Publication Year: Pre-1900 Publication Country: India Title: Prāṇatoṣiṇī
Compiled and composed from the Tantric scriptures by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
the holder of the title Vidyāvāridhi and the head of a circle of scholars (Paṇḍitakulapati).
Published by Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācāryya. Printed at the Kali Press in the city of Calcutta.
Now, the characteristics of the Dvārakā stone, according to the Skanda Purāṇa.

O Nārada, a linga is sometimes seen upon a stone marked by a discus; that should be known as Śrīdhara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. Thus ends the description of the characteristics of Śrīdhara. || 1 ||

In the *Purāṇasāra*, within the *Dvārakā-Kārttika-māhātmya*: "There is a single wheel in the middle portion, white in color and provided with spokes; it is renowned as Śivanābhi, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. "Provided with spokes" means it is joined by a path. [This is stated] in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.

In its lower portion, at the base of the linga, it has the shape of a tortoise and is provided with hooves; known as Śivanābhi, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (From the Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa)

In the lower portion is the tortoise-circle (*kūrmacakra*), white in color and provided with hooves; it is known as the "navel of Śiva" (*śivanābhi*) and bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. The cavity should be one *yava* in measure, while the *liṅga* is said to be half a *yava*; this is renowned throughout the three worlds as the "navel of Śiva."
It is rare. Thus ends the description of the Śivanābhi [mark]. From the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
If that Aghorā, who possesses a mass of matted locks, is worshipped by householders, she is endowed with golden-colored matted locks (p.
691), adorned with golden drops, and on her head there is a cow’s hoof-print resembling a mountain of collyrium; she is the most excellent one named Sadyojātā.
"Bestowing sons, grandsons, and wealth"—thus is the definition of Sadyojāta. In that very same [text]:

"In the middle of the head is the excellent one named Vāmadeva, red in color, joined with white lunar matted locks (jaṭā), and always worshipped by householders. Thus ends the description of Vāmadeva. In that same [text]:

"Somewhat reddish-brown, possessed of black and blue matted locks, and endowed with side-lines—such is the Ishani [lineage] which bestows liberation. Thus ends the description of the Ishana [lineage]. (5)

"Resembling the sun, lightning, and a gem, with matted hair and the moon on its side—that which is designated as Tatpuruṣa is difficult to attain and grants all desires. Thus ends the description of Tatpuruṣa. [6] Whether possessing two, three, four, five, or more marks, it has the shape of a *tāpiñcha* bud.
Sadāśiva is the God of gods. Thus ends the definition of Sadāśiva. || 7 ||

Thus ends the description of the five-fold *kalās* beginning with Aghora. In the *Prayogapārijāta*: "That which has two hubs (*nābhi*) in the form of a wheel, consisting of the nature of Hari and Hara; or that which is joined with a *liṅga* at the hub, white in luster, and provided with hooves—this is known as the 'Hub of Śiva' (*śivanābhi*), which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation."

The sacred field (kṣetra) is composed of Vāsudeva, and the linga is remembered as being composed of Śiva; therefore, one should worship both Śaṅkara and Acyuta in the sacred field of Hari and Hara. A [liṅga] made of hundreds of stones is praised and bestows the fruits of the four goals of human existence.
Now, the majesty of the Dvārakā stone (Dvārakāśilā-māhātmya), as found in the Skanda Purāṇa.

O Goddess! That stone from the wheel-gate (dvārācakraśilā), marked with the noose and auspicious, along with its vessel—that shall be a sacred ford (tīrtha) extending twelve yojanas. O Earth! Wherever one marked with the discus resides, whether in a land of barbarians or a pure region, that area for three yojanas is my own field (kṣetra).

Whoever, being well-composed, dies in its midst as a worshiper, is liberated from a hundred afflictions and is not born again. Whatever action is performed by men in the presence of one marked with the discus— whether bathing, giving gifts, recitation, or fire-offerings— all of it becomes inexhaustible.
Whatever sin has been committed by men through thought or deed over the course of a year—
all that is destroyed by the single act of bestowing the wheel-marked [seal].
Fever, burning sensations, poison, as well as fire and the fear of thieves— all these are pacified.

O Vasundharā! By the mere wiping away of a single mark of the discus (*cakrāṅka*), all *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and *ḍākinīs* go to their destruction. One should install [the mark] endowed with the five discs.
Whether with devotion or without devotion, a person who worships the mark of the discus—even if he is...
One of evil conduct is liberated; there is no doubt in this. He who for a year performs worship, touch, and sight [of the deity] is liberated by the yoga known as Vināśa; there is no doubt in this.
Now follows the specific characteristics of the colors of the stones of Dvārakā, according to the Padma Purāṇa.

Black sesame seeds always bestow death; tawny ones bring fear; speckled ones cause madness; yellow ones destroy wealth; smoke-colored ones lead to the loss of sons; and broken ones take away one's wife and property. White sesame seeds, when perfectly full, [grant prosperity].
They bestow all desired objects. That [lineage] with an unbroken circle is to be worshipped;
it destroys suffering and poverty. Worshipped, the circular and the square [mandalas] grant accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The one with an even circle grants happiness, while the uneven one brings about suffering.

The prohibited stones are also mentioned in that very same [text]: "Those that are perforated, broken, lacking corners, or having uneven circular markings, as well as those shaped like a half-moon—these are indeed not fit for worship. However, there is a specific distinction in the *Yogapārijāta*: "A stone that is cracked leads to the destruction of wealth; one that is too thick..."

One that destroys intelligence should be known as long and life-taking; one that is rough causes the destruction of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). A white-colored stone is to be known as auspicious, as is one marked with a circle of teeth.
The division of forms in the case of a schism in the Saṅgha is stated in the Agni Purāṇa as follows:

Sudarśana has one wheel; Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has two; Acyuta occurs with three, and the god Trivikrama is joined with four. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "vā" (or); thus, the meaning is that Acyuta may have three wheels or Trivikrama may have three. Janārdana has four wheels, and Vāsudeva has five.
Pradyumna has six cakras, and Saṅkarṣaṇa has seven;
Puruṣottama has eight cakras, Navavyūha consists of nine aspects, Daśāvatāra has ten, and Aniruddha has eleven; Dvādaśātmā has twelve.
[The deity] above is Anaṅgaka. In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*, however, the distinction is that [he has] four wheels and four arms.
Furthermore, the specific distinctions based on the types of wheels are also found in that same work: "A stone slab with a single wheel is to be worshipped."
He bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. The god Acyuta, possessing two wheels, bestows the fruit of lordship over the gods.
Janārdana, possessing four wheels, bestows prosperity and destroys enemies.
One should worship him with devotion using fragrant flowers and other offerings.
Vāsudeva, when worshipped with five discs, becomes a lord;
he shall be a protector from the fear of birth and death—of this there is no doubt.
Pradyumna, when worshipped with six discs, shall be the bestower of fortune and fame.

O Bird! By means of devotion, the stone originating from Cakratīrtha is to be known as Balabhadraśilā, marked with seven *caṅku*s. When worshipped, the Lord is pleased and becomes the bestower of sons and grandsons;
Puruṣottama grants one's desires through the nine *vyūha*s consisting of the *vasu* discs. Navavyūha...

The nine-wheeled [liṅga] is difficult even for the gods to obtain; when worshipped, Keśava grants him the highest station. That which is known as the ten incarnations (daśāvatāra) bestows sovereignty with its ten wheels.
By worshipping this [liṅga] marked with wheels, the worship of the ten incarnations is accomplished.
When worshipped with a spirit of devotion, the deity born from the stone at Cakratīrtha bestows supreme sovereignty through eleven [perfections]. Right there,
the God, adorned with twelve discs, is attained when worshipped.

He who bestows infinite fruit for all desires is to be known as the twelve-fold self; when worshipped, he grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Beyond this is the Supreme Self, who eternally increases joy; when worshipped, he, the soul of all worlds, grants the realm of Viṣṇu. Thus it is said.
The stones marked with wheels are described according to their family names; however, there is a specific distinction regarding the region of the single wheel.
In the *Prayogapārijāta*: "There is a distinction regarding the single-wheel [chariot], yet no such distinction is stated [elsewhere].
White and red, red chariots, those of two colors, and those of many colors—if these belong to the single-wheelers, their designations shall be, in order: Puṇḍarīka and Pralambaghna."

"O Brahmin! [The names] Rāma, Vaikuṇṭha, and Viśveśvara—listen to the fruit of worshipping them: they bestow liberation, death, dispute, poverty, and dependence upon others upon the worshipper; therefore, one should avoid them. Thus it is said.
The characteristics of the Dvārakā stone.

In the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*: "Wherever [the deity] is considered to be of a red form, with a head possessing a red luster—even if it is not on a pedestal—having entered the pedestal and performed the rite of consecration (*samprokṣaṇa*), one should install Śiva there; for them, [the rite of] installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is not required."

And it is prescribed: one should cast the burnt, smooth, and wounded *liṅga* into a reservoir of water. Having joined together a *liṅga* that is fit for rejoining, one should perform the installation and other rites.
Or, having taken from a boon a flawless *liṅga* representing the God, preceded by worship, one should place it within the heart.

One should perform the *sandhāna* (reunion) and the *prāṇa* (vitalization) rites as prescribed. Whether the *liṅga* is on the back [of an image], or in an inferior [location], or if it has not been consecrated by a multitude of Śūdras, the wise man, having purified it when a semblance of Rudra (*rudrābhāsa*) has been chosen, should worship it here. This is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* regarding the seeds (*bīja*) of the *liṅgas* and so forth.
The procedure for the upward extraction (*ūrdhvataḥ*) is as follows: for the purpose of destroying all calamities and for the benefit of all living beings,

the extraction (*uddhāra*) and the upward removal (*uddhṛti*) are prescribed for the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*paṇḍikā*), the image, the face, and the *liṅga*, for all the attendant deities (*parivāra*), and likewise for the temple (*harmya*) and the palace (*prāsāda*).
The cause for removal is now stated: when [the image] has cracked, been broken, split, or burnt by fire;

or when it has been carried away by madmen, enemies, or monkeys, or by an elephant; or when the *liṅga*, the pedestal, or other parts have fallen into ruin due to the passage of time—just as the embodied soul [departs] when the body has decayed.
Having abandoned one [body], he approaches another; likewise, the deities abandon worn-out lingas and the like. Then, pretas and vetālas, seeing them decayed, take up residence there;
and because the lingas and such are devoid of essence (sattva), so too do brahmarākṣasas [occupy them].

They cause severe suffering to the performer, to kings, to the kingdom, and especially to that village, including famine, death, and other calamities. Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the rite of restoration (*uddhāra*). Thus ends the procedure for the restoration of the *liṅga* and so forth.
The reversal of that [procedure] is stated in that very same place: "In the case of a self-manifested (svayambhuva) linga, a pedestal (pīṭha), or likewise a bāṇaliṅga,
which has been consecrated by sages, asuras, or gods who know the reality— though the linga may be defective due to decay and so forth— one should not perform its removal."
One should discard [a linga] upon the pedestal of self-manifested (svayambhuva) and other types of lingas.

One should discard among humans any linga defiled by the aforementioned defects and so forth. A linga moved by thieves or others should be reinstalled once it is free of wounds. If, moreover, that linga is indeed free of wounds...

If that should happen, one should install that very same [image] again. Likewise: "One should avoid an image of the attendants that is deficient in arms, feet, or head, or deficient in ears, nose, or mouth. Whatever the material, the dimensions, or whether it be a *liṅga* or an image."

That [liṅga] having been discarded by that measurement, the wise man should fashion it with that same material; he should not cause it to be made with another measurement nor with another material. He should not install one of a different form or lacking the mantra, even if it is excellent. In the case of a liṅga or a temple being carried away by a flood, [he should do so] from elsewhere.

One should establish [the foundation] in a location near that site which is free from obstacles; whether it be a collapsed wall, a ruined mansion, a gate-tower, or a pavilion, one should have it constructed there with the same shape, the same materials, and the same dimensions. How should suitable stones be selected, and likewise, what are the characteristics of those that are not defective?

One should construct a palace made of inferior materials using superior materials; one should not cause it to be built with inferior dimensions or a superior form. One should deliberate upon the aforementioned defects according to the path thus described. Regarding the replacement of a worn-out *liṅga*, pedestal, and so forth—

One should perform that [act]. For that purpose, one need not deliberate over lunar days, asterisms, weekdays, and so forth. A wise person should restore what is dilapidated; he should preserve what is dilapidated but not yet ruined. (From the *Agnipurāṇa*): One should not move a Śiva-liṅga, whether it is well-established or poorly established. One should perform its re-installation with a hundred [offerings].
But [an arrow] made of reed [is effective] with a thousand [shots]. Regarding the characteristics of being well-placed or poorly placed, it is said in that same [text]:
"Even one that is old and so forth is well-placed if it is endowed with worship and other [virtues];
whereas that which is devoid of worship is poorly placed even if it is not defective."

Now, the worship of the Śālagrāma. With the mantra "Oṃ, the Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet; having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by ten fingers' breadth," and so forth, [one should worship] with the mantras of the Puruṣasūkta, one by one.
Having bathed the Śālagrāma with water from a conch shell or with other water using two or three [vessels], having removed the water with both hands or a new cloth,
having placed it upon sandalwood and Tulasī leaves, and having offered sandalwood and Tulasī leaves upon it—

Having placed [the vessel] in a copper or other metal bowl, having established the *sāmānyārghya*, and having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Sun, the nine planets (*navagraha*), Indra, and the guardians of the ten directions (*daśadikpāla*),
one should again perform the installation of the *arghya* and perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with "Oṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth.

Having performed the ritual placement (karanyāsa), one should worship the Śālagrāma stone, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, with the mantras "to the Maker," "to the Destroyer," "to the Sustainer," "to the Ordainer," "to the Sāmaveda," "to the Yajurveda," "to the Ṛgveda," and "to the Atharvaveda," using the formula beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then, taking a flower, one should proceed.
One should meditate as follows: "Om, Nārāyaṇa, who dwells eternally in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne; adorned with armlets, golden earrings, and a crown;
wearing a necklace; possessing a golden body; and holding the conch and the discus"—having thus meditated by means of this [verse].

Having placed a flower upon one's own head and worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), and having meditated once more, one should say: "This is for the water for the feet; *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*. A follower of the Yajurveda says, "This is the *argha*"; a follower of the Ṛgveda says, "This is the *arghya*"; and if one is a singer of the Sāmaveda (*sāmaga*), he should say, "This is the *arghya*."

"An *arghya* man is prescribed in the *Yajurveda* as being without the letter *y*; for the *Chandogas*, it has a neuter gender; and in the *Piṇḍa* [rite], there is a reversal of gender. According to this statement, here is water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), this is fragrance, this is a flower, this is a *tulasī* leaf, and this...

Incense. This is the lamp. This is the food offering (*naivedya*). This is the water for drinking. This is the water for sipping again (*ācamanīya*). This is the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*). Having thus worshipped according to one's ability, one should perform the worship of the syllables (*akṣarapūjā*) as follows: *oṃ oṃ namaḥ*. *oṃ na namaḥ*.

Oṃ mo namaḥ | Oṃ nā namaḥ | Oṃ rā namaḥ | Oṃ ya namaḥ | Oṃ ṇā namaḥ | Oṃ ya namaḥ. Thereafter, one should worship the wheel (cakra). The procedure for the worship of the wheel will be explained further on. The sequence of worship is as follows: Oṃ ācakrāya.
Homage! Thus to the Discus of Victory, to the Excellent Discus, to the Discus that Protects the Three Worlds,
to the Sudarśana Discus, to the Discus that Ends the Daityas, to the Discus that Ends the Asuras, to the Discus of the World, and to the Supreme Discus.

Having worshipped Vāsudeva, the presiding deity of the Śālagrāma stone, with the mantra beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, and having recited [the mantra] according to one's ability, one should offer the recitation with the [mantra] beginning with *guhya*. Then: *Oṃ, O Viṣṇu! Remove my lack of discipline; subdue my mind; pacify my thirst for the taste of sense-objects.*
Extend compassion for all beings and deliver them from the ocean of saṃsāra. || 1 ||

In the lotus-feet of the Lord of Śrī, which are the lotuses that destroy the exhaustion of worldly existence, and which consist of the bliss of Being-Consciousness through the enjoyment of the fragrance of the nectar of the celestial river; || 2 ||
O Lord! Even though our separation has ceased, I am not yours, nor are you mine; for a wave belongs to the ocean, yet the ocean is never the wave.

O Moon who has uprooted the mountains, split the mountains, and destroyed the hosts of enemies that were the demons—when You are seen, the cycle of worldly existence does not prevail, and there is no longer any subjugation by *bhava*. O Supreme Lord! Through Your incarnations as the Fish and others, please bring down that nectar; I, who am terrified by the heat of worldly existence, am to be protected by You. 4–5.
O Dāmodara! O abode of virtues! O Govinda with a beautiful lotus-face!
O Mandara mountain for churning the ocean of worldly existence! May you remove my supreme fear.
O Nārāyaṇa! O embodiment of compassion! Let me take refuge in your feet.
And [his] two feet—may this six-line verse always dwell within the lotus of my mouth. 6.

Thus ends the *Ṣaṭpadī* spoken by Yama. Having taken the *arghya* vessel with this [verse], one should perform three circumambulations (*pradakṣiṇa*). Then, having whirled the conch-shell around one’s head, one should prostrate with either eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) or five limbs (*pañcāṅga*). As follows: "The object of meditation, ever..."

O Great Being! I bow to Your lotus feet—the destroyers of humiliation, the fulfillers of desires, the abode of sacred pilgrimage sites, praised by Śiva and Viriñci, the worthy refuge, the removers of the distress of servants, and the boat for those who have taken shelter to cross the ocean of worldly existence. [1] Having abandoned...

I bow to your lotus feet, O Great Being! You who are most righteous followed the illusory deer desired by your beloved into the forest, forsaking the royal splendor that is so difficult to abandon and yet so coveted by the gods, solely because of the word of your noble brother.

"Oṃ, salutations to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to Him who brings welfare to cows and Brāhmaṇas; salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, the benefactor of the world. Having thus prostrated, one should pray as follows:
"O Lord! In whichever of the thousands of wombs I may enter, in each and every one of them, O Acyuta..."
May my devotion to you, O Acyuta, be ever undeviating. May that intense love which the intoxicated feel for their objects never depart from my heart as I remember you.

"Just as the mind of young women delights in a youth, and the mind of youths delights in a young woman, even so may my mind delight in you. Having said, "Thus I am one who has achieved his purpose," and having contemplated accordingly, he performed dance, song, and other such acts, saying: "Oṃ Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! O mighty-armed one!"

"O destroyer of the afflictions of devotees! Grant me the water from your feet, which pacifies all sins. Having drunk the nectar of the feet with these words, one should take the remainder and [drink] the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, [reciting]: "Om, the remover of untimely death, the destroyer of all diseases, the water from Viṣṇu’s feet..."
"I bear merit upon my head"—by this [formula], one should place [the water] upon the head. As for the fruit of placing it on the head: "It removes untimely death and destroys all diseases;
he who performs the consecration with the water from the Śālagrāma stone is truly bathed."

He who, having been initiated into all sacred fords (tīrthas) and all sacrifices, drinks [this water] and wears it upon his head, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (From the Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa as cited in the Vīramitrodaya). The form of Hari is in the heart, His name is in the mouth, the food offering (naivedya) is in the stomach, and the water from His feet and the remains of His garland (nirmālya) [are likewise received].

"He on whose head Acyuta [resides]... "But at the time of death, he into whose mouth the water from the feet is poured—even one of sinful conduct—he shall go to the imperishable Viṣṇu. Thus is the fruit of consuming the water from Viṣṇu’s feet at the time of death. [One should offer] both water and *tulasī*...

Sandalwood, a twice-born man, a lotus, a bell, a stone, copper, and water from the feet—these nine [are used] with a *ṛc*. The mantra for the water from the feet is the *Puruṣasūkta* verse; such is the definition of the water from the feet.
In the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "He who does not drink the water from the *Śālagrāma* stone, yet places it upon his head..."

One who performs such spilling is called a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). The water from Viṣṇu’s feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births; yet at that very moment, an eightfold sin arises from the falling of even a single drop upon the ground. Before drinking the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, one should drink the water from the feet of a Brahmin.

One who, through delusion, practices what is contrary [to dharma] is called a destroyer of the self. Whatever holy places exist on earth, they are all present in the ocean; whatever holy places exist in the ocean, they are all present at the tip of a Brahmin’s right foot. This is the mantra for drinking the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, which contains the greatness [of that water]. My child!

"I have given this to you; drink the remainder, which is free from old age and death. O God! Grant me constant happiness, victory, and burn away my enemies. This is the mantra for the offering of water from the feet (*pādodaka*), written here incidentally. The mantra for consuming the food offering (*naivedya*): *Oṃ ucchiṣṭabhojanam*.
We are seekers of the remnants of that [offering] by which Hiraṇyākṣa was struck down by the Blue Boar.
As for the specific mantras of Dadhivāmana and others, they should be sought in the *Tantrasāra*. Thus concludes the worship of the Śālagrāma according to the ancient tradition.

Now, the worship of Viṣṇu. From the second chapter of the Sanatkumāra-tantra: Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, having become pure and composed, and having sat upon his seat, he should bow to the Guru with palms joined in *añjali* and contemplate himself as the form of Brahman.
By reciting the mantra repeatedly, one shall become victorious over all disputants.

Then, having bathed and become pure, the preceptor should perform the Vedic rites such as the Sandhyā prayers, as well as the worldly (laukika) duties according to the teacher’s instruction, saying: "I satiate Śrī Kṛṣṇa."

Having recited the root mantra, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Then, having sat at the entrance of the shrine, the wise knower of mantras should wash his feet and bind his topknot (*śikhā*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), the best of practitioners should worship the deities of the gateway. This is the worship of the deities of the gateway.
As previously stated: having expelled the obstacles (*vighna*), one should perform the purification of the hands and the ground;
having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśa, one should perform the worship of Vāstu;
and after worshipping Brahmā, one should thereafter [perform] the seat for oneself (*ātmasana*).

Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the wise one should contemplate, "I am the God. Then, having assigned the seers (ṛṣis) and so forth everywhere, he should thereafter assign the letters of the Mātṛkā. The knower of mantras should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa). [He should meditate on] the Ācakra, the Vicakra, and the Sucakra.

The best of the twice-born [should perform this]: having first placed each of these— the discus for protecting the three worlds, the destroyer of asuras, the Sudarśana, the world-discus, the ender of Daityas, the supreme, and the great— one after another,
he should apply the word "cakra" [to each], and having joined them with the dative case ending.

The word *svāhā* follows immediately after. Likewise, having uttered each limb (*aṅga*), one should apply it individually: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and the mantra for the armor (*kavaca*). These are applied in sequence to the heart, the head, the crest-region (*śikhā*), the body, and the directions, together with their respective powers (*śakti*).

The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with *kuśa* grass and other materials; having performed the placement of the "cage of powers" (*vibhūti-pañjara*), he should then place the "cage of forms" (*mūrti-pañjara*). The learned one should perform the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*) as well as the placement of the hands (*kara-nyāsa*). He should perform the placement of the mantras (*mantra-nyāsa*) and perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) in three ways.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the cage of manifestations (vibhūtipañjara) wherever the ten-syllable mantra occurs; in this manner, one should systematically arrange the placements as stated in the Kalpa. Furthermore, this placement has been adopted by the author of the Tantrasāra himself.
Likewise, one should perform the installation of the conch according to the teacher’s instruction.
Having likewise prepared the *arghya* water and diligently sprinkled the ritual substances,
one should then arrange the pedestal within the [meditative] bodies and worship Dharma and the others, as well as Ananta and the rest, in the heart.

And one should worship according to the prescribed rite. For a householder, the external face [of the deity] is primary; for those in the [other] stages of life, worship is performed at the end. One should worship Bhāskara, Gaṇeśa, Śiva, and Durgā.
Having fashioned a yantra out of copper, one should worship Ananta and the others in its corners. In its corners...

One should always worship Dharma and the others, preceded by Adharma, at his sides; one should also constantly worship the fourteen [deities] beginning with Ananta in the center. Furthermore, the deities beginning with Vimalā are to be worshipped in the filaments (keśara). One should contemplate oneself as the deity.
Having drawn [the deity] out through one's own nostril, one should always worship the God with diligent effort after having invoked Him.

One should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) by means of the seed-syllables beginning with *Ananta*. With care, one should worship the attendants, such as the *Padga*s and the hosts of retinues. Having prepared incense, lamps, and the food offering (*naivedya*), [one should present them].
One should offer [the oblation]. Having recited the mantra prescribed in the Tantra, one should personally worship as if [worshipping] the Deity. (p.

700) Uttering the root mantra with effort, saying "I satiate Śrī Kṛṣṇa," one should satiate [the deity] at the top of the mantra with the water of the *arghya* offering three times. [Then perform] three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having performed the three pervasive [prostrations], the wise one should carry out the ritual application according to the procedure taught in his own Tantra. Thus ends the Sūtra on the Worship of Viṣṇu.

Now, the mantra for the ritual service (upacāra) of Viṣṇu, from the Yoginīpaṭala: "May the boon-bestowing Lord Nārāyaṇa—appearing as the Fish, the Boar, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana—come before me. This is the invocation (āvāhana). [He is seated] upon the footstool of the Lord of the Gods.

"A seat fashioned from lotuses; remain here for the sake of the welfare of all principles, O Madhusūdana!"—thus is the seat. "O God! O Pādma-nābha! O Sanātana! O Viṣṇu! O lotus-petal-eyed one! O Madhusūdana! Accept this water for the feet"—thus is the *pādya*.
Salutation to that Śrī Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of the three worlds, the God of gods, the Noble One, Hṛṣīkeśa. (This is the arghya. O Mandākinī, your water indeed conquers sin;
remove what is inauspicious. Accept this water for sipping (ācamanīya) from me with devotion.
It is offered. Thus, the water for sipping (ācamanīya). "O Waters! You are indeed the earth, and you are light, and you are fire itself.
By means of this water, through the mere act of universal consciousness, I bathe [thee].
Thus, the bath (snāna). O God! This garment is provided, adorned with the colors of sacrifice.

"O Keśava! These two garments, distinguished by their golden hue, are for you. Thus [is the offering of] clothing. "I anoint your body; this very same [anointing] is your activity, O Keśava! This fragrance has been offered by me; please accept it and apply it. Thus [is the offering of] fragrance. [The garment] purified by the mantras from the Ṛgveda and other [Vedas]...
Then, by Padmayoni, [he was given] a sacred thread joined with the Sāvitrī-knot, as well as a rosary of beads.
Thus is the sacred thread (*upavīta*). "Endowed with divine colors and possessed of the brilliance of fire and the sun, these ornaments beautify the limbs of human beings.
Thus is the ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
"O, this divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and sweet-smelling, has been offered by me with devotion! [Thus is the incense.]

"May this incense be accepted. Thus, the incense. "O God! You are indeed the sun, the moon, lightning, and likewise fire; you alone are the light among lights—may this lamp be accepted. Thus, the lamp. "O God! Food of five kinds with six flavors..."
O Keśava! This food offering, accompanied by [these qualities], has been presented by me to you with devotion.

In the forty-eighth chapter of the latter part of the *Matsyasūkta*, there is a specific instruction: "O Madhusūdana! For the sake of the welfare of all beings, please accept this lotus-prepared seat at the footstool of Mount Sumeru. Thus [is the offering of] the seat (*āsana*). "O Lord! [Please accept] excellent water for the feet (*supādya*) for Your feet. [Thus is the offering of] the water for the feet (*pādya*).

"O Padmanābha! O Sanātana! O Viṣṇu! O lotus-petal-eyed one! O Madhusūdana, accept [this]!"—thus is the water for the feet (pādya). "O Lord of the lords of the three worlds! O God of gods! O Janārdana! O Lord of the universe! O Master, accept this arghya consisting of various sandalwood pastes."
Thus is the *arghya*. "The auspicious water of the Mandākinī, which removes all sins—accept this *ācamanīya* offered by me with devotion. Thus is the *ācamanīya*.
4 || "O Mahādeva! Accept with devotion this madhuparka prepared by Brahmā and the other gods and offered by me, O Madhusūdana! Thus ends the madhuparka. 5 ||
"O God, O Keśava! These two garments of yours are endowed with divine cloth, woven from many threads, and produced from gold. Thus ends the section on the garment (6).
[The vessel] was fashioned by the Lotus-born One with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
"O Acyuta! This sacred thread (upavīta), joined with the Sāvitrī-knot, is for you. Thus [is the offering of] the sacred thread. 7.
"Born from the Lord of Forests (Vanaspati), rich in fragrance, and esteemed by the gods; this incense (dhūpa), to be smelled by all the deities, is accepted. Thus [is the offering of] the incense. 8.
"The light of the sun and moon, and likewise that of lightning and fire—you alone are the light of all lights; please accept this lamp. Thus ends the lamp offering. 9.
"And food of four kinds, endowed with the six flavors, offered by me..."

"O Keśava! This food offering is for you with devotion. Thus ends the food offering (naivedya). 10. "May these auspicious ornaments, composed of divine threads and endowed with the brilliance of fire and the sun, grace your limbs. Thus ends the ornaments (alaṅkāra). 11.
In the fifteenth chapter of the third night of the Nāradapañcarātra.
Vyāsa said:
I shall describe the practice for the attainment of imperishable wealth,

which is always cherished by the Lord of Śrī and by the gods headed by Dhananātha; [a practice] well-guarded [and performed] at Dvāravatī amidst excellent palaces radiant as a thousand suns and numerous wish-fulfilling trees when the wind blows.
Likewise, in the pavilion, which possessed walls, door-arches, and pillars made of dripping jewels;
where pearls hung from variegated canopies shimmering with blossoming garlands;
and in the midst of two streams of water shining with rubies.
Beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) from which jewel-gems drip unceasingly,
in a space whose quarters are illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps, one should meditate upon Acyuta seated upon a lotus-throne of the mind that resembles the rising sun, shining like molten gold.

Possessing a splendor equal to ten million rising moons, suns, and lightning flashes; beautiful in every limb, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments; clad in yellow garments, his arms radiant with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus;
wearing a crown of unobstructed, blazing jewels, he touches the bud [of the lotus] with his left foot.

Jāgrat sprinkled the unfading, sprout-like complexion [of Kṛṣṇa]; while Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā, stationed on his right and left, drenched his head with a stream of jewels arising from the jars held in their own hands. At the auspicious moment, Jyotiḥsunandā stood there with the two jars of water for peace (*śānti*) belonging to those two. And by them...

To the right and left stood Mitravṛndā and Sulakṣaṇā; from them, Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā took two jars filled with the essence of the river of jewels and offered them to Vāmana. Surrounding Hari were his sixteen thousand beloved wives.
One should meditate upon [the deities] resplendent with pitchers from which flow streams of gold and heaps of jewels;

outside of them, the eight treasures (nidhis) filling the earth with wealth; and outside of those, all the Vṛṣṇis and the gods and others as previously described. Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self...
One should recite the mantra up to twenty [times]. One should offer oblations with clarified butter for four hundred thousand [recitations] and twenty-two thousand [times].
Śakti, preceded by Śrī, Koṇṭha, Daśānna, Viṃśati, and Ambhaka—[these are the components] of the mantra. Not [otherwise].

Indeed, there is no other Manu like him in the three worlds. The Seer (Ṛṣi) is Brahmā, the metre (Chandas) is Gāyatrī, and Kṛṣṇa is the deity (Devatā). The arrangement of its seed-syllable (Bīja), power (Śakti), and so forth, is exactly as previously stated.
Now, the ritual application (Kalpa) of this mantra, as taught by Sanatkumāra, is being described.

Having performed the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise practitioner should place the six limbs upon the palms and fingers of both hands. Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the mantra,
he should [place] the Mātṛkā enclosed by the mantras, ten times each, according to the paths of withdrawal and emanation.
One should place the principles (tattvas). Again, having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka), one should place the syllables of the mantra upon the body:

on the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, by this [syllable] on the chin, the throat, the base of the arms, the heart, the belly, the navel, the secret place (liṅga), and likewise the foundation (ādhāra).

One should place [the mantras] on the hips, the knees, the shanks, the ankles, and the feet; this is declared to be the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). The maintenance (*sthiti*) extends from the heart to the nose, and the reabsorption (*saṃhati*) begins from the feet.
Having performed [this] five times in this manner, ending with the maintenance, one establishes the pentad of forms (*mūrttipañjara*).

Having performed the placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*), one should carry out the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). The middle [syllables] are said to consist of the letters *guṇa* (three), *agni* (three), *veda* (four), *karaṇa* (five), and so forth. Having formed the mudrā called the *kirīṭa*, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) as before. Thus...
Having meditated, one should worship the deity in the house according to the ritual of the "cage of forms" (mūrttipañjara).
Alternatively, one may worship Viṣṇu; for that purpose, the mantra is now declared.
Having smeared the area with cow dung, one should place the pedestal (pīṭha) there for the image after having anointed it.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with fragrant paste. Within the pericarp, there should be a hexagon;

therein [is] the target (sādhya) facing that [hexagon]. One should oneself encircle him with the remaining seventeen syllables. In the corners starting from the eastern syllable, one should place Śrī, and in the remaining [corners], Susaṃvid.
One should write the six-syllabled *smaragāyatrī* at the joints and on the filaments, three times each;
one should write the *mālāmantra* on the eight petals, six times each;
having written it thus, one should encircle the exterior with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, and draw a *bhūvimba* (earth-circle) on the outside.

Concentrated in all directions and intermediate points, one should write this mantra upon vessels made of gold and other materials as before; whoever wears that which has been thus empowered is honored even by the thirty gods.
Gāyatrī, Kāmadeva, and Puṣpabāṇa [should be placed] with the vocative case endings (ṅe-anta); [we] know... Vidmahe.

"May the bodiless one (Anaṅga) impel [us], joined with *dhīmahi* and *tad*. Having recited this, one should worship Gopāla, who delights all people, with the mantras ending in *namaḥ*. Having uttered 'Nṛtyaṃ te Kāmadevāya' ending in *ṅe* (dative), which is beloved by all people, and then saying 'Mavajana' at the end, as well as the word 'Sammohana'..."

Having uttered "jvala jvala prajvala," one should say "and the heart of the host of Māra; O Śiva, bring [them] under control! This is the Mantra of Madana, consisting of forty syllables, which begins with the seed-syllable of Māra at the start of the recitation.

The subduer of the three worlds: the ground-chamber (bhūgṛha) should be square and adorned with eight vajras. Having worshipped the pedestal as before and having conceived the anthropomorphic form (pauruṣī-mūrti), one should invoke Acyuta there with devotion, perform the ritual of integration (sakalīkṛtya), and worship him.
One should not perform the sequence of nyāsa from the seat (āsana) up to the ornaments; rather, one should perform the emanation (sṛṣṭi),
the maintenance (sthiti), the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), the crown (kirīṭa), the two earrings (kuṇḍala), the conch (śaṅkha), the discus (cakra),
the mace (gadā), the lotus (padma), the garland (mālā), the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem, using perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers.

Having worshipped with the root mantra as before, one should first worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the corners of the pair of fire-walls: the mantras of the head, crest, armor, and eyes, in that order, once each. Then Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha [are to be worshipped] at the bases of the petals starting from the southeast.

One should worship the eight queens, namely Śānti, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Ratī, Īśā, and [the others] as the sixth; then, outside of that, one should fully worship the enclosures beginning with Candravajrā. Thus it is said.
Having worshipped Acyuta with devotion within the enclosure of the seven walls,

one should gratify Him with milk-water mixed with curds, sugar, and ghee. Then, having offered the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and having praised and bowed to Keśava, one should dissolve Him into one's own heart.

Together with his retinue, having bowed and worshipped himself, he should recite the mantra while becoming absorbed in that [deity]. Then, for the sake of prosperity, until the end of the twenty-second [chapter], there is the meditation on the jewel-consecration (*ratnābhiṣeka*).
The house of one who recites this mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and meditations becomes filled.

The earth, filled with all kinds of crops, remains as unobstructed as the palm of his hand, abounding in jewels, gold, and grain. Endowed with sons and friends, he attains the supreme goal at the end.
Having worshipped Govinda with fire using flowers and white rice grains, [he attains this].
Having offered ten thousand oblations with clarified butter, one should cause that ash to be placed upon his head;

for him there shall be an abundance of food, and all women shall be under his control. Or, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations with clarified butter, or with red lotuses soaked in the three sweets; by this, he attains prosperity and sovereignty like that of Indra.

Compassion is certainly not found in one who has not been trained. For the sake of obtaining white garments and the like, one should offer very white flowers with the syllable *hūṃ*. Or, while describing your form, [one should worship] the female deities of the limbs such as the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth, with the thought that they are the ocean of water mentioned at the end of the twenty [syllables].

Then one should meditate upon Acyuta, who, with his two hands granting boons and fearlessness, embraces his beloved by her limbs; he is resplendent as the wielder of the discus, embraced by those two who hold lotuses and lilies in their hands. One should mutter [the mantra] ten hundred thousand times with clarified butter, followed by a thousand-fold oblation.
These two mantras are perfected; they bestow prosperity, friendship, and good fortune upon men.
Preceded by the power of Māra and Śakti, this is the glorious triad of mantras. One should assign names to these mantra-syllables according to the system of the *daśānta*.
Kṛṣṇa, holding a conch, discus, bow, arrow, noose, goad, and a serpent, and blowing a flute with two arms, should be meditated upon as being like the sun; this is the first group of meditations.
In the second [group], one enters that very [meditation]; in the third, there would be ten internal [variations].

One should perform worship with offerings to the guardians of the directions; one should then recite the mantra five hundred thousand times and offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa). Thereafter, the mantras become perfected, bestowing prosperity and splendor upon all beings.

Now, the majesty of the name of Viṣṇu. In the sixteenth chapter of the *Matsyasūkta Mahātantra*: "O Beloved! By chanting the meritorious names of Viṣṇu for a single watch (three hours), a person dwells in Vaikuṇṭha for thousands of crores of kalpas. Indeed, even a single name..."

O beloved! By chanting the second and third [names] with a spirit of devotion moment after moment, one shall go to the world of Viṣṇu. O auspicious one! Indeed, by chanting the meritorious names of Hari with devotion, no fear exists anywhere even amidst all great dangers. Or, while performing...

Or indeed, O beloved, one should perform [this] for a day and night; having led thousands of [his] lineages, he truly attains Me in reality. He who recites the syllables of My name, endowed with qualities and equal to the mantra of devotion, at the three junctions of the day, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.

O Dear One! Those wise men who always worship the Vaiṣṇavas and human beings, being liberated from all sins, go to the world of Śiva. What need is there for further action for those wise ones who utter "Āṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa"?
By means of many mantras that cause the delusion of the mind.
Now begins the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-śatanāma-stotra, from the first chapter of the fourth rātra of the Nārada-pañcarātra, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Vasundharā! O Varārohā! This collection of one hundred and eight names bestows all auspiciousness and grants the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
It destroys millions of great sins (mahāpātaka), bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha),
grants the reward of all recitations and sacrifices, and annihilates evil.

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names [of Kṛṣṇa]. Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting three times the thousand meritorious names, a single recitation of even one name of Kṛṣṇa bestows that very same fruit.
Therefore, this hymn is most meritorious and is the destroyer of sins.

For the one hundred and eight names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa: the seer is Śrī Śeṣa, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this is the application for the recitation of the one hundred and eight names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Oṃ! Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, Vāsudeva, the eternal;
the holy son of Vasudeva, whose human form is a mere play; Hari, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, who is fond of Yaśodā; he who possesses four arms.
Armed with the discus, sword, mace, conch, and lotus; the son of Devakī; the Lord of Śrī;
the beloved son of Nanda the cowherd; the one who brought an end to the pastimes on the Yamunā; and the bestower of grace upon Sucukunda.

Lord of sixteen thousand women, His form sweet with the triple bend; nourished by the nectar of the parrot’s speech, Govinda, the Lord of the wise; wandering about tending the calves, the destroyer of the demon Dhenuka.
He was the shatterer of upturned palm trees, and his form was dark like the tamāla tree.
The Lord of the cowherds and cowherdesses, the Yogi, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;

the Lord of the earth, the Supreme Light, the Sovereign of the Yadavas, the Upholder of the Yadu clan; the wearer of the forest garland, clad in yellow garments, the plunderer of the Pārijāta tree; the lifter of Mount Govardhana, the Cowherd, the Protector of all.

The unborn, the stainless, the progenitor of desire, the lotus-eyed; the slayer of Madhu, the Lord of Mathurā, the leader of Dvārakā, the possessor of strength; he who wanders within Vṛndāvana and is adorned with garlands of tulasī.
The stealer of the Syamantaka jewel was one whose essence was Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The supreme Puruṣa, Māyā, who assumed the form of a hunchback and wore black garments,
was an expert in the great sacrifice involving the Asuras Muṣṭika and Cāṇūra.

He is the enemy of the cycle of existence, the foe of Kaṃsa, the slayer of Mura and Naraka; he is beginningless, a perpetual celibate, and the one who draws away those addicted to Kṛṣṇa. He is the cutter-off of Śiśupāla’s head, the ender of Duryodhana’s lineage, the bestower of boons upon Vidura and Akrūra, and the revealer of his universal form.

The destroyer of Vṛṣabhāsura, the ender of the strength of the demon Bāṇa, the establisher of Yudhiṣṭhira, adorned with a peacock feather as his crest; the teacher of the world, the lord of the universe,
and the master of the flute.
The unmanifest charioteer of Pārtha, the great ocean of the nectar of the Gītā;
whose glorious lotus feet are reddened by the rubies on the hoods of the serpent Kālīya;
Dāmodara, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas; Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman.
He whose vehicle is the serpent-eater (Garuḍa); the stealer of the garments of the gopīs while they were engaged in water-sports;
the one of holy fame; the one to be known through sacred fords; the one to be known through the Vedas; the ocean of compassion; the embodiment of all sacred fords;
the form of all the planets; the one higher than the highest. 108.
Thus, this one hundred and eight names of Kṛṣṇadeva was heard by Kṛṣṇa,
the devotee of Kṛṣṇa, in the past while listening to the nectar of the Gītā; therefore, this hymn which brings pleasure to Kṛṣṇa has been composed by me as I have heard it.

The nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s name is the bestower of supreme bliss; it destroys misfortune and suffering, and increases one's lifespan. Whatever charity, study, austerity, or pilgrimage has been performed in this life [is for those] who recite it.
For those who hear it, the merit shall be multiplied ten million-fold.

It bestows sons upon the childless and provides a refuge for the destitute. It brings wealth to the poor and victory to those desiring triumph. It is likewise beneficial for children and herds of cattle.
It bestows nourishment and increases merit.

It pacifies fevers caused by wind-demons and other ailments, bestowing peace and liberation; it grants all desires instantly and destroys the sins of ten million births. Furthermore, at the end of life, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa removes the fear of the torment of worldly existence. [Salutation] to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Yādavas.
Salutation to the Lord, the master of Rukmiṇī, the knower of Vedānta, the yogin purified by wisdom!
O Great Goddess, a man who recites this mantra day and night shall receive favor from all the planetary deities (grahas) and become most beloved to all, surrounded by sons and grandsons.
"Endowed with the abundance of all perfections, even after establishing the cowherds [in their respective places],
one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Kṛṣṇa. Thus [ends] the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara in the fourth night of the *Jñānāmṛtasāra* within the *Nāradapañcarātra*.
The hymn of one hundred and eight names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is complete.

Now, the prohibition against worshipping Viṣṇu using wooden vessels and the like. In the sixteenth chapter of the Matsya-sūkta: "Carrying the deity oneself, worshipping him in a wooden vessel, and installing him in an earthen vessel—these three are causes of poverty. [Also prohibited] in the hand or on a leaf.

"One should not worship in vessels made of bell-metal, conch-shell, brass, grass, or wooden eye-cups, nor on bark or silver. Thus is the prohibition against the worship of Viṣṇu and others using vessels made of wood and similar materials.

Worship performed in a golden vessel, or one of copper, stone, coconut, or in a fruit, or on a lotus leaf, or on the petal of a *kiṃśuka* tree, or on the leaf of a *caladala*—such worship bestows the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices. (*Kiṃśuka* refers to the *palāśa*; *caladala* refers to the *aśvattha*.)

Thus, in the fifteenth chapter, [is described] the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu with vessels made of gold and other materials. He who offers even a single flower, or even just one, with the *Puruṣasūkta*—by him this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes worshipped. Or even with a single [flower]...
O Goddess! Having recognized [the deity] with a verse and offered a handful of water, one is liberated from all sins by means of the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Likewise, having recited the Puruṣa-sūkta while submerged within the water, one becomes completely freed from the bondage of all karmas.
One is liberated from all sins.
Having learned it, one should daily recite the Puruṣa Sūkta without sloth; in one year, one beholds Vāsudeva, the Lord of Gods. Thus ends the majesty of the Puruṣa Sūkta.
In the sixteenth chapter: One should bathe the one who reclines upon the waters with very cool water;
such a person attains the world of Brahmā for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
By bathing [the image] with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and flowers, one shall attain the world of Brahmā.

p. 708) "By bathing [the image] with water containing jewels one obtains the merit of a Sāvitra sacrifice; by bathing with golden water, the merit of a Kauvera sacrifice; and by the offering of all medicinal herbs, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha). Thus ends the fruit of bathing Viṣṇu with specific substances.

Likewise: "Furthermore, by means of the powder of *kalāya* (horse-gram), or the powder of barley, or the powder of *haridrā-māṣa* (urad-bean), or that produced from rice—one should perform anointment (*udvarttana*);
one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. Thus ends the fruit of anointment.

Likewise: "By washing the Lord of the Gods with a paste of barley and wheat, or with warm water, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa. Thus [ends the section on] the fruit of washing the body of the God with specific substances.
Likewise: "He who offers a footstool and likewise water for washing the face, and rubs [the feet] with a bilva leaf, is liberated from all sins."
Now, regarding the Great Bathing Ceremony (mahāsnāna) of Viṣṇu at that very place: he who performs the Great Bathing Ceremony during the months of Tulā,
Makara, and Meṣa shall dwell for sixty thousand yugas in the world of Brahmā for a long time.

Of each of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), there should be one hundred palas each; or half of that, or half of that again—one should not make it less than that. Likewise, O Goddess of Gods, [the quantity] of oil should be one thousand ghaṭas or one hundred.

Likewise, bathing with half of that, or with a hundred streams, or with a thousand streams, destroys even the greatest sins. O Maheśānī! In the Kali Yuga, half of that [is prescribed], and half of that again;
specifically, twenty-five palas by measure of the decoction, and the same for the warm water.

Likewise, O Maheśvarī, is the number of jars. O Maheśvarī, whoever performs such a bath or causes it to be performed, the sin accumulated over seven births perishes at that very moment. This is done with substances measured individually by four *tolakas* each.
Alternatively, if it lacks four folds, one should not employ it for bathing. Likewise:

"O Goddess of Devas! He who bathes Keśava with water contained in a conch shell while reciting the Viṣṇu-mantra shall deliver a hundred generations of his lineage. O illustrious lady! Having taken the milk of a tawny cow and placed it in a conch shell..."
One obtains the fruit of bathing [the deity] after giving away a thousand maidens in marriage;

half of that is obtained by using the milk of another cow, and double that by using water with *kuśa* grass. One should worship with a great ritual (*mahāpūjā*) using three hundred thousand flowers and leaves; O Goddess of Gods, in the Kali age, it is accomplished with one hundred thousand, according to the tradition.
Specifically: half of that is to be known as the medium [size], and half of that again as the smallest.
Thus concludes the description of the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*) and other such great offerings (*mahāpūjā*).

Now, the majesty of the conch (*śaṅkhamāhātmyam*). In the *Padmapurāṇa*: "O best of Brahmins! Whatever sacred fords (*tīrtha*) exist in the three worlds, their sins are destroyed through service to Vāsudeva; therefore, one should worship the conch."

O Pāñcajanya, born from the ocean and held in the hand by Viṣṇu, fashioned among all the gods— salutations to you! By the mere sight of the conch, how much more so when it is touched, do sins go to their dissolution, like snow at the rising of the sun?
In front of Vāsudeva, a conch shell adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste should remain worshipped;

for him, prosperity is not difficult to attain. Having placed water along with flowers, water, and unbroken rice (akṣata) into the conch, one offers this *arghya* to the Lord, which yields the fruit of the entire earth together with its oceans.

The word "should obtain" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having offered the *arghya* oblation, he who performs a circumambulation with a conch shell has, by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
One should cause the water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), held within a conch shell, to circulate over the head of Hari; [this grants] worldly enjoyment...

O beloved! The one born from the Ocean of Milk indeed grants [her favor] to him who offers water clinging to the *śaṅkha* shell after it has been whirled over Keśava; for Gaṅgā herself bears the Gaṅgā-stream upon her head—what need then has he for the stream of the Gaṅgā?
Now, the characteristics of the *śaṅkha* according to the *Kriyāsāra*:
The conch (śaṅkha) resting at the starting point is considered the most excellent;
one that fills the space between the breasts is middling, while the smallest occurs in sequence thereafter.
A conch with beautiful hips, a mound of dust, smooth, long, and well-traversed is auspicious.
He who is worthy of worship for one with three eyes is he who has fifteen [deities] for one with two eyes. For one with two eyes, there are fifteen.
A conch shell that is dirty, with a low spire, reddish, infested with worms, short,
or possessing a narrow aperture, is not suitable for the worship of the gods.
One that is white as cow’s milk, glossy, with a long neck, large, and well-rounded— [is fit].
That twice-born conch, known by the name Śaṅkha, is either clockwise-spiraled or endowed with a counter-clockwise spiral; possessing the characteristics previously described,
this conch is not very easy to find,
yet it is the foremost for the worship of the gods.

The *Kalpataru* specifies [the vessel] as being one that spirals to the right: "Whoever, with a joyful mind, receives upon his head the water situated in an *auḍumbara* vessel along with a conch shell spiraling to the right—the sin accumulated over seven births perishes at that very moment. Thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
p. 710) Whoever worships Hari with water from a right-spiraling conch, the sin committed during seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment. (From the *Kriyāsāra*)

No defect distinct from [the material] itself exists in copper, crystal, conch, gold, and silver; however, such a defect does exist in other substances. In that case, the conch becomes pure through scrubbing with husks.
(The term *tuṣa* refers to grain husks. — Matsyasūkta, Chapter Sixteen.

Water originating from rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, or pools—all of it becomes the water of the Gaṅgā when drawn up by means of a conch. O Goddess of Devas! Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in the three worlds are present within the conch during the worship of Vāsudeva; therefore, [one should worship] the conch.
One should worship it; by the mere sight of the conch, what need is there to mention when it is touched?

Sins go to dissolution just as frost does before the sun. For one by whom the conch has been worshipped with flowers, water, and unbroken grains (akṣata) in the presence of Vāsudeva, prosperity never departs.

It is difficult to attain. However, he who offers the *arghya* and performs circumambulation with a conch shell has, by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents. He who pours the water from the conch and bathes Keśava with the eight-syllable mantra is liberated.

He too [should be protected] from distress. One should not place the conch on the ground; if it has been placed there, one should wash it again. One should purify it with sandalwood water, milk, or even pure water. *Oṃ*, you were born from the ocean and held in the hand by Viṣṇu; you were fashioned by all the gods.
O Pāñcajanya! Salutations be unto you.
Now, the definition of the *tripadī* (the three-footed stool), as recorded in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*:

The superior *trivṛtā* consists of sixty-four measures and is threefold; the *yantrikā* is considered to have three parts according to the distinctions of superior and so forth. The *siṃhacakraka* is joined with three wheels at each quarter-measure and is located in the half-quarter.

The middle of the foot should be open, and there should be a lion’s face at the bottom of the foot; one should fashion the remainder according to what is aesthetically pleasing. This is proclaimed as the *tripadī*;
it is a three-legged stand used as a support for vessels containing the *arghya* water, the sun [image], or the *naivedya* offering. Thus it is said.
Now, the majesty of Tulasī, from the sixteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.

O Beloved! Tulasī is the most excellent among all leaves and flowers; she is pure, the fulfiller of all desires, belonging to Viṣṇu, and the beloved of Viṣṇu. O Goddess! She bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is the supreme benefactor of all the worlds, and is the highest.

O Supreme Goddess! You, who have attained motherhood and lead one to imperishable heaven, were planted upon the earth in ancient times for the welfare of all the worlds— just as Lakṣmī is dear to Viṣṇu, so are you the beloved of Hara.
Likewise, this goddess Tulasī is not found to have a fourth [comparable];
for as the Gaṅgā is indeed pure and bestows liberation upon all the worlds, so too is this Tulasī the remover of sins for all [beings]. By one who [offers] it with its buds and leaves...

O Goddess! Viṣṇu is worshipped with Tulasī; the meritorious fruit of that act cannot indeed be described. One should not fail to worship the Garuḍa-bannered Lord with a Tulasī flower alone, O fair-faced one, for it is endowed with power equal to a saw. Likewise:
Renowned throughout the three worlds, she is the destroyer of all sins;
the Goddess who grants all desires and brings about every auspiciousness.
In the terrible ocean of worldly existence, Tulasī is the very form of a boat.
This [practice] grants supreme satisfaction to the gods, to Śiva, and to Durgā;
for those afflicted by a multitude of sins, it is the one great medicine. In this regard, they cite this ancient history (itihāsa).
O lady of beautiful countenance, listen to that dialogue between Marīci and Āma! Long ago,
the high-minded lord of the Raghu clan, having worshipped according to the prescribed rites one who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, set his mind [upon this].

Thus he performed his rites there every day at the proper time. In a very short period of time, the best of sages became pleased. He bestowed upon Śrī Rāma a divine garland, supreme among all, consisting of flower-clusters born from a Tulasī grove.

He placed upon the head of Rāma a divine garland composed of the four Vedas. Taking that garland, which was adorned with clusters of blossoms and leaves, and seeing it, the Blessed One became enraged and spoke to the bull among sages: "Aha! What is this arrogance of a Brāhmaṇa?"

"O great-souled one! How has this mass of leaves from a forest tree been placed upon me? For it is said that the blessing of the twice-born should be accepted by those possessed of wisdom. Therefore, O tiger among sages!"
"I bear this contempt for you. Having heard these words of Rāma, which were swiftly filled with rage, the goddess Tulasī cursed the king, the joy of the Raghus:
"O Indra among kings! Because you have discarded me from your head out of pride and arrogance, therefore you shall suffer separation from Vaidehī."
"It shall come to pass. Then, seeing her cursing him, the high-minded Sītā spoke thus to the god, her heart’s beloved, whose eyes were filled with anger. Marīci said:
Be well-pleased, O Great King! I go to you for refuge. I shall relate a wonderful ancient account spoken by the sages. Indeed, O Lord of the Gods, this *tulasī* garland has been given by me;
hear from me its entire and marvelous majesty. For this—

Mahālakṣmī is established in the form of a tree; she is this supreme power of Brahmā, born from the hair-pores of Brahmā. The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and other Vedas are commensurate with her branches and limbs, just as the Gaṅgā [is to the Himalayas].

Just as the Gītā and the Gāyatrī are considered to have emerged from the Lotus-born [Brahmā], so too has this purifier of the world arisen; wherever she abides perfectly, there Lakṣmī is established. Without her, likewise...
Lakṣmī arises for the sake of destruction. Thus was Tulasī, the Mother of the World, herself created by Brahmā; she was brought down to earth for the purpose of protecting the worlds.
Having worshipped her, Mahādeva, the Lord of Devas and Master of Mantras, [conquered] the Asura...

He conquered the one named Ghora in the thick of battle. The narrative concerning the combat with the Asura Ghora has not been written here for fear of increasing the bulk of the work. Likewise: "In this manner, this great goddess Tulasī is the universal form."

"You too should propitiate her; you will certainly attain victory. Having heard these words of the great seer, Madhusūdana bowed his head with reverence and, for the sake of victory, respectfully took the branch of that [goddess] which bestows the fruits of all desires.

Then, having established that dharma, Rāghava returned toward his own home; having planted it according to the prescribed rule, he honored it. Then, by its power, the blessed joy of the Raghus conquered the immensely powerful Yātudhāna.

Those men who worship Rāvaṇa in battle, those who plant [the Tulasi] according to the prescribed rules, and those people who recite [his praises], for them there shall be success. And those who carry a water-soaked Tulasi leaf upon their heads—

Having offered the *arghya* and paid obeisance, liberation stands within their grasp. However, having performed the planting in these places— on a riverbank, in a cremation ground, in barren soil, or in the presence of barbarians— the doer indeed goes to the abode of Yama.

Now, the procedure for planting the *tulasī* plant. In that very same [text]: Having dug a hole one *tāla* deep in the northeast or in front of the house, and having placed therein the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and a peacock’s egg at the break of day, one should plant it during the night, wrapping its base seven times with a thread. At its root...
Having fashioned a circular pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) one cubit in measure, one should then construct a square altar (*vedī*).
Having poured forth a stream of water, a wise man should worship it with perfumes,
flowers, incense, and lamps soaked in ghee.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice and curd-rice, one should say, "Obeisance to Tulasī," and offer the *arghya* for the sake of prosperity. This *arghya* consists of water filled in a conch shell,
along with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), sandalwood paste, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and flowers.
Thus it was spoken.

Now, the meditation on Tulasī is described in that very same place: One should meditate upon the Goddess, whose face is like the new moon, whose lips are like the ripe bimba fruit, who shines brilliantly,
whose slender body is slightly bent under the weight of her pair of breasts, and whose countenance is radiant with a gentle smile.
She has the moon, sun, and fire as her eyes; she is white-bodied, bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons, and is seated upon a white lotus throne.
Now, regarding the praise in that very place, Īśvara said:
I bow to Tulasī, who possesses a gentle form, who is worshipped by all the gods beginning with Indra, who is a celestial beauty, and who grants boons to her devotees. || 1 ||
I bow to Tulasī, who has transcended sound, the point, and the digit; who wears a garland of skulls, who is an ascetic, who is devoted to Vāsudeva, and who possesses a gentle form.
I bow to the goddess Tulasī, who embodies all the gods, who contains the Vedas within her, who is enchanting, who is attainable through yoga, and who possesses a gentle form.
I bow to Tulasī, who knows the distinction between gods and demons, who is adorned with every ornament, the mother of the three worlds, and possessed of a gentle form. 4.
I bow to Tulasī, who possesses the form of Lakṣmī, who has a gentle appearance, holds a lotus in her hand, has a lotus-like face, stands upon a lotus, and has lotus-like eyes. || 5 ||

On the day of the sun’s transit, at the end of a fortnight, and during the eclipses of the moon and sun, whoever recites this while remaining self-restrained shall attain all perfections— without mantras, without recitation,
without sacrifice, without ritual action, without meditation, and without visiting sacred fords.
It shall bring about all accomplishments. Whoever recites or even hears this hymn composed by the Guru, liberation is in the palm of his hand; he is indeed liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Tulasī Hymn in the sixteenth chapter of the Matsya Sūkta.
The mantra for prostration is as follows: "O Tulasī! Grant me prosperity, grant me glory, as well as fame, longevity, and happiness; likewise, grant me strength, nourishment, and righteousness."
With this mantra, however, one should perform a prostration with a concentrated mind.
(p. 714) Now, regarding the wearing of garlands and so forth, as maintained in the *Bhagavadbhaktivilāsa*:

"Then one should wear a garland offered to Kṛṣṇa along with *tulasī* leaves. One should wear ornaments made of *padmākṣa* seeds, *tulasī* wood, fruits, and *dhātrī* [myrobalan] wood, as well as other decorations made of *tulasī* wood."
The Vaiṣṇava [should apply it] on the head, the ears, the arms, and the hands, according to his preference.
Now follows the procedure for wearing the garland, as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having first offered a garland made of tulasī wood to Hari,
he who subsequently wears it himself is indeed the best of devotees.
In that very same place, there is also a censure regarding the wearing of garlands not offered to Kṛṣṇa.
That fool who does not offer to Hari a garland made from *tulasī* wood,
yet wears it himself, certainly goes to hell.
[The garland] should be washed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and consecrated with the root mantra and the *gāyatrī*.
One should indeed fumigate it eight times with incense;
then, according to the rules and with supreme devotion, one should worship it with the *sadyojāta* mantra:
"O garland born from *tulasī* wood! O you who are dear to the people of Kṛṣṇa! I wear you."
Place me, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, upon your neck;

for since you are the eternal beloved of Viṣṇu and dear to the followers of Viṣṇu, O Goddess of Gods, make me likewise eternally dear to the followers of Viṣṇu! O Garland, no sin has been committed by me; you are not my destroyer, O beloved of Hari!

And because it is spoken of for all devotees by him, it is called a *mālā*. Having thus requested according to the rules, the Vaiṣṇava who indeed wears the *mālā* offered around Kṛṣṇa’s neck shall go to the Vaiṣṇava abode. [This is] the obligatory nature of wearing the *mālā*. In that very same place:

In connection with the month of Kārttika: "If a person does not wear a garland made of *dhātrī* fruits around their neck during this time, he is not a Vaiṣṇava, even if he performs the worship of Viṣṇu. (From the Gāruḍa Purāṇa).

Those rationalists of evil intellect who do not wear a garland [of tulasī] do not return from hell, being consumed by the fire of Hari’s wrath. For this very reason, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa, in that same place: "One who is disciplined should not abandon the tulasī garland and should worship Hari; whatever he does..."
All that shall yield infinite fruit. (From the Nāradīya Purāṇa)

Those who have tulasī leaves, lotuses, and rosaries fastened to their necks; those whose upper arms are marked with the conch and discus; or those who bear shining vertical sectarian marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) upon the surface of their foreheads—those Vaiṣṇavas quickly purify the world. Moreover:
He whose pair of arms is marked with signs, whose speech consists of the chanting of the names of the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu),
who bears a most straight-lined sectarian mark (puṇḍra) upon his forehead, and who has a lotus and a string of gems upon his neck;
"I am his servant. This is from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the words of the Blessed Lord.
"He who wears a garland of Tulasī wood around his neck—even if that man is of improper conduct—is indeed [sanctified]; of this there is no doubt. (Skanda Purāṇa)

He on whose body a garland made of *dhātrī* fruit or one produced from *tulasī* wood is seen is indeed the most excellent of *bhāgavatas*. Furthermore, he who wears a garland made of *tulasī* leaves around his neck is, by virtue of possessing Viṣṇu’s own color, worthy of being saluted even by the gods.

A garland made of *tulasī* leaves, or even one fashioned from *dhātrī* fruits, grants liberation to sinners; how much more so for those who serve Viṣṇu! (In that same work, in the section on Kārttika: Furthermore, he who, having placed a *tulasī* garland around his neck, worships Janārdana...
One obtains the merit of ten thousand cows for every flower [offered]. As long as the *dhātrī* garland remains around a man’s neck, so long does Keśava joyfully roll upon his body.
And whichever hairs on men’s bodies the *dhātrī* garland touches with its hand—

For as many days as a man wears a garland of *dhātrī* fruit during the Kali age, for that many thousands of years he shall dwell in the abode of Keśava. For as many thousands of ages as he wears a pair of garlands constantly produced from *tulasī* and *dhātrī*, his residence shall be in Vaikuṇṭha.
And if it flows in the region of the throat, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas. (From the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.)

In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "Whoever wears a garland made of *tulasī* leaves that has been touched by Kṛṣṇa obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices for every single leaf. That man who wears a garland produced from *tulasī* wood bestows its fruit [upon himself]."
The enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu) daily bears [the fragrance] arising from Dvārakā for that man who wears it with devotion;
indeed, no sin remains for him. Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, is always pleased in mind with him.
For the man who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood, there is no need for expiation.

For him there is no impurity even during his physical struggle [with death]. That man who wears a garland produced from *tulasī* wood— having that which is produced from *tulasī* wood as an ornament for his head, on his arms, and on his hands— the Lord Hari dwells forever within the body of that mortal.

Adorned with garlands of *tulasī* wood, one should perform meritorious deeds; in the Kali age, what is offered to the ancestors and the deities becomes ten-million-fold. Upon seeing a garland of *tulasī* wood, the messengers of the King of the Dead flee far away, as if scattered by the wind.
Just as with the petals: if one wanders adorned with garlands of *tulasī* wood, there shall be no bad dreams, no ill omens, and no fear arising from weapons anywhere.

Now, the praise of the Vaiṣṇavas. From the ninth chapter of the first night of the Nāradapañcarātra: "Oh! How truly wonderful is the majesty of the servants of Ananta! They practice disinterested devotion toward the feet of Hari forever."
Those who day and night meditate upon the lotus feet of Padmanābha— which are worshipped by the Lord of Lotuses (Brahmā),

honored by Śeṣa and the other gods, and desired by the Earth herself— seek conversation, touch, and the feet [of the Lord] for the sake of their own purification through speech and wealth for the benefit of all.

O Pārvatī! The pure water from the feet of those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa is remembered as that which purifies all sacred fords (tīrthas) and even the entire earth. Those conversant with antiquity declare that he into whose ear the mantra of Kṛṣṇa enters through the mouth of a twice-born is a Vaiṣṇava who has purified the world.

Merely by receiving the mantra, a person becomes one with Nārāyaṇa; by his mere sport, he purifies hundreds upon hundreds of men. By the mere fact of his birth, hundreds upon hundreds of his ancestors become purified, and through the yoga of action, he immediately goes to Goloka.

He is liberated; he shall effortlessly uplift seven generations of his maternal grandfather and others for seven births. He who accepts a daughter [in marriage] [delivers] seven [generations] of her easily:
her mother, her mother’s mother, his own wife, and seven ancestors from his sons, as well as his brother, sister, and daughter.

A devotee of Kṛṣṇa shall uplift [others]. He has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and is initiated into all sacrifices. He obtains the fruit of all worship and is a practitioner of all vows. He who [recites] the mantra of Viṣṇu...
And by obtaining [the sight] from a Vaiṣṇava, the best of the twice-born, one is liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births;

there is no doubt about this. By the mere sight of those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, one is immediately liberated from the sins accumulated over a hundred births; there is no doubt about this. [This applies to] the Vaiṣṇavas...
O Pārvatī! By sight and by touch, water, fire, and the wind are instantly purified; indeed, the gods constantly long for the sight of Vaiṣṇavas.
Indeed, there is no one more purified than a Vaiṣṇava among all beings in their entirety.

p. 717) The Words of Brahmā in the Tenth Chapter: "Aha!
