The company of Vaiṣṇavas is indeed extremely difficult to obtain even for a moment; it enables one to cross the most terrible ocean of worldly existence and bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation. Thus ends the praise of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Now, the time of the manifestation of the ten incarnations is stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*:

On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the asterism Revatī, on a Monday, during the middle of the twelve nāḍīs, Hari became a fish by day. On the second day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha,
under the asterism Rohiṇī, on a Wednesday, at four ghaṭīs by day, Hari assumed the form of a tortoise.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, when the sun was in Aśvinī,

the Lord Hari became Varāha during the middle eight ghaṭikās of the day. Then, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Rādha, under the Svātī nakṣatra and on a Saturday, he was born at midday.

Nṛhari is the Lord of Kamalā. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra and falling on a Friday, Hari became Vāmana during the course of fifteen ghaṭīs by day. On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, conjoined with Rohiṇī and falling on a Saturday, [the birth occurred] within eleven ghaṭīs.
At night, Rāma became Hari. On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, on a Monday during the Punarvasu asterism, in the forenoon, Janārdana himself became Rāma.
And on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, under the Rohiṇī asterism on a Wednesday, [he became Kṛṣṇa].

At midnight on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, when the sun was in Viśākhā, during the sixth hour of the day, the Lord Viṣṇu himself became Kṛṣṇa; born from a portion of Hari, he became a Buddha. On the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa...

When Saturn was in the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Hari appeared in the form of Kalki during the night, specifically within the middle three ghaṭikās. All the particulars regarding the worship of Viṣṇu should be sought in the *Tantrasāra*; they are not written here for fear of excessive length.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, consisting of the exposition on the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites, in the fifth section (the Bhaktikāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Now, the description of the Mahāvidyās. In the Cāmuṇḍā Tantra:
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī, as well as Vagalā, Siddhavidyā, and Mātaṅgī.

The nature of Kamalā. These ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the perfected sciences (*siddhavidyā*). By the statement "these ten Mahāvidyās," since the status of all of them as Mahāvidyās is established, the specific mention of the term "Mahāvidyā" in the phrase "Kālī Tārā Mahāvidyā" [is intended to emphasize this].
This is for the purpose of establishing that Kālī and Tārā are Mahāvidyās; for this very reason, the *Viśvasāra* states: "Therefore, Mahāvidyā is preceded by 'Mahā'.
Now, regarding the statement "the Siddhavidyās have been proclaimed," since all [of them] possess the status of Siddhavidyā:
If it is asked how it is said that Vagalā is a "perfected science" (*siddhavidyā*), the answer is that it is for the purpose of bestowing accomplishment (*siddhi*) instantaneously.
Now, the majesty of Mahāvidyā and the others, as stated in the first chapter of the *Kubjikātantra*: "In the Kali age, though originally black, she who is white has assumed a blue form;
because she bestows speech through her divine play, she is therefore Nīlasarasvatī. Because she grants liberation, she is always Tārā and Tāriṇī."

She is celebrated as Bhuvaneśī because she is the protectress of the worlds; the Goddess who effects creation and sustenance is celebrated as Bhuvaneśī. She is the bestower of fortune and is eternally the Vidyā; thus she is celebrated as Śrīvidyā. And the Great Goddess, who is beyond all attributes (nirguṇā), is celebrated as Ṣoḍaśī.

Bhairavī is the destroyer of suffering, the dispeller of the misery of Yama. She is celebrated as Bhairavī, the consort of Kālabhairava. O Goddess! O Sovereign of the Gods! You are Triśakti, the giver of time, and Chinnā. O Great Goddess! You are the three qualities (triguṇā), the deluder, and the certain bestower of liberation. [You are] Dhūmāvatī.

Mahāmāyā is the slayer of the demon Dhūmra; the Great Goddess is of smoky form and the bestower of the four aims of life. She is the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, and the benefactor of all worlds. The Goddess is known as Vāruṇī in the syllable *va* and as the Giver of Siddhi in the syllable *ga*.
In the letter *la*, there is indeed the Earth, who is proclaimed as Consciousness;
she is Mātaṅgī, who, due to her intoxicated nature (*mada-śīlatva*), is the destroyer of the Asura Mātaṅga; the Goddess is celebrated as Mātaṅgī because she carries across all calamities.
The goddess residing in Vaikuṇṭha is celebrated as Kamalā; the beautiful goddess residing in Pātāla is Lakṣmī by form. These ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the perfected sciences (Siddhavidyās).

They constantly bestow dharma, artha, and liberation, granting the fruits of the four aims of life; by whatever means possible, they grant their full fruit in the Kali age— even toward those who are destitute and wretched, and especially toward those of base birth, the heretic, the rogue, the slanderer, the meritless, and the undevoted.

O beautiful one! O auspicious lady! This must never be disclosed to those who lack devotion toward their sons, nor to others, for I swear this to you truly and forever. O Maheśvarī, give it only to one endowed with all auspicious marks; indeed, there is certainly no one equal to her in the three worlds.
By merely reciting it once, one is liberated from all sins; by its mere remembrance, O Goddess of gods, one is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
Now follows the description of Bhairava in relation to the Mahāvidyās and others, in the first chapter of the Toḍalatantra.
Śiva said:
Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs! O fortunate one! One should worship Bhairava Mahākāla on the right side of Kālikā;
indeed, Dakṣiṇā always delights together with Mahākāla. On the right side of Tārā, [one should worship] Akṣobhya.
One should worship [her]. O Goddess! During the churning of the ocean, the Kālakūṭa poison arose;

all the gods, together with their wives, fell into great agitation. Because the Halāhala poison was drunk by him while remaining free from agitation, for that very reason, O Maheśānī, he is Akṣobhya (the Unshakeable).
Thus he has been fully glorified. With him, Mahāmāyā Tāriṇī always sports.
One should worship Śiva to the right of Mahātripurasundarī; O Sovereign of the Gods! he has five faces and three eyes, and in each face [is a form]. With him, the Great Goddess always [sports].
She is the curiosity of desire; for this very reason, O Maheśānī, she is celebrated as the fifth.

One should worship Tryambaka to the right of the illustrious Bhuvanasundarī. She who is the primordial Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī) in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld—by her Tryambaka rejoices, and therefore [she is called] Tryambakā.

It is said: "He is proclaimed as possessing power (saśakti) and is worshipped by all tantras. On the right side of Bhairavī, one should worship with supreme effort that very one known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who indeed has five faces."
On the right side of Chinnamastā, one should worship the headless torso (kabandha) as Śiva;

O Goddess, by worshipping the kabandha, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis). Dhūmāvatī, the Great Vidyā who assumes the form of a widow, [is located] on the right side of Vagalā; she has one face.
One should worship [him] who is renowned as Mahārudra, the cause of the dissolution of the universe. One should worship Śiva as Mataṅga on the southern side of Mātaṅgī;
he is indeed Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the cause of the bliss of the world. [One should worship him] on the southern side of Kamalā.

O Supreme Goddess! One should worship Sadāśiva in the form of Viṣṇu; he shall become a perfected one (siddha), of this there is no doubt. And one should worship the Form on the right side of Annapūrṇā.
One should worship Nārada in the region to the south of Durgā— the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the ten-faced deity who bestows great liberation. The syllable *na* is the creator,
the syllable *da* is the eternal protector, and because the letter *ra* has the nature of dissolution (*saṃhāra*), he is Nārada.
Whichever sage is proclaimed as the seer for all other vidyās, he alone is its lord;
one should worship him on the right side.

The time for the manifestation of the Great Vidyās and other [deities] is described as beginning with the "Great Night" (mahārātri) and so forth. As it says in the *Svatantratantra*: "In the month of Phālguna, the lunar day of the eleventh of the dark fortnight is the Great Night."

O Goddess! If the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha falls on a Friday (the day of Bhṛgu) and the eleventh day continues into the night, it is proclaimed as a "Divine Night" (divyarātri). If the new moon (amāvāsyā) falls on a Tuesday, or if there is a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or an auspicious constellation (kularkṣa), or an eclipse, [these are likewise meritorious].

The Bhāvarātri is said to be obtained only through good fortune. Siddharātri occurs on the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) coinciding with the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa) in the month of Caitra. The third lunar day (tṛtīyā) of the bright fortnight in Mādhava is a fierce lunar date (dāruṇā tithi) when it falls under a Kula constellation.
On the fourteenth day of the festival of lamps (Dīpotsava), there is the union with Amā;
O Maheśānī! Kālarātri, Tārā, Kālī, and Priyaṅkarī [are present]. O Devī! Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī is proclaimed as Moharātri. On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, however, it is Krodharātri.
O Maheśvarī! Ghorarātri is proclaimed to occur on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa;
Vīrarātri is proclaimed to occur on the fourteenth day conjoined with Tuesday (Maṅgala), endowed with the letter 'Ma', and joined with the Kula asterism.
The arising of knowledge, however, is described in the third chapter of the third night of the *Nāradapañcarātra*.

Brahmā said: She who was born in the house of Dakṣa as Satī, renowned throughout the world, having become angry with the royal sage Dakṣa, abandoned her body; and having been favored by Menā, she was then born to her, celebrated by the name Kālī, established in all the scriptures.
In the Svatantra Tantra:
"O Maheśānī! That form of Kālī, which bestows liberation directly, was born in the city of Avantī during the day of the Great Night (Mahārātri).
Her majesty has been declared in the Nāradapañcarātra by Viśvāmitra, the best of sages."

Having propitiated the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā), that best of Kṣatriyas indeed attained a new status as a Brāhmaṇa; yet even from him he did not obtain the state of Brahmā. Thus, having gone to all the gods and propitiated them again and again, he remained [unsuccessful].
(p. 721) Having worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord at the instruction of Bṛhaspati, he then attained the vision of Maheśvara and became one who had accomplished his purpose. "O God of gods!
O Mahādeva! O Blessed One, you who are full of compassion! Grant me the status of a Brāhmaṇa."
If you are known to me, grant me my boon.
The Lord said:

"The single-syllable great vidyā of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain; perform its recitation, O mighty-armed one! Then you shall attain the state of a brahmin. Having spoken thus, Mahādeva also vanished from sight.
Viśvāmitra also, having worshipped that Goddess who pervades the universe according to the prescribed rites, did not attain the perfection of the mantra;
instead, out of anger, he cursed her, saying,
"May you be unpropitiable," and then, having approached Śiva, he reviled her in many ways.
To him, Maheśvara spoke this:
The Lord said:
O King, listen with diligence to the reason why he cursed the science:
"You shall attain success through the letter 'ka' mounted upon the letter 'ra', and not otherwise."
Brahmā said:
O Nārada, Śambhu vanished, and Viśvāmitra also disappeared; yet,
having recited the ritual procedure exactly as previously instructed by Śambhu,
that Kālī appeared in person along with Rudra at that very moment.
The Goddess said:
"Choose a boon, O Indra among kings! I shall grant you an auspicious boon; whatever you desire, I will give it to you—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
Viśvāmitra said:

"I have propitiated all the hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā. O Goddess! Why has the status of a Brahmin not been granted to me? Grant it to me! Having heard the king's words, that goddess immediately [looked] at her husband's face.
He gazed upon him with a benevolent disposition and spoke to him by means of a sign.

Mahādeva Śaṅkara, having understood that, embraced him with both hands out of affection and then bestowed the status of a Brahmin upon him. At that very moment, the king attained the state of a Brahmin.
He has certainly gone; he is uniquely skilled in all scriptures and has reached the further shore of all scriptures. Thus ends the *Kālīmāhātmya*.

The third night of the *Nāradapañcarātra* is seen to be of two kinds. In one of these, beginning from the origin of knowledge (*vidyotpatti*) and the manifestation of the Śiva-liṅga, it consists of twenty-two chapters; therefore, having extracted [the material] starting from the origin of knowledge...
It has been written.
However, in the other [text] consisting of fifteen chapters, there are the ritual acts beginning with the morning duties and ending with the procedure for worship; yet—
Since these are almost exclusively the words of the *Kramadīpikā*, there is doubt regarding them in various places.

In the second chapter of the third night of the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Just as she who was born in the house of Dakṣa is celebrated by the name Satī; because she bestows absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), she is remembered as Ekajaṭā;
because she saves (*tāraka*), she is always Tārā; and because she grants speech through her divine play (*līlā*), she is Nīlasarasvatī."

She is called Ugratārā because she delivers from fierce calamities; since she delivers from fierce misfortune, she is celebrated as Ugratārā. In the *Svatantra-tantra*: "When the day of Kālarātri has arrived, during the middle portion of the night, Ugratārā herself is the [saving] power for the sake of delivering one from fierce calamity."
On the western slope of Meru, there is a great lake named Colanā. There, O Goddess, the Mother Nīlasarasvatī herself was born. While she was performing her recitation there, three yugas passed;
then, a mass of splendor issued forth from my upward-facing mouth and, having fallen into the Colanā lake, [merged with her].
At that time, she became blue in color. On the northern side of the lake, there was a most excellent sage named Akṣobhya, who was a portion of myself and intent upon her worship.
She, whose nature is the *kūrca* seed-syllable, assumed the *pratyālīḍha* posture. (From the *Nāradapañcarātra*).
There are seventy million great vidyās and likewise minor vidyās;
O best of sages, their forms cannot possibly be numbered. Once, it is said, Hari came from the northeast to the southwest; he arrived with his body as the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala).
The one whose banner bears Garuḍa [Viṣṇu], and the high-souled Siddhas of supreme splendor stationed there, spoke to that Lord, the Master of the World, in order to restrain him:
"She is the primordial source of all, the eternal one whose form is the universe; by her superior command—"
"You ought to go, O Keśava! You are the teacher of all, the witness of all, and the presiding lord of this assembly.
Indeed, you shall not go, O Blessed One, by any other path; please proceed [by the one we have chosen]. Madhusūdana did not accept those words of theirs, yet Garuḍa proceeded by that very path.
By that very [power], Keśava became paralyzed; at that time, Viṣṇu was unable to proceed from there. Then, having reached the ground, Hari became eight-armed, supporting himself upon Mount Nīla.

Sustaining the universe with all his vital breath, the Lord of the World was indeed unable to rise and became reeling. While Hṛṣīkeśa was thus whirling for two thousand years, the Goddess, the Sovereign, then became enraged and [struck him] with her left hand.
Having wrapped [the image] with the *siddhasūtra*, he cast it into the salt waters. Seeing Keśava fallen into the water, he spoke in astonishment: "What is this? Tell me quickly; dispel my wonder."
Viṣṇu said to me at first, "Perform my rescue quickly. Then, having seized Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the lotus-born one of great splendor, prepared to lift him up; yet he too was bound.

Thus Indra and all the others fell into a state of bondage. Then, after some time had passed, the excellent Jīva, the preceptor of the gods, wandered through all the three worlds but did not see the deities anywhere. Seeing the entire city empty, he went to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Having seen him dwelling there for the full duration of his stay, the Guru was filled with joy;
having propitiated the god Maheśvara with hymns of praise and eulogies,
he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff upon seeing the eternal Lord, and spoke to the Lord of the gods of gods:
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Blessed One, where have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods gone? My mind is utterly terrified by the fear of the asuras."
The Lord said:
And Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods held Kāmākhyā in contempt;
they were perpetually agitated and suffered misery, oppressed within the salt waters.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Lord of the World! O Śiva! Consider a remedy for them; the Daityas strike swiftly, and the city of the gods is desolate.
The Lord said:

"Indeed, here I go quickly to deliver the gods; come with me to the salt ocean, O giver of honor! Having spoken thus, the two of them went to the shore of the salt sea. Although Śiva was capable of delivering them, [he did not do so].

Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of the Universe, assuming a body with a multitude of gods for the sake of establishing the boundaries of those [demons] against Hari, wore the Kāmākhyā-kavaca around his neck.
Extending his left hand and enveloping the gods, Śaṅkara, the Lord of the universe, then raised the deities up. Thereupon, all the hosts of gods,
like trembling trees, fell to the ground and bowed down before Mahādeva.
Again and again. Then, having consoled them, the Blessed One spoke to them appropriately:
"Propitiate Ambikā, the Mother of the World, known as Kāmākhyā. Having gone there with Viṣṇu at their head, they bowed to the Supreme Goddess Kāmākhyā and offered hymns of praise.

Then, with his voice choked with tears and trembling, the devoted Hṛṣīkeśa offered supreme praise with prostrations and hymns. From afar, the eternal Source of the Universe, filled with wrath, spoke: "O evil-minded one! Having shown me contempt, what kind of reverence have you performed?"
"By you—what do you desire? Let a boon be chosen from me, whatever is desired by you."
Viṣṇu said:

"O Mother, in your highly meritorious field, I shall remain day and night in the eight directions along with my Śaktis, always subject to your command. Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the Mother of the World, who is identical with the world, said "So be it," and the giver of boons bestowed her grace upon Hari. Thus [it was told] to you.
"O son! I have related to you a small portion of the supreme majesty of the Goddess Tāriṇī, which is a secret; I am not capable of describing it in detail. Thus ends the Majesty of Tārā.
In that very same [work], in the fifth chapter.
Brahmā said:
Listen further, O best of sages, to this most wonderful secret:
how Mahāmāyā Kālī attained the state of Sundarī while Śaṅkara was dwelling on the delightful peak of Kailāsa. Indra joyfully dispatched all the Apsarases, and they arrived.
They praised Mahādeva, that Maheśvara.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of theirs, he whose banner is the bull then addressed them with gentle speech, which was like the nectar of compassion.
Īśvara said:

"A man is to be known as the guest of a man; of this there is no doubt. For women, a woman is to be known as the guest. Therefore, go to Kālikā. Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord entered that beautiful city and addressed the blessed Goddess Kālī:
To the Supreme Goddess; they too attained that supreme joy which is most difficult to obtain.
In the sixth chapter.
Then the goddess Mahākālī, having reflected again and again, thought:
"Abandoning this form, I shall become Śuddhagaurī, so that Mahādeva will not call me 'Kālī, Kālī'. Having thus reflected in her mind, she vanished from sight.
She had departed. After some time, Mahādeva Śiva also went to his city;
however, Hara did not see Kālī there and remained in that city. Then, after some time, Nārada arrived there and, having bowed his head to the god Mahādeva...

Then the sage stood before the god with his palms joined in reverence. Mahādeva, having touched the best of sages with his left hand and comforted him, engaged him in a holy discourse. After some time, at the conclusion of that conversation there—
The best of sages, having bowed down to the Lord of the Universe, spoke these words with reverence.
Nārada said:
"Where has Kālī, the destroyer of Time, gone, having abandoned you?
Then Mahādeva replied to that sage Nārada: "O best of sages, the Goddess has vanished from sight, leaving me."
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his, Nārada was filled with joy;
thinking to himself, "This is the time for the dispute between Mahākālī and the wielder of the trident," Nārada resorted to meditation and beheld that Mahākālī.
Relying upon the eye of meditation,
that Supreme Goddess, situated on the northern side of Sumeru,
bowed with supreme devotion and approached her who consists of the universe, following the hymn of praise by Nārada.
The Goddess said:
"What can Maheśvara do with my distance?
O Lord of Sages, tell me all that is well with him!
Nārada said:
O daughter of the mountain! O lady of excellent vows! The Great Lord, the God of gods, has made a supreme effort for the sake of marriage; restrain him.
Brahmā said:
Having heard his words, the Supreme Goddess, blazing with anger and her eyes bloodshot, assumed another supreme form— an incomparable beauty that did not exist anywhere even within the three worlds.

It was the highest and supreme of all. There dwells the Blessed Lord, the God of gods, Maheśvara. Having arrived there in an instant, that Supreme Goddess beheld her own reflection within the heart of Śambhu.

Enveloped by great anger, she said to Mahādeva: "O Mahādeva! You are ungrateful! O God, O Supreme Lord, for what reason have you transgressed that agreement which was made by me? Having performed the marriage, you gave me a place within your heart."
"O Śiva!
Having heard these words of hers, the Supreme Lord laughed and spoke to his virtuous beloved in a voice faltering with love.
The Lord said:

"O auspicious lady! I am not ungrateful, nor am I a transgressor of my word. Your reflection has been seen by me within my heart; of this there is no doubt. Meditate, O illustrious one! Behold with the eye of wisdom."

O Goddess of gods! That very shadow then became perfectly established as the supreme [form]. With supreme love, she spoke to the Supreme Lord, the God of gods, the Great Lord, the Ruler of the world who consists of the world: "What is this shadow in my heart?"
O Lord of the World! Tell me, has she been seen?
Brahmā said:
Having heard these supreme words of Kālikā, Mahādeva, the eternal God of gods, spoke with a spirit of love.
Īśvara said:

O Śivā! O Pārvatī! Because you have created the most excellent form in the three worlds, therefore in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, and elsewhere, you are renowned as Sundarī, Pañcamī, Śrī, and Tripurasundarī; and because you are eternally sixteen years of age, you are consequently celebrated as Ṣoḍaśī.

O Sovereign of the Gods! because I saw that shadow in my heart today and became afraid, she is renowned throughout the three worlds as Tripurabhairavī. Since the state of the Blessed Lady is one of a stable mind and full of compassion, therefore [I worship] her, the Mistress of the World, the Queen of the Kings of Kings.
They know her as Ugratāriṇī, as she who dwells in the quarters of space (Dikkaravāsinī),
as she known by the name Lalitakāntā, as Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, as Kauṣikī, and as Devadūtī.
And whatever other forms are remembered— those which are celebrated as Bhuvaneśānī have indeed many divisions: Tripuṭā, Jayadurgā, Vanadurgā, Trikaṇṭakī,
Kātyāyanī, Mahiṣaghnī, Durgā, Vanadevatā, and Śrīrāmadevatā.

Vajraprastāriṇī, Śūlinī, Gṛhadevī, Gṛhārūḍhā, Medhā, Rādhā, and Kālikā—these have been described in brief, O Nārada! As for their divisions, O Sage, by whom could they be told in full detail? Thus ends the majesty of the Ṣoḍaśī.
And its subdivisions.
Likewise: That eternal Kālī, the mother of the worlds, said to her husband:
"Command me, O Mahādeva! I shall assume another form."
The Lord said:
O Mother of the World! Whatever form you desire to assume this very moment, I shall perform all of that in which your pleasure is unwavering.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods! You are the creator of all; O Lord of the Universe! it is by Your power that this is so.
However, O All-pervading One! O Supreme Lord! let Your word be heard:
for Your pleasure, O Illustrious One, I shall establish the bounds of morality after performing most difficult penance.
"Being pleased, make me that very form— whether fair, or reddish-fair, or dark, or white, or whatever other form of mine you prefer, O Lord of the World! The Lord said:
O illustrious one! Fulfill that desire of yours for the welfare of the world; however, my sorrow at being separated from you is indeed difficult to endure.
Brahmā said:
Having consoled her beloved husband, she went to the river Mandākinī.
There, for a hundred divine years, she performed most difficult penance. Then the Lord of Gods, the bull-bannered Bhagavān, appeared before her and raised the virtuous woman up with his left hand.
The Supreme Lord Hara, having cleansed the body of his beloved and made it stainless, bathed Pārvatī in the delightful waters of the Mandākinī; Gaurī then assumed the form of lightning.
She is renowned as Vidyudgaurī; she is Svāhāgaurī, Śyāmā, Śuklā, and Raktagaurikā. Her form is infinite in nature, possessing millions upon millions of forms.
She is Śākambharī, Amalā, Sūkṣmā, Ṣaṭpadī, and likewise Bhrāmarī; she is of manifold colors.
The eternal [nature] has the form of that which is to be traversed.
Thus ends the origin of Vidyudgaurī and the others.
In the tenth chapter: Having seen her own reflection in the heart of Śambhu, the eternal Goddess spoke with a sentiment of love to her own husband, the God of gods:
"O Lord, having seen my own very pure reflection in your very heart..."
"O Lord of the gods! O Lord of the world! I am distressed. If you have affection for me, grant me a place within that body.
The Lord said:

"Right now, O fair-faced one, I shall take half of her body! For me, too, there is incomparable joy in both taking away and giving back a limb. Having said this, Hara split his own body in two with his fingernail, and he formed a single body from both himself and Pārvatī. By those two...
Hara became the Lord whose body is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara) through Hara and Gaurī.

As for the two remaining portions, Maheśvara, having unified them and formed them into a single mass like a lump, cast it into the city of Vaikuṇṭha; even today, it exists in the form of radiant energy.
"Or Maheśvara appeared in embodied form;
all the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha beheld him through the power of their ascetic merit. Thus ends the account of the origin of Ardhanārīśvara and others.
In that very place: once, although the goddess Pārvatī had gone joyfully to the waters of the Mandākinī with her two companions for the sake of bathing,
she— the embodiment of the universe— became dark-complexioned there, afflicted by the arrows of Kāma.

The Goddess, the bestower of joy upon the world—then, at one time, the Great Goddess was asked by those two: "O Supreme Goddess, grant food to us who are afflicted by hunger! She replied: "I shall give it here; wait for me."
After a moment, they asked again, "Give us something to eat now;
wait for us for a little while while we remember.
After another moment, they both said, "Give us something to eat now; you are our mother."
A child should pray to the Mother of all the worlds:
"The Mother provides food, clothing, and so forth for everyone; therefore, O Compassionate One, I pray to you for food for the sake of eating. Having heard this—

Maheśānī spoke these sweet words to them: "Having gone to our home, I shall give [food] to you both. To her, those two supreme *ḍākinīs*, Jayā and Vijayā, replied: "O Mother of the World! We two are tormented by hunger; give us food to eat."
"I am satisfied, O Compassionate One! Act thus, O Mother of the World, O Giver of Boons, O Goddess, to fulfill my desire.

Having heard these gentle words, the Compassionate One, with a pure smile, then severed her own head with the tip of her left hand's nail. As soon as it was severed, that head remained in her left hand.
And she fell; O ascetic, blood issued from her throat in three streams.

As those two streams flowed out through the distinction of left and right, she joined them to the mouths of her companions, while the middle stream she directed into her own forest. Having done this, they all departed from that place.
Just as it came to pass: because her head was severed, she is therefore known as Chinnamastā.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*: "I shall proclaim the severance of arising; she herself is Tārā and she is Kālikā.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, on the supreme mountain Kailāsa, Mahāmāyā was intent upon great passion together with me. At the time of the emission of semen..."
At that time, he assumed a fierce form. Then, two powers (śaktis) born from his own body came into being:
Ḍākinī and Varṇinī by name; Ambikā was with those two as her companions.
Caṇḍanāyikā went to the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river; then, at midday, being afflicted by hunger, she asked Caṇḍikā for food. Hearing that, the auspicious Caṇḍikā laughed and [cut off...].
Beholding her own head and all the directions,
the Ḍākinī gratified them with blood flowing from her nostrils; she caused the goddess Varṇinī of the South to drink the blood.
She satisfied her head with the blood dripping from the base of the neck. Having thus engaged in play, Pārvatī returned home at twilight, placing her own head upon the torso.
Having assumed my own form, which was previously described, I saw it discolored and suddenly became filled with anger; thinking this had been done by others,
I then heard how it came to pass, O Goddess— that portion of myself born of wrath.
Krodhabhairava:
O Goddess of gods! On the day of Vīrarātri, at the end of the day, the supreme Kalā was born as Pracaṇḍikā in that river along with her two companions. Thus it is said.
The Origin of Chinnamastā and Others.
In the twelfth chapter of the Nāradapañcarātra.
Brahmā said:
Seated upon the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels, the great goddess Satī, the beloved of Śambhu,
spoke to her husband, the Supreme Lord, with an expression of love.
The Goddess said:

O Lord of the World! By your grace, nothing whatsoever is difficult for me to attain, since you are the giver of all and the one who brings about the welfare of all. Nevertheless, I desire to go to the auspicious abode of my mother and father.
Īśvara said:

"O Queen of the Gods! O Śivā! This departure of mine is pleasing to me as well. But I have a doubt, O Goddess: will you go there uninvited? Having heard these words of her husband, she spoke these words joyfully: "O Śaṅkara! Once I have gone there, I shall follow after that."
The Lord said:
O auspicious one! O blessed lady, I have now fulfilled this agreement with you;
once you have departed, I shall go for the purpose of bringing you back.
Brahmā said:
In the meantime, Menā celebrated a magnificent festival.
She dispatched Krauñca to where Lord Sadāśiva was; by means of a chariot with the speed of the wind, the son of the mountain arrived swiftly at the place where the Blessed Lord Īśa resided.
Manifesting the very nature of Brahman, Maināka descended from the seat of the chariot even from afar. Having arrived on the ground, that Krauñca prostrated himself like a staff.
His eyes were filled with tears of love, his body was covered in horripilation, and he was trembling.
Then the mighty-armed Mahādeva, his neck bowed with devotion, beheld Krauñca lying upon the earth; lifting him up with his left hand and embracing the son of the Mountain,
he kissed his head while shedding tears from his eyes upon it.
Having inquired after his welfare and well-being, he seated him upon his own lap and spoke with gentle words: "For what purpose have you come here?"
The Krauñca said:
If you have compassion for me, your servant, O Lord! O Master of the World!
I am eager to lead Gaurī, the daughter of Himālaya, there; having dwelt for some months, she will certainly return at your command, O Lord of the Universe!
O Lord, compose yourself!
The Lord said:
Go quickly to Pārvatī and report everything to her.
Brahmā said:

Having heard these words of the trident-bearing god, the Krauñca bird took leave of the Lord of the World and went to where Pārvatī was. Seeing her from afar, that son of the Mountain fell upon the earth; having prostrated with his head upon the ground, he offered praise.
Having touched the feet of the Supreme Goddess, the mighty-armed one stood there filled with humility.
Then Girijā, the daughter of the Mountain, taking him by her left hand,
seated him upon her lap.
Having honored him with blessings, he inquired after the welfare of the mountain.
The Goddess said:
"For what purpose have you come, my child? Tell me before me. It has been a long time since we last saw one another; may it be well with you, and I shall do as you have requested."
The Krauñca said:
All living beings desire even to behold you for the welfare of the world; O Supreme Goddess! Himavat, the king of mountains, and Menā have been granted permission by Maheśa;
O Pārvatī, come quickly with me to their father’s house and [meet] them.
Gladden us! All of us are eager for the sight of you; show compassion for the welfare of the world.
The Goddess said:

"Wait a moment—blessings upon you—until I inform my husband. Having said this, she went quickly to where the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) was staying. Bowing her head with devotion, the devoted wife approached him and said: "Grant me your permission, O Lord! Have mercy on me, O Sadāśiva!"
"By your grace, O Lord of the World! I behold my father, mother, and other kinsmen; brought by you, O Śaṅkara, I shall return."
Śaṅkara said:

"Go quickly, O Pārvatī, O lady of excellent hips, together with Krauñca! If you do not go, O Goddess, there is no doubt that you shall be cursed by them both. Having bowed again to Maheśvara, the God of gods, that goddess ascended the chariot with difficulty along with Maināka.
She departed;
having reached her father’s house in an instant and descended from the chariot, she went with great haste along with Krauñca, moving with the speed of the wind,
to where King Himavat and Menā resided.

The sweet-spoken lady of excellent complexion touched the feet of the two [sages] and stood there. Himavat, the lord of mountains and possessor of great intelligence, having honored that supreme woman and inquired after her welfare and health, embraced her and remained for a long time.
Having obtained wealth, one of great splendor is no longer destitute.
The King of Mountains said:

"Go quickly, O illustrious one! Satisfy Menakā. Having been thus addressed by her father, she went and approached her mother. Having saluted the Mother of the World, she stood before her mother. Menakā, having inquired after her welfare, spoke with a voice faltering with joy.

After a long time, the fortunate Pārvatī, who increases her mother’s joy, was seen; having thus dwelt happily there in her father’s house, she spoke for several months, further increasing their delight.
In the meantime, Śambhu, the king of the gods, taking up a conch shell that was auspiciously marked,
beautiful, lovely to kiss, and captivating,
went to the house of Himavat in the guise of a conch-shell maker, desiring to sell the shells under a pretext.
The destroyer of Tripura gave a conch to the women, yet he did not give one to Pārvatī.
Overcome with affection, Pārvatī, having obtained his consent, said:
"O illustrious one! O Great Goddess! I shall give you this beautiful conch, since it was requested by me, O blessed lady."

"That price must indeed be paid. Having said "So be it," the Mother of the World put on that stainless, divine, captivating, beautiful, and most splendid conch. Then the shell-worker said, "O devoted wife, give the price!"
The Goddess said:
My father is the Himavat mountain; my lord is Śambhu, who is composed of compassion;
my sons are Gaṇanātha and the others; my brother is Maināka himself;
my nephew is Krauñca; and my mother is Menakā.
Whatever you pray for, may it be well with you; I shall grant that to you, without a doubt.
The conch-maker said:
"O fair-faced one, afflicted by the arrows of desire for you, quickly choose me as your husband, O blessed lady;
no other merit is desired by me. Having heard these words of that conch-maker, Pārvatī—
"Who in the three worlds is able to speak such harsh words to me?
This one of wicked intent has set his mind upon Śambhu. Then, O Pārvatī, having established himself in meditation and summoning his fortitude, he beheld his [Śambhu’s] conduct.

Then the Supreme Goddess, smiling, spoke with a face brightened by a gentle smile to that conch-maker, Śambhu: "Go now; may it be well with you; I shall fulfill your heart's desire. O mighty-armed one! Having dismissed him on another day, she who is devoted to the welfare of the world departed.
Assuming the guise of a Kirāta and surrounded by her female companions,

she went to where the Lord of Gods, Maheśvara, was performing his twilight rites; there, assuming the form of Rati, she dwelt with him through dances, songs, amorous dalliances, and abundant food and drink.
The Supreme Goddess. In the meantime, Śambhu went to perform his twilight rites;
having gone to the shore of the lake named Mānasa, Maheśvara beheld that supreme lady, resplendent with the attire of love, accompanied by her friends, and red in hue.
Clad in red garments, perfectly pure, slender, with large eyes and full,
elevated breasts— having approached her presence, the compassionate Lord spoke.
The Lord said:
"Who are you, O fair one! O lady of beautiful hips! For what purpose have you come here? I shall grant your heart's desire; this is the truth, the truth—please show me mercy."
The Cāṇḍālī said:
"O best of gods, I have come here to this Cāṇḍāla settlement for the sake of penance;
O wise one, do not create an obstacle to my desire for divinity!"
Īśvara said:
"I am Śiva, O Queen of the Gods of gods! I am the bestower of the fruits of asceticism.
Now I shall make you equal to Pārvatī; there is no doubt in this. Therefore, O auspicious one, worship me with the sentiment of love. Why do you delay, O Goddess?"
If you desire the state of divinity.
The Cāṇḍālī said:
"O God of gods! O Lord of the world! We have come here for the sake of asceticism;
we have indeed attained the status of deities. Do not create an obstacle for us, O King of Dharma!"
The Lord said:

"There shall be no obstacle for you; what need have you for bodily mortification? Now become my queen, for my word is not in vain. Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord Mahādeva took her hand with his own hand and sat upon an excellent seat provided by her.

Mahādeva Śiva, having embraced her, kissed her face and proceeded to engage in sexual union with her. After sporting with her for some time, Hara assumed the guise of a Caṇḍāla; then his beloved Satī said: "I am not..."
"By what means could you possibly be led astray anywhere? For you, O God, are the preceptor of the gods!
O God of gods! O Lord of the universe! Thus did they take their pleasure with one another in various ways.
And an incomparable love arose between the two, O best of sages!
Then, as they were seated at the conclusion of their dalliance, the virtuous lady spoke to her husband:
"Perform your recitation, O Lord of the World! Grant me my desired boon."
The Lord said:

"O auspicious lady, because you have approached me in this manner in the guise of a Caṇḍāla, therefore this form of yours shall become known as Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālī; there is no doubt about it. She is hidden in all the scriptures. When your worship has been performed at the conclusion of the ritual,"
O Supreme Goddess!
O Śivā! She shall possess all her limbs; otherwise, O Pārvatī, she will not. There is no doubt that your form shall be named Mātaṅgī—a perfected lore, a great lore—and likewise [so].
Tripurasundarī, the goddess Tripurabhairavī, and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Kālī, Tārā, and Mahāvidyā—these are your supreme forms. Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the form Dhūmāvatī; Vagalā, Siddhavidyā, and Mātaṅgī are yours.
This is the body.
Brahmā said:
Having thus granted her the boon, he spoke again to his beloved Satī: "Go to the home of Himavat; as for me, O Lord, I shall go to Kailāsa. Having gone there, [I shall seek] Mahāmāyā..."
"Bring me to my own abode.

Having heard these words of her husband, she prostrated before her lord, offered her salutations, and being granted permission, she departed as she had come. But they, deluded by illusion (māyā), remained there.
They were not aware of anything at all. Thus ends the account of the origin of Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī.
As for another method, it is found in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "Now I shall speak of Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī; listen with careful attention! Nārada questioned Viṣṇu:
'O Lord, tell me the knowledge of song! Hari said to him: 'Formerly, I went..."
To Śaṅkara: There, Śiva was seen, peaceful and crowded with hosts of Mārīcas;

endowed with many sentiments and possessed of various tastes, a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) then arose, and the remnants flowed forth with joy, produced as it were with manifold qualities.

The maiden said: "Give me the remains! Give me the remains! Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, Pārvatī and both of them gave her the remains as a gracious gift with affection. Śiva and Śakti said to her: "O maiden! For those who worship you with recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites,"
And her desires are fulfilled. From that time forward, she is called Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī. Thus ends the account of the origin of Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī in the thirteenth chapter of the Nāradapañcarātra.
Brahmā said:
Once, while dwelling upon the peak of Kailāsa, Girijā, seated on his lap, questioned Hara, whose banner is the bull: "I am tormented by hunger; give me what is appropriate to eat."
The Lord said:
"Wait a moment— blessings be upon you— and I shall give you food thereafter," having said this,
the God of gods, whose banner is the bull, immediately fell silent.
The Goddess said:

"Give me food, O Mahādeva! I am hungry, O Lord of Japa! I cannot endure any delay; I am tormented, O Maheśvara! Hearing these words of his beloved, the ocean of compassion spoke again: "Wait for a moment; I shall give you food."
And having waited again, the Goddess spoke these words once more: "O Lord of the World! Give me food; I cannot endure further delay. Having said this, she took her husband [into her mouth].
He then cast me away. In an instant, a mass of smoke arose from her body.
When that [smoke] had emerged from the body, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, by means of his own Māyā, spoke to his beloved:
"Listen, O beautiful one! Behold, O auspicious and highly fortunate lady, a man!"
"There is no one but me; there is no woman other than you—behold this with your eye of wisdom!
You are a widow; renounce the conch-shell and the vermilion.
O Goddess, O devoted wife, renounce the marks of a virtuous woman! This is your supreme form."

Vagalāmukhī is renowned; because her body is pervaded by smoke, she is therefore remembered as Dhūmāvatī. These two supreme forms of yours are proclaimed as Siddhividya and Prakīrtitā. Just as the form Ugratāriṇī, just as Kālī was formerly Satī, and just as Bhuvaneśānī—just as [these].
O Supreme Goddess! Just as is the form of Chinnamastā, so are you Tripurabhairavī.
Thus ends the arising of Dhūmāvatī.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*, there is another way for its arising.
At the sacrifice of Dakṣa Prajāpati, she who is ever-ready to annihilate all, becoming enraged, cast off her body,
and from that arose a great smoke; from that smoke was born Dhūmāvatī, the destroyer of all enemies, Kālī, with a face as black as the color of Time.
On a Tuesday at the beginning of the night, when the Akṣayatṛtīyā had arrived, the auspicious Dhūmāvatī was born. Thus ends the account of the origin of Dhūmāvatī according to another tradition.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*: Now I shall explain, O Goddess of gods, the cause of the origin of Vagalā.

Long ago, O Goddess, in the Kṛta-yuga, when a disturbance of the winds arose leading to the destruction of all moving and unmoving beings, Viṣṇu became absorbed in anxious thought. And by means of his ascetic penance, [the Goddess] was satisfied.
The Greatly Auspicious Tripurāmbikā, intent on sporting in the water upon seeing the lake known as Haridrā, [is present] at the edge of the Great Yellow Lake; in Saurāṣṭra, Vagalāmbikā exists,
where the splendor born of Śrīvidyā unfolds here and there.
The fourteenth lunar day joined with Mars (Bhauma) and endowed with the letter *ma*,
when conjoined with the Kula asterism, is proclaimed as Vīrarātri.
On that very night at midnight, she dwells in the Pīta lake.
The supreme Brahmāstra-vidyā, which paralyzes the three worlds, was born; that splendor arising from Viṣṇu entered into the Vidyā and Anuvidyā. Thus ends the origin of Vagalāmukhī.
In that very place: Now I shall describe Mātaṅginī, who causes terror to cruel spirits.
Formerly, in the Kadamba forest crowded with various trees, a sage named Mataṅga [practiced] for a hundred thousand years for the sake of subjugating all beings.
She performed penance continuously. There, O auspicious one, a splendor arose from the eyes of Sundarī.
A mass of light appeared there, which became Śrī Kālikāmbikā herself; assuming a dark form, she became Rājamātaṅginī. Thus ends the origin of Mātaṅginī.

In the Svatantra Tantra: Now I shall describe the venerable Bhuvana, the Mother who is the source of the origin of the three worlds. Formerly, Brahmā performed severe austerity in order to create the universe. Satisfied by his austerity, that Supreme Goddess, Śakti, [appeared].

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Tāriṇī herself was born; she is celebrated as Krodharātri, the auspicious one who consists of all powers. She arose from the Ocean of Milk in ancient times through the churning of the sea.

And Ramā, seated upon a lotus throne, resides upon the chest of Viṣṇu; on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, she is the destroyer of the demon Kola. On that lunar day, the Mahāmātaṅginī Kalā was born.
On the eleventh lunar day of the month of Phālguna, which coincides with the weekday of Venus or Mars,
Mahālakṣmī,
the bestower of all auspicious fortune, was born. Thus ends the account of the origin of Mahālakṣmī.

In that very same [text]: "On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, Ghorarātri is proclaimed; on that [day], Mahākāla arose, and the Blessed One himself [was present]. Thus ends the account of the origin of Mahākāla.
The birth of Vaṭuka is said to occur on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha;
the emergence of the teeth is proclaimed to take place on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa;
and the Mahādurgāṣṭamī is remembered as the festival of the Great Slayer of the Buffalo-Demon.
Now begins the section on Kālī. In the fourth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra, the words of Sadāśiva are as follows: "Your form is Mahākāla, the agent of the world's dissolution.
At the time of the great dissolution, Kāla shall swallow everything, because of his act of reckoning (kalanāt)."

She is proclaimed as Mahākāla for all beings; because she is the reckoning (kalana) of Mahākāla, you are the primordial and supreme Kālikā. Because she calculates time (kāla), Kālī is the primordial form of all.
Because she is both time and the primordial being, she is sung of as Ādyā Kālī.

Having again assumed your own nature—which is of the form of darkness, formless, beyond speech, and inaccessible to the mind—you alone remain. Though possessing form, you are also formless; through *māyā*, you take on many forms. You are the beginning of all, yet yourself without beginning; you are the creator, the destroyer, and the protector.

"Therefore, O auspicious lady, it has been told to you: the fruit that one obtains through initiation by means of the Brahma-mantra is exactly the same as the fruit obtained from this practice. (From the *Guptasādhanatantra*, Chapter Six).
O Lord, what is *ālīḍha* like? And what is *pratyālīḍha* like? How is she..."
"Dakṣiṇākālī, who dwells in the cremation ground"—thus is the answer to the Goddess's question.

Her left foot is in the *ālīḍha* posture and her right in the *pratyālīḍha*; Kālī, whose form is that of withdrawal, is the enchantress of the world. Mahāmāyā is the embodiment of fire—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.

Therefore, O Great Goddess! She who dwells in the cremation ground, that Goddess, is in the *ālīḍha* posture at one moment and in the *pratyālīḍha* posture at another moment. O Beloved! Who is able to describe Her who possesses infinite forms, the Dark One? [She is] the Dark One possessing infinite forms.
Bestowing the fourfold aims of human life; from the second chapter of the Picchilā Tantra.

(737) She whose head-jewel and lotus-feet are [worshipped by] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others—Kālī alone is [the deity] in the Kali age; no other god exists in the Kali Yuga. Even for the sake of peace and other goals, that Kālī should be worshipped especially. When faith in the worship of Kālikā arises in the heart...

At that time, there is never any fear of planetary afflictions or diseases. O Goddess! Among all mantras, the Kālikā mantra is the most excellent; by the mere grasping of it, even the lowest person becomes liberated while living. [As stated] in the first chapter of the Kubjikātantra: "In what lineage am I?"
Having arisen, they were intent on accomplishing Kālī. Hearing that, all the ancestors danced with delighted minds; likewise.

The supreme Vidyā is unassailable; in the Kali age, it bestows the full fruit. O Goddess! Kālikā grants liberation and yields swift results in the Kali age. One should receive this great Vidyā, which destroys all sins, from the mouth of the Guru. Likewise: whatever one performs, such as dharma and adharma...
The supreme practitioner certainly receives all of that through the worship of Kālikā. O Maheśvarī! It must be performed according to the traditional injunctions;
O Sureśvarī! for those devoid of the tradition, there shall be no fruit.
Such is the beginning of the censure [of others]. In the Picchilā Tantra: "In this world, those who utter insults against Kālī will have their lifespans exhausted;
their sons and wives will perish, and in the end, they shall go to hell."
Such is the fault of censure and so forth.
Likewise, in the eleventh chapter: "Now I shall declare the mantra of Kālī, by which one becomes an achiever of all aims, a hero swift in all accomplishments, and honored by all the worlds;
merely by the knowledge of which one obtains the fruit of the fourfold goals among all the gods and goddesses."

O beloved! Dakṣiṇā is the primordial nature (prakṛti). I shall proclaim her mantra, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds: having extracted the Yakṣa (Ya) and Skanda (Sa), conjoined with the fire (Ra) and the left eye (Ū), and endowed with the moon (I) and the bindu (M), this is remembered as the seed-syllable (vīja) of Kālī. Having obtained this supreme...
O Goddess who embodies Śiva! This secret, the essence of essences, higher than the highest, allows the practitioner of mantra to effortlessly attain the fourfold aims of life.
O Great Goddess! If this seed-syllable were endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), it would become even more essential; indeed, there is nothing equal to it.

O Maheśvarī! There exists a certain Vidyā; by means of this, one may accomplish pacification, nourishment, and so forth, without delay. [It is effective] in great calamity, in great terror, in the crisis of extreme poverty, in the increase of enemies, in the increase of disease, and in the most terrible [situations].
O Goddess! In times of terror, when fear of kings and the like has arisen— especially within the circle of kings—
one should practice this spoken mantra for exactly one hundred thousand recitations during the wrath of the gods.

In terrifying fear, in the misfortunes of one's home, in fearsome danger, in the wilderness, when standing upon the ground surrounded by bandits, in all rites for pacification, when the loss of wealth is imminent,
or in enmity with one’s own kin— one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; that Kālī protects the practitioner.

Always like Skanda in times of fear; therefore, O beautiful one, worship Kālikā with supreme effort! Without recitation (*japa*), even the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) or the Siddhi-knowledge brings only ruin.
Without fire-offerings (*homa*), there is no sovereignty; without recitation, there is no accomplishment; and without worship, there is none at all.

O Supreme Goddess! there is worship everywhere. Likewise: "O Goddess! these two mantras must not be given even in a life-threatening crisis. If one should give them out of affection, one must perform ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-japa*).
O Maheśānī! by knowing this mantra, one becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, a poet, and eloquent."
He shall become a hero, pleasing to behold by all,
and having attained renown in the worlds, he shall obtain liberation at the end.

In the Guptasādhanatantra, the sixth chapter: "Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the supreme ritual manual for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), by the mere grace of which one does not sink into the ocean of existence."

The mantra that fascinates the three worlds consists of the final vowel joined with fire (the letter *ra*), adorned with the left eye (*ī*), and endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. The final vowel is the letter *ka*. Bhairava is declared to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *uṣṇik* meter is cited as its meter (*chanda*).

The deity Dakṣiṇākālikā is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhis). Her seed-syllable (bīja) is Māyā (Hrīṃ), while the Kūrca-bīja (Hūṃ) is her Śakti. O Maheśānī! Her own seed-syllable is the Kīlaka that deludes all.

The application [of this] is proclaimed to be for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Likewise: On the day preceding the worship, one should first perform acts such as shaving; O Maheśānī, the food should be sacrificial (haviṣya) or a meal free from meat.

Then, on the following day at dawn, having bathed and completed the daily worship (nityapūjā) first with a pure mind like a deity— whether it be the Guru, the Guru’s son, or the Guru’s wife, O lady of virtuous vows— the Guru himself is the one authorized for the worship prescribed in the Āgamas.

O Goddess of the gods! In the absence of a Guru, one should perform the worship and other rites oneself. As stated in the tenth chapter of the Varadā-tantra (p. 739): "One should personally perform the rites prescribed in the Tantras and those mentioned in one's own ritual manual;
or else, one may have them performed by a Guru or by a woman who has sons."

"Otherwise performed, everything indeed becomes useless"— by this [verse], that which was previously considered optional is established as being performed by oneself in the absence of a guru, through syntactic unity with this [text]. The primacy of the substitute over the primary [agent] is established by the force of the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, it follows all the more clearly that if one is personally incapable, a woman who has sons should have the rite performed on her behalf.
He states the fault in performing Tantric worship and other rites through another person.

In the *Guptasādhanatantra*: "O Maheśānī! If the Tantric preceptors perform [the rite] without these [preliminaries], the entire fruit of that worship is devoured by yakṣas and rākṣasas. Therefore, O Maheśānī, the Guru is ordained as the performer. If the Guru, who is the manifest embodiment of Brahman, performs the worship and so forth..."
One should perform it; O Maheśānī! all of that shall become multiplied a hundred crore times. Or else, O Parameśānī! one should personally perform the worship and so forth.
Having personally performed the worship and so forth, whatever materials for worship and the like were used—all of that [shall become multiplied a hundred crore times].

O Supreme Sovereign! One should offer [the offering] before the Guru. O Great Sovereign! Whatever is given to the Guru becomes ten million times more meritorious. Regarding the performance of worship and so forth by the Guru’s wife, there is no need for *homa* (fire sacrifice) and the like; it is stated in that very same source: "O Great Sovereign! If the Guru’s wife should perform worship and the like, [she should perform] the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) and so forth."

In that case, one should avoid performing the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having brought the materials for the oblation, the wise practitioner should place them before the Goddess; having recited the root mantra, he should offer them to Mahādevī. By that, the fruit of the oblation is attained, and the wise practitioner need not offer them into the fire. Likewise, that which was [stated] by the Guru:

O Goddess! all that shall become inexhaustible. O Beloved Goddess! there are many [officiants] such as priests, sons, and others mentioned in the Smṛtis; O Supreme Mistress! one should never have them perform the worship and other rites prescribed in the Tantras.
If one should bring in a domestic priest (purohita) to cause the worship and other rites to be performed, [the result would be otherwise].

All his purposes shall fail, and Kālikā becomes enraged. O Maheśānī! During the time of worship, she should not look at the face of another. For him who performs all acts such as desired worship in the presence of people, all his purposes shall fail, and she becomes enraged.
Kālikā: It is better not to perform worship at all than to perform it in the presence of another.

O Goddess, if one intent on worship should be in the presence of another, he should display the respective mudrās for the worship and other rites prescribed in the Viṣṇu-tantras; by that means, the worship and so forth are accomplished, yet they remain unmanifest.
At any time, O Supreme Goddess, this special rite must be guarded like a mantra in the *Varadātantra*. One should perform the supreme festival during worship involving lamps and other offerings.
With a serene mind, one should perform every action for the pleasure of Bhavānī; therein, devotion is always required.

Whichever one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) may be, lack of devotion toward that deity brings great suffering and causes leprosy. O Goddess, he who abandons his own goddess as well as his own guru and is devoted to another—everything belonging to him perishes. One must not engage in the censure of others.
Never, even for a moment, have I taught that there is anything other than the one Brahman, which is without a second, everywhere. O virtuous one!
It assumes multiplicity only through the distinctions of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). He who worships the One—
He honored them all.
Now, that worship is threefold: consisting of mental and internal sacrifice, as well as external.
As it is said in the fifth chapter of the *Muṇḍamālātantra*: "Mental worship brings about great siddhi and bestows liberation."

The external worship, which consists of the inner sacrifice, destroys the state of being a mere living soul; it is passionate (rājasa) and bestows all prosperity. It grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, destroys all calamities, causes the exhaustion of all defects, and strikes down all enemies.
She is the destroyer of all diseases and the liberator from all bonds.
O Dear One! For heroes and for bound souls (paśus), external worship is considered inferior;
indeed, for those who are purely divine, external worship is declared to be the lowest form. — *Toḍalatantra*

In the third chapter: O Goddess of gods! the procedure for worship is here described in the form of a manual. Having recited the benediction (*svasti*) and performed the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should diligently install the water-pot (*ghaṭa*). One should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) with the mantra and then place the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having sprinkled the doorway with that water, [one proceeds].

One should perform the worship of the door. Having dispelled the threefold obstacles, one should then effect the departure of the spirits (bhūtāpasaraṇa). After worshipping the seat, the wise practitioner should bow to the Guru and the Deity.
Then, having performed the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), the triple clapping of the palms (tāla), and the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with fire—
One should perform the veiling (*veṣṭana*) and then practice the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Mātṛkā and the internal Mātṛkā. Having performed the meditation on the Mātṛkā, one should install the external Mātṛkā; then, having performed the installation of the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*), [one should proceed].

One should perform *prāṇāyāma*. One should perform the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the assignment of the hands, limbs, and phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*). Then, O Goddess, one should perform the sixfold assignment (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), and immediately thereafter the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka*). Thus, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the assignment of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*).

Then, O Goddess, the wise practitioner should perform the pervasive seed-syllable placement (vījanyāsa). Having performed the placement seven times with the root mantra, he should conduct mental worship. He should then offer the special arghya, perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), and again engage in meditation along with the visualization of the eyes.

One should perform the visualization of the mudrās and so forth, followed by the invocation and the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Then, one should perform the *dhenu*-mudrā and others, the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and worship with the root mantra.
One should pray for the command (*ājñā*), worship the limbs (*aṅga*), and worship Kākhā and the others, as well as Bāhmyā and the others, the Asitāṅgas and others, and Mahākāla.
One should worship [the weapons] such as the sword and the lineage of gurus; then one should worship the Goddess again.

Then there is the offering of the bali, followed by the fire sacrifice (homa), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and then the recitation (japa). The wise one should offer the recitation, and then perform breath control, as well as the hymn of praise (stuti) and the armor (kavaca).

Having recollected [the mantra], the wise one should prostrate with the eight-limbed [salutation]. Contemplating "I am Śiva," he should dismiss [the deity] by means of the withdrawal [mudrā]. Having prepared a mandala in the northeast, preceded by the remnants of the *caṇḍālī*, he should hold the *arghya* water upon his head and [apply] sandalwood [paste].
Having accepted some of the food offering at the forehead, one may wander according to one's own desire.

The meditation on Mahākāla is found in the third chapter of the *Niruttara Tantra*, as follows: "One should worship Mahākāla, smoke-colored, endowed with a mass of matted hair, three-eyed, having the form of Śiva, joined with his Śakti, free from affliction, naked, and of terrible appearance."
Having the luster of a mass of blue collyrium, devoid of qualities yet the substratum of all qualities— [I bow] again and again to the abode of Kālī.
The sequence for the worship of the sword and other implements is as described in the *Niruttara*; likewise [in the *Sampuṭa*]:

O Kulasaundari! One should worship a sword and a shaven head in the left hand; likewise, one should worship the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting in the right hand. Thus is the sequence of worship for Asitanga and the others. Furthermore, O Goddess, one should worship the Bhairavas beginning with Asitanga at the four gates.
O Goddess! Starting from the east in sequence, there are two [deities] at each door.
The sūtra for the abbreviated worship is found in the third chapter of the Toḍalatantra.
Alternatively, the mantra-practitioner, being composed, should perform the abbreviated worship: first, having performed the placement of the ṛṣi and so forth,
then the purification of the hands, followed by the placement of the fingers, the pervasive placement, and the placement beginning with the heart.

Three claps of the hand constitute the binding of the directions (digbandha), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma). Then one should perform meditation (dhyāna), the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga), and the placement of the arghya water. Next, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), meditate once more, and then carry out the invocation (āvāhana).

Then, having performed the *jīvanyāsa*, one should worship the Supreme Deity; one should perform the limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*) starting with Kālī and the others, as well as the eight Bhairavas beginning with Brāhmī. Having worshipped Mahākāla, one should then honor the lineage of gurus. After worshipping the sword and other implements, one should worship the Goddess once again.

One should perform worship. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, the foremost of practitioners should recite the mantra (*prajapet*). Then one should perform the offering of the fruit of the recitation into the hand of the Goddess. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, the wise one should prostrate with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*). Having remembered the hymn of praise (*stuti*) and the armor (*kavaca*), [one should conclude].

One should cause the special *arghya* to be offered. Having performed the self-surrender (*ātmasamarpaṇa*), one should dismiss [the deity] by means of the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) mudrā. Having prepared a mandala in the northeast, and having first taken some of the food-remnants of the *cāṇḍālī*, one may enjoy it according to one's own desire.
In the Picchilā Tantra, the twelfth chapter: "I shall explain the procedure for daily worship;
listen, O beloved of my life! For without it, O Goddess, worship and other rites never yield fruit anywhere. Through worship one obtains worship; therefore, one should be devoted to worship."

For one who is devoid of daily worship, no desired object is ever accomplished. Likewise: Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the general offering (sāmānyārghya) at the entrance; there, one should perform the placement of the syllables, the seers, and so forth, and the purification of the hands with the root mantra.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] pervading the hands, the wise one should place the limbs [of the deity]. Then follows the binding of the directions with three claps of the hands (*tāla*), as well as three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*). Meditation upon the desired deity, worship, recitation (*japa*), and the adoration of Kālikā—this very procedure is declared for all.
The sequence of worship: That worship becomes "great" when performed with the sixteen services (upacāras). O Śivā! In the daily rite, one should perform ten or five services.
In the absence [of materials], one should worship with perfume and flowers; in the absence of flowers, with [just] a flower; and in the absence of that, one should worship [with devotion alone].
One should never neglect mental worship even in the absence of vessels, rice, or water;
for if it is neglected, there will be total ruin and calamities at every step. Regarding these two:

The *puraścaraṇa* consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*). In the second chapter of the *Kālītantra*: "First, one should perform the *puraskriyā* according to the prescribed rules. Being pure and fasting on food fit for sacrifice (*haviṣya*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day; at night, with the mouth full of betel, one should recite it while lying on a bed."
"From one hundred thousand [recitations], the mantra becomes perfected; thereafter, the practitioner is fit for ritual application, and not otherwise.

This statement is also maintained in the *Tantrasāra*; however, because later [commentators] observe two hundred thousand [recitations] in this statement, they [interpret it as referring to] the *Aniruddhasarasvatī* written by the author of the *Tantrasāra*.

Because two hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) are seen as what is to be performed, some claim that for these two [mantras] as well, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of two hundred thousand recitations each, divided between day and night. That is not correct;
for even the author of the *Tantrasāra* has clearly stated that the preliminary rite for these two consists of one hundred thousand recitations.

The authority for that should be seen in the statement of the Siddheśvarī contained therein. In reality, however, the "supreme practice" (*para-caraṇa*) mentioned as being [attained] by two hundred thousand [recitations] of these two and of Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is distinguished according to the categories of the *paśukalpa* and the *vīrakalpa*. As it has been said:
As it is stated in the *Svatantratantra* held within the *Śyāmārahasya*: *yathā* (as follows).

During the day, having become pure and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), a man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thereafter, O Dear One, he should perform a fire-oblation with sacrificial food ten times that number. He should then perform libations with water from a sacred ford, or with milk, or likewise with sacrificial food, or with honey, or with water mixed with sugar, O Supreme Goddess!

One should consecrate the Goddess with waters that constitute a tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa); O Dear One, one should then devoutly feed Brahmins who are knowers of the Kālītantra with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) that is a tenth part of that [libation], and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru. O Dear One, the ritual procedure (kalpa) for the bound soul (pāśava) has been told; now hear the procedure for the enemy (vaira).
Thus it is said.

Also, in the fourth chapter of the *Niruttaratantra*: "One who is always pure and eats sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times during the day. One should offer oblations into the fire one-tenth of that amount, perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) one-tenth of that, and receive consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) one-tenth of that."
"O Pārvatī! One should devotedly feed the twice-born with food [obtained] from that [sacrifice], which constitutes a tenth part of it.

The ritual procedure (kalpa) for the *pāśava* [initiate] has been told; now hear the *vaira* [procedure] hereafter. O Goddess! when one watch of the night has passed, one should contemplate one's own lineage. Having begun thus: "The practitioner of mantra, intent on the contemplation of reality..."

One should recite the *kulākula* mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). One should offer oblations into the fire ten times that amount (*daśāṃśa*) with fermented liquors mixed with meat. One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten times that amount with nectar mixed with meat.
O Pārvatī! One should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) ten times that amount with water from sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*).

One should devoutly feed the twice-born with family provisions, giving them a tenth part of that amount. At the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, one should feed the *kula* of the *śaktis*. In their absence, O Maheśānī! one should worship only a single *śakti*. Indeed, if one does not worship a *śakti* during the time of the *puraścaraṇa*, [the rite is rendered fruitless].
His worship, recitation, and fire-offering indeed serve for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). This is also stated in the first chapter.

"By day, the practice is that of the bound soul (paśu), and by night, the practice is that of the Kaula. Rituals such as *puraścaraṇa* are twofold according to the distinction of state (*bhāva*). Therefore, in the *paśu-kalpa*, the *puraścaraṇa* consists of one hundred thousand recitations by day; however, in the *vīra-kalpa*, it consists of one hundred thousand recitations by night."

Siddham. Alternatively, according to the *Kālītantra*, if the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is accepted even in the *Paśukalpa* as consisting of two hundred thousand recitations divided between day and night, then that which is stated in that tantra applies: "One should not practice various conducts, nor should one wander here and there."

"One should not commit violence against living beings, especially against animals; O Goddess, apart from the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), violence is censured everywhere"—by such a statement, the prohibition of various practices would otherwise result in futility. For this very reason, in the *Karpūrādi-stava*, it is said: "The subduer [should recite] the mantra a hundred thousand times..."
Prajāpati, devoted to consuming sacrificial offerings by day and skilled in meditating upon the pair of your feet within his mother’s womb,
should at night— remaining naked and engaged in the pleasure of sexual union— properly recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

"Equal to the Destroyer of Smara upon the surface of the earth"— here, by the words "supreme" (*param*) and "by the diversion of sexual union" (*nidhuvanavinodena*), the preliminary observance (*puraścaraṇa*) for the night is stated to be specifically for those who are like heroes (*vīrakalpa*).
By "the diversion of sexual union," that is, by the bliss of the play of passion (*ratikrīḍānanda*), [the efficacy] of those mantras [is attained].
The procedure for sacrifice has been written in many ways by the author of the Tantrasāra himself; everything regarding it should be looked up there.
Now follows the hymn of one hundred names of Kālī.
Śiva said:
Karālavadanā, Kālī, Kāminī, Kamalā, Kalā, Kriyāvatī, Koṭarākṣī, Kāmākhyā, Kāmasundarī, Kapolā, Karālā, Kāśī, Kātyāyanī,
Kuhu, Kaṅkālī, Kāladamanī, Karuṇā, Kamalārccitā, and Kādambarī.
She who steals away time, she who is full of curiosity, she who is fond of causes; she who is dark, she who is dear to Kṛṣṇa, she who is worshipped by Kṛṣṇa, she who is beloved by Kṛṣṇa;
she who is unconquered by Kṛṣṇa, she who is dear to Kṛṣṇa, she who has the form of Kṛṣṇa; she who is Kālikā and she who is Kālarātri.
Born of noble lineage, a wise woman of good family; fond of the dharma of her clan, she is adorned with desirable qualities and the fruits of desired actions.

She is dear to her family, devoted to her kin, and honored by those of noble birth. Knowing her own lineage, she is like Lakṣmī, worthy of worship, and adorned as if by Mount Kailāsa. Born from the peak [of the mountain], she is Keśinī, the object of desire, the giver of desires, and skilled in the ways of love.
Karālāsyā, Kandarpakāminī, adorned with beauty; Kelambakā, delighting in sport, Kelinī, adorned with playfulness; the beloved of Keśava, Keśā, from Kaśmīra, worshipped by Keśava.

She is the Mistress of Desire, whose form is desire, adorned with the power of granting desires; she is the destroyer of Time, fond of tortoise-flesh, and worshipped by the Tortoise and others; she is the playful one, shaped like a crane, and she dwells upon the tortoise of the earth.

She who dwells in the midst of the filaments of the whorl, she who possesses a whorl, she who is honored by the whorl; she who loves the whorl, she who delights in the whorl, she who frequents the tortoise of the whorl; she who is devoted to the worship of the Virgin (Kumārikā), she who is served by the hosts of Virgins, she who loves the family tradition (kulācāra), she who is dear to the Kaulas.
She who frequents noble families, she who is of noble birth, she who knows the duties of her family, and she who crushes the fears of her family;
she who loves the dharma of desire, she who is desirable, she who is eternal, she whose very nature is desire, and she who can assume any form at will.

She who takes away desire, she who is worshipped in the temple of desire; she whose very nature is the abode of desire, she who is named Kāmā, adorned with desire; she who delights in ritual action and devotion, she who is desirable, she who is golden, and the giver of desires;
she whose garment is the *kola* flower, she who is the *kola*, she who is free from passion (*niṣkolā*), the ender of strife, Kauṣikī, Ketakī, and Kuntī.

Adorned with locks of hair and other ornaments—listen thus, O lady of beautiful limbs, to this secret which is all-auspicious. He who recites this with supreme devotion becomes Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
By the grace of these hundred names, what on earth cannot be accomplished? [Even] Brahmā and Viṣṇu...

O Goddess! By the recitation of this secret [text], Rudra, Vāsava, and the other inhabitants of heaven all became free from their feverish afflictions. O Sovereign of the Universe! This is the truth, the absolute truth regarding the three worlds; there is nothing else, there is nothing else beyond this.

O Mahāmāyā! In the midst of the Tantra, O Goddess Maheśvarī, Karālāsyā, who is clothed in the directions (Digambarā), may become pleased by the recitation of this hymn even without ritual action, O Devī, and even without devotion. I speak the truth, O Maheśānī; there is nothing higher than this.
Indeed,
neither in the physical eye-socket, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the palace of Kailāsa,
is there a science higher than this: the hymn and the armor.
O Mother of the World! In the three worlds, there is never anything [that cannot be attained] at any time—whether by night, during the day, or at twilight, O Sovereign of the Gods!
One should recite this supreme secret hymn with a spirit of devotion; by the grace of these hundred names, [all things are achieved].
The accomplishment of mantras arises for him who recites [this] on a Thursday or a Saturday during the fourteenth lunar day in the latter part of the night; he becomes a successful master,
