a knower of all scriptures, always of noble birth and pure, a knower of the Kula, and he...

O Goddess of the gods! O most beautiful one! He who knows the proper time and knows the Dharma obtains on the surface of the earth the fruit arising from ten million *purascarana* rites simply by reciting this secret [text]. This is the truth, O supreme beauty! O lady of noble limbs! What is not accomplished on earth by the recitation of this hymn?

One certainly becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*; of this there is no doubt. O Maheśvarī! One should recite the *Kālikā-stotra* according to one’s ability at night beneath a *vilva* tree, at the root of an *aśvattha* tree, or beneath an *aparājitā* plant. By reciting it one hundred times, the perfection of the mantra (*mantra-siddhi*) shall be attained.
It is certain.
Thus ends the hymn of the hundred names of Kālī in the eighth chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Now follows the hymn to Mahāvidyā.
Śiva said:

The path of Tāriṇī is difficult to attain; the state of Tāriṇī is difficult to attain. The meaning of the mantra and the consciousness of the mantra are difficult to attain; the practice with a corpse is difficult to attain. The practice in the cremation ground, the practice of the womb, the practice of Brahman, the practice of ritual action, and the practice of devotion [are likewise difficult to attain].
This is the means for liberation. O Goddess of gods! By the grace of this hymn, all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are attained.

Salutations to you, O Caṇḍikā, O fierce one, destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa! Salutations to you, O Kālikā, destroyer of the great fear of Time! O Śivā, protect us, O Mother of the Universe; be gracious.

O beloved of Hara! I bow to the Mother of the Universe, who protects the world, who agitates the world, and who ordains the creation of the world; who is formidable, vast, and terrible, adorned with a garland of skulls, worshipped by Hara, and the one to be propitiated by Hara.
I bow to the beloved of Hara; to Gaurī, the dear consort of the Guru, adorned with ornaments of a fair complexion. I bow to the beloved of Hari, the Great Māyā, who is worshipped by Brahmā.

I bow to Mahāmāyā, the perfected Siddheśvarī, who is accompanied by hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas; she who bestows the perfection of mantra and the perfection of the womb, who is adorned with the *liṅga*, and who is Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune.
I bow to Nīlasundarī, the fierce one who is composed of fierce energy, who acts with fierceness, and who is joined by fierce hosts;
she who is blue, dark as a blue rain-cloud, and beautiful in her azure hue;
she whose limbs are dark, fashioned from the dark, and adorned with a dark complexion.
I bow to Śrī Durgā, the sustainer of the world, who accomplishes all aims; the sovereign of the universe, most formidable, awe-inspiring, and of terrible roar;
the primordial one of the primal Guru, worshipped by the primal Lord.
I bow to the giver of wealth, who is full of food, the lotus-born Mistress of the Gods; I bow to the Mother of the Universe, the beloved of the Moon-crested Lord;
to Tripura, the beautiful young maiden, adorned by hosts of celestial women; to Śivadūtī.

To her who is worshipped by Śiva, meditated upon by Śiva, and eternal; to the beautiful one, the savior, adorned by all the hosts of Śiva; to Nārāyaṇī, who is honored by Viṣṇu, and the beloved of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
The eternal and the non-eternal, devoid of qualities yet possessing qualities, the object of meditation, the one worshipped who bestows all perfections; the Vidyā that grants success,
the Great Vidyā, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī.
I bow to the devotee of Maheśa, the consort of Maheśa, who is worshipped by Mahākāla;
to the sustainer of the world, the crusher of the demon Śumbha;
to her who loves blood, who is red in color, who crushes the red seed, Bhairavī, the one who pervades the worlds.

The Goddess with the flickering tongue, the sovereign of the gods, four-armed, ten-armed, and eighteen-armed, the auspicious one; the Mistress of Tripura, beloved of Viśvanātha, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Auspicious Śivā.
Aṭṭahāsā, Aṭṭahāsapriyā, Dhūmravināśinī, Kamalā, Chinnabhālā, Mātaṅgī, Surasundarī,
Ṣoḍaśī, Vijayā, Bhīmā, Dhūmā, and Bagalāmukhī.

"I bow to Jagattārā, the bestower of all accomplishments and the purifier of all vidyās and mantras, who is the essence for the attainment of mantra-siddhi. O Varārohā! Having thus recited this supreme hymn that brings about success, [one attains the fruit].
O Daughter of the Mountain! One truly attains liberation.
By reciting this hymn on a Tuesday, on the fourteenth day, on the new moon, on a Thursday, or at night on a Friday, one shall attain liberation within three fortnights.

O Śaṅkarī, indeed, the accomplishment of mantras (mantrasiddhi) shall come from the recitation of this hymn. On the fourteenth lunar day, during the latter part of the night, as well as on Saturdays and Tuesdays, one should recite the hymn at the onset of night;
by the mere recitation of the hymn, one shall attain the accomplishment of mantras.
O Caṇḍī! The serpent-lady [Bhujanginī] constantly remains awake through the recitation of this hymn, bestowing unsurpassed success in mantra.
Thus ends the hymn to Mahāvidyā in the eleventh chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.

Now, the armor (kavaca): O Goddess! Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), the uṣṇik meter is declared, and the application (viniyoga), O Queen of Gods, is for the constant accomplishment of the mantra. May Pārvatī protect my head;
may the beloved of the five-faced one (Śiva) protect [it]. May Caṇḍī protect my hair and face, and Bhāratī [protect] my speech.
Beloved of blood—may she protect the throat; may she protect the breast; and may she indeed protect the skull!
Kālī, with her terrifying face, the multiform one, who possesses a variegated bell.

May Durgā protect the base of my chest, and Tripurasundarī the base of my navel; may Tārā protect my entire being, every limb, and everything else; may Viśveśvarī protect the region of my back, and Maheśvarī protect my eyes.

May Kālikā protect the heart-lotus; may she who dwells in the sky protect the throat. May Nārāyaṇī protect my private parts, and likewise Meḍhreśvarī protect the penis. May Jayā protect the pair of feet, and may Caṇḍikā always protect me. May Pārvatī protect my life-force, and Mātaṅgī protect me.
May she protect me always! May Chinnā, Dhūmā, and Bhīmā protect me in times of fear, in water, and in the forest.
May Kaumārī, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhī protect my glory. May Bhadrakālī, who dwells in the cremation ground, protect me eternally; may Sarvāṇī protect me always in my belly.
May Sarvamaṅgalā, the Mother of the World who dwells on Kailāsa, protect me forever with victory.
May Śivapriyā, the daughter of the Mountain, protect my son. May Bagalā protect the three worlds, and may Bhuvanīśvarī protect the universe. And may Sarvanilayā protect every limb of mine eternally.
May Pārvatī protect me; may Cāmuṇḍā, the accomplisher of all aims, protect my pores; may Mahāvidyā, the eternally captivating one, protect my entire universe.

May Liṅga protect Liṅgeśvarī; may Maheśvarī protect [me] at the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha). May the beloved of Sadāśiva protect [me] always; may Sureśvarī protect [me] eternally. May Gaurī protect the region of my joints, and may Tripureśvarī indeed protect [me]. May Sureśvarī always protect [me], and may she protect [me] in the cremation ground and upon the corpse. [She protects me] during the retention of breath (Kumbhaka).
In the exhalation and inhalation within the temple of desire, may the Great Goddess Durgā, known as Kāmākhyā, the abode of desire,
protect me. May Ḍākinī, Kākinī, and likewise Śākinī, Hākinī, and Lākinī protect me eternally.
May Rākiṇī protect me always; may Jvālāmukhī always protect the middle of my face;
may Śivā protect me; may Tāriṇī protect me in prosperity; and may Bhavānī protect me in worldly existence.
May Trailokyamohinī protect all my limbs, and may she protect me in solitude; [may she protect me] in the royal court and during great calamities.
In battle, amidst the peril of enemies, may Bhairavamohinī protect me, the practitioner. May Śrīrājamohinī protect me at the royal gate during calamities.
May Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity, and Bālā protect my strength. [Protect] me always.
"May the consort of Śambhu, the destroyer of Tripura, protect me! Thus, O Goddess, has this secret been told, which is relevant for all times, bestowing enjoyment and liberation,
and granting happiness and all prosperity— [the merit of] whoever recites it upon rising in the morning.
He shall become a preeminent practitioner on earth.
On a Tuesday, the fourteenth lunar day, the new moon, or a Saturday; or on a Thursday, having worshipped the Guru, that best of practitioners who recites this goes to the abode of the Goddess.

Truly, truly, there is no doubt. O lady of excellent hips! If one recites this thus, being devoted with supreme faith, he shall attain the perfection of mantra before long; of this there is no doubt. It is the truth.
Having obtained the fruit of a hundred thousand-fold preliminary rites (*lakṣapūrvacaryā*), one shall go to Śivā;
having reached the royal path of Śiva, the living soul becomes Śiva himself.
By reciting this armor-verse (*kavaca*) and hymn (*stotra*), one certainly attains liberation. Having recited the armor-verse...

If one should worship with this hymn consisting of the ten sciences (*daśavidyā*), the accomplishment of the sciences (*vidyāsiddhi*) and the accomplishment of the mantras (*mantrasiddhi*) will surely occur; of this there is no doubt. The accomplishment of the donkey (*kharasiddhi*) and the accomplishment of the funeral pyre (*citāsiddhi*), which are difficult to obtain on the surface of the earth, become easily attainable without effort through betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*); of this there is no doubt.

"O Maheśānī! He who recites this with devotion at the onset of night, during the night, at the great hour (mahākāla), and at the end of the night, shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati. Thus ends the Mahāvidyā-kavaca in the eleventh chapter of the Muṇḍamālā-tantra.
The worship and other rites for Śmaśānakālikā and others should be sought in the *Tantrasāra*. Now follows the *Śmaśānakālikākavaca*.

The Goddess questioned Śaṅkara, the bestower of boons, the auspicious one, the omniscient Great Lord of all gods, as he sat upon the peak of Kailāsa: "O Blessed One! O Lord of all gods! O Master who grants enjoyment to the deities! O Mahādeva! Tell me, even if it be something to be kept secret, O Lord!"
Tell me that by which the destruction of enemies may occur, by which one's own protection is secured,
and by which one may indeed attain supreme and incomparable sovereignty.
Śrī Bhairava said: O Mahādevī, best among those who know all dharmas, I shall declare to you the wondrous armor (kavaca) of the Goddess,
which accomplishes all desires and, in particular, brings about the destruction of enemies.
It is a protector of men,
a pacifier of all misfortunes, a destroyer of malevolent spells,
a bestower of happiness and enjoyment, and a supreme means of subjugation against hosts of enemies.
They go to ruin, become afflicted by disease,
suffer, are feverish, and likewise fall away from their own desired goals. Of this Śrī-Kālikā-kavaca, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), and Śrī-Kālikā is the deity (devatā).

p. 750) Application for the destruction of hosts of enemies: Oṃ! One should meditate upon Kālī, the Great Māyā, three-eyed and multiformed, four-armed, with a flickering tongue and a face like the full moon, resembling the petals of a blue lotus.
She who tears apart hosts of enemies; bearing a human skull, a sword, a lotus, and likewise a boon-granting [mudrā]; with a blood-red face, possessing a terrifying form with rows of fangs;
ever intent on loud, boisterous laughter, and always naked; seated upon a corpse.

Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads—the auspicious Goddess Kālikā, endowed with a terrible form, the bestower of all desires, and praised by all—one should then recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*): "Oṃ! May the Goddess, who is rich in a formidable form, the bestower of all desires, and auspicious, who is praised everywhere—may she destroy my enemies. Hrīṃ."
She whose nature is *hrīṃ*, and likewise she whose nature is *hrāṃ hrāṃ huṃ*;

she whose nature is *hīṃ hāṃ kṣauṃ kṣauṃ*—may she always subdue my enemies. The Goddess whose nature is *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ*, who liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence; she whose nature is *hasakalahrīṃ*.
May she always slay our enemies—she by whom the Daitya Śumbha and the great Asura Niśumbha were slain. For the destruction of adversaries, I bow to that Kālikā, the beloved of Śaṅkara.
Brāhmī, Śaivī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhikā, Kaumāryā, and Aindrī...
May Cāmuṇḍā devour my enemies! May Sureśvarī, of terrible form and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, whose limbs are encircled by garlands of skulls, protect me always on all sides. Hrīṃ Hrīṃ.
O Kālikā! O Ghoradaṃṣṭrā! O you who are fond of blood! O you whose face is filled with the beautiful glow of blood! O you whose breasts are covered in blood!
Devour, devour my enemies, [named] so-and-so; cut them to pieces, cut them to pieces; destroy them!
Harm! Kill! Kill! Break! Break! Cut! Cut! Exterminate! Exterminate! Drive away! Drive away! Svāhā! Vāṃ vīṃ, I offer my enemy to Kālikā; Svāhā! Oṃ, victory! Victory! Kiri kiri! Kiṭi kiṭi! Kaṭṭa kaṭṭa!
Crush, crush! Delude, delude! Seize, seize my such-and-such enemies! Destroy, destroy! Devour, devour! Rend, rend! O Yātudhānī! O Cāmuṇḍā!
Make all people—the king, the king’s men, and the women—subject to my will; make them so! Expand!

"Grant, grant me grain, wealth, horses, elephants, jewels, divine women, sons, and royal splendor; bestow, bestow them! KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢŪṂ KṢAIṂ KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ SVĀHĀ! Thus has this divine armor (*kavaca*) been described.

Those who always recite this which was [taught] by Śambhu in the past, their enemies certainly perish; their foes go to destruction and indeed become afflicted by disease. His enemies shall forever be destitute of wealth and destitute of sons. Through a thousand recitations, the perfection of the armor-mantra (kavaca) is attained.
Then [the rite] shall succeed; for that indeed was spoken by Śaṅkara.

Having taken charcoal from a cremation ground and having carefully reduced it to powder, one should grind it with water from the feet of a low-caste person and draw the enemies upon the ground with an iron stylus.
Likewise, having placed the hand upon the heart of those who are lowly in form or supreme in head,
the knower of mantras should himself recite the armor-mantra and establish the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the enemy with the mantra.
By the stroke of a weapon, the enemy shall be slain and go to the abode of Yama;
by the heat of glowing embers, he becomes afflicted with fever;
or by rubbing with the left foot, he certainly becomes impoverished—this brings about the destruction of the foe.

This armor-mantra (*kavaca*) has been proclaimed as a means of subjugation, bestowing supreme sovereignty and increasing one's sons, grandsons, and progeny. By reciting it at dawn, especially during the time of worship,
and likewise in the evening, all perfections (*siddhi*) will certainly be attained.
The enemy undergoes eradication and shall be expelled from his country; thereafter, he becomes a servant—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. O Goddess who destroys enemies!
O Auspicious One who bestows all prosperity! O Goddess praised by all the gods! O Kālikā, [I worship] you.
I pay homage.
Thus ends the *Śmaśānakālikā-kavaca*, known as the "Remover of Enemies," from the *Rudrajāmala*.
Since even the practice of the Right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra) pertains to the Śākta domain, the praise of the Śākta is now stated.
Now, the praise of the Śakti, from the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (pātāla), there is no devotee dearer than the Śākta. Among the Sauras, the Gāṇapatyas, and likewise the Vaiṣṇavas, the Śāktas are at the very end—
gradually, step by step, O Dear One!

Listen, O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips! There is no person higher than a Śākta. Even Śaṅkara is himself a Śākta, directly partaking of the nature of the Supreme Brahman—by whom Kālī, Tārā, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, Ṣoḍaśī, Mātaṅgī, and Chinnā have been propitiated.

O Maheśānī! He who has propitiated Bagalāmukhī is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. O Maheśānī! This supreme state of the Śaktas is to be kept most secret. He who knows it within this world is Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
He who constantly worships with joy Him whose lotus feet are adored by Brahmā and the other gods, indeed reaches the very temple of liberation in no long time. (From the Third Chapter)

By worshipping the pair of Pārvatī’s feet, one becomes her servant; would heaven, enjoyment, and liberation not then belong to the Śāktas? Indeed, those lowest of men who utter insults against the Śāktas, they shall surely drink their blood.
The hosts of Bhairavīs and the Bhairavas themselves always harm the ignorant;
they harm the Śāktas, roar, and revile them as great talkers. O Goddess of gods! O Beloved of Hara! She cuts off their heads. Among the Śāktas, there is none superior in heaven.

In the mortal realm and in the netherworld (rasātala), Śaṅkara is to be known as Śākta—the three-eyed one with the moon upon his crest—who, having himself become the bearer of the Gaṅgā, shall roam upon the circle of the earth. (From the Fourth Chapter)
Śiva’s words to the Goddess: "Those beings who are portions of me are Śaivas;
there is no doubt in this. And those who are portions of you are Śāktas; this is indeed the truth, O Daughter of the Mountain!
At the end of many thousands of years, the Śaivas shall become devoted to Śakti, and the Śāktas likewise."

O Goddess Śaṅkarā! Whether they be born in the lineage of Cāṇḍālas, Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, Kṣatriyas, or those originating from Vaiśyas—these devotees of Śakti, O Mother of the World, are never merely human beings; in this world, they behold only [the divine].
With the fleshly eye; likewise, also in the seventh chapter.
Śiva said:

Japa and worship should be performed by means of the power of the Vāmamārga by those of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes. O Goddess, those Brāhmaṇas who are Śākta are considered Kṣatriyas, and the Vaiśyas... [are likewise considered so].

"O Goddess! All Brāhmaṇas are Śūdras, and Śūdras are Brāhmaṇas; O Caṇḍī! Brāhmaṇas are Śaṅkaras, three-eyed, and moon-crested. (From the *Nirvāṇatantra*, third chapter). "All twice-born ones are indeed Śākta; they are neither Śaiva nor Vaiṣṇava."

"Because they worship the Goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable. In the second chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*, after the worship of Śakti, there is a prohibition against other forms of worship as follows:
Concerning Tripurā: "Having performed the worship of her, one should not perform the worship of another; by remembering another, O Goddess, a yoginī incurs a curse. Thus ends the praise of the Śakti.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Mahāvidyā and Others," in the fifth section on Devotion within the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
[This concludes] what was previously written beginning with the words, "One who is intent on the worship of the Kumārīs," and so forth.

Now, at this opportune moment, I shall describe that which was desired according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the Kumārī. Next, the worship of the Kumārī. Regarding that, the definition of the Kumārī is found in the sixth chapter of the Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa.

One year old she is Sandhyā, and two years old she is Sarasvatī; three years old she is the triple-formed (Tridhāmūrti), and four years old she is Kālikā; five years old she is Subhagā, while six years old she becomes Umā.
With seven [years] she is Mālinī; Kubjikā herself is eight years old; with nine she is Kālasaṃdarbhā; with ten, Aparājitā; at eleven, Rudrāṇī;
at twelve, Bhairavī; and at thirteen, Mahālakṣmī. With fourteen...
The Mistress of the Pīṭha is Kṣetrajñā; she is considered to be with fifteen [deities] in the fifteenth [tithi], and Ambikā in the sixteenth.

Having thus gathered them in sequence until the Puṣpa [tithi] arises, one should worship from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the full moon (pūrṇā), according to the divisions of the waxing phase. All that beginning with "one year" and so forth...

In the *Vṛhannīlatantra* as well, there is a variation in both reading and name: "Umā shall be only six years old; the Mistress (nāyikā) is remembered as fourteen; at sixteen she is considered a *carcakā*. However, in the seventh chapter of the *Kubjikātantra*, a specific distinction is stated as follows: "Five years..."

O Goddess! beginning from six years up until she is twelve years old, that maiden shall be a manifestor of her own true form. And likewise, beginning from six years up until she is nine years old, for that duration...

O Maheśānī! For the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of the practitioner, one should recognize her as being born of a noble family (kulajā) from the age of eight until she reaches thirteen years; therein one should perform worship.

From ten years of age until she is sixteen, one should recognize her as a young woman and contemplate her as a deity. Indeed, he who gives food, clothing, and likewise water to such a maiden [gains great merit].

O Goddess! One who gives food equal to Mount Meru and water like the ocean, as well as garments for a thousand crores of years, is honored in the world of Śiva. Indeed, he who gives articles of worship here to a maiden—his deity, being satisfied, regards him as her own son. (From the Viśvasāra)

But, O fair-faced one, when she is eight years old, she becomes Gaurī; at nine years, she is Rohiṇī; and at ten years, she is Kanyakā. Beyond that, she is Mahāmāyā, and from that point on, she is indeed menstruating. This continues from the commencement of the twelfth year until the twentieth year.
She is called Sukumārā, endowed with all the tantras;
she exists in the form of light within the substances of wood, stone, and minerals, O Goddess of Gods, within all living beings.
What more need be said? Where Mahāmāyā is not present, there is nothing at all.
"It exists," thus it has been said.
The fruit of that worship is [described] in the seventeenth chapter of the first section of the Yoginītantra.

"O beautiful one, I am not able to describe the fruit of worshipping a maiden, even with thousands of millions of tongues or hundreds of millions of mouths. Therefore, one should worship that young girl, regardless of her birth; there is no distinction of caste."
O Śivā! In the worship of a maiden, one must act [without discrimination]; O Maheśānī! due to distinctions of caste, one does not escape hell.
A mantra-practitioner intent on doubt will certainly become a sinner; [he must act] with the perception that she is the Goddess herself.

Therefore, one who possesses great devotion should worship her; for a young maiden is indeed the embodiment of all vidyās—of this there is no doubt. O Goddess! O Beloved! if by the power of fortune a practitioner obtains a young maiden born of a family of courtesans, he should strive to secure her even at the cost of his entire wealth.
One should joyfully worship her with gold, silver, and other offerings;
then great accomplishment arises for him, of this there is no doubt.

The place for the worship of the Kumārī and its fruit are also in that very same location. "That region where the Kumārī is worshipped becomes a purifier of the earth; it shall become most meritorious for five *krośas* in every direction. This is stated in the Jāmalatantra in that very same context. [This applies] on all great festival days (*mahāparvan*), and especially so.

Regarding the *pavitraka* [thread]: O Goddess of gods, on the Mahānavamī day, one should worship the *kumārī* (virgin). From that point up to the age of sixteen, she is designated as a *yuvatī* (young woman). In her, there arises the manifestation of *bhāva*; that *bhāva* is considered supreme. She must be protected.

One should carefully contemplate those [lines] as being unbroken. Having performed a great worship and other rites with garments, ornaments, and food, even one of meager fortune who worships thus obtains victory and auspiciousness. Furthermore, by speaking of this to others, there is a great fruit of purpose.

Whoever worships according to the prescribed rite, abiding in the states of the divine, the hero, and the animal, shall attain great bliss within the threefold state—the excellent fruit of divine action. Thus it is said.

Having recited [the mantra] and worshipped a maiden who is endowed with the excellence of her entire lineage, born of various castes, or even originating from various regions, and possessed of both virtues and defects, from the second year onwards until she reaches the eighth year of age; having thus recited and worshipped the maiden—

One who abides in a divine state shall directly obtain the fruit of the tantras and mantras from the worship of a beautiful maiden, through the feeding of maidens and other such acts; there is no doubt that she bestows the fruits of one, two, three, or more seeds. Having given flowers and fruit to them...

Having likewise offered unguents and the like, as well as food offerings dear to children, being permeated by that state of mind and acting with the playful behavior of a child, one should smear his own limbs with that clay.

Endowed with the curiosity for play and conversation regarding what is most dear, one should perform that which is truly pleasing there; thus one becomes a master of supernatural powers (*siddhīśvara*). A maiden is all prosperity; a maiden is the supreme austerity. [One should perform] the fire-oblation (*homa*)...

O Lord, without the worship of the Kumārī, the best of practitioners does not obtain the respective fruits of those actions— be they mantra-recitation, daily rites, the excellent Kaulika rituals, or the great dharma of various fruits. O Hero, the fruit obtained through the Kumārī is ten million times greater.
One may obtain [merit] through worship.

If a family preceptor gives a handful of flowers full to the brim to a maiden, that flower becomes like the gold of ten million Mount Merus; the great merit born of that gift is attained in a mere instant.

One should honor her; by feeding a young maiden, the three worlds are fed. (From the *Kālītantra*, Chapter Eleven): One should perform the worship of the young maiden for the attainment of the fruits of all ritual actions.

In the seventh chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala, having stated: "Now I shall proclaim the worship of the Kumārī, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain," [it continues]: "The place of worship is either a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) or a temple; likewise, a dancer’s daughter or a low-caste girl."
A Kāpālika girl, the daughter of a washerman, likewise the daughter of a barber, the daughter of a cowherd,
the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, the daughter of a Śūdra, and likewise the daughter of a physician.
Having diligently brought together a merchant’s daughter, or even a Caṇḍāla girl, or the daughter of a circle of friends, regardless of which hermitage they reside in, one should worship them.

He who, devoted to meditation on the Self with supreme bliss, performs my worship every day with pure devotion—for him, the worship of virgins and the offering of food to the Sun shall surely come to pass. (p. 756)
The radiant form of both the moon and the fire shines within all things;
through worshipping it, conversing with it, and even eating what is auspicious for it, my own pleasure arises directly. I am the goddess dwelling in secret, the beloved of the god Bālabhairava.
And of Vaṭuka,
my son, who is honored by all the worlds and possesses great majesty— O maiden worshipped by the gods, perform his worship with various ritual substances; the maiden is the deity.

She is proclaimed as the Sovereign of the Universe in every respect. Having brought her for the worship of all the world, the lords of the gods worship the Great Goddess who dwells in Guptabhava. Always filled with a desire for food, she is honored, contented, and smiling; she does not cry in vain.

The Goddess Kumārī is the leader of the gods; she, whose very nature is Sarasvatī, is worshipped by all leaders—by devotees of Śiva, devotees of Viṣṇu, as well as by those who worship other deities. Worshipped by all the worlds, she is necessarily worshipped by the wise. Through her worship, one obtains [the fruits].

Through worship one obtains worship; through worship one attains prosperity; through worship one acquires wealth; through worship one gains the earth. Through worship one attains Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and great luster.
The great sciences become propitious and all the gods [favor him]; of this there is no doubt.
Kālabhairava, Brahmā, Indra, the Brāhmaṇas who know Brahman, the Rudras, the hosts of gods, the Vaiṣṇavas in the form of Brahmā,
the incarnations, those with two arms, the Vaiṣṇavas with four arms, and others.

The guardians of the quarters and the gods, as well as the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, all the Dānavas devoted to various sciences and full of guile, and whoever else exists in the state of affliction— all these are undoubtedly pleased; if I am indeed pure in form, what need is there to speak of other worlds?

Having performed the worship of the Kumārī, one shall bring the three worlds under control; great peace shall swiftly arise, bestowing the fruit of all merit. [From the] Vṛhannīlatantra: O Mistress of the Kula! Great fears, famines, portents, bad dreams, and untimely death—[these are overcome].

Furthermore, whatever else causes suffering to men, those [afflictions] indeed do not prevail simply through the worship of the Kumārī. O Goddess of Gods! One should always worship her in due order according to the prescribed rite; [thus she] destroys all obstacles.
When worshipped, they dispel fear from even most formidable enemies;

the planets, diseases, spirits, vetālas, and serpents go to their destruction. Thus it is stated in the Rudrajāmala: "By the utterance of those respective mantras, one obtains ten thousand merits in an instant through the mantra."

Having performed the *puṭita* [recitation] and having recited it, one shall become a master of accomplishments (*siddhiśvara*). O beautiful god! Whatever method I declare with reference to a specific purpose, that very task must be carried out; do not allow your intellect to waver. Listen accordingly.
O Lord! For the sake of my lineage, [grant] the mantra for the worship of the Kumārī;
it is the great mantra of the Mahāvidyā, a mantra of accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.
By the power of this mantra, the wise one shall become liberated while living (jīvanmukta), and at the end, he attains the state of the Goddess.
Truly, O Ānandabhairava! A mortal shall certainly attain the abundance of happiness in this world and the grace of Madhumatī; grant him rest, O Śaṅkara! [By means of] Vāgbhava.

The agitation of the body occurs through the Māyā-bīja; the eightfold qualities [are attained] through the Śrī-bīja. Through the Śrī-bīja there is the attainment of prosperity, and through the Māyā-bīja the destruction of enemies. By means of the Bhairava-bīja, one attains the power of moving through the air (khecaratva) along with the gods and others.
O Lord! I am indeed the Virgin (Kumārikā), and you are indeed the Youth (Kumāra).

One should worship her either one hundred and eight times, or even just once. When worshipped, she returns the worship; when disregarded, she brings about ruin. The maiden is the Yoginī herself; the maiden is the supreme deity. Asuras, wicked nāgas, and whatever malevolent planets there may be—
The spirits, vetālas, gandharvas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas, and rākṣasas; all other deities whatsoever, and the terrifying ones of the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar;
the earth and all else, the entire cosmic egg with its moving and unmoving beings; and Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— these are pleased, and all are pleased with him who worships a maiden according to the prescribed rite,
O Bhairava, and feeds a young girl (kumārī) with water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth.
Likewise, having worshipped with devotion incense, saffron, and auspicious sandalwood, one should offer them to the young maidens.
The sequence for the worship of the maiden (kumārīpūjākrama) is as follows: likewise.
Having brought forward a beautiful maiden, a virgin who is an excellent consort,

adorned with jewel ornaments and graced by conch-shell bangles, garments, and other finery, one should, O Lord, cause her to offer water with the *vāgbhava* mantra while uttering her name, always meditating upon her with the thought that she is the Goddess herself.

The supreme practitioner should perform worship; O Lord, he should offer water for the feet using the Māyā-bīja along with the deity's name. He should offer the arghya with the Lakṣmī-bīja and sandalwood paste with the Kūrca-bīja. The wise one should cause flowers to be offered to Kumārī using the Māyā-bīja.

Having offered incense and lamps of great excellence with the Sadāśiva mantra, one should worship the Lord of Devas with the Ṣaḍaṅga mantra. O Mahādeva, you who bear the form of bliss, listen to that method on page 758: [it is] composed of great splendor.
Having visualized a radiant heart with the right hands, one should recite [the mantra] after bowing;

hear that mantra, O Śaṅkara! First, having uttered Vāgbhava, then Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Kūrcaka; thereafter, one should utter the seed-syllable of the Preta (the letter *Ra*) together with the Visarga, the Moon (the Bindu), and the Kīlaka.

Having uttered the word *kula*, one should then say *kumārike*. Having pronounced *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, one should then contemplate it upon the head. Having uttered the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which is white in color and consists of all things, one should install it. [One should place] the letter *ha*, beginning with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], and the letter *va*, which is of the nature of the *vāgbhava*.

The practitioner should place the mantra— consisting of *māyā* (hrīṃ), *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ), and *vāgbhava* (aiṃ), ending with *dviṭha* (svā) and bounded by the wife of fire (svāhā)— upon his head. Having visualized [the deity] of black complexion, with a luster like a mass of blue collyrium, in the middle of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the reciter of mantras should perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
For the sake of attaining the *siddhi* of the Kumārī-kula: first, having extracted the *praṇava*, at its end [place] Viṣṇusundarī;

having extracted the word *śikhāyai*, one should then utter *vaṣaṭ*. Then, in the midst of the armor (*kavaca*), having meditated upon the beautiful one—powerful, of great splendor, and resembling the color of the first dawn.
Having uttered the *vāgbhava* syllable, one should then speak the word *kula*. After that, the word *vāgīśvarī*, and then say *kavacāya*.
Then there is the *tāraka-brahma* mantra, which constitutes the network of the armor-assignment (*kavaca-nyāsa*). Then, having meditated upon the three eyes...

The great seed-syllable of great radiance, red in color, adorned by circles of *javā* flowers numbering in the millions upon millions; it shines brilliantly within the sun whose splendor is earned through ten million merits.
Having first uttered the *vāgbhava* syllable, one should then utter the word "Kuleśvarī" followed by "to the three eyes."

At the end of the word "śabda," one should utter "vauṣaṭ" for the mantra of the eye. Then, with the mantra of the practitioner, one should likewise perform two claps upon the palm of the left hand using the middle and index fingers.
That mantra possesses a radiance equal to a mass of light from ten million fierce suns.

Having diligently extracted the syllable *māyā* (the seed-syllable of illusion), which arises from the great space (*mahākāśa*), is a sound that causes intense affliction, and is the word for the weapon (*astrāya*); and having extracted the final syllable at the end of *phaṭ*, the Great Mantra is proclaimed. Then, of her...
Having meditated upon Kuṇḍavilā, the practitioner of mantra, accompanied by his retinue,
should worship with effort using a stream of nectar of splendor; he should satisfy and worship Bhairava and Bālabhairava with devotion.

Having worshipped the deities and their retinues in due order, one should then utter the *Vāgbhava* syllable for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*) through speech. Having first uttered the preceding word, the phrase "to the face, salutation" (*vaktrāya namaḥ*) is proclaimed. Then, having again uttered the *Vāgbhava* syllable, one should extract the word "for victory" (*jayāya*).
Having raised the face in the north, [one should utter] the word "namaḥ" ending in the dative case; then,
having carefully recited the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Śrī,
[the mantra] "kubjike paścimānte ca vaktrāya namaḥ" is uttered.
Then, having uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one should utter the word "Kālike.
At the end of the word "śabda," the mantra "dakṣavaktrāya namaḥ" is proclaimed.
O Lord, O Kuleśvara! Having uttered these syllables of this mantra and having performed worship...
One should worship Bhāskara in due order; one should also worship Caṇḍa, the guardian deity of the directions, as well as Sandhyā and the others.
[One should worship] Vīrabhadra, Mahākanyā, and Kaulinī who moves within the Kula—the eighteen-armed goddess.
One should worship Kālī Caṇḍadurgā, having brought offerings such as food oblations (naivedya) and the like,
adorned with various forms of devotion: milk thickened with ghee, curds, cooked rice, ripe fruits, and whatever else is appropriate for the season, always mixed with honey.

The five principles (pañcatattva) and the substances of the family (kuladravya), which increase one's own auspiciousness; various substances for the food offering (naivedya) prepared according to the prescriptions of their respective tantras; and having thus offered these, adorned with various fragrances, to the young maidens (kumāris).
The highly wise one, having brought cool water, should offer it to them; then,
having recited the beneficial great mantra— which is extremely difficult for a maiden to obtain— the eloquent one becomes a master of spiritual powers (siddhīśvara) together with the root-mantra.
Having offered [the offerings], one should oneself perform the retention of the vital breaths (prāṇavāyu),
while prostrating with the eight limbs and the like, reciting hymns, and bowing down.
The mantra of salutation is also found in that very place: "I bow to the beloved of the Kula, who bestows supreme fortune;
she whose skill in passion is like that of Kumāra, who delights in all spiritual accomplishments, and who wears a garland of coral beads."
"Clad in garments of silver-colored silk, adorned with ornaments of incomparable gold—O maiden whose voice is the world, I worship you. With this mantra, having bowed down, one should worship Tāriṇī.
Having fully worshipped Śiva and Gaṇeśa, the best of practitioners should prostrate; [then he should offer] a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having duly given gifts to the maidens in sequence, he himself should marry off his daughter;
thus the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed. Furthermore, whoever completes the gift of a daughter during an auspicious time [attains great merit].

The fruit of enjoyment and liberation, good fortune, and all prosperity belong to him; the three-eyed Lord Hara dwells eternally in his world. That mortal who gives a daughter [in marriage] obtains the fruit of thousands of crores of holy places and hundreds of horse-sacrifices.

One should cause [the girl] to be married; for as many grains of sand as there are in the ocean, for that many thousands of years, having uplifted each individual family, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. Therefore, the wise person [should act] for the pleasure and satisfaction of their chosen deity.
O Bhairava! Having performed the gift of a maiden, the practitioner attains liberation.
By perceiving each subsequent maiden through that same mental disposition, and visualizing the nature of Śiva in the maiden to be given away, he should meditate upon Śiva in his full form.
The foremost of practitioners should choose as his deity Vaṭukeśa Mahādeva, who is beautiful in every limb, composed of splendor, lovely with fame, and possessing the form of Kālabhairava.

She has the form of a young girl, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, of excellent complexion, her limbs adorned with various ornaments; she is the illuminator of the auspicious vidyā, possessed of a lovely smile, her heart full of great bliss, the auspicious bestower of well-being.

Having meditated upon her whose face resembles the full moon within a twelve-petaled lotus, one should bring forth the gift and cause it to be given with the respective mantra. Thus is the fruit of the sequence for the gift of a maiden.

Now, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Kumārī-mantra. In the eighth chapter: "Now I shall describe the recitation and fire-offering (*japahoma*) of the Great Goddess Kumārī. Having performed a recitation of one hundred thousand counts of either the *māyā* mantra, or the *vāgbhava* mantra, or even the *kālī* seed-syllable, O Lord!"

It consists of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), encased by Sadāśiva and adorned with the *bindu* and the moon; or else, O Lord of the Thirty-three Gods, it may be encased by the *praṇava*. Having recited it one hundred thousand times in due order, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (*siddhi*). One should recite that mantra, O Lord of the Gods!

According to the prescribed rite of one hundred thousand repetitions, one should perform a fire-oblation with bilva leaves smeared with ghee, or else with white flowers or kunda flowers, for the sake of great fruit— one-tenth of that number.
In this manner, one should perform the oblation in sequence with *karavīra* flowers—

either smeared with clarified butter, or used alone, or mixed with sandalwood and agallochum. During the daytime, one should subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and at night, one should be devoted to worship.

One should worship one's own deity with all the substances of the *kula*; there, assuming the form of supreme bliss, one should perform recitation (*japa*) eleven times. At the conclusion of the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations (*homa*) combined with the substances mentioned by me.

Then, having repeatedly purified the vital air (*vāyu*) which is the essence of the life-force (*prāṇa*), and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should joyfully prostrate with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*). O Lord! If, at the time of prostration, one recites this hymn of the armor (*kavaca*), [the following occurs].

Likewise, one should cause the young maidens to recite the great hymn of one's own deity, as well as the *pīṭha-aṅga* and the *kavaca*. Then, O God, having recited the thousand names of the maidens along with the eight [additional names], I— [The text continues: ...having recited [them].

One attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Lord! If one is unable to do that, one who desires perfection should recite the auspicious Thousand Names of one’s own Goddess one hundred and eight times; of this there is no doubt.

O Divine Lord! Listen to their hymn of praise, which brings auspiciousness everywhere. By reciting it, the best of practitioners attains success spontaneously. Having placed all of them before him—cool as millions of jewels—the wise, self-controlled man, with a concentrated mind, should then recite this hymn.

Whether one is devoted to the great divine conduct or possesses a preponderance of heroic sentiment, one should recite [the mantra] in this sequence, being entirely intent on a state of devotion. When offered with a bath of devotion and faith, the Great Vidyā becomes a great service; thus one becomes a possessor of great knowledge.
One will swiftly attain the fulfillment of one's desires.

Now follows the ritual procedure for the worship of the Kumārī (the Virgin Goddess). In this context, a girl who has not yet reached puberty from the age of one up to sixteen years is designated as a *kumārī*. According to her age, the names are as follows: Sandhyā (1), Sarasvatī (2), Tridhā (3).
Mūrti (3), Kālikā (4), Subhagā (5), Umā (6), Mālinī (7), Kubjikā (8), Kālasaṃdarbhā (9), Aparājitā (10), Rudrāṇī (11), Bhairavī (12).
Mahālakṣmī (13); Pīṭhanāyikā (14); Kṣetrajñā (15); Ambikā (16).

These are to be worshipped according to the sequence of increase from the first lunar day (pratipad) to the fifteenth (pañcadaśī). A virgin of any caste whatsoever is highly recommended; specifically, the daughter of an actress, the daughter of a Kāpālika, or the daughter of a washerman.

The daughter of a barber, the daughter of a cowherd, the daughter of a Brahmin, the daughter of a Shudra, the daughter of a physician, the daughter of a merchant, the daughter of a Chandala, and the daughter of one's circle of friends—
having seated such a maiden upon the seat, one should meditate upon her as having the form of a young girl.
The beautiful one, the most excellent of complexion, whose limbs are adorned with various ornaments,
who illuminates the auspicious vidyā, possessing a lovely smile and a heart of great bliss, the auspicious bestower of well-being.

Having meditated thus, having placed a flower upon one's own head, and having worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), one should meditate again, place [the flower] on the body of the *kumārī*, and say: "This is the seat; *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ hsauḥ*, obeisance to Sandhyā Kumārī. Thus.

Having recited the previous seed-syllables, one should worship with the sixteen services beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and so forth, using the names in the dative case in their proper sequence, such as "Obeisance to Sarasvatī Kumārī" (*sarasvatyai kumāryai namaḥ*). This water [is offered] with: *aiṃ saṃdhyāyai namaḥ*.
This is the water for the feet: *hrīṃ*, obeisance to Sandhyā. Likewise the ornaments. Likewise the fragrance:
*huṃ*, obeisance to Sandhyā. These flowers: *hrīṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* to Sandhyā. This incense: *hsauḥ*, obeisance to Sandhyā. Likewise the lamp. This food offering: *aiṃ*.

*Hrīḥ śrīḥ huḥ hauḥ*, I offer this to Sandhyā. Conch-shells, garlands, glowing saffron, and other such items should be offered with this mantra ending in *namaḥ*. In all cases, after the name ending in the dative case, the qualifier "to the Virgin" (*kumāryai*) must be added. Then:

The six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅgapūjā*) and its sequence: Having grasped the heart of the *kumārī* with the right hand and visualized her as consisting of great splendor and white in color, [one recites]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huḥ hsauḥ kulakumārike hṛdayāya namaḥ*. The head is white in color and consists of all things.
Having meditated upon *vaiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ*, [one says] *śirase svāhā*.

Having meditated upon the crest (*śikhā*) possessing the luster of a mass of blue collyrium, [one says] *oṃ śrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. Having meditated upon the armor (*kavaca*), which resembles the first rays of dawn and is full of splendor, [one says] *aiṃ kulavāgīśvari*.

*Huṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*). Then, having visualized the three eyes—which consist of all seed-syllables (*bīja*), possess great luster, are red in color, and are as brilliant as tens of millions upon tens of millions of *javā* flowers—one recites: *Aiṃ kuleśvari netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*. With *Hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*, [one should touch] the palm of the left hand.

One should strike two claps with the index and middle fingers. Then, having visualized Bālabhairava together with his retinue within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of that [lineage], one should worship him with these scents and flowers, saying:
*Oṃ, obeisance to Bālabhairava together with his retinue*. These scents and flowers: *Aiṃ*.
Salutation to Siddhajayā, the eastern face. Likewise, salutation to Jayā, the northern face. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Kubjikā, the western face. Aiṃ, salutation to Kālikā, the southern face.
Oṃ, salutation to Bhāskara and to each of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and to Vīrabhadrā.
One should worship Mahākanyā, Kaulinī, Kalanāmīnī, Aṣṭādaśabhujā, Kālī, and Caṇḍadurgā with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*. Then,
having recited the root mantra of Kumārī or one's own personal mantra according to one's capacity, [one should proceed].
Having performed *prāṇāyāma*, offered the recitation (*japa*), and recited the hymns, armor-verses (*kavaca*), and so forth,
one should prostrate with either eight or five limbs and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Now follows the Hymn to the Virgin (*kumārīstotra*).
Bhairavī said:

The goddesses beginning with Devendra [worship] the one who possesses the rays of ten million moons, the Vidyā residing in Vārāṇasī, the beloved of Vāgbhava, the three-eyed one who moves through subtle actions.

For the sake of prosperity, they worship the maiden Kumārī— the best of goddesses, the mother of the three worlds, who dwells in the root-lotus, whose face is like the moon, and who cuts through fierce agitation.
One should meditate upon the goddess Śivā, who is to be contemplated by hosts of gods, by Śiva, Indra, and ascetics seeking liberation;
she who is the twilight (sandhyā) from which eternal qualities arise, from whom the best of the twice-born and the rising sun emerge,
who possesses beautiful limbs, whose luster is white, who is the Supreme Sovereign, the bringer of auspiciousness, the benevolent one with a broad countenance.
I worship Gāyatrī, the mother of the Gaṇas, the movement of the day, Kṛṣṇā, and Vṛddhā. || 2 ||
I eternally [worship] the youthful one, adored by children, endowed with virtues, the bestower of liberation to the learned,
the nurse (Dhātrī), the pure Sarasvatī, the most excellent of goddesses, the speaker of speech (Vāgvādinī), Caṇḍikā,
the beloved of Śiva in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], the doer of what is dear, and the giver of the knowledge of Vedānta.
For the sake of liberation, I worship her whose form is consciousness, appearing in the body of Yoga. || 3 ||

I bow to the maiden worshipped by the gods in a palace fashioned from a multitude of various jewels, who dwells in the Nandana grove as the perfected seed within the mind; O Goddess, bestow the true meaning upon this body of mine which is otherwise devoid of purpose, having cast aside the mere form of a young girl.
My Mother and Kumārikā are threefold, and she is composed of radiant energy.

I am but a child who has always taken refuge at the lotus feet of Vaṭukeśvara; having abandoned [all else], I worship her who is terrifying with the venom of Hālāhala, who carries the sole seed that causes the blossoming of the path of the Kula, who is formidable with the fragrance of raw flesh, and who bestows desires beyond the reach of ordinary longing.
O Valakumārikā! I worship you upon a white lotus on the head. || 5 ||

I ever worship in the lotus of my heart, upon its solar petals, the auspicious Kālikā— the goddess of time— who is composed of splendor, who delights in the sun, who possesses the power of the *balākini*, who removes the heat of the great sins of the Kali age, who dwells in radiance, who moves with the sun upon the earth, who dispels fear, and who is the very embodiment of light; I praise that maiden, the true knowledge of the crescent moon, who is manifest and bestows spiritual perfection.
I bow to you, the stainless one, the primordial sovereign of forms.
I salute the eternal Umā, the Mother, the beloved of the Śrīkula, who possesses noble lineage, who belongs to the Kaula tradition,
who delights in various yogic sports, the celestial maiden, the perpetual one endowed with austerity,
who is clothed in the specific meanings of Vedānta and established in the particularities of speech.
O Kālapriyā, I [worship] you, the daughter of the king of mountains. || 7 ||
He took as his wife Bhogavatī, who was Kaumārī and Kulamālinī, who instills the fire of agitation among the hosts of enemies,
whose auspicious eyes possess a reddish luster, who bestows the realization of liberation through the supreme path,
and who is a lioness among the lords of the three worlds.
I worship her who is beloved by the five-faced one, who removes fear, and who dispels serpents and other dangers.

Those who constantly worship the beautiful Śrī Kubjikā— the crest-jewel of the lords of kings— who delights in the great splendor of her two lotus-feet, who dispels delusion and other afflictions, and whose hands are most excellent; they shall quickly [attain the goal].
For they proclaimed their wealth, their lifespan, and their sovereignty as pervading the three worlds.

The Lord of Yogins, the Sovereign of the World, the doer of what is dear, the bestower of the glorious *Kālasaṃdarbha*, who flows into the ocean of splendor, and who kindles the fruits of desire from the celestial tree—
for the destruction of the sins of the worlds, [he is praised] by Śivā, the knowledge named Śrī.
I meditate upon him who has Dharma as his vital breath and his constant deity, and who is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who bow before him. 10.

Those of virtuous intellect who joyfully worship Kātyāyanī Bhairavī— the end of all knowledge, the unconquered one, whose face is intoxicated with the delight of passion, whose sandals rest upon the heart-lotus, the essence of the lineage— [dwell] amidst the ocean of supreme bliss.
With its splendor covering all, it was terrifying; [he approached it] for the sake of liberation and for the sake of true fame. || 11 ||
I bow to Rudrāṇī, whose face is like a lotus, who is composed of the splendor of ten million suns,

adorned with various ornaments, and who bestows the bliss of the Kula lineage; I praise the illustrious Māyā, who is accompanied by Kamalā, resides in the heart, and is the creative seed of the lineage.
She who is the embodiment of Vāgbhava, the noble lady of the Kula, born from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*.
I bow to the supreme Varabhairavī, who is like the fire of time at the end of the world upon the surface of the earth,
as red as a lotus stalk or a flower, the purifier of the world's defects;
she who removes the fear of the universe, the sovereign of yoga (Yogeśvarī), who carries me across my thousandfold misfortunes.
I [worship] her, who bestows all enjoyments. || 13 ||
I bow to that Blessed Lady, the Great Lakṣaṇā, who bestows sovereignty;
she is Mahālakṣmī herself on earth, the direct giver of the eightfold prosperity, the destroyer of family turmoil,
and she who resides within the beautiful lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna for the sake of Viṣṇu’s infinite glory.
She who bestows the rank of royalty, the bringer of auspiciousness, the sovereign of the Kaula, at all times.

I salute the Sovereign of the Pīṭhas, the destroyer of Asuras, the auspicious Vidyā, the Leader endowed with all ornaments, the remover of the agitation of the three worlds, the Goddess of Water (Vāruṇī),
the Mistress of the Pīṭha-hosts who overspreads the shadows of the three realms.
She who brings benefit to all, the victorious one, the Goddess whose nature is bliss. (15)

I bow to the Śākinī, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajñā*), who is intoxicated with joy, of noble lineage, fond of spiritual perfection (*siddhi*), and the beloved consort of Śambhu, the illustrious Vaṭukeśvara; she who moves within the great bliss of the wise, who is the manifest emergence of both self and others, and who removes the agitation of one's own mind.
I bow to Mahābhairavī, who shines like silver and reveals the meaning of all speech. || 16 ||
I bow to the Goddess Guṇā, whose face is like the full moon, who appears as if from the center of a lotus, who bears the streams of the great ocean of nectar upon her hundred heads,
who bestows the fruit of prostration, and who brings all kingdoms under her control.
To the supreme Mother, who destroys the fetters of the sense-objects. || 17 ||
I directly worship that goddess Kamalā, the foremost scholar of the Kula, whose body is filled with nectar throughout the three worlds,
and who resides within the center of the thousand petals of the lotus of the twilight (sandhyā).
I [salute] you, Kauleśvarī, the refuge of all divine beings.
O Sovereign of the Universe, O Excellent Kalikā among the host of gods, I bow to you daily with devotion at the fire of the Siddhas;
grant me devotion, wealth, the state of victory, and servitude.
In that [place], Mahāmadhumatī had a wife named Laghugṛhabhāryā. || 19 ||
By the grace of this hymn, one shall become a lord of poetry and speech;

a divine master of the great siddhis, devoted to the state of a hero (vīrabhāva), he attains victory everywhere and becomes beloved of Hara. He shall quickly become a lord of words and able to assume any form at will.
That man shall indeed become a great hero; he certainly becomes divine.

Gradually, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) shall arise, and he will certainly become eloquent. All sciences (vidyās) shall become propitious, all the lords of the directions shall be satisfied, and fire shall attain coolness.
He shall cause the solidification of water; such a man shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, and a king in this world.
He goes to Vaikuṇṭha and to Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva. O Mahādeva! liberation is indeed his who recites this constantly and at all times. For he beholds the lotus feet of Mahāvidyā.

It is certain. Listen, O Lord! I shall explain the ritual of libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the virgins (*kumāris*) and so forth, by the mere libation of which the accomplishment of the *kula* (*kulasiddhi*) will surely arise.
[One should worship] the maiden of the *kula*, who resides in the root-lotus (*mūlapadma*) and sports according to her desire, in a hundredfold [manner].
I satisfy you with the root mantra, O beloved.
O auspicious one, I satisfy Sandhyādevī, who is adorned by a circle of radiating flashes from the great splendor of the Mūlādhāra, with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja). || 2 ||
I satiate Kumārī Śrīsarasvatī, whose limbs are joined with the root lotus, with the substances of the *kula* for the sake of your satisfaction. (2)
I satisfy with supreme nectars the goddess Trimūrti, the leader of the Vālās, who resides in the beautiful root-support lotus and bestows all auspiciousness. 4.
I propitiate with the seed-syllable Śrī that which shines within the six petals of the great lotus of Svādhiṣṭhāna, solely for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. (5)
I satisfy Kālikā, who proceeds to the secret sign of Viṣṇu through the manifestation of the Kula of Svādhiṣṭhāna,
with the nectar of the Kula by means of her own seed-syllable.
Now I satisfy Kuleśvarī, who dwells upon the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, who is composed of great splendor, auspicious, and the crown of all suns. 7.
I propitiate Goddess Umā, Pārvatī, whose body is enchanting, with the seed-syllable of Māyā, within the centers of the lotuses of the maṇipūra.
In the center of the lotus of the Maṇipūra, I satisfy Mālinī, who is worshipped by the three worlds, for the sake of one whose mind is defiled and who possesses right understanding. (9)
I propitiate Kubjikā, the goddess who dwells in Maṇipūra, who is Raudrī, who increases supreme bliss, and who moves through the sky.
I satisfy the Great Goddess, who is intent upon the practice of mantra; I satisfy the Yoginī Kālasaṃdarbhā, whose face belongs to the Kula.
I propitiate the unconquered Mahādevī, the Mistress of the Kula, who bestows power and mantras, who is fierce, and whose tongue is agitated with movement. 12.
I propitiate Rudrāṇī, who is beloved by the great Kaulas, who is perfected, who bestows the happiness of the world of Rudra, who possesses the rays of Rudra, and who is fond of honey. 13.
I propitiate Bhairavī, who is perfected through the sixteen vowels, who destroys the Mahāraurava hell, and whose mind is intent upon the drinking of great wine.
O Mother, I propitiate Mahālakṣmī, the Goddess who bestows boons upon the three worlds, who is surrounded by a garland of the seed-syllable *Śrī*, and who possesses the sovereignty of existence. 15.

I satisfy the one who brings benefit to the worlds, who is beloved by people through both the beneficial and the harmful, the seed-syllable of Ramā, and the mistress of the sacred seats (pīṭha) beginning with Pīṭha.
I satiate Jayantī—the mother of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, the mother of Sūrya, the knower of the field (kṣetrajñā) veiled by Māyā—with nectars. || 17 ||

I offer libations to the one of supreme countenance, who brings joy to the lineage and has reached the further shore; I offer libations to the goddess Ambikā, Mahālakṣmī, who resides within the heart.
The lotus-palms of the feet of all those possessed of consciousness are the auspicious Śrīṣoḍaśī, endowed with the sixteen vowels for the sake of the happiness of the wise;
[I worship] you upon a resplendent lion-throne inlaid with rubies from the ocean of bliss.
I constantly satiate [the deity] seated in the center of a full white lotus.

Those who always attain the supreme liberation through the cause of bestowing knowledge— which consists of the complete satisfaction of the limbs of beautiful hymns well-established [in the heart], and which is composed of illusion— indeed, for them there are no hosts of enemies on the circles of the earth who cause misfortune; rather, they bring all kings under their control.
They become eternally endowed with all yogic powers in an instant. || 20 ||

If human beings recite this [text] known as liberation consisting of satisfaction (tarpaṇa), they shall become endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) and perceive [the truth] within a year; O Lord! through practice for a month, O Master! one becomes a great yogi (mahāyogī).

He who recites this with single-minded devotion shall quickly agitate the three worlds and obtain the fruit of his desire; he shall receive the merit of a libation (tarpaṇa) and attain the fruit of worship through the recitation of this hymn to Kumārī. He who does not perform [this]...
"He who performs the worship and hymn of the Kumārī and the daily auspicious rite shall indeed become like a sacrificial animal;

death awaits him at every step. Thus [it is said] in the Rudrajāmala, in the Uttarakhanda, in the Mahākuloddīpana, in the section on the arrangement of the service of the Kumārī, in the chapter on perfected mantras, in the determination of the divine state.
The hymn to Kumārī in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī is complete.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the auspicious armor (kavaca) of the Virgin Goddess, known as the "Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds," which destroys great sins.
By reciting it and by wearing it, people become great perfected ones (mahāsiddhas) and luminaries; [even] Śakra...
The glorious lord of the gods, Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods; Vahni, composed of perfect splendor;
Dharmarāja, the terrifying one; and Varuṇa himself, worthy of worship by the gods and the sovereign of the waters.

The destroyer of all, the great wind, Kumāra, the lord of elephants, the lord of wealth, the beloved of Śambhu—all these gods are the lords of the directions. You alone are the sovereign, the singular self, the lord of all, whose arising is stainless. By the recitation of this armor (*kavaca*), [may there be protection].

May all the kings and lords of wealth protect [me]. May the Praṇava, the virtuous Māyā who is the essence of the twilight (saṃdhyā), protect my head. May Mahāmāyā protect the upper part of my forehead; may Śrī Sarasvatī protect it. May Kāmākhyā, Vaṭukeśānī, and the Trimūrti protect my forehead.

May Cāmuṇḍā, whose form is the seed-syllable (vīja), protect my face; may Kālikā, who dwells in the sun, always protect my two eyes; and may that ascetic lady, whose nature is the seed-syllable of Kāma, protect the pair of my ears.
May Mālinī, the Goddess of Speech, protect the tip of my tongue;

may Kāmarūpā protect the tip of my palate, and Kubjikā protect the tips of my teeth. May that Goddess, whose form is the *praṇava*, protect my head eternally; may she whose nature is *svāhā* and who consists of the seed-syllable of Śakti protect my upper and lower lips.

May Aparājitā, the most fierce, protect my throat; may the seed-syllable *Kṣrauṃ* always protect my neck, accompanied by Rudrāṇī and Svāhā. May the sixteen-fold Vidyā, possessing sixteen beautiful vowels, protect my heart; and may Mahālakṣmī, the preeminent goddess, protect both my arms everywhere.

May she whose nature is all mantras protect my belly, the mistress of the sacred seat (pīṭha). Likewise, may the Heart Goddess, whose essence is the Vāgbhava mantra, protect my two flanks. May Kaiśorī, whose form is the Māyā-bīja, protect the region of my hips. And may the Yoginī Jayantī protect my pair of shanks.
May Ambikā Devī, who pervades the meaning of the mantra, protect my entire body, she who is surrounded by the *kalluka* [mudrā].

O Lord! May Kamalā protect the tips of my hair; may Naramohinī protect the tip of my nose; may the goddess Caṇḍikā protect my chin; and may Kumārī always protect me. May Lalitā Devī protect my heart and my back.
The dweller of the mountain;

the goddess Triśakti, the sixteenth; the secret *liṅga* is always present. Ambikā is the goddess in the cremation ground, and Bhairavī is within the womb of the Gaṅgā. In the empty house is Pañcamudrā.
May Vajradhāriṇī, who reveals mantras and yantras, always protect me at the crossroads;
and may Caṇḍā, seated upon a corpse and adorned with a garland of severed heads, protect me at the linga.
May the Sovereign Goddess, whose form is Power, protect me in the forest; may the Great Youthful One, who delights in battle, protect me in the great wilderness;

may Sarasvatī protect me in vast waters, in ponds, and in the midst of enemies; may Pṛthvī always protect me on the path through the great sky; and may Rājalakṣmī, as a maiden, protect me in the midst of battle.

May Kulakāminī protect me; may Mahī, who is Arddhanārīśvara and who assumes the form of a young maiden— the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of nine hundred thousand [syllables], resplendent like ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons— protect the soles of my feet.
"May Vāṇī, the bestower of boons and the beloved of Vaṭukeśvara, protect me. Thus, O Lord, I have related to you this most wonderful armor (kavaca) of Kumārī, the lineage-bestower,
which reaches the further shore of the meaning of the five principles (pañcatattva).

Whoever should worship with the hymn of the five principles and the armor, for him there will be the accomplishment of traveling through the sky; of this there is no doubt. He shall quickly become one whose body is like a diamond.

By the grace of this armor (*kavaca*), the yogi who recites it becomes a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) and a possessor of knowledge (*jñānin*). Having recited it during disputes, legal proceedings, battle,
in the *kulamaṇḍala*, on the great road, in the cremation ground, and at the arising of yogic attainments, [one succeeds].
One obtains the fruit; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of the Kula!

This auspicious armor (*kavaca*) for subjugation grants victory everywhere. A practitioner of meritorious vows who recites it daily will certainly become a glorious ascetic (*yati*). [It is] the perfected science (*siddhavidyā*), the Virgin Goddess (*kumārī*).
He who recites or even hears it bestows supreme accomplishment; he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
He attains enjoyment, liberation, contentment, nourishment, royal splendor, and abundant prosperity.
The best of practitioners, having retained it, shall be victorious;

the wise man, having recited this auspicious armor (*kavaca*), shall accomplish even the impossible. It grants great happiness to those of noble lineage and bestows virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.

One should constantly worship the Yoginī during the day and the Kumārī at night; by means of specific ritual offerings, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control, even through the consumption of meat, fish, and liquor.

Having worshipped, recited mantras, and offered libations to the fair-faced goddess with various kinds of food and edibles, fragrant substances, garlands, ornaments of gold and silver, and fine garments; and having honored her through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, ritual applications, and hymns of praise, O Maheśvara!
Whoever recites the Kumārī-kavaca with single-minded devotion shall quickly attain perfection and become a lord of the kings of kings.
He obtains the fruit of his desires, whatever dwells in his mind, by having it written on birch bark.
If one should wear the armor (*kavaca*),

the wise man, facing north, should write it down and wear it on Saturdays and Tuesdays, on the ninth and eighth lunar days, on the fourteenth day, on the full moon, and especially during the dark fortnight.

Even one who is burdened with great sins shall be liberated from all transgressions by wearing [this] on the left arm of a woman; she shall obtain all auspiciousness, become beloved, possess many sons, and be endowed with every prosperity. Likewise, the most excellent of men shall attain glory by wearing it on the right arm.
One should wear [this] on the arm.

In this world, one shall possess a divine body with a splendor equal to that of a lion; in the supreme world of Śiva, one goes, possessing the speed of the wind and free from disease, having pierced through the solar orb to the beyond.

One shall attain liberation by reciting this auspicious armor (*kavaca*), which bestows supreme happiness upon the worlds, removes fear, grants devotion to the feet of Śrī, and arises from the ocean of bliss for the sake of liberation. (p. 770)
Those people who recite this victory, the sole cause for destroying the terrible impurities of the Kali age, attain incomparable merit and reach liberation in an instant.

Thus ends the Kumārī-kavaca, the determination of the nature [of the goddess], within the section on accomplished mantras, in the *Kumārī-kavacollāsa*, which is part of the *Kumāry-upacaryā-vinyāsa* in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Rudrajāmala*, the Northern Tantra.

If one is capable, then one should recite the *Sahasranāma* of the Virgin (Kumārī) as described in the tenth chapter; however, for fear of making this work too voluminous, it has not been written here.

Now, the praise of the Brāhmaṇas. In the third section of the first chapter of the Matsya-sūkta: "Brāhmaṇas are a moving pilgrimage site, free of water yet available at all times; by the very water of their words, defiled people are purified."

In the thirteenth chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Yoginītantra: "The Brahmin consists of all the gods and is the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Born from the splendor of Brahmā, the twice-born is eternally beyond the material world (aprākṛtika). Wherever food is consumed by Brahmins, there Hari himself eats. In that [place]..."
Brahmā, Rudra, the sky-dwelling seers, the sages, the ancestors, and all the deities partake [of the offerings];

of this there is no doubt. A Brahmin consists of all the gods; therefore, one should not treat him with contempt. (From the Seventh Chapter) Therefore, whether he be ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa...
One should always honor [the Brāhmaṇa]. O Goddess! when a Brāhmaṇa is satisfied, all the gods are forever satisfied; O Goddess!
when a Brāhmaṇa is dissatisfied, we ourselves are indeed dissatisfied. O Goddess!
even if a Brāhmaṇa were to commit a hundred wrongs against oneself—

Even so, one who desires his welfare should not cause him distress; nor should he ever show him contempt, O beautiful goddess! For the Brāhmaṇa is the soul of all the gods, and he is indeed manifestly composed of splendor.

In the thirteenth chapter [of the *Bṛhannīlatantra*]: "Those gods always desire a Brāhmaṇa, a maiden, a Śakti, fire, the Veda, and a cow for the purpose of sacrifice in the lands of action (*karmabhūmi*). In the seventh chapter of the *Bṛhannīlatantra*: 'He who, having provided a livelihood for a teacher, causes the twice-born to study—what...'"
One who desires virtue, wealth, and pleasure should not abandon it; know that this merit, esteemed by all, is more meritorious than any other merit.
Likewise, in the Yoginītantra (p. 771): "The curse of Brahmins is difficult to overcome; therefore, one should never provoke it. O beloved! Know that for Brahmins, speech is always their vajra."
In the thirteenth chapter: For one upon whom the curse of a Brahmin has fallen, there is no remedy from afar;
yet for even one bitten by Takṣaka, a counter-measure exists at that very moment.
However, for one struck down by the curse of a Brahmin, a remedy may only occur at the end of a kalpa. And the duration of a kalpa is as follows: [text continues]
It is stated in that very same place:
O Maheśānī! For one kalpa, or three hundred years in the Kali age, there is no liberation from hell for him;
of this there is no doubt. Thus, O beloved, all those born in his lineage are tormented day and night by various kinds of great portents until—
"Extending for seven generations; therefore, O Goddess, one should never despise a Brāhmaṇa under any circumstances. Thus ends the praise of the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, regarding the pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*): [as stated] in the second chapter of the middle section of the *Yoginītantra*.
The Blessed One said:
Having constantly performed the *nāndīmukha* rite for the ancestors in one's own home,
and having worshipped them according to the rules with devotion,
one should thereafter undertake the journey when Venus has moved to the north and the auspicious planets are favorable.

Having obtained permission from one's guru and parents, and especially from the Brahmins, one should feed seven twice-born men and then undertake the journey. One should not travel to the eastern seat during the months of Leo, Sagittarius, or Aries; nor should one travel to the western seat during the months of Aquarius, Gemini, or Pisces.

The wise man, when Mercury is in Taurus, Virgo, or Capricorn, should not go to the southern region; nor should the intelligent person go to the northern region when Mercury is in Cancer, Leo, or Pisces; and likewise when it is in Sagittarius, Taurus, or Virgo.
One should go to the southeast corner. One should avoid [the asterisms] Capricorn, Cancer, and Pisces in the southwest;

one should avoid Aquarius, Aries, and Sagittarius in the northwest; and one should avoid Leo, Pisces, and Cancer in the northeast. One should know this to be the *śūla* (trident). Now listen to [the rules for] the *yoginī*.
O Śaṅkarī!

O my beloved, one should not travel to the eastern region on Saturday, to the western region on Sunday, to the southern region on Wednesday, and to the northern region on Tuesday. On Monday, however, one may go to the west.
O Dear One! On a Sunday, one should not go toward the southeast; on a Monday, especially toward the northeast; on a Tuesday, toward the southwest;
on a Friday, toward the northwest; on a Saturday, likewise toward the northeast;
and on the first and ninth lunar days, O Great Goddess, a traveler should not go toward the eastern direction.

Since the pilgrimage must be performed in the presence of the Yoginīs, one should avoid the fourteenth and the sixth days when traveling toward the west. One should not go toward the southern direction on the thirteenth or the fifth day.

One should avoid the Yakṣa region on the second and the tenth lunar days; one should by all means abandon the Vāyavya region on the full moon and the seventh; likewise, one should not go to the Īśāna region on the new moon and the eighth.

One should avoid Viṣkumbha, Prīti, and Āyuṣmān on the first lunar day (pratipad). One should avoid Saubhāgya and Śobhana on the second lunar day, as well as Atigaṇḍa. One should avoid Sukarmā and Dhṛti on the third lunar day. [Furthermore, one should avoid] Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, and Vyāghāta.

And likewise, O Goddess, one should avoid the fourth [tithi], and similarly, there is corruption on the fifth. Know, O Śaṅkarī, that Vajrasiddhi and Vyatīpāta occur on the sixth; one should also completely avoid Parigha, which is most excellent, on the seventh.
On the eighth day, one should avoid Śivasiddhi and Sādhya;
on the ninth, Śubha and Śakra; on the tenth, Brahmā;
on the eleventh, likewise Indra; and on the twelfth, one should avoid Vaidhṛti.

On the first lunar day (pratipad) when Kṛttikā is present, and on the second lunar day when Jyeṣṭhā is present—one should never set out on a journey during such inauspicious constellations. However, if one is already on a journey, there is no fault; one should simply take care regarding the *karaṇas*. Likewise, [one should avoid setting out] during the birth-month, on the birth-day, and under the birth-constellation.

One should always avoid setting out on a journey on the eighth and ninth lunar days. O Maheśvarī! In times of distress, one may travel at dawn in the western region; at the time of "cow-dust" (dusk), in the eastern region; at midday, in the southern region; and likewise in the afternoon, in the northern region.
One should perform [the ritual] in the northeast at night, in the southwest during the two twilights,

in the southeast at midday, and in the northwest in the morning; or one may perform it at the appropriate time during the conjunctions beginning with the western quarter (Vāruṇa), except on the day of birth, as well as on the eighth and ninth lunar days.
Excepting [the east], one should set out on a journey facing north when approaching the eastern direction;
one should set out facing east when in the west; facing west when in the south;
and facing south when in the north, for the sake of complete success. [The substances are] a flower and barley gruel.
The conch, the kettledrum, Brahmins, kings, cows, an umbrella, a chariot, a vehicle,
and auspicious women are recorded as being on the right side. Likewise, prepared food, a lump of meat, cooked rice, a vessel, and living beings [are also auspicious].

A lump of clay, those who feed on corpses, and all auspicious things on the right are favorable; likewise, a maiden, a couple, a courtesan, women with full jars, birds, and animals moving on the left are auspicious. Curd and fruit in front portend a successful journey.

It is proclaimed to be auspicious. Likewise, when cranes and peacocks go in pairs as one travels, then one should know that success is at hand; otherwise, one should predict obstacles. When vultures, hawks, and crows indeed fly alongside, the traveler should not set out.
The journey [is undertaken] while the obstructing word remains; in the fifth chapter, in the center of Kāmarūpa.
