Having observed the mountain marked by Janārdana, [one should know that] the supreme field named Āgastya is situated between these three: to the north of that mountain, in the northeast of Viraja, and to the south and west of the mountain, at the Śaubhraliṅga. This is indeed the most excellent [of fields]. The triad...

This field extending for a hundred [yojanas] is known as belonging to Aśambhu; one should understand this to be Gayā, while the other is called Lohitya. By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there, the ancestors attain the supreme goal.
One should offer a sweet morsel (*piṇḍa*) into the hand of Janārdana: "O Janārdana! This *piṇḍa* is given by me into your hand; O Lord, you shall indeed be my giver in the next world.
To the east of the Kali-remainder, at a distance of eight bows, that stone [is located].
And for the sake of delivering one's ancestors from the state of being a *preta*,
by offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) there, one is never born again as a *preta* anywhere.
To the southeast of Cakratīrtha, at a distance of two bows, is the *Lola-liṅga*.
One should offer libations with sesame and milk at this supreme sacred ford (tīrtha).
Then, having beheld Janārdana, one is indeed liberated from the three debts. At the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, a Liṅga was established by Śukra, measuring half a bow in length.
I have heard the name Śukreśa. Having beheld the god Śukreśvara, who would not be liberated from bondage? Likewise, having beheld Goleśvara, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
as well as Aṅgāreśa, Siddheśa, Gajāditya, and Gaja.
By beholding Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors;
by beholding the Lord Janārdana after bathing at Gayāgoleśvara— what cause for merit has not been accomplished by men through this?

They lead twenty-one generations of men here to the world of Brahmā. Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist on earth, including the oceans and lakes, they visit Cakratīrtha once every day. On earth, Gayā is meritorious, and within Gayā likewise is Kūpaka.
O auspicious Goddess! Mātṛgayā is eight times more excellent than Kūpa. By going to Mātṛgayā, a son indeed becomes free from debt in an instant.
By offering the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayā, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors. [This extends] to the end of Gayā.

The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) extends as far as Gayā, and that very place is a sacred ford (tīrtha). Likewise: "Whoever offers his own funeral cake here in the great field of Agastya, his lifespan increases gradually by more than two months for each year; and while his parents are still living, the son [attains long life]."

One should perform the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika). O Maheśvarī! Whether there be many sons, or only one son, or a son devoted to yoga; whether the son be afflicted by leprosy from birth, or even if there be no son at all—O Goddess! after forty years have passed, one should personally perform the rites for oneself. He who, with his own hand, performs the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga)...
O Goddess, it is remembered that even for one who has gone to the other world, the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) performed by another yield inexhaustible merit.

One should always perform two bull-releases (vṛṣotsarga) while both husband and wife are alive; however, as long as one's parents are living, a son should not perform funeral rites for them. But when he is intent on going to Gayā, he should perform the Śrāddha...
Having performed [the rites] according to the injunctions, and having assumed the guise of a rag-robe wearer (*karpaṭī*), he should circumambulate the village.

Then, having gone to another village and partaken of the remnants of the *śrāddha* meal, he should proceed while circumambulating and avoiding the acceptance of gifts. He should remain at a distance of one cubit (*aratni*) from a house.
Regarding the journey of Agastya: "The ascent to heaven is like a staircase for the ancestors at every step;
one should always perform the *śrāddha* for Agastya day and night. If the *śrāddha* is performed without meat and likewise excludes Viṣṇu, the ancestors curse him."

The ancestors departed disappointed. O beloved! In an *āma-śrāddha* (a rite performed with raw materials), one should offer raw grain and raw meat without hesitation; otherwise, his ancestors certainly remain with their faces turned downwards.
Furthermore, he who eats a *śrāddha* meal that was prepared with meat but is now meatless [is likewise at fault].

One would go to the Tāmisra hell along with one's ancestors; it cannot be otherwise. He by whom [the food] has been made meatless should perform the Śrāddha without meat; he who eats meat should perform the Śrāddha with meat, O fair-faced one! Also in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Matsyasūkta: "Not..."

O Maheśvarī! One should perform the annual *śrāddha* (yearly ancestral rite) without meat; however, the *śrāddha* on festival days (*parva*) and the *śrāddha* at Gayā are highly commended when performed with meat. One should perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha* and the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha* devoid of meat. A *śrāddha* performed without meat...

If one should eat food containing meat, the ancestors depart disappointed after uttering a most terrible curse. O Śaṅkara! When a Brāhmaṇa has been invited by Śūdras for a Śrāddha, a sacrifice, or a festival, he who feeds that Brāhmaṇa eats excrement.
The meat of the buffalo, the large goat, the deer, and likewise the yak;

the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hare, and likewise the boar; the wild boar and likewise the ram—all these should be offered at a śrāddha ceremony in every respect. However, in the Kali age, the meat of cows [is forbidden].
And that pair [of meat] belonging to a dog; one should also avoid a goat with impaired senses and one that is not black. By the meat of a black goat, [one dwells] for six years on a single path;
by the yak-tail (cāmara), for a hundred years; by the lizard (godhikā), for a thousand years, O Dear One! And for six months...
O Varārohe! [The merit lasts] for one month with tortoise meat; with boar meat for six months;
with rabbit meat for nine months; with śālvaka meat for twenty-two years;
likewise with small wild boars; and with the meat of a large animal, such as the yak (cāmara), it lasts for a hundred years.
One should avoid that which is to be avoided by four or six men;

for that reason, it has been declared as "excessively thick" by the ancient sages. O my beloved! [This applies to] the hide of a buffalo, a cow, a boar, a deer, and even the thick hide of a large goat.

It is praised: the five-clawed rhinoceros (khaḍga) is fit for consumption, as is the pigeon when joined with the rhinoceros. However, O my beloved, one should avoid that which has four faces and is not broad. One should also avoid the monitor lizard, the golden rhinoceros, the yak-tail fly-whisk, and the black [rhinoceros]. One should avoid these.
If a wise man [obtains] a tortoise marked with a wheel, or a lion-mouthed fish, a Rohita, a Rājīva, a Citraka, likewise a Mahāśaṅkha,
a Prauṣṭhika, a Pārvatīyaka fish, a large Rohita fish, and a large Prauṣṭhīka—

One should diligently include the *vṛhacchalla* and the *citra* fish in the śrāddha rite. One should avoid fish that are scaleless and those shaped like serpents. In the case of a scaleless fish, however, two pieces of armor (or protective scales) should be offered in its place. This applies also to items such as *potodhāna* and anything else of deformed appearance.

One should avoid snakes, fat, and female cats; likewise, one should avoid plantains cooked with smoke, sugar mixed with insects, buffalo ghee, and goat's milk at a *śrāddha* ceremony. One should also avoid coconut and palmyra fruit.
One should carefully avoid *kharjara*, *pīnaka*, buttermilk, and milk that is devoid of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One should discard a lamp that uses a cloth wick and visible oil itself.
Likewise, safflower, *nālikā* greens, and *mālatī* flowers [are forbidden] at a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.

One should avoid *paṅkaja* and *karavīra* flowers. With a concentrated mind, one should place the food in vessels of a single kind; first, one should offer it to the gods (*daiva*), and thereafter to the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
One must never place food remaining from the ancestors onto the food for the gods. [The food...]

One should wash [the food] in some cases during an *āmaśrāddha* performed without the sacred fires; however, one should wash the food during a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, at the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), and during eclipses. This statement has also been upheld by the Smārta tradition:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, [the portion] should not exceed eight handfuls due to the transition [of the food]; beyond that..."

One should not give anything deficient in the rite of Śrāddha. O Goddess! O Śaṅkarī! He who performs the Śrāddha in a most beautiful lotus-leaf or under the shade of an Aśvattha tree, which is a leaf of Brahmā, will certainly attain satisfaction for a full hundred years.
In a vessel of *śatapatra* (lotus) wood, infinite satisfaction arises for six months; in a copper vessel, for one month;

and in a golden vessel, for a year. It is said that in a silver vessel the merit is tenfold, and in a vessel of rhinoceros horn, it exceeds a hundredfold. This applies when the *śrāddha* rite is performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) using a vessel of a single material, as well as during the *pārvaṇa* ceremony.

Likewise, one should employ different varieties [of grain] during the period of increase; for that duration of a year, one should indeed employ rice (*vrīhi*). One who observes the vow of rice should avoid it in the *śrāddha* after a year has passed.
[One may use] grain produced in the rainy season and sesame (*tila*) harvested in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Likewise, at the beginning of a sacrifice and during a *śrāddha*, one should avoid grain that has been cooked twice. [One should also avoid] sixty-day grain (*ṣaṣṭidhānya*),
royal grain (*rājadhānya*), great grain (*bṛhaddhānya*), the beloved (*ballabha*), moon-grain (*somadhānya*),
quick-grain (*śīghradhānya*), the red-hand of Bengal (*vaṅgāniraktapāṇika*), the *ketakī*, and the *kalaviṅka*.

One should employ grains suitable for *śrāddha* among the deities, namely: Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Pradīpa, Viṣṇudhānya, Vallabha, Bhogadhānya, Aśoka, and the group of five known as Nāga. These grains are fit for the ancestral rites and should be offered to the gods.

O Maheśvarī! With wheat, barley, and cakes, as well as wild rice (nīvāra) and other divine grains (devadhānya), one should perform the Śrāddha; however, one should carefully avoid grain sown in the spring. By merely eating that food, sin is transmitted.
For men, by eating *śrāvaṇa* grain, one is born poor;
by eating *somadhānya*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
by eating *vṛddhadhānya*, it is said that one becomes wealthy; [and likewise for] *rājadhānya* and *ślakṣṇadhānya*.

By eating it, one attains the world of Viṣṇu; by eating red grain-rice (*raktadhānyaudana*), one obtains the glory of victory. O beautiful one, Nārāyaṇa and Mādhava are my enjoyments; by eating the "thirteen-grain" (*dhānyatrayodaśa*), a man shall obtain renown.
"If a Brāhmaṇa invited to a *śrāddha* does not go, he goes to a terrible hell eternally along with his ancestors. Thus ends the account of the *śrāddha* for pilgrimages and other rites.

Now, the majesty of Kāśī. In the *Yoginītantra*, in the first section (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*), in the sixteenth chapter: following the hymn of praise by the gods who had been defeated by the demon Tripura, [Śiva] made the earth his chariot and the moon and sun his two wheels, and [appointed] Brahmā...

Having made the Vedas the charioteer and likewise the *rajjus* (the cords), having made the gods the parts of the chariot and the immortals as well, having made Sumeru the bow and Vāsuki the bowstring, he placed the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, upon the chariot.

Having made Viṣṇu my arrow, O Maheśānī, the triple city, along with all that is moving and unmoving, including the gods, Daityas, and others, was reduced to ashes by me. Thereafter, O Goddess, I performed a new creation there, wherein this entire world of the moving and unmoving had been turned to ash.

Know that to be the Great Cremation Ground (Mahāśmaśāna), the cause of dissolution for all; there resides the splendor of all the deceased gods. Having become five *krośas* in extent, that splendor likewise fashioned the body of the Triple City (*Tripura*) out of the ashes of the worlds through its power of illusion (*māyā*).

Upon his chest, there, under the guise of death, I praised the Supreme Goddess within that splendor of Mahākālī, who is the supreme embodiment of consciousness. Then, from that splendor, Kālī appeared as the supreme digit;
indeed, that splendor blazing with majesty is called Kālī.
It has been proclaimed: "Only the face of Mahākālī was seen within her splendor;

therefore, it is celebrated by the sages as 'Gaurīmukha' (the Face of Gaurī). O Supreme Goddess! Upon seeing that, bliss arises within me; for that reason, it is sung of by the gods and others as 'Ānandakānana' (the Forest of Bliss)."
Indeed, that entire splendor became identical with Kālī,

just as the spray of water born from the ocean becomes the ocean itself. O Goddess, just as various waters falling into the Gaṅgā [become one], so indeed did the splendor of the immortals become the splendor of Kālī.

O Goddess of the gods! If everything arises as Gaṅgā alone, and likewise as Tejas, O Maheśvarī, then everything becomes full of Kālī; there is no difference, O Maheśvarī! Therefore, Kāśī is certainly Kālī—of this there is no doubt—extending for five krośas.

O Goddess! Kāśī, consisting of the splendor of Brahman, is established as the form of the half-moon and is perceived by all classes of beings. This Kāśī, however, is the Amākalā, devoid of decay or rise.
Therein, O Great Goddess, the Bindu shines as Maṇikarṇikā; that indeed is the nectar of the moon here.
"O beloved! Know the Gaṅgā; O Maheśvarī! Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist there at Kālī—know all that to be nectar, O Goddess, O beautiful lady of the gods!
O Goddess! I bear Tamasā night and day upon my head; therefore indeed is my state as Śaṅkara."

This is indeed certainly true for me: always bearing that Kālī, who extends for five krośas, upon my head, I worship her day and night, swelling with supreme bliss; therefore, my status as the Lord of the Universe is eternal—of this there is no doubt.

There is doubt [regarding this]. O Sovereign of the Gods! He who is the Lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others—he alone is the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara), and none other, O Supreme Goddess! Having become possessed of absolute bliss, I always worship the Supreme One. Thereupon, her grace was bestowed upon him.
Being addressed by embodied beings, the Goddess said:
"O Lord! O Supreme Bliss! You have bestowed bliss upon me; therefore, in Kāśī..."
"O Ānanda, grant bliss always to those who have died.
The Lord said:

Having heard her words, I was immersed in an ocean of nectar. I bestowed the supreme Brahman into the range of the ears of one who was about to die. O Goddess! O Śivā! Always remaining in Vārāṇasī and meditating on the Supreme, those who have died in Vārāṇasī—whether in water, on dry land, or in the atmosphere—are [liberated].

To those into whose range of hearing I give the supreme Brahman, they indeed abandon all action— both good and evil— and by my instruction, they attain the Nirvāṇa of Brahman in an instant. All that, whether good or evil action—
O Maheśvarī! By the grace of Mahākālī and through the yoga of knowledge, one becomes ash.
Whatever part of the body touches Kāśī, that very part becomes Kāśī at that moment.
Merely by touching Kāśī, he meets his death within Kāśī; in that very birth—

O Great Queen! Or rather, in another birth—truly, truly, again truly, it is indeed the truth, O Sovereign of the Gods! Just as the brilliance of fire would burn cotton by its mere touch in an instant, so too would the Śūla-karma be burned away by the touch of the splendor of Kāśī in a moment.

O Śivā! Just as fire consumes a heap of cotton after a short time, so too does a single birth in Kāśī burn away the heap of karmas for men. What more need I tell you regarding the accumulation of merit at the site of Kāśī? Even if there were a woman equal to you [in devotion]—
If there were a person equal to me, or even those born from eggs, born from sweat, born from sprouts, or born from a womb—if they all die in Kāśī by good fortune, they attain liberation.
O Goddess! This Vārāṇasī is auspicious and filled with great splendor; it is perceived by people differently according to the distinction of the Yugas.

Indeed, it is seen that Kāśī is of four kinds: in the Kṛta age she is composed of jewels; in the Tretā age she is remembered as born of gold; in the Dvāpara age she takes the form of stone; and in the Kali age she is auspiciously composed of earth. There exists no sacred field superior to this in the three worlds; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Great Goddess!

I tell you this under oath: O Goddess, he who desires liberation despite being immersed in the cycle of worldly existence, should go for refuge to me alone and remain self-restrained in Kāśī. He alone is a fallen man who has attained wisdom; he alone is the purifier of his lineage. O Great Goddess, even at the end of one's life, [one should not leave] Kāśī.

The twice-born man should depart [from Kāśī]. He alone is the supreme fool; he alone is the destroyer of his lineage, if, having reached Kāśī, he should abandon it in vain like a fool. If one should obtain Kāśī again through the merits of many births, then one must never abandon Kāśī.
Even at the end of one's life, whoever desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra without effort should indeed go by any means to my city, Vārāṇasī. There,
Annapūrṇā shall give food and Sarasvatī shall give knowledge— at the end of one's life.
I am the giver of liberation in Kāśī; what need is there for any other meditation?

The greatness of Vṛndāvana, Kāñcī, and other such places has not been written here for fear of increasing the bulk of the book; seekers should look for it in the fifteenth chapter and others of the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* of the *Yoginītantra*.
The fifth section, titled the Bhaktikāṇḍa (the Section on Devotion), consisting of seven chapters, in the Śrīprāṇatoṣaṇī is completed.
Herein is set forth the glossary for the sixth section, the Jñānakāṇḍa.

First is the fivefold great yoga (pañcamahāyoga); immediately following that, the description of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), the primary proclamation of the restraints (yamas), and likewise of the observances (niyamas).
First is the primary seat, followed by the science of yoga and the obstacles to yoga, and after that, the practice regarding the monastic hermitage.

Then follows the classification of breath control (prāṇāyāma), and subsequently that of the retention of breath (kumbhaka). The four durations for the practice of breath control have thus been proclaimed.

The characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior [levels] of the attainment of *prāṇa*; the fruit arising from washing the body with that very sweat of exertion; the signs of the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*);
thereafter, the fruit of the mastery of the *kumbha* [vessel]; those things to be avoided in yoga, and then those things which bring about success.

Then follows the state of *manonmanī*, which is the indifference toward both the wholesome and the unwholesome for the practitioner; after that, the sevenfold divisions of *kumbhaka* (breath-retention) beginning with "not" (*na*) and so forth; following that, the practices such as *dhauti* along with their results;
then the fruit arising from the practice of the seeker; and finally, the enumeration of obstacles thereto.

The state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā), its fruit, and the obstacle thereto have been described; thereafter, the ten mudrās along with their fruits have been set forth. Thus concludes this first chapter; hereafter follows the meditation on the elements, beginning with earth.

The fruit is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and beyond that is concentration (*samādhi*); this too is a further fruit of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Regarding the division of lunar days (*tithi*), there is a sequential flow of the breath through the left and right nostrils; a fault arises from a contrary movement during exhalation.
In the case of sitting together; in the specific action of Vāyu, the result is determined by the left and right [sides];
even in the specific action of Vāyu, the result depends on the direction in which it is situated during the query;
the result arises from the distinction between full and empty, as does the movement of the channel; likewise, when there is a difference in limbs or a difference in the task.

From that [arise] the five elements and so forth; likewise, their auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, and the determination of that time. There is the knowledge of the elements, their five states distinguished by childhood and so on, their results according to the difference of the days (vāra), and from that, the results of the left and right [sides], as well as the movement of the channels (dhamanī) in the directions.

In the case of wind, the results correspond to one's own channels; thereafter, if it is contrary, the result is likewise contrary. A journey during the position of the *vṛhannāḍī* is auspicious according to the science of winds.
Furthermore, the cleansing of the hand of the flowing channel consists of the positions for departure and their respective results.

The determination of action according to the distinction between full and empty channels: action residing in the left nostril, as well as that residing in the right nostril; the functions residing in the *suṣumnā*, the perception of the forms of the elements and so forth, and the movement of the elements within the division of the five elements—this is the function of the body.

The Determination: The determination of the question consists of the ascertainment of the auspicious and inauspicious by means of the elements (*bhūtas*). Likewise, there is the knowledge of reflection regarding the root and so forth through the elements, as well as the state of the Moon, the time of accomplishment, and the ascertainment of the state of Earth. (p. 781)

The knowledge of the stars through the *tattvas*, the determination of natural movements, the classification of motion by means of departures and so forth, the wind as its deficient cause, and likewise the results regarding the upper directions and so on; victory and defeat based on the distinction of breaths; the application of weapons according to the *tattvas*, and victory and other outcomes in battle through the *tattvas*.

At the time of entry, there is gain and so forth; likewise, at the time of exit, there is loss. In the Void (Śūnya), there is no determination of death or destruction; by means of the Element (Bhūta), there is the determination of location. There is also the determination of victory and so forth, as well as subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa). Furthermore, there is knowledge of the fetus and the auspicious or inauspicious results for the year.
Then follows the thorough knowledge of the causes and so forth of the disease, and from that, its diagnosis;
thereafter, the discernment of death and life, and beyond that, the knowledge of time;
and finally, the knowledge of one's own lifespan for three years and so on.
The knowledge of Arundhatī and so forth, the practice for increasing longevity,

and the praise of the knowledge of one's own voice constitute the second chapter. Then follows the praise of royal yogas, their divisions numbering according to the lunar days, the characteristics of those divisions, and subsequently the *lakṣa-yoga*.

Furthermore, the characteristic of Rājayoga consists of fivefold divisions; Haṭhayoga is twofold, and Jñānayoga follows after that. Then there is the external characteristic, its fruit, and the characteristic of the fivefold space.
Then follows the determination of the sixteen supports (*ādhāra*), the exposition of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*),
the unity of the microcosm (*piṇḍa*) and the macrocosm (*brahmāṇḍa*), the existence of the universe within the body,
the fruit of the attainment of *rājayoga*, and the wonderful secret convention of the lotus (*padmasaṅketa*).

The qualities of the unmanifest and so forth, and thereafter the teaching on yoga; the one qualified for yoga and the very cause of yoga’s perfection; the divisions of yoga, mantra-yoga, and the expansion of laya-yoga;
the knowledge of time and the person (kāla-puruṣa), and immediately after that its fruit; and the means of its practice through the tongue (rasanā).
Then follows the various kinds of fruits; then the proclamation of the conclusion of the third section;
then the description of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) according to the sequence of the gross and the subtle;
Meru is the abode of all the gods, and above it is Satyaloka; below it is Rasātala.
And likewise the worlds; then the description of the extent of the foundational lotus (ādhārapadma) and that of the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
following that, the description of Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka; then the description of Maṇipūra and the description of Anāhata; and the description of Viśuddha.

Therefore, the description of that which is called the Command (*ājñā*), followed by the description of the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*) and the lower face, the seed-syllable of abiding, and the description of the internal structure of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*); this is known as the conclusion of the fourth chapter. [This concludes] the mode of knowledge.
The twofold nature of knowledge, free from duality;

that knowledge, the description of its fruit, and thereafter the form of non-dual knowledge; the knowledge of reality, its praise, the determination of the Self as the witness, and [the analogies of] being the charioteer and the possession of the chariot and so forth.
Following that, [the topics are] the determination of the body and so forth, the determination of the state of the enjoyer’s liberation, and the description of the highest [levels] and so on.
Immediately thereafter, the absence of meditation, worship, and the like for one who knows Brahman; the description of the Self;
the threefold knowledge; the causes of knowledge; and the action that accomplishes liberation.

The exposition of the seed-syllable of Śiva; the exposition of the fetters (pāśa); then, the vision of the non-difference of the individual soul (jīvātman); furthermore, the vision of the absence of birth, death, and so forth in the Self; the determination of the Piṇḍa, Pada, and other categories—this is the fruit born from hearing the Tantra. [This is] the Vidyā-tattva.

From the merit acquired through the praise of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there arises the knowledge of Brahman, which is the determination of the Supreme Self; thereafter, that very knowledge resides in the mendicant (*bhikṣuṇī*), for it is from Brahman that the world originates. The fruit is the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman.

The praise of the Brahma-mantra; the extraction of the Brahma-mantra; the consciousness of the meaning of the mantra and its worship; the hymn to Brahman and its armor (kavaca); thereafter, the offering of food (naivedya) and its fruit;
the praise of its worshipper and the preliminary ritual (puraskriyā) of that mantra; and other things also to be known.
The completion of the fifth chapter has been recorded by the wise according to its proper place.
The twenty-fold wheel beginning with *mātrā* and situated within the wheels beginning with *bāla*—
this indeed is its explanation, which constitutes the completion of the sixth chapter, as well as the *sarvatobhadra* wheel.

The commentary on that, together with its method of exposition; then the hundred-petaled wheel and its commentary; the speech consisting of questions and answers, as well as the salutation and the mantra;
the explanation of those questions, followed by their symbolic conventions; and also the expansion-wheel (prastāracakra) for that.
The commentary on that [section] follows immediately thereafter. This concludes the seventh chapter; other matters should be understood by the wise in their proper place within this work.

This work, delightful with its seven extensive chapters as its blossoms, is a section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*). O wise ones, you who are charmed by its fragrance, know that while it is repeatedly accessible to the world of scholars, its fruit is indeed unattainable except from the mouth of a Guru. O learned ones, forgive my faults!

"Subsisting on the alms of others, O Supreme One, you must purify all my impurities and the like. Because of your great haste to give instructions, it is not possible for me to look back again; this supreme speech has been composed by me. I shall constantly offer my petition."
O terrible ones! Having scrutinized everything, you must purify it with extremely subtle intelligence.
As it is stated in the thirty-sixth chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Rudrajāmala: |||
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said:

One devoid of the knowledge of the three qualities does not perceive [the truth] day or night; day and night, for the sake of knowledge, one does not perceive the physical body. Thus, death occurs for men birth after birth;
therefore, for the sake of ending that cycle of births, one should practice my yoga.

By performing the great yoga of the five immortals (*pañcāmarā-mahāyoga*), a human being becomes immortal. Listen to that method, O Beloved of Life! O One with Lovely Teeth! I shall speak out of devotion to you; do not have any doubt, O Śaṅkara! If this practice of yoga is not told in the presence of anyone else, terrible obstacles [will arise].
How can there be yoga and so forth while [the senses] dwell within the body?

Through the application of yoga, liberation arises; indeed, through its manifestation comes destruction. Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, one should not reveal the yoga, having performed the five-fold immortal yoga every day.
Endowed with devotion, one should recite the *Sahasranāma* and the *Aṣṭaka* of the Goddess Śrī Kuṇḍalī;
O Lord! by means of the breath (*śvāsa*), one becomes a great yogi—of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the yoga-vidyā of the five immortals (*pañcāmara*), which illuminates all vidyās...

Then follows the attainment of the five immortals and the concentration on the eight limbs and so forth. First is the attainment of the five immortals, and then the practice of the minor yoga. I shall explain its method;
listen attentively. In this world, I alone am a true scholar of yoga.

"O Lord! I am indeed the witness of that, for the sake of the elevation of devotees. Now I shall describe to you the practice of the immortal yoga. By practicing thus, one who possesses a constant nature becomes like a sprout of yogas. Through the time spent in yoga, a person certainly attains perfection."
O Śaṅkara, listen now in due order to the five methods of *amarī* (immortality):

the *netī-yoga*, which indeed destroys great phlegm for the perfected ones; I shall next describe the *dantī-yoga*, which pierces the knots of the heart; and after that, the *dhautī-yoga*, which [purifies] everything.
The destruction of impurities: Neti-yoga is indeed supreme; it is the shaking of all limbs and the abdomen.
It is known as the supreme purifying yoga, the cleansing of the channels (nāḍīs).
Thus is the fivefold Amara-yoga, which is beyond the reach of ordinary yogis, to be practiced during the time of Yama and Niyama.

One should worship the rite of the five immortals (*pañcāmarakriyā*). Merely through the accomplishment of the immortals, the boon of immortality shall come to pass. At the time of performing this, one likewise consumes the five immortals.
By consuming the five immortals, one becomes immortal and partakes in the perfection of yoga. Those substances are as follows:

O Supreme Lord! I shall declare before you that [practice] by which those who are deficient do not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. One is indeed the immortal Dūrvā; one should bring its knot.
Another is the goddess Vijayā, Sarasvatī herself in the form of Siddhi. Another resides within the bilva leaf.
The one that brings satisfaction to Śiva is the *amarā*. Another, for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga, is considered the *nirguṇī amarā*.
Yet another is the *kālatulasī*, which most dearly pleases Lord Viṣṇu. These five should be known as *amarās* in the practice of yogic discipline. Of these, double the quantity should be taken.
The leaf of Vijayā is supreme. Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, or Śūdrā, she is honored everywhere. Having collected these substances, one should consume the excellent powder.
At the time of consuming that powder, one should recite these five mantras and so forth, and then eat.
Having performed this, a person shall be released from distress. Oṃ! O Hare, nourisher of the immortals!
You who are born from the source of nectar! O auspicious one, beloved of Hara, always make me immortal! Oṃ! Svāhā to Dūrvā! Thus for Dūrvā.
Furthermore, one should purify all the maidens with the Vijayā mantra: *Oṃ saṃvide brahma* and so forth; *Oṃ brāhmaṇyai namaḥ svāhā*; and *Oṃ Siddhimūlakare!
Devī* and so forth; as well as: *Half [the portion], O subduer of princes! O princess! O wielder of the trident!*

Aiṃ! Salutation to the Kṣatriya; Svāhā! Oṃ, [the mantra] beginning with "ajñānendhana" and so forth. Hrīṃ! Salutation to the Vaiśyā; Svāhā! Oṃ, [the mantra] beginning with "namasyāmi" and so forth. Śrīṃ! Salutation to the Śūdrā; Svāhā! Oṃ, O Goddess who bestows the perfection of the body! O dweller upon the bilva leaf!

Grant me immortality forever; make me equal to Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to the Giver of Śiva, Svāhā! Oṃ, Nirguṇḍī! Supreme Goddess! Over-deity of yogas! May she protect me, O immortal one, O bestower of the perfection of spiritual being! Obeisance! Oṃ, to the Dispeller of Sorrow...
Namaḥ svāhā! Oṃ, O beloved of Viṣṇu! O Great Illusion! O dweller in the flame of Time!
O Tulasī! Protect me always; make me alone immortal! Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Amarā, svāhā! Having again gathered them together in one place, [of] all of them...
One should perform the purification with "Oṃ Amṛte! Amṛtodbhave! and so forth. One should display the Dhenu-mudrā, the Yoni-mudrā, and the Matsya-mudrā.
The wise practitioner should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) according to the sequence of the Tattva-mudrās, even without mantras.

One should offer [the water] upon the head seven times with the name of the Guru; one should cause it to be offered upon the crown of the head seven times with the name of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevī*). Then one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the formula: "I satisfy [you], salutations, salutations.
Prior to this sentence, however, one should utter the chosen mantra (*iṣṭamantra*) of the supreme deity.

Having extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ) that precedes all [mantras], it is traditionally taught that one should then offer oblations into the mouth [of the fire] while first uttering the names of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). Having recited: "Oṃ vada vada, etc., O you who bring all beings under control! O you who have a trident at the throat of the enemy! Svāhā!"— [End of passage]

The best of practitioners, having mastery over the two stages of life (*āśrama*), rejoices in the nectar of the five immortals and is fond of the rules of *Kulācāra*. If one has attained the five immortals, that yogi shall possess a steady mind.
This is stated in the first chapter of the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*, as well as in the section on *Yama*.

Then follow restraint (niyama) and posture (āsana); the fourth is breath control (prāṇāyāma), and withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is the fifth. Retention (dhāraṇā) is declared the sixth, meditation (dhyāna) is called the seventh, and concentration (samādhi) is declared the eighth, which bestows the fruit of all merit.

Thus, Yājñavalkya and others know the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), while the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Kalasa and others practice Haṭha in such a manner; as stated in the fourth chapter of the Niruttara Tantra.
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— these they declare to be the six limbs of yoga.
Withdrawal of the senses is proclaimed to be accomplished by twelve cycles of breath control.
Through twelve cycles of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), auspicious concentration (dhāraṇā) is born.
Those proficient in meditation declare that meditation (dhyāna) consists of twelve cycles of concentration.
Samādhi is said to arise from twelve cycles of meditation alone; that which is supreme within samādhi—

The light is supreme and faces in all directions; when that is seen, no further action remains, and there is no coming or going. (From the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*): "Those ten restraints (*yama*) which have been proclaimed by the seers who perceive reality—the moderate diet among them is the one that is primary, not the others."

Among the observances (*niyamas*), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) alone is primary, not the others. Now listen to the best among the eighty-four hundred thousand postures (*āsanas*). That which was proclaimed by the Primordial Lord (*Ādinātha*) is here called *padmāsana*. Having carefully placed the two upturned feet upon the thighs...
Having placed the two hands palms-upward between the thighs, one should then fix the gaze upon the tip of the nose.
Raising the chin and pressing it against the chest, one should slowly draw in the breath through the base of the teeth with the tongue,
inhaling as deeply as possible according to one's capacity.

One should slowly fill the abdomen; having drawn [the breath] in according to one's capacity, one should slowly retain it in the abdomen; thereafter, one should slowly exhale from the abdomen according to one's capacity. This is declared to be the Padmāsana, which destroys all diseases. — *Grahajāmalam*
In the thirteenth chapter: Placing both soles of the feet upon the thighs and at the end of the genitals—this is the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which destroys all sins. Likewise:
Whether young, old, or afflicted by disease, through gradual practice...
One attains perfection in yoga through mastery over everything. Whether he be a Brahmin or a Śramaṇa,
an elder or even one who is harmful, a Kāpālika or a Cārvāka— provided he is wise, endowed with faith,
and constantly devoted to the practice of yoga— he shall obtain all perfections, being engaged in the ritual action.

How could he be a perfected one (*siddha*) if he performs no action? How can perfection arise merely by reciting the scriptures? Whether he be shaven-headed, or a bearer of a staff, or even clad in saffron robes; whether he be a reciter of the *Nārāyaṇīya*, or one with matted hair, or smeared with ashes—[none of these alone constitute perfection].

Whether one is a proponent of the *namaḥ śivāya* mantra, a worshiper of the Vedic *brahmārccā*, one honored at the twelve sacred sites, or one spoken of as being full of affection for many; or whether one is devoid of ritual action or even cruel—how could such a person attain success? Indeed, the wearing of [ascetic] dress is not the cause of success.

The cause is not that [which they claim]; rather, action alone is the cause of accomplishment. This is the truth, O Sāṅkṛti. How indeed can those who wear the garb of yoga for the sake of their genitals and bellies—being devoid of food and drink—deceive people?

Emaciated men worship with various deceptions, saying, "We are yoginīs," being solely devoted to sensual pleasures. One should gradually avoid those who are ignorant of such practices, devoid of yoga-exercise, yet claim to have achieved their purpose merely through words— those who merely wear the outward garb.

These states, when they have taken possession of one, always obstruct the practice of yoga; one should avoid them with great effort, for no such action bestows perfection. O Sage, during the initial stages of practice, laziness is always the first obstacle, while the second is—
It is proclaimed: the previously mentioned assembly of rogues is the third; the practice of mantra is the fourth;
alchemy (*dhātuvāda*) is the fifth; and the proponent of evil doctrines is the sixth.
Thus, many kinds of obstacles, like a mirage, appear momentarily before one's eyes but become firmly established in the mind.

A wise person, having recognized these [defects], should abandon them. Likewise, one should construct a very beautiful monastery with a narrow door, free from cracks, well-smeared with cow dung or lime with great care, and daily thoroughly swept by untiring attendants using a broom.
And it should be perfumed with fragrant scents and fumigated with guggulu and other incenses. (From the *Grahajāmalatantra*, Chapter Twelve).
The Lord said:

The science of Haṭha is to be kept strictly secret by yogins who desire spiritual perfection. The Goddess [of this science], when guarded, is powerful; but when revealed, she becomes powerless. A solitary hermitage should be established by Haṭhayogins in a region that is easy to traverse, righteous, well-supplied with food, and free from disturbances.
A place with a very small door, free from holes, pits, or hollows, neither too high nor too low, not too long,
properly smeared with thick cow-dung, stainless, cleared of all external clutter,
and outside of which a pavilion, a well, and an altar have been constructed, surrounded by a wall— this is what is prescribed.

O Deliverer from Saṃsāra! This is the description of the Yoga-maṭha. Having stayed in such a maṭha, free from all anxieties, one should practice Haṭhayoga according to the path instructed by the Guru. (From the Dattātreyasaṃhitā).

Free from defects such as feces, urine, and the like, as well as the eighteen [other] impurities, he should avoid sexual union with his wife, or [wear] clothing or even a deerskin; nor should he sit on anything other than a [proper] mat. Having spread out a recommended seat upon that [mat], he should sit.

A seat and so forth. Having sat there, being free from distraction and assuming the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), with the body straight and palms joined, he should bow to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Then, having restrained *piṅgalā* with the thumb of the right hand—

One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* very slowly; having restrained it according to one's capacity, one should then perform the *kumbhaka*. Then one should release it through the *piṅgalā* very gently, not with force.
Again, having drawn [the air] in through the *piṅgalā*, one should slowly fill the abdomen and hold it.

One should exhale the breath slowly according to one's capacity. Having filled [the lungs] with that same [breath] by which one exhaled, one should retain it without conflict. Thus, seated in the morning, one should perform twenty *kumbhakas*; this is the *kumbhaka* known as *sahita*.
Free from all planetary influences, one should likewise perform twenty *kumbhaka*s at midday;
similarly, one should perform twenty *kumbhaka*s in the evening,
accompanied by two *reka*s and *kumbha*s.

One should perform this four times every day, without indolence, day after day. One should continue thus for three months; thereafter, the purification of the *nāḍīs* occurs. (From the *Graha-jāmalam*, Chapter Thirteen: "Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold: by means of exhalation (*recaka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and inhalation (*pūraka*)."

Kumbhaka is considered to be of two kinds: *sahita* (with breath) and *kevala* (pure). That which is performed by first exhaling and then filling [the lungs] is indeed *sahitakumbhaka*. One should practice *sahita* until the mastery of *kevala* is attained. *Kevala* is the effortless retention of the vital air, having abandoned both exhalation and inhalation.
This is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*, which is indeed the *kevalakumbhaka* (pure retention).

One should practice *prāṇāyāma* according to the path instructed by the Guru. As long as the vital air (*vāyu*) remains in the body, so long is it said that there is life; death is its departure, therefore [one should control] the vital air.

One should bind [the breath]. When the vital winds do not move through the channels (*nāḍī*) filled with impurities, how can that state of impurity cease, and how can the purification of the body occur? Only when the entire wheel of channels, which was cluttered with impurities, attains purity, does one truly become a *yogin*.

Capable of sustaining the vital breath, one should then perform *prāṇāyāma* daily with a mind characterized by *sattva*. In this way, the impurities situated along the *suṣumnā* indeed reach desiccation. Seated in the *baddha-padmāsana*, the yogi should fill the *prāṇa* with the lunar breath (*candra*).

Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale again through the solar [nāḍī]. Having drawn in the prāṇa through the solar [nāḍī], one should slowly worship the abdomen. Having performed the kumbhaka according to the rule, one should exhale again through the lunar [nāḍī]. By whichever [nāḍī] one releases [the breath], by that very same one should fill it without obstruction.

Then one should exhale through the other [nostril], and not with force; that is to say, by means of the moon (the Ida) through the left nostril, and by means of the sun (the Pingala) through the right nostril. If one drinks the breath regulated through the Ida, one should subsequently exhale in the opposite manner, having drunk through the Pingala.

Then, having bound the breath (samīraṇa), one should exhale through the left [nostril]. For one who meditates upon the two orbs of the sun and the moon according to this method, the clusters of channels become purified after three months from the beginning of the night. [This should be done] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
And at midnight, one should practice *kumbhaka* breath-retentions up to eighty-four times, four times [per session]. Prāṇāyāma is the great dharma that bestows liberation upon the yogi.
O Goddess! By practicing prāṇāyāma day and night, one abandons the water [of worldly existence]. In the lowest [grade], it is twelve [retentions].

In the determination of *prāṇāyāma*, it is taught that the measure (*mātrā*) is double for the middling [level] and triple for the superior; this should be known from page 789. In the inferior [level], perspiration occurs;
in the middling, trembling occurs; and in the superior, the practitioner, repeatedly seated in the *baddha-padmāsana*, rises up with water.

One should perform the wiping of the limbs with the sweat produced [by practice]; thereby, a radiant glow accompanied by firmness arises in the body. When the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) occurs, then external signs arise in the body of the yogi; I shall describe them in their entirety. [The first is] lightness of the body.

There arises an increase of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) and certainly a thinning of the body. If they practice supreme mastery (*paramābhyāsa*) during the previously mentioned time, thereafter their power in the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*) will be according to their desire. From this desired retention of the vital air...

Success belongs to the Kumbhaka alone. When Kumbhaka is perfected—devoid of both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka)—nothing whatsoever remains difficult for him to attain within the three worlds.

Now, the fruit of the perfection of *kumbhaka*: first perspiration arises; one should perform massage with that. Then, from the gradual and steady retention of the breath, trembling occurs in the body of the yogi seated in his posture.

From practice even more intense than that, the state of the frog (*dārdurī*) certainly arises; just as a frog moves upon the ground by leaping up and springing forth, so does the yogi seated in the lotus posture move upon the ground. From practice even more intense than that, the abandonment of the earth occurs.

Remaining in the lotus posture (padmāsana), he exists having left the earth; indeed, being without support, he then bears a wondrous power. Whether eating little or much, the yogi is never distressed.
There is little urine and feces, and little sleep arises. Worms, scorpions, and...
Excessive sweating and foul odor of the body—these never arise for one who is renowned in all respects. At the time of the first practice, a diet of milk and clarified butter is recommended;
once the practice has become stable, there is no such need to observe those restrictions. Just as a lion [approaches] an elephant...

A tiger may be brought under control gradually; likewise, the vital air (vāyu) is subdued when practiced correctly, otherwise it destroys the practitioner. Through the proper application of breath control (prāṇāyāma), all diseases are destroyed;
through improper practice, all diseases arise, such as hiccups and asthma.

Cough, as well as pain in the head, ears, and eyes, and various other disorders arise from the derangement of the wind (vāyu). Thus ends the section on the disorders caused by the derangement of vāyu.
In the Dattātreyasaṃhitā: "Likewise, I shall describe those things to be avoided that cause obstacles to yoga: salt, mustard, food that is hot, dry, or contemptible;
excessive eating, and frequent sexual union with women, must be abandoned."
Service to the sacrificial fire must be abandoned, especially the company of rogues. In the *Grahajāmalatantra*:
"Excessive eating, travel abroad, idle chatter, the undertaking of restrictive vows, socializing with the masses, and fickleness—by these six, yoga perishes. Thus, these are to be avoided.
Yoga is indeed accomplished through six means: enthusiasm, resolve, fortitude, knowledge of reality, daring, and the renunciation of social contact. Likewise:
pungent, sour, bitter, salty, hot, and green leafy vegetables [should be avoided].

One should know that in this [condition], unwholesome things such as *sauvīraka* (sour gruel), oil, mustard, fish, wine, the meat of goats and other animals, curd, buttermilk, horse gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*kola*), oil-cakes, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), garlic (*laśuna*), and so forth, are unwholesome when consumed with food.

Furthermore, food that has been reheated is [unwholesome]. Food that is excessively salty, or abounding in oil-cakes, tubers, and sour vegetables, is harmful. One should avoid the company of wicked people and the practice of exposing oneself to the heat of fire. Likewise, one should avoid bodily mortifications such as bathing in the morning, fasting, and so forth. Thus end the unwholesome things.
Likewise: wheat, rice, peas, barley, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice;
milk, ghee, sugar-candy, fresh butter, sugar, and honey; ginger, long pepper, *kaṇaphala*, and the five types of potherbs; and divine water such as milk and the like.

The yogi should partake of food that is savory, very sweet, unctuous, delightful, and conducive to the growth of the bodily constituents (dhātus)— food that is desired by the mind and follows the path of Indra.
Thus are the wholesome things.
In the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*: "I shall now declare the means for the swift accomplishment of yoga. Milk, ghee, sweet food, and a moderate diet are recommended.
Having eliminated obesity through the six purificatory acts (*ṣaṭkarma*), one is freed from the afflictions of phlegm, fat, and impurities."

One should then perform *prāṇāyāma*; it is accomplished without effort. O Dear One! By *prāṇāyāmas* alone all impurities are dried up. Having cast off fat, phlegm, and so forth, the sixfold action (*karma-ṣaṭka*) is not approved. If the state consisting of a well-disposed mind [is maintained], the wind...
One should practice diligently; one intent on the practice of *pavana* attains the yoga of the six acts (*ṣaṭkarma*).

Even the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, were intent on the practice of *pavana*, and thus they attained perfection. Therefore, one should practice *pavana* as long as the vital wind (*marut*) is bound within the body.

As long as the mind is free from desire, and if one performs *trāṭaka* between the eyebrows, whence can there be fear for that duration? When the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) has been dried up through the proper restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the wind enters through the mouth, piercing the opening of the *suṣumnā*. In the wind...

When the movement is moderate, steadiness of mind arises; that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady is itself the state of *manonmanī*. To achieve that, one who knows the particulars should perform various types of *kumbhakas* (breath-retentions). Through the practice of diverse *kumbhakas*, one attains manifold accomplishments (*siddhis*).

Now, regarding *trāṭaka*: one should gaze with a steady eye at a subtle object with great effort until tears fall; that, O Great Goddess, is called *trāṭaka*. *Trāṭaka* should be kept secret with effort, like a casket of gold. As for the various types of *kumbhaka*:
Sūryabheda, Uḍḍīyāna, Mūlabandha, Śītkāra, Śītalī, Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Mūrcchā, and Plāvanī—these are the seven types of *kumbhaka*. First is Sūryabheda:
having assumed a comfortable posture, the yogi then binds the *muktāsana* and [inhales] through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*).

Having slowly drawn in the air situated within the fire, one should retain it in *kumbhaka* from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails, until the limit of restraint is reached. Then, the wise practitioner should slowly exhale the air through the left channel (*iḍā*). The fruit of this is the purification of the skull and the destruction of disorders caused by wind (*vāta*).
It destroys the defects caused by worms. This supreme practice of Sūryabheda should be performed again and again. || 1 ||

Now, the practice called Uḍḍīyāna: Having restrained the mouth and slowly drawn in the breath through both nostrils, one should hold the prāṇa with sound until it reaches the end of the throat and the heart, as before; then one should exhale through the iḍā. The fruit [is as follows].
This [practice], bound by the fires and kindled, removes phlegm diseases;
it destroys disorders of the channels, dropsy, the bodily constituents (dhātus), goiters, and other defects. This kumbhaka, called uḍḍīya, is to be performed whether walking or standing. (2)
Now, the sound "śīt": one should always produce the sound "śīt" in the mouth and perform yawning in the nose. By practicing in this manner, one becomes a second Kāmadeva. This is the fruit.

Having attained the circle of Yoginīs, one becomes the agent of creation and dissolution; neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor fainting arises. One’s body becomes autonomous (svacchanda), free from all calamities. Without this, truly, there can be no lord of yogins.

On the circle of the earth, he who constantly drinks the vital breath (prāṇa) through the root of the palate by means of the tongue—with effort, success arises above, and there shall be the destruction of all diseases. || 3 ||

Now, Śītalī: Having drawn in the air with the tongue as before, beginning with the kumbhaka, one should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils, O Dear One! [The fruit: The fruit is that one becomes free from fever, thirst, and hunger; one obtains a cool body and a pleasant complexion; and one conquers all diseases arising from wind (vāta). Thus is Śītalī.
This kumbhaka, named Śītalī, indeed destroys disorders such as abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement, fever, seminal depletion, and thirst; it is truly a nectar.

Now, the Bhastrikā [breathing technique]: Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), O Dear One, with the neck and abdomen held straight, one should carefully close the mouth and exhale the breath through the nostrils.
In that same manner, one should clearly move the vital air (pavana) residing within one's own body; thus it becomes firmly established.

Then, from the heart, throat, and skull, one should forcefully fill the breath slightly as far as the heart-lotus; then one should exhale again in the same manner, filling it again and again, just as a blacksmith would move a bellows with force. In that very way...

One should slowly move the breath residing within one's own body. When fatigue becomes complete during the retention (*bandhana*), then, leaving out the two index fingers, one should firmly press the middle of the nose. Having performed the *kumbhaka* as before, one should exhale the air through the *iḍā*. [The Fruit: The fruit is as follows: by this practice, the fire of digestion increases, all diseases are destroyed, and the body becomes light. One attains the power of flight, and the yogin becomes like a second wind-god. This is known as the *bhujangī mudrā*, which bestows the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*). It should be practiced daily for the purification of the channels. Thus ends the description of the *bhujangī mudrā*.
It pacifies wind, bile, and phlegm; it increases the digestive fire of the body;
it obstructs the *kuṇḍalinī* in the *cakra*; it removes heaviness, bestows auspiciousness, and is pure.
Situated at the mouth of the *brahmanāḍī*, it destroys *kapha* and eliminates impurities.
This kumbhaka known as *bhastrā* should be performed specifically until perspiration arises, thereby piercing the three knots (*granthi*). || 5 ||
Now, regarding *bhrāmarī*: the resonance of the Vedas is the inhalation (*pūraka*), the humming of bees is the exhalation (*recaka*) performed very slowly;
through such practice of yoga by the lords of yogis, a certain creeper of bliss arises within the consciousness. (6)

Now, *mūrcchā*: At the end of inhalation (*pūraka*), having firmly applied the *jālandhara* lock, one should exhale slowly; this is called *mūrcchā*, which bestows the bliss of mental absorption (*manomūrcchā*). (7) Now, *plāvanī*: The abdomen is filled by the internalized wind that has been set in motion [from the base].
Even in deep water, one floats directly like a lotus leaf.

From the *Rudrajāmala*, in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*: "O you who are worshipped by heroes, listen to the rules for the practice of *neti-yoga* (p. 793), by which there shall be the burning away of all phlegm located in the head. One should insert a very fine and firm thread into the nostril and [then] into the mouth-cavity."

Having brought [the tongue] together and joined it, one should rely upon this; again and again, the yogi should constantly rub it by means of moving it back and forth. O Supreme Lord! One should gradually perform the expansion of the cord. By the yoga of *neti*, the cavity of the nose becomes stainless.
But at the time of the movement of the vital breath, O Lord, there is great bliss! || 1 ||

Thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the *dantīyoga*. At the time of cleaning the teeth, one should employ this yoga. The tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana-kāṣṭha*) should be one and a half cubits (*sārddha-hasta*) in length, neither too thick nor too thin, and it should be fresh.
One should carefully take a fresh, unripened tree branch that resembles a lotus stalk, which is supple and excellent. Having taken such a tooth-stick, one should consume it at the time of dawn.
Its tip should be the length of the joint of the little finger; thus [it should be used].

One should perform the chewing gracefully with the rows of teeth; having rinsed that with water, one should slowly effect the withdrawal. The purification of body, speech, and mind should be performed very gradually, until the tip of the wooden stick reaches the root of the navel.

One must necessarily practice daily that which is unagitated and increasingly subtle, until a fracture occurs in the water-wheel (*jalacakra*) within the heart. During that time, every day at dawn, one should perform the dental purification; [for] the fracture of the vessel of phlegm (*kapha*) within the heart [is the goal].
It certainly arises. One attains the bliss of the arrival of the vital breath (*pavana*) which is full of yoga;

the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) arises from *lavaṇa* (the tongue-tip), and acidity arises from *kumbhaka* (retention). Sweetness, vegetables, curd-rice, and eating twice a night—the yogi must certainly employ these.
If one desires yoga here, one should take one part of its own seed and two parts of rice;
having obtained this excellent cooked mixture, one should consume it with ghee and milk. Or else, the wise one should cause the Kundalinī to be satiated with milk alone.

And one should satiate those of the form of the *kula* with milk. O Śaṅkara! If a yogi knows this satiation of Kuṇḍalinī, he shall become a yogi without effort and will certainly become a sovereign of the wise.
In the thirty-seventh chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
I shall explain the *dhautī* yoga, by performing which one becomes stainless; it is an extremely secret yoga that brings about the completion for men. If one does not practice this yoga, then...
He shall meet his death. O Lord! Who on this earth attains perfection without the practice of *dhautī*?
One who, by means of a cloth finer than the finest, measuring thirty-two cubits in length, slowly and gradually [draws it] in by the measure of one cubit at a time—
One should perform the ritual practice for as long as it takes to traverse thirty-two cubits;

by the application of this practice, the yogi becomes such at that very moment. Gradually, the practitioner of mantra becomes accomplished and brings the web of time under his control. Within this [process], the seats are situated within the body.

One should practice; for it is the determination of the meaning of the Tantras that the perfection of yoga is attained on a firm seat. When the mantra is mastered, the attainment of the Supreme (Parā) occurs through the fivefold yogic postures. O Lord! taking this fine garment—eight fingers wide at the sides and thirty-two fingers long—one should grasp this subtle, excellent cloth.
The ascetic should cause [these] to be performed; having conquered his senses, he should always practice knowledge and meditation.
Through improper conduct and the power of the senses, there shall be decline;
through the fault of association with those who commit the primary great sins, various forms of ruin come to pass.
O Mahādeva! This is a virtuous deed worthy of you. Whether one is old, in the prime of youth, or a child;

wherever one may be, by means of this single mantra, one shall become long-lived, immortal, and beloved by the world. Through the perfection of this mantra, one attains all desired perfections and becomes the sovereign lord of all accomplishments. [This occurs] gradually, step by step.
One should always perform that which destroys the defects of time, which severs the knots of the heart,
and increases all the limbs; for one who possesses divine prowess always abandons that desire born of the *dhautī* practice, which is the cause of great death.

Indeed, immediately after the yoga of the messenger (*dūtī*), one should perform the practice of *neḍaṇī*. Merely by the yoga of *neḍaṇī*, one becomes like *neḍaṇī* upon the seat; simply through the accomplishment of *neḍaṇī*, one becomes long-lived and free from disease.
I shall explain the cause of that; listen attentively. Having eaten...

One should wait for one day after eating cooked mung bean rice; one should wait until one's own stomach is empty, remaining free from the desire for solid food. One should repeatedly move the contents within the middle of one's stomach and cause the stomach to rotate like a potter’s wheel.

By the mere movement of all the limbs, the power Kuṇḍalī is set in motion. O Lord! Through the movement of the goddess Kuṇḍalī, consciousness arises. Immediately following this, O God, the cleansing is proclaimed; indeed, by the cleansing of the channels (nāḍīs), [consciousness is purified].

He shall become a treasury of all sciences; he shall attain mastery over the wind and possess mastery over the five elements. The wise man should always and everywhere practice the *muṇḍāsana* posture;
having assumed the *ūrdhvapadmāsana*, he should perform his recitation (*japa*) with his hand held downwards. At that time...

If one is capable of performing the *muṇḍikāsana* for three days, then indeed all the channels (*nāḍīs*) will come under control; of this there is no doubt. Through the yoga of cleansing the channels, the practitioner attains perfection.
How can one who does not know the *neḍaṇī* prepare to perform it? He is truly steadfast.
He who has mastered his senses and possesses intelligence,
yet does not strive to reach the further shore of the practice of *nāḍī-yoga*, must certainly perform the cleansing of the channels and other such preparatory means by way of *nāḍī-yoga*.

O Mahākāla! One who is intent upon the cleansing of the channels (*nāḍī*) indeed becomes like the Lord of the Kings of Kings. Cleansing occurs solely through the retention of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*); without the yoga of cleansing, purification of the body does not arise. [This is] the cleansing of the channels and so forth.

Through the consumption of wind while seated on a skull (muṇḍāsana), the yogi diligently effects the destruction of phlegm, bile, and other humors. Indeed, the grasping of the vital air occurs thus; however, O Lord, one should not practice this solely at the time of the *iḍā* and *iḍā-vaśa-kālaka*, but should always perform it at other times as well. As long as one does not know the *iḍā*, so long will one not [master] the vital air.

One should drink [the breath]; one should not retain it for too long, as that causes diseases of wind (vāta), impurities, and so forth. One should simply count the breaths until the *iḍā* is perfected; and through the mastery of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one comes under the control of the five winds (*pañcavāyu*).
In the *Grahajāmalatantra*: "One whose *medas* (fat) and *śleṣman* (phlegm) are predominant should first perform the six purificatory acts (*ṣatkarma*).
Otherwise, one should not perform them, because of the absence of [excessive] *doṣas*. These six acts are: *dhautī*, *gajakaraṇī*, *vastī*, *naulī*, *trāṭaka*, and likewise *kapālabhāti*."
O Maheśvarī! This sixfold practice (*karma-ṣaṭka*) is to be kept secret; it is the means for purifying the body (*ghaṭa*).
Having assumed manifold qualities, the preeminent among yogis is worshipped. Among these, first is *dhautī*.

One should slowly swallow a cloth soaked [in the liquid], measuring four finger-breadths wide and fifteen cubits long, according to the path instructed by the Guru. Then one should draw it back out; this is the washing, that is, the act of cleansing. [It cures] cough, asthma, splenic disorders, leprosy, and diseases of phlegm.
Twenty [types of impurities] are purified by the grace of the practice of *dhautī*; of this there is no doubt. || 1 ||

Now, the *gajakariṇī*: Expelling the substance located within the abdomen after drawing up the downward-moving wind (*apāna*) to the level of the throat, and [expelling it] through the anal passage by means of gradual practice—that is called the *gajakariṇī*. (2)

Now, regarding enema therapy (*vasti*): Having positioned the anus in water that reaches the navel while seated on a movable stool in a squatting posture, one should perform the cleansing and the application of the enema fluid; this is the procedure for *vastikarma*. By the power of *vastikarma*, diseases such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), and ailments arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* are eliminated, resulting in the destruction of all diseases.

The practice of the Janavasti procedure bestows clarity upon the elements, the sense organs, and the internal organs; it grants luster and the brilliance of fire, and destroys the accumulation of all defects. (3)

Now, the *laulī*: O Supreme Goddess! One whose shoulders are bent should rotate the belly with great speed from left to right and right to left on the ground and so forth; this is the *laulī*. [The Fruit: The fruit is as follows: one attains the state of the *khecarī* and becomes a master of all the *mudrās*. One is liberated from all diseases and is never again subject to rebirth. One becomes a knower of all things and is honored by the gods. One who practices this *laulī* for six months attains the supreme state. Thus ends the *laulī*.

This *laulī* is the crest-jewel of *haṭha*-practices; it always kindles the weak digestive fire, acts as a catalyst for the various digestive processes, bestows bliss, and dries up all defects and diseases.
Now, the *natī* [technique]: One should insert a thread measuring one *vitasti* into the nasal passage and count with the mouth;
this, O Parameśvarī, is the *natī*. [Its] fruit: It purifies the skull, is beneficial for the throat, and bestows divine vision. Whatever disease arises above...
It quickly inclines that [mind] through bowing. Thus, there is only a difference in name between "not-bowing" and "bowing. However, "not-bowing" was explained previously. (5)

Now follows *kapālabhātī*: Like two bellows of a blacksmith, with earrings in a state of agitation—this is known as *kapālabhātī*, which destroys the disorder of phlegm (*kapha*). Thus ends *kapālabhātī* (6).

In the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*: "From practice even more intense than that, great power arises, by which one attains the siddhi of moving upon the earth and becomes capable of conquering those who move upon the earth;
whether it be a tiger, a buffalo, a wild beast, a bear, an elephant, or a lion, he causes them to die."
From the yogin’s striking with his hand, the form of Kandarpa appears just as it is for that yogin as well.
At that time, a great obstacle may arise for the yogin through negligence. Women, falling under the power of that form, desire union with him; if he indeed engages in such union—
One's *bindu* perishes; from the loss of *bindu*, self-destruction occurs and incapacity arises. Therefore, one should avoid contact with women with the utmost care.
For that yogi, success (*siddhi*) shall come through the constant retention of *bindu*. Therefore...

A yogi must protect the *bindu* with every effort; therefore, having entered into the secret, he should mutter the *praṇava* with the protracted (*pluta*) measure for the sake of destroying previously accumulated sins. This *praṇava* removes all obstacles and destroys all defects.
Through such practice of yoga, success arises from the very commencement;

thereafter, for one who constantly practices the breath, the stage of the "jar" (ghaṭāvasthā) occurs. In this way, the prāṇa and apāna, the mind and the vital air, as well as the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), are brought into union without mutual conflict.

In the same way, the state of two jars is well-known and recorded by the yogis. I shall describe some of the signs that may appear therein. One should abandon the fourfold practice previously mentioned, whether by day or by night.
One should practice for exactly one month; every day, one should perform the *kevala-kumbhaka* once. For in this way, there is indeed withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); thus indeed do yogis practice.
It is the yogi who clearly withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses.

Having established the breath-retention (kumbhaka), that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra). Whatever one sees with the eyes, one should contemplate that within the Self; whatever one hears with the ears, one should contemplate that within the Self; whatever one tastes with the tongue, one should contemplate that within the Self.

Whatever limb the skin touches, one should contemplate that very thing as being within the Self. In this manner, the yogi, diligent and unwearied, should daily practice for each watch (yāma) with as many repetitions as there are sense organs. Then, manifold powers arise.
For the yogin, there will certainly arise the power of hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and likewise the ability to travel great distances in an instant.

There shall be perfection of speech, the power to move at will, and the state of invisibility. Furthermore, by the application of excrement and urine, base metals become gold, as well as the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).

And it may arise through the practice of constant application; then the wise yogi should strive for the perfection of yoga. These obstacles exist for the sake of great accomplishment; the wise man should not take delight in them. He should never display his own power to anyone.

Sometimes a mortal may reveal [this] to one endowed with devotion; otherwise, he should conduct himself among people like a fool, like a deluded person, or even like one who is deaf, for the sake of concealing his own power. Otherwise, indeed, there would be many disciples.

Doubt: People always pray to the Lord of Yogis for their respective goals; thus, being preoccupied with performing those activities, one may become lax in one's own practice. Deprived of practice, one consequently falls into worldly existence. Therefore, without forgetting the words of the Guru, one should practice day and night.

In this way, the state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā) arises through the yoga of innate practice. Without practice, this yoga is in vain; it is not accomplished by mere social gathering. Therefore, one should practice this yoga with every effort. Thereafter, the state of familiarity (paricayāvasthā) arises through the yoga of practice.

The vital air (vāyu), having been thoroughly mastered through effort, should awaken the Kuṇḍalinī along with the self and enter the Suṣumnā without obstruction. The mind, together with the vital air, should then enter the Great Path (mahāpatha). Indeed, the Great Path, the cremation ground (śmaśāna), and the Suṣumnā are one and the same.
There are differences in various other doctrines, yet no difference is found in the result. He whose mind,
together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), enters the *suṣumnā* during the day— having discerned what is possible and what is impossible— the yogi [attains this] in solitude.
With effort, one should perform the fivefold retention (*dhāraṇā*), which removes the fear of each respective element.

In the fourteenth chapter of the *Grahajāmalatantra*: "Just as the serpent-king is the support for the earth together with its mountains and forests, so indeed is Kuṇḍalinī the support of all Haṭha-tantras. The "serpent-king" is Ananta. When she, who is asleep, awakens through the grace of the Guru...

Kuṇḍalinī: Then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced; then the path of the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes like a royal highway. Then the mind is without support, and then there is the deception of Time. The path of emptiness (śūnyapadavī) is Suṣumnā, as it has been stated right there:

Suṣumnā, the path of emptiness (śūnyapadavī), the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the great path (mahāpatha), the cremation ground (śmaśāna), Śaṅkhinī, and the middle way (madhyamārga) are synonymous terms. By the phrase "extending like a royal highway" (rājapathāyata), easy passage is indicated. Therefore, with every effort, one should awaken the Goddess.
One should practice the mudrās while [the consciousness] is asleep at the opening of the *brahmarandhra*.
These are: Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, Khecarī, Uḍḍīyāna, Mūlabandha, the bandha known as Jālandhara, and the practice called Viparītakaraṇī.
p. 799) The activation of the power of expansion (*vijṛmbhaṇa-śakti*). This group of ten mudrās destroys old age and death. O Goddess of Gods!
This divine [teaching] has been told, which bestows the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) and is beloved by all the Siddhas.

It is difficult to obtain even for the gods; it must be guarded with great effort like a casket of jewels, and must never be told to anyone, just as the secret amorous dalliances of a woman of noble family are kept hidden.

Now, regarding Mahāmudrā: In the Dattātreyasaṃhitā, [it is said]: "I shall explain with reverence the Mahāmudrā as spoken by Bhairava. One should place the heel of the left foot at the site of the *yoni*. Having pressed down the right foot with both hands..."

One should hold [the breath] firmly. Having placed the chin upon the heart, one should fill it with air again. Having retained it by means of *kumbhaka* according to one's capacity, one should exhale. Having practiced with the left side, one should practice with the right side as well. As for that which is extended—
One should place the foot upon the thighs. In the *Grahajāmalatantra*:
"Having pressed the vulva with the left heel, having extended the right foot, one should hold it firmly with both hands, placing the mouth against the throat."
One should hold the breath above [the head]. Just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like the shape of the staff, so too the Kuṇḍalinī power suddenly becomes straightened.
Then that state of death arises, residing in the two petals; therefore, one should do this very gradually.

One should not emit that [semen] with force. Indeed, this Mahāmudrā is revealed to you out of affection. As for the fruit: the defects such as the great afflictions (*mahākleśa*) and so forth, as well as death and the like, are exhausted; therefore, O Maheśvarī, it is called Mahāmudrā.

Having practiced with the lunar limb (*candrāṅga*), one should practice with the solar limb (*sūryāṅga*). When the number [of repetitions] becomes equal, then one should release the mudrā. Indeed, there is nothing wholesome or unwholesome; even all tastes become flavorless. Even terrible poison, once consumed, is digested like nectar (*pīyūṣa*).

Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, and splenic disorders—all such ailments perish for one who practices Mahāmudrā. This Mahāmudrā, which destroys old age and death, has been described; it must be guarded with great effort and not given to just anyone.
Now, the Mahābandha: Having bound this very mudrā as the Mahābandha, one should practice it. Remaining in the Mahābandha posture on the ground, one should gently strike the buttocks.
This very Mahābandha is practiced by perfected men (siddhas). [One should place] the heel...
One should place the left foot in the position of the *yoni*.

Likewise, having placed the right foot upon the left thigh, one should fill [the mouth] with the breath, fix the chin firmly against the heart, press the *yoni*, contract it, and fix the mind in the center; then one should exhale.

Thus, this is called the Great Bandha (Mahābandha). Having practiced this Great Bandha, which bestows great siddhis, the yogi should practice it on the left side and then again on the right side. This is the obstructer of the upward movement of all the channels (nāḍīs).
It maintains the confluence of the triple stream (Triveṇī-saṅgama) and causes the mind to reach Kedāra;
for just as a woman endowed with beauty and charm is [worthless] without a man, so too Mahāmudrā and Mahābandha are fruitless when devoid of Vedha. || 2 ||

Now, the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha).
