The yogi, established in the Great Lock (Mahābandha), having made the breath flow in a single stream, and having blocked its movement with the wind while holding it with the throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā), being fully composed, should gently strike his buttocks against the ground; [this is done] for both nostrils.

Having drawn [the breath] inward, the wind moves swiftly; scorched by the moon, sun, and fire, it indeed arises for the sake of immortality. Once the state of deathlessness has arisen, whence then can there be fear of death?
Furthermore, the punishment of the king and the binding of the tongue would be beneficial and praised.
The practice of Mahāvedha bestows great siddhis; the three Bandhas are a great secret that destroys old age and death, increases the digestive fire,
grants the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, and removes sin without obstruction for the duration of a watch (three hours).

Every day, for one watch [of the night], he should first perform ablution, then attend upon women, and then approach the fire— this being the dream [vision] for those possessing the right training during the initial stage of practice, which is by nature a mass of merit and always a destroyer of the flood of sins.

Now, concerning Khecarī: There is no food equal to that of the Siddhas, no Kumbhaka equal to Kevala, no Mudrā equal to Khecarī, and no dissolution (laya) equal to Nāda. One should perform the cutting and moving within the body, increasing it through the sequence of Kalās until it reaches the space between the eyebrows.
One directly attains the perfection of Khecarī. In the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*:

"Having turned back the tongue and bound it within the cavity of the skull, with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows—this is the Khecarī Mudrā. In the *Grahajāmalatantra*: "The weapon [the tongue] resembles the leaf of the *snuhī* plant..."

[The instrument] is very sharp, smooth, and stainless. Then, for the sake of maintaining the proper limit, one should cut [the hair] by the measure of a single hair. Having applied powdered rock salt (*saindhava*) and *pathyā* (the *harītakī* fruit), it proceeds [to heal]. When another seven days have arrived, [one should again cut] by the measure of a single hair.
One should sever it. Thus, one who is constantly disciplined should practice in this sequence for six months;
after six months, the binding of the vessels at the root of the tongue is destroyed. Now, the Yoginīs, wearing bamboo bark garments, sever the very root of the tongue in this same sequence.

Alternatively, the yogi who knows the rules for the timing of the practice should wrap the head—the abode of Vāgīśvarī—with a cloth and slowly draw it upward. The "abode of Vāgīśvarī" refers to the tongue;
its "head" is the tip portion. The measurement of the cloth is likewise right there: it should be one *vitasti* in length.

Its length and width are four finger-breadths; it is said to be soft and white for the occasion of wrapping and support. Furthermore, O Dear One, after only six months, through further drawing-in (saṅkarṣaṇa), it increases up to the midpoint between the eyebrows.
From the ear-hole to the corner of the mouth, and from there downward to the root of the chin, it proceeds with gradual movement.

O Dear One! From above the throat, it wanders transversely for the duration of a *krośa*. Then, O Goddess, in the second year, by its own play, having returned from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), it remains there.

O you who are saluted by the wind! Having rubbed [the tongue] at the root of the palate for seven days within oneself, one should purify all impurities according to the previously mentioned method. Having rubbed it with the tips of the fingers, one should place the tongue there; very gradually, up to the end of the head.

The breaker of the great adamantine door-panel; may the Vidyā, renowned throughout the three worlds, be victorious in the past! One should perform the six-limbed practice with this [Vidyā] which pierces the six wheels. She moves through the sky, uninvited, having cast aside all sequences of ritual action, at the arising of the eternal.

O lady of excellent complexion! This practice, which effects the union with the head and the earth, must be performed gradually through repeated training. If its dissolution were simultaneous, the body would go to destruction.
Therefore, O beloved, the yoga should be practiced very slowly by the practitioner. Thus...

Having practiced for three years, one shall certainly enter the Gate of Brahman (brahmadvāra). Having pierced the six wheels (ṣaṭcakrāṇi) and raised up the serpent-power (śaktibhujagī) residing at the base,
one should break through the knot and the great western head that has the form of a rampart, and lead [the power] upward.
Having churned with the mind even the head of the breath-oblation until it is stainless, one should drink that very *liṅga* released from the lunar orb; he is Śiva himself in person.
If a man were to constantly drink with his tongue turned upward the flood of sevenfold nectar— which is delicious, cools the body, removes the fear of sin, and wards off hunger and thirst—
he would indeed attain stability of the physical form and, like Śiva, dwell beyond death and disease.
Misfortune goes to its destruction, and everything spreads forth after wandering through the three periods of time.

The tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse; the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows—this is the Khecarī Mudrā. Having turned the vital energy (kalā) away from the external face, one should cause it to revolve in the triple path (tripatha). That becomes the Khecarī Mudrā, and it is called the Sky-Wheel (vyomacakra).
The yogi who, having placed the tongue at the upper [palate], remains thus for even half a moment,

is liberated from sense objects and from disease, death, old age, and the like. For him who maintains this *mudrā*, there shall be neither disease nor death, neither sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor shall there be fainting.

He knows the Khecarī; he is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma; he is not constrained by time—he who possesses the Khecarī Mudrā. Because the mind moves in the ether (*kha*) and the tongue has gone to move in the ether, this mudrā is named Khecarī and is honored by all postures and salutations.

By whomsoever the aperture above the uvula is delighted by Khecarī-mudrā, his bindu does not leak even when embraced by a passionate woman. Even when the bindu has moved and reached the circle of the womb, it ascends forcefully by means of the power [of the breath] when bound by Yoni-mudrā.
The practitioner of yoga who, having become steady, performs the drinking of soma with the tongue turned upwards, undoubtedly conquers death within half a month. Just as fire consumes fuel,
so does the embodied soul not abandon the body when it is filled with the *soma* creeper.

The embodied soul never abandons a body that is perpetually filled with the digits of the moon. For that yogi whose body is eternally filled with the digits of the moon, even if bitten by Takṣaka, the poison does not spread. Therefore, one should perform this practice constantly, being ever-disciplined and composed.
One should leave the tongue protruding upward and drink the nectar of the Immortal (amaravāruṇī).
I bow to him who is of noble lineage; others are destroyers of their own lineage. By the word "cow" (go), the tongue is indicated;
its insertion into the palate is indeed the consumption of "cow-flesh," which destroys even the greatest sins. This is the bestower of the tongue's entry [into the palate].

It is indeed established by the vital wind (*bhūtavāyu*). From the moon, the world flows; that shall be the nectar of the immortals (*amaravāruṇī*). Having restrained the tongue in the cavity with the face turned upward, one forcibly obtains from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that which has flowed from the sixteen-petaled lotus at the crown of the head.

One should contemplate the supreme Śakti; he who drinks that pure stream of nectar, the water consisting of the waves and digits of her [energy], becomes free from defects, and that yogi, with a body as tender as a lotus stalk, lives for a long time.
If the tongue, dripping with nectar, constantly kisses the tip of the uvula— whether it be salty, pungent,
or like milk or clarified butter—
the removal of diseases, the end of old age, and the vomiting forth of the limbs of the scriptures belong to him.

There may be immortality endowed with the eight supernatural powers, and the attraction of celestial women. There is but one seed-syllable consisting of creation, and one mudrā, which is Khecarī. There is but one God who is without support, and one state, which is Manonmanī. This brings forth wisdom after a very long time.
Endowed with the five principles, the Khecarīmudrā abides in that void which is stainless.
Now, the Mūlabandha:
pressing the perineum with the heel, one should contract the anus; by raising the apāna upward, this is called Mūlabandha. It draws the downward-moving apāna upward.
O Maheśvarī! By means of contraction, I shall describe that as the *mūlabandha*.

Having firmly pressed the perineum with the heel, one should forcefully contract the vital air (*vāyu*). In this manner, the wind (*samīraṇa*), impelled by the *prāṇa* and other breaths, repeatedly ascends upward.

The *bindu* and the root [channel] become one through *mūlabandha*; from that, the perfect accomplishment of yoga arises—of this there is no doubt. When the two vital winds, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, attain oneness through *mūlabandha*, they proceed to the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.

Through the unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa*, and through the depletion of urine and feces, even an old man becomes young by means of constant *mūlabandha*. When the *apāna* moves upward and reaches the region of the *yoni-maṇḍala*, then the long flame issuing from its mouth increases, struck by the vital air (*vāyu*). Thereafter—
When the vital breaths have entered the bound source (the *baddhayoni*), their own essential form is like a lamp smeared with oil that blazes within the body; by that heat, the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī,
being heated, increases in power and, like a female serpent struck by a staff, hisses and attains a straightened state.
Having entered the aperture, one should then proceed into the interior of the Brahma-nāḍī; therefore, O Supreme Goddess, the Mūlabandha must always be performed. || 5 ||

(p. 804) Now, Uḍḍīyāna: Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), when bound therein, flies upward (*uḍḍīyate*) through the *suṣumnā*, it should be known as "Uḍḍīyāna," O Supreme Goddess! It is called Uḍḍīyāna because the great bird, though exhausted, performs a flight (*uḍḍīna*). Uḍḍīyāna.

That indeed is what is called "bandha" (the lock) therein. One should perform it at the forehead in the posterior part of the abdomen, above the navel; for this is the Uḍḍīyāna bandha, the lion that destroys the elephant of death. O Supreme Goddess! Uḍḍīyāna is said to be innate (sahaja).
Through practice, one who is free from drowsiness shall become young again even if old.

By exerting effort to raise the tongue upward from the navel and downward toward the palate, one certainly conquers death after six months of practice; there is no doubt, provided one is established in the vajrāsana posture.

One should firmly hold the feet with both hands; near the region of the groin, one should apply pressure to the binding there. One should direct [the breath] toward the palate, the belly, the heart, and the throat, very gradually, so that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) attains mastery over the abdomen. This applies to all of them indeed.

Among the bindings, Uḍḍiyānaka is the most excellent. O Maheśānī! In Uḍḍiyāna, liberation becomes natural. And in the Dattātreyasaṃhitā: "Uḍḍiyāna is always described by the sages as being innate (sahaja). He who, established in sattva, practices it—even if he is old—"
It becomes youthful. One should diligently direct the *prāṇa* both above and below the navel;
by practicing this for six months, one certainly conquers death—of this there is no doubt. He who constantly practices the *mūlabandha* is indeed a knower of yoga.
Now, the Jālandhara-bandha. In the *Grahajāmalatantra*: "Contracting the throat, one should firmly place the chin against the heart;
this is the bandha called Jālandhara, which produces the imperishable nectar. And in the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*:
Contracting the throat, one should hold the vital air firmly in the heart;

this is the Jālandhara Bandha, which indeed transcends the two nectars. The nectar constantly flowing from the thousand-petaled lotus situated in the skull, which resides within the fire at the navel, attains the state of a drop (bindu).

Just as fire [consumes] for embodied beings, so too one should not drink that nectar, yet one should drink it oneself; through constant practice, it proceeds by the western path and thus makes the body immortal. Therefore, one should practice Jālandhara-bandha. As stated in the *Grahajāmalatantra*: "For it binds the network of channels within the head."

Food does not go [downward]. Therefore, the Jālandhara lock, when applied at the throat, destroys the flood of suffering. When the Jālandhara lock is performed and the constriction at the throat is made, the nectar does not cook in the fire, nor does the vital wind rush upward.
By means of constricting the throat alone, one should firmly retain [the breath] in the two channels;
this is to be known as the Middle Wheel, the binding of the sixteen supports.
These three bindings are supreme and practiced by the great Siddhas. Of all...

O Goddess! One should perform the practice of the Haṭha Tantras. Then, by means of contraction, when the constriction of the throat is quickly effected, the posterior palate comes to the center and the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the central channel (madhyanāḍī). Consciousness, situated in the abode of Brahmā, proceeds to the dwelling of the wind (pavanālaya).

Then death is not born for him, nor likewise old age and the like. Having contracted the root-seat (mūlasthāna), one should perform that which is called the upward flight (uḍḍāna). Binding both the iḍā and the piṅgalā, one should cause the wind to flow toward the western direction. By this very method, the vital air (pavana) attains [its goal].
Through absorption (laya), death as well as old age, disease, and so forth, do not arise.

Now, the reversal of the process (*viparītakaraṇa*): Whatever nectar of divine form flows from the Moon, the Sun swallows it all; by that, the physical body (*piṇḍa*) becomes subject to old age. Therein exists a divine method for binding the mouth of the Sun, which is to be known through the instruction of the Guru. It is not [to be learned otherwise].
And by millions of scriptural authorities: the navel is above and the palate is below;
the sun is above and the moon is below. This practice known as "the reversal" destroys all diseases;
when joined with constant practice, it increases the digestive fire. [One should maintain] a very small diet.

One who abstains from food becomes afflicted by hunger and loses strength; therefore, one should provide abundant food for the practitioner. If he remains without food, the digestive fire would burn his body in an instant. On the first day, he should remain with his head downward and feet upward for a moment.

One should indeed practice for slightly more than a moment day after day; within six months, one will surely destroy wrinkles and grey hair. He who practices this constantly for even a single month becomes a conqueror of his ears. Also, in the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*: "Having joined the anus with the [tip of the] bird..."

One should practice the leftward path with force, so that the vital breath (samīraṇa) repeatedly ascends upward. Through the root-lock (mūlabandha), the prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness; one attains the perfect accomplishment of the Great Yoga—of this there is no doubt.
The practice known as *viparītakaraṇa* destroys all diseases;

for one who is constantly engaged in its practice, it increases the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). O Sāṅkṛti! For such a person, even large quantities of food become small [in effect], and if the food is small, the fire surely causes a burning sensation.
He indeed performs it. O Sāṅkṛti! Rāhu is above and the Moon is below; such is the vision. On the first day, he should remain for a moment with his head downward and feet upward.
Day by day, he should practice for slightly more than a moment. [This results in] strength and the prevention of graying hair.
It is not seen after six months; however, he who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) is a knower of yoga.
Now, regarding *vajroṇī*: *vajroṇī*, *cāmaroṇī*, and *sayonī* are considered to be threefold.

I shall describe their characteristics and how they are to be specifically practiced. Even one who acts according to his own will, without the observances prescribed for yoga, is a yogi if he understands *vajroṇī*.
One becomes a vessel for accomplishment. By practice, one should draw upward the drop (*bindu*) that has gone to the lower part.
Having drawn upward one's own moving drop, one should protect it. In this regard, I shall describe two things that are difficult for anyone to obtain: milk and, secondly, a woman.

One who has mastery over [the breath] should practice contraction properly and slowly with the penis. Whether it be a man or a woman, one who possesses the *vajrīṇī* [yoni] shall attain perfection. With effort, one should gradually increase the "conch" (*kambu*) by means of hissing sounds (*phutkāra*) upon the multitude of arrows. Slowly, slowly.

And one should perform this for the sake of causing the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*). By practice, one should draw upward the drop (*bindu*) situated in the womb of the consort. Having drawn up the drop that has become wrinkled and grey, one should preserve it. Thus, by preserving the drop, one conquers death.

The practitioner of yoga: death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*, while life arises from the retention of the *bindu*. Through the retention of the *bindu*, the body of the yogi becomes fragrant. As long as the *bindu* remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death? The strength of men is dependent upon the *mala*.

Life is dependent upon the semen; therefore, one must protect both the semen and the impurities with great effort. Likewise, a woman during her fertile period should herself protect her menstrual flow and the seminal drop.
Through the proper application of practice, she should draw [the discharge] upward from the penis.

There is also the *sahayoni* (co-uterine) method, which is distinguished from the *vajroṇī* (thunderbolt) method. In the *vajroṇī*, after sexual union, there is the application of an ointment to the limbs of both the woman and the man while they remain seated comfortably, with subtle movements for a moment; this is called *sahayoni*.

O Supreme Goddess! Out of faith, yet due to a predominance of bile (*pitta*), some mortals of fragmented intellect—avoiding the first stream because it is insipid and the final stream because it is too cool—consume the middle stream with their hands. He who drinks the immortal nectar (*amarī*) daily [attains liberation].
Performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) day after day, one should thus practice Vajraṇī; she is called Amarīṇī.
By the contraction of the Yakṣaṇā, that rajas which moves upward is indeed Yoginī. When the past and future are known, Khecarī arises, and one attains the perfection of the body (dehasiddhi).
Through the practice of union with a vajra-woman, this auspicious yoga enjoys worldly pleasures while bestowing liberation. (9)
Now, the activation of the Śakti (Śakticālanam). Kuṇḍalāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī, Kuṇḍalī, Arundhatī, and Devī are synonymous terms.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā [channels], the young girl, the widow, and the ascetic woman—having forcibly drawn her up...

One should grasp that supreme state of Viṣṇu. By seizing the tail, one may awaken even the sleeping serpent; having abandoned sleep, she rises straight up by force. The yogi, established in the vajrāsana, should indeed stir the Kuṇḍalinī.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the bellows-breathing (*bhastrā*); it quickly awakens Kuṇḍalī.
Even for one who has entered the vajra of death, whence then can there be fear of death?
By moving [the breath] for a period of two *muhūrtas*, this [practitioner] draws [the vital energy] upward without fear.
A certain [portion] of the *suṣumnā* has entered the *kuṇḍalinī*. Therefore, the *kuṇḍalinī* has emerged from that *suṣumnā*.
This vital breath (*prāṇa*) constantly leaves the *suṣumnā* and moves with a sound. For that reason, one should constantly cause the *arundhatī*, which contains sound within it, to vibrate.

By the mere movement of which the diseased is liberated from diseases; by whom this power (śakti) is moved, that yogi becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). What is the use of much speaking here? He conquers time with ease.
Through practice, he should constantly rely upon the Aindrī [power] that has emerged [from the body].

"And one should wear on the head that which bestows divine vision. Thus, O Maheśvarī, these ten mudrās have been declared out of affection for you; each one individually swiftly bestows great siddhi upon those who practice self-restraint. Without Rājayoga, the earth is [mere] stone.

Without *rājayoga*, even a varied sleep does not shine. For the wise, the entire procedure for the vital air (*māruta*) is joined with the mind. Even the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*), though auspicious, becomes firm through the steady practice of yogis. Through the postures (*āsana*) and the union of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyoga*), everything is accomplished by means of the *mudrās*.
Even when [the practitioner] has approached [the deity], the Rājayoga of the Mudrās is like the ocean;
and then the supreme Mudrā of the Rudras bestows accomplishment.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Ten Mudrās, Beginning with the Five Immortals," in the sixth section (Jñānakāṇḍa) of the Prāṇatoṣiṇī.

In the *Dattātreyasaṃhitā*, following the five-fold *dhāraṇā*: "I shall describe the earth-retention (*pṛthivīdhāraṇa*), which brings fear to those belonging to the earth-element. One should retain the breath for five *ghaṭikās* below the navel and above the anus; from that, the earth-retention of the vital air (*vāyu*) occurs."
It removes that fear. Because it originates from the earth, death shall not come to that yogin.

Then, one should hold the breath at the region of the navel for five *nāḍikās*. Consequently, there is no fear of water, and death by water does not occur for the yogin. One should hold the breath in the circle above the navel.
There are five *nāḍikās*. This is the *āgneyī* concentration; for him, there is no death by fire.

Indeed, his body is not burned even when cast into a pit of fire. One should hold the breath for five *ghaṭikās* between the navel and the eyebrows, at a distance of two finger-breadths (*prādeśa*); that indeed is it.

The Vāyavī [dhāraṇā]: By holding that wind, no fear shall arise for the yogin. One should hold the wind above the two eyebrows for five *nāḍikās* with effort; this is the Ākāśa-dhāraṇā. Performing the Ākāśa-dhāraṇā, one [overcomes] death.

He truly triumphs; wherever he may abide, he enjoys ultimate happiness. Thus, the yogi should perform the five dhāraṇās according to the prescribed method. Then, for one whose body has become firm, death no longer exists. This is the dhāraṇā of the five elements for one who...
One should practice this; even at the dissolution of Brahmā, death does not exist for him.

Then one should practice that meditation for exactly sixty *ghaṭikās*, restraining the vital breath (*vāyu*), and meditate upon the chosen deity who accomplishes all desired goals. This is meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*).

It may bestow the bliss of the *aṇimā* powers and so forth. One should meditate on the attributeless [Self] like space, and the path to liberation proceeds. Endowed with the meditation on the attributeless, one should practice *samādhi*;
in just twelve days, one shall attain *samādhi* by restraining the vital breath (*vāyu*).

The wise one shall certainly become liberated while living. Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). If there should be a desire to cast off the body, he may relinquish it of his own accord; having abandoned all karma, he shall merge into the Supreme Brahman.

[The fruit is] auspicious or inauspicious. Now, if one has not abandoned [attachment to] one's own body which is dear, one may wander through all the worlds endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth; sometimes by one's own will, having become a god, one may even move about in heaven, or likewise as a human or a yakṣa, according to one's own desire.
In an instant he may become a lion, a tiger, or even an elephant; by his will, he may assume other births.

The wise yogi, a great lord, may act exactly as he desires. This path of the poet, O Sāṅkṛti, is useful for you through the eightfold yoga; it is the doctrine of the perfected ones (siddhas), such as Kapila and others.
I shall speak thereafter: "Due to the differences in practice, there is a difference in that [result], and the fruit is likewise equal.

Immediately following this, Jālandhara and the others were mentioned. Therefore, the wise should discern and understand that according to the system of Dattātreya, one becomes a yogin even without Jālandhara and the rest. [End of] the section on birds.

Having joined the anus with the perineum, one should forcefully practice the leftward path so that the vital air repeatedly ascends upward. Through the *mūlabandha*, the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as well as *nāda* and *bindu*, attain unity; thus one achieves the perfect accomplishment of the Great Yoga—of this there is no doubt.
This is the doubt: The practice known as *viparīta* destroys all diseases;

for one who is constantly engaged in its practice, it increases the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). O Sāṅkṛti! A great amount of food must certainly be consumed by him; if his food intake were small, the fire would cause a burning sensation.
Indeed, he performs it. O Sāṅkṛti! Rāhu is above and the Moon is below; such is the vision.

With head downward and feet upward, one may become so in an instant on the first day. One should practice this for slightly more than an instant, day after day. Baldness and graying hair [shall cease].

After six months, it is no longer seen. He who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) is a knower of yoga. I shall now describe to you the Vajroṇī, which is always guarded by yogis; for it is an extreme secret and must not be given to just anyone. If it is obtained, [give] only one [instruction] to him.

The supreme means for achieving success in yoga consists of two substances: milk and *aṅgarasa*. Of these two, the first is easily obtained. The third [substance] is obtained from strong men who have been won over by women;
and a woman devoted to the practice of yoga should diligently accomplish it for men. Whether it be a man or a woman, [it should be prepared].

Whether that [bindu] or something else, it is female or male in relation to one another. He shall attain perfection through the exclusive means of the mere purpose (*prayojana*). If the bindu has fallen, he should draw it back up and hold it at the crown of the head. For when the bindu is thus preserved, death—
Victory through reality! Death occurs by the falling of the *bindu*; life comes from the protection of the *bindu*.

By the grace of protecting the *bindu*, all yogins attain perfection. One should know the sequence of practice for attaining immortality and for [attaining] a [divine] birth along with [the deity], as practiced by the perfected ones (*siddhas*).

According to the tradition: "By practicing all these [methods] that have been described, in accordance with the proper timing, one will certainly attain Rājayoga; it does not occur otherwise. Success does not come through mere theoretical direction, nor indeed does practice arise [without it]. Having attained the state of Rājayoga..."
It shatters all conceptual constructions. One may perform every action or refrain from performing it according to one's inclination;
likewise, through yoga, the activity of the yogi becomes perfected within. Indeed, that state, when attained, destroys [all worldly bonds] and bestows both devotion and liberation.

Regarding another fruit of *prāṇāyāma*, it is stated in the *Grahayāmala*: "In the bright fortnight the Moon [rises] first, while in the other [the dark fortnight] the Sun [rises first]; starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*), this [alternation] rises, decreasing by three [days] each time. Furthermore, in the *Tripurāsāroccaya*, the rising [of the breaths] is described as being up to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), as follows:
Beginning from the new moon (darśa), the Lord first arises in the left channel for three days;
then for three days in the other [right] channel, and thus it continues in this manner until the full moon (pūrṇā) lunar day.
In this world, for men, the affliction of disease occurs when one lunar fortnight (pakṣa) is reversed;
the loss of kinsmen and friends occurs when two fortnights are reversed; and death shall occur when three fortnights are reversed.

In the *Brahmajāmalatantra*: "When the sun rises at the time of moonrise, or when the moon rises at the time of sunrise, there is inauspiciousness, loss, and agitation; one should employ all that is auspicious [at other times]. At moonrise, this refers specifically to the time determined by the movement of the wind through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*); likewise for sunrise."
At the time determined by the movement of the wind through the right channel, there is a specific ritual action;
furthermore, the auspiciousness resulting from the inhalation and exhalation of the wind through the nostrils is also described in that very same place.
The Moon is auspicious for journeys, giving, marriage, wearing clothes and ornaments, all auspicious rites, and entering [a new home]. For physical conflict, gambling,
battle, bathing, eating, sexual intercourse, legal proceedings, fear, and defeat, the Sun’s nāḍī is auspicious.
It is praised [for these]: enchantment, pacification, divine herbs, and elixirs;
the commencement of learning, stable undertakings, and tasks that must be performed should be done when the Moon is in its course.
In a distant battle, the Moon brings victory; when it is near, the Sun does so. This also applies when the breath flows through the channel (nāḍī) corresponding to the lunar station (pada).

The journey becomes bestowing success. The meaning is that when the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) in whichever nostril is described, a journey preceded by extending one's legs toward that side becomes bestowing success. And likewise during sleep, or in the course of conversation, or even in the embrace of a young woman.

Or rather: he who would drink the moon by means of the sun would become Makaradhvaja (the god of love). At the time of union with a woman, one drinks the moon—the vital breath located in the woman's left nostril—by means of the sun—the vital breath situated in one's own right nostril.
Being deeply absorbed in one's own breath, one draws [the vital energy] inward; the fruit of that is right there.

The Moon-mover destroys poison, while the Sun brings the young woman under control. In the Suṣumnā, liberation occurs; the One God is considered to be threefold. By merely eating [this], those with weak digestion [are restored].

Furthermore, in rites for subjugating women, the wise should always perform the *śayana* (lying down) yoga by means of the *sūryavāha* (sun-vehicle). In cases of pacification, grief, dispute, as well as when one is feverish or unconscious, one should employ the *candracāra* (moon-movement) even for the sake of awakening a virtuous person. [This applies] immediately after eating and so forth.

The essential meaning is that one should sleep on the left side when fatigued and so forth, and on the right side otherwise. If the querent asks while situated in any one of the four directions, above, or below, then [the author] states in which channel the movement of the wind is auspicious.

The messenger (dūta) should be known as being in the upper-left [channel] when situated on the left path; likewise, when situated behind, on the right, or below, he is considered to have entered the solar flow (sūryavāha). Whatever auspicious or inauspicious matter the messenger, having entered the full channel (pūrṇanāḍī), asks about—all that attains success; however, in the void (śūnya), there is nothing.

There is doubt. If, at first, one who has entered the void asks [a question], and afterwards the full [breath] enters, then know for certain that there will be the accomplishment of all aims. Now he states the distinction based on the entry and exit of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*): "At the time of entry..."

Whatever one who has arisen desires for their own purpose, all that they attain as success; there is nothing auspicious in departing [at an inauspicious time]. He now describes the movement through specific channels (nāḍīs) for specific types of rites: "Killing, bewildering, paralyzing, as well as causing hatred and expulsion."

"Perform the impelling, attracting, and agitating [of the breath] during the rising of the solar channel (*bhānunāḍī*); [perform] rites for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and security (*kṣema*), as well as divine herbs and elixirs (*rasāyana*), and practices such as the yoga-exercises during the rising of the lunar channel (*niśākara*). — *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*. [The rising of the elements (*bhūtānām udayam*)...]

A wise person should observe both sides [of the breath] there at first: when the earth-element arises, the mind should be fixed on the nostril as it touches the tip of the nose; when the deity [water] touches below, the movement of water is downward;
when fire rises, its movement is upward; and when the wind touches transversely, its movement is all around.
On the back of the path of the wind; in the god, the vital breath; the fruit is in the *jāmala*.

When the earth and water elements are auspicious, they yield favorable results; fire brings mixed results; and both ether and air cause loss and death for men. Regarding the results of the rising of the earth element during specific actions, it is stated in the *Tripurāsāra*:
The rising of Earth is praised for subjugation and immobilization; the rising of Water is auspicious for pacifying rites, nourishing rites, and other such beneficial acts;
furthermore, the rising of Fire is for quickly performing the killing and rending of enemies, or for expulsion and destruction; and the rising of Air is likewise [for those ends].
For the rites of pacification and neutralizing poison, an arising [of the moon] in the sky is beneficial.

In response to the inquiry as to how long the wind remains in a single channel and by what means the arising of the five elements therein may be known, the *Jāmalatantra* states the duration of the movement through the channels and the arising of the elements according to their respective locations: "The five digits (*kalā*) of each [element] arise in successive order."

They are as follows: earth, water, fire, air, and space. In the center is earth, below is water, and fire flows above; the flow of air moves transversely, while space flows through the junction. This is also stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "In both nostrils..."

The earth is established as the staff, water below, fire above, wind on the sides, and space in the middle; such is the arrangement of the elements within the body. Furthermore, regarding the distinctions of stages such as childhood and so forth therein, it is said in the Rudrajāmala, Uttarakhanda:

In the eleventh chapter: The fifth [element] is proclaimed to reside at the tip of one’s own nose. O Bhairava! That wind which circulates within the middle of the nostrils—one should contemplate existence and non-existence at the upper middle of that nose; it is space (ākāśa).

O Lord! The form of air is indeed fiery; it should be known as earthly in sequence, according to the order of childhood and so forth. When the left [channel] arises, the auspicious Vāmā [energy] is present; in the right, the auspicious Puruṣa is present.
The movement of the winds should be known to extend as far as the sky alone. Kevalam.

When the movement of the breath is in the middle region (madhyadeśa), one should know that as the state of space (ākāśa); this is proclaimed as the state of childhood (bālyabhāva). When the breath moves transversely at the tip of the nose, it is the very rising of the wind; this should be known as mere wandering, which is entirely auspicious.
And: "O All-pervading One! One should know that [the breath] moving transversely in the wind-element is 'Kiśora' (the Youthful).

When the wind moves like a staff at the very tip of the half-nose, one should know that to be the fiery element; through fire, one becomes powerful. One should know that state to be 'Yauvana' (Youth)."

The accomplishment of one's actions will certainly occur when, having reached [the breath], it moves here through the nostril without agitation; then one should know the rising of the water and likewise delusion. Furthermore, with excessive exertion, there is delay and a state of exhaustion, yet one attains the supreme.

When the rising of the Varuṇa-artery brings joy, that which goes downward quickly and slightly upward is beyond perception; when it makes the eastern [artery] weak, then there is the rise of strength from disease. When the earth is elevated, fortune is afflicted by the pain of illness; [when it is] set, [it is likewise].

O Mahādeva! The vital wind (pavana) moves swiftly in both direct and reverse order, according to the distinction between the left and the right. It enters the left nostril [and flows] as Earth and Water;
it is ever intent upon bestowing fruit or the absence of fruit within the circle of the Kula. Of these two, there is indeed the Vāyavī Śakti.
Then one shall obtain the portion of the fruit. This is the description of the different states and their respective fruits, as stated in that very [text].

If it is thus during an inquiry concerning a young woman on the left side, and if a man there asks the question while she is moving to the left, then he will incur disease and a certain loss of his undertaking. This applies if the rise of the wind is on the left and the man is on the right.
When [the Moon] is situated there, one then obtains bad fruit, and the arrival of wealth is difficult to obtain.

There will be a sudden loss of wealth and the destruction of the fruits desired by the mind. There is a breach with friends and disputes; when it is broken, there is no auspiciousness from its rising. The person belongs solely to Varuṇa.

On the right [side] it is auspicious; on the earth and on the right [side] it is inauspicious—this distinction is difficult for even the best to find. One should know, O Lord, the auspicious and inauspicious results of wind and fire when they arise constantly on the right, as well as those of space, if indeed by the power of fortune.

The movement of the wind becomes slow; then, in the middle of the right nostril, there is the auspicious rising of the left [wind]. At that time, one should discern the left [nostril] and the rising of the sound of the wind-fire (*vāyutejaḥ*). Having understood this rising, one should know that in a mixed state there is loss regarding the sound and fear. Thus, if in one's own abode...
The wind blows; at that time, the man stands facing the woman on his left or right side.
Then, just as a human being obtains the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage, so too, by the grace of the wind, he obtains excellent wealth and auspiciousness in another land.
News arrives regarding the attainment of sons; thus ends the description of results according to the distinction between male and female [planets].

In the *Sūkṣmasvarodaya*: On the days of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) prevails; it brings success in all undertakings, especially during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
On the days of the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*) should be remembered.

For one who desires long-term results, the rising [of the breath] remains pure; through the sequence of each successive nāḍī, there is the distinct emergence of the *tattvas*. Within the day and night, twelve transits (*saṃkrama*) are to be known, occurring when the Moon is in Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, Pisces, and Aries.
When Leo, Sagittarius, Libra, Gemini, or Aquarius is on the ascendant, the rising [of the breath] is to be known as occurring in the south;

this is the determination of auspicious and inauspicious results. Thus ends the description of the specific fruits of the *nāḍīs* according to the divisions of the days of the week and so forth. The Moon should remain in the northeast, and the Sun...

In the southwest; when there is a flow in the right channel (nāḍī), one should not go to the south or west. Thus, the knowledge of directions is determined by the specific channels. However, during the flow of the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), one should not go to the east or north; he who goes there becomes an obstacle and does not return. Therefore, in this case, one should not [go].
"Those wise ones who seek the welfare of all and are auspicious should not travel;

for then, in that place, death by crushing (saṅghātamṛtyu) will certainly occur—of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the censure regarding travel in specific directions when the *vahannāḍī* [the vital breath] flows. When the Sun flows on the second day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), [the following applies].
The moon is clearly visible; there is great gain for the man, and gentleness arises.

When the sun rises at sunrise, and the moon rises at moonrise, all undertakings succeed, even those occurring by day or night. Thus ends the description of the results of one's own respective *nāḍīs*.

"When the Sun occurs during the period of the Moon, or the Moon occurs during the rising of the Sun, there will be agitation, quarrel, and loss; one should determine all auspicious matters [accordingly]. Thus ends the critique of the contrary [positions]. Regarding the movement of the Sun, they declare it to be a net [of obstacles], characterized by a mind fixed on a single seat yet unstable, and joined with breath.
At the time of the moon's flow, there is another result for this [ascendant]. However,
if at the time of dawn there is a reversal of the rising, with the Sun situated in the place of the Moon and the Moon in the place of the Sun,
there will be mental agitation in the first month, loss of wealth in the second, and departure in the third.
In the fourth [house], the loss of what is desired is to be known; in the fifth, the glory of sovereignty; in the sixth, the destruction of all objects;
in the seventh, the miseries of disease; and in the eighth, one meets with death.

Thus, according to the difference of days, the results are reversed. When the three times [of day] are unfavorable and the result becomes contrary, then it is declared to yield an evil fruit; if it is slightly deficient [in time], it is very auspicious. [Regarding the position of] the Moon at dawn, midday, and evening—

Divākara says: "Then there is constant victory and gain; however, the opposite brings suffering. Thus ends the fruit of time according to the divisions of time. "Whether on the left or on the right, wherever the breath (svara) is traversed, by making that the first step, the journey becomes one that bestows success. Thus [ends the section].

The fruit of the journey for one whose *nāḍī* is *Vahat*: The Moon brings about the accomplishment of tasks, while the Sun always brings about difficulty. A journey undertaken after placing a full-quarter [of the *nāḍī*] in front yields success. Seven quarters [are required] for Saturn and Venus; these should be understood by the wise. The Moon...

O Rudra! The position of the Sun, Mars, and likewise Saturn, as well as the positions of Jupiter, should always be understood by the wise along with [the other planets]. Thus ends the distinction of foot-marches according to the difference in days of the week.

For traveling quickly to various lands, a slender limb is desired; it should be taken from the opposing side, as there is loss when a quarrel arises. Whichever limb the channel (nāḍī) carries for humans, that is to be taken as the one effecting movement: four parts in the course of the Moon, and five parts in the course of the Sun.
Thus ends the distinction of foot-journeys according to the days of the week.
And thus, this movement accomplishes the supreme [attainment] of the three worlds.
Whichever limb the wind moves through, that limb becomes like a hand; one obtains the desired fruit, with a face as if awakened from sleep. There is no loss, nor indeed any quarrel.
It is not pierced even by thorns; it returns with ease, free from all calamities.

Thus ends the fruit of cleansing the mouth with the "Hand of the Flowing Channel. The Guru, the kinsman, the king, and one's own self—these and others as well are givers of auspiciousness; indeed, [the rite] must be performed when the limbs are complete.

The accomplishment of one's purpose is achieved by the wise. The vowels *ai*, *ī*, *au*, *am*, *u*, *va*, *rṇa*, *ā*, and so forth, as well as other initial compounds, should indeed be employed during the *riktā* lunar days by those seeking victory, gain, and happiness. However, travel toward the north (the direction of the moon) should be undertaken toward distant lands. From them...

Nothing should be given when [the breath] is blazing, nor should there be a turning back of the house. Whatever was previously indicated regarding the attachment to gain and so forth—all that arises without conceptualization within the previous channels (*nāḍī*).
That which was previously explained as the "empty" and the "reversed channel" arises.
And it is not otherwise than as spoken by the Omniscient One:
"In the case of the fire-god (Havyavāha), in the rite of eradication (uccāṭa), in the deception of divine sciences and so forth, or when one is angry, the *svādviṭha* [notes] should be played;
those situated in the full (*pūrṇa*) positions are terrifying. Thus ends the fruit of the full and the empty. On the long road...

The auspicious Moon grants the attainment of desired goals when there are no obstacles; the Sun is praised for swift results in matters of entry and undertakings. Moving through the Moon (Candracārī) destroys poison, while moving through the Sun (Sūrye) brings children under one's control. Through Suṣumnā comes liberation; the One God is established in stillness. He...

The state of yoga belongs to the yogi; even in the locus of yoga, there is fitness. How can one cause the living soul, which is bound to its actions, to proceed upward? When auspicious and inauspicious deeds are performed day and night, then, in accordance with those actions, the result must be experienced.
The movement of the channels. Thus ends the cause for the movement of the channels; however, the method of movement must be learned from the Guru.
Furthermore, for rites involving *iḍā* and *asthira* [karmas], as well as for traveling long distances; for hermitages, mansions, palaces, and the accumulation of goods;
for the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like; and for the two deities, processions, gifts, and marriages.
[It is auspicious] for clothing, ornaments, and decorations; for rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika);
for divine medicines and elixirs (rasāyana); for an audience with one's lord; for journeys, trade, and accumulation [of wealth];
for entering a house, service, and the sowing of seeds in agriculture.

"If the moon is auspicious at the junction [of the breaths] or during exhalation, it is favorable for virtuous deeds. Thus ends the results of the channels of action (*karmanāḍī*) according to specific activities. [It is also favorable] for undertakings such as the commencement of learning, the sight of kinsmen, public discourse, righteousness, initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the practice of mantras.

In the medical treatment of diseases caused by time (chronic ailments), in the awakening of a master, likewise in the mounting of elephants and horses, in the binding of archers, elephants, and horses, in rendering assistance to others, in the depositing of treasures,
and in the investigation of the science of music through song, instrumental performance, dance, and so forth.
When residing in a city or village, when wearing a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) or a parasol (*chatra*), during times of peace, grief, or despondency,

or when one is afflicted by fever or has fainted; likewise, when among one's own kin or relatives of a master, when gathering grain or wood, or when a woman is adorned with ornaments for joy— [in these circumstances, one may wear the *kaupīna*].

Likewise, in the arrival at a seat, O fair-faced one, as well as in the worship of the guru, the giving of gifts, and the movement [of the breath], it is declared that the *iḍā* [channel] bestows success, as do practices such as the cultivation of yoga. Thus are the channels according to specific rites. Even there, one should avoid the elements of air, fire, and space.

p. 817) All actions performed during the day or at night are successful; for all auspicious undertakings, the movement of the moon (candracāra) is praised. Now, as for Piṅgalā: it is likewise [praised] for the reciting and teaching of hard and cruel sciences.
In sexual union with women or visiting courtesans, in boarding large ships and the like, in performing desired rites, in drinking liquor,

in practicing the mantras of heroes, in regions prone to many calamities, in giving poison to enemies and the like, in the study of scriptures, in traveling, and in the prowess of hunting deer and other beasts— [these are occasions for the use of the Vīra vow].

In the fashioning of bricks, wood, and stone; in the harsh grinding of gems; in the practice of singing and the application of mechanical devices and mantras; in climbing mountains for the sake of sight; in gambling;
in the procurement of thieves, elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; in physical exercise; and in the rites of killing and expulsion.
In the performance of the six rites and other accomplishments; in the gathering of protectors, yakṣas, vetālas, and various spirits;
likewise in mounting donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and elephants; in crossing the floodwaters of rivers;
and in the preparation of medicines, writing, and jewels—[these are the means for] killing and bewildering.

Stambhana (paralysis), vidveṣaṇa (enmity), uccāṭana (expulsion), and vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation); in the attraction of vital breaths, in giving, in the sale of a wheel, as well as when holding a sword in hand, in battle with an enemy, in enjoyment, or in an audience with a king;
in eating and in legal proceedings—when these are cruel or blazing, the Sun is auspicious; and likewise immediately after having eaten.

For women with weak digestion, for acts intended to bring others under one's control, and for all cruel deeds as well as various mobile rites, the wise should always perform these during the Sun’s transit;
these are accomplished by means of the Sun—of this there is no doubt. Thus, regarding specific rites.
The fruit of Piṅgalā.

Now, concerning Suṣumnā: when the vital air flows for a moment through the left or the right, that should be known as Suṣumnā, which is auspicious and brings about all success. When the fire situated in that channel blazes with the form of Time (Kāla), one should recognize that as "uneven" (viṣama).

It is the destruction of all undertakings. When the two [winds] flow through that channel by transgressing their proper sequence, then one should know that misfortune has arrived for him. If the wind flows unevenly for a moment in the left and a moment in the right, it portends a contrary result.

O fair-faced one! That which is to be known and that which is to be understood—when both of these are in motion, the wise know that to be "Viṣama" (the uneven). One should not perform cruel or gentle rites; all such actions would become fruitless.
In questions concerning life or death, gain or loss, victory or defeat, [it is so] in the Viṣama [state].

p. 818) He should remember the Lord of the World in the event of its reversal; he should contemplate the Lord, the task at hand, and the practice of yoga and other such duties. Nothing else should be done for the sake of victory, gain, pleasure, or the like, while the *suṣumnā* is being flowed through by the Sun.
Again and again, one may bestow a curse or grant a boon; however, at all other times, it is otherwise.

At the time of the transition of the *nāḍīs* as well as during the transition of the *tattvas*, not even the slightest auspicious act should be performed, such as the giving of merit or charity, even if done ten million times. This applies even when one is situated in the third state on an uneven second day.
One should not even contemplate [this] with the mind; it causes the ruin of one's livelihood and at the time of death, there is no doubt [of this].
When the moon is in front and above, and the sun is behind and on the right—this distinction between the full and the empty must always be understood by the teachers.

The messenger (dūta) is to be known as situated on the left path above, in front, behind, on the right, and likewise below; he is considered to have gone along the solar vehicle (sūryavāha). That twilight (saṃdhyā) is beginningless, unequal, a junction (sandhi), free from food, undisturbed, supreme, and subtle; [all things] dissolve into it.

The junction (*sandhi*) is described as follows: the inquiry regarding the time of the junction is like poison; that junction is called *sandhyā*. One does not say "this Veda, this Veda," for the Veda is proclaimed as the Veda because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) resides therein;
that is what is called the Veda. Thus ends the determination of the division of the three channels (*nāḍī*).
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O Savior from the entire cycle of existence! O Lord, tell me the secret that resides within Your heart.
Śrī Śiva said:

The secret of the knowledge of the vowels is nothing other than the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). The yogi who is devoted to the knowledge of the vowels is considered the supreme yogi. From the five principles (*pañcatattva*) arises creation; within each principle, a principle dissolves.
Beyond the five principles is the Supreme Principle, the stainless Self of all principles.
The names of the principles (tattvas) are to be known by the yogi through the yoga of accomplishment;
for the best of gods indeed know the signs of the wicked among beings. He who knows that everything consists of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—he [is a knower].

The worshipper [should contemplate] that there is no difference in the life-force (*jīva*) of all the worlds, nor any distinction in their essential nature, from the *bhūrloka* up to the *satyaloka*. There is a distinct differentiation of channels (*nāḍībheda*) for each:
the *bhūrloka* is the navel and the *satyaloka* is the head, because those worlds are situated therein, on either the left or the right.

And its arising has also been proclaimed. O beautiful one, listen as I describe the eightfold knowledge of the elements (*dhātu-vijñāna*): in the first [chapter], the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*);
in the second, the junctions of the breaths; in the third, the signs of the vowels; and in the fourth, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself.

The color of the five principles (pañcatattva) is found in the sixth, and its location likewise; in the seventh it is conjoined with sweetness, and in the eighth is the characteristic of movement. Thus, the eightfold vital breath (prāṇa), which is uneven, pervades all that is moving and unmoving. O Goddess! There is nothing else that can remain beyond the primordial sound (svara).
At some time, it should be observed with effort from the hour of dawn; for the purpose of deceiving Time (Kāla), yogins perform their practice [focusing] on the ears,
between the thumbs and the middle fingers, on the two nostrils, and in the mouth.
When one observes two spots on the edge of the eyelashes at a distance of one finger-breadth, there arises in this world of beings, such as the earth and so forth,
a gradual realization of the principles (tattvas).
Having gazed into a mirror with yellow, white, red, and dark-blue dots, [one perceives] that which is free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika).

Therein one should cast the breath; the wise one should understand the vowel *ā* as the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*). Thus is the procedure regarding the elements (*bhūta-prakriyā*). The square, the half-moon, the triangle, and that which is measured as circular—these are not to be understood by means of points (*bindu*), but rather by their forms as the characteristics of the principles.
In the middle, fire flows as both the upper half and the lower half;

and at the transition (saṃkrama), the sky carries the flow of the sacred ford-wind (tīrthavāyu). Such is the method for knowing the elements. Water is white, earth is yellow, and [fire] is red in color.
Fire, the winds, blue clouds, and the sky of all colors—these are the forms of the elements. Fire resides in the two shoulders, the wind at the root of the navel;
earth is in the region of the knees, water at the ends of the feet, and space in the head. Thus [it is said].

Knowledge of the elements arises from the reality of their specific locations. This earth is sweet-tasting; water is astringent and sweet; fire is bitter; wind is sour; and space is likewise pungent. These are the tastes of the elements. Eight finger-breadths...
The wind [element] carries [the breath] four finger-breadths; the earthly [element] twelve finger-breadths;

and that of water sixteen finger-breadths. Such is the movement of the elements. One should know that upward is death, downward is pacification, and likewise transverse is eradication; in the center is immobilization, and the sky [element] is [neutral].

In all cases, the middle [course] is recommended. On earth, one should perform stable rites or mobile rites; in the realm of water, cruel rites; in fire, rites of killing and expulsion; and in air, nothing at all should be performed. In the ether, one should practice the middle course through the service of yoga. Thus it is with respect to the specific elements.

The specific application of the six activities (*ṣaṭkarma*): In all undertakings, one should act during the *śūnya* (void) state; no deliberation is required here. Success is achieved through Earth and Water; death occurs in Fire; destruction follows in Air; and everything in Ether is fruitless—this should be known by those who know the principles (*tattva*). Earth is to be understood as yielding results after a long time.

At that moment, from the essence of water, there would be a loss due to fire and wind; in the ether (nabhas), one obtains what is fruitless. Flowing through the middle, yellowish-red, thin yet stoutly supported, slightly warm—such is the earth-wind (*pārthiva-vāyu*), which accomplishes steady tasks and flows downwards.

The wind that has the sound of a drum, moves swiftly, and is cool to the touch; that wind which is sixteen *aṅgulas* long is auspicious for performing virtuous deeds. That which moves in a whirl, is hot, has the luster of gold, is four *aṅgulas* long, and blows upwards, is a performer of cruel deeds.

The Taijasa [wind] is hot and cold, black in color, moving horizontally, and eight finger-breadths in length. The Vāyu [wind], which is like the blowing wind, should be known as the bestower of success in the practices of movement; it brings forth the qualities of all the principles (tattvas). One should recognize that as the Āvarta [wind], which belongs to the Samīra and conveys the attributes of all the principles for yogins.
It bestows yoga; it is yellow, quadrangular, sweet, and situated in the middle.
The earthly element (pārthiva-tattva) bestows enjoyment; it is twelve finger-breadths in its flow, white, resembling a half-moon, sweet, astringent, and intoxicating.
The Varuṇa-tattva, which brings about gain, is sixteen finger-breadths in its flow;
it is red, triangular, bitter, and flows through the upward path. The Taijasa-tattva is radiant and four finger-breadths in its flow; it is blue, circular in shape, and sweet-sour.

The principle of air (māruta-tattva) is said to reside in animals; it is fickle, eight finger-breadths in its flow, and possesses color and form. It carries a sweet [scent], is unmanifest, and moves everywhere. The ethereal principle (nābhasa-tattva) bestows liberation, yet it is fruitless in all worldly activities. Thus, by means of the specific movement of the fingers...
The reality of that result.

Earth and water are auspicious elements; fire brings about mixed results. Both space and wind cause loss and death for men. Earth is to be known in the east and west, fire likewise in the south, wind in the north, and space occupies the intermediate corners.

When the Moon presides over earth and water, and when the Sun becomes associated with fire, then success is attained without a doubt in gentle and peaceful rites. There would be no gain from earth-related matters;
at night, water brings profit; in fire there is death; on earth there is wind; and [in the Sun] there is ether.

One should burn [the query] in the *sthāna* (station) in some cases; likewise regarding livelihood, victory, gain, agriculture, financial affairs, seeking the meaning of mantras, inquiries concerning war, and going or coming.

When the enemy arrives in the *vāruṇa* (western) station, even if he is situated there on the earth, it is auspicious; [if the enemy] departs from the *vāyuta* (northwestern) [station], [it is also favorable].
"Constant loss [occurs] in Earth, death in Water, and [distress] in Air and Space. Thus are the specific results according to the specific element.

On earth, there should be consideration of the root; the root flows from space. On fire, there should be consideration of the elements (dhātu); the vital principle (jīva) resides in water and wind. Thus is the determination of the root, the vital principle, and so forth, according to the specific element. On earth, there may be many feet; for that which has two feet...

In Vāyu and Tejas there are four quarters, while in Nabhas it is devoid of quarters; thus is the determination of many feet and so forth according to the specific element. Mars is proclaimed as Fire and Iron, Earth as Saturn, and Water as Mercury.
Rāhu is situated in the region of Vāyu and flows through the right nostril; Candra is in Water, and Budha [is likewise].

Earth resides in Jupiter, and wind in Venus; all these are situated in the left nostril (vāmanāḍī) in all matters, this is certain. One should designate the knowledge of roots in the earth element, the knowledge of living beings in water, the knowledge of metals in fire, and emptiness in space. Thus it is said.

According to the division of the elements, the states of the lunar phases (*candrāvasthā*) are proclaimed as follows: contentment (*tuṣṭi*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), excessive play (*ratikrīḍā*), muttering (*japa*), and laughter (*hāsya*) occur in earth and water; deep sleep (*supta*) and knowledge (*jña*) occur in air and fire; that which is called "departure" (*kalpa*) for travelers occurs in ether, followed by death (*mṛtyu*). These twelve should be practiced with diligence.

The instructors should always understand [this]: one should designate the elements beginning with earth as being most powerful in the east, west, and north respectively. These are earth, water, fire, air, and space. Earth [weighs] fifty palas.

One should know that water is forty [palas], fire thirty, wind twenty, and space twenty; the phrase "twenty palas" for space is connected to both [wind and space] by way of the maxim of the crow's eye. And earth [is measured] over a long period of time.

Gain shall occur from water in an instant; one becomes equal to the wind, and success shall arise from fire. Thus is the determination of the time for the results of questions according to their true nature. Earth has five qualities, water has four, fire has two, wind has two, and space has one quality.

This shall be the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Thus ends the measurement of the qualities, such as sound and so forth, within the five elements. (p. 822) That earth which has been fashioned by the agent, manifested, split apart, and passed away, bestows in all undertakings a fruit corresponding to its state. Thus it is said.

The state of Earth: Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇā, Abhijit, and Uttarāṣāḍhā are declared to be the Earth element (pṛthvītattva). Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Ārdrā, Rohiṇī, and Uttarabhādrapadā are Water (toya).
Water is the element that bestows desired fruits. O Dear One! Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Puṣya, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvabhādrapadā, and Svātī constitute the element of Fire (Tejas-tattva).
Viśākhā, Uttaraphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Punarvasu, Aśvinī, and Mṛgaśīrṣā [constitute the element of Air].
And the element of air (vāyustattva) has been thus illustrated. Thus end the constellations of the five elements.
If a being situated in the *bahvan-nāḍī* asks about auspicious or inauspicious matters, all that attains success;
in the *śūnya*, there is emptiness—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the result of questions for one situated in the *pūrṇa-nāḍī* and other channels. Through the *tattvas*, Āma attained victory.

And while Dhanañjaya remained in the state of reality, all the Kauravas were destroyed through the inversion of the truth regarding the head. Yet, by some whose souls are purified of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the truth is known either through the residual impressions of a previous birth or through the grace of the Guru.

Within the city of the body, the wind is the guardian; it is said to be ten finger-breadths [in length] during entry, twelve finger-breadths during exit, twenty-four during movement, and thirty-two during running—running meaning movement with speed. During sexual union it is sixty-five, and during sleep as well.
One hundred finger-breadths [is the distance for specific acts]. O Goddess! The movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is twelve finger-breadths by its very nature;
however, during eating and speaking, its movement is eighteen finger-breadths. Thus is the determination of the outward movement of the vital breaths according to specific activities.

When [the breath] is reduced by one finger-breadth, the departure of the vital breath (prāṇa) is considered to occur; bliss (ānanda) arises at the second, the power of a poet (kavi-śakti) at the third, the power of speech (vāc-śakti) at the fourth, far-sight (dūra-dṛṣṭi) at the fifth, traveling through the sky (ākāśa-gamana) at the sixth, and the piercing of the parts (khaṇḍa-veśa) at the seventh. At the eighth—
In the ninth [month], the eight Siddhis are attained and there is no death; in the tenth, one becomes the ten-fold form (Daśamūrti);

in the eleventh, the shadow perishes; in the twelfth, the movement of the Haṃsa occurs, and one drinks the nectar-essence of the Gaṅgā. For one who performs the breath-filling (prāṇapūraka), even the tips of the nails become edible.
p. 823) Food. Thus has the rule for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) been proclaimed, which bestows the fruits of all undertakings.

It is to be known through the word of the Guru, not by millions of scriptures of knowledge. If, by fate, the Moon is found in the east at dawn and the Sun in the west at evening, and [the Sun] is also in the middle at midday and midnight, then it is supreme.
The true principle proceeds as follows: In a distant battle, the Moon is victorious; when it is near, the Sun is.

In journeys, giving, marriage, entering a city or similar matters, and in all auspicious undertakings, the movement of the Moon is praised. If the lord of the year, the lunar day, and the day is joined with its corresponding *upatattva*, it flows [favorably].

Sometimes, by the turn of fate, a man conquers the enemy army merely by the paralysis of his voice; such a wise man even has power over the world of Keśava. Having placed the *jīvavakṣa* upon the chest of the living and having donned it upon the limbs of the living, the living one who conquers in battle—the living one indeed conquers.

"Movement on the earth and in the water should be undertaken during the auspicious operations of the sword; however, it shall not be so when [the quarters] are ablaze with fire or wind. Thus, according to the specific nature of the elements, is the result—auspicious or inauspicious—of movement."

One should fasten the weapon with the *jīva* [vital breath], and with the *jīva* alone one should release it; one should cast the weapon into the *jīva*, and thus one conquers in battle in every way. In the drawing-in [of the breath] is the *prāṇa* wind, and in the combination is the carrier of the cause (*hetuvāhana*). One should apply the step in the equal-superior [state] and accomplish all tasks.
When the battle with enemies is not yet complete, one who abides in the fullness of reality likewise makes the forest full;

standing alone in the perfection of truth, he conquers the earth. That channel which flows within the body has the deity of disease on its left; even when facing them directly, such is the state of those [channels].
She bestows the fruit of all undertakings. One should first perform the mudrā and afterwards engage in battle. For those by whom every mudrā has been performed, success is certain;
just as soldiers are equal in the flow of a machine or in the drawing up of the sun. Indeed, when it has occurred...

One who desires victory should engage in a debate concerning the principles of wind (*samīraṇatattva*). For one who has been led into these [debates], there is no morning-time obstacle. If one enters into a battle with the wind, then at that time he is always victorious;
there is no doubt. Even if the enemy is before him, wherever [the breath flows] in the channel (*nāḍī*)—

The wind should carry that portion, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself; drawing it up to the tip of the ears, one surely conquers even Indra. From the first lunar day (*pratipad*) onwards, it should be known as full when well-guarded; its power cannot be destroyed by enemies, even those who are most powerful.

At the time of battle, one should place the bow between the thumb and forefinger, as well as upon the big toe; thus, one shall become victorious over ten thousand warriors. When the wind (vital breath) remains situated in the middle during the movement of the moon and the sun, it shall protect the cardinal directions.

A man desiring victory will always find that when the messenger speaks his desire at the time of the inhalation of the breath, his goals attain fulfillment, O beautiful one, precisely through the exhalation. Thus ends the result of questions asked during the time of inhalation.

Gains and other personal objectives, when inquired about or proclaimed, are accomplished when Jupiter (Sajīva) is present; however, there would be loss if Mercury (Niḥsaraṇa) is present. A man is considered skillful when his own [sign] is present, while for a woman, the left [side/sign] is praised. At the time of battle, Kumbhaka [is used], and the movement of women is through the three channels (nāḍīs).

Without the distinction between the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, how can there be a vowel? By the very word *haṃsa*, that *jīva* (individual soul) chants [the mantra] at all times. Whether on the left or on the right, whenever the questioner asks a question, no blow shall arise therein; one should indicate the blow as being in the void (*śūnya*).
The earth element causes injury to the self; the water element resides in the feet;
fire resides in the thighs; the wind element resides in the waist;
and the ether element resides in the head—thus is the determination of injury to be understood as fivefold.
The fatal blow has been revealed in the inquiry regarding the vowels; thus is the determination of the locations of the fatal blows according to their true nature.

When a question regarding the onset of battle is asked, victory belongs first to the *pūrṇa* [breath], and in the second case, when it is *rikta*, one becomes the victor; it is not otherwise. When the question is situated in the *pūrṇa* channel, and the breath has moved into the *śūnya* immediately preceding it, the enemy dies in the place of the *śūnya* that is ahead; of this there is no doubt. This applies to the practice of the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*).

He whose nose is straight shall be victorious; the querent on the right side indicates victory through the southern channel (*dakṣiṇā śirā*). If he asks while the breath is situated in the moon (*candra*), then one should predict peace;
but when he asks while it is situated in the sun (*sūrya*), then know that there will be conflict. Thus it is said.
The explanation of peace and war in a query according to the distinction between the left and the right.

In the case of the Earth element (pārthiva), there will be war; in the case of the Water element (vāruṇa), there is peace; victory indeed occurs in the Fire element (taijasa); defeat or death occurs in the Air element (vāyu) and the Ether element (nābhasa). Thus, through the specific nature of the elements, one gains knowledge of war and other matters.

Or, when the wind is not perceived due to negligence or because it has ceased, if at the time of questioning the wise practitioner should maintain a steady focus, he should— having recognized the motionless state of concentration (dhāraṇā)—
cause the flower to fall upon the hand; whether the flower falls on a full limb or on an empty one.

One should declare its fruit; that fruit is the result of being full or empty. Whether standing or sitting, drawing in one's own vital breath (*prāṇa*), he by whom the breaking of the mind has been performed lives in all undertakings. One should establish the wind by means of the *jīva*, and again cause it to abide by means of the *jīva*; by means of the *jīva* it is brought about.

One who knows the *svara* (vocal/tonal science) always conquers in battle in every way. Through the fruit [of this knowledge], one becomes foremost; otherwise, it may become fruitless in ten million ways. In this world and the next, the knower of *svara* is always powerful. There is fortune amounting to ten, a hundred, or ten thousand, and sometimes the fickle sovereignty of a kingdom, like that of Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
The strength of the lords of the gods would be multiplied ten millionfold.
Śrī Devī said:
"In a battle between humans, victory is likewise declared to be equal. In an even battle...
"When [passion] has arisen among men, how is victory [attained]?
Śrī Śiva said:
One should meditate upon the Reality while the vital breath is steady, and one should offer the steady union as an oblation."

For him, there shall be the accomplishment of his desires, great gain, and likewise victory. The formless has arisen as the world with forms and parts; its form is formless, and in knowledge it becomes identical with that. Thus ends the chapter on the Victory of the Battle of Knowledge.
Now, the rite of subjugation.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Maheśvara! You have described human combat and snow combat; now, O Lord of Gods, tell me of the supreme method of subjugation."
Śrī Śiva said:
One should establish the life-force (jīva) of the Moon within the lunar orb by means of the Sun; thus, the beloved woman remains under one's control from birth.
This has been declared by those whose wealth is austerity (tapodhana). By means of the life-force, living beings are seized; the life-force belongs to the life-force.

It is given: A living being situated in the state of *jāva* (the stage of birth) is one who performs the act of "child-life" (*bālājīva*). He who drinks the seed of Brahman at the time of the third watch of the night, when the womenfolk are fast asleep, is indeed a destroyer of child-life. However, if one recites the eight-syllable mantra (*aṣṭākṣara*) at that time while engaged in sexual union, [that is not so].

In an instant the moon is surrendered and the passionate woman falls into a state of delusion. Whether at the proper time, during an occasion, or even upon embracing a young woman, he should quickly cause her to surrender that very moment and delude the passionate woman. He who drinks the moon by means of the sun shall become the one whose banner is a sea-monster (Kāmadeva). Śiva.

One should embrace her with power during the *prasaṅga* (intercourse), whether on the right side or otherwise. When the Sun is in conjunction with the Sun, there are seven, nine, three, and five [breaths]; when the Moon is in conjunction with the Moon, she becomes submissive during the fourth and eighth watches of the day.
Having made the Sun and Moon equal, one should place them upon all the limbs, the forehead, and the lips.
Having placed one's face upon the *mahāpadma* (the great lotus), one should perform this repeatedly.
This is called "meditative absorption" (*adhyāna*), continuing until one falls under the power of sleep.
Afterwards, at the time of waking, having licked one's throat and eyes, the lover [should proceed] by this method.
One shall bring all women under one's control. O Supreme Goddess, this is the command regarding another [mantra].
Thus ends the section on subjugation.

Now begins the section on conception. When a woman becomes pure on the fifth day during her fertile period, there occurs a conjunction of the sun and the moon with the *jīva* (vital principle), resulting in the birth of a son. When the conch-shell-like channel (*śaṅkhāvalī*) flows with cow's milk toward the earth, she should speak these words before her husband:
"Bestow the embryo with these three words. A woman who has bathed after her menses should drink [the mixture] and employ the knowledge of the fertile period (*ṛtu*);

she shall give birth to a Narasiṃha endowed with beauty and charm. One should employ the knowledge of the fertile period through the fragrance of the Suṣumṇā-sun; [otherwise, one may be born] lacking limbs.

A male is born there with the body of a worm; [if conception occurs] during the odd lunar day (viṣamāṅga), it is by night, and during the even lunar day (dinādhipa), it is by day. When the moon, the eyes, and the fire-principle (tattva) are present, a barren woman may obtain a son.
