At the commencement of sexual union, the sun [is present] for men, and at the end of the union, [the moon].
Sudhākara says: By this application of the ritual, even one who is not a king receives the royal scepter from the gods.
At the commencement of sexual union, the sun belongs to men and the moon (Sudhākara) to women. When the union of both is attained, even a barren woman shall obtain a son. Thus it is said.

The Cause for the Birth of Sons and Daughters: If the lunar channel (candranāḍī) flows at the time of inquiry regarding pregnancy, it will be a daughter; if the solar channel (sūrya) flows, then it will be a son. If both flow, the pregnancy is destroyed. The moon represents a female, the sun a male, and the central channel (madhyamārga) a neuter. In the case of emptiness (śūnya), there is emptiness [of offspring].

In each pair [of signs], there is a miscarriage during the transit; when the Sun's portion is reached, a son is born, but on a Monday, a daughter. In an odd [number of signs] there will be a miscarriage, and in both [cases of even and odd], a neuter child. One should understand this through the principles (tattvas), O beautiful one! Thus it is stated in the *Praśna*.
Knowledge of the child in the womb: In the Māruta [element], conception occurs; one becomes very miserable. In the Divya [element], he is renowned;
in the Vāruṇa, he is endowed with happiness. In the Vahni [element], there is miscarriage and short life. In the Pārthiva, he is an enjoyer, fortunate, wealthy, and endowed with happiness.

One who possesses enjoyments while situated in the womb is most excellent when the principle (tattva) is Varuṇa; however, the embryo perishes in the ether (vyoman). A son is born under Māhendra, and a daughter would be born under Varuṇa. In the remaining [principles], there is either loss of the embryo or death immediately upon birth. [This occurs] in the midst of Ravi.

"The moon has entered the center of the moon; the sun has entered [the center of] the sun. This must be known quickly from a guru, not through millions of sciences and scriptures. Thus ends the section on the Womb (Garbha-prakaraṇa).

Now begins the section on the year: On the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the northern course of the sun, the yogi who perceives the future moment should observe, according to the differentiation of the principles (tattva), that which flows through the right [channel] at the time of the moon's rising, in accordance with the eight principles.

Earth, water, and likewise wind bring abundance of all crops; fire and space bring terrible fear and famine according to the nature of the time. Thus should the results of the elements be known for the year, the month, and the day. [If] cruel and wicked, it becomes mediocre.
In all activities, there may be the ruin of the country, great disease, and the suffering of afflictions and hardships.

At the time of the sun's transition into Aries (meṣa-saṃkrānti), one should examine the changes in the voice; the thinker of truth should then declare the results for the year for the people, regarding the principles (tattvas) residing in earth and the other elements.

The results arising from the day, month, and year [are as follows]: likewise, food will be spoiled by ether, wind, and fire. However, if the earth-element prevails, there will be abundance of food, prosperity, and the earth will abound with crops; there will be heavy rain as well as happiness.
If the fire element prevails at the time of the sun's entry into Aries (Meṣa-saṃkrānti), there will be famine, the ruin of the kingdom, and the onset of most terrible calamities;
the rainfall will be very slight, even less than scanty, and there will be portents, afflictions, fear, meager rain, and pestilences. If the air element prevails...

If [the breath] flows; if at the time of the Aries transit (meṣasaṃkrānti) the element of space (vyomatattva) should flow, even then the wise should know there will be calamity for grain and other crops. Through the element of breath (śvāsatattva), success is granted only to that which is prior and more ancient. As for the Sun and Moon, they are as described in the compendium (saṃgraha).

It bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). In the uneven [period], only the space (*nabhas*) of the fire-principle (*vahnitattva*) is known. One who collects the substances should prepare that; and in two months, there is great value. At the transit of the sun, the channel (*nāḍī*) dissolves and flows forth. That occurs in the wind, and through the conjunction with fire, it is the Raurava [hell] upon the surface of the earth. Thus.
The Section on the Year.
Now begins the section on diseases: If one is afflicted by disease upon the earth, and the lords of water [are] in the water;

if this messenger has gone to the void and subsequently enters the full [house], then even if he is unconscious, he will certainly live—provided for whose sake he inquires, and in whichever limb he is situated.
The living soul situated therein asks: "Does this living soul live, even if afflicted by diseases? If it speaks with harsh or fierce syllables on the right or the left, then that living soul lives;
the Moon yields equal results in due order. And in the form of the letter *Jīva* (J), the nature of Fire [is present], and the form of *Jīva*.

And having observed: if the *jīva* (vital breath) is situated in the *jīvitapraśna* (the inquiry concerning life), the result for him shall be life itself. When the messenger asks while standing on the left-hand path, or on the right during entry, or wherever the vehicle is located—if he stands there and asks, his success is certain, without doubt. And if, in the inquiry, the *jīva* is situated below, it is deficient.

For the living soul indeed lives. A living soul established in upright conduct goes to the abode of Yama; however, if the querent asks a question with reversed syllables on a *riktā* lunar day, a reversal should be understood when there is an unfavorable rising of the planets. When the living soul is situated in the place of the Moon and in the place of the Sun...

The Questioner: If, at that time, he is afflicted by diseases and deprived of life, and the *jīva* (vital breath) is situated in Piṅgalā while the messenger asks on the left [side], then even so the sick man dies, unless Maheśvara is his protector; this occurs through the reversal of one element.
In this world, men suffer the affliction of disease; from the reversal of these three fortnights, there occurs the ruin of both one's kinsmen and friends, and death shall follow.
Now, the knowledge of time:
at the beginning of a month, the beginning of a year, and the beginning of a fortnight, the wise one should examine the time in due order by means of the strength of the movement of the winds.
One should protect the lamp composed of the five elements, which is moistened with the oil of the moon.

By that solar wind (sūryavāta), the vital breath (jīva) becomes firm. If, having bound the wind (māruta), one binds the sun, then through practice the vital breath, though living, deceives even at the time of the sun.
From the sky, the moon flows and sprinkles the lotuses of the body; [one should contemplate] the moon.

The teacher [says]: "The sun [of breath] should be restrained at night and by day. Thus, when there is such an absence [of duality], that yogi will certainly attain immortality; of this there is no doubt. When his vital air flows as a unity throughout day and night, then his lifespan shall be a full three years. For one whose [vital air flows as a unity] for two days and nights...

The constant movement [of the breath] through Piṅgalā is declared by the knowers of reality to signify a lifespan of two years. When the constant movement flows through Piṅgalā three times, the wise declare that his life span is one year. "Sadāgati" refers to the wind (vāyu). [This occurs] at night.

If for one the moon flows by day and the sun flows continuously, one should know that his death will indeed occur within six months. If the sun should flow continuously for one to sixteen days, his death will indeed occur after the remaining days of that month.

If the breath flows fully [through one nostril] while both the sun and the moon are not visible, death occurs within a fortnight; so it is declared by those who know the science of time. If the moon flows fully while the sun is not visible at all, death occurs within a month; so it is declared by those who know the science of time.
He whose urine and feces are discharged simultaneously should be known as one who has departed from his life;
he will certainly die within ten days. Those whose lifespan is exhausted do not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the three steps of Viṣṇu, or fourthly, the Mātṛmaṇḍala. [Arundhatī]

The tongue may become fixed, as may the tip of the nose; the two eyebrows should be known as Viṣṇupada, while the Tāraka is the Mātṛmaṇḍala. Having seen the nine Dhruvas, the seven Ghoṣas, the five Tattvas, the three nostrils, and the single aperture of the tongue, a man certainly dies.
One should observe the bodily mass, which is like the body of a fish in a corner; when the drop (*bindu*) is no longer seen, the man has died within ten days. Thus ends the knowledge of time.

Now, the knowledge of the channels (*nāḍī*): *Iḍā* is known as the Gaṅgā, and *Piṅgalā* as the river Yamunā; between them, *Sarasvatī* is to be known. Through these three, by means of yoga, is *Prayāga*. First, the practice is explained, which produces immediate realization. The yogi sits in the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*).

One should perform uḍḍiyānabandha. Inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) as the third—these must always be understood by yogis for the sake of attaining perfection of the body. Inhalation brings about the equilibrium of the earth element, and likewise, retention brings about stabilization.

One should perform that which increases the protection of life. Recaka (exhalation) removes sin; through Kumbhaka (retention), one attains the state of Yoga. Afterwards, one should remain like a warrior in battle, but one should not cause [the breath] to be bound. One should retain the natural breath with effort according to one's capacity, and then exhale.
The wise one should fill [the channels] by means of the moon-path and the sun-path. The moon drinks the sun;
the sun drinks the moon. Through the mutual state of their times, one may live as long as the moon and stars exist.
Whichever channel flows in whichever limb, perform the awakening of that channel.

Releasing that which is bound at the mouth, or indeed for the sake of knowing others within them, one should obstruct the mouth, nose, and ears with the fingers. This should be known as "the arising of reality" (tattvodaya), O Dear One! It is the act of bringing [the deity] face-to-face; it does not consist of a physical form.
This is the characteristic of the Maṇḍalī: that man in this world who knows [this] is a knower of Yoga, even if he is base.

Free from desire and devoid of fruit, the Yogī should not think of anything at all. Having rendered the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) into the state beyond mind (*unmanī*), he conquers time with ease. Whatever power has been proclaimed for whichever Siddha—

The abyss of qualities: seated firmly in the lotus posture, one should indeed restrain the wind of the anus; one should release the vital breath and so forth during the three-fold *kumbhaka* of the air. When the *prāṇa* is restrained by power, it enters the aperture at the *brahmacakra*; there, the eternal [power] resides on the path of the space of the deposit.

Those few fortunate ones who are devoted to the feet of Śiva attain [liberation]. The yogi who knows this and recites it daily becomes completely freed from all suffering and obtains his desired fruit.
For him who possesses the knowledge of the internal sounds (svara) regarding Śiva, prosperity shall reside at the soles of his feet like his own life-breath.
Just as the sun is among all the gods in the universe,

so too is this holy knower of the Self worthy of worship in the world of mortals; yet he who knows the three channels (nāḍīs) and likewise the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)— with him, no one can be equaled.

The elixir of a hundred thousand crores; the bestower of the single syllable; the one who pierces through the differentiation of the channels—there is no substance on earth by giving which one would not become free from debt. Likewise, the reality of the vowels, battle, and the three divine methods of subjugation proceed thus in the world.

This tantra, O highly fortunate one, is renowned by the yogis who have attained perfection; it bestows success through its recitation. Seated comfortably in a steady posture, O wide-eyed one free from passion, he who meditates upon the Supreme Self shall become [the Supreme].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Branch Consisting of the Knowledge of Vowels," in the sixth section (Jñānakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Now, the Royal Yoga (*rājayoga*). In the *Yogasvarodaya*, the Lord said:
"I shall proclaim the Royal Yoga, which grants success everywhere; listen, for it is more secret than the secret."
O Goddess! O Supreme One beyond all dharmas! O Queen of the Gods! By means of Rājayoga, a man becomes worthy of worship by kings;
the practitioner of Rājayoga becomes long-lived and endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya).
This Rājayoga is of fifteen kinds: Kriyāyoga, Jñānayoga, Karmayoga, Haṭha, Dhyānayoga, Mantrayoga, Urayoga, and Vāsanā. By these, it reigns like the sovereign Lord Brahmā in fifteen ways. Now...
And I shall describe their characteristics; listen, O beloved!

Meditation, worship, giving, sacrifice, recitation, fire-offerings, and other such acts constitute the yoga consisting of ritual action and liberation, which bestows the perfection of *sapiṇḍī*. At the commencement of any task, the mind should form the resolve: "Whatever I do..."
Always performing its practice along with its auxiliary limbs, one should be devoted to *kriyā-yoga*.
Forgiveness, discernment, dispassion, tranquility, contentment, and desirelessness—this union with liberation is declared to be *kriyā-yoga*. Envy, possessiveness, deceit, and violence...
O Madagarvitā! Desire, anger, fear, shame, greed, delusion, as well as impurity;

passion and hatred, disgust, laziness, fatigue, hypocrisy, patience, and confusion—he in whom these do not exist is called a practitioner of *kriyā-yoga*. O Caṇḍī! He alone is liberated and he is the man of knowledge through destruction.
The Lord: That which effects both action and liberation is Rājayoga; it bestows liberation.
I shall now proclaim Jñānayoga; through that knowledge, one attains the state of Śiva. By reciting, remembering, practicing, and adorning oneself with this, one becomes a seeker of Brahman.

The unification of their distinctions, consisting of the eightfold sovereignty (aṣṭaiśvarya), occurs there; where, O Supreme Goddess, are the three sacred sites (tīrtha), the channel (nāḍī), and the triple merit (tripuṇya). He who does not know this within his own body is a yogi in name only. [Therein lies] the nine wheels (navacakra), the support of the digits (kalā), the three lakhs [of channels], and the five voids (vyomapañcaka).

He who does not know this within his own body is a yogi in name only. This is considered by the wise to be the *rājayoga* of this Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*). O virtuous lady! Listen with a single-minded focus as I describe its specific details. At the root-center (*mūlakanda*) and in the region of the perineum, there is one supreme, radiant channel; it is situated above the anus.

In one-third [of the body] is the great channel named Iḍā, possessing the luster of the moon; in the form of Śakti, she bestows all goals through meditation. In the right side is the one called Kulā, having the form of a man and the nature of the sun. In the middle portion is the one called Suṣumnā, whose essence consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Known by those of pure mind, she possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, she grants the powers such as *aṇimā* through meditative concentration.
Having taken her seat within the *suṣumnā* at the nine cakras, listen now as they are described: the *mūlādhāra* has four petals.
Above the anus resides the Great One. In its center, upon a golden pedestal, is the supreme triangular mandala. Therein is the form shaped like a flame of fire, which bestows success everywhere.
Its meditation, consisting of speech, takes place within the mind without the need for a physical seat.

The knower of yoga always perceives the *saṅkarṣa* within all scriptures. At the base of the *liṅga*, however, is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which resembles a seat and possesses six petals. In its center is a great light, radiant like the rising sun, which bestows perfect accomplishment; through meditation upon it, one's lifespan increases.

One attains equality with Kandarpa. The third [lotus], however, is in the region of the navel; it has ten petals and is most wonderful. It possesses the luster of a great cloud and is endowed with millions of lightning flashes.
A light equal to the fire at the end of an aeon is itself situated in its center. Of that...

From meditation, one shall become long-lived, free from disease, the best among beings, liberated from all sins, great, and a shaker of the world. The unstruck (*anāhata*) has eight seats; it is the fourth lotus in the heart, with petals like the sun, a great light, exceedingly subtle, and visible to the eye. It has petals like the sun.

There is a twelve-petaled [lotus]; in its center is an eight-petaled lotus facing upward, possessing great luster. It is the seat of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), and its pericarp is in the form of a liṅga.
This pericarp is called Kālikā, and within it resides Kuṇḍalinī of Padmavatī.

The size of its light is equal to that of a thumb, resembling a jewel. Its life-force (*jīva*) is unattached; it is infinite by virtue of its power and form. Meditation upon this brings the world under control, and one becomes all-pervading like a *khecarī*.
Gods and others become subject to the will of the one who performs this meditation; it is not otherwise. [It brings] the desired and the undesired...

He shall truly become subject [to one's will], truly, there is no doubt; he shall attain his desired success and the arising of qualities such as omniscience. The fifth petal of the lotus is pure, located in the region of the throat. In its center is a single Person, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.

Indeed, incurable diseases perish through meditation upon it, and one attains a lifespan of a thousand years. The sixth wheel, called Ājñā, is located between the eyebrows; it has two petals and consists of a light resembling a flame of fire. It is devoid of the female [seed-syllable] for the male practitioner. Through meditation upon this—

One attains all perfections and reaches the state of being ageless and immortal. In the center of the palate is the middle wheel with sixty-four petals; it is filled with nectar, resembles ten million moons, and is the abode of immortality (*amṛtasthalī*). In its center is the pericarp known as the *ghaṭikā*.
Resembling blood, together with a digit of the moon, it flows there as a stream of nectar.
Having meditated on this and bathed in the nectars, one is forever liberated through yoga.
Insanity, fever, bile, burning sensations, colic, and other pains, as well as headaches, are destroyed.

The state of dullness also perishes. Through immediate meditation, the entire universe is experienced and the dullness of the tongue perishes. In the Brahma-randhra is the eighth chakra, a hundred-petaled lotus of great luster; this is proclaimed as the sacred seat named Jālandhara.

Having recognized the locus of the perfected person (siddhapuṃs), the crest-lock (śikhā) resembling fire and smoke exists as the supreme (parā) form, devoid of beginning, middle, or end, and abiding in the forms of both female and male. Through meditation, one becomes a knower of the end; there is union even in the sky, and one becomes a constant knower of all.

Speaking thus, one becomes great. A living being situated in the midst of the world is freed from the afflictions of the world. That which is beyond the supreme is the ninth, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), the Wheel (*cakra*). There is nothing higher than that; there is nothing more supreme than the Great Supreme.

The Great Wheel (Mahācakra) is the wheel of the perfected ones (Siddhacakra), known by names such as Pūrṇagaurī and others. In its center resides a wondrous thousand-petaled lotus, facing upward within the great face, a supreme locus for the splendor of colors, completely filled with all auspiciousness; there is nothing equal to it.
Its measurement cannot indeed be described by mind or speech. Therein, O Sovereign of the Universe, exists a three-cornered pericarp; there, O Supreme Goddess, resides the seventeenth digit (kalā).
That digit of the Stainless One possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns and the splendor of ten million moons.

Free from cold, heat, and other such dualities, mental suffering shall indeed not arise for the practitioner through this meditation. That which lies above should be known as the abode of infinite supreme bliss;
by meditating upon that, the upward-moving power (*ūrdhvagatakalā*) arises within him. Thus concludes the *Siddhirājayoga*.

The enjoyment of women is great bliss; accompanied by Śiva, the pleasures of song, instrumental music, and diversion increase upon the earth. His meditation is continuous, for merit and sin no longer hold sway.
There shall be a vision of his own true form, and he perceives objects even at a distance.

O Pārvatī, now hear about the practice of *lakṣayoga*, which is easily accomplished. The *lakṣayoga* is fivefold, according to the divisions beginning with the upward-pointing (*ūrdhvalakṣa*). It should be known as the upward-pointing (*ūrdhvalakṣa*), the downward-pointing (*adholakṣa*), the outward-pointing (*bāhyalakṣa*), the middle-pointing (*madhyalakṣa*), and likewise the infinite-pointing (*anantalakṣa*).
And: "O Maheśvarī, listen to their characteristics after knowing their fruit!
Fixing one's gaze upon the sky, one should direct the mind upwards; this upward-pointed focus constitutes oneness with the Supreme Lord, O Queen of the Gods, above the nose."
The gaze should be made steady at a distance of twelve finger-breadths; one should focus on this lower object. Alternatively, this gaze may be made steady upon the tip of the nose.
One who possesses a steady gaze shall have a long life; thus, such a person is endowed with steady vision. [This refers to] the external object.

For those who dwell in reality, that which is to be known reaches them spontaneously; but for those possessed by desire, the outward gaze bestows perfect accomplishment in matters such as visualization. This is the external and intermediate focal point, a desired visualization free from agitation.
Now hear about the internal focal point, which is devoid of directions, intermediate points, and so forth.

O Goddess of Gods! Whether walking, waking, sleeping, or eating—at all times and in every state—one should fix the mind upon the Void (śūnya). The agent and the instigator are the Void; the embodied one is the Void, the Lord (Īśvara). Abiding within the vessel of joy and sorrow, this [self] itself undergoes birth and death.

The form of the inconceivable residing in the jar (the body) assumes a nature free from thought; having abandoned sense objects as being as harmful as poison, and having realized the vital air (māruta), one becomes mindless of designations and is no longer stained by merit or sin. For the space is both external and internal.

This is known as the "internal target" (antarlakṣa). By constantly practicing this, no suffering whatsoever shall arise, and one becomes Śiva. That which is void (śūnya), yet being-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), soundless, and designated by the word "Brahman," and that which is with sound (saśabda) and to be known as "space" (ākāśa)—these are the two distinctions here.

Now I shall describe the characteristics of Rājayoga; when Rājayoga is accomplished by men, the signs of perfection will appear. The mind becomes completely full, and though situated in the world, it remains outside the world. There is no agitation, nor birth, nor death, nor likewise suffering or pleasure.
Difference and non-difference reside in the mind; knowledge, conduct, and lineage are likewise [not inherent].
This is a continuous connection with Prakāśa and Kuśa;
yet He is the illuminator of all, and indeed one for whom difference and so forth have perished. Furthermore, there is no mark of birth for Him.

This one is partless and stainless; this infinite, great light bestows the enjoyment of desire. In his mind, there is neither attachment nor detachment. Even upon attaining a kingdom there is no joy, and in loss there is no sorrow. [He remains] in the silence of the region regarding any object whatsoever.
(p. 835) In some places and at some times, one should maintain an entirely equal vision toward knowledge and ignorance, as well as toward friend and enemy.

Through the state of being an agent attached to enjoyments and so forth, the mind should become like the sky. One may be an agent in the midst of the world, yet even in the midst of the mind, one is actionless. Such a person is called a Rājayogin, whether in happiness or in suffering.

Likewise, joy and sorrow never arise for them, nor does agitation occur in their encounter with the world. Remaining mentally motionless and always equanimous, one should abide forever in that which is eternally radiant, formless, seatless, and without self— just as the wind, moving within space, merges into space.
Spontaneously, when the mind is thus dissolved in space, that is considered the practice of Rājayoga;
it remains untainted by contact with the world, like water on a lotus leaf.

Now, Haṭhayoga, which bestows the perfection of Haṭha, is being described. Having assumed a posture that subdues the breath and removes disease from the body, one should practice inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) with the vital air. Thus, having understood the sequence and its reverse, one should master the breath.
The practitioner of Haṭha Yoga should always perform the sixfold practice beginning with *dhautī*.
O Goddess of Gods! when this [channel] is established and filled with air, the mind then becomes steady, and from that, there is indeed bliss. Through Haṭha Yoga, time [is transcended].

If the dissolution of the mind were to occur, then now hear the second division of Haṭhayoga: one should meditate upon [the point] in space or at the tip of the nose as being like ten million suns, in forms such as white, red, yellow, black, and so forth. Having meditated thus—
He shall possess long life, free from disease and decay; by the grace of Haṭhayoga, this great soul becomes equal to Śiva.
Having become composed of light through Haṭha, he indeed becomes Śiva within.
Therefore, this Haṭhayoga is the bestower of perfection, practiced by the perfected ones (Siddhas). Now...
O Śivā! The characteristic of the yoga of knowledge is now described;

by knowing which, one becomes Śiva, perfected in knowledge, and there is no more rebirth. One who is the self of the universe and the creator of the universe should perceive the entire world as one alone—having thus become disciplined, one is indeed joined [in yoga].

One should practice the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). Wherever one may be situated, the entire world consists of all-knowledge (*sarvajñānamaya*); he who possesses such awakening (*bodha*) is entitled to the authority of knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*). Constantly devoted to the eternal, he attains the *śāmbhavī* mantras, just as [the potential of] a banyan seed [is present within].
On earth, it acts like a tree for its sower: first one, then many;

by its very nature, through the covering of soil and other means, the tree grows day and night, spreading wide with leaves and sprouts. This expansion occurs naturally through sap, flowers, fruits, and seeds.

Thus, he is stainless, eternal, changeless, and untainted; though one, he becomes many, and though vast, he exists in manifold ways through his own creative effort. Composed of the five elements, and subject to the transformations of intellect, *māyā*, and ego, he manifests the universe in this way in its great variety.
Extremely vast as the world and its beyond, there is not even a single atom that exists which he does not know; he who knows this is a knower of reality.

For the stationary, such as mountains and the like, and the moving, such as those who travel through the sky—all this world, appearing in both moving and stationary forms, is that Lord by his own nature and sport.
This [world] shines in the void due to the cognition of emptiness. That object which is perceived as a thing is called "the visible";

that which has transcended being seen is "the invisible," yet at that time one still considers it to be seen. In this way, one perceives the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), crowded with suffering, as a mere differentiation within one’s own body.

Having diligently cast far away [all else], one becomes a wise man through the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). There is but one union with knowledge, and there is but one who possesses the yoga of knowledge. Therefore, that which is to be known is non-different from knowledge;
yet, by means of the discourse on difference, one should set aside all distinctions as far as the earth extends, making them separate from knowledge.

From this vision, one becomes a practitioner of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayogī*), for the yoga of knowledge is indeed singular. Thus, O Great Goddess, through knowledge, the conqueror of time attains the state of Śiva. Listen with diligence, O Goddess, to this distinction of natures; by hearing which, there shall be universal awakening that bestows liberation.
Desiring accomplishment, one speaks of the nature of the self or of earth and the other elements as follows: The self itself is the earth, the sustainer; it is sometimes tender and sometimes firm.
It is sometimes captivating, and it is both pure and impure; it is both foul-smelling and fragrant.

And she is odorless yet intoxicating with fragrance; she has the form of gold, the form of minerals, variegated, and supreme as consisting of jewels. In some places she is white, in some red, and in some yellow and black. She is indeed the fertile soil, always consisting of both poison and nectar. And thus:

The gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, and others, as well as birds and the like; the sick person gathered in happiness, and likewise one whose mind is pacified from anger; endowed with all forms and powers, and thus possessing manifold intellects—this is the divine reality through the power of the elements. The designation "living being" (jīva) is essentially delusion. [This is] the yoga of knowledge.

Changeless, free from suffering, the one Lord; having become the singular embodiment of the Self, he is beyond conceptualization and untainted. By his very nature, he is the infinite consciousness who is happy, sorrowful, and possessed of delusion.
Indeed, that Great One takes the form of both female and male, mutually infatuated with one another, yet remains without a mind.

Through his own state of being, the practitioner of knowledge (*jñānayogī*) remains undisturbed; yet, by his very nature, he may desire enjoyment from garlands, sandalwood, and other such objects of the left-hand path. With a mind fixed on reality, he abides in happiness through that which consists of happiness, even for the sake of the suffering of others—by means of his self, his mind, and his feet.

The wealth of jewels such as sons and so forth—since these are merely the pursuit of the essence within the insubstantial, the intellect of wisdom should arise through the mind. Having attained the discernment of the Self, one who possesses a noble lineage does not perceive the Supreme Self because his flickering mind, blinded by the darkness of sense-objects, fails to see it; for the Self is free from illusion and transcends all categories of reality.
Devoid of the six-fold connection, one who is happy or miserable undergoes birth and death again and again; this is the truth.

Having abandoned the wealth of dispassion and other virtues—which to the intellect are as productive of suffering as poison—one is liberated through the yoga of knowledge, realizing the Self to be equal to ten million suns. As light resides in the sun and clarity in ghee, [so does the Self reside within].

Oil exists in sesame by its very nature; as there is a rabbit in the moon, branches in a tree, and salt in alkaline water, so too does the cycle of worldly existence exist within Brahman, which is indivisible and perfectly complete. Now, O Dear One, hear of the external signs that grant success (*siddhi*); these are indeed known as *dhāraṇās*.

These should be understood in particular. One should meditatively cultivate the absorbed, light-filled, and supremely great [state] as a play. Or else, O Goddess of gods! one should perceive there a smoke-colored form six finger-breadths [in size], or else a red form eight finger-breadths [in size] above the nose.

Alternatively, one should perceive the earth-element (pṛthvītattva) as twelve finger-breadths in measure and yellowish in color; or else, one should perceive there a mass of light equal in radiance to ten million suns, a great expanse of space.
Through meditation upon each of these, one becomes Śiva. [This occurs] in the midst of space, above the space.
Having made the gaze very steady, one sees the sun as a fierce sun even without meditation;
or else, this target (lakṣa) is outside the practitioner, above Śiva, at a height of seventeen finger-breadths, brilliant with light— or else.

The earth-element (pṛthivītattva) resembles molten gold. One should fix one's gaze upon this mark before oneself with a restrained mind. O Dear One! For anyone among those mentioned, the practice of even a single one of these individually results in being free from wrinkles and grey hair, even without medicinal herbs; likewise, all diseases [are cured].
An enemy becomes submissive like a friend; he shall live for a thousand years, honored in all worlds. Knowledge shall manifest at the tip of his tongue even without the study of scriptures.
Arising from the root-tuber, originating from the *brahmanāḍī*, it is white in color.

It remains extending as far as the *brahmarandhra*. Within that, however, exists the supreme [power] known as the *brahmarandhra*; it has the form of a lotus fiber and possesses the radiance of ten million suns and lightning.
This great form moves upward; through meditation upon it, one becomes Śiva.

The eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, become manifest through the complete [practice]. Or, having meditated upon the Moon or the Lord of Light (*jyotirīśvara*) above the forehead, one may destroy diseases such as leprosy; he becomes supremely auspicious and long-lived.
Alternatively, having meditated upon the Sun or the Lord of Radiance (*teja īśvara*) between the eyebrows...
With steady vision, he is honored by kings, liberated while living like Śiva himself;

for having meditated upon the Self as the very form of the Self, he becomes actionless. Free from desire and established in the reality of the Self, he is not like any other who merely holds the status of a king.
Now listen; I shall describe the classification of the channels (nāḍīs) which bestows success.
Outside of Meru is the one named Iḍā, accompanied by Piṅgalā. Suṣumnā stands along the path of the sun, extending as far as the Gate of Brahmā (brahmadvāra). Sarasvatī and Sugandhā, however—

Gāndhārī and Hastijihvikā are to be known between the two ears; likewise, the last one (Śaṅkhinī) is between the two eyes. Pūṣā and Ālambuṣā are situated at the base, and in some places elsewhere as well, O Dear One!
[These channels] extend from the linga-door and the path of the iḍā up to the station of Brahmā, reaching the end of the channels.

In the reverse order, there are seventy-two thousand [breaths]. Now, the ten winds situated within the body are described; they are explained according to their functions and causes, and by means of their characteristics. The prāṇa wind, residing in the heart, performs inhalation and exhalation.

The one known as Yoga makes the Lord yellow and extremely beautiful; Apāna, residing in the region of the anus, performs contraction as well as restraint. Samāna, located in the navel circle, is the nourisher of the channels beginning with Toṣaka and the bestower of luster.

Likewise, the great supreme [vital air] called Samāna is in the midst of the blazing fire; Udāna, however, is in the middle of the palate, and it eats and drinks. Vyāna-vāyu is established pervading the entire body; among these, it effects movement in the body and also maintains stability. [It is located] in the middle of the eyes.

The one named Kūrma performs the closing and opening of the eyes; Nāga is said to be responsible for belching; Kṛkara is known as the upward-moving wind that causes movement; Devadatta is to be understood as the one who produces sneezing;
and Dhanañjaya, whose nature is existence-consciousness (saccidākāra), does not leave the dead body.

Although all of this has already been stated in the *Sargakāṇḍa*, it is mentioned again here for the purpose of making known the relationship between cause and effect; thus, it is not a redundant repetition.
Now, the intermediate characteristic (*madhyalakṣaṇa*) which brings about accomplishment (*siddhi*) is being described: [it is] white...
It may be red, yellow, smoke-colored, or blue;
it has a luster like a flame of fire or a radiance like a mass of lightning;
it may have the form of the solar disc or the lunar disc, or it may resemble the blazing sky.

Or one should meditate on one's own form; one should perceive this body consisting of light within the mind. When these [meditations] have been accomplished, manifold suffering perishes; the impurity of the mind departs, and from that, great bliss arises. Now, O Goddess, space is being described.

By means of five characteristics: the sky is the great sky, the supreme sky, higher than the highest, the sky of reality, and the solar sky—thus the sky has five characteristics. It is eternal, both internal and external, yet it is the formless and stainless sky that must be realized.

One should accomplish the *lakṣākāśa* even without formal practice; likewise, one should contemplate the *parākāśa* as resembling the space between clouds. One should likewise contemplate the *mahākāśa* as a light equal to the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpāntāgni*). And one should likewise contemplate the *tattvākāśa* as having the brilliance of ten million times ten million lamps.

One should meditate upon the sun and the sky as being equal to a drop from ten million suns. He who thus perceives the sky both externally and internally shall wander through the universe like Śiva, free from both sin and merit. By the mastery of these very [perceptions], one may remove evil through the gateway of ritual action.

He who does not know the nine wheels, the support of the kalās, the two hundred thousand [syllables], and the five voids in their entirety, is a yogi in name only. Listen now specifically, O Goddess, to the division of the sixteen supports:
one who possesses a steady gaze and the fire at the big toe of the feet.

The first support according to the principles of yoga is at the big toe; the second is at the base of the foot, which is indeed the supreme base of the foot. Having placed [the weight] upon the heel of the foot, the powerful sage may prevail; or else, [he may place it] at the base of the foot or at the root of the big toe.
One should maintain [the third lock]. The third, however, is the support of the anus (*gudādhāra*), which is the action of contracting the anus;

its expansion and contraction, when stabilized by the *vāyu*, conquers death. The fourth is the support of the penis (*liṅgādhāra*), which is the contraction of the penis; through the practice of contracting the penis...

Situated in the middle of the western staff, one should likewise practice again within that center, known as the Vajra-nāḍī. The movement of wind and mind is threefold: movement, intense movement, and [the state beyond].
The piercing of the three knots is the piercing of that [Vajra-nāḍī] by way of the Brahma-path. [This is] the Brahma-lotus.

Having become filled with wind, the king of yogis remains; by that, there is a paralysis of the vital energy (*vīrya*), and he shall always remain youthful. In the *mūlādhāra*, the *brahmapadma*, and likewise in the six lotuses, he then gradually binds the fifth, the support of the stomach, from death...

This [state], established through dissolution, brings about the destruction of death itself. With this, the one of vast intelligence should cause the breath to move upward from the west. This is the binding of the intellect and the mind; it is the conqueror of time within the fifth support, which is the navel-base.

Therein, one should practice the sixth [stage], which is *prāṇa*. From that, *nāda* arises spontaneously; from *nāda*, liberation ultimately follows. The seventh is the support of the heart; by binding the vital air (*vāyu*) therein, the upward-facing lotuses blossom and it becomes great.

The eighth support there is the throat-support (kaṇṭhādhāra), characterized by the contraction of the throat; it is the lock known as Jālandhara. When that is present, the vital air becomes firm. The ninth is the support of the uvula (ghaṇṭikādhāra);
there, the tip of the tongue touches the [palate] in front. Because it drinks nectar from there, the yogin becomes a conqueror of death, supreme.

The tenth is the support of the palate (*tālukādhāra*). When the tip of the tongue is placed there, and when it moves and milks [the essence], the tongue becomes dull and hangs down. When this tongue reaches the nose and then becomes fixed upon the palate, O Īśvarī, the eleventh is the support born of the palate (*talajādhāra*). During that churning of the tip of the tongue—

The water shall become sweet. When that is drunk, one becomes a preeminent poet, a master of song, astronomy, and prosody. It destroys all diseases, and by supporting the teeth—there being twelve such supports—one should forcefully hold the tip of the tongue between the two [upper and lower] rows of teeth.

Holding [the breath] for even half a ghaṭikā, one destroys all diseases; therefore, this should be known as the thirteenth support, the nose-lakṣa. That which stabilizes the mind and is the great stabilizer of the vital air, wherein the gaze is fixed upon the nostrils—this is the fourteenth support.
When this is performed, one’s own splendor becomes manifest within six months.

The earthly [nature] quickly dissolves through one’s own splendor, which becomes directly perceptible. Likewise, with a steady gaze fixed firmly between the eyebrows for fifteen [moments], the vision becomes stable; it is a peak of ten million rays.
For they flash forth. One should move this sixteenth support of the eyes with the tip of a finger.
Whatever exists within the earth—that digestive fire—will all become directly perceptible through that practice; of this there is no doubt. By means of that, one becomes omniscient.
Thus ends the sixteenth [chapter], the Ādhāra.

Now listen to the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) together with its characteristics: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇasaṃyama), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and especially meditative absorption (samādhi). This is the eight-limbed yoga; now hear the definition of these [limbs].

Listen! Tranquility, contentment, moderation in food, little sleep, restraint of the mind, and an empty inner organ—these are proclaimed as the *yamas*. Having cast fickleness far away and established steadiness of mind, one should always effect a union [of the mind] in a single point.
That state of mind consists of mere vital breath; it is a state of perpetual indifference toward all things and the total abandonment of desire.

Content with whatever is obtained, with one's mind fixed on the Supreme Lord, and the renunciation of honor and gifts—these are the observances (niyamas). And there are as many postures (āsanas) as there are living beings.

Listen first to the manyfold [methods] of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is said to be threefold. Those who are delicate are not capable of breath control while seated; however, by the power of great merit, it can be accomplished by a noble-souled one who meditates on the *iḍā* as having the luster of the moon and with a gentle moon.
One should fill [the breath]. Having filled it according to one's capacity, the practitioner of meditation should perform *kumbhaka* (retention).

Having become the mind of the great light, with the body completely filled by the vital air (*vāyu*), and having terrified the power (*śakti*) with fear, one who is worthy should exhale the air through the *piṅgalā*, which has the color of the sun.
Having meditated thus, one should gradually abandon [the body]. This moth,
by repeatedly drawing near to the fire of wood, should— through the efforts of a great soul— purify the physical frame, having withdrawn the mind from worldly existence and its sensory activities.

And in that very way, having abandoned even that which arises from mental fluctuations, one becomes composed of emptiness. One truly becomes a practitioner of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), wondrously indifferent to all censure. Meditation (dhyāna) is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle; know the gross to consist of mantra.

The subtle [practice], however, is devoid of mantra. Samādhi is unwavering consciousness, free from inhalation, exhalation, and the like. Now listen with diligence to the identity of the microcosm (piṇḍa) and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa).
Whatever elements exist within the macrocosm...
They are also situated within the *piṇḍa*. *Tala* is at the sole of the big toe; above that is *Talātala*; *Mahātala* is between the ankles; above the ankles is *Rasātala*;
*Sutala* is between the shanks; and *Vitala* is in the middle of the knees.

Between the thighs is declared Atala; thus the seven netherworlds (pātālas) are described: Tala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Sutala, Vitala, and Atala—these are the seven pātālas. Now, O beloved, hear of the seven worlds (lokas) within the body: Bhūrloka is at the Mūlādhāra.
From the tip of the *liṅga* comes the earth; from its base, the heavenly world (*svarloka*); at the root of Meru, the world of light (*mahas*);
in the hollow of Meru, the world of beings (*janaloka*); in the channel of Meru, the world of heat (*tapas*); and in the lotus, the mortal world (*martyaloka*).
Thus the worlds are distinct: Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and Janas.

Likewise Tapa; the seventh is Satyaloka, which is known as the sevenfold world (saptaloka). Together with the seven netherworlds (pātālas), these constitute the fourteen worlds. Now, there are four guardians of the worlds situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). By knowing them to be within the "piṇḍa" [the body], one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).

Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are the four deities of the self. In the four-petalled [cakra] at the mūlādhāra, there is the Great One mounted upon an elephant; and in that very place, at the svādhiṣṭhāna, is the Great Hari, the creator of the universe. In the maṇipūra, there is the Great Trident-bearer (Śiva), the lord of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis).
At the palate-door, in the middle of the palate, on the forehead, at the chest-throat, at the *śṛṅgāṭikā*, on the skull, at the uvula,

and in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); these are the nine wheels, the upper wheel, and the three peaks— these twenty-one are to be known as the abodes where the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) reside.
With great effort, the seven continents are now described; listen to them, O beloved!

Jambūdvīpa is in the marrow, Śākadvīpa is in the middle [of the body], Śālmalidvīpa is in the center of the head, Kuśadvīpa is in the midst of the flesh, Krauñcadvīpa is in the skin, and [Puṣkaradvīpa] is in the midst of the body hair.

Gomayadvīpa is thus proclaimed; likewise, Śveta is in the middle of the nails. The earth consists of seven islands: Jambū, Śāka, Śālmala, Kuśa, Krauñca, Gomaya, and Śveta—these are the seven divisions; by these seven divisions, the earth is constituted.

These forms are hidden and stable within the center of the body. Seven oceans are said to be situated within the physical mass (piṇḍa): those consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water. Among these, the salt ocean is located within the sweat.
Sugarcane juice is in the [eastern] face; honey is in the skin; clarified butter, fat, and muscle-fat are in the middle; curd and milk are on the forehead. (p.
843) Virility is in the middle, and nectar is to be known as being in the feet; the great tortoise is situated there.
Now, however, listen to the nine divisions within the nine gates: Bhārata is at the beginning, in the anus.

The regions are Khaṇḍa, Kāśmīra, Trikamaṇḍalu, Dvijakhaṇḍa, Ekapāda, and Vakṣye-samaṇḍala; Kaivarta, Gartta, and Gāndhāra—thus the nine regions are established. Now, the eight mountains are described; listen.
With effort: Sumeru is on the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), and Himālaya is in the middle of the seat (pīṭha).

Likewise, Malaya and Mount Mandara are on the left and right shoulders respectively. O Īśvarī! Vindhya is on the right ear, and Maināka is on the left. Śrīśaila is on the forehead in the middle region.
O Supreme Goddess! Likewise, there is the great mountain Kailāsa situated at the gateway of Brahmā;
Sumeru, Himavat, Vindhya, Malaya, Mandara, Śrīśaila, and Maināka—these are the eight mountains of Kailāsa, as well as all other mountains.
O Maheśvarī! The Narmadā resides within the nine channels of the body.
O Devī! The Yamunā flows in the Iḍā, the Sarasvatī in the Piṅgalā, and the Gaṅgā flows in the Suṣumnā, as well as in the other mutual channels. [These are] the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and the Godā.
The Narmadā, Yamunā, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, Vitastā, and Iḍāvatī;

the flow of rivers and streams in seventy-two thousand [channels]; the twenty-seven constellations (ṛkṣas) here and there within the body; as well as the yogas, zodiac signs (rāśis), planets (grahas), and lunar days (tithis).

O Goddess of gods! Within the waves [of the body], there is the fish-mind, as well as the invocation and installation; in all the limbs, there is the entire circle of constellations, and thirty-three crores of deities reside therein. Likewise, all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) are situated within the center of the body, in the heart.

In the midst of the sky dwell Ananta and the others, as well as Vāsuki; indeed, in the belly within the midst of the sky, other nāgas reside. There also dwell brave gandharvas, kinnaras, vidyādharas, apsarases, and others;
many sacred fords (tīrthas) and castes, as well as guhyakas, truly dwell there, along with infinite perfections attained through wisdom.
Light resides in the heart; the orb of the clouds should likewise be known to be in the falling of tears.
The moon and sun are between the eyes, and the witnesses are in the hairs of the shanks.
Then one should meditate upon the universal form (viśvarūpa), including grass, shrubs, and so forth.
One who is liberated through the vision of the totality attains the enjoyment of heaven and my bliss.

(p. 844) Through reflection on this very [truth], one proceeds, free from disease and sorrow. That action which, by means of action, causes doubt to arise within the mind and manifest externally—that performance of such action is liberation; so he said.

The Blessed One is Śiva; by the mere sight of whom one becomes free from disease and sorrow, the mind attains supreme bliss, and one is indeed celebrated as an ascetic. The seven continents are seen, and from that arises the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). One would come to know all states of being.

Likewise, one becomes possessed of a vajra-body. When bitten by a serpent, no poison shall remain; likewise, hunger, sleep, thirst, heat, and cold [shall cease]. There is no doubt that perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) will be attained. Even during a lightning strike, no injury whatsoever shall occur to the body. Therefore, he is a master of the yoga of wind (*vāyuyogī*).

Upon seeing [this], one becomes endowed with the lineage of the Earth; the eight siddhis, beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as the arising of the Great Lotus (*mahāpadma*), shall come to pass. Treasures will approach his very presence—of this there is no doubt. Wherever he desires, there he may go: whether in heaven, in the mortal world, or in the subterranean realm (*rasātala*).

The Supreme Lord, known as the Command (Ājñā), vibrates everywhere nearby; O Pārvatī, He is capable of causing [bondage], removing it, and also protecting. The wise man should always dwell with his mind within the Self in solitude.
Having achieved the unification of the Self and the mind, he attains the supreme state. The Moon.

As long as the sun remains steady, so long does the body remain established; by addressing that single [reality], one attains the state of constant movement (the True Path). Through the grace of the Guru’s feet, he becomes a wise poet, possessing unwavering tranquility alone; endowed with spiritual perfection, he then attains oneness with That. Now, regarding the lotuses...

Listen to this wondrous secret convention: arising from the distinctions of manifold forms, what indeed is that stainless essential nature? By that, the lotus is renowned as threefold, constituting the body of reality (*tattva*).
Among these, the support is the four-petaled [lotus], where *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* arise; and the Self (*ātman*) abides within this state.
One should become a doer of what is good and what is not good. When this mind is stable, Yama goes away like a captive.

Listen with faith to that which is called the "unstruck" (anāhata), the second [state]: upon the great unstruck seat, there exists an eight-petaled lotus endowed with four corners, facing downwards and surrounded by a city.

Touch, sound, form, taste, smell, intellect, mind, and likewise ego—these are situated there in sequence upon the eight petals. Worship indeed proceeds there in distinct forms; through meditation, there arises the self-luminosity of this [deity], and from that, the lotus is illuminated.
Just as the upward-facing [lotus] is illuminated by the light of the sun,

through constant meditation on the Self, there occurs day by day an increase in lifespan; one becomes gracious in power and free from disease and sorrow— he for whom the practice of the mudrās is perfect and accomplished.
And [she is] Khecarī. The mind consists of consciousness and bliss; consciousness is endowed with moonlight.
The Supreme Self is the great sun; the sun alone is the illuminator. One must constantly effect the unification of light and bliss. Thus it is radiant.
The great sun of light shines as the supreme state; the ever-risen sun of the mind perceives it like the moonlight. In its center is the "navel-maker," the instrument known as *Kula* and *Akula*.
The unmanifest, supreme reality, though impermanent, exists eternally. Therein dwells the One, the Puruṣa.
Beyond that is the supreme state; beyond that is the supreme void; and beyond that is the stainless (nirañjana). These five are said to be endowed with five qualities, which are as follows:
qualitylessness, purity, perfection, and all-pervasiveness.

The qualities of Ānanda are its state of absolute oneness (*kevalatva*). The qualities of that *Tat-pada* (the "That" word) are formlessness (*nirākāratva*), eternity (*nityatva*), self-naturedness (*nijatva*), stainlessness (*nirañjana*), and the state of being without a fixed abode (*nirniketanatā*).
The five qualities [of the *Asi-pada*] are dissolution (*līnatā*), decay (*śīrṇatā*), fainting (*mūrchā*), and the state of being a circle of water (*toyamaṇḍalatā*).

Thus have been fully explained the five stainless qualities of the supreme Void: its innate nature, truth, peace, and the very essence of peace. He who knows this is Maheśvara. Now, listen with diligence as the arising of Vidyā is described.
Ānanda (Bliss) and Paramātman (Supreme Self) are one with Paramānanda (Supreme Bliss);
it possesses the awakening of the arising of the mind of supreme bliss-awakening. From the dawning of consciousness (cid), there is light;
thus these five are likewise. It is indestructible, imperishable, non-dual, indeed unburnable, and unedible.

And thus: these five qualities were proclaimed by Anāda, the enemy of sound (nādavairiṇā), who is like the Supreme Self (paramātman) possessing joy through the manifestation and expansion of rays. Those five qualities are celebrated in five ways: discernment (vicāra), the radiance of splendor (prabhollāsa), and aesthetic state (vibhāva).

Likewise, dissolution; for that reason, five qualities of awakening are proclaimed. Furthermore, the mind of the practitioner, the light of all principles, and the emergence of consciousness—these five qualities should be known specifically as the awakening, the state of the observance, and forgetfulness.
Sakalaprabhā: These five qualities of light are auspicious and produce knowledge; through the knowledge of these, great knowledge arises.
From space comes wind, from wind comes fire, from fire comes water, and from water comes earth.

Their five qualities are likewise: their non-objectivity, non-duality, infinity, graspability, and the movement of the self [within them]. Movement is the shifting [of the breath]; in the remaining [elements], there is a smoke-colored appearance in the ether (*ākāśa*).
Through fire (*tejas*), there is heat, light, a red appearance, a flame, and burning; this arises from light alone.
Laxity, sweetness, and whiteness are in its water; likewise, grossness, form, hardness, and smell are in its earth. Now hear of the five great elements (mahābhūta) within the body:
the five great elements are earth, fire, wind, and space, as well as [water]. And of these...
Listen, O beloved, to the five stages of qualities! Bone, flesh, hair, channels, and skin are the qualities of earth; hunger, thirst, laziness, sleep, and exhaustion are the five qualities of water;
disease, shame, fear, agitation, and retention are the qualities of air. By the knowledge of these alone—

A pure understanding arises in them. Although the qualities of earth and the other elements were already mentioned in the section on creation (*sargakāṇḍa*), they are stated again here by the phrase "by this knowledge" in order to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect. The mind...

Intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*citta*), and consciousness (*caitanya*)—these fivefold forms arise from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The functions of intellect and the other four are to be known as deliberation, non-deliberation, and so forth; however, there are also five qualities, namely: discrimination (*viveka*), tranquility (*śānti*), contentment (*santoṣa*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), and dispassion (*vairāgya*). These are the five qualities.

Listen to the qualities of the ego (ahaṅkāra) belonging to the intellect (buddhi): the sense of "I," the notion of "mine," [the impulse] until the end of the age, as well as violence; likewise, the functions of memory, thought, and resolve, along with hopelessness—these are the qualities of the mind (citta). Furthermore, there are desirelessness, aversion, fortitude, and deliberative reflection.

O Maheśvarī, listen to the three qualities of the mind and the qualities of the individual soul (jīva): resolution, faith, compassion, devotion, and truth—these are the qualities of *sattva*. Renunciation, enjoyment, faith, longing for meaningful objects, and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—these five are the qualities of *tamas*.

Listen! Delight, attachment to taste, quarrels, dispute, the increase of delusion, deception, and likewise sorrow—these are the qualities of *tamas*. Dreaming, waking, and deep sleep, as well as consciousness, are the qualities of the individual soul (*jīva*). Such being the case, O Tattva, that [state] arises from consciousness.

(847) Nature (prakṛti), desire (icchā), action (kriyā), illusion (māyā), and speech (vacaḥ)—these are the five qualities (guṇāḥ). Hope (āśā), thirst (tṛṣṇā), longing (aspṛhā), yearning (kāṅkṣā), and falsehood (mithyā)—these constitute the end of nature. O Beloved! Madness (unmāda), latent impressions (vāsanā), wish (vāñchā), and observation (īkṣitā) are the qualities; refuge (śaraṇam) is the conduct of a noble family (satkulācāraḥ).
The determination of the task is now stated: this secret of yoga must not be spoken in the presence of fools.

Regarding the location for yoga practice, it is stated in that very same [text]: "Yoga should always be practiced in a place free from calamities and devoid of thorns and the like; it should be equal toward pleasure and pain. One should undertake it by resorting to a land with a good king and free from disturbances, in a region rich in all kinds of grain."
Free from greed and delusion, a virtuous person who speaks the truth should neither offer praise nor engage in censure.

Regarding those who are not qualified for yoga, it is said in that same [text]: "He in whose mind there is no compassion, who is always fond of quarreling, who is habitually intent on his own interests and averse to the teacher's business—to him this should not be given, nor should it be spoken in his presence. The negative particle (*na*) is connected to both [clauses].
The meaning is that it should not be spoken; this applies even to one who is qualified for yoga, in that very same context.

Freed from existence and non-existence, and devoid of all grasping, the yogi should always be one who consists of eternal bliss and is constantly engaged in practice. Even in a hostile place that causes suffering, in an unsightly or extremely terrifying location, upon contact with the undesirable, or when faced with deficiency or excess, or with superior strength— [the yogi remains thus].

For one who has become thus, actions are free from conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*). Moving, sleeping, or seeing in this manner, one is not stained by sins or merits. One should always possess the awakening to reality and always maintain moral discipline (*śīla*).
There should be no obstruction of vision regarding others, nor various [distractions] arising from death.

The internal organ of this yogi is indeed inactive; for that proponent of the partless inner self, it is always innate. When everything to be grasped—which is produced by effort—is without cause, and when there is no forceful striving in his mind, he is filled with innate bliss.
A steady gaze must be maintained, and by that very means, the mind must be made supremely steady;

and by that very means, that supreme state must be attained. Now, the majesty of yoga is described, which arises therefrom: through the grace of the guru, from the study of the scriptures, and likewise from right conduct.
From the knowledge of the secret meaning of the Vedānta,
from worship (*upāsana*), from posture (*āsana*), from concentration (*dhāraṇā*), from meditation (*dhyāna*), and from the sixfold means of absorption (*laya*);
and from posture, which brings about the eighty-four types of renunciation and detachment (*vairāgya*).

p. 848) Not through Haṭhayoga, nor by means of excellent medicinal herbs, nor by the practice of *mudrās*, nor through dwelling in the forest despite many hardships, nor by the practice of mantras and the like;
nor through abundant giving, austerity, visiting sacred fords, training in charity, or even by the observance of the three daily junctures (*saṃdhyā*).

Likewise, by the observation of the six [signs] and the moon, the yoga-tattva exists through the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the crown of the head. By one who serves the virtuous, speaks the truth, and partakes of the water from the feet of the Guru, there occurs—through the grace of the true Guru—the turning away from the joy and movement caused by the casting of glances by maidens and others. This is accomplished correctly.
One attains the supreme state. There is no reality superior to that of the Guru; therefore, the supreme state arises from the mere half-nimisha of obeying his command.
One attains a hundredfold great bliss through him; salutations to that venerable Guru!

He who brings about the destruction of the delusions of various conceptual constructions should be known as a true guru, but not one who fosters enmity. Therefore, O Maheśānī, from the very beginning, the true guru is Śiva;
he is a speaker of truth, of virtuous character, devoted to his guru, firm in his vows, and whose soul delights in even the slightest of right conduct.

Endowed with virtues such as generosity and ethical discipline, free from deceit and greed, and born of a noble lineage—such is the true guru; one should strive to be in his company. Through that alone, one attains peace of mind and the supreme state.

In the first chapter of the Dattātreyasaṃhitā, however, it is said: "O Brahmin, yoga is indeed manifold; I shall explain all of that to you: Mantrayoga, Layayoga, and likewise Haṭhayoga, as well as Rājayoga, which is the best among all yogas."
Thus is the classification of yoga.
"Commencement (ārambha), the pot (ghaṭa), as well as familiarization (paricaya), and accomplishment (niṣpatti)—these four stages are proclaimed. Thus ends the stages of yoga.
I shall explain these in detail; if you wish to hear them here, [listen] regarding the limbs (aṅga)."
The wise one, reciting the mantra preceded by the placement of the *mātṛkā* (syllabary), shall thus achieve perfection in the mantra;

that is called *mantrayoga*. One who is of mild capacity may become qualified therein through twelve years of practice; generally, such a person attains both knowledge and the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) beginning with *aṇimā*.

"This yoga is for those of little intelligence; the lowest of practitioners practices it. And that which is called Mantrayoga is considered the lowest among yogas. Thus ends the section on Mantrayoga.
Layayoga arises from the yoga of the mind and through conventions (saṅketa). The Primordial Lord has proclaimed infinite crores of such conventions.
Sāṅkṛti said:
O Blessed One, what is this form of the Primordial Lord? Let it be told.
Dattātreya said:

This is the name of the God of gods: Ādinātha and Bhairava. By his own body, this Lord, through his divine play, became Viriñci; on Śrīkaṇṭha mountain, he was the first leader together with Gaurī, and likewise on Mount Mahendra in the Kadalīvana forest, and on Girikūṭa.

On Mount Citrakūṭa, at the foot of the mountain, out of compassion he gave even to the Śabaras one hundred thousand and fifty thousand [coins] for each person. Indeed, I am unable to recount all of those in detail; however, I shall mention some that were easily acquired through natural habituation—whether standing, walking, or sleeping.

While eating, one should meditate on the void day and night. This is indeed the single convention taught by the Primordial Lord. By the mere act of fixing the gaze upon the tip of the nose, the Supreme is proclaimed;
Śiva resides in the lotus, and the meditation on Bharga is the supreme conqueror of death. HŪM.
Merely by fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, the supreme convention is declared;
even the attainment of the application of ashes is proclaimed as supreme.
By pressing with the big toe of one's own right foot, the supreme dissolution [is achieved]; it is supreme like an arrow striking the ground.
And the supreme bed has been described: if one practices in a secluded place where all activity has ceased, one shall attain perfection. Thus Śaṅkara spoke of many such conventions (*saṅketa*).
That alone is *layayoga*, by which the mind of one who possesses many meritorious conventions has attained dissolution.

"Now, hear [the teaching on] Haṭhayoga. Thus it is said. Here, Haṭhayoga is mentioned first because it is the supreme among all yogas; however, Mantrayoga is written later in the section on yoga as a form of spiritual practice (*sādhana*). [This is stated] in the fifth chapter of the Śivāgama.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Kālapuruṣa (the Person of Time),

by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes a knower of the three times; and I shall describe in brief, as it is taught in the Śiva-āgama, the means by which he is perceived even while situated within the belly of Time.

Having gone to a solitary, secluded place and placing the sun behind his back, he should, with a concentrated mind, gaze at his own shadow at the region of the throat. Then he should look toward the sky;
there he beholds Śaṅkara. *Oṃ hrīṃ paramātmane namaḥ*. [Recite this] one hundred and eight times.

Having recited [the mantra], one then beholds Śaṅkara—Hara, who resembles pure crystal and assumes manifold forms. Through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes the lord of mountains; O Lord! within two years, one becomes the master himself, the creator and the destroyer.
One attains the state of the three worlds, which bestows supreme bliss;
through the yoga of constant practice, nothing remains difficult to achieve. He who beholds that dark-hued form in the stainless sky—

Within six months, that yogin meets with death; of this there is no doubt. If it is yellow, there is disease; likewise, if red, one should indicate the killing of a person; if blue, one should point to the murder of a Brahmin. When it appears in various colors and forms, great agitation arises.

The destruction of the feet, the ankles, and the belly indicates death within half a year, one year, and two years respectively. If the right arm is destroyed, one's own kinsman will certainly die; likewise, if the left arm is destroyed, one's wife perishes.
Doubt [regarding this]: one should predict death upon the destruction of the head, the right arm, or the feet;
without [the destruction of] the head, a man dies within a month, or within eight days if it is the shanks;
but upon the destruction of the shoulders or half the body, [death occurs] at that very moment. [From the] Yogārṇava: "In the morning..."
When the sun has moved behind a mountain and one has long gazed upward with an unblinking eye at one's own shadow, if one sees a white man within that shadow—
yet his ears, shoulders, hands, face, sides, and heart are absent— at that moment, the direction of the sun’s horses (the cardinal points) is determined.
"By the departure of [the breath] from the head, he lives for months equal to the number of earths (1), Vasus (8), eyes (2), and the head (1)—that is, twelve months.
In the *Jñānasāra*, in the second chapter: 'O Goddess, he who, having brought the tongue to the half [of the palate], remains for half a *kalā*, is liberated in an instant.'"

[One should contemplate] by means of [the breath] against disease, death, old age, and so forth. The tongue, constantly [moving] within, reaches as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila). One should imagine the nectar being drunk with the tip of the tongue. Death is conquered in half a month; this is truly true, O Pārvatī! [The practitioner becomes] liberated from all diseases.
There is no doubt that he becomes a lord of yogis; by slowly inhaling the vital air at the root of the palate with the tongue, O Goddess, within six months one will become a great yogi.
Listen now to the specific distinction regarding the union with the taste of the tongue, O Pārvatī: it is destroyed by milk.
It destroys disease and bitter itching. O Great Goddess! By its excellent taste, it destroys the sins of children. By merely tasting the ghee, a man attains immortality.
And from the essence of the taste of honey, he indeed utters the sacred scriptures.

Sweetmeats, pieces of food, and delicious *laḍḍukas*—many such things as these appear from the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*). One may constantly enjoy divine maidens; attraction is always produced. Endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the other qualities, one becomes one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*).
He is born; he should always emit hiccup-like sounds from his mouth, and his nose dilates as he yawns.

By means of such practice, he becomes a second Kāmadeva, who, having attained the assembly of Yoginīs, effects both creation and destruction. O Goddess! He has neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor lethargy.
He is born and becomes as one who has gone to heaven, entirely free from all defects.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Sprout-like Form of Rājayoga," in the sixth section, the Jñānakāṇḍa, of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.

The body is described as a minor Brahmāṇḍa for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of Yoga, as stated in the tenth chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra: "The characteristics of the external region of the Brahmāṇḍa have been explained; within its center, the worlds themselves truly exist."

Fourteen. O Goddess! That very same body resides within the midst of the great Brahmāṇḍa; thus, O Goddess, it exists there in manifold ways within that Brahmāṇḍa. All those who exist in the vast Brahmāṇḍa are also embodied beings of Him, and they likewise abide upon the earth.

Within the great Brahmāṇḍa, there are the forms and bodies of living beings, as well as the vast Brahmāṇḍa itself. O Goddess! Within that are living beings, and within those are the worlds. There is a distinction merely by sight, due to the difference between the gross, the subtle, and so forth.
O Parameśvarī! Whatever kind of thing exists within the Mahābrahmāṇḍa, O Deveśī, all of that indeed [originates] from the center of the Vṛhadbrahmāṇḍa. (From the Fourth Paṭala: Listen, O Devī!
I shall explain the characteristics of the Vṛhadbrahmāṇḍa; and Meru is in the midst of the mountains.
O beloved! It is the refuge of all the gods. O fair-faced one, that great river is situated there in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa).
Above Mount Sumeru is Satyaloka, O beautiful-faced one; and below it, O Great Goddess, lies Rasātala. Thus, in this sequence, the worlds are situated within Meru.
Fourteen [tattvas]. O Maheśvarī! Above the seven netherworlds (pātāla) is the Brahma-lotus;

that lotus is the Ādhāra-cakra, four-petalled, situated in the center of the earth. In the center of that lotus, within the seed-vessel (vījakośa), is the charming Earth-circle (kṣiticakra). The seven oceans exist there in the form of circular enclosures (valaya).
They are established thus: in the center of Jambūdvīpa is a charming four-cornered [mandala];

the triangular one is the abode of Madana, and Kandarpa is its presiding deity. O Śivā, the seed-syllable *laṃ* is indeed the form of Indra, whose vehicle is the lord of elephants; [it resides] in the triangle, the abode of Madana.

Maheśvara exists in the form of the *liṅga*. O Maheśānī! His power of *māyā* takes the form of a serpent; by her alone is the *liṅga* encircled in the shape of three and a half coils. Covering the aperture of the *liṅga* with her own mouth, she remains there eternally. [Therein lies] the seed-syllable of Indra (*indravīja*).
O Varārohā! To the left of the *liṅga*, there is the perfectly perfected abode of Brahmā, most beautiful above the *nāda*.
Therein indeed dwells Brahmā, the creator of the world and the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*).
And on his left side is Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas and Queen of the Gods. Of her—

Having attained grace, it constantly expands the creation. That form which is the abode of Brahmā, extending for a hundred thousand *yojanas*—all of that, O Supreme Goddess, has been described by me as the *Ṛgveda*.
O Supreme Goddess, it is triangular like a sixty-two-fold coiled serpent; that very thing is the mountain.

Indeed, that which is the refuge of all the gods has been described. O lady of beautiful countenance, look first at what is within and outside the triangle! Behold the stationary mountain, the insect, the most excellent animal, the bird, the tree, and so forth, O Goddess! Is there anything on the surface of the earth that does not exist?

Outside the triangle, O Girijā, reside these seven great mountain ranges: the mountain Bahurūpaka, Nīlācala, the mountain named Mandara, Candraśekhara, Himālaya, Suvela, Malaya, and Bhasmaparvata; O Goddess, these dwell within the four corners.
"Indeed, various forms such as grasses, shrubs, and creepers are born and die there according to the very path previously described. Thus ends the description of the *mūlādhāra*.
In the fifth chapter.
Śiva said:
Above this lotus is an auspicious lotus named Bhīma,
having six petals, circular in shape, and adorned with four gates. In the center of that lotus,
within the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa), is the enchanting world of Bhuvarloka, red in color like vermilion.

It was then adorned. Viṣṇu resides above it, with Śrī and Vāṇī at his left and right. The world is created by Brahmā and protected by the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu). That heaven named Vaikuṇṭha is indeed the abode of various gods. On the right side of Vaikuṇṭha is Goloka.
It is the deluder of all. Right there is the goddess Rādhikā, and the two-armed holder of the flute.
It is graced by hosts of gods such as Nārada and others who have mastered the Vedas;
in my knowledge, there is no place equal to Vaikuṇṭha, whether in the beginning or in the middle.
Likewise, on the left, he beholds the luminaries; all endowed with various enjoyments and adorned with various jewels— all the deities beginning with Indra— just as he perceives them all,
even so do all those dwelling upon the earth stand for the sake of offering praise.

The world consists of the Great Reality (Mahātattva) and is adorned by the arms of the Vedas; it is graced by yellow garments, possesses peaceful forms, and is beautified by garlands of forest flowers. Thus, all the devotees shine within Vaikuṇṭha—the realm of Viṣṇu, the assembly of Viṣṇu, and the community of Vaiṣṇavas.

The Form of Viṣṇu: O Supreme Goddess, there is no name other than Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha! That form which is the abode of Goloka does not exist within my own; whether through knowledge, the eyes, or by the yoga of meditation, O Goddess, it consists of pure reality.
Adorned by various deities, in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is the place called Golaka,
the temple of the greed of Śrī Viṣṇu. What greatness can I now describe of that site, which is the enchanting abode of Śrī Viṣṇu in his form as Sattva?
