In that very place, the two-armed wielder of the flute shines eternally; then Viṣṇu, consisting of pure goodness (sattva), certainly protects the world. O Supreme Goddess! Wherein lies the great liberation of the Vaiṣṇava—thus has the majesty of this sacred site been declared by me in brief.

I am unable to describe its extent even in hundreds of lifetimes. Outside the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa), however, is encircled the water-mandala; the beautiful water has the same measure as the Ocean of Milk. It has the form of smoky light and possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons.

The water-mandala, brilliant white in the form of a crescent moon, shines there, O beautiful one! All the rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, appear likewise. All the deities, beginning with Indra, are being incessantly praised, as are the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, and Bhairavas.

With minds always one-pointed amidst various pleasures and delights, they perform the singing of Viṣṇu, being devoted to hymns and bhakti. They perform the Vedic chanting by means of the four-faced Creator (Brahmā). And in that Vedic chanting, there are the six rāgas beginning with Mālava, as well as the thirty-six rāgiṇīs. And in the Vedic chanting...
O beloved! Indeed, these personified beings always perform the chanting of the Sāmaveda with the Mālava-rāga;
likewise, they always recite the Yajurveda with Mallāra, Vāsanta, and Hillola;
and with Karṇāṭa, they always recite the Ṛgveda by the Creator.
O Śivā! This [portion] has been taught with the Śrī-rāga; henceforth, that which was not previously specified follows.
Right here reside those sixteen thousand rāgas. From the singing of the primary rāga of Murāri, every tāla is produced; with that tāla and that rāga, they always sing by the command of the Creator.
Indeed, sages and people distinguish that passion into seasons such as spring, which remain there perpetually. There, the flute-player is adorned with the blossoms of various seasons;
and right there, O Lord, Rādhikā sports in manifold pleasures, speaking thus.
"O Beloved, sing the song of the flute, which causes great infatuation, by which sound the arousal of passion is always produced! Sing with diligent effort that very melody and that very rhythm.
Thus, endowed with bliss, she who delights in the great state of possession shines eternally at your left side."
Rādhikā is affectionate toward her devotees. Likewise: "Those men who first chant the name of Rādhā and then that of Kṛṣṇa—to them I shall indeed grant the supreme goal; of this there is no doubt.
Those people who [worship me] through the path of devotion (bhāva-mārga) and through the path of mantra (mantra-mārga) by means of their guru..."

Those men who worship [the couple] are always equal to me. That woman who worships me as non-different from the male likewise becomes equal to him; of this there is no doubt. Whether with devotion or even without devotion, if they chant the pair with devotion to you, [they attain the same].
"I shall grant you my own state; listen, O Rādhikā! Thus ends the description of one's own abode (svādhiṣṭhāna).

In the sixth chapter: Above this lotus is a great lotus, very difficult to obtain, having ten petals, blue in color, innate, and of a formidable form; it is a most beautiful lotus adorned with the letters from *ḍa* to *pha* accompanied by the moon (the bindu). In its center...
The well-perfected seed-syllable of fire dwells eternally within the seed-vessel; externally, in its third part, is that which is called Traipura, resembling nine suns and shaped like a svastika.

O Goddess! This place, known as Svarloka, is worshipped by all the gods; it possesses the form of the seed-syllable of fire (Ra) and is eternally mounted upon a ram. Indeed, the abode of Rudra is right there, the destroyer of great delusion. The Great Vidyā Bhadrakālī resides on the left side.
She is beautifully adorned; Bhadrakālī is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), eternally effecting destruction.

By Brahmā the world is created, and it is protected by him in the form of Viṣṇu. The Supreme God, in the form of Rudra, is the eternal cause of destruction; indeed, he who is in the form of Rudra shall destroy it.
O Goddess, what is there on the surface of the earth that cannot be accomplished through the speech of Rudra together with Bhadrakālī?
That form which was previously described as Goloka, the enchantment of all— beyond that, indeed, in every respect,
lies the world of Rudra, four times greater, eternally bestowing the great liberation.

Rudra, whose limbs are adorned with ashes; Bhadrakālī, the Great Vidyā, is in the north-western direction of Rudra. Then, by always worshiping Kālī, the Great Vidyā, with great effort, one becomes the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Goddess! and the Lord of Goloka.
Devoted to praise and devotion, by the grace of Kālī’s feet, he shall become a protector of the worlds.

For the sake of protecting the worlds, that flute-player (Muralīdhara), accompanied by his wife, shall always dwell in Goloka after having propitiated Bhadrakālī. And by the grace of Kālikā, [he shall dwell there] with Viṣṇu.
It is always being enjoyed; therefore, Viṣṇu, who is devoted to the Great Being (Mahāsattva), is the protector. Thus ends the description of Maṇipūra.

In the seventh chapter: Above this lotus is a supreme, stainless lotus, adorned with twelve petals and resembling a red bandhūka flower; it bestows empty fruits upon those who desire them and is like the vermilion of the ocean of accomplishments. Within the seed-vessel in the center of the lotus...

The auspicious six-cornered mandala; in the center of the mandala is the charming seed-syllable of Vāyu (Ya), adorned with its own seed-syllable and graced by four arms. He is the Lord of the three worlds, the Sovereign worshipped by all. That Vidyā is Bhuvaneśānī, [revered] throughout the three worlds.

She is worshipped; that Goddess stands on the left side of Īśvara. O auspicious one! O Sovereign of the Gods! This Maharloka is the place of worship. Therein, the best among those who know Yoga performs mental union (yoga). For her limbs are lovely, reddened with vermilion, and she is fashioned from crystal.
Therefore, all human beings perceive the light; the gods, endowed with all their limbs, remain there eternally. Those dwelling on earth perceive it as circular and luminous;
those who go to the heavenly world (Svarloka) all perceive it as having form, yet they do not perceive any distinction of limbs.
They behold the observation of gross forms. Just as the people dwelling on earth spread across the surface of the earth, even so, O Pārvatī, all the deities abide in heaven.
Brahmā resides in the *bhūrloka*, Janārdana in the *bhuvarloka*, and [Viṣṇu] in the *svarloka*.

Śambhu, the agent of dissolution, dwells there eternally; he is the Lord of Brahmā and the others, the creator of all, and the Sovereign. He is the embodiment of the Lord of all and the Sovereign who creates everything.
O Goddess, that which is called Goloka is always resplendent in such a form.

Therefore, O Goddess! Maharloka is a hundred times more beautiful; it is a hundred times more extensive, and everything there is a hundred times [greater], O Śivā! How can I possibly describe the majesty of Maharloka? For he who should dwell in Maharloka—

He is intent upon the nature of the universal whole (*sāmānyabhāva*). Therefore, having received his command, the lotus-born Brahmā suddenly creates the one-hundredth part [of that essence] as Muralīdhara in Goloka.
By his command, the two-armed Muralīdhara protects the worlds. Thus indeed, in the form of Rudra...

He withdraws the entire universe; since the Lord is the creator of all, for that very reason, O Maheśvarī, He is the Sovereign (Īśvara), the creator of all, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), immovable, and auspicious (Śiva). Having attained Bhuvaneśī, the Lord is the master of all and the Sovereign. For this very reason, O Maheśānī, He alone is [the Supreme].
She is the bestower of liberation. That Goddess is the Mother of the Universe (Viśvamātā) and the one who performs the protection of the universe.

She is the giver of liberation to all worlds, the bestower of release, and the Universal Mother (Viśvamātṛkā). Without Bhuvaneśī, the Lord (Īśa) is unable to accomplish anything; for this very reason, that Goddess is the bestower of liberation.
"Sarvarūpiṇī. This is the description of the Anāhata [cakra], in the eighth chapter.
Śaṅkara said:
Above this is a stainless lotus, the cause of universal enchantment, endowed with sixteen petals, and the destroyer of the darkness of delusion; it is like [a flame] in the midst of smoke.

Likewise, O Beloved, there is Vahni, consisting of light; and in the center of the lotus, within the pericarp (varāṭa), is the most beautiful Janaloka, which pacifies the darkness of great delusion. Outside of that is the lunar orb, adorned by hosts of gods, singers, and sages. [This is] of Goloka...

This place is a hundred thousand times more difficult to attain; its length and likewise its breadth have been described by me as being a hundred thousandfold greater than Goloka, O Goddess—of this there is no doubt. Within the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa) on Maṇidvīpa is an excellent six-cornered yantra.
In the center of the yantra is a bull whose body is half that of a great lion;
above it is Mahāgaurī, and on her right side is Sadāśiva. He has three eyes and five faces, with three eyes in each face, and his limbs are adorned with sacred ashes.
The brother of the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa), the god clad in a tiger skin, adorned with the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others;
the bestower of desired objects to the worlds, the destroyer of the worlds' fears,
the producer of enjoyment for the worlds, the giver of liberation to the worlds, and the eternal creator of bliss.

The Lord is the all-pervading Ardhanārīśvara; in some places the God consists of light, and in others he is devoid of form. He is the worshipful form of the gods and the sovereign form of the gods. The Lord is eternally the bestower of liberation upon the devotee and the giver of the state of Viṣṇu.

O Caṇḍikā! The greatness of that Lord—who, having made Goloka his own, protects the devotee by bestowing upon the worshiper with bilva leaves His own state of union (sāyujya)—is now described in detail. She who is Gaurī, the Mother of the World, whose nature is half the body of Brahmā;

That Great Goddess consists of the three qualities (guṇas); by means of one quality, the wielder of the Pināka bow, Sadāśiva—the creator of all—attains union with her. Thus ends the description of the Pure Abode (viśuddhasthāna).
In the ninth chapter.
Śaṅkara said:

Above this lotus is the extremely rare lotus of knowledge (*jñānapadma*), joined with two other lotuses, in the form of the orb of the full moon. Within the seed-vessel in the center of that lotus, one should remember the city of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). In its center is a nine-cornered yantra.

It is indeed extremely difficult to attain. In its center is the seed-syllable of Śambhu, possessing form in the shape of a *haṃsa*. The *haṃsa* is the supreme Brahman in form, manifest as the form of Śiva;
O lady of beautiful hips, it has the syllable *tāra* as its beak and possesses wings for departing and returning.

The pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti has the three *bindus* as its eyes; it is the playground of this *haṃsa*, worshipped upon a golden lotus. Thus, the *haṃsa* is on Maṇidvīpa, and upon its lap is Paraśiva. On his left side is Siddhakālī, whose nature is eternal bliss. Of her—
Having attained grace, Maheśvara, the creator of all, [bestowed] this world of austerity (tapoloka), O blessed lady,

which is difficult for all the worlds to attain; where the gods, beginning with Brahmā, always practice meditation— a world of austerity that cannot be reached even by mind, nor by yoga, nor by penance.

O Śivā! The four characteristics of Goloka are as follows: those gods who reside in the worlds of Brahmā, those deities and others in Vaikuṇṭha, and he who dwells in the world of Śambhu—these are solely devoted to devotion. O Śivā!
Even through austerity, the state of Tapoloka cannot be attained; there is nothing equal to Tapoloka.
O Sulocanā! In the midst of the world, indeed, Sālokya [residence in the same realm] is in Maharloka; Sārūpya [attainment of a similar form] is in Janaloka;
Sāyujya [union] is in Tapoloka; and Nirvāṇa is indeed above that. Therefore, the gods beginning with Brahmā always desire Tapoloka. Thus, O beloved, the sixfold sequence has been described to you.
The definition: "That knowledge by which the practitioner attains immortality and liberation while living (jīvanmukta),
and having known which, he shall never again enter a mother’s womb"—
thus ends the description of the locus of knowledge.
In the tenth chapter.
Śaṅkara said:
Above the region of the lotus of knowledge is a thousand-petaled lotus, a great downward-facing lotus situated in the center of Mount Sumeru; it is white, red, and likewise yellow.
It was black and green as well, adorned with various colors and diverse, wonderful forms;

in one moment it was white, in a moment red, and in a moment beautifully yellow. O lady of lovely limbs, in whichever moment it appeared white, or the supreme green color, or a variegated form, it was beautiful.
O Goddess! In every single moment, that lotus is thus adorned in various ways, just as the abode of Goloka is always manifest.
There, the Lord of Goloka is devoted to the sentiment of bhakti; O Goddess, he is the Lord of Kailāsa.

One should constantly practice the yoga of meditation. Thus, all the gods beginning with Brahmā, and the lords of the three heavens beginning with Indra, are entirely devoted to praise and devotion, remaining forever in a state of humility. O Maheśānī! There, in that very place, Muralīdhara dwells a hundred thousand times over.

O beloved! O Supreme Goddess! There, Rudra performed a hundred lakhs [of recitations] and Brahmā performed a hundred lakhs every day; many cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) came into being. In their midst, Brahmā established the Lord of Kamalā, Śiva, who possesses manifold forms, in that very place.
Then one should establish [the deities]. For thus, O Supreme Goddess! one should duly install the various powers (*nānāśakti*).

Having joined the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā with their respective powers within every cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), one should perform the installation of the cosmic egg. Within the earth, they abide in the lotus of Brahmā.

Human beings and so forth—O Goddess! all these, as well as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the worlds within it, the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*), and right there the seven heavens—thus, within every body, the fourteen worlds are contained in a wheel. O Supreme Mistress! in every single body, there is a cosmic egg.

There is no doubt in this matter. Likewise: "The abode is of many forms and is the support of all bodies; in its center is Satyaloka, the cause of Mahārudra, fashioned from gold as radiant as the sun by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu); and in the directions is the circle of water."
Likewise, there is a full moon disc; around it are *pārijāta* trees, and in the center is a *kalpa* tree.
Near the *kalpa* tree is a temple of light. Om!
It resembles the rising sun and is adorned with four gates.

Accompanied by soft musical instruments and adorned with perfumes and flowers, in its center, O Goddess, is an altar; and there, O Beloved, is the lion-throne of jewels. Within that, Mahākālī, the Supreme Self, exists in the form of a chickpea, her essence veiled by Māyā.
From the state of equal parts, he is indeed Mahārudra; he alone is the Self, for he is indeed Mahāviṣṇu;

he alone is the Self, he is Mahābrahmā—the distinction between them being merely one of names. A single form has three names: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. In the perception of diversity, it is the mind [that creates the difference].

For such a person, liberation is not found. O fair-eyed one! There, hundreds of thousands upon hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) are born; there Brahmā resides, there Viṣṇu, and there Rudra is established. Having thus performed the creation of the cosmic eggs, the eternal Viṣṇu—sa... [he...]

Having fashioned a living form as well as the body of a creature, the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) thus eternally creates the manifold universe. Indeed, even while remaining quality-less, he is the very cause of perfection in the form of Viṣṇu; some say he is Brahmā, while others say he is Viṣṇu.

It is proclaimed: Some say that Rudra is the Great One, the primordial single deity, stainless, the god joined with the primal Śakti, whose form is shaped like a chickpea; he is the light of a lamp for the magical net (*indrajāla*), the embodiment of the moon, sun, and fire, the great light, formless, the sphere of light (*goloka*), and the one with the beautiful face.

Then, O Goddess, in the Satyaloka, within the seed-vessel (bījakosa) in the auspicious palace of the Cintāmaṇi gem, one should meditate upon the Stainless One (Nirañjana) seated upon a jeweled lion-throne. Devoted to worship and meditation, one should worship one’s own Guru in His presence, O Goddess, together with His consort, who is like unto a mountain of silver.

One should meditate upon the God, who is joined with his beloved, as being deep red, possessing a beautiful face, and whose nature is self-luminous; [one should meditate on him] situated upon one's own head,
just as they perceive a mountain within the center of a mirror in the great thousand-petaled lotus.

In this manner, one should contemplate the Lord. For thus, O Beloved! He is composed of Brahman and consists of supreme liberation; He is the direct abode of the Attributeless (Nirguṇa) and the abode of Mahākāla, O Śivā! Wherein He eternally resides, formless and immovable—His form [is as follows].

Supreme bliss is the Lord of the worlds, both transcendent and immanent; the Goddess Kālī is eternal bliss, the supreme, who illumines time. The primordial power Mahākālī brings about the liberation of the gods. Just as a tree is born from the earth and dissolves back into the earth, so too a bubble is born from water.
Just as [a substance] dissolves in water, and just as lightning, having arisen in a cloud, dissolves back into it;

even so, the gods beginning with Brahmā arise from Kālikā. Likewise, at the time of dissolution, they dissolve back into her again. O Goddess! Without the knowledge of Śakti, liberation is a mere mockery.

It is conceived thus: by one part she becomes Brahmā, by one part Janārdana, and by one part Śambhu, O fair-eyed one! She who is the other is Mahākālī, like the ocean to rivers and the like, yet like the water in a cow’s hoofprint.

O Śivā! Just as the waters of the ocean would know nothing of the hoof-print of a cow, so too Brahmā does not know [Thee], nor does Viṣṇu know Śaṅkara. Just as the gods and others are produced by Kālī as the creator of the universe, so too at the time of dissolution...
Furthermore, he dissolves into her. Therefore, Kālī is the bestower of liberation (nirvāṇa), while the man is the bestower of heaven.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) is situated in the southern direction; terrified on all sides, he flees by the name of Kālī. Hence, she is known as Dakṣiṇā among the three.

She is sung of in the worlds: "Since the attributeless Puruṣa is created and dissolved by Kālī, she is therefore celebrated in the three worlds by the name Dakṣiṇā. She is Vaśyavidyā, Mahāvidyā, Kālikā, and Jagadambikā. That Kālī possesses a formal form, yet her form is that of a chickpea."

Devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs, she has the form of the moon, sun, and fire. O fair-faced one, her abode is said to be Satyaloka; O sinless one, that place is always to be prayed for by all the gods. What more need I say now regarding the majesty of that place?
O fair-eyed one! Regarding a thousand-petaled lotus, even on a single petal there are a thousand spheres of light;
therefore, it cannot be described. Even with a thousand lifetimes and a hundred million tongues, I am indeed unable to describe the beauty of that single petal. Therefore, you yourself—
O Pārvatī, O lady of excellent gait! Cease this [mental] state. How can I possibly describe the splendor that exists within the filaments? Within that, O Goddess, is the pericarp;
within that, the seed-vessel (*bījakoṣaka*). In the center of the seed-vessel, however, is the supreme ocean of nectar.

Extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, it possesses most beautiful and excellent waters. In its center, O beloved, is Maṇidvīpa, a thousand yojanas in extent; all around it are Pārijāta trees and a magnificent grove of Kadamba trees. In the middle stands the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, and there is a supreme palace of light.
It was provided with four gates and adorned with golden ramparts;
it was accompanied by gentle music and endowed with perfumes and incense.
O Goddess! In its center was an altar, attended by thousands of celestial maidens intent upon service.

Consisting of fifty syllables; above that, O Maheśānī! O Śivā! is the jeweled lion-throne. Mahākālī and Mahārudra are of the form of chickpeas. It is the eternal, great light, like the glow of a lamp in a magical illusion. [From] the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra* held within the fourth *ullāsa*.
The Goddess said:

O God of gods! O mighty-armed one! O you whose nature is creation, preservation, and dissolution! One should meditate upon the tranquil Guru, accompanied by his Śakti, situated in the center of the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown of the head, which is red in color and faces downward. [One should likewise meditate upon] the Great Śakti in the Mūlādhāra.

[She is] the one who assumes the form of Kuṇḍalinī. If the visualization proceeds in sequence through all the lotuses with [the head] facing downward, then how could there be meditation upon the Guru and the Deity there? And how could [the Guru] be situated in the lower part, established in the Ādhāra?
Mahādeva said: "O Goddess, praised by heroes! What you have spoken is indeed appropriate; there is no doubt that such a suspicion arises in this matter, O Supreme Sovereign! It shall now be told."

It is the cause for the destruction of doubt. O Goddess of gods! Those lotuses are situated within the *suṣumnā*, and they are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and consist of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*). All that, O Goddess, is the lotus facing in every direction; both worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and renunciation (*nivṛtti*) are [contained therein].

The two states (bhāva) reside within the individual soul (jīva): the path of engagement (pravṛtti) pertains to the transmigrating being, while cessation (nivṛtti) pertains to the Supreme Self. During the contemplation of the state of engagement, one should contemplate the faces as facing inward; however, by means of the yoga-path of cessation, they should always be contemplated as facing upward. It is precisely thus, through the distinction of these states.
No doubt arises in the heart.
In the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*, however, a specific detail is stated as follows: "On the outer region of Meru,

at the heads of the Moon and the Sun, the Suṣumṇā channel— composed of the three qualities and consisting of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire— is situated in the center between the left and the right."

The root called *vajra*, which has a body entwined with the blossoming flowers of the *dhustūra*, remains for a short time within the bulb; it matures at the top of the region of the penis and should be blazing in its middle part.

In the midst of that is Citriṇī, radiant with the Praṇava, attainable through yoga by yogins, comparable to a spider’s thread, situated within the center of Meru amidst all the lotuses; having pierced through them,
she shines intensely with the arrangement of their interlacing, awakening pure consciousness in their midst.
The Brahmā-nāḍī resides within the primordial deity, emerging from the cavity of the mouth of Hara.

She is like a play of garlands of lightning, appearing as a shimmering thread within the minds of sages; she is exceedingly subtle, the awakening of pure knowledge, and the absence of all worldly pleasures, radiant pure states, and the like.
Her mouth is the gateway to Brahman, a region delightful with a shower of nectar that flows forth from it.
They say that this very place of the knot is the mouth, by means of the channel known as Suṣumnā.
Then, the supporting lotus is attached to the mouth of the *suṣumṇā*, situated below the penis and above the anus;
it has four red petals, faces downward, and is beautiful with a rising golden luster, joined by the letters from *va* to *śa*.

With the letters of the Vedas: In this [mandala], upon the earth, there is a four-cornered wheel surrounded by eight radiant tridents; it is brilliant yellow in color, with limbs as tender as lightning, and therein resides the seed-syllable of the earth within the water.

Therein shall dwell the infant Creator, who is adorned with four arms, mounted upon the lordly elephant and other mounts, whose splendor in his lap is equal to the rising sun; he possesses the beauty of a lotus-face, shines with the Vedas as his arms, and has the fourfold Vedas as his ornaments.
And the goddess known as Ḍākinī, radiant with four arms resembling the Vedas, with red eyes,
possessing a brilliance like many rising suns, and always carrying the light of pure awakening, shines forth eternally from the region of the mouth under the name Vajra.

Situated in the center of the pericarp is that corner known as Tripura, shimmering like lightning, tender, and capable of assuming any form at will. Within its center, the wind named Kandarpa blows perpetually;
there resides the Lord of Life, who, laughing even at a cluster of Bandhujīva flowers, is like ten million suns.

The Light: In the center of that is the self-manifested (svayambhū) in the form of a *liṅga*, tender as a drop of molten lotus, facing west, the light of knowledge and meditation, with a form like a fresh sprout.
Dwelling in Kāśī, the playful one shines forth, laughing with a continuous stream of oiliness from the mass of rays of the entire multitude of rising full moons;
he manifests in the form of the whirlpools of the river. Above him is the opening of the door of Brahman, subtle and shimmering with the grief of the thread of poison, enchanting the world.
Covering her own mouth with sweetness, resembling a conch-spiral,
the abode of the playful charm of a fresh garland of lightning, sleeping like a serpent upon Śiva,
she shines with a radiant triple-coil (trivṛtti) and a half-turn; and as the Kulakuṇḍalinī, she warbles sweetly.

She by whom the life-force of the worlds is sustained through the modulation of the breaths of inhalation and exhalation, and by means of the various sequences of distinctions in the composition of her tender speech, which is made manifest by rows of intoxicated bees.

Within the hollow of the root-lotus shines a row of intense radiance. In its center dwells the Supreme Power (Parā), most skillful in her arts, subtler than the subtlest, eternally blissful, exceedingly restless in her mutual union, and possessing a garland of shimmering rays; by whose light the entire vessel of the cosmic egg and all else are illuminated.
This very Śrī Parameśvarī shines; may she, whose awakening is eternally dawning, be victorious.
Having meditated upon this, which shines with the brilliance of ten million suns within the path of the central lotus,
that lord of men becomes instantly a master of speech and a delighter in all branches of knowledge; he possesses eternal health,
and being the self of the mind and soul, he attains infinite great bliss.
With words and compositions of speech, he of pure conduct serves the preceptor of all the gods.

Another lotus, as red and beautiful as a stream of vermilion, is situated in the center of the *suṣumnā* at the base of the banner; it is surrounded by limbs and covered with musical instruments having the color of lightning.
And with those ending in Purandara (Ra) adorned with the bindu;
within that, shining forth, is the unmanifest sky, and then the orb of Varuṇa (Va),
which is like a lotus, graced by a half-moon, as white as the autumnal moon— the stainless seed-syllable Vaṃ.
May Hari himself, mounted upon a sea-monster (makara), protect you— He who reclines upon His lap,

possessing a splendor beautiful with a dark-blue luster; clad in yellow garments, bearing the fullness of early youth, wearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and holding the Vedas in His arms.
Right here she, Rākiṇī, shines eternally, possessing a splendor like the luster of the interior of a blue lotus;
her limbs are constantly graced by the beauty of various uplifted weapons, and she is adorned with divine garments and ornaments.
With intoxicated minds.
Now follows the praise of knowledge, from the third chapter of the Nigamakalpadruma.

Through knowledge one attains liberation; through knowledge comes the destruction of sin. Through knowledge one becomes a hero in action, and through knowledge one transcends the state of a bound soul. Through knowledge one attains the divine state;
therefore, knowledge is preeminent. Everything is purified by knowledge, and indeed, it is through knowledge alone [that this occurs].

The Purifier: Just as fire burns away all wood, shrubs, creepers, and the like, so too are all the fruits of karma burnt away by knowledge. Knowledge is indeed twofold, distinguished by the divisions of duality and non-duality. By means of dualistic knowledge, that which is performed in this age—both merit and sin—is [consumed].
In this age, by the measure of the knowledge of non-duality (*abheda-jñāna*), one's prior karma and other such factors are consumed;

furthermore, one shall not be born again, and as a non-dualist, one attains liberation. Otherwise, even in a hundred thousand *lakṣa*-yugas, one who possesses the knowledge of duality (*bheda-jñānī*) never attains liberation, heaven, or similar states—of this there is no doubt regarding Śambhu.

Where is the sequence of non-duality determined, and by what action? For the differentiation of bound souls (*paśu*) is indeed declared to be the divine state. The hero who knows both difference and non-difference should place the non-sequential within the sequence. If he should act through the sequence while wandering free from desire, then—

The ritual action that yields the fruit of isolation (kaivalya) should be understood according to its sequence; however, if desire—whether higher or lower—should bind it, then even through the sequence, that [desire] remains inferior, constrained by the fetters of the bound soul (paśu). Whether one, two, or in reverse order, it must be purified.
Through diligent effort, a person who discerns distinctions attains liberation; through the perception of duality, one becomes a partaker of their own karma.
Now, the knowledge of non-duality (advaitajñāna), from the sixth chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.

As long as there is a personal identity (ātman-bhāva), so long does this manifold diversity exist; so long are actions considered to be distinct, and so long are they held to be of various kinds. So long do the gods remain differentiated—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, and Varuṇa.
Kubera and the guardians of the directions—all these separately—[are surpassed by it].

O Goddess of gods! As long as there exists the manifold activity consisting of women, men, and neuter beings; as long as the *vilva* leaf remains distinct from the *tulasī* leaf on the earth; and as long as the *javā*, *droṇa*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *karavīra* flowers remain distinct [from it].
And furthermore, O Queen of the Gods! Truly, by means of a *tulasī* leaf, one remains a divine hero for so long, yet for that long one remains in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*).
For that long there is the notion of duality in the Tantra, and for that long there is separate ritual action toward the God.
O Mother of the World! Only then does the realization arise regarding Hari and Hara—[she who is] Karālavadanā.
Kālī, Śrīmadekajaṭā, Śivā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhairavī, Chinnā, and Bhuvaneśvarī; Chinnā, Annapūrṇā, Vagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, Vāṇī, and Rādhikā; and Ceṣṭā—each distinct from the other.

Action is diverse, and the collection of practices is diverse; as long as unity does not arise in the lotus-feet of Bhavānī, so long it does not occur. When non-duality arises in the supremely purifying lotus-feet of Tāriṇī, and likewise when the essence of knowledge is produced within the abode of the heart-lotus, then unity comes to be.

O lovely-limbed one! O Śaṅkarī, among all living beings! Indeed, how can it be said that there is oneness among living beings, when—only upon the arising of the knowledge of oneness—is there oneness of Śiva, Śakti, and all living beings within the lotus feet of Tāriṇī? This is not so.
If it is argued that it was appropriate to speak thus at that time because of the relationship between the served and the server, that is true;

however, this was said for the purpose of instructing those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) regarding devotion mixed with knowledge (jñānamishrabhakti). For this very reason, he will later state that "devotion is unfailing. As for one who is liberated, there is only certain, singular knowledge.

He has no need for instruction because he is entirely free from anxiety. For him there is neither sin nor merit, neither heaven nor hell, neither pleasure nor pain, nor likewise fear of diseases; there is neither fear nor grief—indeed, all [is absent].

The universe is composed of Brahman. Whether she be born of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Vaidya, a Śūdra, or an Antyaja, the knowledge that delivers (Tāriṇī-vidyā) is exactly as it is—just as the knowledge itself is.
O Maheśānī! O beloved! when such knowledge indeed arises, at that very moment it is [the true] Vidyā.
O Queen of the Gods! This [knowledge] is the adversary of ignorance; there is no doubt that it arises here. One shall become composed of the bliss of Brahman.

Non-dual, beyond the qualities (*guṇātīta*), devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), and transcending primordial nature (*prakṛti*), one joined with supreme bliss will certainly attain liberation. This is the truth, indeed.

I speak the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one! There is nothing superior to the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and there is no god higher than Sadāśiva. At that very time, after a short period, the realization "I am He" arises.
Having indeed abandoned the notion of manifoldness and having grasped the sattvic state which is identical with the Supreme Self—having taken hold of it...

O Varārohā! One becomes a knower of the supreme reality (*paramārtha*). There is nothing higher than knowledge; there is nothing, there is nothing, O fair-faced one! Having attained the supreme reality, one is indeed liberated from the bondage of the body.
Likewise: "O Daughter of the Mountain! Various distinct practices have been taught by me in various tantras."

O Goddess! when there is knowledge of oneness, then one attains perfection. O Mistress of the Universe! O Pārvatī! when the mind becomes equal toward both the immobile and the mobile, what is not accomplished here and in the hereafter? O Mother of the World! in this way, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.
Likewise, at the end, through the knowledge of reality, one shall attain nirvāṇa; [as stated] in the eleventh chapter.

As long as there is indeed diversity, so long shall there be distinction upon the surface of the earth; so long shall there be caste and lineage, so long shall there be various names; so long shall all gender be distinct, for the social orders (varṇas) are indeed separate; so long shall there be friends and enemies, and so long—
O beloved Caṇḍī! As long as you have not been born, so long do wife and kinsmen exist; so long is there worship of various kinds through mantras, yantras, offerings, and the like;
so long does merit exist, and so long does that which increases merit exist; and so long do "you," "I," and "this" arise. But once you are born, O Caṇḍī, all this ceases.
Knowledge is the adversary of ignorance; knowledge is the destroyer of ignorance, and it increases both knowledge and ignorance.
That great knowledge which is the savior is the adversary of knowledge and ignorance. Therefore, O lady of excellent limbs!
having produced knowledge upon the earth, one attains nirvāṇa, that is, liberation; this is the truth.

O Tripurasundarī! Unwavering devotion to the lotus feet of Śrī Durgā arises only then; at that very moment, the knowledge of Brahman—so difficult for even Brahmā to attain—is born. [So too do the realization of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra and the other celestial dwellers, as well as the Bhairavas and Gandharvas.
Those who are intensely eager for the practice of knowledge— there is no learning equal to the knowledge of Brahman,
no ritual action equal to the knowledge of Brahman, and no wisdom equal to the knowledge of Brahman; it does not exist, it does not exist at any time.

In this world, there are two types of selves, distinguished by engagement and withdrawal: the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) and its renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Thus it is stated in the *Vājasaneyisaṃhitopaniṣad*, as cited in the commentary composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya on the *Taittirīyaka*: "These two alone..."

"The two paths have emerged from behind you; the path of action is indeed before them, while renunciation alone follows after," so it was said. "Now, these are the two paths upon which the Vedas are established: the dharma characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and that which is declared as withdrawal (nivṛtti)."

Therefore, in the *Kāmyakāṇḍa* and the *Bhaṇḍikāṇḍa*, various forms of worship of the Lord as a qualified, gross-bodied deity were described for the sake of achieving the human goals of those following the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛttimārga*). Now, however, [the text describes the practice] for those following the path of renunciation (*nivṛttimārga*).

The reality of the Self is declared for the purpose of worshipping the most subtle Lord who is beyond qualities (*nirguṇa*). As it is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*: "The world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is fashioned by *māyā*; having known thus that the one Supreme Brahman alone is real, one becomes happy."

Having abandoned name and form within the eternal, partless Brahman, he who has attained firm certainty regarding reality is liberated from the bondage of karma. Liberation does not come through recitation, burnt offerings, or even hundreds of fasts; rather, it comes by knowing "I am indeed Brahman."

The embodied being becomes liberated. Also, in the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "He who performs self-contemplation for even a moment, thinking 'I am Brahman,' his sin accumulated over ten million births perishes in that very instant. In the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*: "The Self is the witness and all-pervading."
He is full, true, non-dual, and higher than the highest; though dwelling in the body, he does not dwell in the body.
Knowing this, one becomes a partaker of liberation.

Now, if the Self is intended as the witness (*sākṣin*), then how can a chariot— which is common to that transmigrating being produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), who is subject to knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā*) and is destined for both wandering in *saṃsāra* and proceeding toward liberation— be postulated? As it is stated in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad:
In the third chapter (of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad): "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot.
Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. They say the senses are the horses, and the objects are their paths. The Self, when joined with the senses and the mind..."

"The wise call him the enjoyer. Thus [it is said]. The venerable Śaṅkarācāryas explain this as follows: "Know the chariot-owner"—that is, understand him to be the master of the chariot—because the body is being drawn along by the senses, which stand in the place of horses yoked to the chariot.

The state of being a chariot. Know, however, that the intellect (*buddhi*), characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*), is the charioteer; for the body has the intellect as its primary guide, just as a chariot has a charioteer as its primary guide. Know the mind (*manas*), characterized by volition and conceptualization, to be the reins.

For the instruments, such as the ear and others, proceed when grasped by the mind, or like reins. They call the senses, such as the eye and others, "horses," because those skilled in the construction of chariots perceive a similarity in their pulling of the body-chariot. When these senses have been thus conceived, [they likewise conceive] the objects of perception.

Know the paths to be the objects such as form and so forth. The wise, those who possess discernment, declare that the Self—when joined with the body, senses, and mind, meaning conjoined with the body, senses, and mind—is the "enjoyer" and thus the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). For it is not the isolated Self alone [that is the enjoyer].
The state of being an enjoyer belongs to that [Self] only as produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect; this is true.
By the statement "though situated in the body, it is not situated in the body," the stainlessness (nirliptatva) of the Self is shown.
Therefore, with the intention that for one who is stainless, the status of an enjoyer is not possible without the status of a witness (sākṣitva), the Self [is described].

It has been stated that [the Self] is the witness. Now, in response to the inquiry as to how—given that a single Self alone is indicated as abiding or remaining in all bodies—it can be so, the Upanishad itself provides the answer: "But he who is devoid of knowledge..."
Then, by means of an uncontrolled mind, his senses become unsubdued, like the vicious horses of a charioteer.
But he who possesses discernment and always has a controlled mind, his senses are subdued, like the good horses of a charioteer. Therefore, then—

If it is intended that the Self, whose nature is consciousness, possesses only the status of a witness, then [the text] removes the doubt as to who experiences liberation or transmigratory existence by stating: "But he who possesses discernment,
who is possessed of the mind, and who is ever pure— he attains that state from which he returns no more."

He who is devoid of discernment, lacking a controlled mind, and always impure, does not attain that state and instead enters into the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Having abandoned all conceptualization of forms, names, and so forth—like the play of a child—he who is established in Brahman is liberated; there is no doubt in this.

Doubt: If a form imagined by the mind were an obstacle to the liberation of men, then kings and human beings [would likewise be hindered] by a kingdom obtained in a dream; and those who perceive the Lord in images made of clay, stone, minerals, wood, and so forth, would suffer in vain through their ascetic penance.

Without knowledge, they certainly do not attain liberation. Whether they are emaciated by the restraint of food or bloated with food taken at will—if they are devoid of the knowledge of Brahman, can they achieve final deliverance? Are there even serpents who, subsisting on air, leaves, grains, or water, become partakers of liberation?

Beasts, birds, and aquatic creatures are liberated [by this]. The realization of the true nature of Brahman is the highest state; the state of meditative absorption (dhyāna) is middling; praise and recitation (japa) are the lowest state;
external worship is the lowest of the low. In Yoga, the oneness of the individual soul and the Supreme Soul is the true worship of the servant and the Lord.

For one who knows that "all is Brahman," there is neither yoga nor worship. If it is objected: "But many kinds of yoga have indeed been described; why then is the mere identity of the individual self (jīva) and the Self (ātman) called yoga?"—it is true. Those other yogas are merely secondary, as they consist of actions such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the like.
The primary yoga, however, is indeed the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Self (*ātman*). And so it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:

"Yoga does not come from the lotus posture, nor from gazing at the tip of the nose; those skilled in yoga declare that the identity of the individual soul and the Self is yoga. Thus it is said in the *Mahānirvāṇa*.
For one in whose mind the supreme knowledge of Brahman shines resplendently, what need is there for recitation,
sacrifices, austerities, restraints, or vows?
For one who perceives that Brahman is Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss— unitary by its very nature— [what further rites are required]?

For one who has become Brahman, what need is there for worship, meditation, or concentration? There is neither sin nor merit, neither heaven nor rebirth; there is neither an object of meditation nor a meditator for one who knows that "all is Brahman. This Self is eternally liberated and untainted amidst all things. What [need is there for ritual action]?

Why do the dull-witted desire liberation from that which is their own bondage? They have themselves fashioned this universe, inconceivable even by the gods; yet it shines everywhere as if unentered, though it has entered, just as space exists both outside and inside all things in every respect. In that very same way...

For the Self, as the witness, shines in its own nature in that form; there is no childhood or old age for the Self, nor youth or birth. It is eternally of one form, consisting of pure consciousness, and entirely free from modification.
Birth, youth, and old age belong only to the body, and not to the Self—even those who perceive them [do not see them in the Self].

Those of unrefined intellect perceive through illusion; just as one sees the sun reflected in the waters of a river in many ways, so too does one behold the Self as manifold within the body due to illusion.

In the fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*: "The Self is indeed eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects. It is one, yet appears divided through delusion born of *māyā*, and not by way of its own nature.
Therefore, for me there is no duality, no phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and no recollection [of it], just as [the nature of] space..."

The space within a jar is said to be the great space; likewise, delusion is declared to be twofold, namely as the self in the form of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). I am not the body, nor the vital breath, nor likewise the sense organs; I am not the mind, nor the intellect, nor the thought-organ, nor the ego-sense. I am not...

There is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air; neither space, nor sound, nor touch, nor taste; indeed, there is neither smell, nor form, nor illusion, nor I, nor the cycle of worldly existence. I am the Self, eternally of the nature of the witness, and I am Brahman itself.
"Only this: 'I am that Brahman, not a transmigrating being; there is never anything other than Me.
Thus one should know one's own Self; this is proclaimed as Samādhi. In Samādhi, he is of pure form, indeed the very sound of the Fourth (Turīya); the portion of the Fourth is Parā."

Power is of the nature of the *bindu*, the absolute Brahman. One should know the individual soul (*jīva*) as being in the state of the Lord (*īśvara*); "I am He" is most certainly true. Just as foam, waves, and the like arise from the ocean and are again dissolved back into the ocean, even so the world is dissolved into the Self. For whom the Supreme Self is thus...

Manifested as distinct, he attains the supreme state, himself directly realizing the ultimate nectar (*parāmṛta*). When consciousness shines eternally and universally within the mind, it then spontaneously becomes one with the yogis through the removal of all obstructions. When all...

He perceives all beings within his own self, and he perceives his own self within all beings; then he attains Brahman. When, established in samādhi, he does not perceive any beings as separate, he then becomes one with the Supreme and remains as the Absolute alone. Then...

The knowledge of Brahman alone is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease; when that arises, one becomes Śiva. Therefore, liberation comes from such knowledge and not otherwise, even through millions of meditations or the powers of mantras and medicines, by which [the body] might merely be worn away.
Poison that has been consumed is digested; likewise, all the karmas of the knower are digested in an instant.

When the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is known, wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption. "I am Brahman, and there is no other in this; I am liberated."

One should meditate: "I am of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, possessing an eternally liberated essence. He who is thus endowed with *samādhi* is considered to have attained perfect composure. Having declared, "I am Sadāśiva," the ascetic (*yati*) may wander according to his own will; he is not smeared by sin, nor is he bound by *karma*.

Just as fire instantly burns away the impurities of melted gold, so too does one who has surrendered the self to Brahman destroy all karmas. Having abandoned the Deity residing within the self, one meditates upon a deity outside; having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in his own hand, he wanders about.
By means of craving for glass.
In the eleventh chapter of the *Muṇḍamālātantra*: "Knowledge should be known to be twofold:
that which is difficult to know even by the mind, and [the other]. Knowledge is called the supreme reality (*paramatattva*);
knowledge is the means for accomplishing the object to be known. The other [kind] is knowledge whose object is delusion."

This is considered common. And thus, the remaining threefold [knowledge] is inferior and devoid of reality (*tattva*). O lady of noble hips! The knowledge of reality is difficult for even the lords of yogis to attain. Without the thorough knowledge of reality, worship and recitation are fruitless. There is but one God, and I am that one.

The self is not distinct from the body—O Maheśānī! [It is not distinct] from a pot, from a cloth, from the wheel of time, or from a tree. When one possesses such knowledge consisting of reality (tattva), then one is liberated before long. Its worship and meditation are indeed for various purposes.
Visiting sacred fords, taking refuge at the feet of Tāriṇī, remembering Manurāja, wandering indeed upon Kulācala, association with the virtuous, service to Viṣṇu, worship of Śaṅkara,
and devotion to the pair of feet of Kālikā.

The cause of knowledge. [The text] also demonstrates that ritual action (*kriyā*) is a means to liberation in the second chapter: "O Caṇḍī! He who worships Kālikā with devotion and through ritual action, that living being attains the state of Śiva—this is the truth, the truth; there is no doubt. Likewise: "Always..."

The ritual must be performed; by means of ritual, the best of practitioners attains supreme accomplishment. Therefore, he should never abandon it. This statement, which pertains specifically to the householder, will become clear in the first chapter. Where is Yama? Where is austerity?

Where is Viṣṇu, and where is Kali, the destroyer of merit? One should always contemplate the truth regarding every mental affliction. Having adopted this method, the wise person should mutter the mantra and meditate;
such a person attains the state of Śiva in a very short time.

That which was previously stated—that the difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) consists solely of their limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—will now be clarified, as it is said in that very same [text]: "The individual soul is Śiva; Śiva, the Lord, is that very soul.
When pure, he is Śiva; when bound by fetters, he is the individual soul; when released from fetters, he is Sadāśiva."

Regarding the fetters (*pāśa*), it is stated in the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "Compassion, shame, fear, sorrow, and disgust as the fifth; family, conduct, and caste—these eight are proclaimed as the fetters. Bound by the fetters is the individual soul (*jīva*); released from the fetters is Sadāśiva."
In the third chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra: "Rice remains bound by its husk, but in the absence of the husk it becomes pure grain;
so too the living being (jīva) is bound by karma, but when liberated from karma, he is Sadāśiva."

Likewise: "Just as an oblation thrown into water is not [perceived] there as it was before, so the Self is said here to exist as distinct from the qualities (*guṇas*). Just as water mixed with milk becomes milk itself, there is no distinction."

In the same way, it is so with the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). Just as the disks of the moon and the sun [are reflected] in jars filled with water, when the jar is broken, the moon and the sun dissolve into the water itself. The supreme Śiva, the Self, is neither born nor does He die; this is the knowledge of the Self.

O Caṇḍī! Having reached [the Lord], the soul certainly crosses over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of saṃsāra and always attains the state of Śiva. Also, in the second chapter of the Kaṭhopaniṣad: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die; this one has not come from anywhere, nor did anyone ever become anything. He is unborn and eternal."
This ancient one is eternal; he is not slain when the body is slain.

This is also found in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "He is merely the wise one" (*kevalaṃ vipaścit*); here, the distinction lies in the second quarter [of the verse], which reads "sometimes" (*kadācit*) instead of "having been, he shall not be again" (*bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ*). Likewise, in the sixth chapter: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is to be known as Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, who is forever free from passion."

O lady of excellent hips! The reality of Brahman is difficult to attain even for the gods. Likewise: "O lady of noble complexion! Through knowledge, the individual soul attains the state of Śiva. One should worship the wondrous lotus feet of the Guru, as well as those of Pārvatī and Śaṅkara, in a single-minded manner; he alone is indeed liberated while living."
"O fair-faced one, those who are absorbed in the *piṇḍa*, absorbed in the *pada*, and absorbed in the *rūpa*—those who are absorbed in that which transcends the *guṇas* are liberated;
of this there is no doubt. 'I do not know the *piṇḍa*, nor the *pada*, nor the *rūpa*, O best of gods! Let it be told!'—following these words of the Goddess's question, [the Lord replied: "
Śiva said:

The *piṇḍa* is the power of Kuṇḍalinī; I am established in the *pada*. O lady of excellent hips! Form as well is indeed meditation—of this there is no doubt. He who worships the great power Mahākuṇḍalinī, that female serpent, has achieved his purpose, he is blessed, and he is a divine and most excellent hero.

Likewise: "Those who are divine lords of practitioners (*sādhaka*), those heroes who are the best of practitioners, and even the bound souls (*paśu*)—though they may be experts in the meaning of all scriptures—they are to be known as mere *paśus*.
The practitioner attains liberation; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one! Listen, O Goddess, Mother of the World!"

(873) O Goddess of gods! One who hears this Tantra, the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, shall attain the nirvāṇa of Brahman. One should not raise the doubt as to how the attainment of Brahman occurs through hearing the Tantra; for this is the Tantra-śāstra known as the Āmnāya, which is the very nature of the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Because it reveals the knowledge of reality (*tattva*), the Veda and other scriptures are considered the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); others are not so.

Thus says the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "Two knowledges are to be known," as those who know Brahman declare, "the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*). Among these, the higher consists of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.

The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual manuals (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiṣam). Now, there is another [knowledge] by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained. But if the higher knowledge (parā vidyā) is external to the Ṛgveda and so forth—being outside the Vedas—then how can it be the Upaniṣad?

Supreme knowledge would be the means to liberation; yet [you claim] that those Smṛtis which are outside the Vedas are remembered as such because they are false views, fruitless, and unworthy of acceptance. Consequently, the Upaniṣads would also be outside the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas. And if they were outside the Ṛgveda and the others...

Others, however, maintain that although this distinction is purposeless, it is not so because the intended subject is the knowledge of the object to be known; for here, by way of primary importance, the knowledge whose object is the Imperishable (Akṣara) to be known through the Upaniṣads is intended as "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā).
The term "collection of words" (śabdarāśi) is not used [here]. However, by the word "Veda," a collection is intended everywhere.

For even upon the acquisition of the collection of words, the realization of the syllables and so forth does not occur without internal [effort], characterized by approaching a teacher and the cultivation of dispassion.
Because it is possible [to attain liberation through them], there is a separate treatment of the knowledge of Brahman as the "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā).
He speaks in praise of the knowledge of Brahman in the first chapter of the Gāyatrī Tantra:
All knowledge remains as such only so long as true wisdom has not arisen.
Once the state of the knowledge of Brahman is realized, all [other forms of knowledge] become obscured.
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans; but that which belongs to Śambhu— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

Knowledge is hidden like a woman of noble family. All sciences reside within the body, and all deities reside within the body; one obtains all sacred fords (tīrthas) residing within the body through the word of the Guru.
Indeed, the science of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) brings about happiness and liberation for men. [Regarding] action and inaction...

In that way, all this recitation ceases. For this very reason, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*: "Having studied all the scriptures and having diligently realized the ultimate reality, one should abandon all scriptures like a seeker of grain discards straw. Also, in the *Gītā*: "The objects of the three qualities..."
"O Arjuna, be free from the three qualities," and so forth. In the *Gāyatrītantra*:

"Just as fire is within wood, fragrance in a flower, and clarified butter in milk, so too is the Lord, devoid of merit and sin, within the body. [This is] of the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*).
The second chapter of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad demonstrates that this is the fruit of merit accumulated over many births:
"Even by many He is not obtained for hearing; though many hear Him, they do not know Him. A wonder is His speaker, skillful is His obtainer; a wonder is He who knows Him."

Instructed by the virtuous, this is not easily understood when proclaimed by an inferior man, for it is to be contemplated in many ways. It is not uttered here by one other than [the Supreme]; there is no voice here, for that which is subtler than the subtle is beyond reasoning and cannot be measured. This wisdom is not to be attained through mere logic.
It has been declared by that very one for the sake of true knowledge, O dearest one; you have attained it, being one whose conduct is truth. May a seeker like you, O Naciketas, arise among us!
I know that what is called "treasure" is impermanent; for that which is eternal cannot be attained by means of things that are transient.
Therefore, I have built the Nāciketa fire-altar with transient materials and have thereby attained the Eternal.

Having seen the attainment of desire, the foundation of the world, the infinity of sacrifice, and the further shore of fearlessness— the great, wide-striding Stoma as the firm basis— you, O wise Naciketas, have steadfastly renounced it. That [Self] is difficult to see, hidden, entered into deeply...

"Having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that God is hidden in the cave [of the heart], dwells in the depths, and is ancient— the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. Having heard this from here, having fully grasped it, and having attained this righteous doctrine, a mortal who holds fast to it rejoices, for he has found that which is worthy of joy."

I consider the lotus of Naciketas to have been opened. Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, and other than the past and the future; that goal which all the Vedas proclaim.
"That which all austerities declare, and desiring which they lead the life of celibacy—that goal I tell you in brief: it is Om. Thus [it is said] in the eighth chapter of the Nityātantra.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O Savior who delivers the world from its distress! O Maheśvara, tell me: what is the meaning of the name 'Paramātman'? The Lord said:

Well asked by you, O blessed lady! Listen as I tell you that by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while living. O Great Goddess, it is in the place called Virajā, within the great lotus-seed vessel (mahāpadmavarāṭaka), at Puṣkara—the king of holy sites—through the supreme union with Vaikharī.

Formless, the supreme light, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman; omniscient, devoid of qualities, eternal, non-dual, and established in all—when one becomes composed of light through union with Mahākuṇḍalinī, at that very moment, O Goddess of the Gods, this Supreme Self should be meditated upon. [The individual souls and others...]
O Supreme Sovereign! They are proclaimed to be her portions.
In the second chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
The Goddess said:

That which has been described as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest, by the worship of whom a mortal attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation—by what means, O Blessed One, does the Paramātman become pleased? What is His practice, O God, and what mantra is proclaimed for Him? What...
O Lord! I wish to hear in truth the nature and the method of meditation upon the Supreme Lord, the Highest Self; please tell me out of compassion.
Sadāśiva said:

Out of affection for you, I shall speak of that supreme reality which is dearer to me than my own life; that Brahman is to be known as the supreme, consisting of existence, consciousness, and the universe, in its true essential nature.

Or by means of the characteristics, O Maheśvarī! The essential nature of Brahman is remembered as pure existence, devoid of distinctions, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and the true being of the three worlds. It is to be known through the yogas of meditative absorption by those who possess an equal vision toward all things.

That Brahman is to be known by its characteristics as that from which the universe has arisen, by which it is born and sustained, and into which all things dissolve; [it is to be known] by those who have transcended dualities, who are free from conceptual construction, and who are devoid of the superimposition of the body upon the Self. However, the knowledge of Brahman belongs only to renunciants.

[This applies] to householders. And likewise, in the first [chapter] of the *Muṇḍaka-bhāṣya*, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya says: "Although all those belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*) have the right [to pursue] knowledge alone, nevertheless, only those established in renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) [attain liberation]."

By stating that the means to liberation through the knowledge of Brahman is not conjoined with ritual action, and by saying "practicing the life of a mendicant through the yoga of renunciation," [the scripture] demonstrates this. Furthermore, because of the contradiction between knowledge and action,
one cannot perform ritual action even in a dream alongside the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.

It is possible. Since there is no specific restriction of time regarding knowledge (*vidyā*) and since it possesses a fixed cause, a limitation by time or action is untenable. As for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found among householders—such as their being the agents who bestow the knowledge of Brahman—that does not overturn the established principle.

"It is not possible to subvert [this], for even by a hundred injunctions it cannot be made that darkness and light coexist in one place"— thus they say. Then, having begun with "In this dharma, what would be as follows," and stating "one who is intent on serving mother and father," how was it said?

If it is argued that this is because the service of mother and father is possible only for a householder, we say no; for if this were the case, one would have to say "when this dharma is undertaken," otherwise the description "one devoted to the benefit of others" would not be consistent. This is because one who is solely intent on Brahman lacks knowledge of both self and other. [End of section on] Brahman.
The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad describes the creation of the world: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web],
as herbs arise from the earth,
and as hair and body hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe emerge here from the Imperishable."

The method for the knowledge of the Self is found in the third *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "He who knows this supreme abode of Brahman, wherein the universe is deposited and shines forth brilliantly—those wise ones who, free from desire, worship that Puruṣa, they indeed transcend this brilliance. He who [desires] desires..."

One who desires, thinking [of objects], is born again and again through those desires. But for one whose desires are fulfilled and who has perfected the self, all desires dissolve away even here in this world.
This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning;
he alone whom this Self chooses is able to attain it, for it is he whom the Self chooses as its own body.
This Self is not attained by one who is devoid of strength, nor through negligence, nor through austerity lacking its proper signs.
But for that wise man who strives by these means, this Self enters the abode of Brahman.
He states the fruit of attaining the knowledge of Brahman: "Having attained this, the seers—
satisfied by knowledge, perfected in self, free from passion, and tranquil— having reached the omnipresent everywhere, those wise ones, with disciplined minds, enter into all."

p. 877) "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they, having become supreme immortality at the time of the final end, are all liberated in the worlds of Brahman. What was previously stated regarding the "knowledge of Brahman for renunciants" is [the subject] here.
This has been made very clear by the Upanishad:

"The fifteen parts (kalās) return to their foundations, and all the deities return to their respective deities; the actions and the self consisting of knowledge—all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]. Just as rivers..."

Flowing into the ocean, they go to their setting, abandoning name and form. In the same way, the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. He who knows this supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his family, there shall be no one who does not know Brahman.

"He becomes [liberated], he crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil; released from the knots of the cave [of the heart], he becomes immortal. Also, in the *Mahānirvāṇa-tantra*: "If, through merits accumulated over many births, a true Guru is obtained, then, having received [the teaching] from his mouth..."
He shall attain the fulfillment of his birth; having placed the four aims of life in his hand, he rejoices both in this world and the next.
He is blessed, he has achieved his purpose, he is successful, and he is righteous. He has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices; he is proficient in all the scriptures.

Established throughout all the worlds, O Śivā! Blessed is the mother and blessed is the father of one who has brought this mantra—the great jewel—within the range of his ears; that family is purified.
His ancestors are satisfied and rejoice together with the gods, singing songs of praise.

With their bodies marked by horripilation upon hearing this verse, they said: "In our family has been born a preeminent scion who is an instructor in the Vedas. What need have we for funeral cakes offered at Gayā?
What need for śrāddha rites and libations at sacred fords? What need for gifts, recitations, or fire-offerings?"
What need is there for other numerous means? We have attained imperishable satisfaction through this virtuous son. Listen, O Goddess, honored by the world! I speak the truth, the absolute truth:
for those who worship the Supreme Brahman, what is the use of other means?

Merely by receiving the mantra, the embodied soul becomes composed of Brahman. O Goddess of Gods! For one who has become Brahman, what is there to be attained in the three worlds? What can the angry planets, vetālas, paṭakas, and the like do to him? At the mere sight of him, they flee.

Turning their faces away; fashioned with the Brahma-mantra and enveloped by the splendor of Brahman, what fear can he have of houses and such things? He is like another Mārtaṇḍa (the Sun). Seeing him, they are seized by terror and flee, just as elephants do upon seeing a lion.

They perish like moths in a fire. For that embodied being who is established in Brahman, there is no evil whatsoever. Since he is purified, cleansed, and intent on the welfare of all living beings, who would seek to cause him harm, except for one who seeks his own destruction? Those who bear him malice...

Wicked and sinful men who offer instruction on the Supreme Brahman commit treachery against their own selves, for [the Guru] is remembered as none other than that [Brahman]. He is the virtuous one who benefits all and acts for the welfare of everyone; O Goddess, when harm is done to him, who indeed could remain free from affliction?
O Śivā! That which is to be known through the intellect as one's own true nature (svarūpa) is indeed [the goal] indicated by the characteristics (lakṣaṇas).
For those who desire to attain that through characteristics, the means (sādhana) has been prescribed therein.
O beloved! Listen attentively, for I shall explain that means; first, O Primordial One, I shall speak of it.

The extraction of the mantra of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is as follows: having first extracted the *praṇava* (OM), one should utter the word *saccit*; at the end of that word, one should say *brahma*. This is proclaimed as the extraction of the mantra. When combined according to the rules of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*), this seven-syllabled mantra is thus considered.
O Goddess of gods! This mantra is considered to consist of six syllables when deprived of the *tāra*.

This praise of the mantra is also found in that very same [text]: "It is the supreme of all mantras, directly bestowing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. There is no dependence on the attainment of the *mātṛkā* and so forth, nor is there any defect caused by enemies, friends, and the like. There is no requirement for a lunar day (*tithi*), nor a constellation (*nakṣatra*), nor likewise a group of zodiac signs (*rāśi*)."
For those of both noble and ignoble lineage, there is no restrictive rule; no ritual refinement is required here.

In every respect, this is a mantra that grants accomplishment (*siddhi*); no deliberation need be made in this regard. For the sake of the mantra’s meaning, for the consciousness of the mantra—no deliberation need be made in this regard. For the sake of the mantra’s meaning...

The practitioner who does not know the consciousness of the mantra does not achieve success in that mantra, even if it has been recited ten million times. Therefore, O Dear One, I shall explain its meaning and its consciousness; listen!
By the letter *A* is the protector of the world, by the letter *U* is the destroyer, and by the letter *M* is the creator of the world.

The meaning of the *praṇava* has been declared. Consciousness (*cit-caitanya*), which eternally abides by its own will, is proclaimed [as such]. O Īśānī! It is called *brahman* because it is one, non-dual, and vast. O Goddess! The meaning of the mantra, which grants the desired accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the practitioner, has been told.

This is indeed the consciousness of the mantra, for it is the presiding deity. O Supreme Goddess! Knowledge of that bestows success upon devotees. O Queen of Devas! Its presiding deity is all-pervasive, eternal, inconceivable, formless, beyond speech, and stainless.

O Pārvatī! By means of *vāṅmāyā* (aiṃ), *kamalā* (śrīṃ), and so forth, devoid of the *tāra* (oṃ), various *vidyās* are bestowed, such as *māyāśrīsarvatomukhī*. With the *tāra*, or even without the *tāra*, each individual word, or by way of pairs of two, this mantra becomes manifold.

Now, regarding the method of worshiping the Brahma-mantra, it is stated in that very same source: Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having bowed to the Guru who bestows Brahman, and having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity; as before, one should bow to Brahman.

This is remembered as the morning ritual (*prātaḥkṛtya*). Likewise: "Now, O Śāmbhavī, I shall describe the procedure for the *sandhyā* of the Brahma-mantra, by performing which a human being on earth attains the perfection of Brahman—at dawn, at midday, and in the evening, in whatever place and upon whatever seat."

Having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman as before, O Goddess, the best of practitioners should perform one hundred and eight recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra. Having offered the recitation according to the rules, the wise one should prostrate as before. This *sandhyā* has been described by me; it is in every way the means for attaining Brahman.

O lady of beautiful limbs! Listen to the Gāyatrī, which destroys all sins. Having uttered "Parameśvarāyai" ending in the dative case (ṅe), immediately thereafter say "vidmahe. O beloved! One should then say "paratattvāya parato dhīmahīti. Thereafter, O Īśānī! one should say "tanno brahma pracodayāt. This [is the Gāyatrī].

The Śrī Brahmagāyatrī bestows the four aims of human life. Whatever action one may perform—whether it be sacrifice, worship, bathing, drinking, or eating—one should accomplish it with the Brahma-mantra. O Goddess! at the commencement of all rites, one should say "That is good" (tat sat).

May this mantra, "brahmārpaṇam astu," be employed during the acts of eating and drinking. Sadāśiva is indeed its seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is declared to be its meter (chandas), and the Supreme Brahman—the inner controller of all and devoid of attributes—is its deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of human life.

Thus it has been proclaimed. O beloved! Listen as I describe the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa*. First, one should recite "Tāra" (Oṃ), then "Saccideka" (the One Being-Consciousness), and then "Brahma" along with the entire mantra.
O Maheśvarī! [These are to be placed] on the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and the two little fingers.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods! With a well-composed mind, the practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the palms and backs of his hands,
using the mantras ending respectively with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*,
according to the procedure prescribed for *nyāsa*.

In this very manner, [the breath] is regulated from the heart down to the feet; thereafter, one should perform *prāṇāyāma* with either the root mantra or the *praṇava*. O Pārvatī! Holding the left nostril with the middle and ring fingers of the right hand, [one should exhale] through the right nostril.

The practitioner of mantra, holding his right nostril with his thumb, should fill the breath while reciting this root mantra through the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention). He should then recite it thirty-two times;
thereafter, he should slowly release the air through the right nostril while reciting it sixteen times.

O Goddess worshipped by the gods! One should likewise perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) through the left nostril, and again through the right nostril as before.
This is declared to be the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) in the practice of the Brahma-mantra. Thereafter, one should perform meditation.

The means for accomplishing the desired goal of the practitioner: situated in the center of the heart-lotus, it is beyond distinction, free from desire, knowable through Hari, Hara, and Vidhi (Brahmā), and attainable by yogis through meditation;
it destroys the fear of birth and death, is the very nature of existence and consciousness, and is the seed of all worlds.

I praise the Brahman-consciousness. Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Brahman with mental offerings, one should worship it with supreme devotion for the sake of attaining union (*sāyujya*) with Brahman.
One should offer fragrance as the earth-element (*mahītattva*), flowers as the ether-element (*ākāśa*), and incense...

One should offer the lamp as the fire-principle (taijasatattva) and present the food offering (naivedya) to the Supreme Self (paramātman) by means of the water-principle (toyatattva). Then, having mentally recited the great mantra,
the best of practitioners should offer it to Brahman and subsequently commence the external worship.

Having purified with this mantra the substances present— such as perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, and whatever foods and drinks there may be— and having meditated upon the eternal Brahman, the wise man, closing his eyes, should offer them to the Supreme Self.
"The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, the fire is Brahman, and it is offered by Brahman;

through that concentration on action as Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained. Then, opening his eyes and having recited the root mantra according to his capacity, he offered that recitation to Brahman, and [recited] the hymn and the armor.

One should recite: "Listen, O Maheśānī, to the hymn of Brahmā, the Supreme Self, by hearing which, O Goddess, the practitioner attains union with Brahman. Salutations to You, the Existent One, the refuge of all worlds; salutations to You, Consciousness, whose nature is the universal form."
