Salutations to the non-dual reality, the bestower of liberation; salutations to Brahman, the all-pervading, devoid of attributes.

You alone are the refuge, you alone are the most excellent, you alone are the cause of the universe, possessing the form of the cosmos. You alone are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the world.

You alone are the supreme, immovable, and free from conceptual construction; you are the fear of fears, the terrifying one, the refuge of those who are terrified, and the purifier of purifiers. You alone are the sole ruler of the highest states, the ultimate protection for others.
Of all protections! O Supreme Lord! O Master! O Indestructible One in all forms! O Inexpressible! O Unreachable by all the senses! O Truth! O Inconceivable and Imperishable! O Pervasive One!
O Sovereign of the Manifest Reality, the Ajapa-mantra, and the Speaker! May You protect me from misfortune! That One...

We remember that One alone; we worship that One alone; we bow to the Witness of the universe. We go for refuge to the One Reality, the Supportless Ordainer, the Lord, the boat for the ocean of existence, the worthy sanctuary. This is the *Pañcaratna* (Five-Jewel) hymn of Brahmā.

"Whoever, having become purified, should recite this [hymn] to the True-Existence-Consciousness Self (saccidātman), shall attain union with Brahman. He who recites it daily at twilight, especially on Mondays, should—being wise—cause his kinsmen and those established in Brahman to hear and understand it. Thus [it is said].
The Praise of the Five Jewels is completed.
Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the armor named *Jaganmaṅgalakavaca*, by the recitation and wearing of which one certainly becomes a knower of Brahman.
May Śiva, the Supreme Self, protect the heart; may the Supreme Lord, the protector of the world, protect the throat.
May the All-Seeing Lord protect my face; may the Soul of the Universe protect my hands; may the one composed of consciousness protect my feet;
and may the eternal Supreme Brahman always protect all my limbs.
Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of this auspicious armor (kavaca) for the world, and its meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh.
The supreme deity is Brahmā. The application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.

Whoever recites this Brahma-kavaca, preceded by the ritual placement upon the sages (ṛṣinyāsa), shall attain the knowledge of Brahman and become directly one with Brahman. Having written it on birch bark...

If one should wear a pill placed in gold upon the neck or the right arm, one shall become the master of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*). Thus has this supreme armor of Brahman (*paramabrahmakavaca*) been revealed to you;
it should be given to a beloved disciple who is wise and devoted to the Guru. Thus ends the Brahma-kavaca.
It is finished.

Having thus performed the worship together with his own people and kinsmen, the wise man should partake of the *mahāprasāda* of Brahman, the Supreme Self. In the worship of the Supreme Lord, there is neither invocation nor dismissal; [this applies] everywhere and at all times.

One should accomplish the means for attaining Brahman. Whether unwashed or having bathed, whether having eaten or being hungry, one should always worship the Supreme Self with a pure mind. With this Brahma-mantra, one may partake of food, drink, and so forth; that very same [offering] is given to the Supreme Lord.

It is a great purifier. While even the defect of touch exists regarding the water of the Gaṅgā and [images of] Śiva and others, no fault arises from touching or not touching an object offered to the Supreme Brahman. Likewise: "In this matter, there is no consideration of caste, nor any consideration regarding what has been tasted by others (leavings) and so forth; nor is there any restriction of time here."

Purity and impurity are likewise [determined by this]. Furthermore: "Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or burdened by other sins, by receiving grace even once, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
One obtains that fruit which is the result of bathing and giving charity at three and a half crores of holy fords (tīrtha)."

A mortal [attains perfection] through the practice dedicated to Brahman. Likewise: "All actions become meritorious, and evil deeds turn into good deeds; here, acting according to one's own will is prescribed for the accomplishment of the Great Mantra. What need has he for Vedic conduct, or what need has he for Tantric conduct?"

For the wise one who is established in Brahman, conduct according to his own will is declared to be the rule. For him, there is no fruit from what is performed, nor is there any fault from what is not performed. There is neither obstacle nor transgression in the practice of this great mantra. O Great Goddess, in this dharma, one should be a speaker of truth.
One who has conquered the senses, is devoted to the welfare of others, free from transformation, and always a refuge;
devoid of envy, without hypocrisy, compassionate, and pure-minded; one who brings joy to his mother and father and is intent on serving them. Likewise, with thirty-two thousand...
The preliminary rite (puraskriyā) for this [mantra] consists of recitation; the fire-oblation (havana) is one-tenth of that,

the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that, the sprinkling (secana) one-tenth of that, and the feeding of Brahmins, O beautiful one, is one-tenth of that, during the performance of the purascarana rite by the practitioner of mantra.

In this [practice], the discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten is to be abandoned; there is nothing to be accepted or rejected. There is no rule regarding the purification of time, nor any determination of place. Whether one is a non-devotee or a devotee, whether one has bathed or not bathed, one should accomplish the supreme mantra through conduct according to one’s own will.

The practitioner [should know that] for the wise, liberation occurs regardless of where death takes place. This is stated in the first chapter of the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra*: "Whether at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, or at the mouth of the Apā [river], wherever the wise man dies, he is liberated right there."
One shall attain liberation.
The states of the five elements arising from breath were previously described;
now, while describing the fivefold state according to the distinction of colors, he has also shown another purpose based on color.

In the *Brahmajāmala* as cited in the *Narapatijayacaryā-svarodaya*, the vowels within the *mātṛkā* are declared to be sixteen in number. Of these, the last two should be abandoned, and four are neuter.
Among the remaining ten vowels, each one should be applied to a pair [of consonants].
In the pair [of consonants], the vowels and so forth should be known from this point onward as short in the arising of the five vowels.

For the vowels are the utterance of the Mātṛkā, and the three worlds are pervaded by the measures (mātrā). Therefore, everything in the three worlds, including the moving and the non-moving, originates from the vowels. The five vowels beginning with *a* are Brahmā and the others.

There are five deities; the five digits (kalās) beginning with Nivṛtti; the pentad of powers (śaktis) beginning with Will (icchā); the various divisions of the wheels (cakras) beginning with Māyā; the five elements beginning with Earth (dharā); and the objects of the senses beginning with smell—these are declared to be the arrows of Kāma.

The lump (piṇḍa), the word (pada), likewise form (rūpa), that which transcends form (rūpātīta), and the stainless (nirañjana)—this knowledge, which abides in the differentiation of vowels, is always known through the Guru. The vowels beginning with 'A' are five;
their eight divisions are these: measure (mātrā), color (varṇa), seizure (graha), life-force (jīva), zodiac sign (rāśi), and lunar mansion (bha).

Regarding the *piṇḍa-yoga*: "That by which one who is asleep speaks, or by which one goes when called—therein, the vowel belonging to the first letter of the name is indeed the 'vowel of the measure' (*mātrāsvara*). Thus ends the wheel of the vowels of the measures (*mātrāsvaracakra*).
One should write the letters from *ka* to *ha*, excluding *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṇa*, beneath the vowels.

In a horizontal row of thirty-five squares, the vowel situated directly beneath the first letter of a person's name is called the "vowel of that letter" (varṇasvara). The letters *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṇa* are not mentioned [in this context], as they do not occur at the beginning of a name.

If they exist, then the worlds should be known [to be situated] in their proper order. If, however, in the name there should be a consonant characterized by a conjunct letter (*saṃyuktākṣara*), the first letter of that [conjunct] is to be taken;
thus it is stated in the *Brahmajāmalatantra*. This concludes the Wheel of Vowels and Consonants (*varṇasvaracakra*). In the absence of vowels, Aries, Leo, and Scorpio [are assigned].
Virgo, Gemini, and Cancer; Sagittarius and Pisces under the vowel *u*; Libra and Taurus under the vowel *e*;
Capricorn and Aquarius under the vowel *o*. These are the vowels of the planets that preside over the zodiac signs.
One should place the planet below its corresponding vowel, whichever planet is the lord of the sign. Thus ends the Vowel-Circle of the Planets (*Grahasvaracakra*).

The *ha*-group consists of sixteen syllables, while the groups beginning with *ka* consist of five syllables each. The *ya* and *śa* groups consist of four syllables; such is the number of syllables proclaimed for the groups. One should take the vowels from the syllables of the name and divide the total by five, according to the number of syllables in the groups.

The remainder is known as the *jīvasvara*. Thus ends the wheel of the *jīvasvara*. In the vowel *a*, Aries and Taurus [are assigned]; the six signs beginning with Gemini are in the vowel *i*; the three signs beginning with Gemini are also in *i*; Leo and Cancer are in the vowel *i*; Virgo and Libra are in the vowel *u*; and the three divisions of Scorpio are in the vowel *u*.

In the vowel *e*, the last [portion] of Scorpio, the Bow (Sagittarius), and six [degrees] beginning with Capricorn; in the vowel *ai*, the last three degrees of Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—thus is declared the "Lord of the Signs" (*rāśisvara*), arising according to the sequence of the nine divisions (*navāṃśa*). Thus ends the Wheel of the Lords of the Signs. In the vowel *a*, there are seven constellations (*ṛkṣa*).
And according to the sequence beginning with Revatī, five [vowels] each begin with the letter *i*; thus is the rising of the vowels of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣasvarodaya*).

Thus ends the Nakṣatra-svara-cakra. The number [of syllables] is derived from the vowels of the mātrās and the letters; likewise, the number is derived from the seed-syllable vowels. When these are combined, the remainder divided by five (the arrows) is here called the Piṇḍa-svara. Thus ends the Piṇḍa-svara-cakra. Having generated the vowels from the name according to the distinctions of the letters beginning with the mātrās—
"When the sum [of the letters] is divided by nine, the remainder therein is considered the *yogasvara*. Thus ends the wheel of the *yogasvara*.

The eight natural vowels beginning with *mātrā* have been declared as those born from names. I shall now describe their ascensions (*udaya*) occurring over periods of twelve years and so forth, according to the sequence beginning with *prabhava*.

The rising of the vowels begins from the non-vowel (the svara-less). The rising of each of the twelve years lasts for twelve years. Its internal rising (antarodaya) is one year, one month, two days, forty-three ghaṭīs, and thirty-eight palas. [1 | 1 | 2 | 43 | 38 | 1].

Each year begins with the *prabhava* cycle and so forth; the rising [of the vowels] starts from the vowels beginning with 'a'. The duration of a twelve-year cycle minus one year is the annual portion within the annual *svara*: 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 43 | 38 | 2. The vowel-less (*asvara*) is the lord in the southern course, while the *isvara* is the lord in the northern course. The enjoyment [of the years] occurs according to half the measure of the annual portion.

In the six-monthly division of vowels: 0 | 0 | 16 | 21 | 49 || 3 || The five vowels beginning with *a* arise in the sequence of spring and the other seasons. Within each [season], there are five vowels; thus, seventy-two days arise. (p.
885) || 72 || Six days belong to the wealthy and generous one (*vadānyāḍhya*); the palas are thirty-four (*vahni-veda*). This is the internal arising (*antarodaya*).
Of this [breath], during the rising of the *svara* within the channels of the seasons (*ṛtunāḍī*), [the duration is] 6 days, 32 ghaṭīs, 43 palas, and 4 vipalas.
In the months of Nabhasya, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Vaiśākha, the vowel *a* arises;
in Āśvina, Śrāvaṇa, and Āṣāḍha, the vowel *i* is known as the leader (*nāyaka*). The vowel *u* occurs in Caitra and Pauṣa;
the vowel *e* occurs in Jyeṣṭha and Kārttika; and the vowel *o* reaches its rising [in the remaining months].

In the months of Māgha and Phālguna, the interval of sunrise (antarodaya) is said here in the context of the monthly *svara* to be two days, three *abdhi*s (twelve) *nāḍīs*, and thirty-eight *palas*. [0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 43 | 38]. The one without *svara* (*asvara*) is the lord of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣeśa*).

The Lord is the master of the bright fortnight. The enjoyment [of the lunar day] belonging to the other half of the fortnight is calculated from half the duration of the month: 0; 0; 1; 21; 49. || 6 ||

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the sequence beginning with the letter *a*, the five lunar days (*tithi*) starting with Nandā arise; thus the rising of the day-sound (*dinasvara*) occurs according to its respective lunar day and so forth. At the beginning of the lunar day, there are five *ghaṭikās* and twenty-seven *palas*; this is declared by the learned to be the "internal rising" (*antarodaya*) of the day-sound. (0 | 0 | 0 | 5)

27 || 7 || The rising [of the breath] occurs within the measure of the interval between two lunar days (tithi) during the ghaṭikā-svara; this should be understood according to the method described in the Ādijāmala. The ghaṭikā-svara consists of five ghaṭikās and twenty-seven palas. Its internal rising is said to have a duration of half a ghaṭikā. 0 |||

0 | 0 | 0 || 30 || 8 || From their own positions and according to their own time, [the cycles] ending with twelve years, days, and nāḍīs [arise]; then again, at the end of that rising, within eleven risings, this measurement of time—
years, months, days, nāḍīs, and palas— is proclaimed by me in due order.

In this *Svarodaya*, there are five methods. Whatever *pala* has been consumed by the twelve-year *svara* and the others, that consumption is divided according to the specific *svara*; the quotient is the elapsed *svara*, while the remainder of two is to be known as the current *svara*.
In this [system], the elapsed *svaras* are to be understood from the quotient, and the remainder is declared to be the rising *svara*.

The vowel that is consumed by the sixty [units] and so forth becomes "arisen" (*udita*). For that arisen vowel, there shall be five stages—infancy and so forth—according to the power of the name-vowel and their respective durations of time: infancy, childhood, youth, and old age.
Likewise, one who is dead bestows results according to his own state; there is no doubt in this matter. A child brings some profit, while a youth grants half the profit.
A young man bestows all success, whereas in an old man there is loss, and in a corpse, ruin.
In matters of travel, war, dispute, loss, evil, or affliction by disease, the Bāla-svara (the "Child" tone) is inauspicious;

however, it is auspicious for auspicious events such as marriage. In all auspicious undertakings and likewise at the time of departure, the Kumāra-svara (the "Prince" tone) brings success; in battle, one who bears its mark is victorious even if wounded. This applies to both auspicious and inauspicious matters.

In all practices involving mantras, yantras, and the like, it bestows every accomplishment, especially in journeys and warfare; likewise in giving gifts, worshiping the deities, initiation, and the recitation of secret mantras,
one becomes auspicious with an elevated voice, whereas in battle there is defeat and fear.

When the *mṛtyusvara* (death-sound) arises, men should not perform any auspicious rites such as marriage, nor any inauspicious ones such as battle. The sounds of death— whether belonging to the dead, the elderly, the child, the youth, or the young man— are all to be understood as possessing progressively greater strength.

By those who know the *svara* system: whichever vowel occupies the fifth position from another is the giver of death; in the third position, it brings prosperity; and the remaining positions yield middling results. Death occurs when the name has a weaker *svara*, victory when the name has a stronger *svara*; and when the *svara* of the name is equal, there will be equality [of fortune].
The junction (*sandhi*) refers to victory and defeat. In the first vowel, there is equality; in the second, there is half the result;

in the third, the result is full; in the fourth, there is bondage; and in the subsequent one, destruction. When the enemy’s *mṛtyu-svara* (death-vowel) has arrived and one’s own *yuvan-svara* (youth-vowel) has arrived, one should commence [the action] at that time.

In battle, victory becomes certain. At that time, the *mātṛka* [vowels] should be taken for the day, as well as the consonants and vowels; the planetary vowel (*grahasvara*) should be known for the fortnight, and the life-force vowel (*jīvasvara*) for the month. For the season (*ṛtu*), the zodiacal sign and its degree (*rāśyaṃśaka*) should be taken; for the six-month period, the asterism (*dhiṣṇya*) arises; and for the year...

The *piṇḍasvara* is to be known as lasting for twelve years in its conjunction; it is powerful at all times, and the *varṇa* is all-pervasive—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one must diligently examine the auspicious and inauspicious aspects of the *varṇa* everywhere. Just as the footprints of other animals enter into the footprint of an elephant, and just as rivers [enter the ocean].

In the oceans; just as the deities reside within the body of Hari, so do the vowels stand as the source of the fruits of the consonants. One should always perform the practice of mantras and yantras, as well as the application of the yantra;
perform downward-facing rites during the strength of the *mātrā* vowels and the strength of the consonant-vowels.
Every action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, should be performed; it grants success in all undertakings,
especially at the time of battle— whether for killing, bewildering, paralyzing,
causing hatred, expulsion, subjugation, dispute, conflict, or destruction.

One should undertake all activities such as travel and drinking during the *svarodaya* of the planets (*graha*). One should perform the commencement of studies and marriage during the *svarodaya* of Jupiter (*jīva*). Furthermore, one should construct temples, gardens, palaces, and establish deities during the *svarodaya* of Jupiter.
The royal consecration and initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed when the vowel corresponds to the current zodiac sign (rāśika). Peaceful rites (śāntika),
nourishing rites (pauṣṭika), entering a new home, sowing seeds, the marriage of a woman, as well as journeys,
and the destruction of enemy territories should be undertaken during the Bhāsvatodaya.

The battle of the digits and the envelopment; likewise, the commander of the army and the minister should be appointed at the arising of the *piṇḍaka*. One should accomplish yoga through yoga, that which resides in the body and arises from knowledge—the first being *āṇava*, the second *śāmbhava*, and the third *śākteya*—as well as the lunar days and the days of the week.

The constellations have been explained individually; now, having combined them all together, one should apply them in the *Varṇasvarodaya*. One should avoid that day on which the first letter of a person's name corresponds to a [fatal] constellation born of the lunar day (*tithi*), the weekday (*vāra*), or the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*), because it causes loss and death for that person. By this—

On that day, the wise practitioner should accomplish the killing of enemies and other rites through the application of vowels, as well as the employment of mantras, yantras, and rituals, and the induction of delusion. There are twelve states, beginning with the vowel of childhood, corresponding to the twelve signs of the zodiac; these occur according to the sequence of sunrise and sunset, measured by the duration of the vowel's enjoyment.

The states (avasthās) arise within the vowels according to the day known as the *ghaṭikā*, the fortnight (*pakṣa*), the month, the season (*ṛtu*), the solstice (*ayana*), the year, and the twelve-year cycle. [The durations are: 27 *bhāga-palas* (degrees), 5 *ghaṭīs*, one and a half months and two days;
1; 230; and 6 fortnights and months.

The determination of the state (avasthā) occurs sequentially. One should divide the measure of the consumed vowel by its own respective duration. The elapsed state is determined by the elapsed count; the remainder is considered the [state] produced at that time.
In the east, the master is the vowel *a*; likewise, the lord (*īśvara*) is in the south; the vowel *u* is in the west.

In the northern sector, the neutral tone (*udātta*) resides in the center. One should avoid the fifth direction from whichever direction a tone rises in for all undertakings, especially at the time of departure. When a questioner asks a question while remaining stationary, one should avoid the direction in which the tone has set.
Loss, death, fear, and ruin arise; there is no doubt in this matter. || 18 ||

The vowel of the *ghaṭī* (unit of time) arises from the vowel of the lunar day (*tithi*) at the beginning of that day. I shall now declare the results of that [vowel] starting from the vowels of the "child" (*bāla*) state in a query. Having calculated the number of elapsed *ghaṭīs* of the lunar day as the result, one should divide by 327 (the constellations and fires); the remainder is the vowel produced at that specific time.

A question asked with a specific purpose in mind yields its corresponding result; however, where nothing is specifically indicated, the outcome for the querent—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is determined by the following: If the query occurs during the rising of Bāla, it grants only a small gain in matters of profit; in matters of disease, there is a long-lasting illness; in travel, loss; and in battle, defeat. (1)
At the time of the rising of the Kumāra [Navamī], there is abundant gain; there is the destruction of diseases and victory in battle;

a journey at this time grants success everywhere. At the rising of the Yuvan [Daśamī], one may obtain a kingdom and the immediate cessation of afflictions; one becomes a slayer of enemies in combat, and a journey is likewise successful.
It shall yield fruit. In the Vṛddhodaya [yoga], there will be no gain; for those who suffer, it increases their affliction. In battle, one suffers defeat, and on a journey, one does not return.

4 || When a person born under the rising of an even (Mṛdu) sign asks about his own purpose, all of that should be known as bringing death; in battle, there is death accompanied by defeat. 5 || 19 || Odd vowels are considered male, while even vowels are considered female. When their respective vowel-ascendancy (svara-udaya) has occurred—

The strength of men and women shall be determined as follows: for the sake of conception, if the male vowel arises, a son is born; if the female vowel arises, a daughter is born. If both arise together, twins are born; if it is lost, there is loss; and at the transition (saṃkrama), there is the death of the mother. When the day-vowel and the [corresponding] consonant-vowel belong to males, a pair of males is born; when they belong to females, a pair of females is born.

One should determine the male-female pair within the womb from those two [letters]. Whichever vowel-syllable corresponds to the color of that which belongs to the birth asterism or the birth-quarter (janmapāda), by that the nature of the life-force (nāḍīsvara) of living beings here is to be known. [Such a person is] fickle, timid, and foolish.
One born when the *bāla* (rising) of the voice is in the *svarodaya* becomes miserly, lacks control over the senses, and speaks much that is untrue. (1)

Resolute, skilled in the arts, devoted to women, fortunate, and happy; long-lived, heroic against enemies, and born with the rising of the prince (Kumāra); endowed with all auspicious marks, he becomes a renowned king. A child born during the rising of the youth (Yuvan) is victorious in battle at all times. || 2-3 ||

A man born when the Moon is in its period of increase (vṛddhodaya) is devoted to righteousness, full of desire, discerning, possessed of steady courage, truthful, and of virtuous conduct. But one whose birth occurs during the period of decline (mṛtodaya) is afflicted by suffering, envious, cruel, deluded, and has impaired senses; he is lazy in all undertakings and wicked.

For the first lunar day (*tithi*), three syllables (*varṇa*) are prescribed; for the remaining two, two syllables each are considered. Thus, the number of syllables in the *tithi*-vowels (*tithisvara*) should be known within the triad of lunar days. [The results are] birth, loss, and likewise death, corresponding to the lunar day and so forth. When the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) corresponds to birth, there is gain; when it corresponds to loss or death, there is no death (i.e., survival).

Doubt [is resolved] || 20 || In the *Svarodaya*: "That which was stated in the *Jāmala-tantra* has been understood through the grace of the Guru. I shall now declare the daily results derived from the breath-sounds (*svara*), which illuminate the actions of men; [namely,] the yoga, the piṇḍa, the asterism (*ṛkṣa*), the zodiac sign (*rāśi*), the so-called life-force (*jīva*), the planets (*kheṭa*), the syllables, and the breath-sounds."
Having generated them by name, one should place eight [signs] ending with Mātra in sequence.

Beneath those, one should write the eight vowels, increased by twelve years; these are conjoined with their own enjoyment (*bhoga*), and the enjoyment consists of an eleventh part. These, beginning with the conjunction (*yoga*), possess increasing strength in successive order.

The vowels are born from names; the vowels arising in time must also be known by those who know the vowels. Having placed the numbers according to the measure of the Vedas beneath the vowels beginning with *a*, arranged in their proper sequence, they are known as *viṃśopaka*s. In the conjunction...

The twelve-year states are to be understood collectively within the year; the annual state is known from the Bhasvara [system] and the northern course from the Rāśisvara. The monthly state is derived from the Jīvasvara, and likewise the fortnightly state from the Grahasvara. The daily state is to be known from the Varṇasvara, and the hourly state from the Mātrāsvara.

If a period exceeding twelve years is situated within a vowel such as 'A' and so forth, it will not be auspicious there, even if it is auspicious according to the five states (*pañcāvasthā*). The two vowels at the end of the "old" (*vṛddha*) group are defective, as is the first half of the "child" (*bāla*) group; the remaining one and a half [vowels] should be known as auspicious.

Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious: those [planetary periods] such as the twelve-year ones that are situated within their own internal risings should be placed together on one side if they are auspicious, and separately on another side if they are inauspicious.
From the middle of this pair of heaps consisting of the nature of the auspicious and inauspicious, when one is subtracted from the other...

The remainder should be known as the result for that day. When the remainder is multiplied by twenty and divided by sixty-four, the quotient obtained therein indicates the auspicious and inauspicious points (viṃśopaka). This applies to the yoga according to its own function, and to the piṇḍa at the end of the body.

From friends [the result is known] in the sign (rāśi); from one's own family in Jupiter’s [position]; from an enemy planet in the accent (svarita); from its own lord in the color (varṇa); and from women in the measure (mātrā). Having understood this, the wise man should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results for the day.
The explanation, the procedure, and the terminology for these are now stated. For example: (p.

It does not arrive. In that regard, the meaning is that the *mātrā* (vowel quantity) and the *svara* (vowel sound) which belong to the first syllable—the initial letter—of the name, are called the *mātrāsvara*.

For example, in the name Rāmatoṣaṇa, because the vowel *ā* is joined with the letter *r*, the vowel *a* is the *mātrāsvara*. [The passage beginning with] "the letters starting with *ka*" (*kādītyādi*) follows.

Six lines should be drawn in an east-to-west sequence. Likewise, eight lines should be drawn in a south-to-north sequence; thus, there are thirty-five squares. In that [grid], the letters *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, and *o* are placed at the beginning of the first square.

[These letters] have been written. Now, in the five cells of the second row, which consists of the northern and southern forms and is devoid of the letters ṅa, ña, and ṇa, these letters are placed: ka, kha, ga, gha, and ca. In the five cells of the third row, these letters are placed: cha, ja, jha, ṭa, and ṭha.

In the fourth [group] are ḍa, ḍha, ta, tha, and da; these are in the fifth; dha, na, pa, pha, and ba are in the sixth; bha, ma, ya, ra, and la are in the seventh; and va, śa, ṣa, sa, and ha are to be written in the eighth, respectively.
Since the first letter of a person's name falls beneath a particular vowel by being written below it, that vowel belongs to him.

Regarding "the phoneme-syllable" (*varṇasvara*): as stated, the first phoneme of the name is the letter *ra*, which falls below the letter *e*; therefore, its phoneme-syllable is *e*. Regarding "if [there is] a name," etc.: if there should be a conjunct consonant at the beginning of the name, then it is the first phoneme of that conjunct.

It is to be taken. For example, in the name *Prāṇakṛṣṇa*, the letter *pa*—which is the first consonant—is to be taken; by that, the vowel of that name is the letter *u*. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of a vowel" (*asvare*) and so forth:
beneath the letter *a*, Aries, Leo, and Scorpio are to be written. Likewise, beneath the letter *i*.
Virgo, Gemini, and Cancer; the rest is clear. *Mṛga* is Capricorn (*makara*).
Regarding "the lord of the sign" and so forth: one should write beneath whichever sign that planet is the lord.
And the lords [of the signs] are as stated in astrology: Mars is the lord of Aries and Scorpio; Venus is the lord of... [and so on].
Venus is the lord of Taurus and Libra; Mercury is the lord of Virgo and Gemini;

Jupiter is the lord of Sagittarius and Pisces; Saturn is the lord of Aquarius and Capricorn; the Moon is the lord of Cancer; and the Sun is the lord of Leo—these are considered the lords of the signs (kṣetrādhipas). Thus, whichever sign is situated below its own [ruling] vowel...

That fallen tone of his is called the "planetary tone" (*grahasvara*). For example, in the name Rāmatoṣaṇa, because the vowel situated beneath the letter *ra*—which is the planetary tone of the zodiac sign Libra—is [present], that vowel is the planetary tone for him.

p. 891) "Sixteen," and so forth: the *a*-group (*avarga*), ending with the *visarga*, consists of sixteen syllables. The *ka*-group, *ca*-group, *ṭa*-group, *ta*-group, and *pa*-group each consist of five syllables.
The *ya*-group and *śa*-group each consist of four syllables; such is the count among the groups (*vargas*).

It is proclaimed as follows: having added up the numerical values of the letters of the name according to their respective classes (*varga*) and sounds (*varṇa*), one should divide by five. Whichever number remains as the remainder after the division—that being the count within the pentad beginning with *a*—by that number it is designated as the "living vowel" (*jīvasvara*). For example:

In the name *Rāmatoṣaṇa*, there are two *repha*s (the letter *r*), two *ā* vowels, and five instances of the letter *m*. The convention is that the combined form of these letters is not to be taken; therefore, the vowel *a* is not to be taken after the letter *m*.
There is one *t*, three *u*s, thirteen *y*s, and two *ṇ*s.

When those five are added together according to that convention and the resulting thirty digits are divided by five, no remainder remains. According to the convention that in the absence of a remainder the divisor-digit is to be taken, the vowel of the soul (*jīvasvara*) for that name is the syllable *o*. [This applies to] Meṣa and so forth.

In the sequence of nine divisions, Aries and Taurus, along with six divisions of Gemini, are to be written under the vowel *a*. Thus, under the vowel *i*, there are three divisions of Gemini, as well as Leo and Cancer. Similarly, under the vowel *u*, Virgo and Libra, along with the first three divisions of Scorpio, are placed.

In the vowel *e*, the six remaining degrees of Scorpio (*vṛścika*) and the first six degrees of Sagittarius (*dhanus*) and Capricorn (*makara*) are included; in the vowel *o*, the remaining degrees of Capricorn (*makara*), as well as Aquarius (*kumbha*) and Pisces (*mīna*), are included.
By this, in the [alphabet] named Rāmatoṣaṇa, because the letter *ra* falls upon the first degree of Libra (*tulā*), it is a vowel (*usvara*).

Regarding "the lord of the zodiac" (*rāśisvara*): [it refers to] the letter *a*, and so forth. Beneath the vowels, one should write the seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Revatī and ending with Ārdrā, according to their sequence. Likewise, because there are five groups of five starting from the vowel *i*, they are written beneath the letter *i* as follows: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Under the letter *u*: 12.

"From the mother," and so forth: whatever number is obtained from the vowel of the mother and the vowel of the father, that [number] and whatever number belongs to the vowel of the *jīva* (the soul-vowel) should be combined; the summing of these three figures must be performed. That [sum] is then to be divided by five.

That which remains after the subtraction, among the five vowels, is to be known as the *piṇḍasvara* according to the number of the remaining digit. For example, in the case of one named Rāmatoṣaṇa, the *mātrāsvara* is the vowel *a*, whose numerical value is one; the *varṇasvara* is the vowel *e*, whose [numerical value is two]. (p. 892)

There are four numbers for the *jīvasvara*, which is the vowel *o*; when these are added to the three groups of five numbers, they become ten. When the number ten is divided by five, a small remainder remains; therefore, that is the *osvara*, and it is called the *piṇḍasvara*. [Regarding the phrase] "mātrādi" and so forth:

Having combined all the individual numbers of the seven groups of consonants ending with the vowels starting from *mā* (ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa), divide that total by five. Whatever remainder remains, the vowel corresponding to that numerical value is the "yoga-svara" (conjunct vowel). For example, in the name Rāmatoṣaṇa, [the process for] the vowel of the *mātrā* (syllabic weight) is as follows: [Note: The specific calculation for the name "Rāmatoṣaṇa" would follow here, applying the aforementioned rule to its constituent syllables.]
The number for the phoneme-sound (varṇasvara) is eleven; the numbers for the planet-sound (grahasvara) are four;
the numbers for the life-force-sound (jīvasvara) are three; the numbers for the zodiacal-sign-sound (rāśisvara) are five;
the numbers for the lunar-mansion-sound (nakṣatrasvara) are three; and the numbers for the aggregate-sound (piṇḍasvara) are five.
When all the digits are combined and that total of twenty-four is divided by five, four remain; therefore, for him, the sound is called *yogasvara*. || 8 ||

"Proktā" and so forth. These eight vowels, beginning with *mā*, are innate (*svābhāvika*) and produced by name. The meaning is that I shall describe the arising of these vowels—the conventional usages such as childhood and so on—born from the twelve-year cycle, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, the lunar days, and the *daṇḍas*.

Beginning from the vowel *a* of the year *Prabhava* and so forth, these vowels arise individually in a cycle of twelve years according to the sequence of the sixty-year cycle, starting with *Prabhava*.
Thus, by repeating this twelve times each, there is the arising of the four vowels beginning with *i*. In this regard:

In the *asvara* [cycle]: Prabhava 1, Vibhava 2, Krūra 3, Pramoda 4, Prājāpatya 5, Aṅgirā 6, Śrīmukha 7, Bhāva 8, Yuvan 9, Dhātṛ 10, Īśvara 11, Bahudhānya 12. In the *īśvara* [cycle]: Pramāthin 13, Vikrama 14, Vṛṣa 15, Citrabhānu.

In the *Ratnamālā*: "The time of Śakra and Indra (the Śaka year), multiplied by twelve and added to twenty-two hundred and sixty-four, is divided by one thousand nine hundred and seventy-one. The quotient is disregarded;
the remainder, when divided by sixty, gives the Prabhava and subsequent years. This is for the purpose of calculating the [expired] years. Excluding the current year.

That which remains, having been filled by the suns (twelve) with the waves of the sky (zero), when divided in reverse order and then divided by thirty (the fires of the sky), yields the portions, months, and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows: the Śaka year is placed separately in two locations; there, one is multiplied by twenty-two (ākṛti) and filled by twenty-two.

By naming the *ākṛti* meter as "twenty-two syllables," the convention "twenty-two" (*dvāviṃśati*) is established for it. [The number] four thousand two hundred ninety-one... [is derived from] the moon (1), the Nandas (9), the horses (7), and the pairs (2).

That *aṅka* combined with the *srai*s should be divided by the number one thousand eight hundred and seventy-five (1875); it must be divided by as many [units] as it is able to go. That quotient, obtained, is to be added to the previously established *Śaka* year figure.

It should be added. The remainder obtained by dividing by sixty is then treated as before: when the remainder of the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty is [calculated], the years beginning with Prabhava occur. If the remainder is one, it is Prabhava; if the remainder is two, it is Vibhava, and so forth. This is the meaning of the phrase "excluding the year" (*varṣavarjam*).

That which remains after subtracting the years— that is, the remainder exceeding the years— is divided by five hundred and nineteen (519). Whatever remains as the quotient should be multiplied by twelve (the sun) and then divided by sixty (the waves of the sky), according to the rule "in reverse order."
The remaining figures after being divided by sixty are the *daṇḍas* (minutes). The quotient obtained from dividing by sixty is the degrees (*aṃśakas*).
When divided by thirty, the remainder represents the days;
that is to say, the figures obtained [from the division] are to be known as the months. This begins with the sixty-year cycle starting from Prabhava.
Among those, the first twenty belong to Brahmā, the second to Viṣṇu, and the third has Rudra as its presiding deity; they are excellent, middling, and inferior respectively.
Now the procedure is being set forth on the first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in the Śaka year 1742.

The Śaka year is 1742. Multiplied by 22, it becomes 38324. Added to 4291 (the sum of the moon [1], Nanda [9], horses [7], and pairs [2]), it results in 42615. This very number, divided by 1875 (the arrows [5], mountains [7], Vasus [8], and moon [1]), yields 22.
The remaining figure is 1365. This, when multiplied by twelve (12), becomes 16380.
As before, this is divided by the figures beginning with "śaśāṅka" (1875) to obtain the months: 8.
The remainder is 1380; this, when multiplied by thirty (30), becomes 41400, as before.
Divided by the figures beginning with "arrows and mountains" (1875), the quotient obtained is 4; the days are 22.

The remaining figure, 150, multiplied by sixty (60), becomes 930. As before, divided by the figures beginning with "arrows and mountains" (1875), the quotient obtained is 4; these are the *daṇḍas* (minutes). The remaining figure is...

1500 increased by sixty becomes 1600; multiplied as before by the figures 1875 (starting with "arrows" [5], "mountains" [7], etc.), the quotient obtained is 48 *palas*. There is no remainder whatsoever. By this, [the result is] 22 years, 8 months, 22 days, 4 *ghaṭīs*, and 48 *palas*.

These have arrived through the process of calculation (*samudāyaprakriyā*). As reckoned in the Śaka year 1742, they became 1764; 8 months; 22 days; 4 *daṇḍas*; and 48 *palas*. Divided by sixty, the results obtained are 24 years, 8 months, 22 days, 4 *daṇḍas*, and 48 *palas*. Therein, for the purpose of knowing the vowels (*svarajñāna*) pertaining to the twelve-year cycle:

When divided by twelve, the elapsed vowel is the second, *i* (4); the third, *u*, is the current vowel. Therefore, the rising of the vowel *u* occurs at twelve years. Here, the internal rising (*antarodaya*) based on the elapsed and remaining [time] will become clear later. This is its internal rising.
The internal rising of this twelve-year period is obtained by dividing twelve by eleven; the resulting years are 1, months 1, days 2, ghaṭīs 43, and palas 38—this very [value].
"One year," and so forth. By this, years, months, days, and *daṇḍas* are to be converted into *pala*s. For example: having multiplied the year by twelve, one adds the month;
having multiplied that by thirty (30) and converted it into days, one adds two (2) days; [then] the days...

Having multiplied the *daṇḍas* by sixty (60) and added the *daṇḍas* therein, and having multiplied those *daṇḍas* by sixty (60) and added the *palas*, the resulting quotient—namely the *pala* measure of the daily rising of the zodiacal sign—is 943,440.
This is the divisor for the elapsed year of the *prakṛti*, which is multiplied by twelve (12). Then [multiply] by three (3).

Having multiplied the months by thirty (30), added the days therein, and then multiplied that by sixty (60), one adds nine *daṇḍas* (p. 895). Multiplying that by sixty (60) and adding the *palas*, one divides by the measure of the *antarodaya-palas*; the resulting quotient is 2. By this—

The vowel *u* begins the twelfth [sign], and the vowels beginning with that—namely *o* and *a*—are the two vowels in the intermediate rising (*antarodaya*) during the period of enjoyment (*bhukti*). The vowel *i* is the present one. The remaining seconds of the portion (873,740), when subtracted from this measure of the intermediate rising in seconds, result in the seconds yet to be enjoyed (*bhogya-pala*).

In this case, when sixty has passed and been subtracted from the elapsed [period], the obtained years are 3 months, 2 days, 42 ghaṭīs, and 20 palas; the remaining years to be traversed are 5 months, 0 days, 1 ghaṭī, and 18 palas. Furthermore, the duration of the internal rising (antarodaya) is everywhere exactly one-tenth of the years and so forth, having been converted into palas.

The method for knowing the arising of the elapsed [period] is as follows: whatever elapsed portion in *pala* there is of the twelve-year vowels and so forth, that elapsed portion, when divided by its own respective duration, yields a remainder of two; this will be explained further ahead. Thus ends the annual calculation of the twelve vowels.

"Prabhava" and so forth: for each individual year beginning with Prabhava, the vowels and so on are placed below it. Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, and Prajāpati—these five years belong to the five vowels beginning with 'a'. Thus it continues further.
Five years for each of the five vowels. Thus, in the annual vowel, there is a repeated enjoyment twelve times.
The enjoyment of the intermediate rising of the twelve-year cycle, when reduced by one year, occurs within the annual vowel.

The *bhukti* (daily motion) of that [planetary day] is the daily motion of the internal rising (*antarodaya*). Years: 0; Months: 1; Days: 2; Daṇḍas: 43; Palas: 48. The arrangement for the present case is as follows: the years elapsed since the last solar return (*ābdika*) are 0;
months: 8; days: 22; daṇḍas: 4; palas: 48. Here, in the calculation of the elapsed solar period, there are the vowels *a* and *e*.
The vowel *u* is the current one. Therein, the elapsed time is 8 months, 22 days, 4 *daṇḍas*, and 48 *palas*.
The measure of the interval converted into *palas* is 943,440; this is the measure of the divisor and the dividend converted into *palas*.
From the division therein, the quotient obtained is the elapsed vowel; in the second cycle, the current vowel is *kāra*.

The remainder of the *bhaga* (degrees), when divided by sixty, gives the days, *daṇḍas*, and *palas* of the *bhogya* (portion yet to be traversed) in this *bhogapala*; this is the annual *svara*. Regarding the solstitial *svara*: in the south, during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) within the six signs beginning with Cancer, the vowel *a* is the *svara* [4]; in the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*)...
In the six months beginning with Capricorn (makara), the vowel *i* is the sixth-month vowel and the vowel of the sun’s transit (*mayana*).

According to the measure of half the year’s duration, that which is the measure of the internal-rising movement (*antarodaya-bhukti*) within the year is halved to become the internal-rising movement consisting of vowels, months, days, daṇḍas, and palas.
This is as follows: [p. 896] * Vowels: 4 * Months: 4 * Days: 4 * Daṇḍas: 4 * Palas: 4 This constitutes the internal-rising movement for the period of half a year.

From the *palīkaraṇa* (conversion to units), the divisor (*hāraka*) is 4 and the day of purification (*śuddhidina*) is 3. From this point, during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), the days elapsed in the month are converted into *palīs*. Dividing by the divisor, the resulting vowel is the sixth;
in the second cycle, the current consonant is obtained from the remainder of the division, representing the elapsed and yet-to-come [vowels].

The days, degrees, and minutes of arc to be traversed from the vṛtta obtained by dividing by sixty constitute this interval; thus begins the operation [of the calculation], according to another authority.

Regarding the phrase "from the letter A": those [days] whose rise occurs sequentially during the six seasons, beginning with the piercing of the vowels starting from the letter A and ending with the piercing of the final vowel, are to be understood as such. It is stated that for each individual [vowel], there are seventy-two days of rising (72). There are five vowels (5) and six seasons (6).
Thus, by including the preceding vowel within twelve lunar days (tithis), there are seventy-two (72) days. In this way, the arrangement of the five vowels consists of seventy-two [units];
the measure of the internal rising (*antarodaya*) is six days, and so forth, [including] days, *daṇḍas*, and *palas*. Here, the *pala* of the internal rising serves as the divisor (*hāraka*).

In Vaiśākha and other months, by calculating the elapsed days in solar order, one obtains the current vowel-sound (svara) as the quotient of this verse-number divided by the divisor; thus, in spring, the vowel *a* arises, and the fourth vowel, *ā*, is currently present. In the current [month],...

From the calculation of the elapsed and remaining *pala* of the [day] already consumed, the remaining *pala* are the remaining days, degrees, and *pala* obtained by dividing by sixty; this should be considered in the same way for what follows.

The seasonal sounds (*ṛtusvara*). Regarding the month of *Nabhasya*: therein, the vowel *a* arises for the months of Bhādrapada, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Vaiśākha; likewise, the vowel *i* for Āśvina, Śrāvaṇa, and Āṣāḍha; and the vowel *u* for Caitra and Pauṣa.

The letter *e* arises in the months of Jyeṣṭha and Kārttika; the letter *o* arises in Māgha and Phālguna. Here, two days constitute the monthly vowel; thus, the internal arising (*antarodaya*) of the first [vowel] occurs. Day 2, Daṇḍa 43, Pala 38. This, converted into palas, is 9818. For this very reason, the month begins with the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇādi*) according to the sequence of the vowels.

Starting from the beginning of the dark fortnight, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the previous day is reduced by one; the resulting quotient obtained here by the divisor is five vowels, which reside in the sixth vowel. And that, according to the sequence beginning with *ka*, is the second occurrence of the form of the letter *ā*.
The elapsed *pala* of that [current] vowel is divided by sixty; from this, six vowels are obtained, and the seventh is the current vowel.

In the case of the second cycle beginning with *kāra*, the vowel *i* is the current one. Its elapsed and remaining *palas* are divided by sixty, resulting in the *pala* of the day and *daṇḍa* of the cycle.
The month-sound.

Regarding the term *asvara*: those [factors] which consist of the fortnight (*pakṣa*), having the nature of the fortnight, are to be known as occurring within—that is, in the middle of—the *antarodayabhukti*, the monthly *bhukti*, and the half-measure (*ardhamāna*). The measure of the interval between the rise of another measure is the *antarodayabhukti* of the fortnight; and that is—
A day is one *daṇḍa*, which is this *pala*; from the conversion of *palas*, the *hāraka* [is determined].

On the first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the elapsed days are converted into *palas*; what is obtained here by the *hāraka* is therefore called the "sound of the maker of the bright fortnight. That very same [value] is the *antarodaya*.

The first form is the present; by that, the portion of the experienced and the portion of the experience-able, when divided by sixty in this [context], become the palas of days and dandas—this is the "sound of the fortnight" (pakṣasvara).
Regarding "beginning with *a*": by the sequence beginning with *a*— namely,

the sequence in which the letters *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, *o*, and *au* are written horizontally in a row— one should place below that, in that same order, the five lunar days beginning with Nandā (the first day of the moon, etc.), repeated three times.

Having written down the daily sunrise of the days (*dinasvarodaya*) every day, it occurs and comes to pass exactly as it should, according to its respective lunar date (*tithi*) and so forth; for instance, the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar dates (*pratipad*, *ṣaṣṭhī*, *ekādaśī*) are beneath the letter *A*, and on those dates, there is the sunrise of the letter *A*.
On the second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days, [the vowel] *i*; on the third, eighth, and thirteenth, *u*;
on the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth, *e*;
and on the fifth, tenth, and full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), *o*. Thus it is with respect to the lunar days.

The rising of the vowels is to be considered. For this [vowel], the duration of its internal rising is five *ghaṭikās*, [fifteen] *daṇḍas*, and twenty-seven *palas* (27). Likewise, the measure of the rising of the lunar day (*tithi*) is five *daṇḍas* and twenty-seven *palas*.
From the *dhāraka* value of 327, which is converted into *palas*, one subtracts the *daṇḍas* elapsed of the current day of Vaiśākha.
When reduced by the divisor which is the elapsed portion of the day, the result is the elapsed, the remaining, and the current solar [time].
That [result], through the process of superimposition and subsequent repetition, becomes the *kāra*; by that, the elapsed *pala* and the remaining *pala* are obtained.
Here, when divided by sixty, the *daṇḍa-pala* results; this is the meaning [to be understood] hereafter.

"Having calculated the number of *ghaṭīs* elapsed in the lunar day (*tithi*), one should then convert them into *palas*. The vowel produced at that time is found in the remainder [obtained by dividing] by 327 (the asterisms multiplied by three). Thus it will be stated. Regarding the "arrangement of the cycle" (*cakranyāsa*) for the vowel of the *ghaṭī* (p.
898), because it resides therein, he explains its immediate arising as a relevant digression with the words "of this."
The internal rises (*antarodaya*) of this lunar-day rise (*tithyantarodaya*) have a measure of half a *daṇḍa*, based on the measure of half a *ghaṭikā*. Thus ends the section on *svara*.

"By the measure of the rising of the other lunar day" means that the rising of the *ghaṭī-svara* should be known— that is, understood— by means of the previously mentioned measure of the rising of the other lunar day, because there is no difference between the sixth and seventh [units] of the *ghaṭī-svara*. This is according to the procedure set forth in the *Ādijāmala*, the foundational source text.
It has been stated thus: there is an internal rising (*antarodaya*) of the letter *u*, which is the tenth of the fifty *daṇḍas*;
by that, fifty-seven (*57*) *palas* have been consumed. Therein, the internal rising lasts for half a *ghaṭikā*, until the *pala* of the second letter *ā*; this is the *ghaṭī-svara*.
He explains how the internal rising and so forth occurs: "Twelve years," and so on.
The eight vowels, beginning with *a* and ending with *au*, [correspond] to twelve years and so forth; by virtue of their configuration,
their own duration, and their own time— that is, by the measure of their own enjoyment through the period of twelve years,
months, and days— they rise and set therein, and within that, they arise again through eleven risings according to the measure of their own enjoyment.

Thus it is questioned. For this very reason, when there is a desire to know the internal rising (*antarodaya*), it is indicated by the eleventh [chapter] that whichever portion is obtained in a given place, that becomes the measure of the internal rising there; therefore, it was previously treated in that very manner. Regarding the word "year" (*varṣa*): here, in the fivefold *Svarodaya* known as the "internal rising," [it is explained] in five ways.
I have explained the measurement of time and the measurement of the observance (samaya) in due order as years,

months, days, nāḍīs, and palas; just as in the twelve-year cycle there are five [units] beginning with the year, so too there are the monthly vowels, the days of the solstice, the days of the season, the days of the fortnight, and the days of the day.
Regarding the staffs and so forth in the *ghaṭikā*, and the *pala*s and so forth:
he says "twelve years" (*dvādaśābda*) for the purpose of knowing the elapsed time and the currently experienced *svara*.
One should disregard the *pala* that has been consumed of the twelve-year *svaras*.
The sound (*svara*) should be determined by its enjoyment (*bhoga*), with an interval of eleven units obtained for each;
that which is obtained is to be known as the enjoyed sounds (*bhuktasvara*), while the remainders are the current sounds (*vartamānasvara*).
When these current enjoyed *pala*s are subtracted from the divisor *pala*s, the enjoyed and the remaining (*bhuktabhogya*) *pala*s are established.
In that case, when the period of sixty years and so forth has been experienced, and the portion to be experienced (*bhogya*) is derived from what has already been experienced (*bhukta*),
the measure of the current period to be experienced is obtained from the measure of the experienced and the remaining to be experienced.
This sequence is explained in the commentary on the *Svara* [chapter] of the *Dvādaśābdī*.
It is to be followed.

Regarding the phrase "of the arisen": for an arisen vowel, when combined with the letters of its name, there shall be five states, such as infancy and so forth, according to the measure of their respective durations and the authority of the time-periods to be experienced by each. He describes these states: "The first is infancy" refers to its own state.

The [Bāla-svara] yields results according to its state, such as "the ignorant should be employed" or "you shall be patient," and so forth. Regarding the question "What is the benefit? and so on: in these matters—the loss of property, being bitten by a snake or similar creature, or being afflicted by disease—the Bāla-svara is prohibited.

The meaning is that, for instance, when the *bāla-svarodaya* (the rising of the "child" breath) occurs, it yields forbidden results in the loss of wealth, the presence of venomous insects, and disease; however, it bestows auspicious results in marriage and other such virtuous undertakings. Furthermore, in the case of journeys, battle, initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the instruction of mantras, [it is forbidden] during the *mṛtyu-svarodayas* (the risings of the "death" breaths).

The clear emergence of the vowels (svara-udaya) begins from the "child" (bāla) stage; the names [of the years] begin with the "conjunction" (yoga) vowels and so forth. There are eight vowels, and for each of them, the twelve-year period and so on ends at the "child" stage. The remainder is the emergence within that interval.
The arrangement of the five vowels beginning with "child" will become clear further on.

He states the relative strength of the vowels as being either deficient or superior: "The dead," etc. It should be understood that the *vṛddha* (mature) is stronger than the *mṛta* (dead), and the *kumāra* (youthful) is stronger than that. This is the meaning: when one person has the rise of a *mṛta* vowel and another has a *vṛddha* or other vowel, then the latter person attains victory in battle over the former.

He will depart. Regarding the voice of a child, that note which is in the fifth position from it is said to be "dead," as it bestows death. When the war-note arises in the third position, there is prosperity in all undertakings. As for the remaining notes—those of the child, the youth, and the old—they are called "bound" and "death."
If the sound is weak, death occurs; if there is an excess of rising sounds, victory. In the case of equality, there is parity;
"samatā" means the meeting of the two combatants, or "sandhi," which implies that victory and defeat are equal.

Regarding "ekasvara" (single tone): if both combatants have the same [tone] under the influence of the child (*bāla*), then there is equality; victory and defeat are equal. In the second case, the result is half [that] relative to the child;
in the adolescent (*kumāra*), there is half-victory; in the youth (*yuvan*), the full result; in the elder (*vṛddha*), there is bondage—that is, imprisonment.

"And victory over the enemy. Regarding "of the enemy": when the fifth vowel, the vowel of death, has arisen for the enemy, victory in that case for one's own youth is certain. He first demonstrates the production of the vowels from the name and birth [as promised] on page 900, within the twelve and so forth, the eight vowels.

Regarding the phrase "at that time": it should be understood that at that specific time, the *mātrā-svara* arises within the *ghaṭī-svara*. Likewise, during the day, having commenced with the *varṇa-svara* on the lunar day (*tithi*), one should know that according to the system of the stages beginning with childhood (*bālādi*), the *pakṣa-svara* arises, and within that, the *graha-svara* arises. In the month, [the *graha-svara* arises] within the *māsa-svara*.

The *Jīvasvarodaya*: the consideration of childhood and other stages based on the *jīvasvara*. During the season (*ṛtu*), when the *rāśyaṃśasvara* is operative, the determination of childhood and so forth is governed by the *rāśisvara*. For example: the consideration regarding the *naraharināmasvara* occurs within six months; likewise, there is the possibility [of birth] according to the *ayanasvara* and the *nakṣatrasvara*.

The determination of childhood and so forth is based on that limit. Regarding the year (*abda*), the arrangement of childhood and so forth is determined by the *piṇḍa* (the aggregate) and the vowel of the *piṇḍa*. In the twelve-year cycle (*dvādaśavārṣika*), there is the "vowel of yoga" (*yogasvara*); the determination of childhood and so forth is based on that limit. For example:

In the system named Rāmatoṣaṇa, there are eight types of names derived from the vowels of the mātrās and so forth: the vowel of the *mātrā* is the letter *u*; the vowel of the *varṇa* is the letter *e*;

the vowel of the *graha* is the letter *ka*; the vowel of the *jīva* is the letter *ka*; the vowel of the *rāśi* is the letter *ka*; the vowel of the *piṇḍa* is the letter *ka*; and the vowel of the *yoga* is the letter *ka*.
These are the eight [names] born of the names, beginning with the vowels of the *mātrās*.

These were written first. Regarding the extraction [of time] starting from the *ghaṭī* and ending with the twelve-year cycle, they were written first according to the gross sequence (*sthūlakrama*), and then according to the sequence of internal rising (*antarodayakrama*). Where there is a desire for knowledge concerning the gross or the subtle, beginning with the child and so forth, this [method] is to be employed here. For example:

The *mātrāsvara* is said to be the gross sequence; the *ghaṭīsvara* is that which has the letter *ka* as its limit and is the fifth. In the *antarodaya-ghaṭīsvara*, the rising of the letter *ka* constitutes the *mātrāsvara*. Thus ends the *bālasvarodaya*. In this manner...

The letter *kāra* arising from the vowel *a* (varṇasvara) is said to be the fifth when limited by that [vowel], and it is prohibited. Here, the arising of the letter *kāra* from the intermediate vowel (*antarodaya*), limited by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), is the fourth; being "mature" (*vṛddha*), it is fruit-bearing. The letter *ukāra* arising from the vowel of the planet (*grahasvara*) is likewise [fruit-bearing] when limited by the vowel of its own side.

The letter *kā* arising by way of the gross sequence is the second *kā*, which becomes the Youth (*kumāra*); even in the internal rising, that *kā* is also the second *kā*, the Youth, and thus it bestows its fruit. Likewise, the vowel *a* is the Life-force (*jīva-svara*), whose rising occurs in the month; the monthly vowel, however, is *kā*. That [is the second *kā*].

The emergence of another vowel occurs through a sequence of increasing coarseness starting from the letter *ca*; and since that [vowel] is the second after *ka*, it bestows the fruit of youth (*kumāra*). Likewise, the letter of the *rāśi-svara* arises during its transit;
and the letter of the *ṛtu-svara* is the third after the *rāśi-svara*. Thus ends the *Svarodaya*. The letter *kāra*.
"The risen one is the lord of the mass of living beings"—thus is the rising of the *bāla* (infant) sound. In this way, the maker of the *nakṣatra-svara* (stellar sound) arises;

its calculation is the rising, and that is the third from the *rāśi-svara* (zodiacal sound)—this is the *svara-udaya*. The *antara-udaya* is the maker of the arising (*kārodaya*), and that is the third from the *nakṣatra-svara*—this is the *yuvan-svara* (youthful sound). Thus.

The vowel *kāra* that constitutes the *piṇḍasvara* is its rising (*udaya*) as the annual vowel (*vārṣikasvara*). That *kāra* which constitutes the annual vowel is the fifth from the *piṇḍasvara*. In the intermediate rising (*antarodaya*), the rising of *kāra* is the fourth from the *piṇḍasvara*, being increased (*vṛddha*). Thus is the *kāra* of the *yogasvara*. Its...

In the twelve-year cycle, there is an arising (*udaya*). In the twelve-year cycle, the vowel *svara* is the second [vowel] from the *yoga-svara*. *Kumāra* is the internal arising (*antarodaya*), and *kāra* is that very same *yoga-svara*.
Thus ends the arising of the children (*bālodaya*). These [terms], beginning with *mātra* and ending with *yoga*, belong to the vowels derived from names.
Regarding the twelve annual vowels— beginning with the vowel of the *ghaṭī* placed in the sequence of the reversal of the speed of time—
one must contemplate within one's heart the refutation of the sequence of the arising of the eight vowels.
In this context, the excellence of the "eight vowels born from the name" (*nāmajāṣṭasvara*) must necessarily be taken into account.

He demonstrates that the *varṇa* is powerful at all times, stating: "The *varṇa* is powerful at all times. The *varṇa*—that is, the *varṇa*-sound—is powerful, meaning it is strong and bestows its own fruit at every time throughout the twelve-year cycle; there is no doubt in this matter. He states a qualifying attribute containing a reason: "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpī*).

It is all-pervading (*vyāpī*) and pervasive (*vyāpaka*) with respect to all [factors] such as the *mātrās*, vowels, and planets, because it is that which pervades them; for by the power of its [specific] syllable and vowel, even those [other factors], though exceedingly strong, become productive of results independently of them. Therefore, for this reason, one should [strive] with every effort.

One should examine what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. When [it occurs] at the foot: just as other footprints enter into the footprint of an elephant, so too do the vowels of the measures (*mātrā*) and the consonants beginning with *ka* enter into the locus where the fruits of the seven letters arise, for the purpose of yielding their results.

In some places, the reading is *varṇaphalodayasthāḥ*. This means that they stand at the rise [of the day] having placed the results of the *varṇa* (color/letter) foremost; that is to say, they are strong by virtue of the strength of their *varṇa*. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: in battle, when considering the strength of the *varṇa*, the *varṇa*-strength should be specifically taken into account. By "yoga," he means the *yogasvara*.

One should accomplish the yoga that brings about knowledge of the body: the *āṇava* [yoga], which arises from the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā*; the *śāmbhava*, which has Śambhu as its object; and the *śākteya*, which arises from Gaurī and others. Thus ends the exposition on the wheel of vowels. Regarding "the phonemes" (*varṇa*): [The text continues: ...the phonemes are the letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'KṢa'. By means of these, one should contemplate the supreme reality. The *āṇava* [yoga] consists of the contemplation of the phonemes as the support for the emergence of consciousness. The *śāmbhava* [yoga] consists of the contemplation of the phonemes as the dissolution of all objective phenomena into the state of Śiva. The *śākteya* [yoga] consists of the contemplation of the phonemes as the creative power (*śakti*) of the Lord. Thus is the description of the wheel of phonemes. [The text concludes: ...Thus is the explanation of the wheel of phonemes. As for "the phonemes" (*varṇa*):...

Demonstrating the arrangement of children and others based on the specific manifestations of lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays (*vāra*), and so forth, as distinguished by their respective colors and vowels, he says: "The lunar day and the weekday," and so on. The *tithi* refers to the *nandā* group and others;
the *vāra* refers to Tuesday (*maṅgala*) and others. All [of this] is presented individually, according to a distinct sequence.

All that which has been spoken together is situated in the locus of all sounds (*sarvasvara*); having gathered it there into a circle, one should effect the arising of the phonemes and vowels (*varṇasvarodaya*). This is the meaning: the five phonemes beginning with *a* are the vowels;
below them are placed the powers of the vowel-wheel (*svaracakra*), the lunar days (*tithi*), the weekdays (*vāra*), and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

Regarding the childhood state of the *bāla* vowel: when the name Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa occurs, the letter *ka* is present; therein, the vowel *i* is the *bāla* vowel of the syllable. Beneath it, situated within the wheel, are the lunar days (*tithis*) of the second, seventh, and twelfth. These bestow the fruits of childhood and so forth, as well as youth and so forth. Thus, when the name Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa is encountered, the vowel *i* is the *bāla* vowel of the syllable; below that, situated within the interior of the wheel, are the lunar days of the second, seventh, and twelfth.
The two weekdays, Mercury and Moon, below that are "children" (bāla); the asterisms situated within the wheel below those two children are "children";
and the subsequent lunar days, weekdays, and asterisms are to be treated as "youths" (kumāra) and so forth.
In this same manner, the ritual procedure should be performed even with another name.

Regarding the phrase "of whom": for that person whose name-letter—the first syllable of the name—and whose lunar day (*tithi*), weekday (*vāra*), and asterism (*nakṣatra*) have passed away, one should avoid that day among his desired undertakings, provided that it is a day on which the fifth vowel of that [deceased] has arisen. That day is the very day of the asterism.

This causes his ruin and death. By this [means]: when, through this conjunction of vowels (*svarayoga*), the death-vowel (*mṛtasvara*) arises for the enemy while one's own [vowels] such as the infant (*bāla*) and others arise—specifically the youth (*kumāra*) and adult (*yuvan*) stages—then the [enemy's] similarity of phonemes (*sāvarṇya*) and so forth [is destroyed].
On that day, the wise scholar should accomplish—that is, perform—the rites of mantra and so forth.

Thus ends the exposition on the wheel of the vowels according to lunar days, weekdays, and asterisms. Regarding the individual results for children and others, he says "bāla" (child) and so on: the states beginning with the vowel of the child are equal in number to the suns (twelve).

And these [energies] arise according to the sequence of the measure of their own enjoyments: in the day known as the *ghaṭikā*, in the fortnight (*pakṣa*), in the month, in the season (*ṛtu*), in the solstice (*ayana*), in the year, and in the twelve-year cycle; there are twelve divisions [in the year]. In the solstice (six months), there is one-twelfth part per fortnight; in the year, there is one-twelfth part per month.
In twelve years, for each single year in succession, the respective states (*avasthā*) arise according to the measure of the *bhoga* (duration). Regarding the measure of the elapsed vowels:
by one who wishes to know the state of a vowel such as *bāla* and so forth within the *ghaṭī*-vowels and others, [the following applies]—p. 903.

That which has been consumed should first be converted into *palas* individually and divided by twelve, which is the number of its own periods of enjoyment. When the division is performed, the result obtained is the remainder of the elapsed period; however, in the case of the remainder of the current period—
By means of the elapsed and remaining [units], when the elapsed [portion] is divided by sixty and so forth, the elapsed time is obtained;
when the remaining [portion] is divided by sixty and so forth, the remaining time—the present state—is arrived at.
For example, in the sequence: the third lunar day of the month of Nāma; here, its elapsed *daṇḍas* [are as follows].

In the desire to determine the twelve states (*dvādaśāvasthā*), one should convert the elapsed *daṇḍas* into *palas*, add those *palas* to that [total], convert the elapsed lunar day (*tithi*) into *palas* by dividing it by twelve, and then divide that [sum] by the circle consisting of fifteen *daṇḍas*. The result obtained is: four states have been traversed.

The remainders of the divisions are those pertaining to the present fifth [period]. When this divisor has been subtracted, the portion to be experienced (bhogya) in both cases is obtained by dividing by sixty; from this, the elapsed and remaining time in the fifth state consists of two and a half *daṇḍas*.
However, where there is the possibility of calculating days and months, the month is obtained by dividing the *daṇḍa* by sixty;

and in this context, it has been stated that either the twelfth or the fifth of the twelve *avasthās* yields the result for food (*aśana*). In the same manner, the *ghaṭī-svara*, *akṣara-svara*, and other *avasthās* should be calculated for other matters.

The verses concerning the states (*avasthā*) are written here in the text: "The states beginning with the sound of a child are: *Śūlā*, *Bālā*, *Śiśuhāsikā*, *Kumārikā*, *Yauvanarājyadā*, *Kleśapramodā*, *Jaritā*, and likewise *Mṛtā*. (1) "Then there are *Svasthā*, *Ābhṛtā*, *Meghanigharṣa*, and *Vṛddhā*..."

Mahodayā brings peace, yet she is not a woman; Vṛddhā is her equal, for she too is a source of virtue and bestows auspiciousness. Dvādaśikā resides in the boy. Utsāha, Dhairya, Ugrajarā, and Balā, along with Maṅgalyayogā and Sakāmapuṣṭi, Śākhī, Siṃhā, and Bandhanīśvarī—[these reside in the young girl].

The twelve-fold [night] named Śāntā occurs in the period called Youth (yuvā). Indeed, those remaining [nights] are deficient and fruitless; they are capable of causing a fall from [one's state], bringing painful sleepless nights, and being associated with mental distress. Likewise, there is the fierce night of old age, the twelve-fold night of death, and the night of growth. And having bound [the mind] with anxiety...
The remaining [deities] are the Obstructress (Pratighātakī), the Earth-born (Mahījvalā), the Ocean-born (Bhavābdhijā), and the Life-taking (Prāṇī).
Kirā is the Divider (Bhedakarī); Vadādyā brings death, and there are twelve born of Death who cause the destruction of life.

Thus, there would be sixty states, yet the fivefold state always persists. In all of them, the fruit should be understood as being consistent with their respective names. From the first verse [onward], these are:
*śiśuhāsikā* (the laughing child), *yauvanarājyadā* (bestowing the sovereignty of youth), *meghanigharṣā* (the thundering cloud), and *vṛddhā* (the aged).

And [she is] the source of qualities (guṇodayā). And [she is] the young girl (bālā) who possesses enthusiasm, fortitude, and fierce speed, who nourishes desire, and who is the remainder of deficiency; she is sorrowful, night, sleep, born of the earth (mahījavā), and the giver of the fire of existence (bhāvavahnidā). Thus are the states (avasthā). "In the former" means: in the former region, the Lord of Sound (asvara-svāmī).

Thus, the eight vowels beginning with *a* [rotate]; the vowel *o*, which is the sound of Nandā, rises in the east; there, the sound of Aśani [the letter *ṛ*] rises in the south, and so forth. Regarding the south: whichever vowel on whichever lunar day always rises, that [vowel] moves toward the fifth direction from that one.

One should avoid [these] in all undertakings, especially during a journey. For example, since the vowel *i* corresponds to the southern direction on the second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days, its fifth direction—the eastern quarter—is to be understood as such. In that case, because the dead-vowel (*mṛtasvara*) has arisen there, the central direction is established.

When the doubt arises as to how this should be performed, [the rule is: on the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days, when the letter 'A' rises in the eastern direction, one should enter its fifth house; one should not go to the middle of a palace or to houses situated above or below, such as attics or basements—this is how the connection should be understood.

"Ask" means: if the questioner asks a question while focusing on the fifth direction of the *svara* that has arisen in its sequential order during the various states (*avasthās*), then loss and so forth will occur;
there is no doubt in this matter. Likewise, because the second form arises in the southern direction.
The meaning is that when the questioner remains in the state where [the vowel] has set in the eastern direction, the result itself must be declared.

Thus ends the explanation of the vowels of the directions (*dik-svara*). Regarding the vowels of the lunar days (*tithi-svara*), after demonstrating the results from a question concerning the vowels such as "Bāla" situated in the internal rising (*antarodaya*), he says: "at the beginning of the lunar day," etc.; that is, at the commencement of the lunar day.

Starting from the *tithi*-svara, the *bāla*-svara and the others proceed; thus the *ghaṭī*-svara rises. When there is a question regarding that, I shall state the strength of that *bāla*-svara and so forth; he describes the manner of its rising with the words "tithi" and so on. Whatever number of *ghaṭīs*—in the form of *daṇḍas*—of the *tithi* have been elapsed, that number [is multiplied] by sixty.
Having multiplied [the result] and made it into *pala*s,
one should divide that by thirty-seven (37); the quotient obtained is the elapsed *svara* counting from the *tithi-svara*, and the remainder is the *svara* occurring at that time.

The sound of the current moment (tātkālika-svara) must be known; that very sound is to be given as the sound of the *ghaṭī* at the rising of the next lunar day (*tithi*). Regarding the sequence of the sounds of the letters of the rising [day], there is a fixed arrangement of "child" (*bāla*) and so forth;
however, since it is stated that in the case of the *ghaṭī*-sound, the arrangement of "child" and so forth proceeds from the sound of the *mātrā*, it is considered unsettled.
The section [on] the result: it demonstrates the state of being a recipient of the fruit with the words "with reference to whom.

The meaning is that for whichever person a question is made with reference to, the fruit arises for him; he becomes a recipient of the fruit by virtue of the vowels of that person's name, such as "Bāla" and so forth. Wherever there is a certain name...

It is not indicated nor revealed there; rather, the auspicious and inauspicious fruit to be described must be stated specifically for the questioner. He states this fruit in five verses, beginning with "O Kumārī," which are clear.
He states another question through the division of odd and even: "The vowels *o*, *a*, *i*, and *u* are masculine;
they know the even vowels *ī* and *ū* to be feminine. Thus it is for others as well, according to their own gender or the gender of their respective class.

Strength arises for both men and women. Thus, when the male tone (puṃsvara) prevails in the [relevant] positions such as the Bāla and others, a man is strong; whereas if it is subordinate, there is the birth of a son. Likewise, regarding women, he says another thing for the sake of the embryo: "In a query concerning the embryo, if the male tone prevails, there is the birth of a son; if it is equal [to the female tone], [there is no birth]."
