Regarding the birth of a daughter: when the question concerns the arrangement of even-numbered vowels and the final vowel, it is a pair; however, at the conclusion of the lost vowels, there is loss, and the destruction of the fetus should be predicted. At the transition and the commencement of the vowels, the death of the mother occurs.

He states what is suitable for a twin conception with the words "of the day and the breath-sound" (*dyunāḍīsvarayoḥ*). "Day" (*dyu*) means daytime; "breath-sound" (*nāḍī*) means a *ghaṭī* (unit of time). When those two—the day-sound and the *ghaṭī*-sound—are determined, if they are both male, there is a pair of males (*puṃyugmam*, i.e., two men). If the two sounds are female, there is a pair of girls (*kanyādvayam*). If they are male and female, [there is a boy and a girl].

If one sound is discordant and the second is concordant, then one should predict or declare that there will be a pair in the womb—a son and a daughter—when asked about a twin pregnancy; this is the instantaneous sound (*tātkālikasvara*). Regarding "the birth asterism" (*janmarkṣa*): it refers to the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) and the birth quarters (*janmapāda*).
The syllable-sound (varṇasvara) which corresponds to the letter in the square of the *śatapadacakra* assigned to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of one's birth—
just as the four syllables "kekī-ha-hī" correspond to the four quarters of the Punarvasu mansion— is [the determining factor] by that [syllable].
In the first and second *pādika*s, there is the letter *ka*; its vowel is *a*.

In the third and fourth, there is the letter *ha*; its vowel is *o*. The vowel of the [letter] born in those *pādika*s is called the "channel-vowel" (*nāḍīsvara*); it is the nature of living beings here.
The meaning is that it is established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). He states the purpose of the *nāḍīsvara* at birth with the verse beginning "and pale" (*ca pāla*).
The result of the *tithisvara*, the *viśiṣya*, or the *tadantarodayasvara*—which are superior to the *nāḍīsvara*—in determining the fortune of children and others is clearly stated in five verses.
The determination of the nativity based on the sound at that time.

Now, he explains who would be the victor in a battle between two warriors: the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ja*, as well as the five short vowels—*ka, kha, ga, gha, ca, cha, ja, jha, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ta, tha, da, dha, a, i, u, e, o*—these are powerful during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). The remaining [letters]...

The letters *dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha*, as well as *ā, ī, ū, ai, au*—all these are strong during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Regarding "a single vowel" (*ekasvara*):
where a single vowel occurs at the beginning of the letters in both [fortnights] separately, there the strength of the fortnight (*pakṣabala*) is to be taken.

According to the distinction between the white and black fortnights: just as in the case of the two syllables *karma* and *gharma*, which belong to the same lunar fortnight, the vowel of the first letter—the letter *ka*—belongs to the white fortnight, while the letter *va* belongs to the black fortnight; thus, those two [syllables] belong to their respective fortnights.

Since each [vowel] is victorious through the division into white and black, he expresses the state of being one or the other within a single category by means of speech that unifies the vowels, saying: "a syllable of a single category."

Between two warriors whose names begin with letters belonging to the same side, if the vowel of the first letter is *ka*, and if it occurs once, then in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) he who is fair—meaning of fair complexion—is certain to conquer; whereas in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), he who is dark—meaning of dark or swarthy complexion—is certain to conquer. As for example: [text omitted].

*Karmu* is fair-complexioned (*gaura-varṇa*), while *gharmu* is "other than white," being dark-complexioned (*śyāma-varṇa*). The vowel for both is the same, the letter *a*. Among them, there is one [digit] and five;

therein, because *karmu* is fair-complexioned, he is victorious in the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), and because the other is dark-complexioned, he is victorious in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "in which": in that case where there is only one vowel in a single-syllable word, and the two consonants (the *yodha*) are either both light (*gau*) or both heavy (*kṛṣṇa*), or one short and one long— there, if the short vowel is the syllable nearest to the vowel according to the order of writing, then it becomes the winner (*jayī*).

p. 907) The meaning is that if the long vowel of those two becomes a syllable following a vowel, then one becomes victorious. Regarding "pramāṇa": *pramāṇa* refers to shortness and so forth; *nāmajākhya* refers to the letters [of the names], such as the color white and so forth. If there is *aikya*, that is, equality, among these for the two combatants, [then victory follows].

In that regard, the strength for battle should be understood according to the distinction between the attacker (yāyin) and the defender (sthāyin). Having clarified this very point, he establishes it with the words "of two combatants" (*yodhayoḥ*). When there is equality (*samatā*)—that is, identity—in all respects such as the measure (*pramāṇa*) and so forth mentioned in the previous verse, and when a youthful (*yūn*) or fatal (*māraka*) *svara* has arisen, [the outcome is determined].

The first [vowel] is the "mover" (*yāyī*), and the one who exerts himself first is the victor. Likewise, in that same manner, when the vowel is situated in the "child" (*bāla*), the "old" (*vṛddha*), the "final" (*antima*), or the "dead" (*mṛta*), the stationary opponent (*sthāyī*) is the victor. Regarding the results for each lunar day (*tithi*) among the seven syllables situated above the three child-lunar days, he states [the result] starting with "of the first lunar day."

Above the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days (tithis) are the seven syllables: a, ka, cha, ḍa, ḍha, ba, bha. For these, those same lunar days are the "children" (bālas); on them, the letters of the first lunar day, the *pratipad*, are the letters a, ka, and cha; likewise for the remaining two.

Two syllables are considered for the sixth and eleventh [tithis]. Thus, on the sixth there are the letters *ḍa* and *dha*, and on the eleventh, *bha* and *ba*; in this manner, the number of syllables for the three tithis within the vowel of the tithi should be known. Regarding the phrase "syllable-tithi, etc.," this refers to whichever tithi corresponds to whichever [syllable].

That lunar day (tithi) becomes his [corresponding] letter. Then, according to the sequence beginning with one and so forth, for every triad of lunar days, there is [respectively] "Yama" and so on, as well as "Death. Thus, for three months, for the letter *ka*, the first (pratipad) is named after birth, the sixth is named after death, and the eleventh is named after death. Herein—
He states the individual results beginning with "Śrījanmani" and so forth. Thus concludes the determination of the specific varieties of vowels.

Inquiring by means of the distinctions of vowels as to what the fruit for a person might be on this day, he says: "That which has been stated. I shall declare that fruit of the day from the vowel—beginning with the vowel 'a' and known by its measure (mātrā)—as it pertains to men; of what nature is it?
The phrase "the illumination of dharma and so forth for men" is an elliptical expression that includes others as well;
whatever [is taught] in the *Jāmalam*, the *Jāmalādī*, and other such works, has been known by me through the grace of my guru and by means of his instruction.
Demonstrating the method, he says: "By yoga," and so on.

Having produced those eight sounds—the sound of yoga, the sound of the vowels, the sound of the zodiac signs, the sound of the life-force (*jīva*), the sound of the planets, the sound of the letters, the sound of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and the sound of the prosodic measures (*mātrā*)—one should establish them;
one should write them in the order of horizontal rows. "Of that" means: below that [set] beginning with the sound of yoga.

One should write down the eight vowels at the beginning of the name, produced from the twelve-year period and so forth— arising from the twelve years, years, half-years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, and ghaṭīs— and joined with the enjoyment of the vowels.

He describes the enjoyment (*bhoga*) together with the gross sequence and the internal measure of rising; "enjoyment" means that which is obtained as the eleventh part, and the meaning is that the arising of the enjoyment of whatever [period]—whether a year or otherwise—is assigned to whichever [day]. The "gross measure" refers to the enjoyment obtained for each [unit] by means of the eleventh part.

Just as in the twelve-year cycle, first one year, then two days, [the values] are 1, 1, 2, 43 [in terms of] *loka*, *abdhi*, and *nāḍikā*, along with their *pala*s and so forth; and according to the respective sequence of the eight groups (*aṣṭānīkāni*), therein lie the vowels beginning with *ya* (the *yoga-svara*) and ending with the final vowel (*kānta-svara*).

The classification of the Bālā and others among the *svarādhika* notes is as follows: "In ascending order. Those who know the musical notes (*svara*) should understand that these notes possess increasing strength in successive order. What are they? They are the eight [categories] beginning with *yoga* and ending with *mātrā*, which are produced from names—that is, derived from their designations—and likewise, in that same manner, they also bring about the arising of results.

All [vocal sounds] beginning from twelve years and ending with the *ghaṭī* (one hour) are said to be fully arisen; they should be understood as possessing increasing strength in successive order. Just as the *piṇḍasvara* is stronger than the *yogasvara*, and the *nakṣatrasvara* is stronger than the *piṇḍasvara*, so too in this sequence is the annual [sound] stronger than the twelve-year sound.
The meaning is that the svaras of the rainy season and so forth should be understood in this same sequence even further ahead.

Regarding "akārādi" (beginning with the letter 'a'): having written [the vowels] in the sequence beginning with 'a'—namely *a, i, u, e, o*—one should place beneath them the four Vedas, numbering four and corresponding in measure to that [sequence]. This means that those who know the vowels have accepted this as being particularly beneficial. As for the purpose:
Therefore, because there is an arrangement of the number four within each of these eight vowels,
it shines forth as two categories— the auspicious and the inauspicious. Thus,
regarding the names and the eight vowels previously mentioned, [one should consider] the states such as childhood arising during the twelve-year period.

Indicating from where and where that [calculation] is to be considered, he says "from yoga" (*yogāt*). From yoga—that is, from the *yoga-svara*—the states of childhood and so forth occur during the twelfth year. The meaning is this:
whichever vowel among those beginning with 'a' is declared in the *svara* of the twelfth year, that [is the relevant one].

With reference to the measurement of the *yogasvara*, it should be specifically established in its subtle internal arising (*antarodaya*) by means of the vowels beginning with the "child" (*bāla*) and so forth; likewise, the seven states (*saptāvasthā*) are described hereafter. Among these, the "child" state is to be understood by means of years. For example, from the *piṇḍa*:

The state (avasthā) is determined from the *piṇḍa-svara* for the annual [calculation], from the *vārṣika-svara* for the yearly [calculation], from the *bha-svara* for the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), from the *ayana-svara* for the solstices beginning with Capricorn and Cancer, from the *rāśi-svara* of the two signs [concerned] for the zodiacal signs,

from the *ṛtu-svara* for the seasons, from the *jīva-svara* for the life-force, and from the *māsa-svara* for the month; the states such as infancy (*bālā*) and so forth are derived from the planet (*graha*).

The states of childhood and so forth are to be considered from the planetary tone (grahasvara), the fortnight tone (pakṣasvara), the phoneme tone (varṇasvara), the lunar day tone (tithisvara), the mora tone (mātrāsvara), and the hour tone (ghaṭīsvara).

Regarding the phrase "twelve-year period": the time-period consisting of twelve years, characterized by the vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, and *o* in this manner, is established as the *samaya*. If that [period] should be auspicious during the five states—that is, while the sequence beginning with *a* is situated within those five states—[it is favorable].
If it yields inauspicious results and produces forbidden fruits through the sequence of the internal rising (*antarodaya*), then it would not be auspicious; likewise,
if it is not auspicious during the five states— namely the states consisting of year, month, day, *nāḍī*, and *pala* according to the *Svarodaya* system— then it would not be auspicious.

It would not be so; or rather, even if [the planet] is auspicious in five states, or even if it is auspicious in five states according to the sequence of child and so forth, or by the sequence of year, month, day, and so on, if an inauspicious zodiac sign remains according to the method described for the daily practice (dinacaryā), then—

It would not be auspicious. When that which is inauspicious in five states is inauspicious in those five states, then the auspicious planet is not auspicious and the inauspicious planet is not inauspicious; at that time, the result should be declared according to the sequence of the remainder—this is the intended meaning. For example, as for those vowels beginning with *ba* (*bālādi*).
Among those [planets], one situated in its house of rising (antarodaya) is auspicious, while the lord of its house of setting (astarāśi) is inauspicious;

having calculated the twenty-point value (*viṃśopaka*) for the syllables situated above them and written down the figures for both the auspicious and inauspicious categories, one should apply the rule of "subtracting the smaller from the larger."
By way of elimination, if it is a sign of an auspicious planet, then it is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious.

Having ascertained the current *svara* in the general manner described by the sequence beginning with "twenty," the result should be declared below it according to the influence of the planet situated there, as per the remainder.

If there are twenty or more auspicious planetary divisions (koṭis) according to this sequence, and an equal number of inauspicious ones, then a mixed result should be declared; however, if there are more auspicious divisions remaining, then also a mixed result should be declared.
Gains and losses are determined by the strength of the planets presiding over the elements, the roots, and the life-force.
In this context, the sequence of those respective substances must be considered.
For the purpose of establishing the previously mentioned results for the day, he states the rule regarding children and others: "The vowels" (svarāḥ).

The vowels *vṛddha* and *asta* (the long vowels and the *aṣṭama*-vowels) are defective; they yield forbidden results. Likewise, [the vowels] *vṛddha* and *mṛta* (the long vowels and the *mṛtyu*-vowels) are defective, yielding forbidden results.

The first half of the *bāla* [period] is the initial fruit of the *bāla* [period]; likewise, it is "corrupt" (*duṣṭa*) in meaning. The remaining one and a half [units] belong to the *kumāra* and *yuvan* [periods], together with the latter half of the *bāla*. In that context, it is by this manner [that it is understood].
The knowable consists of the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Regarding the "twelve": those eight [periods] beginning with the twelve-year cycle which are situated within their own internal risings are auspicious; however, the vowels—namely the infant (*bāla*), the upper half, the youth (*kumāra*), and the adult (*yuvan*)—when combined with the twenty added [units], should be placed together in one place as inauspicious.
The twenty-point values (viṃśopaka) for the vowels representing the child, the first half-deceased, and the old should be established.
For each of these—child and so forth—there are four points.
The "child" has a value of two in both cases because its results are mixed; this applies there at the time of the first half.
Twice inauspicious. || 42 || At the time of the latter half, twice auspicious. || 42 || Regarding "auspicious and inauspicious":

The meaning is that from between the pair of heaps consisting of the auspicious and the inauspicious, when one is subtracted from the other, the remainder— whether it be an auspicious heap or the form of an auspicious heap— is the result produced on that day. This refers to the results of illness and so forth.

In response to the inquiry "From where might it be? he says "By twenty. When the remainder—the residue remaining after subtraction—is multiplied by twenty and divided by sixty-four (i.e., the quotient obtained when the portion is taken by sixty-four), that which is obtained therein, among those [factors], constitutes the auspicious *viṃśopaka*s.
These reveal auspiciousness. For example, when there is a single gain, it is calculated by yoga; when there are two gains, it is by summation (piṇḍa).

From one up to eight, the result is derived from the end of the measures (mātrā). "From what has been stated for each" means that having assigned the number four to each of the five vowels, the total becomes twenty; by that—
The vowels from *yoga* to *mātrā* are eight in number,
and the vowels from twelve years to one *ghaṭī* are also eight in number;
therefore, by multiplying these eight by eight, the total number is sixty-four.

The intended meaning is "one who performs the division. Regarding the reading *netra* (eye) in the phrase "divided by four and five," it means that a division by fifty-four (*catuḥpañcāśat*) is to be taken there.

He asks: "When the number [of planets] such as conjunction (yoga) is obtained, how can there be a result through a sequence starting from one? He says: "In conjunction" (yoge). When the number one is obtained through conjunction, it is due to one's own karma—that is, from one's own activity—regarding the body; when the number two is obtained regarding the body, it is from one's own [natal] asterism (nakṣatra).
If [the planet] Jupiter is obtained from the fourth number in the house derived from friends,

there is happiness or sorrow from one's own family; if obtained from the fifth number, it is from one's own wealth— or according to the reading "svacitta" (one's own mind)— from one's own mental state.

It is as follows: when the number of planets is counted from the planet itself and divided by seven, the result obtained from the enemy (the seventh house) indicates suffering caused by enemies; when the number of letters is counted from the letter itself and divided by seven, the result obtained from the master (the lord of the sign) indicates suffering caused by those who must be served;
and when the number of all [planets] is counted from eight and divided by eight, the result obtained from the eighth house indicates suffering caused by women.

The manner in which there arises either an auspicious or an inauspicious result is stated here in general; it is now written for the purpose of making it half-manifested. For whichever name, such as Devadatta or another, one desires to know the daily result, that name—
Having generated the eight vowels beginning with *mātrā* in reverse order, starting from the vowel of union (*yogasvara*),

and having written them ending with *mātrā* in a transverse sequence, one should specifically generate the eight vowels according to the internal rising sequence— distinguished by the gross sequence and ending with the *ghaṭī* of the twelve-year cycle.

Having written that [table] below in sequence, one should establish therein the respective states of infancy, childhood, and so forth, starting from the *yoga-svara* and the others; then, one should write here the twenty *viṃśopaka*s of the five *svaras*, each established in a group of four. It is as follows:

At the time of the latter half of childhood, assign two [units] to the youth and four each to the adult and the young; having thus calculated the auspicious heap, write it down. At the time of the former half of childhood, assign two [units] to the old and the dead, and write the number four each in the inauspicious column.
The result that remains between the two heaps of the auspicious and inauspicious is the fruit corresponding to that name.
In that regard, whatever remains is multiplied by six when at twenty, and divided by sixty-four;
the quotient obtained is the number of those vowels already traversed in the *saṃkhyāyoga* and other systems.

For the purpose of knowing the arising of that [result], the eight vowels of the twelve years, existing in their respective states of rising and situated in the forms of "past" and "future," were previously written on the first day of the bright fortnight of the Śaka year one hundred and all its common and additional [days]. Likewise:

They are written here for the purpose of daily observation: the eight vowels beginning with *mā* (ma-ā-ī-ī-u-ū-ṛ-ṝ), starting from the mother-vowel (*mā*) and proceeding in reverse order, beginning with *yoga* and so forth.
Although their origin occurs first within the forms of the twelve-year cycle and so on, starting with the *yoga*-vowels and others, therefore the vowels [are presented] right from the beginning.

One ought to establish it. Even there, since that establishment does not occur apart from the arrangement of the seven notes (*svaras*) beginning with *ṣaḍja* (the *mātra*), the intent is that it is described in the remaining portion. Here, regarding the internal arising of the twelve-year periods and so forth:

Regarding the classification of states such as "child" (bāla) and so forth based on the limit of the *yogasvara*: the author of the *Yogasvarakāra* states that the letter 'u' arises in the twelfth year from that limit. This is the latter half of the child state. In an auspicious zodiac sign (*śubharāśi*), the *piṇḍasvara* is the letter 'e', which has the number two; the year arising from that limit is when the letter 'u' emerges.
The "old" [vowel] of that [consonant] is the fourth number of the inauspicious group.

The vowel *e* is the "star-sound" (*nakṣatra-svara*) and is the limit for the solstice (*ayana*); when it has arisen in the auspicious group, its number is four. The vowel *ṛ* is the "zodiac-sound" (*rāśi-svara*) and is the limit for the season (*ṛtu*); when it has arisen...
The second half of that [verse] concerns the child (*bāla*): in a benefic sign (*śubharāśi*), the number is two;
the vowel *u* (vasva-ro) is the month starting from that point, and the vowel *i* (udita-kāra) is the boy (*kumāra*);
in his sign, the number is four; the vowel *a* (graha-svara) is the planet, and the fortnight (*pakṣa*) begins from that point.

The letter *kāra* [is assigned] the number four in a benefic *rāśi*; the letter *kāra* of the vowel (*svara*) is the limit for that day, and the letter *kāra* arisen during the day in an extremely inauspicious *rāśi* is also its number four. The letter *kāra* of the *mātrā* (vowel measure) is the limit for that;
the letter *kāra* arisen during the *ghaṭī* is the "child" (*bāla*), and its latter half is thus defined.
In the auspicious heap, there are two numbers. By this much, through childhood and the latter half, there are six; for the two youths, eight; for the young man (*yuvan*), four;
and by rounding [the total], eighteen (18). In the auspicious heap, there are eight, including *hv* and *tva*.
For the three children who have previously eaten half, there are six (6).
By rounding [the remainder], the number in the inauspicious heap is fourteen (14).
From two heaps, one heap must be subtracted from the larger heap. In the present case—
For a young person, the remainder obtained by subtracting the eighth house from a more auspicious house is the residue.
If the [natal] position is situated in that auspicious house indicated by the residue, the result will be auspicious.
If the residue is four, when multiplied by twenty, the result is eighty (vṛtta). In this case—

The remainder obtained by dividing by sixty-four is as follows: thus, the second current *piṇḍa* is a vowel; it is auspicious, and its auspicious fruit should be considered regarding the body—the term "body" being indicative of death, meaning one's own people. Thus, in the common [calculation].

Even when the vowels are determined according to the twelve-year cycle and other such periods, one must establish the states of infancy, childhood, and so forth for the name-born vowels for each individual, and then perform the respective rites and daily results accordingly. "In this way" means: in this manner, the learned scholar...
Having understood whether [the action] is auspicious or inauspicious, one should declare the result.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of Bālā and Others, Whose Fruits are Attained through the Instruction of the Teacher of Śikṣā," in the sixth section on Desired Objects within the *Śrī-Prāṇatopiṇī*.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the wheel that illuminates the three worlds, renowned as the Sarvatobhadra, which produces immediate conviction. By laying down ten lines extending upwards and likewise ten lines extending transversely, a wheel consisting of eighty-one squares (81) is produced.

There is no doubt in this matter. The vowels beginning with *a* should be placed in the squares starting from the northeast (Īśa) and proceeding through the intermediate directions in sequence, following the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*), numbering sixteen and arranged in four turns. A wise person should write the lunar mansions (*dhiṣṇya*) beginning with Kṛttikā in the eastern direction and so forth.

In groups of seven by seven, these twenty-eight letters—*ava*, *ka*, *ha*, *ḍa*—are to be written in the east; *ma*, *ṭa*, *pa*, *va*, *ta* in the south; *la*, *ya*, *bha*, *ja*, *kha* in the west; and *pa*, *sa*, *da*, *ca*, *la* in the north. These three groups of three begin with *vṛṣa* (the bull) and so forth.

The wise one should know the twelve zodiac signs, ending with Aries, according to the sequence starting from the eastern direction and following the path of creation. In the remaining squares, one should likewise write the five lunar days beginning with Nandā, and the seven weekdays in the order starting with Tuesday (Mars). [The signs] for the Sun are Aries and Libra.

Taurus and Scorpio are declared the exaltations of the Moon; Capricorn and Cancer for Mars; Virgo and Pisces for Mercury; Cancer and Capricorn for Jupiter; Pisces and Virgo for Venus; and Libra and Aries for Saturn. These are proclaimed as the high and low signs. Saturn, the Sun, Rāhu, Ketu, and Mars are the malefic planets.

The remaining [planets] are auspicious planets. Mercury joined with a malefic planet, as well as the waning moon, is likewise malefic. In whichever asterism a planet is situated, from that point there occurs a threefold piercing (vedha): by virtue of planetary aspect, here [it occurs] in the left, the front-facing, and the right directions. [This applies to] the portion already traversed (bhukta).

A lunar mansion that is being traversed, has been traversed, or is pierced by a malefic planet should be diligently avoided in all auspicious and inauspicious undertakings. When a planet is retrograde, its aspect is directed to the right; when it is swift, its aspect is to the left; and during its direct motion, its aspect should be known as intermediate.

In the five [planets] beginning with Mars: when the Sun is in the second house, the planets are swift (śīghra) in the ghaṭīyantra; they are known to be even (sama) when the Sun is in the third; they are slow (manda) when the Sun is in the fourth; they are very slow (mandāḥ) when the Sun is in the fifth or sixth;
they are retrograde (ativakra) when the Sun is in the seventh or eighth; and [they remain so] when the Sun is in the ninth or tenth.
A crooked motion arises. When the Sun is in the eleventh or twelfth [house], they again attain swiftness. Rāhu and Ketu are always retrograde; the Moon and the Sun are swift-moving.
Because their motions possess a single nature, there is always a threefold creation for these [planets]. The malefics are retrograde.
Those situated in their natural states are gentle, while those moving swiftly are cruel. *Gha*, *cha*, *ja*;
*ṣa*, *na*, *ṭha*; *dha*, *pha*, *ḍa*; and *sta*, *jha*, *ña*—this is the triad.
The triad [of letters] is pierced by the piercers that dispel phlegm (kapha) in sequence:
*gha-ṅa-cha* by the piercing of Raudra; *ṣa-ṇa-ṭha* when the planet is in Hasta;
*dha-pha-ḍa* in Pūrvāṣāḍhā; *kha-jha-ña* in Uttarabhādrapada; and *ra-vi-śa-sa* and *ya-ja* therein.

The letters *ṅa* and *ña*, as well as *au*, pierce one another; when there is a piercing by auspicious or inauspicious planets, the second letter is pierced by the first. In the case of a piercing, vowels beginning with *a* (short) are considered the piercers; there is no piercing by a single [vowel], but rather a piercing of both [letters] occurs. This applies to a piercing consisting of even vowels, as well as to the *anusvāra* and *visarga*.

When a planet is situated in the first or last quarter between two adjacent asterisms, it pierces the four syllables beginning with the vowel of the preceding asterism; through such piercing by one or more malefic planets, results arise for men in due order:
agitation, fear, loss, disease, and death. [In the asterism...]
If an Akṣara is pierced, there is delusion; if a Svara is pierced, loss; if a Tithi is pierced, fear of disease;

if a Rāśi is pierced, great obstacles; one pierced by five [lines] does not live. Piercing by one [line] causes fear in battle; piercing by two causes loss of wealth; by three piercings, defeat occurs; and by piercing [by four], death.

Regarding the four planets: as the malefics bring evil results, so the benefics bring auspicious ones. However, a benefic conjoined with a malefic should be known as yielding malefic results. When pierced by the Sun, there is mental anguish and loss of wealth; when pierced by Mars, it causes suffering from disease; and the same applies to Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu.
[The planets] bestow obstacles [when they pierce]. When the Moon pierces, there is mixed results for men; and when Venus pierces, there is the attainment of pleasure.

When Mercury pierces, there is wisdom; Jupiter is the bestower of all auspiciousness. Full strength is known to exist when [a planet] is in its own sign, three-quarters in a friendly sign, and half in a neutral sign.

One quarter [of the strength] is when situated in the house of an enemy. And this strength of both benefics and malefics is determined by their positions; the same result should be understood for benefics, while for malefics it is the reverse. Whatever numerical strength arises from the conjunction of positional and piercing strengths—
Having ascertained the strength of the objects to be pierced according to their number, one should declare the result.

When a planet is retrograde, the result is doubled; when situated in its exaltation, it is tripled. The result is that which arises from its own nature when it is in direct motion; when situated in its depression, the planet yields half the result. [The calculation involves] the lunar day, the zodiacal sign, the degrees, and the asterism.

That which is pierced by a malefic planet must be diligently avoided in all auspicious and inauspicious undertakings. One who exerts effort during the time of such piercing (vedha-velā) does not rejoice in marriage, nor does he return from a journey;
yet a sick person is freed from disease. Such piercing occurs during the period of illness.

The occurrence of a cruel planet [indicates] death through retrograde motion; even in a direct course, one is afflicted by disease. At the point of piercing (vedha), there shall be defeat; in a fortress, fragmentation occurs.
There indeed is the entry of the enemy and the slaughter of warriors where [the piercing occurs].

In whichever direction the Sun is situated, starting from the zodiac sign of Taurus (Vṛṣa) and so forth, that direction is to be known as "set," while the remaining three directions are always "risen. The vowels located in the northeast (Īśāna) are to be known as being in the east; those in the southeast (Āgneya) and south (Yāmya) [are in the southeast]; and those situated in the southwest (Nairṛta) are in the west (Vāruṇī), while those in the northwest (Vāyavya) [are in the north].
They are considered to be gentle: the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), vowels, consonants, zodiac signs (rāśis), lunar days (tithis), and directions.

All of these are to be known as having set where the sun has set for three months. When a lunar mansion has set, there is illness; when a vowel has set, loss and likewise grief; when a sign has set, obstacles and likewise fear; and when five have set, [great calamity].

Death is certain. Travel, battle, dispute, the construction of gates, palaces, or mansions, and any other auspicious undertaking should not be performed by men facing the direction of the setting sun. For a man who stands in the direction of the setting sun...
The first syllable of a name is [the indicator]. That man is to be known as afflicted in all undertakings and struck by fate.

In the case of a poet, a fortress, or a battle—a great conflict involving four divisions of the army—warriors who have set (or declined) should be avoided if one desires victory in combat. When a constellation has risen, there is nourishment; in the case of a letter, there is gain.

There is happiness in the *svara*, victory in the *rāśi*, and the attainment of rank through splendor (*tejas*) when the *tithi* and the rising of the *pañcaka* coincide. At the time of inquiry, if the ascendant (*lagna*) is pierced by malefic planets, it is auspicious if it is aspected by benefics; if by mixed planets, the result is considered mixed; and the same applies if it is not pierced by planets.

The fruit of whatever *lagna* is [predominant] should be understood according to its own nature. That which has been described regarding the *cara* and other [movements] in the aspect (*īkṣaṇa*) and the quadrant (*kendram*) [should also be considered]. For one whose vowels, lunar days (*tithi*), and *svara*s are pierced on both sides by malefic planets, as well as his zodiac sign (*rāśi*) and asterism (*dhiṣṇya*)—these five—their death does not occur.

Doubt arises [regarding the following]: A circle, a city, a village, a fortress, a temple, or a capital—these perish in their respective order when pierced by malefic planets situated in both [the ascendant and the seventh house].
Furthermore, when there is a piercing by malefics in two or three asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā according to the *kūrma-cakra*, all [are destroyed].
The regions beginning with the navel perish in due order when there is a piercing (vedha) in Kṛttikā,
Puṣya, Revatī, and Punarvasu, respectively; this piercing occurs among the castes,
beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, affecting oil, vessels, liquids, and grain.

Quadrupeds such as elephants and horses—everything becomes highly valuable where a malefic planet is situated. When there is a conjunction with a malefic configuration (*krūravedha*) and the occurrence of a secondary affliction (*upagraha*), for that person there is death, without a doubt, either from disease or even in battle. [Calculated] from the Sun.
The fifth fire-altar (dhiṣṇya) is to be known by the name Vidyunmukha;
the eighth is declared to be Śūla, and the fourteenth is Sannipāta.
One should know the eighteenth to be Ketu, Ulkā would be the twenty-first, and [the next] is the twenty-second.

In the twenty-third *kalpa*, Vajraka; and in the twenty-fourth, Nirghāta—these eight secondary planets (*upagraha*) are said to always cause obstacles during departures and in all undertakings. [The four types of planetary positions are] Janmabha, Karma, Ādhāna, and Vaināśa.
This group of eight asterisms (dhiṣṇya) is collective, pertaining to the Saṅgha, and common to all people.

Having understood the piercing (vedha) of the king by birth, region, and consecration—these being the nine bases—one should declare the results, both auspicious and inauspicious, through the gentle and cruel planets. [The first is] the birth asterism (janmabha).
The tenth birth-star is designated as *karman* (action);

likewise, the twenty-first is *ādhāna* (foundation), and the twenty-third is *vināśaka* (destructive). The eighteenth star is named *sāmudāyika* (collective), and the star known as *sāṅghātika* (congregational) should also be understood.

Indeed, it is the sixteenth [house] alone. For the body, the collection of kingdoms, that which is designated by caste, name, and wealth, the country, the teaching, the asterism, the kingdom-asterism, and the consecration—these are all [determined by this]. If the birth-asterism (janmabha) is pierced, there will be death; if the action-asterism (karmabha), there is indeed affliction; and if the conception-asterism (ādhānabha), there is exile.

If there is a break in the *varṇa*, there will be destruction; likewise, if there is a break in the *sāmudāyika*, there is undesirable loss; if there is a break in the *jāti*, there will be the ruin of the family;
if there is a break in the *abhiṣeka*, there will be imprisonment; and if there is a break in the *deśa*, there is the collapse of the country. A cruel person is better [than this].
From auspicious [planets], there is auspiciousness; when conjoined with malefic planets, death occurs and not otherwise.
There is fear, defeat, and slaughter; death conjoined with both [fear and] defeat results in death.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which was stated in the *Brahmajāmalatantra* regarding the auspicious and inauspicious results arising from the piercing of planets within the diagram of eighty-one squares (*ekāśītipada-cakra*). When there is a conflict or piercing by one or more malefic planets, one obtains the result according to the piercing; [this applies to] the lunar day (*tithi*) and the lunar mansion (*dhiṣṇya*).

The vowels, the zodiac signs, and the letters are indeed the fifth; on whichever day [a letter] is pierced from the Moon, on that day shall be the auspicious or inauspicious result. Place, time, and the commodity—these three must be considered by the wise at all times in determining value. Piercings are to be examined at every moment.

Place is said to be threefold: the country (*deśa*), the region (*maṇḍala*), and the location (*sthāna*). Time is also described as threefold: the year, the month, and the day. Furthermore, substance is considered to be threefold: the element (*dhātu*), the root (*mūla*), and the life-force (*jīva*). Now, I shall explain this triad of triads.

The lords of the [twelve] places are the planets beginning with the Sun; the lords of the regions (deśeśas) are Rāhu, Saturn, and Jupiter; furthermore, the lords of the [nine] divisions (maṇḍala) are Ketu, the Sun, and Venus; the lords of the stations (sthāna) are the Moon, Mars, and Mercury;
the lords of the year are Rāhu, Ketu, Saturn, and Jupiter; furthermore, the lords of the month are Mars, the Sun, and Venus.

The Moon is to be known as the lord of the day (the Sun). The lords of the elements (dhātus) are Saturn, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and Mars; the lords of the planets (jñas) are Mercury, the Moon, and Jupiter; and the lords of the roots (mūlas) are Ketu, Venus, and the Sun—these are the planets that are lords of merchandise. Rāhu, Ketu, the Sun, Jupiter, and Mars are considered male planets; the female planets are [Venus and the Moon].
Venus and Mercury are white and cool-rayed; the neuter planets are Saturn and Jupiter. Venus and the Moon are lords of the white color;

Mars and the Sun are lords of the red color. Mercury and Jupiter are yellow; Rāhu, Ketu, and Saturn are considered black. Among the planets, whichever one has a retrograde rising (vakrodaya) is more powerful at the time of its rising.
That very planet is considered the sole lord of its own sign, as well as of the country and other factors.

A planet possesses full strength when it is in its own domicile and in retrograde motion. When another planet is situated ahead of or behind it, the strength is determined by the *trairāśika* (proportional) method. Furthermore, strength is full when the planet is in its exaltation and diminishes when situated in its debilitation degree.

The strength within the interval should be understood by the wise through the rule of three proportions (*trairāśika*). In this manner, the piercing (*vedha*) of the lords of the houses and other positions should be determined for each house. Friends, enemies, and neutrals must be considered with great care; [one should consider] their own friends, equals, and enemies.

Regarding the piercing (vedha) based on position and other factors in sequence: a benefic planet bestows auspicious results in proportion to four, three, two, or one quarter; likewise, a malefic planet produces inauspicious results by one, two, three, or four quarters. A planet that pierces, seeing with its full aspect, [bestows results] by that quarter.

The planet is the fruit; it should be understood that it produces results otherwise than [normally] according to its aspect. Within the circle of signs beginning with Aries for the vowels, syllables, and signs, that piercing (vedha) of the vowels and syllables is also considered to occur by virtue of the planet's aspect. The vowels and syllables are as stated in one's own wheel for the piercing of the lunar days (tithi).

Regarding the *pīḍakas*: the results arising from aspects are determined by the lunar day (*tithi*), the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), and the planet itself according to its own aspect. Whether malefic or benefic, Venus is a piercing planet on the piercing lunar day (*vedhyatithi*). It bestows its full result, yet its strength during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is equal to that of the planet [it aspects]. The degrees of the planet should be understood as complete.

The aspect is always [considered] by the wise. Furthermore, in a piercing (vedha) devoid of aspect, there would be no good or bad result whatsoever. A benefic planet, piercing while viewing with a full aspect within the fivefold [categories] such as color and so on, shall bestow five *viṃśopaka* points; a malefic shall bestow four.

In whatever place and for whatever duration the piercing (*vedha*) occurs regarding the color and other attributes of the target, the aspect (*dṛṣṭi*) should be declared by the wise through inference based on those *viṃśopaka* units. Thus, wherever auspicious or inauspicious results arise according to these *viṃśopaka*s, their nature should be understood through this very method.
Auspicious and inauspicious; the calculation of one-twentieth of the current price applies to them respectively.
One should bestow the auspicious and inauspicious results derived from the current price.
Wherever there is a [malefic] aspect, there is the destruction of the country, affliction of the people, death, and likewise the slaughter of living beings.

In that region, there will clearly be a severe famine within the kingdom; where trees produce fruit and flowers even out of season, and where the eating of the flesh of one's own kind occurs, there will be a terrible famine. There, an invasion by a foreign army and famine shall prevail within its own realm during the [wrong] season.

Where there is a reversal, famine shall occur in that region; earthquakes, the falling of dust, and the falling of blood shall arise. Even in a land endowed with every happiness, there will be fear due to piercing.
Just as a lamp illuminates everything within a house from all sides, so it is for this [region].
The wheel that protects from all sides, which illuminates primordial wisdom.
Its explanation—the procedure and the convention—is now stated: "going upwards" (*ūrdhvaga*).
Having laid down ten lines in the order from east to west, one should again lay down ten lines there in the order from north to south. By this, eighty-one squares are formed.

There, in that grid, one should write the vowels beginning with *a* by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*) in the corner-cells starting from the northeast (*īśāna*): first in the northeast corner, then in the southeast, then in the southwest, and then in the northwest; thus, they should be written four times around, following the sequence of seven groups for each of the cardinal directions starting from the east.

One should write the twenty-eight lunar mansions, beginning with Kṛttikā, in the first row in the four directions; below that row, one should write the twenty syllables beginning with *ava* and *ka*; and below that row, one should write the twelve zodiac signs, beginning with Taurus (*vṛṣa*).

In the remaining five squares, one should write the five lunar days beginning with Nandā. Therein, in the northeast (Īśāna), one should write the four vowels a, u, ḷ, and o; in the southeast (Āgneya), the four vowels ā, ī, ḹ, and au; in the southwest (Nairṛta), the four vowels i, ṛ, e, and aṃ; and in the northwest (Vāyavya), the four vowels ī, ṝ, ai, and aḥ.

Then, in the eastern direction, one should write the seven lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā in the first row; in the second row, [the letters] ava-ka-ha-ḍa; and in the third row, [the signs] Vṛṣa, Mithuna, and Karkaṭa.
Below that square, one should also write the lunar days (tithis) beginning with Nandā. Then, in the southern direction, as before.

Following the sequence of rows, one should write the signs beginning with Aries (meṣa) up to Pisces (mīna), as well as the *bhadrā* [tithis] starting from Leo, Virgo, and Libra. In the western direction, as before, one should place the Sun and Mars in the square of Nandā, the Moon and Mercury in the square of Bhadrā, and Jupiter in the square of Jayā.
One should write Śukra in an empty house and Śani in a full house.
To understand the strength of the planets, he states their positions of exaltation and debilitation, beginning with "Aries for the Sun," and so forth.
Since the consideration of all auspicious and inauspicious matters indeed depends upon the planets, he describes the malefic and benefic nature of the planets.

Regarding the phrase "Śanyarka": Saturn (Śani), the Sun (Arka), Rāhu, Ketu, and Mars (Maṅgala) are malefic (krūra); Mercury (Budha), Jupiter (Guru), and Venus (Śukra) are benefic (śubha). However, Mercury joined with a malefic is considered evil. Likewise, the waning Moon (kṣīṇacandra) is considered diminished (kṣīṇa) according to the science of astrology (jyotiṣa), from the latter half of the eighth day of the dark fortnight onwards.

"The moon wanes for as long as the eighth day of the bright fortnight; otherwise, the moon becomes full. He states the purpose of this explanation with the words "in which," etc.: in whichever wheel [the moon resides], the lunar mansion upon which the planets depend proceeds together with that mansion in a counter-clockwise direction—left, front, and right.

There would be a triple piercing (vedha). In the lunar mansion occupied by the planet that has already passed through it, the portion yet to be traversed (*bhogya*) precedes; that which follows the lunar mansion is "traversed" (*ākānta*), meaning it is presided over by the planet. The meaning is that no ritual action should be performed therein.
He describes the aspect of vision (dṛṣṭiphala) as follows: when the five planets beginning with Mars are moving retrograde (vakragāmin), a rightward vision (dakṣiṇā dṛṣṭi) is to be understood;

here, the result of a rightward piercing (dakṣiṇavedha) is to be declared. When they are moving direct (śīghragāmin), there is a leftward vision (vāmadṛṣṭi), and the result of a leftward piercing (vāmavedha) is to be declared.

In the case of mean motion (madhyacāra) and natural motion (prakṛtagati), the aspect (dṛṣṭi) should be known as "facing" (sammukha) when [the planet] is in front; in that case, the result of a direct piercing (sammukhavedha) is to be declared. He states the period of retrograde, swift, and other motions of the planets with the words "joined with the sun" (sūryayukta); [meaning] together with the sun.
Planets situated in a single zodiacal sign become "set" (asta) at specific degrees. And it is said in the *Jyotiṣatattva*:

"When joined with the sun, they have gone to the next sign and are thus 'risen' (udita). When the sun is in the second [sign] from the sign occupied by the planet—that is, when the sun has reached the sign immediately following the one occupied by the planet—the planets are 'swift' (śīghra)."

They become swift-moving. Thus, in due order, when the Sun is situated in the third sign, the planets have equal movements as they naturally do. When the Sun is in the fourth [sign], they become slow, with movements equal to the previous full circle. Likewise when the Sun is in the fifth sign...

When the Sun is in the seventh or eighth house, the planets move in extreme retrograde motion. Likewise, when the Sun is in the ninth or tenth house, the planets attain their natural, non-retrograde motion. When the Sun is in the eleventh or twelfth house, the planets move with swiftness.
...they come to be. This retrograde, swift, and other such motions belong only to the five beginning with Mars (*maṅgala*). Regarding the specific motion of the others, he says: "Rāhu and Ketu.
Because Rāhu, Ketu, the Moon, and the Sun share a single motion, they always possess three aspects.
The gaze is always directed to the left, right, and center. Regarding the term "cruel" and so forth:
malefic planets, when in retrograde motion, become exceedingly cruel; likewise, benefic planets, when retrograde, become exceedingly auspicious. And thus it is said of those two:

In the case of both auspicious and inauspicious retrograde motions, the result is auspicious or contrary according to the sequence of their aspects. However, whether moving in their natural course or retrograde, when situated in their own signs or their own nature, auspicious planets (saumya) become exceedingly auspicious in both ways.

Thus, even though they are swift-moving, the gentle and cruel planets become auspicious when the four syllables *ka-pa-bha-da* are pierced; likewise, the triad *gha-ṅa-ch*, the triad *ṣa-ṇa-ṭha*, the triad *dha-pha-ḍa*, and the triad *tha-jha-ña*.

It becomes pierced in due order. Thus, when the letter *gha* is pierced, the three letters *gha*, *ṅa*, and *cha* become pierced. Likewise, when the letter *pa* is pierced, the three letters *ṣa*, *ṇa*, and *ṭha*; when the letter *bha* is pierced, the three letters *dha*, *pha*, and *ḍa*; and when the letter *da* is pierced—

When the three letters *tha*, *jha*, and *ña* are pierced in sequence, and when the lunar mansion Ārdrā is pierced, the four letters *ka*, *gha*, *ṅa*, and *cha* are pierced. Likewise, when the lunar mansion Hasta is pierced, the four syllables *pa*, *ṣa*, *ṇa*, and *ṭha* [are pierced].
When the *pūrvāṣāḍhā* lunar mansion is pierced, the four letters *bha*, *dha*, *pha*, and *ḍa* are pierced;

when the *uttarabhādra* lunar mansion is pierced, the four letters *da*, *tha*, *dha*, and *ña* are pierced respectively. These two [groups of letters] are those mentioned in the statement beginning with "when the sun," ending in the same case-ending.

There are two vowels; between them, when one is pierced by auspicious or inauspicious planets, the other is also pierced. Likewise, when one of the two, the anusvāra or the visarga, is pierced, the other is also pierced.

Regarding "in a corner" (koṇastha): when a planet is situated in the final quarter of one and the first quarter of another among the pairs of asterisms located in the corners— namely, Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā, Aśleṣā and Maghā, Viśākhā and Anurādhā, or Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā.

In each of the four vowels beginning with *a*, there occurs the piercing (*vedha*) of the full moon, the fifth day, the tenth day, the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), and the new moon (*amāvasyā*). For example,
if a planet is situated in the final quarter of Bharaṇī and the first quarter of Kṛttikā, then [the piercing occurs].
p. 921) The four vowels beginning with *a* are pierced together with the full lunar day (*pūrṇātithi*).

This should be understood to apply likewise to the other corners as well. Regarding "one," etc.: in the case of a piercing by one malefic, there is agitation; in a double piercing, fear; in a triple piercing, loss; in a quadruple piercing, disease; and in a quintuple piercing, [death].

Death. Regarding the passage beginning with "Ṛkṣa" and so forth: when a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is pierced by a malefic planet (*pāpagraha*), there is "confusion," which means a derangement of the intellect. The rest is easy to understand. He states a specific rule regarding battle: "In the case of one [planet]" and so forth;
if the letters of the name and so on are pierced by one malefic planet, there is fear in battle; by two [malefics], [there is greater danger].
The meaning is that with three [planets] there is loss of wealth, and with four there is death.
He states the results of the auspicious planets as follows: "arketyādi" (beginning with the Sun), etc.; "bhṛgusutaḥ" is Venus, "maṅgalaḥ" is Mars, and "sauriḥ" is Saturn.
"Candret yādi" (beginning with the Moon), etc.: if the Moon is waning, then there is an inauspicious result;
when the Moon is full, then there is an auspicious result—it bestows auspicious results in every respect.

The strength of the planets is such that their results will be accordingly; thus he demonstrates their strength with the verse beginning "In their own sign" (*svakṣetre*), which is easy to understand. Furthermore, this positional strength (*sthānabala*) of both benefic and malefic planets is equal; however, the results should be understood as being the reverse. When—
When a malefic planet possesses full strength, its result is then slow; when a benefic planet possesses full strength, it is then exceedingly auspicious. "Tithi," etc. [refers to the following].

The meaning is that whichever lunar day (*tithi*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), or ninth-part (*navāṃśaka*) is pierced by a malefic planet, as well as whichever lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is pierced, those must be avoided;

no auspicious rite should be performed therein. Regarding the result of such piercing, he says "does not prosper" and so forth, which is easy to understand. If a king constructs a fortress upon a pierced lunar mansion or similar [inauspicious] position...
The meaning is that "khaṇḍi" refers to fragmentation; its breaking occurs, which is the intended sense.
One who acts as a "kaviḍāka" (a maker of confusion) is well known; his entry takes place into a fortress constructed according to the directions of the piercing constellations (*biddhanakṣatra*).
Thus, when that enclosure is made there, it results in the slaughter of the warriors. But here—

It should also be inferred that if the first letter of the name of a member of the army, or of a person besieged, or of a fortress and so forth, is pierced by a malefic planet, [the same result follows]. "Where" means that whichever direction—east and so on—in which the Sun is situated within three signs starting from Taurus, that direction is to be known as set; this is the meaning. The remainder...

The directions arise as follows: "Īśāna" [refers to] the vowels situated in the northeastern direction—namely the four forms *a*, *u*, *ḷ*, and *o*. They should be known as being located in the east; when that [direction] has set, they too should be known as having set. The same applies elsewhere regarding the constellations (*nakṣatras*).

(p. 922) In whichever direction the Sun is situated through the sequence of traversing the three signs (*rāśi*), all the asterisms (*nakṣatra*), colors, signs, lunar days (*tithi*), and days of the week (*vāra*) located therein become eclipsed. He states the result of that in the verse beginning with "nakṣatra": it is easy to understand. Regarding "yātrā" [etc.]: auspicious matters such as journeys, and inauspicious matters such as death.

The meaning is that men should not perform [the rite] facing the eight directions. Regarding the phrase "in the direction of the setting" (astāśāyām): that man whose name-syllable is situated in the direction of the setting should be known as one who is as if struck by fate. The two hands are easy to understand. Regarding "attainment of the desired object at the feet" in the question: this refers to the ascendant at the time of the query (praśnalagna).
If it is struck by an inauspicious [planet], then it is inauspicious; if it is struck by a auspicious [planet], then it is auspicious;
if it is struck by both auspicious and inauspicious [planets], then it is mixed. "Struck by planets," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should declare whatever result arises according to the planetary aspects, as well as the results produced by the nature [of the planets], for an ascendant afflicted by a planet whose form consists of the three types—movable, fixed, or dual.
This is the intended sense: whichever ascendant is [placed] in this wheel...

If [a planet] is afflicted by another planet, its results should be declared according to the aspect it casts from a quadrant (kendragata). However, if that planet is an evil one other than its own [lord], then the failure of the undertaking should be predicted; if it is auspicious, then [success].
If the accomplishment of the matter is mixed, then a mixed result should be declared.

Regarding the designations "movable" (*cara*) and so forth, it is stated in the *Dīpikā*: "These signs, Aries and the rest, are taught in succession as having the names 'movable,' 'fixed' (*sthira*), and 'dual-natured' (*dvirātmaka*). As for the passage beginning with "by the malefics" (*krūraiḥ*), etc.:

If one's complexion and the other five factors, as well as the mandala and so forth, are afflicted by malefic planets through either the fifth or the reverse order, then that [person] perishes; "mandala" refers to the country.
A *nagara* is a place where a king resides; a *durga* is a fortress such as a citadel; a *devālaya* is well known;

a *pura* is a capital city marked with the name of a king. Regarding the phrase "Kṛttikā and so forth," in the *kūrmacakra*, the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are divided into groups of three each, constituting the limbs in a sequence of nine parts.

These are the established rules. In that regard, if a triad of lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā is afflicted by malefic planets (*krūra-biddha*), the regions situated at the navel perish; the same applies elsewhere. This is the intended meaning: if, in both the tortoise diagram (*kūrma-cakra*) and the all-auspicious diagram (*sarvatobhadra-cakra*), there should be a lunar mansion afflicted by malefics, then [the corresponding region perishes].
The regions marked by those constellations perish and become greatly afflicted. If [the moon] is pierced in Ekacakra, then they are slightly afflicted. Regarding Kṛttikā:
when Kṛttikā is pierced, a Brāhmaṇa is pierced; likewise, when Puṣya is pierced, a Kṣatriya is pierced.

A Vaiśya [is born] under Revatī, and a Śūdra under Punarvasu. In that regard, if there is a piercing by a benefic planet, the result is auspicious; if by a malefic, it is inauspicious; and if by a mixed one, the fruit is mixed. According to another opinion, however, [the result is determined] even by piercing from other [asterisms], as Varāhamihira said: "The three Pūrvās together with Kṛttikā [belong] to the first-born [castes]..."
The constellations Uttara-phalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarā-bhādrapadā, along with Revatī, Anurādhā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī, are for the farmers.
The constellations Ārdrā, Hasta, Abhijit, and Aśvinī, they declare to be for the merchants. Mūla, Aśvinī, Svātī, and Śatabhiṣaj—these are for the thieves.

The dignity of the fierce-born [caste] lies in their sovereignty. The Moon, Citrā, and the asterisms presided over by the Vasus, having attained the status of masters over those who serve them; likewise, Serpent, Viśākhā, Śravaṇa, and Ārdrā are indicated as belonging even to the Cāṇḍāla-born. Regarding "equality" (taulya): equality...
Merchandise refers to goods fit for barter, such as gems, liquids, ghee, oil, and so forth. Grain refers to crops;

"high value" means being more expensive, while "low value" means being cheaper—this is the meaning. When there is a benefic *vedha* (piercing), there is an abundance of food. "Malefic *vedha*" is easy to understand. He now states the *upagraha* (secondary conjunction): "from the sign of the Sun," and so on.

This is easy to understand. Regarding the asterism of the channels (*nāḍī-nakṣatra*), he says: "In birth... and so forth. These six asterisms are to be known as common to all people. The asterism of the caste (*jāti-bha*) has already been mentioned. The asterism of the country (*deśa-bha*) is to be known through the first syllable of the country's name in the *Śatapadacakra*. In whichever asterism...

The nakṣatra under which a king’s consecration takes place is called the *abhiṣeka-bha* (consecration asterism). Regarding that, the results of malefic piercing have been explained; however, auspicious results are to be declared [if the piercing is by benefics]. As for the "tithi," on whichever day there is a piercing—whether auspicious or inauspicious—it is pierced by the moon's piercing among the five [categories] beginning with the lunar day (*tithi*).
Wherever and whenever there is a piercing by the moon (candravedha), the predicted result for that [planet] should be declared.

When the conjunction with the moon occurs during the fivefold period beginning with the lunar day (tithi) and so forth, then the aforementioned result arising from the planet on that day should be declared. Regarding "the place": merchandise refers to goods for sale.
"Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the elements from gold down to earth. "Root" (*mūla*) refers to those from trees down to shrubs.

"Living being" (*jīva*) refers to those from humans down to insects. Regarding "region" (*deśa*) and so forth: Rāhu, Śani, and Bṛhaspati are the vowels of the regions; Ketu, Āditya (the Sun), and Śukra are the lords of the mandalas; and Candra (the Moon) and Budha are [the lords of] the lunar mandala.
The lords of the houses are as follows: Rāhu, Ketu, Śani, and Bṛhaspati are the lords of the year;
Ravi, Bhauma, Budha, and Śukra are the lords of the months; Candra is the lord of the day;
Śani, Rāhu, and Kuja are the lords of the elements (dhātus); and Budha, Candra, and Bṛhaspati are the lords of the living beings (jīvas).

The lords of the planets are Ravi (the Sun), Ketu, Śukra (Venus), and Āmūleśa (Rāhu). Rāhu, Ketu, Soma (the Moon), Jīva (Jupiter), and Maṅgala (Mars) are the male planets (*puruṣādhipāḥ*). Śukra and Candra are the female planets (*strīgrahau*). Śani (Saturn) and Budha (Mercury) are the neuter planets (*napuṃsakau*).
Regarding the term "in the house" (*gṛhe*): it means in one's own house, that is, in one's own zodiac sign (*svasvarāśau*), such as the Sun in Leo, and so forth.

When the degrees traversed in retrograde motion are in the opposite direction, [the planet is strong] in its own domicile (*svaharmya*) or its own house (*svagṛha*), as well as in the houses preceding and following it; this is its full strength, known as the *trairāśika* (triangular) strength. "High" (*ucca*) refers to half [of the maximum distance]. In the interval between the high and low points, [strength is determined] by proportion according to the *trairāśika* rule.
The strength should be understood [as follows]. Regarding the increase: for every thirty-minute division (triṃśāṃśaka) from the limit of the exaltation, there is a loss of ten seconds (vikalā) each;
likewise, for every thirty-minute division from the limit of the fall (nīca), there is a loss of ten seconds each.

"Vṛddhi" (increase) and "evam" (thus): the meaning is that one should consider the piercing (*vedha*) with respect to each respective domain of authority, such as the regions and so forth. In this manner, regarding the house (*gṛha*), one must reflect upon which planets are piercers, which are friends, which are enemies, and which are neutral. For example, the Sun is the lord of the mandala.

Its friends are the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter; if the mandala is pierced by them, then there is an auspicious result. Mercury (Saumya) is its friend, so [piercing] by it is not prohibited; Saturn and Venus are its enemies, so piercing by them yields contrary results. This should be understood in the same way for others as well. Regarding "one's own friend":

Regarding the country and other factors, such as the country-mandala and trade, a benefic planet bestows auspicious results through its aspect upon oneself, one's friend, an equal, and an enemy, by means of four, three, two, and one-quarter [of its full strength] respectively.
Likewise, in the case of an aspect upon oneself, the result is full; upon a friend, it is reduced by one quarter; and upon an equal, it is half.
"In the case of piercing by an enemy [planet], the fruit is one-quarter," it is said. A malefic planet bestows adverse results;

likewise, in the case of piercing by its own [sign], the fruit is one-quarter; in piercing by a friend's [sign], half the fruit; in piercing by a neutral [sign], three-quarters less one-quarter (i.e., three-eighths);
and in piercing by an enemy, the full [fruit]. "Pierced" means looking at the pierced sign with a full aspect.
Whenever a letter of a particular sign is pierced, it then produces its result by a quarter [of its full effect],
according to the aspect; here the sequence is reversed,
such that here the result of the *kapāla* (half) is produced by a full aspect, and the full result by a quarter aspect, while the half-result is produced by a half-aspect.
Three quarters [are seen] by looking at three quarters; half [is seen] by looking at... [he] says "varṇa" (color).

Among the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries, for those whose initial letters are a, i, u, e, and o, the Sun or Mercury— by virtue of the arrangement of these letters— bestows the fruit of piercing (vedha) upon the signs situated in their respective degrees according to this sequence, through the influence of planetary aspects.

That piercing (vedha) is also considered to be by color and so forth; wherever there is a piercing by a degree (aṃśaka), there is also a piercing by the color and vowel (svara) of its corresponding ninth-part (navāṃśa). In that case as well, the result [is determined] by the aspect of the planet upon the zodiacal sign of the pierced ninth-part. This refers to "vowel and color" (svaravarṇa).

p. 925) Among these, those which are the letters (varṇas) are said to be born from the names as described in the Svaracakra; they are declared in one's own cakra according to the name. For example, for a name beginning with the letter *ka*, the letter is *ka* and the vowel is *a*. In this way, each has its own respective letters; when pierced by malefic planets, such [letters] are afflictors, as are those pierced by lunar days (tithi-vedha).

It is indeed a *pīḍakā*. Likewise, regarding the lunar day (*tithi*), one should understand the results arising from aspects—whether auspicious or inauspicious—due to the aspecting by benefic or malefic planets upon whichever sign (*rāśi*) and whichever color [corresponds to that day], according to the sequence of their own aspect or quarter-aspect (*pādadṛṣṭi*). Regarding "inauspicious": whether it be a malefic planet or a benefic planet, in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*)...
When performing the *tithi-vedha* (piercing by lunar day), it bestows its entire fruit as calculated through aspect;

however, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), it bestows only half of that. Regarding the word "planet" (*kheṭa*): scholars should always consider the aspect to be full when the planet is at its degrees (*aṃśaka*), because if there is no aspect in the piercing, [the result is nullified].
The construction [of the sentence] contains a logical reason: "there would not be even the slightest fruit, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

Regarding the term *saumya*: when the fivefold set consisting of color (*varṇa*), vowel (*svara*), asterism (*ṛkṣa*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), and lunar day (*tithi*) has been thus pierced (*viddha*), the planet is the piercer (*vedhaka*).

It bestows auspicious or inauspicious results. Regarding "Saumya": looking with a full vision at the five [categories] beginning with color in the directions starting from the east of the Sarvatobhadra-cakra, one should pierce twenty-five units (upakās), counting the fallen foot.
A benefic planet bestows a result known as five twenty-fifths (pañcapañcaviṃśopaka).
A malefic planet bestows a result of twenty-four twenty-fifths (caturviṃśopaka) for every quarter (pāda).
In the triad of signs beginning with Taurus, the letters are the *avadahaḍā* vowels, and the constellations begin with Kṛttikā.
In the triad beginning with Leo, the letters are *ma*, *ṭa*, *pa*, *ba*, and *bha*; the seven asterisms beginning with Maghā correspond.
In the triad beginning with Scorpio, the letters are *ṇa*, *ṣa*, *bha*, *ja*, and *sa*; the seven asterisms beginning with Anurādhā correspond.
In the triad beginning with Aquarius, the letters are *ga*, *śa*, *da*, *ca*, and *la*; the seven asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā correspond. Thus it is.
The constellations (nakṣatras) and the colors of the zodiac signs (rāśis) should be known; if those planets aspect them with a quarter-aspect (pādadṛṣṭi),
one should calculate five viṃśopas for each quarter-aspect by means of benefic planets.
"By the wise, these should be known as measured by the inauspicious [planets] through the aspect of the feet. Regarding "piercing" (vedha):

In the piercing (vedha) of the five [factors] beginning with color (varṇa), as well as in the piercing of the position (sthāna-vedha), the wise should state the *viṃśopaka* values by inference from whatever strength of aspect (*dṛṣṭi-bala*) exists and whatever aspect is present. "In this manner" means:
in this way, whether in the case of an inauspicious or a auspicious planet, according to the distinctions in the strength of aspects and so forth.
Viṃśopakas occur according to the sequence of their arrangement; the viṃśopakas of benefic planets (p.
926) should be held together in one place, and the viṃśopakas of malefic planets should be held in another. Among these, whichever are less than the others should be subtracted from the greater.

These are to be purified. Whatever remains visible therein should be marked as either auspicious or inauspicious, and its result declared. The meaning of the phrase "wherever there is such-and-such a vision" is explained in detail below.
In a piercing (vedha) between the second and tenth houses, there are twenty-five points (pañcaviṃśopaka); likewise in a piercing between the ninth and fifth houses.
Ten *viṃśopaka*s [are assigned] when [a planet is] in the fourth or eighth house; fifteen each when in the third or ninth;
and twenty when in the seventh. Thus it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* regarding aspects:
"A one-quarter aspect occurs in the tenth and third houses; a half-aspect occurs in the ninth and fifth."
There is a quarter-look at two signs, a full look at four and eight, and likewise a full look at seven equal [signs].
For all malefic planets, sixteen *viṃśopaka*s are produced through a full look, as four *viṃśopaka*s arise for each quarter-increment of aspect. Thus it is.
In due order, wherever there are auspicious or inauspicious *viṃśopaka*s,

one should write down the auspicious planetary *viṃśopaka*s in one place and the *viṃśopaka*s of cruel planets belonging to the enemy's army in another; then, whichever [total] falls upon a particular spot, that [result] pertains to that spot.
Having caused [the others] to fall, if two remain belonging to a benefic planet, then by that inference the result is auspicious;
if they belong to a malefic planet, then the result is inauspicious.
"Varttamāna," and so forth: among those commodities for sale,
regarding the price of present goods such as grain and the like,
according to the previously mentioned method, by means of the distinctions of their names, asterisms (*nakṣatra*), vowels, consonants, lunar days (*tithi*), and zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
The calculation of twentieth-parts (viṃśāṃśa) should be performed until their mutual subtraction results in zero.

Then, by calculating the value based on the remaining portion of the twentieth-parts: if only one remains among the benefic planets and so forth, the price is reduced by twenty parts; if two remain, [the reduction is] two parts.

[This applies] when [the total] is decreasing. In the same way, it should be considered when [the total] is increasing. Wherever the fivefold set beginning with color (varṇa) for a country and so forth is added to the remainder of the auspicious and malefic *viṃśopaka*s in this sequence—increasing by one, two, three, and so on, up to twenty parts in the middle.
The price alone becomes higher, and both auspicious and inauspicious results are produced.

Thus, wherever there is an initial piercing by a malefic planet, some inauspicious object must be considered even because of that piercing. Wherever the fivefold qualities—such as color and so forth—of a region and the like are pierced by an auspicious [planet] alone, [the result is favorable].

In that case, it is extremely auspicious; where there is merely evil, it is extremely inauspicious. Where there is the piercing of a *bhūta*, one should calculate *viṃśopaka*s according to the division of aspects (*dṛṣṭibheda*).
From the auspicious and inauspicious *viṃśopaka*s, the auspicious or inauspicious result should be declared. (p. 927)

Regarding "the country" (*deśa*) and so forth: in whatever country there is a piercing by a malefic planet, if its aspect becomes intensified according to the method described, that country's destruction occurs. Likewise, in that country, there will be affliction for the subjects and various calamities; there will be the destruction of the king and famine throughout the realm.

Wherever there is affliction by malefic planets in the *kūrmacakra* or even in the *sarvatobhadra*, the destruction of that region and so forth, as well as results such as the oppression of the subjects, will inevitably occur.
He demonstrates all these omens [with the words] beginning with "even at an improper time" (*akāle’pi*), etc., regarding whichever region and so forth.
When flowers, fruits, or the like appear on trees at a time other than their natural season—that is, at an improper time—there one consumes the flesh of one's own kind;
a human consumes human flesh, and likewise for those of other species as well; therein lies the Raurava hell.

Wherever there is a terrifying famine, there also occurs the arrival of a foreign army. Even in a land with a good king—that is, one with a virtuous ruler—there may be famine. Regarding the phrase "of the season" and so forth:
in whatever region there is a reversal of the seasons, that is, an abnormal order.

Riddles and the like, which are appropriate for the month of Pauṣa and so forth, occur during the summer and other seasons, just as heat occurs during the cool season in the common order of things, or cold during the summer. Furthermore, in that case, the reversal of the cause, like the reversal of the property (*dharma*), is difficult to discern; such is the case with earthquakes.

And so forth. Due to piercing [the diagram] in a location endowed with all comforts, there arise long-lasting earthquakes caused by malefic planets, the falling of dust, a rain of soil, or a rain of blood. "Just as a lamp":
this Sarvatobhadra-cakra is likewise an illuminator of knowledge, just like a lamp.
It illuminates the interior of the house. Just as the knowledge of objects situated within a house arises by means of the light of a lamp, so too, from this Sarvatobhadra-cakra,
knowledge regarding all objects arises.
I shall describe the wheel of one hundred squares, which arises from the asterisms, signs, and degrees.
The asterisms, signs, and degrees are to be known from the initial letter of the name.
A wise person should draw lines running horizontally and vertically, numbering eleven (the number of Rudras). Thus it is produced.

There is no doubt that there are one hundred squares; having placed Avakahaḍa and the others in the directions starting from the northeast (rudra-dig) in sequence, one should apply five pure letters at a time in due order. By combining each with the five vowels, make each letter fivefold.

One should place three consonants each in the *ku*, *pu*, *bhu*, and *du* positions. In the *stambhana* [rite], when it is associated with the *raudra* [direction] and *īśāna*, there should be *k*, *gh*, and *ṅ*. In the *stambhana* [rite] known as *haste* and *āgneya*, there should be *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, and *ṭha*. In the *stambhana* [rite], there should be *bh*, *u*, *dh*, *pha*, and *ḍha*.
In Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Nairṛta (Svātī) there is *hatha*; in Vāyavya (Anurādhā) and Bhādra (Pūrvabhādrapadā) and Uttara (Uttarabhādrapadā), there is *jhañā*.
Thus, the four pillars (*stambha*) should be known by those learned in the science of vowels.
The lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā each consist of four syllables; including Abhijit, there are one hundred and one [syllables] in the Śaka [system].

Twelve more [verses follow]: "Whichever planet—whether malefic or benefic—is situated in the square of a lunar mansion's degrees, auspicious results are to be known from its aspect by benefic planets, and inauspicious results from malefic planets. With mixed planets, the result there is mixed; through non-aspecting (nirvedha), the result is neither auspicious nor inauspicious. As it has been said:
In the Sarvatobhadra [diagram], one should likewise consider here all the auspicious and inauspicious results arising from the piercing (vedha) by planets and secondary planets (upagrahas).

The meaning of this is as follows: I shall describe a hundred-square grid diagram (*koṣṭhacakra*). Of what nature is it? It is "originating from the syllables of the lunar mansion divisions" (*ṛkṣāṃśākṣarasambhava*); that is, its origin is from those syllables which will be described later, corresponding to the portions (*aṃśāḥ*) of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*), namely the *pādas*.

"Of which that [is the name]" means that it is composed of those respective syllables. The portion relating to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is to be known by means of the initial letter of the name. He describes the arrangement of the wheel with the words "transverse," and so forth.
The number of Rudras is eleven; the lines run both transversely and upwards.
