One should write eleven [syllables] in the order from east to west, and likewise eleven in the order from south to north. Starting from the northeast corner,
in the first five squares of the eastern row, one should write the five syllables *ava*, *ka*, *ha*, *ḍa*, and *e*.
One should apply and write [the syllables] joined with only the pure vowel *a*:
thus, beginning from the southeast corner, in the five squares of the southern, western, and northern rows, [one writes] *ma ṭa pa ra ta iti*, *la ya bha ja sva iti*, and *ga śa da ca la iti*.

One should write the five vowels in sequence: *a-i-u-e-o*. By means of this conjunction of the five vowels, the written syllables constitute the five elements (*pañcadhātu*). The intended meaning is that one should write them in successive rows below one another as *a-i-u-e-o* and *va-vi-ve-vo*. In the middle of what has been written, in the positions of *ku-pu-bhu-du-stha*, there are three others.

"One should make three syllables" means one should write them. Thus, on the pillar situated in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa) under the asterism Ārdrā, one writes the four letters *k-u-gh-a-cha*; likewise, on the pillar in the southeast corner (agnikoṇa) under the asterism Hasta, one writes the four letters *p-u-ṣ-a-ṇa-ṭha*. On the pillar in the southwest corner (nairṛtakoṇa)...

In the *pūrvāṣāḍhā* lunar mansion, the four syllables *bhu-dha-pha-ḍha* are on the pillar in the northwest corner; in the *uttarabhādrapada* lunar mansion, the four syllables *ha-tha-jha-ña* [are on the pillar]. Thus, there are four syllables for each of the four measures (*mātrā*) and so forth.
The four pillars should be known by those who understand the established rules of musical tones.

Regarding the phrase "the sacrificial hearths" (*dhiṣṇyāni*) and so forth: among the inscribed syllables, beginning with the letter *a*, [the hearths] are formed by groups of four syllables each, together with the *Abhijit* constellation.

There are twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras), beginning with Kṛttikā. In this system, each nakṣatra consists of four quarters (aṃśas), totaling one hundred and twelve in number. By this [allocation]: *a, i, u, e* belong to Kṛttikā; *o, va, vī, vu* belong to Rohiṇī; *ve, vo, ka, ki* belong to Mṛgaśiras; *ku, gha, ṅa*... [and so forth].
Cha, ā, r, d, r, ā—Ārdrā. Ke, ko, ha, hi—Punarvasu. Hu, he, ho, ḍa—Puṣyā. Ḍi, ḍu, ḍe, ḍo—Aśleṣā.
Ma, mi, mu, me—Maghā. Mo, ṭa, ṭi, ṭu—Pūrvaphalgunī.
Ṭe, ṭo, pa, pi—Uttaraphalgunī. Pu, ṣa, ṇa, ṭha—Hastā. Pe, po, va, vi—Citrā. Vya, ve, vo, ta—Svātī.
Ti, tu, te, to: Viśākhā. La, li, lu, le: Anurādhā. No, yā, ye, yu: Jyeṣṭhā.
Ye, yo, bha, bhi: Mūlā. Bhu, bha, pha, ḍha: Pūrvāṣāḍhā. Bhe, bho, ja, ji: Uttarāṣāḍhā. Ju, je, jo, tha: Abhijit. Khi, khu, khe, kho: Śravaṇā. Ga, gi, ge, go: [Dhaniṣṭhā].

Dhaniṣṭhā; Śo, Śa, Śi, Śu, Śatabhiṣā; Śe, Śo, Da, Di, Pūrvabhādrapada; Ha, Kha, Jha, Ña, Uttarabhādrapada; De, Do, Ca, Ci, Revatī; Cu, Ce, Co, La, Aśvinī; Li, Lu, La, Lo, Bharaṇī. Thus are the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

He demonstrates the purpose with the words "in which lunar mansion" (*yadṛkṣāṃśake*) and so forth. Whether a malefic or a benefic planet, one should pierce the first letter of the name of the man—of the person—from the asterism in which that planet is situated, again by means of a diagonal sequence (*tiryakkrameṇa*). The word "if" (*yadi*) is to be supplied here.

He states the result of the piercing (vedha) in the verse beginning with "saumyavedha" and so forth: in the case of a benefic piercing, the result is auspicious; in the case of a malefic piercing, however, it is inauspicious. When there is a piercing by mixed benefics and malefics, the result is mixed—both auspicious and inauspicious. If there is no piercing at all, there is nothing [to be determined]. Whatever [result] arises from a planet in the Sarvatobhadra-cakra based on the piercing of planets...
The result has already been stated; it applies here as well. *Pepīvavīti* refers to the constellation Citrā;
therefore, for one named Rāmatoṣaṇa, the constellation Citrā is situated in the third quarter of the zodiac sign Libra.
This same rule applies to the constellation of anyone else as well.

But upon seeing the questioner during a query, having mentally bowed to Sarasvatī with the words: "I salute that Bhāratī, who speaks through the mouth of the questioner regarding the objects contemplated by the mind, who possesses form and color, and who is affectionate toward her devotees"— thereby having prostrated to Sarasvatī in one's mind;
Having recited the seed-syllable *Vāgbhava* or one's own chosen mantra one hundred times, one should ask:

"For what purpose have you come here? Tell me," and so forth. Then, having understood the ascendant (*lagna*) and its nine-divisional parts (*navāṃśaka*) by means of the first syllable of whatever the questioner says first;

By means of planetary piercing (grahavedha) and by means of planetary aspect (grahadṛṣṭi), one should declare the elements, roots, livelihoods, and so forth, as well as the colors, forms, and other characteristics, along with their auspicious and inauspicious effects.
There shall be thirteen vertical lines and likewise ten horizontal lines;
therein there will be one hundred and eight squares. Having written the *ka*-group nine times in the first, eighth, second, and seventh squares, [one should place] the first [vowel] in each.

In the sixty-third [cell] from the two *naṭas*, the *ya* and *śa* groups are in the fourth, and likewise the group in the fifth; those beginning with *ta* are in the ninth and twelfth, and those beginning with *pa* are in the remaining two cells. These are to be known in the combination of four syllables according to the sequence starting from Aśvinī.

The nine divisions (navāṃśakas) of the letters in the zodiacal circle beginning with Aries are as follows: Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter; these should be placed above the grid cells according to the letters of the grid. From the letters of the grid...

The Moon should be known as arising at that time; all results—gain or loss, victory or defeat—are dependent upon it. [The remaining degrees] are obtained by dividing the product of the desired nāḍīs and the lunar mansions by sixty, using the portion of the Moon traversed starting from Aśvinī.

From that calculation, the moon for that time is determined. When the moon is in a cruel sign or a cruel syllable, there is no auspiciousness in any undertakings; however, it is indeed auspicious when in a benefic sign—such is the determination of the moon in the *prastāra* (astrological grid).
[The sequence of numbers is: four (4), three (3), seven (7) sages, twelve (12) suns, seven (7), nine (9) Nandas, three (3) qualities, and five (5) arrows.
Twelve months, seven mountains, twelve lords, and twenty-four praises—these are the fixed values for the zodiac signs.
The constant values (dhruvas) for the degrees of the month and so forth are: three, seven, four, five, seven, five, three, four, eight, five, six, and five.
A degree is to be multiplied by a degree; this product, increased by the constant value, is then [divided] by its own multiplier.

The wise man should then multiply [the result] by the root-figure and divide it by sixty (60), five (5), twelve (12), two (2), three (3), two (2), and twelve (12) respectively. These are the results in *nāḍīs* for the Moon, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Sun-Saturn pair. These are their respective *yaśas* (glories).
p. 931) The results of the *vargas* arise from the daily fruit (*dinaphala*). What [fruit arises] from a fortnight, a month, a year, or by means of solstices and years?

At the time of inquiry, at marriage, at the conjunction [of planets], at birth, and in the case of confusion—thus has the excellent fruit of the Moon been proclaimed in all the scriptures. Thus [it is said].
The Prastāracakra (the wheel of expansion).
The meaning, the procedure, and the convention of this are now stated. "Thirteen," and so forth:

by this, nine squares are formed in twelve positions according to an upward and downward sequence. Therein lies the arrangement of the groups of letters (*varga*). Following the sequence of nine parts, there are nine [letters] in each of the twelve [squares].
Showing that they become "pādikā," he says "the *ka*-group," and so forth. Having written the first letter of the *ka*-group (*ka*,

*kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*) nine times in nine ways— by means of nine squares in an upward and downward sequence— in Aries (the first sign) and Scorpio (the eighth sign), and likewise [in the other signs],...

In the second [house], which has the form of Taurus, and in the seventh, which has the form of Libra, one should write the initial letters of the consonant groups, beginning with *ca*. In the third and sixth, which have the forms of Gemini and Virgo, having written the letters beginning with *ṭa*—
namely, the *ṭa*-group— one should likewise write the *ya*-group, the *śa*-group, and the *ava*-group (*a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*) in the fourth, which has the form of Cancer.

One should write the letters *aṃ* and *aḥ*, which are the forms of the fifth [house], in the form of Leo; the letters of the *ta*-group (*tādyān*), which are the forms of the ninth and twelfth [houses], Sagittarius and Pisces; and in the remaining two squares, the letters of the *pa*-group (*pavargavarṇān*), which are the forms of Capricorn and Aquarius. Regarding "four-syllabled," etc.: *ka*.
By combining *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* in this sequence, the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) beginning with Aśvinī are formed.

Therein, by means of nine letters each, which constitute the nine divisions (*navāṃśas*) in the form of quarter-steps (*pādikās*), the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśis*) and their respective degrees are established. Thus [ends] "Bhauma."

One should arrange or write [the table]. At that very time, when the measure of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) occurs, the Moon—situated within the portion occupied by one of the twenty-seven lunar mansions—is to be known as being located in a specific ninth-part (navāṃśa) consisting of the letters of the grid and their respective quarter-parts. "The desired nāḍīs" [refers to this].

The desired *daṇḍas* are filled by twenty-seven; then, by dividing by sixty, one obtains one lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). When fifteen *pala*s or more remain as the remainder, that is the first quarter of the lunar mansion, and within the subsequent thirty parts of *daṇḍas*.
The second quarter [is calculated] upon that within forty-five palas;
the third quarter upon that within sixty [palas]; and for the fourth quarter, the contemporary moon should be placed at each respective remainder. By this, the following is established:
That which is obtained by dividing by sixty is the lunar mansion already traversed (*bhukta-nakṣatra*), and whatever remains is the one currently being traversed (*bhujyamāna*).
In that regard, if the sum of the figures for the lunar mansions traversed by the moon exceeds twenty-seven,
then one should subtract twenty-seven and establish the moon as it stands at that time.
One must proceed toward the arising of truth.

He demonstrates the method for making [the time] instantaneous: the desired nāḍīs, which are the daṇḍas traversed by the asterism, must be multiplied by twenty-seven, the number of the lunar mansions (dhiṣṇya).
Therein, in the divisor which has a remainder obtained by dividing by sixty, because of the division by sixty, [the result] is placed in front.
When the remainder in the count of elapsed asterisms is added to the body of the asterism currently being traversed—

arranged in vertical order from top to bottom, excluding the current sequence— and joined with the asterism-number traversed by the Moon, such as Aśvinī and so forth, if twenty-seven are subtracted from that sum, the remainder [is the result].
The elapsed asterism (*nakṣatra*), the remainder,

and the portion of the next asterism being traversed by the moon— thus is the moon at that time determined. The duration for the transit through an asterism, however, is two *daṇḍas* plus thirteen *palas*.
This is the meaning. However, an exception occurs in the case where the duration of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is less than or greater than sixty [units].

He demonstrates their results with the verse beginning "krūrakṣetrākṣaram": when the Moon is situated in a syllable belonging to a cruel mansion—that is, in a syllable corresponding to the zodiac sign of a malefic planet—it is not auspicious for any undertakings.

When the Moon is situated in an auspicious field (*kṣetra*), under an auspicious planet, sign (*rāśi*), or asterism (*nakṣatra*), it is called an auspicious time (*śubhakāla*). The determination of the Moon has been explained in the *prastāra* diagram. To address the doubt as to when the aforementioned results will manifest, he says: "The results of the *nāḍīs*," namely, the *ya*-group and the *śa*-group.

The *nāḍī* and *phala* [periods] yield results within the day; therein, when the moon traverses one quarter [of the circle], there are thirty-three *palas*, and beyond that, success in the task is certain. Thus, for the traversal of each successive quarter, having made the measurement of that quarter circular—

The rule regarding the *daṇḍa* (stick) form must be stated: that [period] lasts at most five *daṇḍas*, provided the remainder of the *rāśi* (zodiacal sign) is less than three *palas*. In the arising of the daily result (*dinaphala*), which yields the stated results over one day, what is the *ka*-group? The *ka*-group pertains to the fortnight (*pakṣa*). The *ca*-group pertains to the month (*māsa*). The *ṭa*-group [pertains to the year].

Regarding the seasons: the *tavarga* and *pavarga* [consonant groups] correspond to the two solstices (*ayana*) and the year (*abda*). The *tavarga* pertains to the six-month period, while the *pavarga* pertains to the year as the bestower of fruit. Regarding the "time of inquiry":
in these matters, the position of the Moon is concealed in all the scriptures by this method.

At the time of making a formal inquiry, at a marriage, or at the commencement of a rite, one should consider the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness based on the Moon of that specific time. Thus ends the Prastāracakra.

Victorious is Prāṇakṛṣṇa, honored by all, the refuge for the distressed, preeminent through the dissemination of his fame earned by meritorious deeds, most excellent, uniquely pure, one whose new renown is proclaimed even by scribes,
who has dispelled the poverty of the virtuous, and the glory of the heart of Gauḍa.
Its branches are inscribed with the handwriting of Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa; its fragrance, like that of blooming flowers, has perfumed the quarters of the sky;
it is attainable only by those of pure being (*sattva*) and its essence is accessible only to the most diligent practitioners—[this tree] resides within the heart of Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa.
May it spread joy.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], containing the *Pañcapuṣpa-stavaka*, in the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī* composed by Paṇḍit Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya, with the approval of Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa.
The section on knowledge is completed.
She who delights in the battle-play made manifest by the exultation of Mahākāla, her braid of hair loosened,
clad in the sky, her face perspiring; glossy as a fresh rain-cloud,
with eyes reddened by the blood offered upon a corpse— she always dwells in the chamber of darkness within my heart like a flash of lightning.
May it flash forth within me! Now the seventh chapter, known as the "Section on the Attributeless" (Nirguṇa-kāṇḍa), is being prescribed.

First therein is the *nirghaṇṭa* (glossary), which is the determination of the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*) and so forth. Then follows the fruit of the three states, the three states during the forenoon and other periods, and finally, the seed of accomplishment (*siddhibīja*) within the state of the bound soul.

Praise of the Divine Hero; the characteristics of the animal [sacrifice] and others; the determination of what should and should not be done by them; thereafter, the determination of the superiority and other qualities of the three states (bhāva);
then, the description of the three states according to their divisions such as the "commencement" (ārambha) and so forth; and finally, the exposition of the states (bhāvanirūpaṇa).
Then follows the definition of *brahmacarya* (celibate student life), the various fruits of wearing copper [amulets] according to the different parts of the body, and the fact that in the Kali age,
only the first three stages of life (*āśrama*) are to be known by the wise; as well as the duties of the householder, hospitality, and the worship of the ancestors.
The characteristics of a wife; the avoidance of another's wife; the nurturing of sons, daughters, and so forth;

what is to be done and what is not to be done by a householder—these and other matters are to be understood according to their respective contexts. The duties of the mendicant stage of life and the prohibition thereof in the Kali age [are also to be understood].

The ten names of the Avadhūtas, followed by the determination of the Avadhūta; their duties, characteristics, and subsequent praise; the statement "Oṃ tat sat" as the designation, its fruit, and its glorification;
and the description of the different modes of conduct—this is recorded as the next section.

Following that is the procedure for the Full Consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), then the other consecrations, the praise of the hero (*vīra*), and the heroic deeds (*vīrakṛtyaka*). The drinking of wine according to the ritual rule is prohibited otherwise, yet it is sanctioned by the scriptures. Immediately thereafter is the provision for the alternative practice (*anukalpa*) in the absence of the [required] substances.

(p. 934) The censure of drinking unfermented liquor, the qualification of the Brahmin, therein the connection with its fruit, and thereafter the fruit of liberation from the curse; the fruit of recitation when attached to the [five] essences, as well as the mental disposition—this is the determination of the Dharma of the five *makāras*.

The fruit of the five *kārakas*, the condemnation of worship performed without them; the five principles (*pañcatattva*) for Vaiṣṇavas, the purification of the five principles; thereafter, the description of the *svayambhū* flower and so forth, the manner of their origin, and their purification as well.

The sequence for the placement of vessels, including the mantras and other causes; the sequence for the libation (tarpaṇa); the description of the mudrās of the principles (tattvas); the determination of the locations for the libation according to the sequence of the different states of being; and the purification of the principles—this concludes the second chapter.

First, there is the worship of the Hero (Vīrapūjā), wherein the mantra consists of twenty-two syllables; then the ritual placement of the seer and other factors (ṛṣyādinyāsana), meditation (dhyāna), and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) and so forth. Following that is the worship of Mahākāla, and after that, the censure of others (paranindā).
The attainment of the fruit occurs through half the recitation (japa), and the seed-syllable (bīja) is the cause of success (siddhi).
Then follows the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) according to the distinctions of caste, such as Brahmins and others;

then the sequence for the accomplishment of the rosary (*mālāsiddhi*); then the sequence of the *Kūlavaṭī*; then other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the three applications (*prayoga*). [Without these], accomplishment does not arise.
Furthermore, there is another method therein; the means consisting of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth;
the procedure for the second initiation; the praise of the Great Mantra; the purification of the mantra and so forth;
the hundred names of the second [initiation]; and after that, the *vīra-homa*.

Then follows the fruit of the gift of material substances and the fruit of the various types of liquor; next is the section on the *mahāśaṅkha* (great conch), and thereafter the salutation to Aśoka and the others. After that is the procedure for mountains and other locations, followed by the mantra of salutation. Then follows the censure of performing rites in cremation grounds and the like, and the consequences of not performing them.
The tasting of the nectar (*rasāsvāda*) of the heroes and its fruit immediately thereafter;

and likewise, the accomplishment of the six activities (*ṣaṭkarmasādhana*) of the heroes immediately thereafter—this is recorded as the conclusion of the third chapter. This is the conduct of the *kula* and the characteristic of one born of the *kula*.
Immediately following that: the Kulācāra (the conduct of the Kula) is twofold; thereafter, the duties of a Kaula;

the prohibition against censuring the Kaulas; the determination regarding the Gṛhāvadhūtā (the householder-ascetic); the nocturnal rites and the Kulācāra; then the praise of the Kaulas; and finally, the section on the internal sacrifice (Antaryāga).

Then follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (*jñāna-homa-vidhi*). Next is the sequence of the Śrīcakra, followed by the censure of greed and the drinking [of wine] (p. 935). Furthermore, there is the description of the characteristics of the ignorant worshiper regarding the censure of drinking and so forth. Then comes the essential [instruction] on the five purifications and the description of the mandala. Regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*):
Then follows that which is prohibited and that which is prescribed; thereafter, the purification of substances and so forth;

then the sequence of the lineage of gurus; then the sequence of the Kula conduct; then the prohibition against unworthy recipients (kupātra) and the like; immediately after that, the prohibition against those who have not bathed and others from using Kula substances; and finally, regarding the touching of what has been left over (ucchiṣṭa).

Beyond that is the prohibition; the fault of removing vessels and materials, the obstacle to the *cakra* accompanied by pacification rites (*śāntika*). In the intense outpouring (*prauḍhollāsa*), there follow the signs of the intoxication of knowledge for the wise.
In the *cakra*, one must avoid jesting and the like, and conceal the recipients (*pātra*). Whatever rite is performed in association with the uninitiated (*paśu*)—

Avoiding idle talk and the like; avoiding the scriptures of the uninitiated (paśu); censuring those who lack faith; worshipping the teacher, the Śakti, and others with the thought that they are the deity, even without personal desire; forbidding the use of force; and not saluting raw meat and such things.
Following that is the prohibition against disparaging the Kula scriptures and so forth;

then comes the description of the nature of bliss, the censure of excessive drinking and the like, the fault of drinking for the sake of mere pleasure, the secondary alternative (anukalpa), and finally the prohibition against datura and similar substances.

And indeed, even in every secondary rite (anukalpa), there is the censure of practicing the five principles (pañcatattva) without the traditional lineage (pāramparya). For those bound by worldly ties (paśus), the practice of the five principles is a great sin.
Then follows the determination of the performance of the Cakra (cakrānuṣṭhāna) and the salutation of the worthy recipient (pātra); as well as the measure of the worthy recipient (pātramāna).

The investigation into the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) of the power (*śakti*) of the Lord of the Wheel; then the hymn of peace (*śāntistotra*), followed by the determination of the sequence for the completion of the wheel;
the narration of the hymn of bliss (*ānandastotra*), and the determination of the manifestation of bliss (*ānandollāsa*). Thus ends the fourth section.

The conclusion is now declared: the performance of the rites to be carried out by the five wheels (*cakrapañcaka*), the names of the wheels, the presiding authority of the wheels, the determination of the power (*śakti*) and so forth of the illustrious Royal Wheel (*rājacakra*), and thereafter the determination of the purification by the nectar of the power of the Great Wheel (*mahācakra*) and so forth; [this concludes] the section on the Wheel of the Deities (*devacakra*).
Immediately after that is the determination of the Śakti and so forth; likewise, following that, is the determination of the Śakti and so forth within the Vīracakra.

Then follows the determination of the Mātrās and so forth, the exclusion of those who do not know the secret signs (saṅketa) and the unworthy heroes (vīra), and subsequently, the determination of the Śakti and so forth for the Paśucakra, as well as the worship of one's own Kula-Śakti.

First, then [the following]: the worship of Paraśakti is intended solely for those who have perfected the mantras; likewise, the ritual practice for the realization of Śakti, the determination of the seats (pīṭhas) of the limbs of Śakti, the fruit of recitation (japa) in various locations, the fruits of the various Śaktis, and the worship of Śakti in the head and other parts [of the body].

And the determination of the *japa* [of mantras], as well as the *liṅga*, mantras, *japa*, and so forth; then the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Following that is the description of the accomplishment of desires in the *cakra*;
then another [section on] the practice of the creeper (*latāsādhana*), and after that, the purification of the bed (*śayyāśuddhi*).

The description of the nine powers (*nava-śakti*), the characteristics of the Kāpālikīs and others, the specific enumeration of courtesans, and the fruit of the reverse recitation (*viparīta-japa*). That power (*śakti*) bears names such as Kālī according to the sequence of age;
furthermore, there is the accomplishment of the *Śyāmā* and other vidyās through union with specific powers (*śakti-viśeṣa-yoga*), as well as their practical application.

The meditation on the Yoni, the hymn of praise following that, the armor-mantra (kavaca), the application of the Yoni-yoga, the determination of the fruit of recitation, the determination of the nine flowers, the ascertainment of the excellence of Śakti, the fruit offered to Śakti,
and the abiding of the deity within the limbs of Śakti.

The practice of other women as a means of attainment, union with another's wife during worship, the presence of all sacred fords within the female body, and then the ritual procedure for the worship of the *yoni*. Following that, the fruits of recollecting the *yoni* and so forth, and the worship of the *yoni* itself, which is devoid of [rituals such as] invocation (*āvāhana*).

From that [section] follows the fruit resulting from drinking the water used for washing the feet of Śakti and so forth; immediately after that is the majesty of Bhaga-tattva and Kuntalī; and "the bonds" marks the conclusion of the fifth chapter. Other matters are to be understood according to their respective places.

O wise one! Behold this very section, composed by Rāma to please [you] through the profound and diligent contemplation of the essence of existence within the midst of the scriptures; if you desire to be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence, which is devoid of [intrinsic] qualities.
Now follows the determination of the meditative cultivation (*bhāva*). From the sixth chapter of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrajāmala*.

O Lord! Listen in detail to the nature of the deity established in the state of a bound soul (paśu): he who constantly performs the worship of Durgā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva is indeed remembered as the "supreme bound soul" (uttama-paśu). He who performs the worship of Śiva alone is a practitioner (sādhaka).
The illustrious and supreme among the *paśus* is he who dwells together with Śivā;
the wise one who is solely Vaiṣṇava is considered the middle among the *paśus*. Those who constantly perform service to the elements and the deities are the middle *paśus*.

They have been declared to dwell in hell, of this there is no doubt. O Great Lord! Having performed service to you and service to me, as well as service to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, and then having performed service to all other beings, to the leading women, to the Yakṣiṇīs, and to the Bhūtinīs— [p. 937] ... [they shall attain the fruit].

[She is] the bestower of auspiciousness. Those who always perform service to Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and others, as well as those supreme men who perform service to the venerable Tāraka-Brahman—for them, the deities such as Bhūta and the rest, who grant all desires, are not difficult to attain; one should avoid [the path of] the animal-path (paśu-mārga).

A person devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu [should perform] daily śrāddha, as well as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vandana), libations to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa), visiting deities, visiting sacred seats (pīṭha), visiting holy fords (tīrtha), obeying the commands of the guru, and the daily worship of the deity. (Second Paṭala)
A mortal established in the state of the animal (paśubhāva) will certainly attain the great siddhi. [From] the sixth chapter.

Listen now with due respect regarding the rebirth of the bound soul (*paśu*): suddenly, that soul attains perfection and becomes equal to Nārāyaṇa. Possessing a four-armed body, with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in hand, and mounted upon Garuḍa, he goes to the city of Vaikuṇṭha.

By the grace of Mahāvidyā, he becomes the very nature of the Great Dharma. Having first established the state of the bound soul (*paśu-bhāva*)—the great state that bestows the supreme perfection of all things—he should subsequently perform the necessary rites. [He then attains] the state of the hero (*vīra-bhāva*), the great state.
The most supreme among all states; thereafter, the state of divine being, exceedingly beautiful and yielding great fruit. Thus are the states.
Regarding the fruit of the disposition (*bhāva*), it is stated in that very same place: "The man who desires the fruit, who seeks liberation,

who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, and who desires knowledge, wealth, and jewels— such a person should perform the three divine dispositions, which are the supreme means for accomplishing the disposition."

Through devotion, one obtains a kingdom, wealth, jewels, and great fruit; whatever fruit is gained by worshipping ten million lingas in Vārāṇasī, a mortal obtains that very fruit in an instant—of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the fruit of devotion.
The fruit of the specific state (*bhāvaviśeṣa*) is also described in that very same place: "In the first ten *daṇḍas* [of the day], the animal state (*paśubhāva*) occurs;
likewise, in the ten *daṇḍas* at midday, the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) is declared; and in the ten *daṇḍas* of the evening, the divine state (*divyabhāva*) [occurs]."

It bestows auspiciousness. Alternatively, one may worship the desired deity and other deities in the state of a *paśu* (bound soul). By chanting the mantra until the end of his life, the practitioner (*mantrī*) shall attain great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*). Even by means of the mere *pīṭha-brahman* and the great *ṣoḍhā-āśrama*, the practitioner remains established in the state of a *paśu*.

One shall attain singular accomplishment. If the mantra-practitioner abides in the path of Kula, he will certainly obtain accomplishment regarding the Great Kaulika deity situated in the preceding and following [stages].
If the Vidyās are propitiated, then there arises the state of a Hero (vīrabhāva). By the grace of the state of a Hero...
One shall attain a divine state. Those best of men who embrace the divine state and the heroic state are, without a doubt, masters of the wish-fulfilling tree and its creeper of desires.
Having become an ascetic devoted to meditation and proficient in mantra and tantra...

By wandering through the great sacred seats (mahāpīṭhas), an ascetic shall become liberated in person. What need is there for any other effort if one possesses the [proper] disposition and so forth? Merely by grasping my true nature, a man shall become a knower of wisdom; the perfection of speech and the power of words shall swiftly arise.

She who reaches the heart; Lakṣmī remains in the house having abandoned Nārāyaṇa—there is no doubt that my supreme, perfect vision is fixed upon his body. He certainly attains perfection; this is the truth, the truth, O Sadāśiva! Likewise: "The disposition is indeed threefold."

O Lord! From the sequence of the divine, heroic, and animal [methods], there are likewise three types of gurus here, as well as the mantra-deities. O Mahādeva! The divine state is the most excellent, bestowing all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The second is declared to be middling, and the third is censured by all. Likewise, from much recitation...

O Mahādeva! Mantras and Tantras do not bestow their fruits through burnt offerings (*homa*), physical austerities (*kāyakleśa*), and other such elaborate practices; rather, they do so through *bhāva* (inner disposition). Likewise: "First, O Kaulika, listen with diligence to the divine *bhāva*.
It is the Vidyā worshipped by all the gods, filled with a mass of splendor, consisting of light, and [pervading] the world."
Having dissolved all conceptualization of form.
In the eleventh chapter: "The divine state is threefold, arising from the Vedas, the Āgamas, and discernment (*viveka*).

The meaning of the Vedas is declared to be the lowest; that which originates from the Āgamas is the middle; and that which arises from the blossoming of discernment is declared to be the highest and fruitful. In that very [chapter], the state is threefold..."

The sequence of the Divine, Heroic, and Animal [methods]—that which arises solely from the Divine and Heroic is declared to bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*). One should know that to be the supreme, an ocean of the essence of bliss (*ānanda-rasa*).
The intermediate is the radiance of the scriptures (*āgama-ullāsa*), the state of the Hero (*vīra-bhāva*) endowed with ritual action, born of the Vedas.

And for the sake of the fruit, one indeed attains the state of a beast, which is the lowest of dispositions; it is pervaded by all forms of censure and is the most base of states for a beast. In the highest [state], there is the highest knowledge, which bestows the perfection of being upon men; in the middling [state], there is that of Madhumatī.

Arising from the tradition of my own lineage, it removes untimely death and is exceedingly difficult for ordinary beings to attain. O Lord! Without the state of a hero (*vīrabhāva*), it is never accomplished. When [it concerns] the base, it always explains the base, expressing censure and its meaning. When... p. 939)

If one does not engage in censure, then one shall obtain the fruit thereof; even in the state of a beast, success will be attained if one constantly practices this Veda. One should always contemplate the meaning of the Veda, delighting in the sound of its recitation, remaining free from all censure, and avoiding violence and laziness.

If a practitioner established in the state of being remains free from greed, delusion, lust, anger, pride, and envy, he attains accomplishment even if he is in the state of a *paśu*. O Mahādeva! For those on this earth who know that the state of a *paśu* is the state of the Great Being (*mahābhāva*), what is there that cannot be achieved? Through the practice of exertion, they attain that very state.
The entire world depends on labor; even the deities depend on labor.
The entire world depends on labor; supreme austerity depends on labor.
Family tradition and the characteristics of bestiality depend on labor.
Merely by knowing the meaning of the Vedas, one attains the state of a beast, which is dear to the Kula.

Furthermore, the Smṛtis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, as well as those things ordained by the meaning of the Vedas, describe the various types of spiritual dispositions and stages of life (*bhāvāśrama*) in that very same place. Having studied all the scriptures...

Having known the reality, the wise man should abandon all scriptures like a seeker of grain discards chaff; having become a knower, the best of practitioners should take refuge in the essence of existence. According to my spoken word, the ritual action of the Veda must be performed within the Veda.

The characteristic of those who are like cattle, [afflicted] by fatigue and burning, has thus been described. The purposeful activity of the scriptures must always be performed through the conduct of my family (matkula). This is the characteristic described for the heroes, the exalted ones, those who follow my body, and those whose essence is the reality of my family’s conduct.
For those whose consciousness is firm in their actions through the knowledge of the aphorisms on discernment, and who maintain an attitude of equanimity toward all things,
the mere state of being [devotion] is indeed the means. For,
having seen that everything moving and unmoving everywhere has its origin in the lotus-feet of Me, whatever action one performs—

It is unshakeable and bestows the attainment of the fruit; it is the state of those whose minds possess unbroken knowledge—this is the meaning for the discerning. It is described as the characteristic of those who are divine through stainless bliss. On this earth, that great hero who knows the threefold divine state never perishes.
The supreme practitioner, if he practices by relying sequentially upon the divine state and the others, that supreme practitioner attains great siddhi in the divine state.
O Lord! Without the divine state, he who desires the vision of my lotus feet—

O Mahādeva! How does that deluded practitioner [attain] the state of a Paśu in the first [stage], the state of a Vīra in the second, and the state of a Divya in the third? O Śiva, protector of the three worlds, hear the manner of those [stages] in sequence.
He who knows the distinctions of the three states, who discerns the six supports,

who understands the reality and nature of the five principles, and who is ever devoted to divine conduct— he alone becomes illustrious, having reached the further shore of all that is to be accomplished, and shall wander through the world like Śiva himself.

Endowed with the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), through a state of purity in all things, one performs the practice of the mass of bliss (*ānandaghana*). Whether by recitation (*jāpana*) or retention (*dhāraṇa*), the mind comes under control through effort. In a solitary and secluded place, one certainly becomes a perfected one (*siddha*). At that time, for the sake of the seed-state (*bījabhāva*), there is indeed mere being (*bhāvamātra*).

The Means of Accomplishment: Success is attained through devotion, and nowhere else but from the Hero. Having worshipped at night during the twilight hours and the like, with one's mouth filled with betel, and being completely filled with the bliss of Vijayā, one should take the unity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) into one's mind.

One who, free from fear, recites [this] throughout the entire night in a solitary house, shall become a servant of Kālikā, the most excellent among the divine ones. Having thus understood these three states of being, he who then accomplishes the ritual becomes endowed with the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*).
Having become [thus], one certainly becomes omniscient.

And in the seventh chapter of the Kubjikātantra: "O Goddess! There are three types of contemplation (bhāva), according to the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu). O beautiful goddess, one should contemplate the entire universe as the form of the Deity;
one should contemplate the whole world as consisting of woman and the person as being the form of Śiva, within non-duality."

But that which is the very self of the deity—meaning its nature is that of the deity—[is all]. If it is argued that because everything is understood through the contemplation of non-difference to consist of Śiva and Śakti, then acts such as bathing should not be performed, [the following] is stated in that very same [text] to dispel such a doubt: ... [The text continues with the specific citation] ... just as it is said there.

O Goddess! One should perform daily bathing, daily giving of gifts, recitation and worship at the three junctions of the day, wear clean clothing as an undergarment, possess firm knowledge of the Vedas and the Shastras,
likewise firm knowledge of the Guru and the Deity, firm knowledge of the Mantra, and the worship of the ancestors and the gods.

Likewise, O lady of pure smiles! the offering to Bali, as well as the Śrāddha rite, are daily duties. O Goddess, O Maheśvarī! one should regard an enemy as equal to a friend. O Maheśānī! one should avoid the food of all others; however, O Maheśānī! the food of the Guru should be eaten.
For the sake of all accomplishments, O Great Goddess! one should completely avoid the miserly and the cruel.

Upon seeing one who reviles the deities, one should not even engage in conversation with them. O Goddess! one should speak the truth and never a falsehood; one should worship solely with a divine disposition.
O Goddess! The wise one should daily contemplate the worship of the Guru as the Supreme Sovereign.

Everything is of the form of the deity and has the nature of the Parameṣṭhin. Remaining constantly with one-pointed focus, one should worship the Guru at the three junctions of the day; O Maheśānī, [the Guru] is equal to the Guru himself.

One should pay homage, O fair-faced one! Having seen the soles of women's feet, one should always regard them as the Guru. O Goddess, one should make the body—adorned with sandalwood paste and blood, most beautiful—like the supreme Gandharva deity.

O Goddess, O Maheśvarī! One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with either ashes or red sandalwood paste, and adorn all limbs with rudrākṣa beads. Having become Bhairava himself, one should worship the eternal Goddess and offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) every day.

O Maheśvarī! For the sake of attaining the state of divinity, having taken up the pledges (samayas), one should perform worship and other rites; O Maheśvarī! Worship should indeed be performed at midnight. O lady of beautiful countenance! Upon seeing a Kula-tree, one should likewise perform prostration and salutation.
And every day, O Maheśvarī! one should worship the Goddess at night alone, never by day.
At night, O Maheśvarī! with the mouth full of betel-leaf, one should recite the mantra. And everything, O Mahādevī! one should offer to the Supreme Goddess.

In that very same [text], it speaks of the censure of that state of being which consists of the notions of what is to be done and what is not to be done regarding the nature of a bound soul (*paśu*): "O Goddess, those who are devoted to the Vedic path, who are intent on the performance of rituals, and who are attached to the fruits of action—these are called *paśus*. They are deluded by the darkness of ignorance and are bound by the fetters of ritual action. They do not know the supreme reality, nor do they perceive the Self. They are subject to birth and death, and they wander through the cycle of existence. They are devoted to the worship of various deities, yet they do not know the one Lord. They are intent on the attainment of heaven and the like, and they are averse to liberation. They are bound by the ropes of desire and are immersed in the ocean of worldly existence. They are devoid of discrimination and are always overcome by passion and hatred. They are devoted to the enjoyment of sense objects and are averse to the contemplation of the Self. They are bound by the bonds of karma and are subject to the three qualities (*guṇas*). They are deluded by the power of Māyā and do not know their own true nature. They are devoted to the performance of sacrifices and the giving of gifts, and they are intent on the study of the Vedas. They are bound by the fetters of ritual action and are subject to the cycle of rebirth. They are devoid of devotion to the Guru and are averse to the teachings of the Śāstra. They are bound by the ropes of attachment and are immersed in the mire of worldly existence. They are devoid of knowledge and are always overcome by delusion. They are devoted to the enjoyment of sense objects and are averse to the contemplation of the Self. They are bound by the bonds of karma and are subject to the three qualities. They are deluded by the power of Māyā and do not know their own true nature."

Those who delight in the state of beasts and possess only the form of beasts—such a person should never touch a yantra or recite a mantra at night. They always harbor doubt regarding the offering of oblations (bali) and doubt regarding the tantra; they perceive the mantra as a mere collection of syllables and maintain constant lack of faith in the guru.
One who perceives images as mere stone, or as a deity only when they are broken; O Goddess of Gods!

one who worships the deity without selfless devotion; one who constantly bathes out of ignorance; one who strikes the deity every day; and he who utters insults against all—O Maheśvarī! he [is a destroyer].
Thus, one who possesses the nature of a beast is proclaimed to be the lowest. Also, in the first chapter of the *Nityātantra*:

"One should never worship the Goddess at night, nor during the twilight, nor in the afternoon. O Goddess! One should avoid sexual union except during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*). O Maheśānī! One should renounce meat and the like."
During the five festival days, one who is devoted to the observances should perform whatever else is prescribed by the Vedas.
Thus ends the censure of the state of being a sacrificial animal.

The superiority of the divine (divya) and heroic (vīra) states is also mentioned in that very same place: "The divine state is the highest, the heroic state is middling, and the animal (paśu) state is the lowest, O Goddess; this is the truth, there is no doubt. Mantras established in the animal state consist merely of the form of letters."

O Maheśānī! One must awaken the realization of the divine nature; therefore, indeed, one should accomplish this with effort through the state of a Vīra. O Goddess! having seen a woman of the Kula, especially a Kula-tree, and likewise a Kula-dwelling, O fair-faced Goddess, one should offer salutation.

O Maheśānī! O Varānanā! One should pay homage to a woman of noble family, one who is proficient in the Tantras and Mantras, a female messenger (dūtī) devoted to sacrifice, or likewise a courtesan or an unchaste woman—whether she be old or young.

In the tenth chapter of the Picchilā Tantra: "The divine hero and the one of great disposition; the lowest is the state of a bound soul (paśu). A Vaiṣṇava, through the state of a bound soul, should worship the Supreme Lord.
O lady of excellent hips! In the mantra of Śakti, the state of a bound soul is terrifying."

O Maheśānī! Through divine heroes, the highest siddhi is born. There is no difference between the divine and the hero; the hero is exceedingly exalted. I shall describe the divine and the heroic, who are considered the best of all states. O Dear One! Without Śakti there is no worship, nor is there [worship] without fish and meat.

One should never perform worship without both the mudrā and sexual union. The vulva of a woman is the support for worship; [substitutes] made of gold, silver, or kuśa grass may be used. In the absence of all these materials, there is a secondary ritual option (*anukalpa*) in the Kali age. Or else, O Supreme Goddess!

One should perform everything mentally. Mental bathing is declared to be the Vedic way; one is always a follower of the Vedas through the mental path. Where one partakes of a great mental worship after eating, that indeed is the mental meal.
One may mentally enjoy a woman, whether she be one's own or another's. [Mental]...

The supreme practitioner may accept liquor, meat, and so forth; likewise, he should perform the mental offering of the *svayambhū* flower. He should perform mentally the hair of the vulva and so on, and mentally worship the vulva. He should perform everything mentally, for by that the practitioner attains success. Not [otherwise].

In the Kali age, that which is the natural conduct does not exist for one whose mind is filled with doubt; rather, through a purely mental disposition alone, one may attain all perfections. (From the second chapter of the Nigamakalpadruma).

O Supreme Lord! The commencement and the conclusion of the *paśus*, the *vīras*, and the *divyas* are each distinct. The conclusion of the state of *paśu* and the commencement of the state of *vīra* constitute the commencement of the *divya*.
And it is indeed the destroyer of the state of heroism; just as childhood, youth, and old age are dear in their sequence; just as the flower, the fruit, and the seed follow one another in order;
and just as milk, butter, and clarified butter, O Maheśvara! Just as...

O Bharata! Know that the work of volition and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) constitute the threefold nature arising from the commencement of action. The entire world, both moving and unmoving, originates from ignorance; bound by the ropes of ignorance, I create it here again and again.

Ignorance is the root of action as long as one does not find reality; once reality has arisen, there is no longer any latent impression (vāsanā) regarding action. Listen now to my words concerning the cause and effect even for that person who is free from latent impressions and has received initiation preceded by [the proper rites].

Therefore, O Maheśānī! For the Vīras, the Paśu is the cause; for the Divyas, the state of being a Vīra is the cause. Consequently, there is nothing else whatsoever. If anyone abandons my word and does not practice purification, no purpose is served by him.
They share in their desired families. For this very reason, it is stated in the fifty-first chapter of the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
"The state of a *paśu* lasts for only one birth until the age of sixteen; thereafter, the state of a *vīra* persists until the age of fifty. [This occurs] in the second part.

The heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) is the third, which is divine (*divyabhāvaka*). Thus, O Dear One, through these three states alone, the unity of states (*bhāvaikya*) arises. Through the knowledge of this unity, the Kula practice becomes identical with the Divine. For state is a mental quality; one should always practice it with the mind alone. [This applies to] those in the stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*).

Since the apprehension of existence (*bhāva*) has already been discussed, and there is now a desire to know the stages of life (*āśrama*), the stages of life are being defined. Among them, because studentship (*brahmacarya*) is the first to be encountered, it alone is defined at the outset.

In the fourteenth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*, it is said: "Listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess! I shall explain the worship of Brahmā, by the mere performance of which a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. One intent on the meditation of the deity should wear saffron-colored garments."

Delighting in a diet of fruits and roots, he should collect cow's milk; he should not accept rice produced from [ordinary] fields, nor water brought by a Śūdra. Except during the fertile period, he should never approach his own wife. O Maheśānī! Even though he is a householder, he is a celibate.

The Guru is always [to be served]; at times he may indeed be indifferent, or even become the presiding authority over the disciple’s duties. O Caṇḍikā! for such a disciple, there is never any spiritual welfare. O Goddess! the nails, hair, and so forth must never be discarded by the celibate student (brahmacārī); he must always maintain a state of constant devotion.
Devoted to meditation, he should carry a single trident or wear one with three prongs;
he should also place a rudrākṣa bead joined with copper upon his pair of ears.
The fruit of wearing copper is stated in the second chapter of the *Yogasāra*.
By wearing it on the arm, copper removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by wearing it on the hands, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
by wearing it on the ears, copper yields the fruit of ten million tīrthas; and on the neck...
By retaining [this] copper, the yogi shall attain liberation. The word "tāmram" (copper) is used in the accusative case with the sense of the genitive.
The fruit of the holy life (brahmacarya) has been explained in the Nirvāṇatantra, in the fourteenth chapter.

"O Goddess! Wherever there is a celibate (brahmacārī) whose wealth is austerity (tapodhana), in that place prosperity becomes stable; of this there is no doubt. However, in reality, for a Kaula, there is no stage of life known as celibacy (brahmacaryāśrama). This is stated in the eighth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra:"
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:

O observer of excellent vows! Four castes and stages of life have been described, as well as the specific conduct for each caste and stage. However, from the Kṛta age down to the Kali age, five castes are proclaimed: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
O Maheśvarī! For all these castes, there are indeed only two stages of life (āśramas).

O Primordial One! Listen to their rules of conduct and duties; I shall speak to you. Previously, the activities arising from the Kali age were already described for those who are devoid of austerity and Vedic study.

"Even for men of short lifespan, how can there be physical exertion sufficient for the effort required to overcome the afflictions? O beloved! There is no stage of life equal to celibacy (brahmacarya), nor even the forest-dweller's life (vānaprastha).
In the Kali age, only two stages of life remain: that of the householder and that of the mendicant. Thus it is written.
In some places, there is a hermitage because of the observation of legal proceedings.

p. 945) Now, regarding the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*). In the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "Now I shall declare the characteristics of the householder; listen, O Caṇḍikā! One should practice the recitation [of scripture], fire-offerings (*homa*), the honoring of guests, the worship of the gods, the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), family traditions, and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)."

One's own wife is always to be honored; indeed, one's own wife is a deity. One should perform mental worship and practice mental recitation (*japa*). Mental action is indeed the great dharma; there is no sin in that which is mental. (From the *Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*); all the ritual acts of a householder [are likewise mental].

O Śivā! In the Kali age, the rites taught in the Āgamas [must be followed]; by no other paths can success in ritual action ever be achieved for householders. O Goddess! In the Kali age, whether they be Brahmins or members of the other castes, and whether they belong to either of the two stages of life (āśramas), all are equally entitled to these. Indeed, for all without exception—

The sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed according to the path of Śiva. For other types of rites as well, the characteristic marks of the rite (*karmaliṅga*) are distinct for each. One becomes a householder immediately upon birth; through the sacraments, one enters a stage of life (*āśrama*). One should first undertake the state of a householder (*gārhasthya*).
O Maheśvarī! When knowledge of reality has arisen according to the prescribed rule and detachment is born, then one should renounce everything and take refuge in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
One should acquire learning in childhood, wealth and a wife in youth, and [spiritual practice] in maturity.

Having performed one's righteous duties during the fourth stage, the wise man should renounce; yet, having abandoned his aged mother and father, his devoted wife, and his infant son, he should not enter the state of the Avadhūta. [One should likewise abandon] mothers, fathers, children, wives, and kinsmen.
Even his kinsmen—if one renounces the world having abandoned these, he becomes a perpetrator of a great sin;

he would be a slayer of mother, a slayer of father, a killer of a woman, and a murderer of a Brahmin. Furthermore, that Brahmin who departs for the stage of the mendicant without first satiating his ancestors and others is no longer a true Brahmin.
One should perform the sacraments prescribed for one's respective caste according to the Śaiva path; this is the dharma in the Kali age.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord, what is the duty of a householder, and what is that of a mendicant? Tell me of the purificatory rites and other duties for a Brahmin and for those who are not Brahmins.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:

The householder’s life is the primary dharma for all those born as humans; I shall describe that very thing first, O Kaulinī, hear it according to its true essence. A householder should be established in Brahman and devoted to the knowledge of Brahman; whatever action he may perform, let that be offered to Brahman.
One should offer [these]; one should not speak falsely, nor should one perform what is impossible elsewhere. A householder should be devoted to the worship of the deities and guests.
Regarding the guest (*atithi*), as stated in the sixth chapter of the *Nāradapañcarātra*:

"By whomsoever a guest is honored, the entire universe is honored by him. Indeed, Hari himself is pleased with him whose guest is pleased. All the deities are perpetually present in the house of the guest; they are the very shrines (*tīrtha*)."
All merits, vows, austerities, sacrifices, truth, good conduct, righteousness,
and virtuous deeds— all these depart together with those who have failed to honor their guests.
When a guest returns from one's house with his hopes frustrated, both his ancestors and the gods [depart as well].
The fires of meritorious dharma, as well as fame, stability, fortune,
the beloved deity, and the guru, depart in despair, abandoning the man who has committed sin—
even those who have killed women, cows, or the ungrateful, or those who have slain Brahmins or violated the teacher’s bed.

By those who betray trust, the wicked, and those who harm their friends; by those who destroy truth, the ungrateful, and those who destroy their reputation; likewise by sinners, by those who avoid conversation, by those who sell their daughters, and by those who steal the *soma* plant.

By those who give false testimony, by those who seize the property of Brahmins, and likewise by those who misappropriate what is to be established; by those who keep bulls as beasts of burden, by temple-priests, and likewise by those who act as priests for entire villages; by those who eat the food of Śūdras, and by those who eat at a Śūdra’s funeral feast (śrāddha).
By Brahmins who have turned away from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by those who are violent and destroyers of men, by those lacking devotion toward their guru,

by those afflicted by disease, by those who constantly speak falsehoods, by Śūdras who approach the wives of Brahmins and even those who approach their mothers, and likewise by those who harm the Aśvattha tree and by their own wives.

He who fails to honor a guest incurs a fault equal to that of those who kill their parents, those who kill those who have sought refuge, and those among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who steal stones or gold— indeed, he is as one who has directly slain his own mother and father.
A householder should always, with every effort, serve the manifest deity.

O Śivā! when the Mother is pleased; O Pārvatī! when the Father is pleased; then, O Goddess, may there be your satisfaction, and the Supreme Brahman is propitiated. O Primordial One! you are the mother of the worlds, and the Father is the Supreme Brahman.
Furthermore, what austerity can there be for householders that would bring you pleasure?
Having understood the proper time for each occasion, one should provide them with a seat, food, clothing, drink, and even objects of enjoyment; one should speak to them with gentle words.

One should always speak kindly; one who follows the wishes of his parents and the king is a son who purifies his lineage. One should avoid arrogance, mockery, and excessive talk in the presence of one's parents if one desires one's own welfare. Upon seeing his mother or father, [he should behave with humility].

Having bowed, he should rise with all haste; he should not sit down without permission while remaining under his father's command. He who, intoxicated by the pride of learning or wealth, should show disrespect toward his father, goes to a terrible hell, excluded from all dharma. [He should likewise serve] his mother and father...

A householder should not eat while neglecting his children, wife, guests, and siblings, even when his own life-breaths are at his throat. He who eats only to fill his own belly, having deceived his elders and kinsmen, is censured in this very world and shall become a denizen of hell in the next. [Thus speaks] the householder.

One should protect one's wife, practice learning, and nurture one's sons; one should protect one's own kin and kinsmen—this is the eternal dharma. The body was nurtured by the mother and further developed by the father;
he who, having been affectionately instructed by his own kin, abandons them, is the lowest of men. For their sake...

O Maheśānī! He who, even after undergoing hundreds of hardships, constantly pleases [his wife]—this indeed is the eternal dharma. That man is blessed in this world, he is successful, and he is a knower of the supreme truth;
that man on earth is established in Brahman and true to his word. [He does not neglect] his wife...

One should strike her [only] on rare occasions, but always protect her like a mother; one should not abandon her even in the midst of terrible hardship, provided she is a virtuous wife devoted to her husband. While his own wives are present, a wise man should not touch another woman with a wicked mind, for otherwise he would become a denizen of hell. He should sleep and dwell in solitude.

A wise man should avoid another's wife and refrain from improper speech; he should not display his prowess to a woman. He should constantly satisfy his wife with wealth, clothing, affection, faith, and truthful words, and never do anything unpleasant to her. [This applies even] at festivals or public processions.

A wise man should not send his wife to sacred fords or the homes of others when she is deprived of her sons and ministers. O Maheśānī! With whatever man a devoted wife is pleased, all dharma has been performed by him; he is indeed beloved.

For a period of four years, the father should fondle and protect his sons; thereafter, until they reach sixteen, he should instruct them in virtues and knowledge. When the sons are over twenty years of age, he should employ them in the affairs of the household. Then, regarding them as equals, he should manifest affection toward them.

A daughter should likewise be protected and instructed with great effort; she should be given in marriage to a learned groom, accompanied by wealth and jewels. In this same manner, one should [care for] brothers, sisters, nephews, as well as kinsmen, friends, and servants.

The householder should protect and satisfy them. Therefore, the householder should protect those who abide by their own duties, those residing in the same village, those who have arrived as guests, and even neutral strangers. O Goddess, if a householder does not act in this way while possessing wealth, he should be known as nothing more than a beast; he is a sinner and despised by the world.

One should not indulge in excessive sleep, laziness, physical exertion, or the grooming of hair; nor should one be overly attached to food or clothing. Moderating one's diet, sleep, speech, and sexual activity, one should be pure, humble, clean, and skillful in all undertakings. One should be brave toward the enemy.

He should be disciplined in the presence of kinsmen and elders; he should not despise those who are contemptible, nor should he slight those who are proud. Having ascertained through living together their friendships, business dealings, conduct, and innate dispositions, as well as their reasoning, he may then place his trust in them. This...

A wise man, observing the conduct of those who are base, may feel resentment; yet he should not display his own inner state nor transgress his fortitude. One who knows the Dharma should protect his own reputation and manliness, as well as that which was spoken for the sake of concealment and whatever has been done for the benefit of others.

One should not disclose [the matter]. Even if it has been committed in writing, there is defeat in a case involving contemptible conduct. Whether by a great or a small teacher, one who is renowned should not litigate. One should not engage in that which destroys knowledge, wealth, fame, and dharma, nor where one might incur only pride, misfortune, the company of the wicked, or false malice.
One should abandon [worldly concerns]. Actions follow one's state, and rituals follow the established rules (samaya).

Therefore, having observed both the state and the rule, one should perform the rite. One who is devoted to yoga and protection, skillful, righteous, and kind to kinsmen, should be moderate in speech and moderate in laughter.

But one should especially be respectful toward the venerable. Having conquered the senses, with a serene mind and good thoughts, one should be firm in one's vows. Vigilant and far-sighted, one should purify the contacts of the senses.
A wise person should speak words that are truthful, gentle, pleasant, and beneficial. [One should avoid] self-exaltation...
Likewise, one should avoid censuring others. He by whom a reservoir, a tree, a resting house on the road, or a bridge has been established has conquered the three worlds.
In that family where the parents are contented and kinsmen are affectionate, [the ancestors] sing:

By whose fame the worlds [are known], by him the three worlds have been conquered; he for whom truth alone is the vow, who possesses compassion for the distressed in every way, and for whom desire and anger are subdued—by him the three worlds have been conquered. Furthermore, O Goddess, purity is twofold, distinguished as external and internal.

The dedication of oneself to Brahman is known as internal purity (*āntarika-śauca*). The removal of impurities by means of water or ashes, whereby the purification of the body is achieved, is called external purity (*bāhya-śauca*). In this context, sacrificial ashes (*yājñika-bhasma*) are the best, though clay (*mṛtsnā*) is also acceptable.

She is free from impurity. External purification is prescribed at the conclusion of sexual intercourse, at the end of urination and defecation, after eating, when touched by filth, and upon contact with excrement. However, O Śivā, what is the use of much speaking here? A householder should perform whatever rite of purity and impurity ensures that his mind becomes pure.
One should perform that. The three daily *sandhyā* rites should be performed according to the Vedic and Tantric traditions in their proper order.

One should perform worship according to the rules, with distinctions such as the various modes of adoration (*upāsanā*). Likewise: the offering of the water of honor (*arghya*) to the Sun and the recitation (*japana*) of the *Gāyatrī* mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times.

Or even ten times, O auspicious lady! There is a rule for recitations in every daily rite; however, only Śūdras and those of other castes have the right [to perform them] according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas, O Goddess!
From that, all perfection shall arise.

In the second chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "The householder possesses a divine form adorned with sandalwood and other ornaments. This householder, appearing in the form of a virtuous person, is the father of all. He is ever devoted to giving, illustrious, and always intent upon sacrifice."

One should diligently establish the five *tattvas* in the middle of the house; at that very moment, one becomes a master of all *siddhis*, of this there is no doubt. O Maheśānī! whatever deliberations regarding mantras there may be, or any disparagement of the group of *siddhas* and others—all that pertains to the householder.

The Sage has determined: the best of practitioners, having reflected well, should take up a great mantra—whether it be a single syllable, a *kūṭa*, or a *mālāmantra* and so forth. O Goddess of Gods! there is no need for such deliberation regarding a mantra obtained in a dream; yet even so, a householder must reflect well upon a great mantra.
For one who carries a staff, there is no need for ornaments when initiated into any mantra.

(p. 950) Having entered the stage of a householder, he who delights in the knowledge of reality is liberated from all sins; he is indeed Maheśvara himself. [The merit that comes] from the gift of food...
O beautiful goddess, whatever fruit is obtained through the gift of water belongs entirely to the householder, and not to anyone else!
In the eighth chapter of the Nityātantra.
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord! The characteristics of the Kaula conduct have been described. How, O Master, does it exist among householders and kings? The Lord said:

O Goddess, due to the differentiation of the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—the eternal Kaula Dharma exists within all beings. Sattva arises through the yoga of devotion as the sole cause of all manifestation; for this very reason, O Maheśānī, householders...
The Sāttvika state is considered [the highest]. Through the yoga of action (karmayoga), Rajas arises; the king is the performer of action.

For this very reason, O Maheśānī, the king is remembered as being characterized by Rajas (rājasika). Śambhu, the Lord of Yogins and Supreme Lord, abides in the state of Tamas; for this very reason, one should take refuge in the state of Tamas.

Free from attachment. O Maheśvarī! The Śakticakra, the Rājacakra, and the Vīracakra—therefore, O Parameśvarī, these must be performed in due order. [As stated] in the seventh chapter of the Kubjikātantra:
"O Sureśvarī! Having seen the Aśoka tree, the Bilva tree, and the Śivā (the jackfruit tree)..."

One should perform prostration for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. O Goddess of the Gods! One should pay homage to the owl, the Śaṅkhacilla bird, and the vulture, as well as to Mahākālī;
thus one shall obtain victory in battles. [One should also visit] a crossroads and a cremation ground.

One should especially pay homage [to them]. O fair-faced one! One should also pay homage to the knower of the Tantra and the Avadhūta. Upon seeing a practitioner (upāsaka), one should always speak sweetly. O Goddess! Without the observance of the rules (samaya), success (siddhi) shall never be attained.
Therefore, one should indeed receive it with great effort; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now, regarding the stage of the ascetic (yatyāśrama), it is stated in the thirteenth chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra:

Endowed with all auspicious marks, the Brahmin should proceed; having gone into the presence of Daṇḍin, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff, saying: "O Lord of the gods of gods! You alone are the savior;
you alone are the protector of the worlds; protect me, who have come to you for refuge."
In the word *vastā*, the causative sense is intended, meaning "one who causes to dwell" (*vāsayitā*).
Having heard this, Daṇḍadhārin respectfully asked the people: "Who are you?
Whose son are you? Tell me, by what means did you come here? Hearing those words, the Brahmin—

(p. 951) He uttered the offering of himself: "Born indeed in a lineage of Brahmins, I am such-and-such, possessed of discernment. I have no father present before me, nor do I have a wife, sons, or the like. My parents are dead, as are my brothers and other children."
"Afterwards, upon the loss of my beloved wife, I was indeed overwhelmed with extreme grief;

therefore, O Lord, grant me the supreme stage of life (paramāśrama). By this it is indicated that while one's father and others remain, the ascetic stage (yatyāśrama) is not possible; [only] after abandoning them does the staff [of renunciation] become one's."
In that very context, the words of the staff-bearer (Daṇḍin), containing a statement regarding the fault of the upholder [of the vow], are as follows:

"O best of the twice-born! Make true what was indeed spoken in my presence. By the fault of speaking falsehood, one is surely deprived of the path of Brahman; of this there is no doubt. O twice-born one, speak before me!"

O Supreme Goddess! For him who maintains the staff while his beloved wife remains in the prime of her youth, everything indeed becomes fruitless. O Goddess! For him who maintains the staff while his parents are still living, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is fruitless, and he goes to the hell named Raurava.

"He will go [to hell]. O Supreme Goddess! For him who possesses a wife and likewise a son due to his state of childishness, the undertaking of renunciation is indeed in vain; both that teacher and that disciple fall into the hell named Raurava. Having heard such firm words as these...

"Only one who carries a staff and has conquered his senses should receive the gift of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and eternal liberation. Having heard such words revealing the faults [of worldly life], and having again heard a firm statement from his father and others confirming the certainty of death, he—
The syntactical connection is that one should offer the gift of renunciation (sannyāsa).
He states that method: "At the beginning, the Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear the ten-syllable mantra first."
The venerable Śaṅkara said:

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the supreme ten-syllabled mantra, by the mere hearing of which even a fool assumes the form of Viṣṇu. O Queen of the Gods, if a male practitioner recites a Śakti-mantra without knowing that great mantra, he [is lost].

One would become a Brahmarākṣasa. Even if one were a knower of reality (tattvajñānin) without knowing that great mantra, he would nevertheless go to hell; such is the consensus of the Veda. Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the supreme vision of the mantra: the seed-syllable *mayā* and the seed-syllable *badhū*.
Lakṣmī, Kālī, and Pāśaka; Gaganam, Pakṣibījam, and Vahnikāntā—O Dear One! Thus, O Caṇḍī, this unsurpassed ten-syllable mantra has been declared to you.
By knowing which, one attains immortality; of this there is no doubt. Of this...

By the mere act of grasping it, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa; by the mere grace of this, the bearer of the staff (daṇḍin) shall attain liberation. O Supreme Goddess! One should recite this ten-syllable mantra over the staff;
from this mantra, great mantras are born—of this there is no doubt. All...

The conduct of the gods arises certainly from the *daśārṇa*; yet the practitioner of the Great Vidyā does not perceive the *daśārṇa*. In this world he is poor, and in the next he becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
Therefore, O Queen of the Gods, the Guru should diligently cause the *daśārṇa* to be heard; [it is] exclusively—

The supreme practitioner should listen but not recite [the mantra] himself; he who causes the ten-syllable mantra to be heard is that man, the most excellent of gurus. O Goddess, when one is the giver of the mantra, he alone is remembered as your guru.
O Goddess, he who gives the ten-syllable mantra is indeed the supreme guru, just as it is said in the *Amarataraṅgiṇī*:
All rivers are unequal; O Goddess worshipped by the gods, there is no mantra equal to that of Daśārṇa.
Likewise: Hereafter I shall declare the form of the staff-bearing [vow]:
one who is virtuous in form, a householder, a Brāhmaṇa, and a proclaimer of Brahman.

Having completely abandoned all illusion, he is devoted to all dharmas; he has conquered his senses and conquered his anger, maintaining equanimity toward all castes, as well as toward son and enemy, during the twilight hours and likewise during rites for prosperity. There is no attachment to body or life, whether today or at the end of the age.

For one whose mind finds delight in knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman, the assumption of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) must be performed by Brahmins for the sake of liberation. That Brahmin who bears the staff is Nārāyaṇa himself; they are born with four arms.

Merely by wielding the staff, and having heard that, one should cause the great undertaking to proceed; one should travel with speed for a *krośa* or two *krośas*. The preceptor and the disciple, according to the rule, should stand one behind the other, [the disciple saying]: "Wait, wait, O mighty-armed one! Do not [leave] me!"
Do not depart after abandoning me. You are a disciple who is a Paramahaṃsa; there is no one equal to you on this earth. You must forgive my offense; you alone are the one who bears the form of Viṣṇu.
You alone are worthy of worship by the worlds; you alone are honored by all. You alone are the Supreme Haṃsa; please remain.

"Stay! Do not go!"—O Goddess, because the disciple utters these words to Daṇḍin, that supreme *haṃsa* lies bewildered upon the path. And for the sake of beholding him alone, the deities in the intermediate space are present together with their consorts.

Accompanied by their retinues, they arrive from the cardinal and intermediate directions. At this moment, the staff-bearer (daṇḍī), firm in his vows, should console the excellent disciple; having uttered the *phutkāra* sound many times with this mantra, he should restore the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) once more through those *phutkāra* sounds, which possess the force of the wind.

It is said that at that very moment, another birth for that very person occurs. Observing this other birth, the Guru should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). Having brought [the child] near the staff, he should perform the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana). Addressing him as "You are so-and-so," he should offer a flower into the fire.

One should deposit [the disciple] there; having established him by this name, one should perform the great consecration (*mahāsaṃskāra*). Furthermore, O Goddess, for the sake of the disciple's knowledge, the staff-bearer [the Guru] should say: "Listen, O disciple! O you of great fortitude!
Take my words to heart. For him, another birth is indeed more dear than life itself."

One should transform [one's perception]. This body is of the nature of a corpse; of this there is no doubt. Be detached from everything, and do not seek satisfaction through the pursuit of food. Eat only that which is given by a Brāhmaṇa. One should always practice the five principles (pañcatattva) with a hidden disposition.

Having conquered the senses, always perform mental worship, always perform mental libation, and diligently practice mental yoga at the navel-pit during the three junctions of the day. Diligently perform both mental enjoyment and renunciation; having become a conqueror over the six internal enemies.
