By the mere act of wielding the staff, a man himself becomes Nārāyaṇa; of this there is no doubt. Seventeen generations on his father’s side, thirteen on his mother’s side, and the seventh generation on the side of his wife—he shall become Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. Thus it is said.

Having heard his words, the disciple spoke these words: "I shall perform without ceasing that which was told to me for the sake of liberation. The five principles (pañcatattva) must always be practiced;
tell me, from what [practice] does the gain arise? Where indeed does the staff-bearer reside?"
Surrounded by many disciples, go there and strive diligently to distinguish [the true teacher] from among the many disciples;
or else, proceed with effort into the midst of heroes. Indeed, the knowledge of reality departs from the presence of a householder; one must travel even to a very great distance to where he dwells.
The leader of the family; the mendicant’s conduct is not for his own sake, but rather for the sake of the deity. (p.
954) Upon seeing the teacher’s wife, however, he should go for alms with a concentrated mind, saying:
"O Mother, give me alms; I shall satisfy Kuṇḍalin. Having spoken thus, then...

The staff-bearer (Daṇḍin) should perform the great consecration (*mahāsaṃskāra*). Having brought [the disciple] near the staff, he should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite. Then, holding the hand, he should again offer eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the syllable *hūm*.
He should perform the purification of the limbs (*aṅgaviśodhana*) in reverse order. Thereafter, he should perform...

With effort, one should maintain an inner sacred thread (*antaryajñopavītaka*); I consider its crest to be the crest itself, which one should place in the midst of the betel nuts (*pūga*). One should then fix the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) upon that very [crest] by means of the root-mantra.
Having smeared the betel nut with clarified butter and clay, one should then purify it. That betel nut...

One should cast [the materials] into the center of the sacrificial pit with the root mantra. Then, the wise one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). O Dear One! He should then dispatch that betel-nut (pūga), together with the sacrificial thread and the top-knot (śikhā). There, he should recite the root mantra one thousand times, plus eight hundred more (gajāntaka-sahasra).

And then, O beautiful one, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the mantra of Kālikā; or else, one should cause him to hear the supreme, rare mantra of Tārā. Having recited the root mantra, by the diligent consumption of betel nut and ashes, at that very moment—

One who visibly wears the inner sacred thread (*antaryajñopavīta*) is indeed Nārāyaṇa himself; of this there is no doubt. Having procured a *vilva* staff, one should procure a single bamboo staff as well.
One should diligently perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of Kālikā upon the *vilva* staff, followed by the placement of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*).
Having fashioned the staff, one should contemplate the Goddess within it. One should unite the consciousness residing in the bilva fruit with the bamboo staff.
O Supreme Goddess, this staff is the very form of the chosen deity! One should perform the placement of the staff in the right hand of the disciple. Having brought the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu)...

The wise man should recite the Vāruṇa mantra; he should pour the Vāruṇī water therein and then recite the Mūla-mantra one hundred and eight times. Having recited it, he should place it in the person's left hand. He should carefully clothe him in a reddish-brown (gairika) garment. Merely by holding the staff, a man becomes Nārāyaṇī.
It shall be so. Until today, contemplate Mahāmāyā upon the staff; then perform the worship of Mahākālī upon the staff with your heart. For you are indeed Nārāyaṇa in person;
be devoted to dharma and adharma. Your mother, father, and master—all are at the end of the staff.
Thus ends the undertaking of the supreme stage of life.

p. 955) Regarding the manner of the staff-bearer’s (*daṇḍin*) wandering for alms, it is stated in that very same [text]: "The wise man, having addressed Nārāyaṇa, should go to the door of the house of the twice-born householder, even if it is very far away. In that same [text], it describes what the householder must do immediately after the arrival of the staff-bearer:

Having heard this, the householder should join his palms in reverence; and seeing a staff-bearer at the door, the best of Brahmins should prostrate himself. O Dear One! He should diligently offer alms, excluding honey and meat. Having received the alms, O Goddess of Gods, he should depart like a thief.

He should wander. The manner of staying for a *daṇḍin* is also described in that very same place: "O Goddess, he should cause his residence at night to be in the house of a householder; likewise, having gone to a city, he should stay for three nights;
then, having gone to a sacred site (*tīrtha*), he should dwell there for seven nights. Upon seeing a *daṇḍin*...

The duties of a Brāhmaṇa have been stated in that very same [text]: "Upon seeing a staff-bearer, a Brāhmaṇa should bow according to the prescribed rule, O Goddess of Devas! Whether the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) is full of water or empty, the best of the twice-born should make that vessel full by the mere sight of it."

The fruit of giving water in a *kamaṇḍalu* is also mentioned in that same place: "If one should offer even a drop the size of the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass into a *kamaṇḍalu*, he certainly obtains the fruit of giving the seven oceans. The censure of giving water is also in that same place: "If, out of delusion, he should not give..."
He would become a refuge for calamities; furthermore, he would become a tree for thirty thousand years.

Thus, O Caṇḍī, I have told you the supreme practice of maintaining the renunciant’s staff (saṃnyāsa-dhāraṇa). It must never be spoken in the presence of an uninitiated person (paśu), even at the cost of one's life. In truth, however, the taking up of the staff in the Kali age—
It does not exist; for it is prohibited by such statements as "long-term celibacy and the carrying of a water-pot," which are upheld in the *Udvāhatattva* and other works.

Also, in the eighth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra: "O Goddess, even in the stage of life of a mendicant (*bhikṣuka*), the carrying of the staff prescribed in the Vedas does not exist at all in the Kali age, because the knower of reality possesses that Vedic consecration. [Rather,] he maintains the stage of the *avadhūta* according to the procedure for Śaiva consecration."

"O blessed lady! That very [practice] called the taking of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) has been taught for the Kali age in the second night of the Nārada-pañcarātra: 'In the Kali age, the taking up of the staff is not at all a cause of liberation;
rather, it is contrary to the Vedas and leads to the opposite result,' and so forth."
And because it has been prohibited [in other texts]. As for that which is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*:

O Caṇḍikā! There is no renunciation (saṃnyāsa) anywhere other than with a Brāhmaṇa. That man who, out of delusion, practices it elsewhere is indeed a refuge for sin. O Queen of the Gods, my beloved of life! Listen with a secret disposition: O fair-faced one, the five principles (pañcatattva) must always be served by a renunciant.

If death does not occur within twelve years, one should cast one's staff into the water and become a Paramahaṃsa. Devoted to the conduct of an Avadhūta, such a Haṃsa is the most excellent of all; he is renowned as Ānanda, and Sarasvatī [resides] within him for twelve years. Thus it is said.
The statement also refers to [the practice] other than the Kali age. "Sarasvatī" is a specific designation among the ten types of *āvadhūtas*; its authoritative source is as follows:
"Tīrtha, Āśrama, Vana, Araṇya, Giri, Parvata, Sāgara, Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, and Purī—these ten are proclaimed. Thus [it is said]. Their definitions are found in the *Bṛhacchaṅkaravijaya*.

As held by Vidyāraṇyasvāmin: One should bathe at the holy confluence (tīrtha) of the three rivers characterized by "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and other such mahāvākyas, with the realization of the true meaning of reality; he is called a "holy place" (tīrtha). One who is mature in the adoption of the stages of life (āśrama) and is free from the snares of desire [is likewise so called].

Freedom from coming and going—this is the defining characteristic of this stage of life (āśrama). He who dwells in a delightful region by a waterfall or in a forest, liberated from the bonds of hope, is called a Vanaprastha (Forest-dweller). Constantly established in the forest, in the grove of bliss (Ānandanandana), having renounced all this—

The universe indeed has bliss as its defining characteristic. He who dwells eternally on an excellent mountain, who is devoted to the practice of the Gītā, and whose intellect is profound and steady, is called "Giri" (the Mountain).
He who, being mature through meditation and concentration, dwells at the foot of mountains and discerns the essence within the essence, [is likewise so called].

He who is proclaimed as a mountain dwells deep as the ocean, possessing a wealth of forest jewels, and never transgresses his boundaries; he is thus proclaimed as the ocean. He who is ever under the control of the knowledge of musical notes, who speaks with melodic tones, is a lord among poets, and indeed knows the essence within the ocean of worldly existence—[he is the true singer].

Sarasvatī || 8 || One who is filled with the weight of knowledge casts off all burdens; he does not know the burden of suffering—he is proclaimed as Bhāratī. Filled with the essence of wisdom, established in the state of the perfect reality, he is eternally devoted to the station of Brahman. || 9 ||

He is called by the name Purī. (10) Even now, those who perceive the *Kevala-nirvāṇa-tantra* act in such a manner. Furthermore, the state of being an *avadhūta* belongs only to those in the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramin*). Thus it is said in the *Yoni-tantra*: "Among the stages of life, the *avadhūta* stage is the greatest."
There, by means of the family yoga, I attained the state of a Great Deity.
Now, the stage of the Avadhūta, from the eighth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:

O Goddess! In the Kali age, the stage of the Avadhūta is called Sannyāsa. Listen now to all that must be performed according to the prescribed rule: when knowledge of Brahman has arisen and all ritual actions have ceased, one who is proficient in the science of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) should enter the stage of Sannyāsa.
Having abandoned his aged parents, his young wife devoted to her husband,

and having left behind capable kinsmen, one who goes forth into homelessness shall become a denizen of hell. Having completed his household duties and satisfied the scriptures, he should depart from his home free from possessiveness and devoid of desire.

Having conquered his senses, a man desiring to depart from his home should call together his kinsmen, relatives, villagers, and neighbors, and seek their affectionate consent. Having obtained their permission and bowed to the Supreme Deity, he should [leave] the village.

Having circumambulated [the teacher] and become indifferent toward home and possessions, one who is liberated from the snares of saṃsāra and nourished by supreme bliss should approach a Kulāvadhūta who knows Brahman and pray as follows: "O Brahman! This [life] of mine in the householder stage has now passed away."

"O Master! Grant me the favor regarding the undertaking of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Having considered that one has ceased from household duties, and having observed him to be peaceful and discerning, the Guru should direct him toward the second stage of life (the life of renunciation). Then the disciple, having performed his bath and with self-restrained mind—"
Having performed his daily rites, he should worship the gods and sages, as well as the ancestors, for the sake of liberation from the three debts.
The gods are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, together with their retinues;
the sages are Sanaka and others, and likewise the divine sages are Atri and others. Here, those who are the ancestors to be worshipped are as follows:
I shall speak; listen to them as well: the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather;
likewise, O Goddess, the mother, the grandmother, and the great-grandmother;
and similarly, the maternal grandfather and so forth, as well as the maternal grandmother and so forth. [One should worship] the sages in the eastern direction.

One should worship the gods in the south and worship the ancestors; one should honor the maternal grandfathers in the west during the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). One should offer two seats each, starting from the east in due order. Having invoked the gods and others there in their proper sequence, one should perform the worship.
Having worshipped them according to the rules, one should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to each individually.
Having offered the rice-balls in due order according to the ritual for offering piṇḍas, one should, with palms joined in reverence, pray to the ancestral deities: "Be satisfied, O ancestors! O gods!"

O divine sages, O Mothers, O Gaṇas! In the state that transcends all qualities, may you soon discharge my debt. Having requested freedom from debt and having bowed down again and again, one should perform the *ātma-śrāddha* (the ancestral rite for oneself), liberated from the three debts; for the grandfather is indeed the self itself.

O Goddess, for the sake of offering oneself to the Self, the wise man— whose father and great-grandfather are all [the ancestors]— should perform the rite of the Self. Facing north and seated upon a prepared seat as before, he should invoke his own ancestors, offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and worship them.

One should spread *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, southward, and westward respectively, for the purpose of the *piṇḍas*, according to each specific rite; having completed the *śrāddha* rituals by the path shown by the Guru.
One desiring liberation should recite this mantra a hundred times for the sake of purifying the mind: "Hrīṃ!

We worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of nourishment. May he release me from death, as a cucumber from its stem, but not from immortality. According to the method of practice, [one attains] knowledge.

Preceded by the construction of the mandala, the Guru, having placed the water-pot (kalaśa) there, should commence the worship. Then, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman by way of the Śāmbhava path,
the knower of Brahman, having performed the worship, should carry out the installation of Brahman.

Having offered the oblations as prescribed by the ritual intention into the fire previously consecrated, the Guru should summon the disciple and cause him to offer everything [within himself] into that fire. First, having offered with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should perform the *prāṇahoma*. [The offerings are]: Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.
The winds. There, one should then perform the oblation for the sake of liberation from the impurities of the body:
earth, water, fire, wind, and space; smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, in their respective order; and then speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals.
Furthermore: the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*).

These are purified at the end of my feet; one should utter the word "pada. *Hrīṃ*, may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—thus [ending] with the "dviṭha" (the letter *ḥ*). The twenty-four principles (*tattva*) are the ritual actions (*karman*).

And having offered Vedic oblations into the fire, one should then contemplate the body as being inactive and like a corpse. Having visualized it as a corpse—devoid of all ritual action—one should remember that Supreme Brahman and remove the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) while reciting: *aiṃ klīṃ hūṃ*.

Having removed the sacred thread from his shoulder with the mantra, the knower of reality should hold the *yajñasūtra* in his hand, recite the three *vyāhṛtis*, utter the wife of fire (*svāhā*), and cast it, smeared with ghee, into the fire. Having thus offered the sacred thread while reciting the *kāmabīja*, he should cut it.
Having placed the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) in one’s hand, one should apply it into the midst of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*): "O Daughter of Brahmā! O Śikhā!
You are indeed eternal and in the form of a child. A place is being offered in the fire; go, O Goddess! Salutations to you!
One should then utter the *kāma*, *māyā*, and *kūrca* mantras, followed by the wife of Vahni (*vahnijāyā*).

The ancestors, the gods, and likewise the divine sages, relying upon the crest-lock (śikhā), all those who perform acts of dependence dwell upon the crest-lock. Therefore, having satiated all those divine sages, ancestors, and deities, by the relinquishing of the crest-lock and the sacred thread, the embodied soul becomes composed of Brahman.
It may be so: for the twice-born, renunciation occurs through the abandonment of the sacrificial thread and the topknot;

for Śūdras and others, however, the consecration occurs only after offering the topknot into the fire. Thereafter, having released his topknot and thread, he should prostrate like a staff before the Guru. The Guru, having raised him up—

He should say this into the right ear of the disciple: "Thou art That, O one of great wisdom! Realize: 'I am He,' the *haṃsa*. Free from possessiveness and free from ego, conduct yourself happily according to your true nature.
Then, having discarded both the water-pot and the fire, the knower of the reality of Brahman [should realize] that very form of the Self.
Having recognized [the Guru], one should bow with the head: "Salutation to you, salutation to me;
salutation to you, salutation to me, salutation, salutation! You alone are He, and I am indeed you, O Viśvarūpa! Salutation be to you!
[This is for] those who worship the Brahma-mantra, who know reality, and whose selves are conquered, by means of their own mantra.
Upon the cutting of the topknot, one becomes a renunciant (saṃnyāsin).
For those purified by the knowledge of Brahman, what is the use of sacrifices, ancestral rites (śrāddha), or worship?
For those devoted to acting according to their own will, no transgression is found. Therefore...

Free from duality, desireless, and steady-minded, the disciple should wander on this earth as one who is truly Brahman itself, devoid of the sense of "mine. Liberated from injunctions and prohibitions,
free from the concern for acquisition and preservation, the knower of the Self remains equanimous in pleasure and pain— steadfast, self-conquered, and free from longing.
Steadfast in soul, though he has encountered suffering, he remains free from longing even when happiness is attained;

ever blissful, pure, tranquil, indifferent to worldly concerns, and undisturbed; he shall not cause agitation to living beings, but shall always be devoted to the welfare of all creatures, free from resentment and fear, and self-controlled.

Free from conceptual construction and free from effort, one should be liberated from sorrow and hatred; one should be the same toward enemy and friend. Enduring cold, wind, and heat, one should be equal in honor and dishonor. Equal toward the auspicious and the inauspicious, one should be content with whatever object is obtained by chance. Free from the three qualities (*guṇa*) and free from doubt.

One should be free from greed and not accumulate possessions. Just as the entire world of falsehood is established by relying upon truth, so too the body depends upon the Self; one who understands this does not suffer.
The senses alone perform their respective functions individually; the Self is merely the witness.

Being untainted by knowing this, one shall partake in liberation. A renunciant should avoid accepting gifts of base metals, censuring others, falsehood, dalliance with women, attachment, and malice toward others. He should maintain an equal vision toward all—toward an insect, a deity, and likewise a human. All...

A wandering mendicant (parivrāj) should recognize Brahman in all actions; whether it be the food of a brahmin or the food of a dog-cooker, since it has come from the same source, he should eat it without discrimination, considering the place, the time, and the food itself,
always through the study of the scriptures on the supreme self (adhyātma-śāstra).
Through investigations into reality, the Avadhūta, devoted to the conduct of his own choice, should pass his time.

He should never cremate the dead body of renunciants; rather, having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he should either bury it or immerse it in water. This applies to mortals who have not attained yoga.

O Goddess! For those who always long for sensual desires, worldly engagement arises from their power amidst the turmoil of karma. Even here, they are devoted to meditation, worship, and the practice of recitation;
knowing that alone to be the highest good, they possess firm resolve in that very path. Therefore, [follow] the ordinances of action.

These have been proclaimed for the purification of the mind. For that purpose, various names and forms have been imagined by me. O Goddess! Without the knowledge of Brahman and without the renunciation of ritual action, one who performs ritual action for a hundred aeons shall not become a vessel for liberation. [Such is the case for one who is] a Kulāvadhūta, a knower of reality.

A man liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is the very form of Nārāyaṇa; therefore, a householder should worship him as such. By the mere sight of a mendicant (yati), one is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of visiting sacred fords, observing vows, performing austerities, giving gifts, and offering all sacrifices. Thus ends the stage of the Avadhūta.
Its subdivisions are [discussed] in the fourteenth chapter (ullāsa).
The goddess spoke.
Two types of stages of life (āśrama) have been proclaimed: namely, the householder and the mendicant. (p.
961) Why is this heard—that there are four kinds of Avadhūtas?
I desire to know this; tell me in truth, O Lord! [Regarding] the four kinds of Avadhūtas...
The characteristic, with its specific distinctions.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:

O Dear One! Those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others who worship the Brahma-mantra should be known as ascetics (yatīs), even while living in the householder stage of life. Furthermore, those men who have been consecrated by the rite of full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should be known as Śaiva Avadhūtas and are worthy of worship.

O you who are worshipped by noble families! May the Brahman-avadhūtas and the Śaivas, who abide by the highest conduct, perform all rites perpetually according to the path proclaimed [by us], except for that which is offered to Brahmā and that which is offered to the Cakra; likewise, they should avoid forbidden food and water.

They shall never accept [these things] from the Brahmāvadhūta-Kaulas who have received initiation. O fair-faced one, the Dharma and the codes of conduct have already been declared: bathing, renunciation, drinking, giving gifts, and the protection of a wife.
Everything [is established] through the path of scripture for both the Śaiva and the Brahmāvadhūta.
In the Nirvāṇatantra, in the fourteenth chapter.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:

Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain how one becomes an Avadhūta. One who is ever devoted to the ultimate reality (tattva) should know the form of the Hero (Vīra). Whatever form has been described as the supreme assumption of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), all actions are performed in that very form.

The one beloved by heroes should perform it; O Dear One! just as one would practice the shaving of the head for a staff-bearer on the new moon day, so indeed should one perform the shaving of the hero’s head. [One should shave] the unadorned mass of hair, leaving only a hanging tuft of locks.

Or he may adorn himself with a garland of bones, or even wear rudrākṣa beads; the lord of heroes may go naked, or else wear only a loincloth; he should smear his limbs with red sandalwood paste and use ashes as an ornament for his body.
In the second chapter of the *Yogasāra*:
"O Dear One! A yogin should always carry a human skull, a wooden staff, an axe, and a deerskin, just like [the Lord].
The yogin should carry a *khaṭvāṅga*, garments of bark, and a skull-bowl."

One should wear the moon [on the forehead] especially with sandalwood paste and other unguents. O son, one should always wear slightly reddish-brown clothing. "O virtuous one" (*sata*) is an address to Śiva.
The wise one should wear that wheel known as Sudarśana; where the yogin plays the lute, the tawny drum, the *maḍḍu*, the *ḍiṇḍima*, the *jharjhara*, and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).

In which hermitage does he reside? [It is said] in the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "O Daughter of the Mountain! Forgiveness, generosity, and meditation through a state of childlike innocence—[this is the path]. 'I am Śiva, I am Bhairavānanda; I am liberated, the leader of the Kula. A mantra devoted to such a state of being, endowed with its proper cause, is Sadāśiva."
One should always practice the service of consciousness and the service of the cause; that person will undoubtedly become manifest as the very form of Sambhu. — *Mahānirvāṇatantra*
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, and even one of common birth—
all five have the entitlement for the consecration of a Kulāvadhūta," as stated in the *Nirvāṇatantra*.

Through the state of a hero (*vīrabhāva*), the Brāhmaṇa attains liberation in Nirvāṇa; the Avadhūta Kṣatriya and the Mahāyogin do so as well, without a doubt. Even a Vaiśya may become his own true nature, and even a Śūdra becomes possessed of the world. The Brāhmaṇa attains the complete fruit, which is the state of Nirvāṇa.

A Kṣatriya attains three parts of the fruit by virtue of his heroic nature; that of a Vaiśya is two parts, and that of a Śūdra is one part. The individual names of the ten Avadhūtas have been stated previously; now, [regarding] them...
In that very [context], for the purpose of formally accepting [the state] as primary, he states the specific definition of the "womb" (garbha) and the designation [of its names]:

"O Daughter of the Mountain, listen to the description of the Avadhūta! [The womb consists of] the forest (vana), the wilderness (araṇya), the speech (bhāratī), the mountain (giri), and the city (purī)."

Staying in a single place, one should practice the desired meditations and so forth; he who bestows mantras through austerity is proclaimed as a *vana* (forest-dweller). With disheveled hair or matted locks, he should always be like a madman; O Daughter of the Mountain! he is an internal yogi, a great hero, and one who has no attachment to the forest.

He who is learned in various scriptures, skilled in various rites, and who meditates upon the stainless [Goddess] as his own chosen deity— he alone is the heroic Bhāratī, a possessor of great knowledge,
one who has conquered his senses, a hero with arms perpetually raised and hair disheveled.

The Digambara: That best of men who meditates with equanimity everywhere—apart from his chosen deity (iṣṭadevī)—is proclaimed to be a mountain. He should constantly wander through various countries, sacred seats (pīṭhas), fields (kṣetras), and holy sites (tīrthabhūmis), and he should perform worship there with diligent effort.

Constant meditation upon the deity as well as the worship of the illustrious Guru, and being steadfast in internal sacrifices—he is indeed a hero and a true Purī. O Goddess! For him whose devotion to the Avadhūta stage of life is perfectly firm, Kālī becomes pleased; what, then, cannot be accomplished on this earth?

Having beheld the Avadhūta, one should perform worship as if [beholding] Śambhu. One should diligently offer the five tattvas according to one's capacity; O Supreme Goddess! if one is incapable, one should satisfy him with devotion. (From the Mahānirvāṇatantra). The Bhaktāvadhūta is of two kinds.

Based on the distinction between the complete and the incomplete: the complete one is known as the *paramahaṃsa*, while the other is remembered as the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*). If one who has performed the *avadhūta* consecration should be weak in knowledge, then, while remaining in the abode of the world, he should purify himself.
Protecting the marks of his own caste and performing only his prescribed duties, he should always be devoted to Brahman and thus accomplish the supreme knowledge.
In the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra: "The Avadhūta is Śiva himself;
Sadāśiva is the Avadhūta. The goddess Śivā is the Avadhūtī.
Listen to what is inauspicious for the Avadhūta. Among the four stages of life (āśramas)..."

The stage of the Avadhūta is great. And the Avadhūta is of two kinds: the householder and the one who follows the funeral pyre. He may be clothed or naked, following the prescribed rules for conduct; he may have a wife or remain celibate forever, laughing loudly (aṭṭahāsa) and wandering with directions as his only garment. O Goddess of Gods! such is the householder-avadhūta; the second, however, is—

Sadāśiva [states]: Regarding the performance of ritual action by the Avadhūta with the mantra *oṃ tatsat*, the Mahānirvāṇatantra says: "Uttering the mantra *oṃ tatsat* and contemplating 'I am That,' one who has always taken refuge in dispassion (*vairāgya*) should perform the actions appropriate for oneself while doing so."

Unattached to actions, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, one should strive to uplift oneself through the discernment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Regarding this very point, he states the fruit of action for all by means of the designation "It is *sat*": "Whatever action one may perform with the mantra *oṃ tat sat*..."
Whether he be a householder or indifferent, that [merit] shall accrue to his desired object;
likewise, the completion of the rite performed with that mantra occurs right there.

Recitation, fire-offerings, consecrations, and all other ritual acts—accomplished with the mantra "Oṃ Tatsat"—will undoubtedly be complete and perfect. What need is there for many other mantras or numerous other means? By means of this Brāhmaṇa-mantra, all rites [are fulfilled].

One should accomplish it. It is easy to practice, free from excessive difficulty, and bestows the complete fruit. O Ambikā, there is no other means superior to this Great Mantra! Having written it down, one should wear it upon the body or in a city district; his home becomes a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*), and his body [is likewise sanctified].

It shall be meritorious. O Goddess of the gods! This mantra—*oṃ tatsat*—is the essence of the essences of the *nigamas*, *āgamas*, and *tantras*; it has been spoken truthfully before you. For the fourfold categories of principles (*tattvas*) and other entities as well, there is no need for purification by other mantras.

If it has been purified by this [means], then seeing the form of existence everywhere and muttering that great mantra which is that very reality, one who acts according to his own will and possesses a pure mind is indeed the sovereign of the Kaulas on earth. Through the recitation of this, one becomes accomplished; through the contemplation of its syllables, one becomes liberated.

The embodied soul is directly composed of Brahman; one should recite this mantra for this very purpose. This great mantra consists of three parts and is the cause of all causes. By the practice of this mantra, one becomes a conqueror of death himself. Or else, it may consist of pairs of words, each [pair] individually.
Or even just the single word; O Great Goddess! by reciting this, the practitioner shall become a possessor of siddhis.
Thus ends the praise of the mantra.
In that very same [text], it is stated that the Śaiva-avadhūta has no authority over any ritual action (*karma*).
For one whose entire karma has been shaken off by the purificatory rite of the Śaiva Avadhūta, there is no eligibility for rites performed for the gods, nor for ancestors, nor for the ṛṣis.
Now, concerning the Paramahaṃsa: among the four types of Avadhūtas, the fourth is called the Haṃsa.

The other three are rich in yogic enjoyment; all are liberated and equal to Śiva. The Haṃsa should not engage in sexual union with women nor maintain possessions; he merely experiences the fruits of his past karma (prārabdha).

He should dwell free from prohibitions and injunctions; he should abandon the marks of his own caste and the duties of householders. As one in the fourth stage, he should wander the earth without resolve and without effort, always content in his own self-nature, devoid of grief and delusion, homeless, and patient.

He may be free from attachment and free from affliction; for him there is no offering of food or drink, nor does he require meditation or mental concentration. Liberated, fully released, beyond the pairs of opposites, the ascetic is devoted to the conduct of the *haṃsa*.
Thus, O Goddess, have I described to you specifically the characteristics of these four types of *kula*-yogins.
For these holy ones who are my very own form, through seeing them, touching them, conversing with them,
and pleasing them, the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites is attained by those born as human beings.
(p. 965) Now, the different types of conduct (*ācāra*). The conduct of the Vedas has already been described;
now that of the Vaiṣṇavas and others is being stated. In the first chapter of the *Nityātantra*:
"Now I shall declare, O Great Goddess, the supreme conduct of the Vaiṣṇavas, by the mere knowledge of which time [is conquered]."

He should keep his hands joined in *añjali*; always devoted to the observances according to the sequence of Vedic conduct, he should never engage in sexual intercourse nor in conversation about it. He should avoid violence, censure, crookedness, and the eating of meat. At night, he should avoid garlands and mechanical devices.
One should never touch [impure things]; O Goddess! one should worship Viṣṇu and offer all actions to Viṣṇu. O Goddess! one should always contemplate the entire world as being composed of Viṣṇu.
Such is the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava.

Likewise: "Listen, O fair-limbed one! O fortunate lady! To the Śaiva practice, which is very difficult to attain, and which is established within the Śaiva and Śākta [traditions] according to the sequence of Vedic conduct—its specific feature, O Great Goddess, is solely the slaughter of animals. Now listen; I shall speak."

O Adrijā! Because this [path] was formerly resorted to by the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, for that very reason, O Maheśānī, it is called Dakṣiṇācāra. This practice is the first to have been set in motion for both the Divya and Vīra [classes].

One should worship the Supreme Goddess according to the very sequence of Vedic conduct; having taken up Vijayā at night, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. [From the Third Chapter: "O Bhadrā! O you who are beautiful in every limb! Listen to the Divine-Vīra doctrine; I shall explain it in brief."

The fifth practice is the most excellent. O Maheśānī! During the days, being a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and composed in mind, one should worship the Goddess at night according to the secondary ritual of the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
Listen to another [instruction], which I shall declare as the essence of essences, higher than the highest, within the knowledge consisting of the bliss of Brahman.

Out of affection for you, O Pārvatī! This compendium of knowledge, hidden within the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas, is established, O Goddess, like fire within wood. Just as there is no actual slaughter of a horse in the performance of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, even so...

O Supreme Mistress! No fault exists in the sacrifice. O Pārvatī! That which is pure and impure becomes pure through purification alone. O Great Goddess! This indeed is the defining characteristic of the Siddhānta conduct. [From] the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*: "Having bathed..."

Wearing white garments and likewise dressed in pure attire, always devoted to the worship of the gods and intent upon Viṣṇu during the day, and at night offering all materials such as substances and the like in the best possible manner according to the rules with devotion— he shall obtain the full fruit of it all.
He will subsequently establish the family tradition. Thus end the varieties of conduct.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Knots Consisting of the Determination of the State of the Fettered (Paśubhāva) and Other States," in the seventh section on the Attributeless (Nirguṇakāṇḍa) of the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Now, the Full Initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). From the tenth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
This supreme rite was once kept secret throughout the three worlds;

by performing it with secrecy, men attained liberation in former times. But in this powerful Kali age, when the path of Kula has been made public, one should perform the consecration either at night or during the day, for there is no [attainment] without consecration.

A Kaula [is so called] simply by the consumption of wine. One who has received the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) becomes a Kaula, a lord of the circle (cakrādhīśa), and a worshiper of the Kula. There, on the morning of the initiation, for the pacification of all obstacles, one should [worship] Vighneśa with offerings according to one's capacity.

The Guru should perform the worship. O Dear One! If the Guru is not authorized for the auspicious full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), then one who has been consecrated as a Kaula should accomplish all of that. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this [mantra] is proclaimed to be the letter at the end of *kha* (the letter *ha*) joined with the nasal bindu (*hrīṃ*). Its sage is Gaṇaka and its meter is...

The deity is Nivṛttivighna (the Obstacle-Remover). He is employed for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the rite to be performed. One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the root mantra conjoined with the six long vowels.
Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should meditate upon Gaṇapati, O Śivā!

Having the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and a broad belly; holding in his lotus-like hands a sword, a noose, a goad, and other desired objects, as well as a jar filled with wine that shines in his reddish palms;
with his head illuminated by the crescent moon, having the face of a lordly elephant, and his cheeks moistened by a citron fruit—[I bow to him].
Worship Gaṇapati, whose ornaments are bound with the lord of serpents, and who is clad in red garments and red unguents.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should worship the Power of the Seat (pīṭhaśakti). [These are: Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpiṇī, Ugrā, Tejasvatī, Satyā, and Vighnavināśinī in the center. Having worshipped these starting from the east, one should worship the Lotus-Seated One (kamalāsana).

Having meditated again upon Gaṇeśāna and worshipped him with the fivefold offerings (*pañcatattvopacāra*), the most excellent practitioner, O Kaulinī, should worship Gaṇeśa, the Leader of the Gaṇas, the Lord of the Gaṇas, and the Playful Gaṇa in the four directions—
namely, Ekadanta, Vakratuṇḍa, Lambodara, and Gajānana.
And one should worship Mahādeva, who is formidable, smoke-colored, and the destroyer of obstacles;

then one should worship the Śaktis headed by Brāhmī and the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas). Having fully worshipped their weapons, one should dismiss Vighnarāja. Having thus completed the worship—

One should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of Vighneśa and feed the knowers of Brahman and the Kula-practitioners with the five elements (pañcatattva). Then, on the following day, having bathed and performed the daily obligatory rites,
one should offer gold and sesame seeds for the destruction of sins committed since birth.

O Dear One! For the sake of satisfying the Kaulas, one should feed at least one person; having offered *arghya* to the Sun, and having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the nine planets, and the hosts of Mothers, one should perform the *vasudhārā* rite. For the success of the ritual, one should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
Then, having gone to the side of the Guru and prostrated, one should pray as follows: "Come, O Nātha!
O you who follow the family tradition! O beloved of the lotus-clan! O ocean of compassion, place the shade of your lotus-feet upon my head! O highly fortunate one, grant me your command!"
"In this auspicious *pūrṇābhiṣeka*, may I attain the unimpeded accomplishment of the rite through your grace! O child, by the command of Śiva-Śakti, perform the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*!
By the teaching of Śiva, may the accomplishment consisting of the fulfillment of your heart’s desire arise! Thus [he gave] the command of the Guru.

Having attained this for the sake of pacifying all calamities and for the acquisition of longevity, prosperity, strength, and health, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Then, having made the resolve, and having honored the preceptor with garments, ornaments, decorations, and pure ritual implements, one should choose him as the teacher. The preceptor [should enter] into a pleasing house.
Variegated with red ochre and other pigments, adorned with colorful banners and flags, and beautified by fruits and flowers;
graced with garlands of networks of tinkling bells and illuminated by moonlight;
and rendered free from even a trace of darkness by rows of lamps fed with ghee.
In a place well-perfumed with incense containing camphor and yakṣa-dhūpa,
adorned with fans, chowries, peacock feathers, mirrors, and other ornaments, one should construct there an altar made of clay, four fingers high and measuring one and a half cubits.

Then the venerable Guru should construct the Sarvatobhadra mandala using powders made from unbroken grains (akṣata). He should perform the ritual of worship according to the procedure prescribed in the respective tantra. Having performed this, he should purify the five principles (pañcatattva) according to the previously mentioned method. Having thus purified the five principles—

In the previously prepared maṇḍala, one should place a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; having washed it with the *candrabīja* mantra, adorned it with curd and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and established it with the *brahmabīja* mantra, one should mark it with vermilion (*sindūra*) by means of Śrī.

p. 968) One should fill that [vessel] with the causal [substance] by means of reciting the root mantra, using the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, adorned with the *bindu*. Alternatively, one may fill it with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or pure water; [and place] the nine gems or gold within the jar.

He should cast it away. The treasury of compassion should place a sprout derived from the *panasa*, *uḍumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vakula*, or *āmra* trees into its mouth with the *vāgbhava* mantra. Furthermore, having uttered the *ramā* and *māyā* mantras, he should set down an earthen bowl provided with fruit and unbroken rice grains.
O fair-faced one! One should bind its neck with a pair of cloths upon the sprouts;

for Śakti, red cloth is prescribed, while for Śiva and Viṣṇu, white cloth is proclaimed. Having remembered Sthāṃ, Sthīṃ, Māyā, and Ramā, and having stabilized it within the interior of the jar, one should deposit [the deity].
One should arrange the five principles (pañcatattva) and nine vessels. The vessel for Śakti should be made of silver, the vessel for the Guru of gold, and the Śrīpātra should be a great conch-shell;
the others may be fashioned from copper, stone, wood, or metal.
One should avoid [unfit vessels] and prepare a vessel according to one's capacity for the worship of the Great Goddess (Mahādevī).
Having arranged the vessels, one should satisfy the Gurus and the Goddess.
Then, the wise practitioner should worship a jar completely filled with nectar (amṛta) and, having displayed it—

One should offer incense, lamps, and an oblation to all beings. Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditated, and invoked Maheśvarī, one should worship the desired deity according to one's capacity, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth. Having performed and completed the fire sacrifice (homa)...
The practice of the Kumārī-Śakti: O Śivā! That Guru should worship [her] with flowers, sandalwood, and garments, saying:
"May the Kaulas, who observe the Kula-vow, show favor toward my disciple;
may you grant your permission for the rite of the Full Consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka). Thus he asks.

The lords of the wheel (cakreśas) should say with reverence to the guru: "By the grace of Mahāmāyā and through the power of the Supreme Self (Paramātman), this disciple has become perfected and devoted to the Supreme Reality (Paratattva). Then, having worshipped the Goddess, the guru and the disciple should worship the jar (ghaṭa) [with the mantras] Kāma, Māyā, and Ramā.
Having recited [the mantra], he should move the supreme jar. "Arise, O Brahma-jar!"— thus the Guru, facing north,
filled with compassion, should consecrate [the disciple] with these mantras that are about to be described.
Sadāśiva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the Śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka; the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh;

the deity (devatā) is Ādyā; the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be the Praṇava; and its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the purpose of the Śubhapūrṇābhiṣeka. May the gurus consecrate me with this substance.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; and Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Bhavānī—the Mothers—consecrate you. May Ṣoḍaśī, Tāriṇī, Nityā, Svāhā, and Mahiṣamardinī—may these consecrate you.

With water purified by mantra: "May Jayadurgā, Viśālākṣī, Brahmāṇī, Sarasvatī, Bagalā, Varadā, and Śivā—may these sprinkle you! And may Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vanamālinī, Indrāṇī, Vāruṇī, and Raudrī [do the same]."
May the Śaktis consecrate you! || 4 || May Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Umā, Kṣamā, Śraddhā, Kānti, Dayā, and Śānti always consecrate you!
May Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahānīlasarasvatī, and Ugracaṇḍā... || 5 ||
And may Pracaṇḍā always consecrate you. (6) May Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, and Bhārgava-Rāma consecrate you with water.
(7) Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, and Bhayaṅkara—

May Kapālī and Bhīṣaṇa consecrate you with water. May Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, and Mahogrā always consecrate you. May Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and likewise Pavana [consecrate you].

May Dhanada and Maheśāna, the lords of the directions, sprinkle you. (10) May the planets—the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—along with the lunar mansions, sprinkle you. (11) [May] the lunar mansion, the *karaṇa*, the *yoga*, and the days [of the week] [bestow blessings].
May the fortnights and the days, the seasons, the months, and the years always consecrate you. 12.
May the oceans— those ending with the salt, sugarcane, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk,

and fresh-water oceans— consecrate you with water purified by mantra. May the great serpents beginning with Ananta, the birds beginning with Suparṇa, and the trees beginning with the Kalpa-vṛkṣa [consecrate you].

May the lords of the directions sprinkle you—those who move through the netherworld, the earth, and the sky, who travel for the sake of well-being, and who are gratified by the full consecration—with water. May they consecrate you.
May misfortune, ill-repute, diseases, dejection, and likewise sorrows perish, struck by the seed-syllable of Kālī through this consecration. 16.
May the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and those *grahas* who cause misfortune flee and perish, struck by the seed-syllable of Ramā. May the defects caused by malevolent spirits,
those arising from hostile mantras, and the defects born of mind, speech, and body [be destroyed].
May they perish through this consecration! May all calamities be destroyed;
may all prosperities be firmly established; through this complete consecration, may all desires be fulfilled.
Having thus performed the ritual sprinkling with twenty-one mantras,
the Guru should cause the initiate to hear once more the mantra obtained from the mouth of the sacrificial animal (paśu).

Addressing them by the names previously mentioned and making the practitioners of power (śakti-sādhakas) understand, the Kaulika Guru should recount the narrative beginning with Dadya and ending with Kulanātha. O Goddess! having worshipped his own deity in the Guru who has heard the mantra, he should thereafter honor the Guru with the offerings of the five elements (pañcatattva).

Having given cows, land, gold, garments, vehicles, and ornaments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, one should worship the Kaulas who are of the nature of Śiva. Having performed the Kaula worship, the wise man—
calm and endowed with great humility— should touch the feet of the venerable Guru with devotion.
Having bowed, one should pray as follows: "O Śrīnātha! Lord of the worlds! My Lord!
O ocean of compassion! Fulfill my heart's desire by bestowing the supreme nectar. O Kaulas, who are the manifest form of Śiva, grant me your command for the sake of my disciple."
I give the supreme nectar to the disciplined one. O Lord of the Wheel! O Supreme Sovereign!
O Sun to the Kaula-lotus! Make this true disciple successful;
grant him the nectar of the Kula, having received the command of the Kaulas, which is filled with the supreme nectar.

He should place the purified drinking vessel into the hand of the disciple. Having drawn the Goddess from his heart into the Guru by means of the ash adhering to the *sruva* ladle, he should apply a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) upon himself, upon the disciple, upon the *kaulas*, and upon the *kūrca*. [The term] *kūrca* refers to the space between the eyebrows. Then, he should bestow the principles of grace (*prasādatattva*) upon the *kaulas*.

One should cause [the disciple] to be served; one should provide food and drink according to the rules for the performance of the meal. Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the auspicious and complete consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which is the sole generator of the knowledge of Brahman and the means for attaining the fruit of Śiva-hood. [It may be performed] for nine nights, seven nights, or five nights.
For three nights, or alternatively, one should perform the full consecration for even a single night.

O Maheśānī! regarding this rite of refinement (*saṃskāra*), five ritual procedures (*pañcakalpa*) have been proclaimed. During the nine-night rite (*navarātra*), the *sarvatobhadra* mandala should be prepared; during the seven-night rite, the *navanātha* [mandala].

In the *Pañcarātraka*, there is a five-petaled lotus; O Dear One, in the *Trirātra* and *Ekārātra*, as well as in the *Sarvatobhadra* and *Navanābha* mandalas, nine jars should be established by the practitioners. In the five-petaled [lotus], five jars are to be placed.
O Goddess, on an eight-petaled lotus, one jar is prescribed;
one should worship the deities of the limbs and the coverings upon the filaments and other parts.
By the mere sight of Kaulas who have attained perfection through the full consecration and whose souls are stainless— [The text continues: ...by the mere sight [of them], [one attains merit].

Purification of the Guru is prescribed through touch or smell by the Śāktas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, Sauras, and Gāṇapatyas alike. A virtuous practitioner who has taken recourse to the Kaula path should accomplish this with great effort; likewise, there should be the worship of the Śakti and the five elements (pañcatattva), and so forth.
One should purify [it] by means of the ritual procedure for one's own chosen deity, but one should not become the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara). Likewise:
Many applications and various ritual acts have been described;

for the Kaula who is solely devoted to Brahman, renunciation and performance are equal. Indeed, knowing that the one supreme Brahman alone exists pervading the universe, and that every action is permeated by it—
O beloved! Even those who worship with a sense of duality reach that [Brahman] and enter into it;
everything is Brahman, and everywhere Brahman alone remains as the ultimate conclusion. He alone should be known as a true Kaula, liberated while living—of this there is no doubt.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), according to the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*.

On the morning of the consecration, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles, the Guru should worship Gaṇeśa with offerings according to his capacity. If the Guru is not authorized therein, then he should accept an initiated Kaula as his Guru and have everything performed by him. *Gam* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Gaṇeśa.

Having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), sat upon his seat, and sipped water (*ācamana*), he should perform the ritual actions beginning with the placement of the *arghya* offering and ending with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Then, he should perform the ritual placement of the seers and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*) as follows:
Gaṇaka is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Nīvṛt is the meter (*chanda*), and Vighnarāja is the deity (*devatā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) in order to pacify all obstacles for one who has completed the ritual of self-initiation (*svakarttavyapūrṇābhiṣeka*).
On the head: *oṃ gaṇaka-ṛṣaye namaḥ*. In the mouth: *namo nīvṛc-chandase*.
In the heart: *namo vighnarājāya devatāyai*. *Gāṃ* to the heart: *namaḥ*.
Having performed the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* with these [mantras] and the like, and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra,
one should meditate as follows: [He is] the color of vermilion, three-eyed, with a broad belly,
holding a sword in his lotus-like hands...

Worship Gaṇapati, who holds a noose, a goad, and a lotus, with his red hands shining with a water-pot full of wine; whose crown is illuminated by the crescent moon; who has the face of a lordly elephant; whose cheeks are moist with a citron fruit; who is adorned with the king of serpents; and who wears red garments and red unguents.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should worship the powers of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*) upon the yantra or the jar, as follows: "Oṃ, these are the fragrance and flowers; obeisance to Tīvrā.
In this same manner, everywhere, with the *praṇava* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, [one worships] Jvālinī, Nandā, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
One should worship [the goddesses] in the sequence starting from the east: Ugrā, Tejasvatī, Satyā, and Vighnanāśinī in the center.

Then, offering these perfumes and flowers with "Oṃ, obeisance to Kamalāsana," and having meditated again, one should place them upon the water-pot and other vessels, and invoke Gaṇeśa with "O Gaṇeśa, come here! followed by the offerings of water for the feet (pādya) and so forth.
Having worshipped with the offerings of the five principles (pañcatattva) and in the four directions, these scents and flowers are offered:
"Obeisance to Gaṇeśa; likewise to Gaṇanāyaka, Gaṇanātha, Gaṇakrīḍa, Ekadanta, Vakratuṇḍa, Lambodara, Gajānana, and Mahādeva."
One should worship Vikaṭā, Dhūmābhā, and Vighnanāśana everywhere with incense and flowers, using mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. [Likewise, one should worship] Brāhmī,
Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Nārasiṃhī.

Having worshipped with the mantra "Obeisance to Mahālakṣmī, to the guardians of the directions beginning with Indra, and to the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt," one should then recite the root mantra as much as possible, offer the recitation, prostrate, and dismiss [the deity] with the words, "O Gaṇapati, forgive me. Then...

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) as prescribed in the *Dīkṣāpaddhati*, one should feed the knowers of Brahman, the members of the lineage, and the practitioners with the five principles (*pañcatattva*). Then, on the following day, having bathed and performed the daily rites, one should utter "Oṃ tat sat" and say: "Oṃ, today, etc., in such-and-such month, when the moon is situated in such-and-such zodiac sign..."
On this day, in the month of Bhāskara, in such-and-such a fortnight, on such-and-such a lunar date, I, Śrī-Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such a lineage,

desiring the destruction of sins committed through both knowledge and ignorance since birth, offer this gold with a *tilaka* mark, dedicated to the deity Viṣṇu, to a Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such a lineage and name as available.

"I have bestowed [it]. Having thus uttered this, he should cast the golden *tilaka* as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then, for the satisfaction of the *Kaulas*, he should set aside one portion of food. Then, having offered the *arghya* to the Sun and worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the nine planets.

Having performed the worship of the sixteen Mothers beginning with Gaurī, the pouring of the Vasudhārā stream, the recitation of the Āyuṣyasūkta, and the Abhyudayika Śrāddha, one should go to the presence of the Guru, prostrate, and pray: "Oṃ, come, O Lord! O Kula-practitioner! O Beloved of the Nalinī family!"
"O ocean of compassion! Place the shadow of your lotus feet upon my head!

O illustrious one, grant me your command for this auspicious and complete consecration! By your grace, may I attain the successful accomplishment of this rite without obstacle. Then the Guru shall say: "Oṃ."

"O child! By the command of Śiva and Śakti, perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka). May the perfection consisting of the fulfillment of your heart's desire arise by the decree of Śiva. Having thus received the permission of the Guru, [the disciple says]: "Today... [etc.
...I, of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Amukadevaśarman, desiring the attainment of longevity, prosperity, strength, and health..."

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) as described in the tenth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra," one should recite either "oṃ yajjāgrataḥ" or "oṃ devo vaḥ.
Then, having performed the ritual acts beginning with "oṃ sādhu bhavān āstām," [one should honor the disciple] with garments, ornaments, and so forth.

Having worshipped the Guru with the cause for purification, [one should recite]: *Oṃ adya* etc., in the rite of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) as taught in the tenth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*:
"In this rite of full consecration, [I initiate] the venerable *Amukānandanātha* of the *Amuka* lineage..."

The disciple says, "I choose you as my guru, so that you may perform the duties of a guru. The guru should say, "Om, I am chosen. Then the disciple says, "Om, perform the duties of a guru as prescribed. [The guru replies], "Om, I shall do so according to my knowledge."
The Guru should say: "Then, in a beautiful house well-painted and adorned with variegated banners, flags, and the light of moonbeams, well-perfumed with incense such as guggulu and the like,
and where even a trace of darkness has been dispelled by rows of lamps fed with ghee..."
Upon an earthen altar four finger-breadths high and measuring one and a half cubits,
one should construct a Sarvatobhadra or other mandala using powders of five colors.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows: having constructed a Sarvatobhadra mandala for the nine-night consecration,
a Navanābha for the seven-night consecration, a Pañcābja for the five-night consecration,
and an eight-petaled lotus for the three-night or one-night consecration, therein—

One should perform the placement of the jar (*ghaṭasthāpana*) as described in the *Dīkṣāpaddhati*. Then, having purified the five principles (*pañcatattva*) and so forth, one should place curd and parched grain (*dadhyakṣata*) into the jar with the lunar seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ*. One should establish the jar with the Brahma-seed-syllable *oṃ*. [With] *śrīṃ*...

One should place vermilion in the jar with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī. One should fill the jar with the syllables from *kṣa* to *a* accompanied by the nasal bindu, using the root mantra and the syllable *ṭha*. Alternatively, one may fill it with water from a sacred pilgrimage site or pure water. [Then] the nine gems...
Or one should place gold inside the vessel.
One should place the five young shoots (*pallava*) of the *panasa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vakula*, and *āmra* at the mouth of the vessel with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, *aim*.
One should place a new shallow bowl (śarāva) containing fruit and unbroken rice (akṣata) upon it with the mantra "Śrīṃ" and "Hrīṃ.
One should bind the neck of the jar with a pair of cloths. The procedure there is as follows:
with red [thread] for the Śākta [tradition], and white for the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava [traditions]. Then, [one recites] "Sthāṃ Sthīṃ Hrīṃ."

Having stabilized the jar with the mantra *śrīṃ*, one should place nine vessels starting from the south between the jar and the *śrīpātra*. The sequence there is as follows: the vessel for Śakti is made of silver, the vessel for the Guru is made of gold, and the vessel for the Vīra...

The great conch-shell may serve as one's own vessel, or likewise other vessels made of stone, wood, or metal may be prepared. Then, one should satisfy the Guru and the Goddess with the *kāraṇa* offering. Thereafter, according to the procedure prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), [one should offer] into the full jar of the *kāraṇa*.
Having fully worshipped the deity, having recited the mantra according to one's capacity and offered the recitation (*japa*),

having performed the offering of oblations (*bali*) and so forth, having recited the hymns (*stava*) and armor-verses (*kavaca*) and so forth, and having offered one thousand and eight or one hundred oblations, [one should worship] with perfumes, flowers, garments, garlands, vessels, and other such items.

Having worshipped the Kumārī, the Śakti, and the practitioners (sādhakas), [the officiant] recites: "Oṃ! May the Kaulas, who observe the Kulavrata, show favor to my disciple; may you grant your consent for the consecration of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka). When the Lord of the Cakra (cakreśvara) recites this, they should say: "Oṃ."

By the power of Mahāmāyā and by the majesty of the Supreme Self (Paramātman), you shall become a perfected disciple (pūrṇa-śiṣya) devoted to the supreme reality (paratattva). Then the Guru, having had the Goddess worshipped by the disciple in the previously mentioned jar, and having muttered "Śrī" and "Hrīṃ," should move the jar [with the mantra]: "Oṃ uttiṣṭha."

"O Brahma-kalaśa! O bestower of the desired perfections of the deities! Fulfill this person's heart’s desire with water filled from all sacred fords (tīrthas). Having recited this, [one should consider]: Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the disciple’s chosen deity is the divinity (devatā), and the Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja); [this is used] for the attainment of longevity, fame, strength, health, and so forth.

The application for the Full Consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*): Oṃ! May the Gurus—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you. May the Mothers—Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Bhavānī—consecrate you. May Ṣoḍaśī, Tāriṇī, Nityā, Svāhā, and Mahiṣamardinī [consecrate you].
May these [goddesses] consecrate you with water purified by mantras:
Jayadurgā, Viśālākṣī, Brahmāṇī, Sarasvatī, Vagalā, Varadā, Śivā, Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vanamālinī. (3)
May Indrāṇī, Vāruṇī, and Raudrī—the Śaktis—consecrate you.
May Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Umā, Kṣamā, Śraddhā, Kānti, Dayā, and Śānti always consecrate you. [And] Mahākālī.
May Mahālakṣmī, Mahānīlasarasvatī, Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā,
and the others always consecrate you. May Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, and Bhārgava-Rāma consecrate you with water.
May Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhonmatta, Bhayaṅkara, Kapālī,
and Bhīṣaṇa consecrate you with water. May Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, and Mahogrā always consecrate you.
May Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, as well as Kubera and Īśāna—may these lords of the directions sprinkle you with water. || 10 ||

May the planets— Ravi, Soma, Maṅgala, Budha, Jīva, Śita, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu, together with the lunar mansions— consecrate you. May the lunar mansions, the Karaṇas, the Yogas, the days of the week, the fortnights, the days, the seasons, the months, and the years consecrate you.

Always. || 12 || May the oceans—the salt, sugarcane, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and freshwater oceans—consecrate you with water purified by mantras. || 13 || May the great serpents beginning with Ananta, the winged beings beginning with Suparṇa, and the trees beginning with the Kalpa-tree [consecrate you]. || 14 ||
May the lords of the directions— those who move through the netherworld, the earth, and the sky, who travel for the sake of well-being,
and who are gratified by the full consecration— sprinkle you with water.

15. May misfortune, ill-repute, diseases, dejection, and likewise sorrows perish, struck by the seed-syllable of Kālī during this consecration. 16. May the spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, as well as those planetary influences that cause calamity, flee and be destroyed.

Struck by the seed-syllable *Rām*, may the defects caused by malevolent spells (*abhicāra*), those arising from the mantras of enemies, and the defects born of mind, speech, and body be destroyed through this consecration. May all calamities perish;
may all prosperities remain firm through this complete consecration.
"May all desires be fulfilled. (19) Having thus consecrated the disciple with these mantras, the Guru should again cause him to hear that mantra which was obtained from the mouth of the *paśu*.
Addressing the disciple by the previously mentioned name and informing the practitioners of the *śakti*:

The preceptor should give the name ending in Ānandanātha to the disciple. Having heard the mantra from the guru, the disciple, having worshipped his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), should honor the guru with the five principles (pañcatattva). Then, he should give the guru a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of cows, land, gold, clothing, vehicles, and ornaments.

Then, having worshipped the practitioners of the Kaula-śakti with the five elements (pañcatattva) and touched the feet of the Guru, one should pray as follows: "O Śrīnātha! O Lord of the worlds! O my Lord!
O ocean of compassion! Fulfill our heart's desire by bestowing the supreme nectar (parāmṛta). Then...
The Guru says: "O Kaulas, who are the manifest forms of Śiva! Grant me your permission;

I shall bestow the supreme nectar upon this humble and worthy disciple. They should say: "O Lord of the Cakra, O Supreme Sovereign, O Sun to the lotus of the Kaulas! Make this worthy disciple one who has achieved his purpose."

"Give this nectar of the Kula to such-and-such a person. Having thus received the Kaula command, he should give the *kāraṇapātra* (the vessel of the cause) along with the purification to the disciple.
Then, he should apply a tilaka on the foreheads of everyone using the ashes clinging to the *sruva* ladle. Thereafter, having completed the circle (*cakra*), [he should proceed].
"One should dwell as one pleases. Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.
Immediately after the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), however, in the Vāmakeśvaratantra,
in the fifty-fourth chapter:
Bhairava said:

One should construct a pavilion according to the rules and prepare the articles for worship. The preceptor, who is a *paramahaṃsa*, should perform the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣecana*). Having placed the nine gems in water and having filled the water-pot (*kumbha*) with water—[as stated] in the fifty-second chapter—one [should use a pot] that is not too short.

The eight excellent vases should not be too long; they consist of the nature of consecration and are adorned with jewels and other ornaments. Furthermore, in the northeast, one should place a pitcher adorned with gold and other materials, and one should wrap all the vases with cloth.
Preceded by garlands and sandalwood paste, may all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
the oceans, the lakes, the streams, the most meritorious pools, the rivers flowing through the subterranean realms (pātāla),
and all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) take up residence within this jar, empowered by the recitation of the seed-syllable of Ramā.

One should offer a sprout; the offering of fruit should be done with the *kūrca* mantra, and a stable form with the female seed-syllable (*strīvīja*). One should place vermilion with the fire-seed-syllable (*vahnivīja*) and a flower with the *preta* mantra.
A wise person should offer *dūrvā* grass with both the root-mantra and the *praṇava*. *Hūṃ Phaṭ*.

One should perform the striking with a *darbha* grass blade while reciting the mantra "Svāhā. One should worship the Goddess in the *īśa*-pitcher according to the procedure stated in the *saṅkalpa*. Then, one should worship the retinue (*āvaraṇa*) according to the procedure stated in the *saṅkalpa*.
The wise expert in the *tantra* should diligently offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the procedure taught in the *Āgama*.

One should perform the *kuśaṇḍikā* rite there; one should offer oblations with a *vilva* leaf according to the rule of being smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). One should worship the Goddess again with the sixteen services (*upacāras*).
O Goddess! the wise one should again worship the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) with diligence. Then, [one should offer] the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having given [the gift], one should perform the worship of the Guru; one should worship eight beautiful altars and also worship young maidens.
In the fifty-fourth chapter: "O Goddess of Devas! At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the consecration with water-pots (*kalaśa*). I shall specifically declare its mantra;
listen with reverence: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauḥ putra! tvaṃ sarvasiddhīśvaro bhava* (O son! may you become the lord of all supernatural powers)."

Thus, with the eastern water-pot, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple. With the mantra: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kroṃ hauḥ haṃ saḥ, putra! tvaṃ vetālo bhava* (Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kroṃ hauḥ haṃ saḥ, O son! may you become a Vetāla), the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple with the fire-pot alone. [With the mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ haṃsaḥ, putra!* (Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ haṃsaḥ, O son!)
"May you become a master of the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as *aṇimā*. With these words, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple with the southern jar. "Oṃ huḥ hrīṃ krīṃ śrīṃ! O son!
May you become a master of the *añjanā* siddhi. With these words, the Guru should sprinkle the disciple with the southwestern jar (*nairṛta-kalasa*).
Auspicious! *aṃ āṃ aiṃ kroṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*, O son!
May you become a master of the supernatural powers beginning with *laghimā*. With these words, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious child with the water-pot of Varuṇa.
*oṃ āṃ aiṃ krīṃ hrīṃ*, O son! May you become a master of the desired supernatural powers (*kāmyasiddhi*).
"Be so!"—with these words, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple with the *marut-kalaśa*. "Aiṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ!
Son, may you become a master of the siddhis of immobilization (*stambhana*) and the rest!"—with these words, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple with the *kuvera-kalaśa*. Haṃsa Aiṃ Hrīṃ.

Having first performed the naming ceremony with nine new names, the Guru should sprinkle the auspicious disciple with the water from the Īśāna-pitcher, saying: "O son! May you become a master of the siddhi of ākarṣaṇa (attraction). Thus ends the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) up to the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The best of practitioners should perform [this]. Thus ends the section on consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

(p. 978) Now, the praise of the hero (*vīra*). In the sixty-third chapter of the *Utpattitantra*: "O Goddess! O Supreme Sovereign! Wherever a hero dwells—whether he be divine or otherwise—all sacred sites (*tīrtha*) reside there for the sake of the hero's accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*). He who is a hero is Śiva himself, the very God; of this there is no doubt. Where...
O Goddess! A hero shall dwell there; who could have any fear? There is no untimely death there, nor likewise any fear of famine; O Goddess! there is never any fear of oppression by kings there.
Now, regarding the heroic deed (*vīrakṛtya*) in that very same context: A hero (*vīra*) should always be devoted to the family tradition (*kulācāra*) and associated with the family (*kula*).
O Maheśvarī! He should practice the service of *saṃvit* (consciousness) and drink the soma. O Goddess! A hero of exalted mind performs [this] in every way; he is indeed divine.
The deity is smeared with applications of sandalwood and agallochum, and well-anointed with the scents of red sandalwood;

of this there is no doubt. The hero is grey with ashes on his limbs, acting like one intoxicated, constantly devoted to drinking liquor, and intent upon offerings and worship. [He is] a man, a goat, and a buffalo.
The ram, the boar, the hare, the porcupine, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise—these ten are traditionally listed.
Furthermore, the monkey, the donkey, the elephant, the horse, birds, and so forth—with offerings of such creatures, one should worship one’s chosen deity. Likewise, daily...

One should perform the occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites day after day; likewise on the day of one's own *kula*-weekday, under the *kula*-constellation, and on the lunar day of *candana*. O Beloved! having established the wheel (*cakra*) fashioned for Bhairavī as before, O Supreme Goddess! one should duly perform the purification of the liquors (*surā*) once the [rite] has commenced.

In the Bhairavī-cakra, all castes are the best of the twice-born; when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes are distinct once again. [Objection: But surely, since drinking liquor—which is said in the Smṛtis to produce great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—is prohibited, one who is "addicted to drinking liquor" [would incur sin].
If it is asked how [the statement] "the purification of the gods" is consistent [with this], the answer is true:
it should be understood that those various statements prohibit drinking except on specific occasions or for ritual purposes; otherwise, [it would be contradictory].
Because they would contradict the Vedas, those respective Smṛtis would incur a loss of authority. And thus,
in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and the Vājapeya rite, one takes the cups of *surā* (fermented liquor), and one takes both the cups of *soma* and the cups of *surā* for the Vājasṛts.

"Invoke the drinkers of *surā*, etc. Furthermore, the purification of *surā* has been stated by means of [the mantra] "The swan dwelling in purity," etc. (p. 979). If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the other Vedic text stating that 'liquor is not to be given, not to be drunk, and not to be accepted'?"—it is not so, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning.

You suspect a fault; for indeed, its meaning is that liquor—which is distinct from what is to be given to the deities—is not to be drunk and not to be accepted by them. Or rather, it may be intended to prohibit the giving and drinking of liquor in other contexts, such as in the case of a *nimitta-yajña* (an occasional sacrifice).

It should be understood as *śruti*. One must not argue that, based on the consistency of such statements as "the human horse-sacrifice (*narāśvamedha*), liquor, and [other rites] excluding the *kaula* [tradition] are for the twice-born," the Vājapeya and other sacrifices pertain only to eras other than the Kali Yuga; for this has been refuted by Vidyākaravājapeyin and others.
Because it is determined even in the Kali age according to its name,
a twice-born man should offer both the Vijayā and the Anukalpa in every age.

The conclusion of those of dull intellect— that the sacrifice may be accomplished by means of a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) based on such statements— is incorrect, because it has been stated that a secondary alternative is only prescribed when the primary [means] is unavailable.

And likewise, in the fifth chapter of the *Niruttara-tantra*: "In the absence of the [actual] substance, one should worship the Supreme Deity with substitutes (*anukalpa*); and in the absence of wine, a twice-born man should offer cow's milk in every age. From such statements, it follows that the performance of the sacrifice is accomplished by means of a substitute.
The established conclusion for those of dull intellect is that [the primary substance] must indeed be unavailable, since it is stated that there is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).

Thus, it is said in the fifth chapter of the *Niruttara Tantra*: "In the absence of the [primary] substances, one should worship the Supreme Deity with secondary alternatives. And: "In the absence of wine, a twice-born man should offer cow's milk in every age."

It has been stated for this very reason: "There is no fault in eating meat, nor is there fault in drinking liquor; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit. Thus, the absence of fault regarding the drinking of liquor was stated by Manu, or rather, it refers to the drinking of *surā* that has not undergone ritual consecration (*asaṃskṛta*).

As it is said in the *Utpattitantra*: "By drinking unconsecrated liquor (*asamskṛtā surā*), a Brahmin becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). But by drinking consecrated liquor (*saṃskṛtā surā*), a Brahmin [becomes pure] like a blazing fire.
A Brahmin may drink liquor during the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice and in the *Kulācāra*; elsewhere, however..."

By drinking [surā] intentionally, one is indeed fallen from the status of a Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, it should be understood that the scriptural prohibitions regarding *surā* refer to those who have not undergone consecration (*anabhiṣikta*), since in that very context, the rules for the drinking of *surā* by all [classes] are observed. Some evidence for this has been written down.

And that which is to be written is found in the third chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*: "O Pārvatī, there is no doubt that the Brahmin is the lord of all sacrifices. In the great sacrifice of Sautrāmaṇī, there are four [classes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇa; for the Brāhmaṇa, there is great liberation through the drinking of wine."

Priyaṃvadā! O Supreme Goddess! O Daughter of the Mountain! It is the truth, the absolute truth, that if a Brāhmaṇa should partake of [the offerings] such as drink and so forth, he becomes the very form of Śiva at that very moment.
