Just as water merges into water, as fire merges into fire, and as space [merges] when a jar is broken, [he merges] into the wind.

Just as the wind [dissolves], O beloved! so too, O beloved, by means of drinking wine, a Brāhmaṇa merges into Brahman, the Supreme Self, O Daughter of the Mountain; there is no doubt in this. The great liberation beginning with *sāyujya* is ordained for Kṣatriyas and others; without drinking wine, O Goddess, the knowledge of reality does not arise.

[The status of a Brahmin] is thus obtained. For this very reason, O Daughter of the Mountain! even if a Brahmin should practice the drinking of liquor, he does not cease to be a Brahmin provided he performs the recitation of the *Vedamātṛ* (the Mother of the Vedas). O Goddess! when one possesses the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), then he is called a Brahmin. Brahman is the nectar of the gods; that indeed is the worldly [reality].

Regarding the statement: "Surā; because it provides enjoyment (*bhoga*) alone, it is proclaimed as *surā*," which appears to be a scriptural injunction permitting a Brāhmaṇa to drink liquor—that too refers specifically to an initiated (*abhiṣikta*) Brāhmaṇa. For it is said: "In initiation, having abandoned one's own respective caste, one certainly attains the state of Śiva."

If it is asked, "Since there is no consideration of caste for one who has been consecrated according to the previously cited statement, how can this be 'for the sake of the consecrated'?"—this is true. Know that this statement regarding drinking is intended for one who is weak in knowledge and who guards the signs of his own caste. Alternatively, [it may be understood otherwise].

The statement prohibiting the drinking of *surā* is for the purpose of forbidding the drinking of that which has been cursed. *Surā*, however, is indeed purifying throughout the four ages; it is only through a curse that it becomes undrinkable.
Therefore, as a preliminary form for the release from that curse, it may indeed be drunk; thus he says in that very same place regarding the three mantras: [The three mantras]...

One should always recite that which grants liberation from the curse of Brahmā and other such afflictions; for by that alone, the liquor becomes composed of Brahman. Just as fire becomes radiant by the mere placing of an oblation, so too does liquor become the bestower of liberation by the mere act of releasing the curse. Therefore indeed, O Goddess of Gods!

A Brahmin should practice drinking [the nectar]. He is a true Brahmin, he is a knower of the Vedas, he is an Agnihotrin, and he is one who has been initiated. O Goddess, what more need be said? He alone is of the nature of the Nirguṇa (the attributeless Self).
O Goddess, this path to liberation must be guarded from the multitude of the uninitiated (paśus) against disclosure.

There would be a loss of spiritual attainment (*siddhi*), and she would not be subject to reproach otherwise. If it is argued that she is unfit to be accepted even for the sake of releasing a curse, then the acceptance of the *Gāyatrī* by Brahmins would likewise be inconsistent; for in that case as well—

"Because of the sight of the curse," as stated in the *Utpattitantra*: "O Supreme Goddess, one should by all means consort with a woman of noble family; one should take pleasure in a beautiful young woman who is intoxicated and full of passion—whether she be an actress, a skull-bearing ascetic, a courtesan, or a distinguished lady of the *haḍḍi* class."

O Supreme Goddess! O Beloved! regarding a Śūdra woman, a Mleccha woman, or a Yavana woman—there is no consideration of "mother's womb" apart from the mother's womb. A hero devoted to the Kula conduct and dedicated to the Kula worship should perform the recitation (japa) after drawing [the essence] from the union of the Bhaga and the Liṅga.

If the mind becomes motionless, what need is there for an eclipse of ten million suns? When the mind is moving, disease arises; when it is motionless, it becomes as steady as a mountain. Likewise, O Goddess, the practice with corpses and the supreme practice with creepers, as well as the practice with funeral pyres—O Goddess, through these, perfection is attained.

In the Kali age, O Maheśvarī, wherever there may be a great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Mahākālī, the offering of a human sacrifice—even by force—will result in affliction. Therefore, O Goddess, the offering of humans and other such beings has ceased; from that time forward, O Queen of the Gods, one should avoid these two types of offerings.
This statement refers to [the practice] other than that of the intense Kali age; as it is said in the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra:
In the Kali age, the state consisting of divine heroism never exists; for men, the accomplishment of mantra occurs only through the state of the bound soul (paśu).
In the sixty-fourth chapter of the *Utpattitantra*: "O Mahādeva! What is existence (*bhāva*)? O Maheśvara! Who is the hero (*vīra*)? O Deva! How is one divine? Tell me yourself, O Śaṅkara!
Following this question from the Goddess, Mahādeva said: "Existence, however, is a mental quality (*mānaso dharmaḥ*)."

But how may that [practice] become complete with its ancillaries? O Maheśānī! It becomes one with the supreme Brahman, free from conceptual construction. O Devī! Śiva alone is the cause of the mental [state], there is no doubt.
A hero is one who has mastered the mantra; a hero does not [become so] through the drinking of wine. But in the Kali age, in the land of Bhārata...

The people dwelling in Bhārata drink liquor in every house and thus indeed fall from their caste. There is no difference between the divine and the heroic; one becomes a knower through the practices of the Kula. One who knows the three threads, follows the Kula conduct, and possesses knowledge is remembered as a Kula-guru. [He knows] the six chakras and the sixteenfold [reality].
The three worlds are the five voids; how can those yogins who do not know them within their own bodies attain accomplishment?
Now, the Five Ms (pañcamakāra), according to the eleventh chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra.
Śaṅkara said:

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the reality that is supremely secret. Having heard it, O beautiful one, guard it with effort as you would your own womb! [From] the seventh chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*: "Listen, O Goddess!
I shall proclaim the reality that is supremely secret, according to the very sequence for the extraction of mantras."

I shall tell you all of that: join the letter *bha* with *ta*, and make the final letter of *tha* joined with *ya*. Again, join *bha* with the nasal dot (*bindu*), and make it joined with the vowel *ā* and the nasal dot. Having uttered the seed-syllable of the Moon (*caṇdabīja*), make it joined with the vowel *a*.
Again, the letter *bha* ending in *ta* (bhta), joined with *vāyu* (ya);
again, *bha*, O Maheśānī, adorned with the fifth vowel (*u*); make it the letter *tha* ending in *ra* (thra), mounted on *vahni* (ra) and joined with the letter *ā*; again, *bha*, O Maheśānī!

Endowed with the vowel of the Sun (Ra), joined with the letter Ta and the letter Ma, and the letter Dhā joined with the vowel A—O Goddess! these five principles are hidden in all the Tantras. In the first chapter of the Kaivalya Tantra, it is said: "There is nothing higher than the five principles."

For the Śāktas, [liberation occurs] through the mouth and the release. By the fifth alone, the practitioner becomes perfected. Among these, O Great Goddess! the Supreme Reality (paratattva) is distinguished. Likewise:
By the first yoga alone, the practitioner becomes Bhairava; by the second reality (tattva), he attains the state of Mahābhairava; by the third reality, the practitioner assumes the form of Śiva;
by the fourth, O lady of noble hips, he becomes a bearer of the form of Rudra; and by the supreme [reality], he attains transcendence.
"He is equal to me, without a doubt. O Goddess! Alcohol, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—this is the *pañcatattva* for the sake of liberation and *nirvāṇa*.
O Goddess! This group of five 'M's (*makāra-pañcaka*) is difficult even for the gods to obtain. Thus it is said in the *Kāmākhyātantra*.

In the fifth chapter: With wines, meats, as well as fish, with ritual gestures (mudrās), and even through sexual union—with women together, the great practitioner should worship the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā). Otherwise, great censure is proclaimed.

By the wise and the gods, [this is taught] through body, mind, and speech; therefore, one should be devoted to the ultimate reality (*tattva*). That man who, having received initiation (*dīkṣā*) into Kālikā-Tāriṇī, does not practice the consumption of wine, shall fall into ruin in the Kali age. He is excluded from both Vedic and Tantric rites of recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*).

He alone is called a non-Brahmin; he alone is a "hand-murkha" (an elephant-like fool). His libation even to his ancestors is equal to the urine of a female dog. If, having obtained the Tārā-mantra in the Kali age, one does not practice the conduct of a hero (vīrācāra), he shall attain the state of a Śūdra with that very body, and not otherwise.

In the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*: "O Goddess! That wine which is declared on earth to grant liberation in all undertakings—its name is 'Tīrtha,' and its drinking is very difficult to attain. As for the meat ordained by the gods, it is fit to be eaten by Śūdras."

That purification, when performed according to rule with Vedic mantras, is declared to be the highest. O fair-faced one! Those various fish which are said to be fit for consumption have been described by me in secret as the fish that bestow spiritual perfection (siddhi). [Likewise,] parched rice and roasted grains...
Wheat, chickpeas, and so forth—O Goddess! its name is *mudrā*, which bestows liberation. O Beloved! that which constitutes sexual union through the yoga of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*—O Goddess!
its name is proclaimed as the fifth. First, however...
Liquor is the first, and meat is the second; fish would be the third, and the mudrā is the fourth; one should know the fifth to be the fifth—these five are thus remembered by name.

The derivation of the word *matsya* and others is found in the seventeenth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava-tantra*: "Because he pacifies the impurities of *māyā* and the like, because he demonstrates the path to liberation, and because he is free from the eight types of suffering and so forth, O Goddess, he is proclaimed as *Matsya*; furthermore, because he generates auspiciousness."
Because it bestows consciousness and bliss, and because it is dear to all the gods, it is called *māṃsa* (flesh).
Likewise: "O Goddess! Among all [the elements], the fifth shall be dear to me as my very life.
O Goddess! Without the fifth, how can one recite the Caṇḍī-mantra? O Beloved! If one harbors delusion regarding the five *kārakas*, O Goddess, how can there be accomplishment for him?"

How should one recite the Caṇḍī-mantra? The syllables *ma*, *ka*, and *ra* indicate the supreme Brahman, which is bliss (*ānanda*). Now, regarding their fruit, it is stated in the eleventh chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "O Daughter of the Mountain, through the drinking of wine, one attains the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) and supreme liberation (*mokṣa*)."
By the mere eating of meat, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person;
by the mere eating of fish, Kālī becomes manifest;
by the mere practice of *mudrā*, a Brahmin assumes the form of Viṣṇu; [and] by sexual union...

"A great yogin is equal to me; of this there is no doubt. Likewise: "Having brought forth a single Śakti, the Kaulika practitioner alone, with great effort, should worship her by means of the five principles (pañcatattva). By doing so, he shall attain perfection (siddhi) that does not fall within the range of vision of others," as stated in the Śaiva [Tantra].
O Sulocanā! This knowledge of reality has been proclaimed in the Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, and Cāndra [traditions].

Now listen with diligence to that which is in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], O Goddess of the Gods! In the twelfth chapter: the principle of the Guru, the principle of Mantra, the principle of the Mind, the principle of the Deity, and the principle of Meditation—this is the fivefold principle.
O fair-faced Pārvatī! Out of affection, I shall first explain the true nature of the venerable Guru.
Residing within the body, he possesses great luster and is equipped with an oil-soaked wick;
through the Guru’s bestowing of mantras, that thread becomes ignited. For he is indeed the very body of the deity.

It arises certainly from the mantra; for this very reason, its essence is undoubtedly of a divine form. Whatever is the potency of the Lord is itself of an imperishable nature. By that [potency], the body of the living being consists of phonemes (varṇa); of this there is no doubt. [This is stated] regarding the phoneme of the mantra.

O Supreme Goddess! They consist of all the phonemes (varṇas). O Goddess! This reality of the phonemes is my very essence; I am myself the God and none other, stainless and possessing the form of the Deity.
One should meditate upon the Divinity everywhere, even in grass, shrubs, creepers, and the like. Through such meditation, one attains [the goal].

Everything is attained through meditation; one who possesses the form of Viṣṇu attains perfection through meditation, for without meditation nothing is accomplished. Thus, O Sovereign of the Gods, I have told you the truth regarding the Vaiṣṇava, by the knowledge of which a man becomes immortal and takes on the form of Viṣṇu. Those [who do not know this] are indeed not men.
Sometimes they go to the abode of Yama.
The method for purifying the principles (tattva-śodhana), however, is found in the second chapter of the Kaivalya Tantra.
The illustrious Śiva said:

Listen, Pārvatī! I shall indeed describe the procedure for their purification. Having seated oneself in the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should perform the cupped-hands gesture (karapuṭa). One should pay homage to the Gurus on the left, meditate upon Gaṇapati on the right, and, having paid homage to the Goddess in the center, perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform [the ritual]. Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkās* upon the body, one should perform the placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.

One should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *kalpa*. Afterwards, O Maheśvarī, having drawn a triangle or a hexagon mandala upon the ground—
p. 985) Upon that, one should place a pure jar (*ghaṭa*). The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "a triangle or...

indicates a conjunction (*samuccaya*), like the letter *ca* used in the rule of "injunction by association" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*). Therefore, the meaning is that both of those mandalas must be constructed.

Because it is in agreement with the words of the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* which will be spoken [later], and because it is in agreement with the words of the independent *Tantra*, by that [method] it is also well-founded. Having performed the sprinkling many times with the syllable *phaṭ* again and again, then, upon that, the cause—
And one should establish [the deity] with the root mantra alone, O Goddess of gods! Indeed, [one should do so] with the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order as well.

Furthermore, the wise practitioner should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with the *phaṭ* mantra. Then, having joined the seed-syllable of the power of space (*viyacchakti*) with the fourteenth vowel, and endowed it with the *nāda* and *bindu*, [one should proceed].

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times over it. Then, one should recite the root mantra, followed by the *māyābīja*. Having displayed the *dhenu*, *yoni*, *gālinī*, *trikhaṇḍa*, and that which is known as *mīna* [mudrās], O lady of excellent limbs, one should hold the jar and recite the mantra: *oṃ ekameva*.

The Supreme Brahman is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle; by means of that, I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin born of *kaca*. Oṃ! O Goddess, born from the solar disc, arisen from the abode of Varuṇa, composed of the seed-syllable of Amā!

May [she] be liberated from the curse of Śukra. Oṃ! If the Praṇava is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth, O Goddess of Devas, may she be cleansed of the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. Then, one should likewise [meditate upon] the syllable *va* joined with the six limbs and conjoined with the *bindu*. Thus...

O Kulasaundari! Having recited the mantra together with its causal syllable and endowed with its phonemes and letters, the practitioner of mantra should then meditate upon his own mantra. He should meditate upon Anandabhairava according to the instructions of the Tantra—as red in color, four-armed, three-eyed, and auspiciously bestowing boons.

One should worship that auspicious God Śiva, who wears a mass of matted hair, whose neck is adorned with Vāsuki, and who holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a skull-cup, a mallet, and an excellent noose, and who is clothed in a tiger skin. O Maheśānī! having meditated thus upon Him...
One should worship in the center. Then, one should cast it out with this mantra: *māyābījam* (the seed-syllable of Māyā), followed by *huṃ phaṭ*.

Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī within that [space]: the goddess Ānandabhairavī, whose hands shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, of terrible form, of excellent hips, and three-eyed.
"Clad in red garments, red in color, most fierce, accompanied by a thousand Bhairavas, and praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others—I worship Śivā.
O Maheśānī! having meditated thus, one should worship with that very mantra. [One should contemplate] the unity of those two.

Having meditated upon Gāyatrī, one should mutter [the mantra] ten times. Having uttered "Bhairavam" ending in the vocative case (ṅe), immediately thereafter one says "vidmahe"; then after that, one should say "sudhādevyai"; then one should say "dhīmahī"; then "tanno devi"; and finally, at the end of that, "pracodayāt. Thus, O Goddess, it has been told to you.
The Gāyatrī is the supreme syllable. By the mere remembrance of it, the purification of substances occurs. Through its grace, I am the Lord; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
In its center, one should write the root mantra once with *vilva* twigs, and worship it with a red cloth.
One should conceal the nectar with a cloth. The meaning of the word *kāraṇa* (cause) is explained in that very same place.
O Pārvatī! Since it is proclaimed as the cause of all things— of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as of the objects of the senses— and since, O Maheśānī,
it is indeed the cause of our very bodies, I am Mṛtyuñjaya, O Vīreśī!

O Goddess of gods! O Blessed One! When the Kula is served with a mind that is free from modification and free from conceptual construction, by the grace of heroic action, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. O Great Goddess! One who is free from conceptual construction undoubtedly partakes in liberation; O Lady of excellent limbs! One who possesses conceptual construction [falls into] Raurava.
He certainly goes.
Now, the purification of meat and so forth is described in the third chapter.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Supreme Goddess! O Beloved! I shall describe the purification of meat and other substances.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should worship upon the maṇḍala Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Ananta, and likewise the Earth. In the center of that, one should place the meat.

O Pārvatī! Having consecrated the fish and the *mudrā* with the *huṃ* seed-syllable, one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with *phaṭ* syllables. The best of practitioners should display the *dhenu-mudrā* and others with the *vāruṇa* mantra.
Then, he should recite the *māyā*, *badhū*, and *śrī* seed-syllables in sequence, as well as the purification mantra (*śuddhi-mantra*).

Reciting the root mantra with devotion, one should say: "O Mistress of the Gods! Make pure the meat and the fish, O Kuleśvarī! [Make pure] the divine mudrā produced from grain for the sake of worship, O Kulanāyikā! Then, O Beloved, one should mutter *hūṃ phaṭ* and the *vāruṇa* [mantra] over it.
And one should perform the recitation of the root mantra ten times in the center of that.

Now, regarding the purification of the *śakti*, in that very same [text]: "O Dear One, I shall now describe the purification of women. Having placed her either in front or on the right upon the mandala, one should draw the Tripura-mandala on her forehead with vermilion."
The wise practitioner should apply collyrium to the eyes while reciting the root mantra;

he should then cause the Śakti to consume various other substances before him. Having meditated upon the desired form [of the deity], he should place betel in the mouth, and then [worship] with the mantras of the six limbs.

One should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Then, having performed the placement of the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should perform the placement of the seers and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*). Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times on the head. One should also recite the Kāma-bīja and the Baddhi-bīja in the heart and at the navel.

O Pārvatī! The practitioner of mantra should recite *Śrīṃ* at the secret place, all the seed-syllables (*sarvabīja*) [at the heart], *Vāgbhava* at the head, *Kāma*, *Kuṇḍalī*, and *Kulakuṇḍalī*; by reciting the seed-syllable of Śakti, he shall become a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). He should cause *Māyā* to be heard in the left ear.
O Maheśvarī! O Queen of the Gods! In this manner, the purification of women is accomplished through this sequence. Thus ends the purification of the Śakti.

Regarding the fruit of pure *śakti*, it is said in that very same place: "O Pārvatī! Whatever the Mother of the World, once propitiated, declares—all that attains truthfulness; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. And for those who have been initiated, O Queen of the Gods, there is never any impurity whatsoever."
The purification of the five *m*’s (*pañcamakāra*) and so forth, as maintained in the *Śyāmārahasya*, is as follows:

Having drawn a dot within a triangle situated inside a hexagon on one's left, and having fashioned a circle and a square on the outside, and having sprinkled it with water from the general *arghya* vessel,
one should worship there, saying "Obeisance to the Support-Energies" (*adhāraśaktibhyaḥ*). Having washed the support with "Obeisance," [one proceeds].

Having placed [the vessel] upon the mandala and worshipped it with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten digits (kalās)," and having rinsed the water-pot (kalaśa) with "Phaṭ," worshipped it with the *kāraṇa* mantra,
and adorned it with red cloth, garlands, and so forth, one should [place it] upon the support with the thought that it is the Goddess, saying "Oṃ."
Having established me [as the deity], one should worship the support (ādhāra) with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten digits";

then, having fully worshipped the vessel (kalaśa) with "Aṃ, obeisance to the sun-maṇḍala consisting of twelve digits," one should worship it with "Uṃ, obeisance to the moon-maṇḍala consisting of sixteen digits."
Then, having struck the substance with *darbha* grass while reciting "phaṭ," having veiled it with the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā while reciting "huṃ," having gazed at it with the root mantra,
having sprinkled it with water while reciting "namaḥ," and having taken up the fragrance three times with the root mantra while reciting "oṃ."
Having placed a flower in the vessel, one should draw a triangle in the midst of the substances with the mantra *hasauḥ*.
Having worshipped with *hasauḥ hasauḥ namaḥ*, [one offers] the vessel to *hrīṃ krīṃ paramasvāmini paramākāśaśūnyavāhini candrasūryāgnibhakṣiṇi*.

"Śiva-śiva svāhā. Having thus held the jar and recited this ten times, one should then recite over it: "Aiṃ hrīṃ krīṃ, let us know Ānandeśvara; let us meditate upon Sudhādevī; may Urdhvanārīśvara impel that [knowledge]. This is the liberation from the curse (*śāpamocana*).
One should perform [it].

Thus it is said in the *Svatantra*: "Then, having brought the divine causal [substance] contained in a jar, wrapped in a red cloth and adorned with a red garland, O Maheśānī! on the left side there is a square mandala; therein..."

O fair-faced one, one should establish [the deity] with devotion, perceiving it as the Goddess, within the mandala, the pitcher, the ritual substance, the fire, the sun, and the lunar orb; this is the meaning of "one should worship."

And in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "On the left side, having drawn a hexagon with the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in its center, one should place there a water-pot (*kumbha*) made of gold, silver, copper, or even earthen—provided it is not made of iron. Thus it is stated in another Tantra.

And the mantra-practitioner should place [the vessel] upon a support—a jar made of gold, silver, bell-metal, or even clay, provided it is flawless. Regarding the specific fruit of each jar made of gold and so forth, it is stated in that same source: "A golden jar is said to bestow enjoyment (*bhoga*); a silver one..."
Likewise, [a vessel made of] bell-metal bestows liberation, while that made of clay brings about peace and bestows nourishment.
Now, regarding the mantras for liberation from the curse, it is stated in the Kumārī-tantra:

"Listen further, O Goddess of gods! Hear from me those mantras by which no fault arises, O Goddess, in acts such as drinking and so forth. 'The Supreme Brahman alone is one, consisting of both the gross and the subtle...'"
"O Dhruva! By this [mantra], I shall destroy the sin of Brahmin-slaughter arising from your hair.
O Goddess born from the solar disc! O you who have originated from the abode of Varuṇa! O Goddess consisting of the seed-syllable *Amā*!
May [he] be released from the curse of Śukra. The *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of the Vedas."

"If it consists of the bliss of Brahman," so it is said. Therefore, O Goddess, even truth does not remove the sin of killing a Brahmin for you! Having thus consecrated the auspicious liquor with these three mantras, one should offer it to Kālikā; thereafter, one may partake of the food offering (naivedya). Thus, O Goddess, are the three mantras.

Holding the jar, one should recite [the mantra] three times. Then, one should recite three times: *oṃ vā vī vū vai vau vaḥ brahmaśāpavimocitāyai sudhādevyai namaḥ*. This is the release from the curse of Brahmā (*brahmaśāpavimocana*). Then: *oṃ śā śī śū śai śau śaḥ*...

One should recite ten times: "Obeisance to the Goddess Sudhā, who has been liberated from the curse of Śukra. Thus ends the liberation from the curse of Śukra. Then: *aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ krāḥ krīḥ krūḥ kraḥ krauḥ kraḥ*, "Liberate [her] from the curse of Kṛṣṇa; cause the nectar to flow, cause it to flow! Svāhā! Thus.
One should recite it ten times. Thus ends the release from Kṛṣṇa’s curse.

Now, in the *Uttaratantra*: "Oṃ haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasur antarikṣasadd hotā vedisad atithir duroṇasat | nṛṣad varasad ṛtasad vyomasad abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijā ṛtaṃ bṛhat. Recite this three times over the substance. Then, in the midst of the substance—
One should meditate upon Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī, as follows:
The god who resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons, who has eighteen arms,
five faces, and three eyes; who stands in the midst of an ocean of nectar,
seated upon a Brahma-lotus, mounted on a bull, and is blue-throated.
Adorned with all ornaments, holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, sounding a bell and a ḍamaru drum, the God holds a noose and a goad,
and wields a mace and a club, a sword and a shield, and a paṭṭiśa and a mallet.

The best of practitioners should meditate upon the Lord of the gods, who is red in color, holding a trident and a staff, possessing a variegated shield and a severed head, with hands granting boons and fearlessness. Having thus meditated, one should recite:
*hasakṣamalavarayūṃ ānandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ*. Thus [one worships] Ānandabhairava.
One should recite it three times.
Then one should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī as follows: One should contemplate the Goddess Sudhā,
who possesses the luster of ten million times ten thousand moons, white as snow, jasmine, and the moon,
having five faces, three eyes, and endowed with eighteen arms.

Having thus meditated upon her who is intent on producing all bliss, the wide-eyed one smiling and facing the God of gods, [one should recite]: "To Hasakṣamalavarayī, the Goddess of Nectar, Vauṣaṭ. Having thus worshipped Ānandabhairavī, one should draw the Śakticakra in the center of the ritual substances.
Then, having written in three rows in a clockwise direction the syllables *aṃ* 16, *kaṃ* 16, and *khaṃ* 16 in sequence,

one should write *haṃ*, *laṃ*, and *kṣaṃ* in the center. Then, having contemplated the state of nectar (*amṛtatva*) within the substance resulting from the union of Śiva and Śakti, [one should seal it] with the Dhenu-mudrā.

Having rendered [the water] nectar-like by reciting the seed-syllable *vaṃ* of Varuṇa and the root mantra eight times, and while contemplating the jar as being composed of the deity, one should hold the jar and recite [the following]. Thus is the purification of the substance (*dravyaśuddhi*).

Thus it is said in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "And then, O Dear One, one should meditate on the substance in the center as resembling blood; it is adorned with the three syllables *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* arranged in three rows beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.
Within the previously mentioned Yoni-mudrā, at the union of Śiva and Śakti, [there arises] nectar."

One should contemplate the substance eight times and recite the *amṛta* mantra eight times; then, having taken up the jar, one should recite the root mantra eight times. This, O Goddess, is the cause served by the hosts of gods;
for this very reason, her name is "Sure" (the Divine One) throughout the three worlds, and because of it, Keśava [is associated] with her fragrance.
With incense, the Kaulika should worship the supreme goddess, the auspicious Kālikā of the South.

Now, the purification of meat: *Oṃ pratadviṣṇustavate vīryeṇa mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro gariṣṭhā yasyoruṣu triṣu vikrame dhiyanti bhuvanāni viśvā*. With this [mantra], one should purify the meat. Then: *Oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*.
"Sweet-smelling, increasing nourishment—may I be released from death, as a cucumber from its bond, into immortality. Thus ends the purification of fish.

Oṃ. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. Oṃ. The inspired poets, ever-vigilant and full of praise, kindle that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Thus is the purification of the mudrās.
Oṃ! May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the womb for Viṣṇu; may he shape the forms. May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. Bestow an embryo, O Sinīvālī;
bestow an embryo, O Sarasvatī! May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place an embryo within you.
Now, regarding *svayambhūkusuma* and so forth, as stated in the second chapter of the *Muṇḍamālātantra*.

The first flower that arises on a creeper in the temple of Kāma, even if it is devoid of contact with fire—one should offer that to Mahādevī. O Goddess! That is known as the Svayambhū flower, the Raktacandana, as well as the Triśūla flower and the Vajra flower.
O fair-faced one! As an alternative rite, [use] red sandalwood, which is dear to Hara.

In the second chapter of the *Samāyācāra-tantra*: "O fortunate one! At whatever age a woman’s first menses occurs, she should immediately take [the substance] called the 'Self-Arisen Flower' (*svayambhūkusuma*), which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to obtain, always for the sake of pleasing the deity, if—"

O Goddess! By the power of fortune, one obtains this second flower; thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should perform the unsurpassed bath for his own deities. O fair-faced one, he shall obtain his desire—this is the truth, the absolute truth!
This secret has been told for the purpose of bathing the deities. Not... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
O Goddess! One should perform the consumption of both of these;
that is to say, of both this *śaktikusuma* and the *svayambhūkusuma*. Likewise:
O beloved! For women whose husbands are living, one should have the fifth [mark] made;
whatever substance belongs to her vulva is said to originate from the *kuṇḍa*. One should likewise have the fifth made for women whose husbands are dead; whatever substance belongs to her vulva—

That which arises from the *kuṇḍagola* is thus described. O beautiful one, listen to what should be done in the absence of the flower arising from the *kuṇḍagola*: in the absence of the *svayambhū* flower, O fortunate one, one should offer all the flowers of creepers and whatever flowers belong to trees to the deity.

The flower of Aparājitā, that which is the Vajra-flower, the flower of Karavīra, the flower of Bandhujīvaka, the flower of the lotus, and the flower of Campaka— these flowers, O beautiful goddess, are especially suitable.
O beautiful one! Having taken all these—varvara flowers, leaves, and bilva leaves—for the purpose of worship, for the attainment of all auspicious fortune.

In the first chapter of the *Utpattitantra*: "O Great Goddess! He who performs worship with self-arisen flowers after having offered oblations with self-arisen flowers is indeed a hero and is Śiva himself. In the second chapter of the *Gandharvatantro*: "Having brought a divine maiden..."
The practitioner should place [the mantra] upon the body of one who is endowed with youth, consecrated with the root mantra, of virtuous character, and sweetly smiling;
whose heart is always full of bliss, who is devoid of pity and shame, devoted to the guru, well-attired,
and intent on the worship of the deity.

The practitioner should place the five corpses, which are the five objects of desire; the mantra-wielder should place the five peaks and the fifty *mātṛkās*. Having taken up the divine garland, the practitioner who has conquered his senses should then recite the *Svapnāvatī* mantra one thousand times.

By this very procedure, there shall be a great attraction. One should worship the Supreme Goddess in her house of passion (*madanāgāra*). Having bound the *sarvasaṅkṣobhiṇī* mudrā, one should cause the *yoni* to vibrate. One should contemplate her as being the very embodiment of Kāmeśvarī.
The supreme practitioner, meditating upon himself as being of the very nature of Kāmeśvara,
remains himself unshaken while practicing the fifth [rite];
he must personally and with great effort protect her flower until it is [offered].
One should worship her daily with betel, perfumes, and flowers;
having diligently provided satisfaction through various flavors,
foods, and drinks, one should bring her joy with garments, ornaments, jewelry, and the like, at the appropriate times.
One should diligently take that flower oneself, according to its appropriate form;

for it is indeed the self-arisen flower (*svayambhūkusuma*). This divine self-arisen flower is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds; the best of practitioners obtains it and thereby accomplishes what is otherwise unattainable on earth.

One should always worship [the deity] directly with that very *svayambhū* flower; by reciting the *Svapnāvatī* Vidyā, swift attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) will occur. Indeed, gods, planets, *nāgas*, *dānavas*, and *rākṣasas*, as well as kings and all women, will constantly become subject to one's will.
Whoever performs worship daily with Svayambhū flowers and recites [the mantra] over a divine rosary shall obtain all their desires.

Now, the purification of the *svayambhūkusuma* and other substances: *pluṃ sluṃ mluṃ śluṃ svāhā! O Amṛte! O Amṛtodbhave! O Amṛteśvari! O Amṛtavarṣiṇi! Cause the nectar to flow, cause it to flow, svāhā!* This is the purification of substances derived from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*. Then:

Having veiled everything with "HŪM," having rendered it nectar with the *dhenumudrā*, having performed the three *tālas* and the binding of the ten directions, one should recite the root mantra seven times over that;
this is the purification (*śodhana*). [The mantra: *HASAKṢAMALAVARAYŪṂ ĀNANDABHAIRAVĀYA VAṢAṬ*.

Having thus worshipped Ānandabhairava and holding the *arghya* vessel, one should recite: Aiṃ Krīṃ Sauḥ! O great vessel, arisen from the fragments of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), produced from the entirety of essences, filled to the brim—bring forth the nectar of immortality (*pīyūṣa-rasa*)! Aiṃ.

O You who possess the form of Akula! Place Your spontaneous vibration here, O You who hold the moon of the nectar of speed and whose hand bears the bliss of the single flavor of the [divine] fragment! Klīṃ! O Supreme One, whose form is the nectar residing in Akula, who bestows the knowledge of purity! O You whose form is moist with compassion! Bestow the state of immortality upon this object! Sauḥ!

Having made it delightful as one with that very form, and having become of this same nature, manifest within me in the form of supreme nectar! Aiṃ sluṃ vluṃ aṃ, O Nectar, O Source of Nectar, O Showerer of Nectar, cause the nectar to flow, cause it to flow! Svāhā! Aiṃ.

*Vadavada vāgvādini aiṃ klīṃ klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru kuru aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ mahāmokṣaṃ kuru hauḥ hasauḥ.* Having consecrated the ritual vessel (*kāraṇa*) with this mantra, one should invoke the Goddess therein, perform the triple *tāla*-clapping, and carry out the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).
Having veiled [the vessel] with the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā, having rendered it nectar with the *dhenu* mudrā,
and having displayed the *yoni* mudrā, one should worship it with "Hasauḥ Namaḥ. Then, having displayed the *śaṅkha* mudrā therein,
having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should cover the vessel with the *matsya* mudrā.
Having recited the root mantra ten times, one should contemplate the vessel as having the very form of the Goddess.

Then, having received the command of the Goddess, one should place the vessels between the jar (ghaṭa) and the śrīpātra. Next, near the jar, one places the guru-vessel, and after that, the bhoga-vessel.

One should place the vessel for the Śakti, the vessel for the Yoginīs, the vessel for the Vīras, the vessel for the bali offering, and the vessels for the water for washing the feet (pādya) and for sipping (ācamanīya), just as one does for the general arghya. Then,
with the Tattvamudrā and using the *kāraṇa* [liquor] containing fish, meat, and so forth, [one should take from] the Śrīpātra onto one's own head.

Having offered libations three times with the mantra "I satisfy Śrī Ānandabhairava," and having offered libations three times— or once— with the respective mantra "I satisfy the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of the Guru Amukānandanātha," one should likewise satisfy the supreme, the intermediate, and the supreme-most Gurus.

Then, one should satisfy the Goddess—along with her weapons, her vehicle, and her retinue—in the heart with the nectar from the *śrīpātra*. As for the *tattvamudrā*, it is as described in the fourteenth chapter of the *Niruttara Tantra*:

O Pārvatī! By joining the thumb and the ring finger of the left hand, one should offer libations to the Goddess Kālikā, together with her weapons and her retinue. The thumb is said to be the Lord Bhairava, and the ring finger is called Śakti; O Goddess, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, one should satisfy the Deity. This is the libation (tarpaṇa).

O Goddess! [The practice] is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior. The superior belongs to the divine state (divyabhāva), the middling to the heroic state (vīrabhāva), and the inferior to the fettered state (paśu). These correspond respectively to the heart, the yantra, and water. Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi). This has been stated in the Śruti:
May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna breaths be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā! || 1 ||
Oṃ! May earth, water, fire, air, and ether be purified for me; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil. Svāhā! || 2 ||
Oṃ, [I offer] my primordial nature, ego, intellect, mind, and ears, and so forth. || 3 ||
Oṃ, may my skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and speech [be purified], and so forth. || 4 ||
Oṃ, [I offer] my hands, feet, anus, genitals, sounds, and so forth... || 5 ||
Oṃ, may [the elements] whose natures are air, fire, water, and earth [be established] for me, and so forth. || 6 ||
Oṃ, may my touch, form, taste, smell, and sound be purified; I am light, and so forth.
Having recited these seven mantras, wiping the palm with the [left] hand,
drawing a triangle on the right hand, and having placed the purity resembling the *kalās* within the center, facing the south, north, and front of the triangle;

Having grasped one [flower] with the union of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger of the left hand, at the end of the root mantra, recite: *hrīṃ śrīṃ ātmatattvena sthūladehaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. Having thereby accepted the purification of the lower part, [recite] *hrīṃ śrīṃ vidyātattvena*...

"I purify the subtle body, svāhā!"—with this, having accepted the one situated on the right, [one says]: "hrīṃ śrīṃ, by means of the Śiva-principle, I purify the supreme body, svāhā!"—with this, having accepted the one situated on the left, [one says]: "hrīṃ śrīṃ, by means of the All-principle, [I purify] that which rests upon the three principles."

"Jīvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā. Having accepted this with the left middle finger, having purified both hands with a cloth, one should wipe all the limbs with the two hands; this is the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi).
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Full Initiation and Other Rites," in the seventh section on the Attributeless (Nirguṇa-kāṇḍa) of the glorious *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Now, the worship according to the conduct of heroes (vīrācāra). In the third chapter of the *Kṛkalāsadīpikā*:

"O Goddess worshipped by heroes! First, the 'Illuminator' (dīpanī) must be explained; by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while living. She is the one to be illuminated among all the gods."
O Pārvatī! This knowledge, which bestows the fourfold aims of life, is proclaimed among the Siddhi-vidyās.
Without this, no knowledge ever attains perfection. O Maheśvarī! Even without worship, without meditation, and without ritual conduct, a practitioner may become liberated through knowledge alone.
He is free from great sin. In his family there is no poverty; in his lineage there is no one who is unlearned. (p.

995) One may give up one's life, one may give wealth, one may even give up one's family and women, but, O Great Goddess! one should not give this knowledge to just anyone. [The three seed-syllables of Kālī.]
Immediately after that, there is a pair of *kūrca* syllables (*hūṃ hūṃ*). O Goddess! likewise, there are two *lajjā* seed-syllables (*hrīṃ hrīṃ*) followed by "Dakṣiṇe Kālike.

Again, those same seed-syllables follow, ending with the beloved of Fire (*svāhā*). This is the mantra. Bhairava is declared its *ṛṣi*, and *uṣṇik* is cited as its meter (*chanda*). Dakṣiṇākālikā is declared the deity.
It is concealed in the Tantra. O Queen of the Gods! O Beloved! The seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), the kūrcam, and the lajjā [syllables] are to be applied in sequence.

The nyāsa on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the nyāsa on the hands (karanyāsa) are proclaimed to be performed with Māyā. [One should meditate upon] the Great Goddess, whose face is formidable, who is terrifying, with disheveled hair, naked, and four-armed.
Adorned with a garland of severed heads,
her upper left lotus-hand holds a sword with a freshly cut head,
while her lower right hand grants fearlessness and her upper right hand bestows boons; she possesses the luster of a great cloud.
Dark-complexioned, adorned with skeletons in her hands, with a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck and smeared with dripping blood; possessing terrible fangs and a gaping mouth,
with full and elevated breasts, she stands upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
Having thus meditated with effort upon her who is afflicted by perverse passion together with Mahākāla,
the practitioner of mantra, endowed with devotion, should worship the retinue with great care using intoxicants, meats, red flowers, red lotuses, and crimson garments.
One should worship the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā), O Goddess, beginning with Ādhāra-śakti;
likewise Prakṛti, Kūrma, Śeṣa, and the Earth; as well as the Ocean of Nectar, Maṇidvīpa, the House of Cintāmaṇi, the cremation ground (śmaśāna), and the Pārijāta tree.
At its base, the best of practitioners should place a jeweled altar; upon that jewel, he should set a pedestal. In the four directions, he should place the gods and Śivas, holding human skulls.

One should worship Dharma and Adharma, and so forth, with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Self of Knowledge. Then, in the filaments starting from the east, one should worship Icchā (Will), Jñāna (Knowledge), and Kriyā (Action), as well as Kāminī, Kāmadā, Rati, Prīti, Śrī, and Ānandā, O Maheśānī, in the center.

O Maheśānī! The wise one should place Manonmanī, Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā on the outside of the hexagon. One should place Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, and Dīptā upon the petals of the triangle, as well as Mātrā.
One should likewise place the Mudrā and Mitā in another triangle. All [the goddesses] are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands (p.
996), adorned with garlands of severed heads, holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) with their left hands, possessing pure smiles, naked, and having laughing faces.

Adorned with their respective vehicles—having meditated thus with diligence, one should worship them on the eight-petaled lotus: O Dear One! Brahmāṇī, Nārāyaṇī, and likewise Māheśvarī, Aparājitā, and Kaumārī.

The wise one should worship Vārāhī; having worshipped Nārasiṃhī, he should then conquer [the obstacles] from the south. O Goddess! One should worship Mahākāla with effort during the interval of inverted sexual union—he who is naked, with disheveled hair, and of fierce appearance. Having thus worshipped with diligence, [one should proceed].

One should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. If one worships the Goddess without wine and without meat, one incurs the curse of the deity and, upon death, experiences hell. O Goddess! If a practitioner recites [the mantra] without [union with] another's wife, even by a hundred crore recitations, for him—

Success is not attained [otherwise]. Women are the goal, women are the life-breath, women are success—of this there is no doubt. When women are remembered, Kālī is remembered; of this there is no doubt.
O Beloved! [Place] the throat upon the throat, the face upon the face, and the breast upon the breast in the temple of the Kula.

Likewise, O Goddess of the gods! that man who recites the mantra after having paid the fine, Kālikā herself becomes manifest through even half of the recitation. O Goddess! having caused him to drink the *kula-rasa* as is appropriate, and having drunk it oneself, one should recite the mantra; success (*siddhi*) occurs, and not otherwise. And of this—
He for whom exhaustion arises during the practice is said to be ineligible for the groups of Kālikā mantras.
For the *puraścaraṇa*, it is said that one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) suffice; for Kṣatriyas, it should be two hundred thousand, and for Vaiśyas, three hundred thousand. But for Śūdras...

A preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of four hundred thousand [recitations] is prescribed. O Goddess! One should recite it for just one hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), pure during the day; and at midnight during the night, having drunk the *kula-rasa*, O Beloved! accompanied by a group of *kula* women, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. Thus, according to the stated injunction:

One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitations]; one-tenth of that is the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and one-tenth of that is the consecration (*abhiṣecana*). O Supreme Goddess, it is proclaimed that one-tenth of that is the feeding of Brahmins. One should perform the fire-oblation and the libation with the nectar of the blooming flowers. Thus...
One becomes accomplished through mere practice and not otherwise. O Goddess! one attains mastery over speech;

O Beloved! one attains stainless poetic skill. Through wealth one becomes like Kuvera, and through knowledge one becomes like Bṛhaspati. Having lived until the end of the kalpa, one shall attain liberation at last.
At the time of commencing the ritual application, O Goddess, the wine shall become milk or it may become blood;
the meat shall become flowers. The vessel of wine shall become empty, especially the vessel of meat; and the flower shall be the interval between the artistic divisions (kalā).

There may be another flower; O Dear One! butter is equal to meat, and meat becomes a flower. Having understood this, the best of practitioners gradually attains [success]. O Goddess! he who has conviction in this matter obtains it—of this there is no doubt. [This] mental union [is attained] in half that time.

O lady of excellent complexion! It may be done with effort. O lady of excellent complexion! A garland made of gold, silver, pearl, coral, and ruby—this quartet of garlands has been prescribed; one should string the garland together in equal proportions using silk thread.
O Pārvatī, one who is in her menses and staying at home—[should fashion] a very beautiful image in the form of a serpent with red [pigment].

One should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with nectar (makaranda). Having uttered the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the *māyā* (hrīṃ), the pair of *kūrca* (huṃ huṃ), the words *māle māle*, and the beloved of fire (svāhā)— [The mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ huṃ huṃ māle māle svāhā*.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times, one should consecrate it. O fair-faced one, one should bathe it in the middle of the pedestal within an empty house. Then, O Goddess, the wise one, having carefully taken that rosary and having recognized its proximity to success (*siddhi*), should perform a great festival. [One should take] a sixteen-year-old...

Having carefully brought a very young woman, he himself should rub her with fragrant unguents and bathe her with pure water. Having worshipped her with the splendor of divine ornaments and with fragrant, divine flowers, he should feed that fair-faced woman with sweet foods.
One should carefully make her drink the *āsava* liquor and drink the certainty that consists of that very essence.

Then, when she desires pleasure, the wise mantra-practitioner should delight her; having placed a garland in her hand, he should ask for it from her. Taking the garland given by her, [he should offer it] to the Brahmins.
Then one should feed [the disciple]. At that time, one should recite [the mantra] at midnight; [the deity] becomes manifest directly, and not otherwise.
Even there, if no sign of attainment occurs, the wise one should enter into the midst of the *kalā*s. Having tied beautiful silken threads on the four sides of the couch—
Having secured twenty-two knots with roots encased in *ramā*, and having placed a *pāñcālī* and a *saindhavī* for the sake of self-protection, one should cause her—
sixteen years of age— to be seated upon a cloth according to the sequence to be described.
Having diligently brought a foreign creeper and especially a courtesan,
one should offer them divine flowers. One should feed them sweet foods, clothe them in linen garments, anoint them with divine perfumes, and personally adorn them with ornaments.

The practitioner should delight [the consort] with supreme devotion for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*). Accomplishment occurs through even half of the recitation; it does not happen otherwise. O Maheśānī! Without wine, one never succeeds.
Therefore, at the outset, having drunk it with effort, the wise man should cause her to drink it as well.
If one has no confidence even in that regard, O Goddess, one should perform the Cāruhoma sacrifice. Fearless at midnight,

in a cremation ground or likewise in a desolate wilderness, having performed the bath and other rites with perfumes, preceded by the washing of the feet, one should place there a vessel made of gold or silver.

Likewise, O Maheśānī! having fashioned that [liṅga] out of copper according to one's means, one should worship the Supreme Goddess during the night portion [of the day], with the secondary offerings (upacāras) according to one's capacity, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth. Having performed the worship of the Goddess, [one should then prepare] the flour...

One should cause it to be cooked thoroughly. Having carefully placed [the offering] in the *caru* as a circular ball made of four types of flour, one should then have the practitioner drink the *caru* and worship within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The mantra-master should worship Raktā, Ghanā, Balākā, Nīlā, Kālī, and Kalāvatī, as well as the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), at the gates.

With diligence, the practitioner of mantras should worship the planets according to the sequence of the four corners. Then, with the *hūṃ* mantra, the practitioner should offer a stream of oblation, and subsequently the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) according to his capacity.
For the sake of attaining success, he should cause it to be heard with the root mantra, accompanied by honey. Thus the oblation is offered.

The practitioner of mantra should cover the sacrificial fire with a yellow cloth; then, with diligence, he should worship Dakṣiṇakālikā with incense, lamps, and food offerings, and thereafter perform circumambulation. A quantity of flour equal to the number [of circumambulations] results in gold and other precious materials.
O Dear One! If success should be achieved by a single performance, then the oblation is performed with a second;
O Sovereign of the Gods, silver is obtained with the third, and iron is said to be obtained with the fourth.
Having understood one of these, one should accomplish the supreme Siddhi.
When Kālikā has been perfected, it is said that even the state of Indra is difficult to attain.

All this has its root in the Guru; therefore, one should worship him first. By his grace alone one becomes perfected, and not otherwise. Even in that case, if there is no conviction [in the Guru], [success will not be attained].

Then one should perform a circumambulation. On the day of the new moon, at midnight, having cast off all fear, one should go to a cremation ground or a remote wilderness and worship the Goddess with offerings of liquor and meat,
with delightful incenses and lamps, and with food offerings (*naivedya*).
O lady of excellent complexion! likewise, with food mixed with meat, with red garments,
and adorned with golden ornaments, while muttering the root mantra restrained by anger,
one should perform circumambulation and prostrate oneself constantly on the ground like a staff.

O Girijā! O Maheśvarī! From the beginning of the night until the end of the night, if fear should arise therein, then one should become even more firm. Having engaged in *dantādanti* (biting with the teeth), one should recollect the mantra with the mind alone. Indeed, the sound and the crest-lock (*śikhā*) are surely heard.

It is seen on dry land. O Goddess! if there were sound there, it would be a quality of a quality (*guṇaguṇa*). Then, being attached to another creeper, the task is performed just as before. At that time, O fair-limbed one, the divine speech becomes most beautiful. Having recognized the necessary accomplishment (*siddhi*), [one proceeds].
Then one should perform a great festival. Even so, if there is no conviction [of success], one should then perform the *bhaga-yāga*.
Having diligently brought a young woman who is desirous and especially in her menses, one should carefully adorn her with one's own ornaments. Having personally massaged her...
O Śivā! Having honored her with perfumes, ornaments, garments, and having fed her with sweet foods with supreme devotion, one should strip her of her clothes and place her upon a raised bed;
thereafter, one should perform the worship.
Equipped with various ritual materials, one should fashion a yantra right there using red sandalwood and lac. One should worship Bhaganāsā, Bhagaprāṇā, Bhagadehā,
and Bhagastanī upon the eight petals, and worship the Goddess in the center.

The practitioner of mantra, desiring a vision of the Goddess, should worship with devotion using red perfumes, red garlands, and beautiful red garments. O Goddess, at that time, when she desires pleasure,
he should enjoy her like a creeper until he performs the fire-offering (homa).

Then, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the nectar of the flowering [plant]. Oṃ, salutations to you, O Bhagamālā! O auspicious one who bears the form of the *bhaga*! O you whose form is the *bhaga*, O highly fortunate one, the sole bestower of enjoyment and liberation! By the grace of the Goddess, may [this be accomplished] for me.
Success shall be attained! O Kālī! O you whose form is the digit of Time (Kālakalā)! O Kulīnā! O you whose form is the Kula!

By the grace of the path of the Kula, success shall be mine. Having praised her thus, O Maheśānī! O Deveśī! one should mentally recite the thousand-fold *kūrca* seed-syllable and the *Nārasiṃha* mantra.

Within a hundred [days], she herself, though mad, will speak when she appears in person. The beloved will certainly tell [you]; there is no need for hesitation here. Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme secret, more secret than the secret, rather than [making it] public.

There would be a failure of one's purpose; therefore, one should guard [the practice] with effort. O Maheśānī! If one is unable in this regard, one should employ the *kalāvaṭī* rite. Having combined saffron, sandalwood, and camphor, one should grind them together. O Deveśī! One should recite the mantra a thousand times and worship the Goddess. [One should also worship] a passionate woman...

One should worship with devotion and cause a *tilaka* to be made upon her head; by the mere act of subjugation, one should wear it oneself on one's own head. O Supreme Goddess! *Ramā*, *Vāṇī*, and *Bhavānī*, likewise *Sarvasammohinī*, joined with the syllable *ṅe* and ending with the beloved of Fire (*svāhā*)—this is the mantra. By this...
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead with [the mantra] recited one hundred times.

One should diligently worship Kalā, adorned with various ornaments. Having drunk [the water] oneself with care, one should carefully cause her to drink as well. Then the goddess herself will produce divine speech; of this there is no doubt.
Having become thus, O lady of excellent limbs, one should then apply effort. Or else, O Goddess of the lords of gods,
the wise man, having become naked, should gaze upon another woman who is naked and recite the mantra with undivided mind, beginning from the latter part of the watch (yāma).
Vigilant regarding the two times [of worship],

and having worshipped the chosen deity with offerings of moderate meat, one should station Gaṇanātha, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and likewise the Yoginī at one's own side, sword in hand, for the sake of protection.

O most beautiful one! One should worship with offerings of meat and food mixed with meat; having lit a lamp of ghee, one should then worship the Goddess. Then, for one who recites [the mantra] a thousand times, a vision of the deity will occur. Or else, having become observant of the rules (niyama)...
O Goddess! For the sake of attaining perfection, one should daily recite [the mantra] encapsulated by the *bhūtalipi* and other syllables a thousand times.

One should practice constant remembrance day and night, consume only sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and always diligently wear washed garments. Furthermore, one must avoid conversing with barbarians (*mleccha*).
One should diligently avoid flour-based foods; one should subsist solely on milk, or else eat only barley-gruel (yāvaka). One may subsist on vegetables, or water, or even remain without food.
Having reached a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), one should dwell there, or else reside on the earth or with a beloved maiden.

One should worship with effort the one adorned with various ornaments. O lady of excellent limbs! when the month is complete, at midnight, free from fear and situated in the midst of a circle of creepers, one should perform the great worship with various kinds of liquor, meat, and other offerings.

Having thus worshipped with various offerings according to the rules and with devotion at all times in the abode of darkness (the cremation ground), perfection is attained by merely reciting [the mantra] one thousand times; it is not otherwise. That Goddess comes in person—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. O lady of beautiful hips! She comes in person, and one becomes equal to the moon.

O fair-faced one! O Goddess! For the sake of attaining the power of ointment (*añjana*), the power of sandals (*pādukā-siddhi*), the power of the sword (*khaḍga-siddhi*), and the power of immortality and freedom from old age, as well as the power of the Madhumatī, there is no doubt that these are achieved for the purpose of attaining the power of beautiful women (*kāminī-siddhi*). Furthermore, a hundred celestial maidservants come under her control; it is not otherwise.
Whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld, wherever he desires to go, all the celestial nymphs (ceṭikās) lead him there;
of this there is no doubt. If the practitioner recites [the mantra] for Rambhā or even Ghṛtācī, that goddess arrives at that very moment; no deliberation need be made in this matter.

O Goddess! One shall attain death at will; what else shall I tell you? This secret rite of Dakṣiṇā has been told to you out of affection for you, O lady of excellent hips, within thousands of Tantras—of this there is no doubt. Alternatively, having approached a courtesan, one should worship her with a spirit of devotion, together with her.

One should mutter the mantra and drink the *āsava* (fermented liquor) incessantly; having offered it with supreme devotion, one should diligently cause her to drink it as well. O fair-faced lady, having understood this procedure, the wise man should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) every day for one month, and there must always be the feeding of Brahmins.

When the month is complete, the supreme practitioner, joined by the creeper at midnight, should worship the Supreme Goddess according to the very sequence of direct worship. Standing in the midst of great darkness, he should recite the mantra with one-pointed mind; O Goddess, success arises at that very moment—this is the truth!
I tell you: or else, a wise man should fashion a Pāñcālī from Nimba wood;

having gone to a secluded place, O beloved, in a great forest, he should perform the ritual of worship there for that image which has the form of his beloved, though not yet consecrated, and whose head is toward the constellation Revatī. Having bathed it... [he should proceed].
One should perform the ritual procedure for practice. O beautiful one! One should inscribe the mantra upon the ground with sandalwood paste.

O beloved! One should place the *pāñcālī* there upon a red cloth. Having gone there, O beloved! one should plant stakes in the four directions. Right there, one should install the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) secured by their respective mantras.

Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginīs in the directions of the moon (the north), the mantra-practitioner, endowed with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), according to the prescribed rite, [should recite]: "Oṃ! And whatever spirits (*bhūta*) are stationed here, white ones in the form of *kuṣmāṇḍas*, and the *yoginīs*..."
The Yātudhānas and those who are exceedingly fierce, the Gandharvas who create obstacles,
the Kinnaras, the ants, the Cipiṭas, the Śaṅkaras,
those with terrible fangs and great ferocity, and the Sūcīmukhas who are great sinners.

"May all those who delight in evil deeds, having been struck by me, depart at the command of Śaṅkara. Having properly uttered the *kūrca* mantra, one should strike them vigorously with unhusked rice grains (*akṣata*).
Then, having diligently worshipped the Goddess according to the procedure for the great ritual (*mahāpūjāvidhāna*), [one should proceed] from there...

The wise one should write the root mantra on the forehead of the doll; O Goddess, one should worship the appropriate deities upon its limbs: Kālikā on the forehead, Bhadrakālikā on the eyes, Guhyakālī on the ears, and Siddhikālikā on the tongue.
One should diligently worship Śmaśānakālikā on the head, Mahākālī on the chest, Kālikā on the hips,
and Śrīyonikālikā on the throat; having thus worshipped with care,
one should recite the root mantra a hundred times in the heart while in a place of profound darkness, in a desolate spot, or in a temple of the gods.

By merely reciting it one thousand times, she becomes manifest; it is not otherwise. Or else, one should take refuge at the root of a plantain tree in the midst of a cremation ground and worship her with supreme devotion, adorned with various ornaments, accompanied by offerings of liquor and meat.

Standing in the midst of a group of young women, one should mutter the mantra throughout the night; he becomes manifest, and not otherwise. Or else, O Supreme Goddess! one should fashion a divine rosary from the seeds of the *karṇikāra* tree, O Pārvatī, using a red cloth and the blood from the house of a menstruating woman.

One should adorn [the deity], O Supreme Goddess! Furthermore, O Goddess, one should incense [her] with the smoke arising from black agallochum (kālāguru), O lotus-eyed one, having worshipped the Goddess with great effort. Through the offerings of wine and meat, she becomes manifest; it is not otherwise. Thus it has been told to you.
O Goddess! This supreme [teaching], more secret than the secret, has been told. Through disclosure, there would be a loss of siddhi;
therefore, one should guard it with great effort. Alternatively, O lady of excellent limbs, having carefully burnt the Kākajaṅghā creeper, one should likewise adorn one's own body with its ashes.
Then, O Goddess of gods, having stripped off his clothes, the wise man, with a single-minded soul, should recite [the mantra] upon the funeral pyre;
he shall become manifest, and not otherwise. Or else, he should plant [the seed] in the earth where boars have fed, and there, having worshipped the Goddess...

O Supreme Goddess! One should worship with various delightful substances, including the use of wine and meat. Having worshipped with diligent effort, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. Then, O lady of excellent hips, [the goal is attained] directly; there is no need for further deliberation here.
Reflection: Or else, O lady of excellent hips! one should perform the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vidhi*).
Having brought a human skull, or even that of a cat, O Pārvatī!
and having carefully placed a fresh cow-skull upon the ground, one should then install the pedestal and meditate upon the Goddess.
The practitioner should worship her at midnight, provided with liquor and other offerings.
The practitioner should recite [the mantra] with supreme devotion up to one thousand times. Then, O Goddess, she will become manifest;
there is no need for deliberation on this point. Or else, O Mistress of the Gods, having approached a beautiful woman...

Having drunk from her lower lip with effort, one should fill it thoroughly with camphor. One should likewise apply saffron to her vulva and honey to her ear. Then, O Supreme Goddess, having enjoyed that beloved woman while reciting her mantra, [one should consume] that saffron and that...

Having carefully mixed it with honey, and having applied that very mixture as a tilaka, the practitioner, free from fear at midnight, should recite the mantra a thousand times; then she will appear before him in person.
Or else, O fair-faced one, having diligently fashioned a yantra with blood drawn from one's own body, [one should place the mantra] therein.
One should worship the Goddess with offerings of wine and meat and with *arka* flowers, O fair-faced one!

Success is attained by merely reciting [the mantra] a thousand times, and not otherwise. Or else, O Supreme Goddess, the wise man should dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā; having observed two fasts, he should perform [the rite].
Having bathed without sloth, one should then worship the Goddess with delightful incense, lamps, and offerings of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna). Restraining one’s speech, one should eat oneself.
Having eaten and drunk together with his wife at midnight, free from fear, he should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, O Queen of the Gods.

Then, O fair-faced one, success is attained! Alternatively, staying at the foot of a banyan tree, naked, with hair disheveled, and being entwined by creepers, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
Then, O Goddess, he shall become manifest; there is no need for hesitation here. By this practice as well—

If it does not manifest directly, then, O Goddess! I shall explain a most wonderful method. If it does not manifest directly through even one application, one should perform a second, or perhaps a third, O Beloved! If [it still does not manifest] by the third—

I shall tell you the means for attaining success therein: upon a cloth that is white, red, yellow, or blue, one should fashion an image of the Goddess, beautiful in all her limbs. One should worship her in her wrathful form with captivating red garments, and having performed full adoration, one should recite the mantra of the Goddess there within the yantra.

A thousand [recitations] are performed there with a rosary fashioned from red sandalwood seeds; then, O Dear One, having carefully kindled a fire with wood from the Śālmalī or Nimba tree, one should worship the fire therein. Then, one should write the mantra upon the forehead of the effigy.
O Varānane! O Goddess! Then one should heat the Sindūra-puttalī (the vermilion image) in the fire.
One should strike it with the root mantra and protect it with the root mantra. One should wash it with pure milk or else with curd-water. Then one should recite the syllable *Hūṃ* a thousand times.
O Supreme Goddess! Then, O Goddess, [the deity] will manifest visibly; there is no need for deliberation here.

Or else, O Pārvatī, O Goddess, one should strike [it] with the Nārasiṃha [mantra]. During the day, the man should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remain like a celibate student (brahmacārī); at night, his mouth should be full of betel leaf.

Standing in the center of the circle of the palm-leaf mandala, O Queen of Gods, one should recite the mantra encased within the *nārasiṃha* [mantra]. Then, by merely reciting it one hundred thousand times, he becomes manifest; it is not otherwise. He will certainly become manifest, just as my own word says. Or else, O lady of excellent hips, with iron from a ship...
O Pārvatī! Having fashioned a trident with effort, one should depict the Goddess upon a cloth.

One should worship her with diligence using red sandalwood and flowers. Having worshipped her with diligence, one should duly invoke the deity of the pedestal (pīṭhadevatā) upon her limbs with devotion.

One should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. One should diligently worship the trident, which is sharp and exceedingly difficult to obtain. Having uttered the two weapon-mantras: "Oṃ! O Great Trident! Salutations to you, the destroyer of all Daityas," [one should then strike] the chest with the trident.

By effort alone, that Kālī comes; of this there is no doubt. She will certainly manifest before one's very eyes, just as my word says. Alternatively, having carefully inscribed the seed-syllable of Kālikā a hundred times on the first leaf with saffron using a golden stylus, [one should recite] the mantra.

O Goddess of gods! having drawn [a figure] upon the ground, one should bring the beloved there; one should worship the Goddess, adorned with various ornaments, upon her body. At midnight, one should recite the mantra in a secluded place together with the beloved; one should then recite the mantra one thousand times.

(1005) One will certainly become manifest [as the deity]. Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme secret, more secret than the secret. This must not be disclosed, O Goddess; one should guard it like the offspring of one's own mother.

In the fourteenth chapter: O beautiful one! [I shall speak] of the secret Vidyā of Dakṣiṇā, O Pārvatī! [And] of Mahākālī, of Mahāvidyā, of Siddhikālī, of Śmaśānakālikā, and of Nāyikā, O Daughter of the Mountain! Of those Nāyikās...

O Queen of the Gods! The method of accomplishment shall now be told. It has been spoken, O Supreme Goddess! and it must also be spoken, O Pārvatī! The seed-syllable of Kālī, O Great Goddess! is the mantra that is the highest of all the high. O Goddess, this Vidyā is renowned as consisting of three qualities and is exceedingly difficult to obtain.

O Beloved! one should perform everything as previously stated, and the fruit shall be exactly that much. O Noble Lady! the mantra may end with *namaḥ*, or it may end with *vaṣaṭ*. O Goddess! the great mantra may begin with *hrīṃ* (lajjā) or begin with *aiṃ* (vāgbhava). O Lady of Excellent Limbs! this mantra [is found] in all tantras.
It is concealed. Bhairava is declared its seer (ṛṣi), and Uṣṇik is remembered as its meter (chandas).

All matters such as worship and meditation have been proclaimed as before. O Goddess! The entire method of practice (sādhana) has been proclaimed as before. This is the celebrated three-syllabled vidyā.
It is proclaimed that [the mantra] ends with *svāhā*. This five-syllabled Great Vidyā is concealed in all Tantras.

All matters such as meditation and worship have been described as before. O Goddess! The entire method of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is accompanied by a host of creepers. The one-syllabled Great Vidyā also ends with *svāhā*.

The three-syllabled mantra is thus remembered. O Supreme Goddess! its practice is performed with the offerings of wine and meat. The great vidyā of one syllable is proclaimed to end with *svāhā*, or, O Great Goddess! it may end with *phaṭ* or *vaṣaṭ*, or, O Great Goddess! it may end with *namaḥ*.

The bestower of all accomplishments! O lady of excellent hips! The seed-syllable of the East [Hrīm], O lady of beautiful countenance! Kālī and the lunar [Aim]—this great vidyā of Kālikā is concealed in all tantras. O lady of excellent hips! The seed-syllable of the Earth [Lm], O lady of excellent hips! Kālī, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava [Aiṃ]—these, O Goddess, are the syllables of the mantra.
The [mantra] of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain. For these excellent mantras, Ugrabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi); the meter is known as Anuṣṭubh; and Dakṣiṇā is said to be the deity.
(p. 1006) Now, O Maheśānī! I shall declare the auspicious [mantra] of Guhyakālī.

O Devī! It consists of the three seed-syllables of Kālī followed by Guhyakālī; this Vidyā is said to end with *svāhā*, and it is considered the supreme Vidyā. Alternatively, it should be known as ending with *namaḥ*.

That [mantra] is also remembered as ending with *vaṣaṭ*. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kālī, one should extract the seed-syllable of the Earth (*dharā*). Having extracted the seed-syllable of Lajjā, one should extract the seed-syllable of Kūrca.
This Vidyā, said to end with *svāhā*, bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. O Goddess, [the mantra consists of] the pair of Kūrca and Lajjā.
Likewise, Kālī is proclaimed; this Vidyā, ending with Svāhā, is declared to be hidden in all Tantras.
Of these very Vidyās, the metre is remembered as Uṣṇih. Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the Seer (Ṛṣi), and Dakṣiṇā is remembered as the Deity. O lady of excellent hips, there are three Kūrca-mantras.

Indeed, it is proclaimed that [the mantra] ends with *svāhā*. Having extracted the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kālī, one should likewise utter the words "Kālī Kālī" and then the word "Mahākālī," ending with *svāhā* according to the prescribed proportions. This great mantra (*mahāmanu*) of Mahākālī is renowned in all tantras. [The seed-syllable of] Kālī...

Having extracted Mahākālī joined with *ṅe* and ending in *svāhā*, this Vidyā is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*). Having extracted the seed-syllable of Asitā and the word "Mahākālī" twice, ending in *svāhā*, this Vidyā is said to increase great prosperity. [The names] Kālī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā [are used].

The syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) followed by *sphreṃ* is proclaimed as the supreme; this mantra, O Goddess, ending with *namaḥ*, is considered to bestow liberation directly. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kālī, one should extract the seed-syllable of Lañjā (hrīṃ). Then, O fair-faced one, the word *Siddhikālī* in the dative case (*ṅe'-anta*) ending with *asitā*.

For these very vidyās, the meter (chandas) is declared to be Gāyatrī. Its deity is Mahākālī, the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga). O beautiful lady, Kālikā may end in Svāhā or even in Phaṭ. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Lajjā (Hrīṃ), one should extract one's own seed-syllable: [this is] Siddhikālī.

Then, this [mantra] ending in *ṅe* and ending in *svāhā* is proclaimed; that Great Goddess ending in *namaḥ* bestows the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*). Having extracted this *asitā*, one should extract the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhavānī. O Supreme Goddess! The *vāgbhava* is then remembered as the *parā* seed-syllable. Then the word *kālī-kālī*.
Therefore, the word for the attainment of success follows; this Great Vidyā ending with *phaṭ* is concealed in all Tantras.

O Goddess! [There are] the three seed-syllables of Ramā, likewise the three seed-syllables of Lajjā, and the three seed-syllables of Kāma, O Goddess! And Siddhikālī joined with *ṅe* [and ending] with *svāhā*.

The Vidyā has been declared as the lamp illuminating the path to liberation. For these gentle Vidyās, Gāyatrī is said to be the metre (chandas). O Goddess! Kapila shall be the seer (ṛṣi), and Siddhikālikā the deity.
Having extracted the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kālī, one should take the word "Śmaśānakālikā" joined with the suffix "ṅe".

O Supreme Sovereign! O Fair-faced One! Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kālī and the seed-syllable of Kūrca, this Vidyā ending in Svāhā is said to bestow all siddhis. O Beloved of the Excellent! O Maheśvarī! [The mantra consists of] two Kūrca-syllables and the seed-syllable of the Goddess.
