This Vidyā bestows all accomplishments and is not in conflict with any scripture. Viśvāmitra is declared to be the sage, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter. The goddess Śmaśānakālikā is hidden within all Tantras. O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign! The practice (sādhana) of these [mantras] has been previously described.

The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for all of them shall now be described; through this application alone, success is attained, and not otherwise. For Śmaśānakālikā, there is the sitting upon a *kalā* (digit); O Maheśānī, the application of the *kumārī* (virgin) is prescribed in the place of the *kalā*.

O Maheśvarī! A girl who is eight years old, or less than twelve, should be seated on the four sides [of the vessel], having been fed with sweet food. The practitioner should worship her with supreme devotion and then eat himself. He should carefully make her drink the *āsava* (fermented liquor), and then he himself should drink it as well.

One should recite the syllable *sa* and the syllable *gha*, joined with the syllable *la*, one hundred and eight times into the ear of each of them individually. Having worshipped him with great effort and placed him upon one's chest, O Goddess, the practitioner, with undistracted mind, should recite the mantra accompanied by the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). In this...

O Goddess! When she desires pleasure at the proper time, then the practitioner of mantra should delight her so that no pain arises. There should be a gradual drinking of the lips, a gradual pressing of the breasts, a gradual insertion into the secret place, and a gradual embrace, O Beloved! If pain should arise therein—
At that time, it is the destroyer of success. In this manner of practice, Kālī becomes manifest; not otherwise.

Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme secret, more secret than the secret. If there be a lack of devotion, a lack of ritual action, or a lack of following the prescribed rules, then success will be delayed and shall be fruitless.
It is never born. One should not harbor distrust, nor should one practice indolence, O Pārvatī!
Having extracted the essence of all the most excellent mantras, O Pārvatī—just as butter is within milk, or as fire is within wood—so too [is this].

O Goddess! The essence has been extracted; there is no doubt about this. Indeed, these mantras of yours are self-perfected and hidden in all the tantras. Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; it must be guarded with great effort.
In the fourth chapter of the Toḍalatantra: "Listen, O fair-limbed one! O fortunate lady!

[I shall describe] the great worship of Tārā. Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra, one should then bow to the Guru as a deity. Having purified the water, one should then wash both hands and feet."

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra, one should then contemplate the seat (pīṭha). O Goddess! Having tied the topknot (śikhā), which destroys various obstacles, and having purified the ground and the seat, and having tied a knot in the cloth, one should then perform the purification of body and speech.

The purification of the flowers: having prepared the *yantra*, the lord of practitioners should arrange the ordinary *arghya* offering. Having worshipped the guardians of the gates, he should commence the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

He should then worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭha-śakti*), such as Lakṣmī and others, and thereafter worship the mantra of the pedestal. [He should perform] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

I shall now declare the specific distinction that exists here, O Goddess of the Suras! By means of the *haṃsa* joined with the *kūrca* and through inhalation (*pūraka*), the practitioner, together with Kuṇḍalinī, [unites] the self and the twenty-four seed-syllables (*bīja*) therein.
O Mistress of the Gods, the practitioner should burn away sin by means of Māyā while those [syllables] are dissolved into the Supreme Self.

O lady of excellent hips! the wise one should reduce a person who has the luster of collyrium to ashes by means of *kumbhaka*. O Queen of the Gods! one should exhale the seed-syllable of the bride along with the ashes.
Then, O Supreme Goddess! one should contemplate a mass of nectar on the forehead by means of the *pūraka* and the *kūrca* mantra.

During the retention of breath (*kumbhaka*), one should recite the mantra *āṃ hrīṃ krīṃ* ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*) eleven times in the heart. Then the wise one should meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable *āḥ*;
above that, he should further meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable *ṭāṃ*. Above that...

One should again meditate upon the syllable *huṃ*, resembling the color of a dark blue cloud. Above that, one should again meditate upon a chisel adorned with [the letter] *vi*. Above that is the supreme *bindu*, the imperishable form of Śiva, which is a thousandth part of a grain of sand.
It is extremely difficult to attain. Within the *bindu* is the Jewel Island (*maṇidvīpa*), extending for a hundred *yojanas*.
Within the *bindu* is the supreme light, a sphere in the form of a bubble.
O Goddess! Just as one perceives a reflection within a single bubble, so too is the vision [of that light].

One should perform the ritual action with the eye of wisdom. In the center of that, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a jewel-island consisting of golden sand; all around it, he should contemplate the enchanting Pārijāta tree.
In the middle, he should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), and upon himself as being identical with Tāriṇī.
Resembling the rising sun, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, equipped with four gates, adorned with golden ramparts, beautified by many chowries, bells, and celestial maidens,
provided with gentle breezes, and decorated with perfumes and incense— in the midst of that [palace]:

One should meditate upon the altar, adorned with various jewels; one should contemplate the supreme parasol fashioned with golden threads. Beneath that, O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a jeweled lion-throne;
there, one should meditate upon the Goddess according to the yoga of the prescribed visualization.

O Goddess! One should worship with the articles of offering mentioned in the *Yogasāra*. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth. One should perform the binding of the ten directions with three claps and snapping of the fingers. Then, having performed the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhā-nyāsa*), [one should proceed].
Immediately thereafter, having established the pervasive [deity] and the special *arghya*, one should purify the five principles (*pañcatattva*).

Having invited the goddess Sudhā, one should perform the *vipañcīkaraṇa*. Taking a flower in the *kumbha* vessel, one should worship it three times within the triangle; likewise, one should worship Vāmadeva three times.

Having spoken thus, one should mutter the *khecarī* mantra ten times. Likewise, the wise person should mutter the *Ānanda-gāyatrī* and the *ṛc* three times. O Goddess of the Gods! By muttering the [mantras of the] directions, the wise one causes the curse of Brahmā, the curse of Śukra, and the curse of Kṛṣṇa to vanish; thereafter, he should recite the triad of mantras.

O Dear One! Having recited the *Pāvamāna* mantra three times over the knife, the corpse, and the venerable *tiraskariṇī* (curtain), one should perform the purification rites and so forth. O Goddess! One should recite the *Vāruṇa* mantra three times and the *amṛta* mantra seven times. Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* within the *vidyātattva*, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) eight times.

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī, one should then contemplate, "I am Śiva. After purifying the meat and the fish, one should perform the purification of the *mudrās*. The best of practitioners should then purify the *Śakti* and the *Kula-flower*, [offering them] to the gods, the ancestors, and the sages.

One should satisfy one’s chosen deity. Taking the purified substance, one should pour it as the special *arghya* offering. Then, having meditated upon [the deity] as consisting of Brahman, one should perform the worship and meditation.
Having brought [the consciousness] from the location of the nose and placed the flower upon the seat—
Then, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should display the five mudrās.

Having worshipped with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should again display the mudrās. Then, having performed the placement of life-force (*jīvanyāsa*), one should worship with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*). Having worshipped the six limbs, [one worships] Akṣobhya.
One should worship below. Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one should worship at the bases of the petals.

One should sacrifice to Kālyā and the others preceded by Mahā, as well as Vairocana and the rest. Then, having worshipped the Goddess again, the wise practitioner should offer the bali. Thereafter, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).

One should perform meditation on the mantra. O Maheśānī! Having performed the recitation (japa), one should offer it into the hand of the Goddess. Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the acceptance of the principles (tattvasvīkāra). Having given [the remainder] to her and having drunk [some] oneself, the best of practitioners should recite. Having drunk again and again, and having recited, [one should proceed].

Liberated along with ten million lineages, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for each vessel. Then, having remembered the hymn of praise and the armor, he should prostrate with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*).
Thereafter, the special offering (*viśeṣārghya*) should be presented, and he should offer himself, assuming the form of Rudra.

Having become [the deity] oneself, one should dismiss [her] by means of reabsorption. O Maheśānī! Next, perform the assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and then *prāṇāyāma*. Having drawn a mandala in the northeast, [one should worship] Caṇḍālī, preceded by Ucchiṣṭa, and Nirmālyavāsinī, ending with the vocative suffix *ṅe*.
Salutations again and again to Caṇḍeśvarī! One should wear the remains of the offering (nirmālya) upon the head and sandalwood paste on the forehead.
One should draw a bindu in the place of the Guru and wander like Bhairava.
O Goddess! The abbreviated mental worship, which is devoid of [external] principles, should be performed here according to what has been taught therein.

A wise person should not transfer [the offering] to anyone else; O Goddess, by transferring it to another, Tāriṇī becomes enraged. What was stated there refers to the section on external worship (vāhyapūjā). O Pārvatī, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) and mental worship belong only to Śakti.
In the twelfth chapter of the Picchilā Tantra: "At the very moment the great mantra is heard with focused attention, even the most massive sins residing within the body are destroyed.
O Maheśvarī! I shall now describe the application of mantra-purification and so forth; [first], mantra-purification..."

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should then form the mantra-crested lock (mantra-śikhā). Having recited the Kallukā-mantra over the head, one should then recite the Mahāsetu-mantra. One should recite the Nirvāṇa-mantra at the navel and then meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī. Then, having performed prāṇāyāma—
One should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Then, having performed the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, one should recite the *saptacchada* [mantra] once.
O Dear One! One should recite the mantra encased by the *dhruva* [syllable] seven times.
O Maheśvarī! Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning of the mantra, one should recite it once; or else, [one may place] the *praṇava* [at the end].

O Supreme Goddess! Having placed either *māyā*, *vāgbhava*, or *dīpanī* at the beginning of the mantra, one should recite it seven times. O Queen of the Gods! In the case of the *Kālī* mantra, one should recite *krīṃ* as the root syllable seven times.
And having placed the *vidyā-mantra* at the beginning of the mantra, one should recite it seven times. [One should worship] one’s own guru...

Having visualized [the Guru] on the crown of the head and the Goddess in the heart, one should then perform the recitation while contemplating oneself as the form of Kāmakalā. At the end of the recitation, one should meditate upon Śiva,
and at the end of that meditation, recite again— either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times.

One should recite the mantra. O Śivā! Having first uttered the *dīpanī* of Śyāmā—the Jewel of Knowledge (*vidyāratna*)—one should recite it seven times; thereafter, the dedication of the recitation (*japasamarpaṇa*) follows. For other [deities], one should recite the *praṇava*, the *māyā*, or the *dīpanī* at the beginning of the recitation; having recited the *setu* seven times, [the recitation is concluded].

One should recite the mantra ending with the *praṇava*. Afterwards, one should offer the recitation and perform *prāṇāyāmas*. The procedure for the recitation here has been stated as a supplementary detail.
Now follows the hymn of one hundred names of Tārā.
The illustrious Śiva said:

Tāriṇī, Taralā, Tanvī, Tārā, the young creeper (Tarūṇavallarī); she whose form is the shore (Tīrarūpā), dark as a boat (Taraśyāmā), with slender and diminished breasts (Tanukṣīṇapayodharā); the fourth state (Turīyā), the tremulous (Taralā), of swift gait (Tīvragamanā), the blue-flowing river (Nīlavāhinī);
Ugratārā, Jayā, Caṇḍī, the glorious Śrīmadekajaṭā, the auspicious Śivā, and the youthful Śāmbhavī.
Chinnabhālā, Bhadratāriṇī, Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Nīlā, Kṛṣṇā, Nīlasarasvatī; the second is Śobhinī, Nityā, Navīnā, Nityanūtanā;
Caṇḍikā, Vijayārādhyā, the Goddess Gaganavāhinī, Aṭṭahāsyā, Karālāsyā.
You are Carasī, worshipped by Aditi; you possess all qualities and are to be propitiated by those with qualities; you are worshipped by Hari, Indra, and the gods.

You are fond of red, have red eyes, and are adorned with blood and wine. You are fond of offerings (bali), delight in offerings, and are Durgā, the powerful, and Valā. You are fond of strength, delight in strength, and are fully worshipped by Balarāma.
The Mistress of Half-Hair, whose hair is adorned with the Lord of Hair (Viṣṇu);

she who wears a garland of lotuses, whose eyes are like lotuses; she who is named Kāmā, the daughter of the Mountain; she who is Dakṣiṇā, the skillful Dakṣā, born of Dakṣa, and devoted to the right path; she who loves the *vajra* flower, who is fond of red, and is adorned with exquisite ornaments.

(1012) Māheśvarī, the beloved of Mahādeva, adorned with five ornaments; Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā, who is the form of the vital breath (prāṇa); and Gāndhārī as the fifth, worshipped by the five-faced one and others—this, O Goddess, is the secret that has been told.
Most wonderful! By hearing this, one attains liberation through the grace of the goddess Tārā.

Whoever recites this secret hymn of praise to Tārā shall wander upon the circle of the earth endowed with all accomplishments (siddhis). For him alone there shall be success in mantra; my own unsurpassed success [is granted] to him.
"It is so, O Mahāmāyā! This is the truth, the truth; there is no doubt.

Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this at night on a Monday or a Tuesday, for him alone shall there be the perfection of mantra, and he shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati—whether with faith or even without faith."

One who recites this secret [mantra] shall, in a very short time, become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and attain the state of Śiva. O Goddess! By reciting it one thousand times, one obtains the fruit of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). Thus, those who, being constantly disciplined, worship You while meditating upon You, they have achieved their life's purpose, O Maheśānī!
"From the bondage of death and saṃsāra. Thus ends the hymn of the hundred names of Tāriṇī in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.

Now, following the *Tāriṇī-stotra*, in the *Mahānīla-tantra*: "O you of terrible form! O Great Death! O you who bring all enemies under control! O Goddess, granter of boons to your devotees, protect me who has come to you for refuge! O Goddess worshipped by gods and asuras! O Goddess served by *siddhas* and *gandharvas*!"
O Goddess, remover of dullness and sin! Protect me who have come to you for refuge!

O You endowed with a mass of matted locks! O You who imitate the flickering tongue [of Agni]! O Goddess, bestower of swift intellect! Protect me who have come to you for refuge! O You of gentle form! O You of terrible form! O You of fierce form!
Homage be unto you! O you whose form is creation, salutations to you; protect me who have come to you for refuge.

With a single-minded focus on the eighth, fourteenth, and ninth lunar days, one attains perfection within six months; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. Grant me intelligence; grant me glory.
Grant me, grant me the power of poetry! O Goddess, take away my evil intellect;

protect me, who have come to you for refuge! O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods beginning with Indra, O embodiment of compassion! O Tārā, whose face is the lord of stars (the moon)! Protect me, who have come to you for refuge! One seeking liberation attains it.

One seeking liberation shall attain liberation; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth; and one seeking knowledge shall acquire knowledge, such as logic and grammar. That person who constantly recites this hymn attains these benefits:
his enemies go to ruin, and he becomes possessed of great wisdom.

Whether in times of affliction, in battle, during the recitation of mantras, in giving charity, or likewise in fear, for one who recites this auspicious hymn, there is no doubt of its benefit. O Goddess of the Gods! by praising the Sovereign Goddess with this hymn, one attains all desires and becomes a treasury of all knowledge.

Thus has been told to you this divine hymn that bestows the power of Sarasvatī; O Maheśvarī, there is no hymn superior to this within the Tantra. Thus ends the Tāriṇīstotra in the second chapter of the Bṛhannīlatantra.
Now, the Vīra-homa. In the fifth chapter of the Kaivalya-tantra: "Listen, O Pārvatī!

I shall explain the procedure for the external homa, O beloved. It was previously taught in detail by Vyāsa across all the Āmnāyas; I shall describe it here in brief, by means of which a person may attain liberation."

Having drawn a triangle upon the ground, the practitioner should then establish the fire with the root mantra and the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Having invoked the Goddess there along with her retinue,
he should worship her with various ritual substances with a mind free from conceptual distraction.

O Mistress of the Kula! One should first offer an oblation with liquor while reciting the root mantra; then one [should offer] with meat, fish, and a seal (mudrā), together with the sweepings fallen from the base of a plantain tree.

One should perform oblations with clarified butter, either once or three times; there is also one oblation with ghee and red flowers. O Goddess of the Gods! two oblations with *kuṇḍodbhava* are prescribed;
an oblation with cow’s milk mixed with ghee is especially distinguished as being performed once.

O beautiful one, in a pure place, one should recite "hum" ten times while using *gopīcandana*, vermilion (*sindūra*), *vīrapuṣpa*, cow-products (*gavya*), and *vilva* leaves; then a single oblation (*homa*) should be made into the fire with cow-products,
followed by a single offering of oil-cakes mixed with salt, and then the root-mantra.

The practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, O Beloved! Having recited, praised, and bowed, he should dismiss [the deity] within the fire-mandala. Thus has been told to you, O Goddess, the means for attaining liberation, O Dear One! There is nothing higher than this; I tell you this as the truth. This is the supreme secret.
One should not reveal this to ordinary people; from such revelation, there will be a loss of accomplishment—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Thus ends the Vīra-homa.

Having thus worshipped and offered oblations, one should partake of the substances, drinks, and so forth, together with the initiates (*sāmayika*). Regarding the fruit of giving substances to the Goddess, it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālātantra*: "O Goddess, having worshipped the Great Goddess with wine, meat, *kalā*, and various kinds of food..."
Having thus fully satisfied him, by the very fruit of that offering of liquor, one shall become a great lord of yoga.

The varieties of *surā* are described in that very same [text]: "Surā is said to be of two kinds: *sphāṭikī* and likewise *ḍākinī*. By the gift of *kāñjikī-sphāṭikī*, there is unsurpassed increase of wealth;
by the mere gift of *ḍākinī*, one will certainly become a subduer of all. [This is done] with the *kāñjikī-mudrā*."
O Goddess! He who worships the Supreme Goddess shall become a master of great siddhis and dwell for hundreds of kalpas. O Great Goddess! For the giver of food, there is unsurpassed great siddhi.
Now, regarding Mahāśaṅkha, in the second chapter of the Nityātantra:
Īśvara said:

O sinless one, I shall tell you the greatness of the Mahāśaṅkha. It must always be guarded like one's own source of birth, even in the midst of a crowd of animals. O fair-faced one, Mahāmāyā is in the form of the Bhaga; she is intent on satisfying the seed (śukra), the lore that attracts the world, and the secret of the universe.

In that very place, the essence of the worlds is grasped in the form of a seed. That seed, O Supreme Goddess, consists of the fifty letters. Having reached the womb, it becomes bone, endowed with the marrow of the embryo; even half of that bone exists.

"O Goddess of the Gods! Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times with rosaries made of ordinary beads consisting of fifty letters, that same fruit is proclaimed to be gained by a single utterance with a rosary of bones. Thus ends the fruit of recitation with the great conch-shell rosary.

Regarding what must be avoided when making that garland, it is said in that very same [text]: "One should avoid one who has died by his own will, a woman, a Brahmin, an animal, as well as a sick person, a Yavana, an old man, and also one who has been initiated. Regarding what is to be accepted, it is also stated in that very same [text]: "[A stone] struck by a thunderbolt or bitten by a snake..."

Or one who has died after falling into water, or one killed by a tiger or similar beast, or one who has died facing the enemy in battle— these are the foremost among the low-born Śūdra castes, such as the Caṇḍālas and others.

In the fourth chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*: "O Goddess of gods! For one who has died in battle, [an image] made from the bone of a *caṇḍāla*—and especially from the skull—is proclaimed as the 'Great Conch' (*mahāśaṅkha*). In the *Nityātantra*: 'For this very reason, O Maheśānī, [one should wear] a garland of bones around the neck.'"
In my first chapter: Having taken recourse to the great conch rosary, one should proceed to the state of a hero.

Now, the method for making a garland of human bones: In the second chapter of the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra*: "O lady of excellent complexion! A garland strung from the finger-bones of a man according to the divisions of the joints bestows all accomplishments and grants liberation; it may also be strung with veins."

The garland should be made with a red cloth; a garland strung with human veins, O Dear One, bestows great siddhi. Also in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "Having brought the severed head of a fallen man, [the garland] should be touched with basil, cow dung, and likewise with water from the Gaṅgā."
That rite of his should be performed by practitioners who are neither Yavanas nor Brahmins; and they should know that it must remain untouched by Śālagrāma stones and the like.

Now, regarding the consecration of the great conch-shell rosary, it is as follows: having first prostrated there to the Guru, one should consecrate the prayer rosary. Having performed the daily rites, the practitioner of mantra should worship the rosary in due order with: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ klīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus.
Having consecrated it seven times with the mantra, one should place it in a vessel such as a cup or bowl. Then,

having invoked the Goddess together with her retinue there by means of the *āvāhanī* and other mudrās, and having worshipped her with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should transform her into nectar using the *vam* syllable and the *dhenu-mudrā*, and veil her with the *kavaca*.

Having covered [the vessel] with the *matsyamudrā* and meditating upon that garland as having the form of the Goddess, one should perform the sprinkling of the *bindu*. Therein the mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā | oṃ hūṃ svāhā | oṃ hraḥ svāhā | oṃ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ svāhā*.

Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā | Having thus performed the sprinkling of seven drops of arghya and having incensed the musk, one should lift it from the vessel such as a cup and consecrate the garland. The mantra for that is: Oṃ...

Hrīṃ śrīṃ, O Great Vajra-holder! O You of most terrible form! O You upon the circle of rough great bones! Enter [me], grant all accomplishments! Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā! Oṃ, O Great Skull-bearer! O You of most terrible form! Svāhā!

Having addressed [the deity] with this, worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), performed the kindling (*uddīpana*) with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmavīja*), worshipped with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), inflamed with the *mātṛkā* mantra, one should encircle [it] with the syllable *oṃ*. Then: *hūṃ hrīṃ hūṃ oṃ hūṃ śrīṃ hūṃ oṃ hūṃ*.
HŪṂ OṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ HŪṂ OṂ SVĀHĀ | OṂ HŪṂ MAHĀYOGINI! TRIBHUVANATĀRIṆI! DWELL IN THE MIDST OF THIS GREAT CONCH-BONE;
GRANT ALL SIDDHIS; ACCEPT AND CAUSE TO BE ACCEPTED THESE OFFERINGS OF SURĀ AND MEAT; HRĪṂ.

"Śrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having offered the *bali* with the aforementioned substances by means of this [mantra], one should dismiss the Goddess with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and place the rosaries in a secluded spot. Regarding the term "dropping of the drop" (*bindu-prakṣepa*), "drop" here means a drop of liquor (*surā-bindu*). Having thus purified [them],...

The Tantrikas maintain that the consecration of the rosary must also be performed according to the procedure for the purification of garlands. As stated in the Tantra: "A rosary obtained unexpectedly [is purified] by means of a rosary known as the *mahāśaṅkha*;
likewise, those made of bone are proclaimed to be *mahāśaṅkha*. Here, by the word "bone" (*asthi*), [the following is meant].
"The Tantrikas maintain that it is to be grasped from the region of the qualities (guṇa) and so forth. Thus ends the consecration of the great conch rosary.

In the seventh chapter of the Kubjikātantra: "O Sovereign of the Gods! Having seen an Aśoka tree, a Bilva tree, and a jackal, one should offer salutation for the sake of attaining all desires and goals. [Likewise, having seen] an owl, a Śaṅkhacilla bird, and a vulture..."
O Sovereign of the Gods! One should pay homage to Mahākālī and shall obtain victory in battle.
One should especially pay homage to a crossroads and a cremation ground.
O fair-faced one! One should pay homage to a knower of the Tantras and an Avadhūta, as well as to a practitioner at all times.
Having seen [this], one should speak sweetly.

In the sixth chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*: "O Maheśvarī! If by chance one should be on a mountain, in a desolate place, in a lonely spot, in an empty pavilion, at a crossroads, or in the midst of a *kalā*, one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, bow down, and then depart as one pleases."

Upon seeing a vulture, one should diligently pay homage to Mahākālī; likewise, upon seeing a jackal, one should pay homage to Kṣemaṅkarī, who is the messenger of Yama. Furthermore, upon seeing a curlew, a hawk, a crow, or a black cat, [one should offer salutations].

The mantra for saluting these is found in that very same [text]: "O slender-waisted one! O great fierce one! O you with loose hair! O lover of offerings! O you whose face is pleased by the Kula practice! Salutations to you, the beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having seen a corpse in a cremation ground, while walking clockwise around it and bowing down with this [mantra]...
Through mantra, the practitioner of mantra shall attain happiness. O you with terrible fangs! O you with a gaping mouth!
O you who utter the sound "kiṭi"! O you who strike with a loud and excellent roar! Salutations to you, O Caṇḍanādinī! Having beheld Tripurāmbikā with red garments and red flowers.
Having beheld her, a person should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and recite this mantra:
"O You who resemble the *bandhūka* flower! O Tripura! O Destroyer of fear!
O You who have arisen from the dawning of good fortune! Salutations to You, O Lady of excellent complexion! Likewise, [salutations] to the dark-colored one..."

Having seen Puṣpa, Rājāna, Rājaputraka, Hastyaśvarathaśastra, Kālavīra, Śiva, Mahiṣa, and Kulanātha, as well as Mahiṣamardinī, or having prostrated before Jayadurgā, one is not touched by obstacles. O Jayadevī! O Mother of the World!
O Full One! O Primordial One! O Thou of the Triple Deity! O Goddess who grantest boons to thy devotees!

O Thou adorned with a garland of severed heads! O Thou drenched in streams of blood! O Giver of Boons! I bow down to thee! O Goddess who removest all obstacles! Salutations to thee, O Beloved of Hara! [Salutations] to these...

If they do not act in this manner through mere sight, having placed the *śakti-mantra* before them, their accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not arise. How could that sinful soul—who performs the killing, expulsion, or harming of these [beings] by means of snares and the like—be my devotee? Thus ends the section on the deeds of the hero (*vīrakṛtya*).
Now, for the sake of the heroes' attainment of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*), the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) is [described] in the fifty-third chapter of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*.
Bhairava said:
In the exposition of the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*), the *tantra* becomes more extensive.

I shall describe to you briefly some of their characteristics: in the science of poetry (*kāvyashāstra*) there are nine aesthetic flavors (*rasas*), while in Yoga eight flavors are traditionally taught. Indeed, [the varieties] are of eighteen kinds.
In the Vidyā, they are fully proclaimed; in the yoga of devotion, the nine sentiments (rasas) are remembered as the seasons regarding the object of experience.
O Goddess, the rasas beginning with the fifth are remembered as fifty-five. I shall explain the divisions of these rasas; listen attentively, O beloved!

In the treatises on poetry (*kāvyashāstra*), there are nine [rasas]: the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the comic (*hāsya*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), the loathsome (*vībhatsa*), the tranquil (*śāntaka*), and the furious (*raudra*). Furthermore, [the eight limbs of yoga are] restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇasaṃyama*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and... [samādhi].

O Great Goddess! O Beloved! Concentration (samādhi) is eightfold, as described at length in the Yoga scripture. Metre (chandas) is the feet of the Veda; grammar (vyākaraṇa) is remembered as its mouth; phonetics (śikṣā), O Maheśānī, is its nose; and ritual procedure (kalpa) is said to be its hands. Astronomy (jyotiṣa), O Goddess...

That eye is called Nirukta, and the ear is said to be Śrotra. The four Vedas, along with Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya-vistara, Dharmaśāstra, and Purāṇa—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās). Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharva—these are the three [additional ones].

The eighteen branches of knowledge are joined with the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), as are the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*). They are: reflection, glorification, meditation, remembrance, service at the feet, worship, salutation, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender. Thus, O Goddess, are the nine sentiments within the yoga of devotion.

These have been proclaimed: garlands, perfumes, women, beds, garments, and ornaments. O Supreme Goddess! In this realm, the seasons and the aesthetic flavors (rasas) have been described. There are five flavors to be tasted: the molasses-based (gauḍī), honey-based (mādhvī), sugarcane, fruit, and grain. Those who know the flavors and the emotional states (bhāvas) within these are indeed connoisseurs (rasikas).

[These] are remembered [as follows]: O Supreme Goddess! the rite of action (kṛtyavidhi), the rite of recitation (japavidhi), the rite for the purification of substances (dravyaśodhanikavidhi), the rite of external worship (bāhyapūjāvidhi), and the rite of mental worship (mānasikapūjāvidhi). O Goddess! the rite of preliminary service (puraścaryāvidhi) makes the sections on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) fivefold. O Goddess! the rite of action is threefold: morning, evening, and...
Likewise, having experienced all the flavors and performed the ritual actions throughout the day,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana).
In the fifty-fourth chapter.
The Goddess said:

O Lord! How is it that you speak of mantras and how do you speak of the Vedas? With words concerning those various rasas, you seem to delude my mind. O Master, tell me now the cause for cutting through this doubt; for there is a great curiosity from hearing such a marvelous narrative.
Great.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

The words of the Tantras and the Vedic utterances are the cause of all knowledge. I shall explain the classification of the aesthetic sentiments (rasas); listen with attention to me. The erotic (śṛṅgāra) is to be known as arising from the heroic (vīra), and within it reside compassion and the others; likewise, the erotic and so forth, as well as loathing and so forth.

It should arise from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). But when, O Goddess, the erotic sentiment indicates the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then supreme peace (*paramā śānti*) attains the state of Rudra.
Listen to the meaning of these sections from me, O you who are dearer than life! Without the foot, there is no body.
No movement is found, O beloved! One should never enter the path of the Vedas through mere metrical form (chandas).

Without ornamentation, O Priyaṃvadā, meter would not shine. The distinction between the eye and the beyond (parokṣa) is the same as that of the science of light (jyotiḥśāstra), [which concerns] the moon and the sun.

Through grasping, light attains perceptibility; the Vedic branch becomes the Nirukta, and through the branches, Brahman is born. When the act of singing is being heard, devotion arises toward Brahman; at that very moment, the function of singing occurs within the mouth and the nose.
Without song there would be no dance; dance is born from song.
The science of phonetics, drama, and the like are considered to be grammar of words.
O lady of pure smiles! Because of the relationship of inseparable concomitance between these two, the Vedas [are likewise established].
Devoted to the exposition of Brahman along with its six limbs,

Mīmāṃsā, together with Nyāya, definitively establishes Brahman. For the sake of the living being’s knowledge of Brahman, there is an investigation into the Supreme Self in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras.
O Dear One! Through the investigation of its systematic arrangement and so forth, the Purāṇas are constantly born from that very source.

A living being intent on the bliss of Brahman, yet eager for self-preservation, should thoroughly study Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda. Furthermore, O Goddess, through the process of synthesis—
And the practitioner who possesses full knowledge [should worship] with honey,
sugarcane juice, milk and other such things, fruits and grains, with perfumes, garlands, and the like, O Goddess,
as well as with garments, ornaments, and so forth; upon the bed, the form of a woman.

One should worship the Mother of the Universe. O Goddess! In the worship of women, the means for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) is the worship, the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), which is proclaimed to be fivefold. A hero should master all of that for the sake of attaining the Goddess. In worship, it is ninefold.
And the effulgence of the rasa of devotion arises. Then, having practiced yoga, the ascetic (yati) becomes established in samādhi. Therefore, O Maheśānī! I have already stated this previously:
"O beloved! Having experienced all fifty-five vowels within the sphere of the ritualistic sections (karmakāṇḍa)..."

O beloved! One becomes free from desire; when one is free from desire, the fruit is wondrous, and by that the deity is satisfied. An embodied being, having taken recourse to a body, should not abandon action; rather, having completed the divine rites through such acts as the pilgrimage to the Goddess, [one attains the goal].
From the bliss of the essence of perfect knowledge, one certainly becomes liberated while living.
Now follows the accomplishment of the six rites for heroes, from the fourth chapter of the first section of the Yoginītantra.
The Goddess said:

O God of gods! O one adored by the world! O you who are saluted by gods and asuras! Now I wish to hear the means for accomplishing the six heroic rites (vīra-ṣaṭkarma), which are auspicious for meritorious kings throughout the stages of life beginning with childhood, and for women established in spiritual perfection.
Of all those who revel in enjoyments.
p. 1020) He stated the six rites in that very same place:
The Lord said:

O Supreme Goddess! pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), as well as inciting enmity (vidveṣa), eradication (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa)—these six rites are proclaimed. O Mother of the Universe! out of affection for you, I shall describe [the practice] concerning Tāriṇī, Kālikā, and Chinnā, which brings about swift accomplishment.
Furthermore: Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mātaṅgī, Kulakāminī, Durgā,
and Bhadrakālī— for the sake of accomplishing rites at the beginning of any action, a hero endowed with his own power should worship them with the sixteen types of offerings.

Regarding the six rites, he states the location for the rite of killing—excluding the other five—right there [in that same work]: "One should perform the five rites in an empty house, a great forest, or even in a temple; however, the rite of killing should be performed upon a corpse, or in its absence, on a cremation ground."

I shall describe the garments to you: the primary one is to be known as the sky-clad (naked state), and the second is the tiger skin; in its absence, one may use red linen, but no other garment should be employed.
He describes the vessels for worship according to the sequence of rites such as pacification (śānti) and others: "For the first [rite] a golden vessel, and for the second a silver one;

for paralyzing (stambhana), a stone; for inciting enmity (vidveṣa) and eradication (uccāṭana), copper; and for killing (māraṇa), a skull is auspicious. Furthermore, the man [who serves as the officiant] should be a Brahmin or another caste, young, and dark-complexioned."

In times of famine or death from disease, these [rosaries] bring auspiciousness to the practitioner. In their absence, O Beloved, one should perform japa with crystal beads or with *indrākṣa* seeds. Or else, O Queen of the Gods, on a seat that is soft or gentle; or on a *muṇḍa*, O Goddess, or on a tiger skin, O Beloved!

Within one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits on all sides, one should practice while remaining firmly seated; one should not entertain fear there. O Maheśānī! When fear arises, one should remember the mantra spoken by Bhairava.
Then, with the "Vajra-net" [mantra], one should strike the pair of jaws; thereafter, [one is protected] from all beings.

At the end of the *kūrca* mantra, the *mantra* of Bhairava follows. Then the practitioner should offer the *bhūtabali* in accordance with the Dharma. And that oil, O Maheśānī! having rubbed [the body] with it, one should perform the rite of Kālakañcara.
By means of the conjunction of Tuesday and other such days, one should perform the fivefold ritual (*pañcakarma*). And on Saturday, O Goddess! the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) is performed.
It is certain, O Goddess worshipped by heroes! No ritual action whatsoever should be performed during the junction of night, O lady of pure smiles!

(p. 1021) First, O Śivā, the wise one should properly recite his own mantra, joined with the appropriate breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), for the sake of attaining the fruit of the practice and as a great means of self-protection. Then, on the day of purification...
When one watch of the night has passed, the practitioner, having worshipped the Kulavilāsinī with the five substances beginning with *mā* (meat),
naked and with all his hair disheveled, O Kulakaulika!
joined with the Śakti and constantly recollecting her in his mind, should mutter the Vidyā, O Maheśānī, for a number of times equal to the letters *ha* and *kṣa*.

Preceded by the worship of Śakti, the wise one should daily feed other Kaulikas at the end of the day. He should offer meat, wine, and fish, two hundred oblations each. O Śāmbhavī, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, who is the very form of Śambhu.

O Maheśānī! If a divine being or a preeminent hero should perform [this rite] according to the method thus described, he would lead even the gods [to his side]. O Kāntā! No hesitation arises; he will certainly partake of the fruit.
O Deveśī! In the Great Application (mahāprayoga), one should offer a black goat as a sacrificial oblation at the conclusion of the worship.

O Goddess! One should constantly worship the fire with one-tenth of the [offering] portions. The procedure has been described everywhere according to the sequence of the divine (divya), the heroic (vīra), and the animal (paśu) [initiations]. One attains the fruit through this sequence; by transgressing it, one becomes a sinner.
Thus, the proper scope of the six rites has been fully told to you. It must be kept secret from the wicked.
When seen in the presence of a common cowherd.
The Goddess said:
O Lord! What kind of liquor is auspicious, or what kind of power is auspicious? O ocean of compassion, tell me according to what is appropriate for the six duties (ṣatkarma).
The Lord said:

The honey-wine (mādhvī) is declared to bring peace; for subjugation (vaśya), the crystal-like wine (sphāṭikī) is auspicious. For paralyzing (stambhana), the ḍākinī-wine is to be known; for causing enmity (vidveṣa), the flour-wine (paiṣṭikī) is considered best. Likewise, for eradication (uccāṭana), the molasses-wine (gauḍī); and for killing (māraṇa), the bhairavī-wine is prescribed. O Goddess, the characteristics of these have been told in the *Kulamohana*.

Regarding the distinction between the powers (*śakti*), it is said in that very same [text]: "The *padminī* is declared to bestow peace; the *śaṅkhinī* is considered suitable for subjugation (*vaśya*). O Goddess! The *nāgavallabhā* is praised for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*);
likewise, the *ḍākinī* is excellent for killing (*māraṇa*) and brings death to enemies."

The characteristics of the *padminī* and others are also described in that very same place: "She who has a fair complexion, long hair, always speaks with nectar-like words, has red eyes, and is of good character—that *padminī* is auspicious for spiritual practice (*sādhana*). Indeed, she brings about the accomplishment of mantras; she is the *śaṅkhinī*, so it shall be."

She who has long limbs is Śaṅkhinī, the one who causes the enchantment of the world; she has a dark body and an auspicious form, neither short nor excessively tall. She has long hair, is slightly stout, speaks softly, and is Nāginī; she has a dark body, a slender frame, and protruding teeth.
Intoxicated and tormented, with short hair and a long nose, always speaking harshly, perpetually angry, tall-bodied, and prone to loud cries; shameless, devoid of laughter,
sleep-addicted, and a great eater— she is declared to be that *ḍākinī*, who is praised in the yoga of death.

O Goddess! These Śaktis, born of all castes—whether with children, young maidens, or those who have given birth to sons and so forth—are auspicious. They should be worshipped as beloved women with devotion and the family nectars (kularasa).
The Goddess said:
"By which specific mantra does a practitioner of mantras become a partaker of the six rites? [Tell me] each of those mantras, O Maheśānī, if I am dear to you! Śrī-Īśvara said:

The single-syllable mantra of Kālikā, the three-seed-mantra of Tārā, and the eleven-syllable mantra of Vajravairocanī are indeed declared to be stealers of all splendor. What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O beloved of my life! [It is accomplished] by the seed-syllable of Śakti alone.
O Goddess, one who recites [this] with a concentrated mind certainly attains the fruit; it is not otherwise, O you who are praised by heroes!

If the wicked were to obtain the fruit and the upright were to be fruitless, then, O Maheśānī, everything here would be in vain. I am the creator, as well as the sustainer and protector in matters of protection.
O Śivā! Even so, the accomplishment of the fruit occurs; this is a marvel, O Daughter of the Mountain!
Thus, O Goddess, I shall describe to you specifically the rite of killing (māraṇa):
the word ending with the letter *sa* (sānta), joined with fire (*va*), adorned with the left eye (*ī*), followed by a pair of *kūrca*s (huṃ huṃ), O Goddess!

"Kill so-and-so, the two! This fourteen-syllable mantra, ending with *svāhā*, is a destroyer of enemies. Having taken charcoal from a *khadira* tree, especially on a Tuesday or the eighth lunar day, one should carve an effigy in the likeness of the enemy upon a copper plate at night, [placing it] on the head.

Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra in the eyes, forehead, heart, hands, navel, private parts, hips, back, and the two feet according to the prescribed sequence, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) therein. Then, having formed the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should meditate upon the Goddess who bestows victory.

One should meditate upon the goddess who destroys enemies for the sake of their destruction— long in form, black in color, with her head perpetually raised upward, naked, and chewing a pair of human skulls in her hand. Thus...

O Śaṅkarī! Having meditated [on her], one should, with the left hand, offer [the offering] with brick powder while reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to the destroyer of enemies. O Maheśvarī! Then, one should offer a stream [of liquid] mixed with turmeric powder with this [mantra]:
"Drink, drink the blood of so-and-so! followed by "flesh..."

The mantra is: *khādaya khādaya hrīṃ namaḥ*. Having performed worship at midday or at midnight, one should recite it one hundred and eight times on the eleventh day; then disease will surely afflict the enemy, of this there is no doubt. On the twenty-first day plus one *daṇḍa*, the death of the enemy shall indeed occur.

Alternatively, I shall describe another method for the destruction of enemies: having taken the dung of a bull, one should worship it with warm water; one should perform the recitation (*japa*), worship, and other rites in reverse order.
One should collect the bull's dung while saying "Salutation to Mahādeva," and [the cow dung] while saying "Salutation to Śiva."

One should perform the ritual union with the mantra; then, one should establish the vital breaths [of the enemy] with the words, "Salutation to Paśupati. O Maheśānī! Having drawn an image of the enemy in a vessel of iron using charcoal from the *khadira* tree, one should install Śiva therein. Then...

One who is well-composed in meditation should meditate upon Mahārudra: Rudra stationed upon the chest of the enemy, possessing a radiance like a blazing fire, holding the hair with his left hand and drawing out the vital breath with his right; the god clad in human skin and entwined by great serpents and other creatures.

Having invoked [the deity] with effort using "O wielder of the Pināka bow, come, come here," and so forth, the best of practitioners should bathe [the image] while saying, "Salutation to the Trident-bearer. He should worship with water for the feet and other offerings, saying, "Salutation to Maheśvara. Then he should worship the forms beginning with Īśāna in reverse order.

O Maheśvarī! From the southeast corner up to the end [of the directions], according to the previous method, one should recite the root mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" twenty-eight times. Then, with the left hand, one should dismiss [the deity] saying, "Huṃ, forgive me! [And address:
"O Ajita! Kaiśava! Viṣṇu! Hara! Satya! Janārdana! Haṃsa!"

"Nārāyaṇa! Svāhā"—one should mutter this mantra once. "Huṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Vāsudeva, Svāhā, obeisance"—one should also mutter this once. In this way, O Goddess, the concealment of the enemy occurs truly and directly within eleven days; it certainly happens, O Goddess, truth, truth.
O Three-eyed One! Thus is the concealment of enemies.

(p. 2024) Now, regarding immobilization (*stambhana*): O Great Goddess! I shall describe the supreme immobilization of enemies. One should obtain a cooking pot from a potter; it should be one that was made by the artisan himself, clearly unglazed. Having brought it...

O Goddess of the Suras! Having likewise placed stale ashes from the middle of a cremation ground into a cooking pot, along with a layer of dried *nālikā* leaves, and having positioned it upon the ashes, O Maheśvarī! one should make an opening in the northeast on a Saturday.

O beautiful lady, when it is midday and the place is deserted, O beloved, I, the Great Goddess, remain there near the pit in the garden on all four sides to protect you from thieves. O Goddess, with a mind intent on leaping forward, one should perform circumambulations upon the ground for that same duration. Then...

O noble lady! Having circumambulated the ground counter-clockwise, one should again go to the vicinity of that pit. There, in that very secluded spot, having planted an iron pin into the pit and placed upon it a cooking pot along with a water-jar, one should cover it with earth.

Having filled that pit, one should return home; O Goddess, there shall indeed be a paralysis of movement for thieves and others. O God, this supreme yoga is difficult to obtain on the surface of the earth by you [others].
Piśācas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, Brahma-rākṣasas, and Dānavas—[of these...]
Likewise, no other destiny arises there; rather, the abundance of wealth and sons increases day and night, and a righteous intellect is born day by day— of this there is no doubt.

In the *Vṛhannīlatantra*: Now I shall further proclaim another supreme method of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), by the mere knowledge of which mantras are accomplished instantly. O Goddess! One should have an image fashioned from one *pala* of silver, or half a *pala*.

O Maheśānī! O Śivā! Having made an image of the person to be subjugated (sādhya), and having placed half a *pala* of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) as well as turmeric powder there—after digging a pit measuring one and a half cubits (*sārddhahasta*) and casting it therein, O beautiful one!—and having provided a red seat there, one should enter with the mind fixed upon that [target]. In the four directions...
O Maheśānī! One should fix the banner. Seated upon a red seat and facing the east, one should begin the recitation (*japa*). O Goddess, daughter of the Mountain! Know this to be the rule for worship.
There, the preceptor (*deśika*) should place a jar filled with sesame seeds.

The wise practitioner should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra. Having placed [the image] below and having worshipped it with a rosary of coral, he should perform the recitation (*japa*). Through ten thousand recitations, he then becomes fit for the ritual application (*prayoga*). First, having uttered the *praṇava*, [he should utter] the *māyābīja*.
The second [mantra]: "Who are you? (*kā tvam*), followed by *tvallākinīyuktam*, adorned with the moon on the left ear (*vāmakarṇendubhūṣitam*).

Then one should utter the word "red" (*raktapadam*), and immediately after that, "O Cāmuṇḍā" (*cāmuṇḍe*). Then, having placed the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhyanāma*), one should say "bring under control" (*vaśamānaya*). This mantra, ending with the wife of fire (the *svāhā* suffix), should be recited ten thousand times.

One should perform the fire-oblations (homa) and other rites according to the measure of ten parts and so forth. Having bathed in the morning, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), being pure and having subdued the senses, one should recite [the mantra] starting from the morning until midday. O Goddess of Devas! O Auspicious One! When the recitation is completed, one should offer oblations day after day.
By performing a fire-oblation with *jāti* flowers, one shall bring [the deity] under control; of this there is no doubt.
One should satisfy the Supreme Deity with water mixed with camphor. First, having uttered the *praṇava*, one should then pronounce "Cāmuṇḍā."

"O beautiful one, know the mantra ending with *agnijāyā* (svāhā). O Goddess of the Gods, by propitiating the Supreme Deity according to this very procedure, success arises through its application; there is no doubt in this. Thereafter, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*)."

O Maheśānī! [One should recite] the Praṇava and thereafter Cāmuṇḍā; one should then consecrate [the disciple], and subsequently one should perform the consecration with the Hṛdaya-mantra. O Deveśī! One should then feed Brāhmaṇas with a tenth part of that [mantra-repetition]. When this has been done, O Maheśānī!...

This is the supreme method of subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter—this is the truth, the truth, without a shadow of doubt. O Goddess, it becomes like the god of love to women and like a pacifier to enemies;
for as long as life lasts, O Sovereign, it acts like the arrow of Smara—of this there is no doubt.
It is true, O Goddess worshipped by the hosts of gods! One should grind the root of white Aparājitā together with *rocanā*.

Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should then apply it as a *tilaka*. One will bring others under control; there is no doubt here—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī! Even the moon and the sun would then become powerless.
One shall become a partaker of fruitlessness. One should propitiate Cāmuṇḍā with great effort using a red cloth. O Dear One!

Gold should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's means. O Fair-faced One! One should perform a grand worship at the beginning and the end. By practicing this for five days, [one may influence] a king...
One should bring [it] under control. O Great Goddess! For your pleasure, that which is difficult to obtain on earth has been told.

(p. 1026) Now, regarding the rite of inciting hatred (*vidveṣaṇa*). In that very same [text]: "O Maheśānī! O beloved! Listen with a one-pointed mind to the rite of inciting hatred! Having drawn the images of a crow and an owl upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) with the juice of *karavīra* or likewise with *dhustūra*, [one should perform it] against those who are the targets (*sādhya*). O Maheśvarī! [The targets']...

The practitioner, having inscribed the mantra together with the names, [should recite]: "Whatever enmity exists between these two, may such enmity arise between so-and-so and so-and-so. The mantra, ending with the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā), causes all-encompassing hatred. Then follows the worship of that deity Mahākālī.
Bestower of auspiciousness! O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation (japa) five thousand times.
Now, regarding killing (māraṇa): in that same [text], "Listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved, to the specific procedure for killing: a black cat should be killed, and its head [used] therein."
The best of practitioners should lead it [there] and prepare it with vermilion.

O Great Goddess! O Beloved! one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) upon its tongue. Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should joyfully recite the name of Kālī, fashioned from one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*) as a three-syllabled mantra.
Then one should perform the recitation (*japa*). By ten thousand recitations, one may slay the enemy before oneself.
Having invoked Śmaśānakālikā there, one should then worship her.
One should offer a garment adorned with iron ornaments to the Goddess, facing the south.

Then one should recite the mantra; thus the mantra becomes perfected. O Great Goddess! O Beloved! Having cooked food, one should cause it to be given in a secluded place. If, having offered a *bali* at midnight, one digs [the remains] in the house of an enemy, O Queen of Gods!
within seven days the enemy goes to the abode of Yama. Thus has it been told to you, O Goddess!
This is considered the essence of essences; yet, O lady of noble form, it has been revealed once more out of affection for you.

In the sixth chapter of the Kāmākhyātantra: "O Śāmbhavī! Having worshipped the Great Goddess with the five principles (pañcatattva), and becoming filled with great bliss, one should accomplish the great practice. O Maheśānī! One should purify one's own urine with the Kūrca-bīja."

One should satisfy the terrible Bhairavī with the name of the enemy and drink [the substance] oneself; one should cast it into the ten directions, into the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), and even into the fire. Having become naked, one should wander there;
the destruction of the enemy will certainly occur. A hero should feel no disgust toward semen, blood, or urine.
If Bhairavī is angry with him, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.

For example: O Śivā! Taking a clay vessel, one should write the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Having encased it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*yaṃ*), one should pour one's own urine into it. O Maheśānī! One should recite the *māyā-bīja* (*hrīṃ*) one hundred and eight times. O Devī! One should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to Bhairavī; [this results in] killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*).
O Pārvatī! Taking his own urine with his left hand, the best of practitioners should place it, purified, into the vessel of Bhairavī. O Maheśvarī! The enemy becomes insane or dies;
he will certainly become deluded, agitated, or even brought under control.

The pacification of these is found in the Yoginītantra. O Omniscient One, listen to the rite of pacification (*śāntika*) by which the practitioner may live: first, having taken Urvaśī, followed by the supreme bringer of the end of the age, then three Dhūminīs joined with two breasts—of this mantra...
O Queen of the Gods! O Great Goddess! one should perform the recitation (japa) eight thousand times;
the deity is Annapūrṇā.
One should worship her with various kinds of edible foods endowed with diverse flavors—namely, that which is to be chewed (carvya), that which is to be sucked (coṣya), and so forth.

Likewise, one should offer delightful things to be licked and drunk; and one should perform the fire-oblations (homa) and other rites according to the measure of one-tenth and so forth. O beautiful one! Through the oblation of lotus flowers, peace is attained. One should satisfy the Goddess Annapūrṇā, the supreme goal, with honey.

O Goddess of the Gods! On the Rathame day, one should fill a jar with water and worship the Goddess, the beauty of the gods, having invoked her into that jar. O Goddess of the Gods! If one performs this ritual application with this mantra, every disease shall be destroyed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Six Ritual Acts including Vīrācāra Worship," in the seventh section on the Nirguṇa-kāṇḍa of the Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī.

Now, the Kulācāra. In the third chapter of the Nityātantra: "I shall declare the ritual procedure for Kulācāra; listen with careful attention. By the mere knowledge of which, the agent becomes Sadāśiva, the destroyer. There is no restriction of direction or time, nor any restriction of lunar days and the like; there is no [such] restriction."

O Queen of the Gods! Regarding the practice of the Great Mantra, the characteristics of the Kaulas are described in that very same place: "Sometimes refined, sometimes fallen, and sometimes like spirits or *piśācas*, the Kaulas wander upon the surface of the earth, assuming various guises. (p. 1028) In the mud...

O Goddess, beloved! He for whom there is no distinction between sandalwood and a son, nor between an enemy and a dear one; who makes no difference between a cremation ground and a palace, or between gold and grass—he, O Queen of the Gods, is proclaimed a Kaula.
Having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Āgamas with the staff of knowledge, this is the essence, O Great Goddess.

The Kaulācāra is thus established in the *Samayācāra-tantra*. Listen further to the twofold conduct (*ācāra*) distinguished by the categories of "moist" (*ārdra*) and "dry" (*śuṣka*). The moist conduct is to be understood as being endowed with the five *makāras*; the dry conduct is proclaimed to be devoid of the five *makāras*.

"O Goddess! In the Kali age especially, the practice of Ārdra yields fruit. In the first chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*: 'The Kula practice, which is the great knowledge, must be guarded in the presence of the uninitiated (paśu).
O Mahādevī, O Pārvatī, it must be protected like one's own womb. [One should not reveal] the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas..."

O Pārvatī! Among all those scriptures, the Kula-ācāra is indeed the very essence and is extremely difficult to attain. Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, it is impossible to describe the majesty of the Kula-ācāra; nevertheless, out of restlessness, I shall say something.
I shall speak; listen to me. The entire universe has its root in Śakti; supreme austerity has its root in Śakti. Relying upon Śakti, one may dwell in any hermitage whatsoever.
Possessing the power appropriate for a practitioner and following the command of the practitioner, one shall be happy in this world.
Having entered the body of the Goddess, he dissolves therein; the supreme practitioner, having attained great siddhi, goes to the abode of Hari.

In the fifth chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra: "Those who dwell upon the earth having taken refuge in the Kula-dharma, they become Śivas; by virtue of the Kula-dharma, those living beings become Śivas.
One who belongs to the Kula should be known as Śaṅkara himself; one who belongs to the Kula is Hari himself; one who belongs to the Kula is the god Vāsava."

The grandfather is indeed of noble birth; all sages are of noble birth, and the ancestors are remembered as being of noble birth. Likewise: "O fair-faced one! Whether he be a fool or a scholar, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya-born, a Śūdra, or even a Caṇḍāla, O lady of excellent complexion!—all are equal and of noble birth."

This is the means for accomplishing all goals. Listen, O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips! Hear my words, O lady of pure smiles! One who is skilled in the beauty of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is proficient in all rites.
From the erotic arises creation; from the erotic arises passion (*rati*).
Śiva is pleased by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and Pārvatī as well;
O Queen of the Gods! whether the sound of a blow be graceful or harsh, by the mere word "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*), people shall attain the supreme goal. Women are gods; women [are the deities].

Virtuous women alone are the true ornament. One should never harbor hatred toward women, nor should one direct blame or blows against them. O Goddess of Gods! One who is devoid of compassion and shame should strictly avoid such conduct.
He who, on this earth, understands that the form of a woman is the form of Tāriṇī, is indeed the Lord of Śrī himself.

He who is to be known as the Lord of Pārvatī is the one to be known. Likewise: "The living soul who delights in the path of the Kula is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. A creature intent on the purpose of the Kula-dharma should wander upon the Kula-path.
Taking refuge in the Kula-flower, he should resort to the stage of life of the Kulīna. (From the Sixth Chapter).

One should resort to the family lineage (*kulavāra*), the Kaula, the family dharma (*kuladharma*), and the family vow (*kulavrata*), as well as supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and indeed that which is supreme bliss itself. In that very same [text], he states the fault [of failing to do so] even with such words as: "There is no devotion for those of noble family (*kulīna*)," and so forth; and: "In the one of noble family there is no higher intellect, nor in the one of noble family is there a higher goal. Nor...

"Supreme devotion is found in the noble-born, not supreme ritual action in the noble-born. The living being who speaks thus indeed does not attain liberation at all. O Goddess of Gods! Heaven is right here; the abode of Kailāsa is right here.
Right here are devotion, worldly enjoyment, and unfailing liberation; right here is both pleasure and heaven.
O Śaṅkarī! O Mistress of Tripura! Liberation is indeed within the grasp of the followers of Śakti;
I speak the truth, there is no doubt.

In the eleventh chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "In whatever region whatever conduct is prescribed for the accomplishment of mantra, one who is distinguished by that conduct is indeed proclaimed as a Kaulika.
And in the fourth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*: "One whose self is purified by the conduct of the Kula..."
One becomes directly identical with Śiva. Where there is an abundance of enjoyment, what talk can there be of yoga? Yoga is the absence of enjoyment, whereas the Kaula enjoys both.

Now, regarding the fruit of Kaula worship, it is stated in that very same place: "O lady of excellent vows! If even a single person who knows the Kula-tattva is worshipped by someone, all the gods and goddesses are worshipped; there is no doubt about this.
The fruit that one would obtain by giving away the earth filled with gold—ten million times that [is obtained from worshipping such a person]."

One obtains merit and virtue from the worship of the Kaula. Even a dog-cooker (outcaste), if he possesses knowledge of the *kula*, excels a Brahmin. A Brahmin who is devoid of the *kulācāra* conduct is the lowest of dog-cookers. There is no dharma higher than the Kaula dharma within my own system of knowledge.

By the mere performance of which a man becomes a knower of Brahman—this supreme path remains hidden amidst the turmoil of worldly beings. It shall become manifest after a long time, when the powerful Kali age has fully set in.
Indeed, as the Kali age proceeds, I speak the truth, the absolute truth: they shall not remain [without it].
On this earth, the Kaulas are the true men, while others are but beasts.

Now, the praise of the family tradition (*kulācāra*). From the second chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "O Goddess! Having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Āgamas with the staff of knowledge, I—who know the essence—have extracted the Kula-dharma. On one side [stand] all..."

Dharmas consist of sacrifices, sacred fords, vows, and so forth; and on one side is the family dharma (*kuladharma*), which, O Dear One, is superior therein as the *kaula* [tradition]. Just as rivers, flowing straight or winding, enter the ocean, even so all the *samayas* (observances) enter into the *kula* alone. Just as [all footprints] are absorbed within the footprint of an elephant...

It shall become the station for all living beings; likewise, all the *samayas* have indeed entered the *Kula*. Just as there is [the difference] between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly, so too is the great difference between other *samayas* and the *Kaula*, even among all philosophical systems (*darśanas*).

Without practice, human beings obtain liberation in the Kaula system immediately; of this there is no doubt. Likewise: "If one is a yogi but not an enjoyer, or if one is an enjoyer but not a knower of yoga, then the Kaula doctrine—which consists of both enjoyment and yoga—is therefore the soul of all, O Dear One! In it, enjoyment becomes yoga."

O Mistress of the Kula! In the Kula-dharma, even manifest sin acts as merit, and saṃsāra itself acts as liberation. O Goddess! Even the foremost sages and deities such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are devoted to the Kula-dharma; what then need be said of human beings? Having abandoned...
One should understand all phenomena according to the various systems of the Gurus;

indeed, one should discern the *kula* if one desires prosperity for oneself. Through the practice performed in previous births, the knowledge of the *kula* becomes manifest, even without instruction or the like, like the cognition of one who has just awakened from sleep.

Regarding the prohibition of the *kulācāra* during the day, it is stated in the fifty-first chapter of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* (p. 1031): "The *kulācāra* is not to be practiced during the day, except by one who possesses complete knowledge. O Goddess, the practice is of two kinds, distinguished as *vāma* and *dakṣiṇa*."

"The right [hand] is for birth alone, while the left is for consecration," as stated in the first chapter of the *Niruttara-tantra*. "One should perform the *kula*-rites at night and the Vedic rites by day;
by day and by night, the yogi should worship the Goddess according to the distinctions of yoga," as stated in the *Vāmakeśvara-tantra*.

O Goddess! O Beloved! Through the propitiation of the Guru and the practice of mantra, the stage of the Avadhūta is indeed the greatest among the four stages of life (āśramas). A practitioner of steady mind should enter the stage of the Avadhūta.

Free from desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, the Avadhūta Śiva is manifest before me, as dear to me as my own life, O beloved! The Avadhūta is of two kinds: the householder and the sky-clad (naked ascetic). There is also the one with clothing, the one with a wife, the devotee, the practitioner, and the pure one.
O Goddess of the Gods! One who is devoted to the Guru, a man of wisdom, a performer of both external and internal dharma,

intent on the practice of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga), dedicated to breath control (prāṇāyāma), free from desire, whose self is purified by knowledge, and devoted to the worship of Śiva— he is a Gṛhāvadhūta.

And the second is Sadāśiva. Indeed, he is the naked ascetic (avadhūta), devoted to the fivefold conduct; ever-blissful, ever-peaceful, clothed in the directions (naked), the giver of all, the enjoyer of all, belonging to all castes, and always delighted in dharma and action. [He does not exist] in the Kali age.

One should purify liquor, for there is no transgression of approaching those who should not be approached. Householders may perform their duties with *avadhūta* [liquor], while those who are naked (*digambara*) must act accordingly. Between *saṃvit* (consciousness) and *āsava* (alcoholic extract), consciousness alone is superior;
by the mere drinking of consciousness, one is a hero and a practitioner. Such is he.

O Beloved! One who knows the ritual procedure becomes noble; at that very moment, a divine state arises—of this there is no doubt. O Goddess! Those Śāktas who are Brāhmaṇas, those Kṣatriyas who are known as Brāhmaṇas, and those Vaiśyas who are Brāhmaṇas, O Goddess—all Śūdras are the best of the twice-born.

Internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, and in the assembly considered Vaiṣṇava, the Kaulas wander upon the earth assuming various forms. He is both an initiated householder and a perpetual ascetic; he is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, yet he is not equal to Śiva.
There is doubt [regarding this]. External worship should be performed according to the instructions of the Guru;

however, worship consisting of internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is the most excellent of all worships. External worship should be maintained as long as knowledge has not arisen; but once knowledge has arisen, O Mistress of the Gods!
The cultivation of the form of the deity; or else, the wise practitioner should accomplish [the goal] by taking recourse to the form of the deity.

In the fifth chapter of the Kāmākhyātantra: "He is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, he is a Vaiṣṇava, he is a Śākta, and he is a Gāṇapatya; he is a Śaiva, a knower of the supreme truth, and he alone is fully initiated. It is the consensus that all sacred fords (tīrthas) here are purifying."

O Girijā! The Kaula is the purifier of all sacred fords; what need is there for further words? Blessed indeed is his mother, blessed are his father and the rest, blessed are his kinsmen and family, and blessed are those people who converse with him. All his ancestors rejoice and joyfully sing his praises. Even...
In our own family, someone will arise who possesses knowledge of the lineage.

Now, the inner sacrifice (*antaryāga*). From the sixth chapter of the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra*: One should meditate upon and worship the God with the mind, speech, and heart. Indeed, that practitioner in this world who is devoted to the inner sacrifice—O Mahāmāyā! [is the true yogi]. *Antaryāgaṃ mahāmāye!* (The inner sacrifice, O Great Illusion!)
It is inaccessible even to practitioners. Indeed, the cosmic egg is the body of all living beings;
whatever qualities exist in the cosmic egg reside within the physical frame.
The body is composed of the skin and is flooded with various fluids, joined with the lunar orb.

Adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*, the body of Śaṅkara is difficult to attain even for others and bestows liberation; O Mahāmāyā, as long as liberation has not been attained, so long indeed must the practitioner [remain].

In the fourth chapter of the *Nityātantra*: "Now I shall describe the internal worship; listen, O you who are beautiful in every limb! By knowing this, the practitioner does not enter the womb of a mother again.
One should contemplate the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, coiled like a serpent, in the *ādhāra* with the *pūraka* [inhalation]."
O Maheśānī! Then, having joined the six wheels by means of *pūraka* (inhalation), the wise practitioner should lead [the breath] to the temple that is the mass of a thousand blisses. O Supreme Self!
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the adept shall become eternally happy. [The lotus] is thus blossomed.

By its power, the entire body becomes [purified]. One should visualize a sixteen-petaled lotus outside the *anāhata* [cakra]; in its center, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate an excellent ocean of nectar, one hundred *yojanas* in extent, circular in shape, and radiant.

O Supreme Goddess! In the center of that is the enchanting Maṇidvīpa, adorned with gardens made of Pārijāta and other trees. O Great Goddess! One should meditate upon the Kalpavṛkṣa tree situated in the middle space, surrounded by those endowed with the four Vedas.

Adorned with four branches, O Goddess! one should contemplate at its base a palace of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi), fashioned of gold, resplendent with a collection of various jewels, encircled by a girdle of coral, and beautified by bells and chowries. In the center of that—

O Supreme Sovereign! One should contemplate a jeweled altar; above that, O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon a captivating jeweled pedestal (*maṇipīṭha*) described in one's own *Kalpatantra*, which has the form of a womb (*yoni*). O Supreme Sovereign! Between the eyebrows is that supreme lunar vessel (*candrapātra*).

O Goddess, one should cast that nectar situated there into that womb; by means of that very [nectar], one should contemplate [it] in the center of the womb having the form of lightning. From space arises wind; from wind, the sun is produced;
from the sun, water is produced; and from water, the earth is produced. By this very procedure...
One should contemplate the body of the Goddess as consisting of the five elements, endowed with all the sense organs, equipped with all weapons, and adorned with every ornament.
Having bathed at the holy site of Puṣkara, one should worship the Supreme Deity with three vessels for water for the feet.
O blessed one! O fair-faced lady! One should likewise prepare three vessels for the *arghya* offering, as well as three vessels for the *ācamana* rite.
O Goddess! Having then assigned eight bathing vessels to each petal, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the two feet with the nectar-like waters of Kuṇḍalinī from two vessels.

O Supreme Sovereign! One should then take the water from the feet. Having mentally divided the *arghya* offering three times according to the distinction of the three qualities (*guṇa*), Kulabhairava should bring the Goddess on a golden swing.
He should bathe her with honey, perfumes, and so forth, using eight golden jars. With silk...

One should remove the water from the body using a body-cleansing cloth. Then, having offered a silk garment to the Goddess, one should clothe her in it. Having offered a bodice, one should then offer a conch shell made of ivory upon her four arms to Mahādevī.

Having presented various ornaments to the Goddess, the supreme practitioner, with a mind imbued with devotion, should assign them each to their respective places. Then, having applied fragrant oil to her tresses,
Kulabhairava should perform the grooming of the hair with a golden comb.
Then, having tied the *tribali* (the three folds of skin on the abdomen), one should arrange the mass of hair.

The wise practitioner should apply a *sindūra* tilaka between the eyebrows with collyrium. He should then adorn the eyes of the Goddess with a golden probe. Having applied lac-dye (*alaktaka*) to her feet, [he should proceed].
Upon the tips of the claws of his lotus-like hands, he should offer a pair of anklets set with priceless gems; the pure devotee should offer a pair of sandals fashioned from gold;
and he should present a crown constructed from various jewels.

One should apply an ointment to the Goddess with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, *kuṣīda*, saffron, and the like, as well as with the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* substances. One should offer thousands of red lotuses to the Root Goddess; then, having brought her back to the throne, one should again [offer] her upon a golden swing.

O Maheśānī! One should offer fragrance to the Goddess by means of the twenty-four principles (tattvas). One should offer a lamp, which is the form of light, to the Goddess.
