One should give clothing, a fly-whisk, the sun, and an excellent mirror. O Maheśānī! [One should also offer] the moon and the parasol.

Likewise, one should offer a girdle of six lotuses and a bell consisting of the sound of the *anāhata* [cakra]. Then, one should present an ocean of the nectar of immortality, and thereafter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*) filled with the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) along with Mount Meru, to the Goddess. Bliss...

Then, having offered [the oblation], the partless Kulabhairava should gratify the Supreme Goddess with dances, songs, and instrumental music, consisting of the most excellent sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which have arisen from the dancer that is the mind. Having worshipped her in this very manner according to the rule...
One should recite the mantra.
In the sixth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*, there is a certain specific point as follows:
"Abandoning the deity residing within oneself, one indeed searches for a god outside;
like one who, having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in his own hand, wanders about out of a craving for glass. Having made [the deity] manifest before one's eyes...

One should worship Śivā, who resides in the heart, within the heart. O Supreme Goddess! Whatever be the ornaments and vehicle of whichever deity, one should contemplate that very same [form] during its worship.
Now I shall describe internal worship, by which one becomes identical with the Divine; [this is done while] seated comfortably on a seat.
Facing either the east or the north, one should meditate upon an excellent ocean of nectar within one's own heart; in its center is an island of jewels consisting of golden sand,
[adorned] with celestial wish-fulfilling trees such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta.
[It was] with trees in full bloom, divinely adorned on all sides, bearing flowers and fruits eternally; its quarters were made fragrant by the scent of various sweet-smelling blossoms,
crowded with swarms of bees delighted by the fragrance of fully opened flowers, and filled with the warbling of flocks of cuckoos.

O Goddess! One should meditate upon that divine tree, the enchanting Kalpavṛkṣa, situated in the midst of it— a place whose horizons are made resonant by sound, adorned on all sides with celestial, shimmering golden lotuses, pearls, flowers, garlands, buds, and golden archways.

O beautiful one! [The tree] has four branches and represents the four Vedas, endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). It is adorned with yellow, black, white, red, green, and variegated flowers, shining with many kinds of blossoms. O Goddess! It is graced by cuckoos, bees, and many other birds.
Having thus meditated upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), one should contemplate beneath it a jeweled pedestal (ratnavedikā). Above that,
one should visualize a vast and expansive jeweled pavilion (ratnamaṇḍapa), resembling the rising sun, adorned with jeweled stairways, strewn with rows of banners, and provided with four doors.
Richly adorned with various jewels and embellished with jeweled ramparts,
it was presided over by the world-protectors stationed in their respective places,
and frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Mahoragas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases.
It was filled with throngs of celestial women sporting in all directions, devoted to dance and instrumental music;
it was adorned with banners attached to networks of tinkling bells and embellished with great rubies,
lapis lazuli, gems, and yak-tail whisks.

O Goddess! One should meditate upon a great ruby pedestal in the center of that [lotus], adorned with large, brilliant pearls hanging down, and anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and other perfumes; it is beautified by four corners and shines with the rays of the rising sun and moon.

There, one should meditate upon the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), which is of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. O Maheśānī! Upon that lion-throne, one should place a cushion of flowers. Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa), one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess there upon the corpse-lotus seat (pretapadmāsana).
Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deities within oneself.
Having offered the venerable jeweled sandals and led [the deity] to the bathing chamber,
one should perform the ritual rubbing with camphor, agallochum, and musk while [the deity] is seated upon the lion-throne.
Likewise,
having performed an anointing of the Goddess with musk mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron, combined with various fragrances,
one should apply scented oil with divine water and flowers.

Having brought water with thousands of golden jars, one should contemplate the Supreme Deity as bathed therein. One should wipe her body with fine silken cloths (*dukūla*) and likewise dress her in silken garments. One should groom her hair with a comb and bind it according to the prescribed rite.

One should offer a silk cluster adorned with locks of hair and various jewels; anklets for the feet, and a pearl from an elephant's tusk at the tip of the nose. One should offer flower garlands and ornaments according to one’s capacity, and an ointment should be applied to all the limbs.
Sprinkled with fragrant sandalwood, the heart-center is adorned above by a golden, elegant bodice.

One should meditate upon the Goddess in *samādhi* and perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth. Having performed the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), one should always worship her within *samādhi*.

One should worship Śivā, who resides in the heart, with the sixteen services: one should offer a jeweled lion-throne, utter a welcome, and inquire after her well-being; O Goddess, one should offer water for the feet at her feet and present the arghya offering upon her head, as well as the supreme nectar for sipping (ācamana).

One should offer it into the lotus-face; one should place the *madhuparka* in the mouth and perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times in the mouth. One should offer divine, well-prepared *paramānna* (exquisite rice) contained in a golden vessel, combined with the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), accompanied by various side dishes, and resembling an ocean of nectar.

One should mentally offer a mountain of meat, heaps of fish, and likewise foods that are to be eaten, swallowed, licked, chewed, and sucked, as well as betel-leaf with camphor. Then, one should perform the worship of the Goddess’s enclosures by means of the mind alone.

Thus, having propitiated her within the mind alone, one should mutter the mantra; having performed a thousand or more recitations, one should offer water to the Goddess. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—therefore, this is declared to be the couch of the Great Goddess.
The practitioner-yogi should prepare a bed resembling the foam of milk, adorned with various flowers— a flower-bed— therein for the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods. He should contemplate her,
who delights in manifold pleasures, and satisfy her with dance, song, and instrumental music.
[To the] Supreme Goddess. Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the sake of making the worship fruitful.

Now I shall explain the fire-oblation by which one may attain the state of pure consciousness. Then, one should offer oblations into the fire of consciousness within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) consisting of the lower [elements].

In the fifth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*: "One should offer the heart-lotus as a seat with the nectar flowing from the thousand-spoked [cakra]; one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the two feet and mentally present the respectful offering (*arghya*)."

With that nectar, one should prepare the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) as well as the bath-water. One should conceive of the element of space (ākāśatattva) as the garment, and the element of fragrance (gandhatattva) as the perfume. One should conceive of the mind (citta) as the flower, and the vital breaths (prāṇa) as the incense. And for the purpose of the lamp, one should offer the element of fire (tejas-tattva), and likewise the food offering (naivedya).

One should offer the ocean of nectar, the bell of the unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*), the wind-element as a fly-whisk (*cāmara*), dance representing the functions of the senses, and likewise the flickering of the mind as various kinds of flowers, for the sake of accomplishing one's own spiritual state (*bhāvasiddhi*).

Absence of deceit, absence of egoism, absence of passion, and likewise absence of pride; absence of delusion, absence of hypocrisy, and likewise absence of hatred and agitation; absence of envy and absence of greed—these are proclaimed as the ten flowers. Non-violence is the supreme flower, and restraint of the senses is a flower.
"Compassion, forbearance, and knowledge are the flowers; beyond that is the fivefold flower.

Thus, one should worship with these fifteen flowers, which are flowers of disposition (*bhāva*). [One should offer] the ocean of nectar, the mountain of meat, the parched mountain of fish, the heap of mudrās, and the excellent devotee.
Likewise, milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee; that flower which is the nectar of the lineage (kulāmṛta);
and the water used for washing the pedestal (pīṭha). Having offered the oblation (bali) consisting of the two transformations—lust and anger—one should perform the recitation (japa).
The rosary is said to consist of the phonemes (varṇa), constrained by the thread of Kuṇḍalinī, together with the bindu.

Having uttered the phonemes, one should recite the root mantra. From the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, both in direct and reverse order; then, beginning again from the letter *la* up to the end of the *Śrīkaṇṭha* mantra, one should mutter it. This is known as the reverse order (*viloma*), and the letter *kṣa* is called the *meru*.

Together with the final letters of the eight groups [of consonants], one should then recite the root mantra and the eight [syllables]. Having thus chanted one hundred and eight times, one should offer it with: "O Primordial Mother Kālī, whose nature is light, accept this internal recitation within the abode of the innermost Self; svāhā!"
"Salutations be unto you! Having offered this recitation, one should prostrate with the eight limbs of the body with devotion.
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), one should commence the external worship (vahirpūjā).

Now follows the internal oblation (*antarhoma*). In the seventh chapter of the *Nityātantra*: "O beautiful one in every limb! Listen, I shall explain the procedure for the oblation of knowledge (*jñānahomavidhi*), by the mere realization of which Sadāśiva becomes the agent and the destroyer. O you who are worshipped by heroes! Having meditated upon the Self as a square, [one should contemplate] the Self and the Inner Self."

O Parameśvarī! O Queen of the Gods! One whose self is supreme knowledge should form a square with these four [lines]. One should contemplate within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) in the form of a womb (*yoni*).
One should likewise fashion the girdle (*mekhalā*), the three lines, and the enclosure (*valaya*) as bliss (*ānanda*).

O Goddess of the Gods! There, Kulabhairava should unite the fire of knowledge (jñānāgni), which is known as sound and has the form of the Mātṛkā. Then, with the syllable "Hum," [he should cast it] into the fire of consciousness (saṃvidagni). O Goddess! Here, these letters become the wordless Brahman; merit, sin, conceptualization (vikalpa), and volition (saṅkalpa) [are likewise dissolved].
O Goddess worshipped by heroes! O Sovereign Lady! O Pārvatī! One should contemplate these sacrificial offerings—both what is to be done and what is not to be done—and meditate upon the Root-Vidyā;
one should offer them with the mind as the sacrificial ladle. Then, consisting of pure consciousness, one shall directly attain the state of the Supreme Brahman.
Now, the five oblations; [as stated] at the end of the root [text] in the *Śyāmārahasya*:

With the mind as the sacrificial ladle and the oblation, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses into the fire whose nature is the consciousness at the navel, which is ever-kindled by knowledge. Svāhā! With this, one should offer the first oblation.

Then, at the end of the root mantra: "O Knower, in the fire of the Self, with the ladle of the mind, I constantly offer the activities of the senses as an oblation of merit and demerit through the path of the *suṣumṇā*. Svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer the second oblation. Then, at the end of the root mantra:
Supporting [the vessel] with the hands of light and space, I offer into the fire that which is filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit by means of the ladle of *unmanī*.
One should prescribe the third oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of fire (*svāhā*). By this, one performs the third oblation.

One should offer [the oblation] at the end of the root-mantra: "I sacrifice the universe into the fire of consciousness— which blazes within without external fuel, which is the adversary of the darkness of illusion,
and which is the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays."
Or [the sequence] beginning with the earth and ending with space.
Now, the procedure for the Śrīcakra, from the fifth chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "Without a support, there is a fall [of the vessel], and the Mothers are not satisfied;
therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should prepare a support according to the rules—a tripod support."
They say it should be six-footed or four-footed; or else, O Goddess, one should make it circular and beautiful. Thus ends the description of the vessel’s support.
[The vessels] made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, skull, gourd, or clay; as well as those from coconut, conch, and pearl-oyster shells.
A wise person should fashion an alms-bowl produced from a sacred tree;
one should avoid that which is too thin, too thick, cracked, or broken. Thus ends the description of the bowl.
Gold, silver, and copper [bowls] grant all accomplishments and are used for rites of pacification (*śāntika*).

A stone bowl is for the purpose of immobilization (*stambhana*), while one made of clay is used for subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like; a coconut shell is for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), and a tortoise-shell bowl is likewise. A conch shell bestows knowledge, and a pearl oyster shell grants wisdom. Bowls made of skull or gourd also bring about the accomplishment of yoga.

The vessels made from the Puṇyavṛkṣa tree remove all sins. O Goddess of the Gods! among those mentioned, one should prepare a single vessel for this specific rite. Thus ends the fruit of the vessel according to the particular ritual action.

Immediately following this, having described the preparation of the clan-substances (*kuladravya*) and so forth, one should cause other intoxicants to be prepared as the causes for the wine: the juice of the *pānasa* fruit, grape-wine, honey-wine, date-wine, palm-wine, sugarcane-wine, that produced from honey, *sīdhu*, *mādhvīka*, *aireya*, and that produced from coconut.

These eleven types of liquor grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation; however, O Dear One, the twelfth, the spirituous liquor of grain (surā-madya), is the best of all. Spirituous liquor is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī). That made from flour brings about all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis), while that made from molasses bestows worldly enjoyments.
O Dear One! Madhvī is said to grant liberation, while Surā is dear to the deity. Thus ends the description of the three kinds of liquor.

A rosary made of *ekṣu* (sugarcane) bestows knowledge; one made of *mādhvī* (honey-tree wood) grants sovereignty. A rosary born of *tāla* (palmyra) is praised for paralyzing [enemies], while one of *khārjūrī* (date-palm) destroys foes. One made of coconut bestows prosperity, and the *pānasī* (jackfruit) yields auspiciousness. A rosary made of *madhūka* (bassia latifolia) produces wisdom, as does the *mādhvīkā* (grape).
It is the destroyer of diseases, O Maheśānī! It is called Maireya, and it removes all sins.
This is the eleventh fruit of liquor.
[Liquor] produced from milky trees, that which arises from bark, āsava produced from honey-flowers, and that produced from rice.

By merely smelling its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices (*śatakratu*). By mere contact with it, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (*tīrtha*). O Goddess! By drinking it, one directly attains the fourfold liberation (*caturvidhā mukti*). In the absence of liquor, a pill (*vaṭikā*) is prescribed; it is described in that very same [text].

Having thoroughly mixed alcohol, meat, and so forth with Vijayā and well-blended with the eight fragrances (aṣṭagandha), the wise one should knead them, form them into pills (vaṭikā), and then collect them. In the absence of alcohol, however, one should dissolve the pill in water and perform the libation (tarpaṇa); in the absence of a pill, [one should do so] with another substance.

The libation (*tarpaṇa*) is described in that very same [text]: "One should satisfy [the deity] with buttermilk mixed with jaggery and honey, or one may do so with *sauvīra* vinegar; one must not omit this rite. If it is omitted through negligence, one incurs the curse of the deities. And meat is said to be of three kinds."

O Dear One! Among those moving on land, in water, or in the air, one should prepare whichever is available for the purpose of libation (tarpaṇa). Even by the mere sight of meat, the fruit is equal to that of seeing wine.
In sacrifices to the ancestors, gods, and others, injury to living beings is ordained; however, it is not for one's own sake.
Violence has never been enjoined, O beloved! One should never cut down even a blade of grass without cause;
yet, having killed for the sake of the gods or for the sake of the twice-born, one is not tainted by sins.

In the absence of meat, a substitute for meat has been prescribed in that very same [text]: "In the absence of meat, however, having taken garlic, fresh ginger, or ginger-root (nāgara), one should worship the Goddess;
otherwise, it will be fruitless. This applies in the absence of fish, meat, or their respective substitutes.

Satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) has also been described by means of a single substance alone in that very same [text]: "One should satisfy [the deity] even with liquor devoid of fish, meat, and so forth; one should not perform worship with substances lacking fish and meat. The fruit of satisfaction is stated in that very same [text]: "The flesh..."

By satisfying [the deity] even once with a mere sesame seed, or even half a sesame seed, along with a *bindu*, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices. There is no other merit equal to the *Kula* worship in the three worlds;
therefore, he who worships with devotion becomes a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

O Sovereign of all four castes, stages of life, men, women, and eunuchs! He who, though unlearned in the scriptures, knows the sacred teachings, is devoted to his guru, firm in his vows, and delights in honoring his lineage— he shall be most dear to me.

"O Sadāśivā! You are always worshipped; like a celestial consort, you should grant fruit both in this world and the next. Regarding the fault of one who performs this [rite] without the family worship (*kulapūjā*) and so forth, it is said in that very same [text]:
'That person of wicked intellect who performs this without the family worship goes to hell.'"

[This practice] is formidable for those who are unable to perform worship with the twenty-one families (*kula*). Regarding those [who are] incapable of such worship, the ritual procedure is stated in that very same [text]: "Therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the family-worship (*kulapūjā*);
one obtains all accomplishments (*siddhi*), and no doubt should be entertained in this matter."

If one is unable to perform the propitiation (*ārādhana*), one should provide the materials for worship. If one is not even able to give those, one should at least observe the act of worship. It is stated in that very same source that even for the Śaivas and others, worship may be performed with family-owned materials (*kuladravya*) in the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, and Saura traditions.
O Pārvatī! In the presence of a *gaṇa*, or in the Buddhist, Pāśupata, Sāṅkhya, Vrata,
Kalāmukha, Sadakṣa-vāma-siddhānta, or among the Vainikas and others,
worship performed without wine and meat, and without the substances of the *Kula*, shall be fruitless.

"O Goddess! one should perform the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), austerity, and vows; otherwise, it shall be fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes. It appears that he who claimed there is an absence of family tradition (kulācāra) among Vaiṣṇavas has not heard such statements as these."

Regarding the fruit of performing the family tradition (*kulācāra*), it is said in that very same [text]: "Just as those who move within the inner circle are dear to a king, and not those who move outside, so too, O Goddess, those who are devoted to the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) are dear, and no others. Those who offer meat and wine with both hands out of devotion generate [merit]."

And Ānanda, those Kaulikas are dear to Me. Our supreme form, characterized by Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, manifests through the enjoyment of the *kuladravya* (substances of the Kula), and not otherwise.
The inner radiance arising from the Self, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech, [manifests] through the enjoyment of the *kuladravya*.

It does not arise otherwise, O beloved! When the Kula-substance is consumed by one who perceives the true meaning of the Kula-principle and who views all things with equanimity, the possession of Bhairava arises. Just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen by means of a lamp, so too is the Self, which is shrouded by Māyā, [revealed] by the drinking of the substance.

It is seen, O Dear One! Those people who drink the family substance (kuladravya) purified by mantra and offered to the Guru and the Deity—for them, there is no further need for drinking mother’s milk. Wine is Śakti, meat is Śiva, and the devotee thereof is Bhairava himself. From the union of these two, bliss arises, which is liberation.
It is said: Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that resides within bodies.

Liquor is its manifestor; therefore, it is drunk by yogis. One who is free from attachment, fearless, heroic, beyond dualities, devoid of curiosity, and who has determined the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras [should drink] the Giver of Boons.
One should drink the Vāruṇī liquor.
The fruit of giving conditioned material objects is explained in that very same place.

O Pārvatī! Through drinking the nectar purified by the refinement of mantra, the state of divinity arises, which liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence. It should always be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa;
by a Kṣatriya when entering battle; and by a Vaiśya at the time of tilling the soil.

Regarding the funeral rites for a Śūdra: O Goddess! having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, [one should proceed]. Regarding the drinking of family property (liquor) out of greed for wealth and so forth, the fault lies in that very act.
Remembering the Guru, one who drinks wine and eats meat incurs no fault;

indeed, for the sake of satisfying all the gods and for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, one may partake of honey and meat. However, if one consumes them out of mere craving, he is a sinner.

For the purpose of illuminating the meaning of the mantra, for the sake of stability of mind, and for the cessation of the bonds of worldly existence, one should practice the drinking of honey-wine (*madhupāna*). He who consumes wine and other intoxicants merely for the sake of pleasure is a sinner; [one should drink] only to please the deity.

Indeed, [the practitioner] is free from desire. O Dear One! It is said that the consumption of intoxicants such as fish, meat, and liquor is a fault except at the time of sacrifice; just as the drinking of Soma is ordained for Brahmins during sacrifices, so too is the drinking of honey-wine.

The ritual performed at the proper time bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Having correctly understood the underlying disposition from the Kula scriptures of the venerable Guru, one should practice the five mudrās; otherwise, one becomes a sinner. Without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation of the mantra, [one should not proceed].

Even a Kaula who drinks according to the rite of drinking animal flesh (paśupāna) shall go to hell; for he who, being unaccomplished in Kaula knowledge, desires to consume that substance, O Goddess, is a great sinner, excluded from all rites. [This applies to] the evil-minded one who lacks the conduct of the observance (samaya) and follows his own whims.

There are no accomplishments for one who falls from their lineage; therefore, one should not associate with such a person. He who discards the injunctions of the scriptures and acts according to his own whims attains neither success nor the supreme goal in the hereafter. He who conducts himself according to his own will...
Deprived of the purificatory rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*), he shall never attain a good rebirth,

despite asceticism, pilgrimages, vows, and the like. He who drinks unrefined substances, engages in sexual intercourse by force, or eats meat killed for his own pleasure, shall go to the Raurava hell.

Those who follow the Kaula path yet observe the vows of the fettered (paśu), mocking both sides, remain in the Raurava hell for as many years as there are hairs on their bodies. Likewise, those who resort to the substances of the Kula while adhering to other doctrines remain for a period measured by the number of hairs on the body of one who eats the Palāśa leaf.
It is said: "Having brought the group of senses from its own object, one should unite them within the Self;
O Goddess, he becomes an eater of flesh, while all others are slayers of living beings.
Without awakening the power of the Paśu, and having awakened that of the Kaulika... (p. 1043)

He who serves that Śakti becomes a servant of Śakti; he is filled with the bliss of the union of the supreme Śakti and the Self as a couple. He who remains thus experiences true sexual union, whereas others are merely servants of women. [This concludes the description of] the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the five mudrās, beginning with these.
O Kulānāyikā! O Goddess! he who, having learned [this] from the mouth of the Guru, practices it, is liberated.

In the sixth chapter (Ṣaṣṭhollāsa): Characteristics of the worshipper and so forth. O Goddess! He who is accompanied by worship and consecration, who knows the true meaning of the scriptures, who is devoted to the deity and the guru, and who constantly performs the rite of adoration, O Dear One!—he who knows the secrets of the Kula tradition, who is eager for the propitiation of the deity, and who is endowed with the instructions of the guru.
O Kulanāyikā! One who is pure in soul, exceedingly joyful, free from anger and greed, and turned away from the vows of the *paśus*, should worship facing [the deity] and offer libations, O Dear One!
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the worship of the Śrīcakra through the application of mantra; that I shall now explain to you.

"I myself accept [this] with reverence; through the knowledge that 'I am Bhairava,' I am endowed with qualities such as omniscience. Having reflected thus, the lord of yogis should be devoted to the Kula worship. O Goddess, the Kaulika who, endowed with such characteristics and firm in his vows, worships you— [The text continues: ...he shall attain the supreme state. He is liberated from all sins and becomes one with me. There is no doubt that he attains the fruit of all mantras. By him all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are worshipped. By him the ancestors are gratified, and by him the world is sustained. Therefore, O Goddess, you should always be worshipped by one who desires liberation. Thus ends the [chapter on] the worship of the Kula. May there be auspiciousness. May there be success. Om. Tat Sat. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. Śrī. He is the vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Seated comfortably in a solitary, secluded place in the forest, free from disturbances, facing either east or north, one should perform the fivefold purification of the self, the place, the substances, and the deity. O Goddess, as long as one does not perform this...

How, then, can there be worship of the deity? Having thus performed the fivefold purification, one should thereafter perform the sacrifice. That worship is to be known as fruitful; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
O beloved, worship without a maṇḍala is said to be in vain.
Therefore, having drawn the mandala according to the rules, one should worship there.

The characteristics of the mandala are described in that very same [text]: "The universe, established pervading all, has the form of an unbroken circle; that by which the three worlds are adorned is the mandala of Sadāśiva. The garden should be square, and Kāmarūpa is circular."
The triangle [of Jālandhara] has the luster of the upward-facing moon, and Pūrṇagiri shall be [the circle]. Having worshipped the mandala, one should thereafter place the supports in sequence:
the common [vessel], the vessel for the Śrīguru’s enjoyment, and the five vessels for the bali offering; or there may be two vessels or three vessels.

One should not use a single vessel. Having established [the offerings] from one's own right to the left and having worshipped them with *āsava*, the knower of the ritual procedure should worship [the deity] with the root mantra, O Mistress of the Kula! Therein, one should place fish and meat in the measure of a *māṣa*.
Regarding the types of liquor prohibited for libation (*tarpaṇa*), the same text states:

"Libation becomes fruitless when performed with things that are undesirable, stale, leftover, foul-smelling, devoid of fragrance, caused by [impure] motives, or contained in another's vessel. [Likewise,] unrefined liquor [is forbidden]."
It bestows evil, strife, disease, and suffering;

it destroys longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, wealth, and grain. Therefore, having consecrated the family property according to the prescribed rite, one should then worship [the deity]. Otherwise, both the consumer and the giver go to hell.
There is no doubt.
The method for purifying liquor is described in that very same place.

Substance purified by inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), mantra, and mudrā becomes fit for libation (*tarpaṇa*) and is a cause of delight for the deity. Regarding the purification mantra for each of the five *makāras*, it is stated in that same source: "First, *haṃsaḥ sadasat*..."
"Pratadviṣṇo" is the second; "Tryambakaṃ" is the third; the fourth begins with "tatpuruṣāya"; and the fifth, following the ritual procedure, is the mantra beginning with "Viṣṇur-yoniḥ.
O Ambikā! Having consecrated and worshipped [the mantras] one, two, three, four, five, and twice four times respectively—
One should worship the vessel with the *dhenu-mudrā*.

This great vessel, filled with pure substance, is produced from a fragment of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), originates from all essences, and is indeed filled with the essence of nectar (*pīyūṣa*). With that pure substance as well...

O Dear One! One should worship oneself with pure flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), using the previously mentioned mantras for the ritual placement (nyāsa). One should worship the lineage of the venerable gurus upon the head and the pādukā at the mūlādhāra.

Regarding the sequence of the lineage of gurus, it is stated in that very same [text]: "In the divine stream (divyaugha), there are Ādinātha and his Śaktis; Sadāśiva and his wife; Īśvara and his wife; Rudra and his son;
Viṣṇu and his beloved; and Brahmā and his consort—these are said to be the twelve."
In the lineage of the Siddhas (siddhaugha), Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta, Ribhukṣaja, Dattātreya, Daivataka, Vāmadeva,
and thereafter Vyāsa and Śuka— these eleven are proclaimed. In the lineage of the Manus (mānavaugha):

Nṛsiṃha, Maheśa, Bhārgava, Mahendra, Mādhava, and Viṣṇu—these six are proclaimed [as the members of the Divyaugha]. O Goddess! One who joins with "Namaḥ" the supreme Śiva in the Divyaugha, Mahāśiva in the Siddhaugha, and Sadāśiva in the Mānavaugha, then...
Having worshipped the pedestal, O Beloved, one should invoke the Goddess:

"O You who dwell within the forest of great lotuses! O You whose form is the bliss of the Cause! O Mother, benefactor of all beings! Come, come, O Supreme Goddess! O Queen of the Gods, easily accessible through devotion!"

"O you who are endowed with all ornaments! Remain steadfast here for as long as I worship you. Having invoked the Goddess with this mantra, one should worship her with undivided mind; having meditated upon her and displayed the mudrās, one should honor her with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings.

Now, the Wheel of Family Conduct (*kulācāracakra*). From the eleventh chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "If an elder who has been initiated is devoid of the family worship (*kulapūjā*) and other rites, then a younger [initiate], if he follows that lineage, should perform the family worship in his presence. Then, toward him...

Having gone and paid obeisance to the Guru as is fitting, and having reported all of that to him, one should eat the remainder, O Pārvatī! If, during the course of the worship, the Guru, an elder, or another worthy person arrives, the disciple should bow and inform them of his presence; he should conduct himself according to their permission. And [regarding] the elder...

O Kulnāyikā! When the disciples of two younger brothers are stationed together in one place, the conduct toward them is said to be like that toward those worthy of worship. O Goddess! If one arrives at an unknown time, one should consider the sequence of precedence; having remembered his own Guru, one should satisfy him through equal entry. This is the daily worship during the day.

One should perform occasional worship at night; this is the scriptural determination regarding both [daily and occasional rites], as well as rites for specific desires. One should not perform worship after bathing, nor while seated, nor after eating, nor while talking idly, nor if one is unadorned with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, ornaments, garments, and so forth.

Or, one should not perform the worship of the Kula without having laid down the body [in the prescribed posture]. O Dear One! It is said that worship performed without mantra, libation without meat, and drinking without Śakti are fruitless. One may perform the Śrīcakra alone, but one should not worship with only a single vessel.

One should not worship with only one hand, nor drink with only one hand. O Goddess! One should not worship with fish, meat, or fermented liquors in the presence of a *paśu* (an uninitiated person). One should enter the *cakra* after bowing, and exit only after bowing. O Goddess! The sight of the Śrī-cakra is the destroyer of sins for the eyes.

O Goddess! one should contemplate those who follow improper conduct, those of good conduct, those established in the *cakra*, and the *śakti-kaulikās* with the thought that they are Śiva and Gaurī; one should not despise them.
Having gone to the house of the Kula-teacher, one should do so with devotion for the purification of sins.

One should request the nectar-scented [substance], and in its absence, drink water. Having bowed with devotion, one should receive the vessel offered by the family preceptor according to his capacity; otherwise, one would go to hell. This applies even if one has eaten without having bathed.

O Mistress of the Kula! He who, out of greed, consumes the Kula-substance shall incur poverty. One who wears a turban, one in a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one surrounded by attendants, one who turns his face away, or one who is quarrelsome—such a person must not drink the nectar of the Kula.

By spitting the nectar of yoga, by wandering about with a vessel of liquor, and by drinking through an upward-pointing tube, one incurs the curse of the deities. O Dear One! Those who sit upon the same seat, eat from the same vessel, and drink water from the same cup, they go to hell. He who...

O Kulīśānī! If one consumes the family substances (kuladravya) while the Guru resides in the same village, or while his kinsman, his son, or his elder brother who serves as the family preceptor (kuladeśika) is present, without their permission, he shall go to an inexhaustible hell.
O Pārvatī! One who is impure from eating (ucchiṣṭa) must not touch the family substances within the circle (cakra), nor outside.
Having washed both hands, one should cause the family substances to be offered.

O Dear One! Having lifted up the vessel of liquor, one should not fill that same vessel [again]. One should never place the vessel of enjoyment back into the jar of wine. Within the circle (cakra), with a mind of purity, one should perform the washing of the hands and other such rites.

The deluded soul who performs [these acts] shall become a vessel for calamities. He who discharges spittle, impurity, urine, or downward wind into the center of the Śrīcakra becomes a *paśu* (a bound soul) for the Yoginīs. [Likewise, he who does so] when the jar in the center of the Cakra is broken, or when the vessel has fallen to the ground.
O Dear One! When the lamp is extinguished, one should construct the Śrīcakra for the sake of pacification;
this is just as the realization of the wise and the intoxicated occurs when there is intense exhilaration.
O Beloved! The wise chant mantras, meditate, offer praise, and prostrate; they awaken others, inquire, and rejoice. Intoxicated, they laugh, walk about, and debate with one another;
they weep, desire prosperity, and criticize—such are the wise, O Beloved!

One should avoid joking, idle chatter, caviling, excessive talk, indifference, fear, and anger in the midst of the *cakra*. O Great Goddess! One should not wander within the *cakra* with a vessel in hand; nor should one stand still while holding a full vessel in the hand.
O Beloved! One should not speak for long while holding the vessel in hand; O Ambika! one should not criticize the recipient.

One should not touch the vessel with one's feet, nor let a drop fall to the ground. O Beloved! it should not be given with only one hand, nor without the *mudrā*. One should not move the vessel from its place.

One should not make a clutter of vessels. One should not drink liquor with noise, nor should one fill it to the brim. One should not strike one vessel against another, nor should one let a vessel fall to the ground. One should not lift a vessel that has a base [for another] and place it on a surface without a base. Nor should one leave an empty vessel...

One should not make a vessel [of another], nor should one brandish it, O Beloved! A wise man should not step over a vessel, nor should he ever overturn a vessel. Having washed it, one should conceal the vessel; such is the command, O Supreme Goddess! When a Kaulika whose inner radiance is unkindled looks upon a bound soul (paśu), having recited—
He who might associate with the scriptures of the fettered (paśu), or with the wives of the fettered;

or who might engage in sexual union with the fettered, or perform the rites of the fettered; or he who, out of affection, greed, or even fear, gives the Kula-substance situated within the Śrīcakra to the fettered—[he is a sinner].
One may become a beast for the Yoginīs. One should not engage in verbal dispute even with an enemy in the midst of the *cakra*;

one should regard such a person as equal to one's father or mother, and endure them. Likewise, if the mind rejoices upon seeing women, sons, friends, and so forth, it will likewise rejoice upon seeing the Kaulikas.
He shall be beloved by the Yoginīs.

Likewise: One should always worship with devotion and must not place [the offerings] in the hands of a *paśu*. O Pārvatī! One should enjoy the Kula scriptures as one's own wife; one should avoid all *paśu* scriptures like the wife of another. Just as milk placed in a dog’s hide is not to be drunk, [so too are those scriptures].
It may be [performed] by the twice-born. Likewise, the Dharma from the mouth of a beast must not be heard by the Kaulikas.
He who hears the Kula conduct and he who speaks it according to the scripture—both of them truly go to the assembly of Yoginīs and Vīras. As for those who lack faith in this matter...
O Mistress of the Family! In the family dharma, they do not return from hell until the dissolution of all beings.

Likewise: One should not cause [the following] to perform [the rite]: the Guru’s Śakti, the wife of a hero, a maiden, one observing a vow, one with deformed limbs, one with mutilated limbs, or even a hunchback; and likewise a daughter.
One should not desire one's sister, granddaughter, daughter-in-law, or even a beloved woman in the presence of the Guru (p.
1048). One should not engage in mutual embracing. [One should avoid] a dark woman, a fair woman, a dark-complexioned maiden, a slender-waisted woman, or a captivating woman.

One should worship a woman established in youth with the thought that she is a deity; one should never, even once, violate a Kula-yoginī by force. O beautiful lady of the Kula! One should desire her who is herself aroused within the center of the wheel.
[One should offer] raw meat, a jar of wine, an intoxicated elephant, and a perfected ascetic.

Seeing a mango tree and an *aśoka* tree, young maidens absorbed in play, a single tree in a cremation ground, a multitude of women, and a woman dressed in red garments, one should bow with devotion. [One should likewise bow to] the Guru, the Śakti, the elder son, and the younger son.

The family preceptor; the scriptures of the Kula vision, the Kula substances, and the Kaulikas; those who incite, those who indicate, as well as those who recite, those who show, those who instruct, and those who awaken;
those appearing in the forms of yogis, yoginīs, and siddhas; the maiden, and the young girl.
One should not revile or feel disgust toward a woman, even if she is naked or insane; one should not mock her or treat her with contempt.

One should never speak unpleasant or untruthful words to anyone, even to a woman of noble family. One should not call a woman of noble family "ugly" or "black. One should not test the devotion of one's disciples.
And regarding what has been done or left undone by heroes: one should not look at a woman who has fallen, who is naked, who is insane, or whose breasts are exposed.

One should not take pleasure with a beloved woman during the day, nor should one gaze upon her private parts. Whatever woman exists in the world, she originates from the lineage of the Mothers; the Kula-yoginīs become enraged [if this is transgressed].
One should not transgress against women. Even for a hundred offenses, one should not strike a woman even with a flower.

One should not enumerate the faults of women, but rather manifest their virtues alone. The Yoginīs of noble lineage always reside within the trees of the family; one should not eat from their leaves, but should instead worship them.

In particular: one should not sleep beneath a family tree, nor should one commit any act of violence against it. Upon seeing it, one should pay homage with devotion and never cut it down. The *śleṣmātaka*, *karañja*, *nimba*, *aśvattha*, *kadambaka*, *vilva*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *tintiḍī* are the ten [trees].

It is taught: A Kaula should avoid these five: the penance prescribed by Bhṛgu, falling [from a cliff], renunciation, the observance of vows, and undertaking pilgrimages. [Likewise, he must avoid] the killing of a hero, drinking intoxicants in vain, stealing the property of a hero, and sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero.

And association with them is the fifth; this is declared to be a "great sin" (mahāpātaka) in the Kula lineage of the Kaulikas. In the Śaiva [tradition], it is the thorough knowledge of the principles (tattva); in the Gāruḍa, the swallowing of poison;
in Jyotiṣa, the eclipse; in the Kaula, it is grace and restraint.
Now follows the description of the nature of Ānanda, from the first chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*.
Bliss is supreme Brahman, the supreme power, and Sadāśiva. Without bliss there is no falling away, and the deities find no satisfaction.
O Bhairavī! All things, such as the purification of substances and so forth, are for the sake of bliss; [all] is in bliss.

One must never consume [it] while it is being produced. From excessive drinking, one becomes intoxicated, and recitation, worship, and so forth become fruitless; O Goddess, the destruction of the intellect occurs. Therefore, one should consume it in moderation.
For him who consumes it for the sake of pleasure, calamities lie at every step.

From excessive agitation, extreme censure by the world arises. Likewise: "Perceiving everything as consisting of Brahman, he is not tainted by faults; but whoever here acts out of delusion or even through negligence, he is the lowest among practitioners and becomes a denizen of hell."
Certainly; he would be censured in this world and would go to hell in the next.

Now follows the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). In the *Samayācāra-tantra*: "In the absence of products of the cow (*gavya*) and so forth, one must never omit the daily rite (*nitya-karma*). He who omits it through negligence certainly attains hell.
The fourteenth substance has been proclaimed; listen to it individually."
Among those, two substances are never to be accepted:
milk, curd, buttermilk, ghee, honey, jaggery, sugar, cold water,
sugarcane juice, coconut water, *āsphena*, *vijayā*, and *unmatta*.
Poison is likewise. O Goddess! The *dhūstūra* is poison; it is a substance whose very nature is to take away life.
As for other substances that a man might drink for the sake of pleasure, they are just like that.

In the absence of all substances and so forth, ginger is prescribed; one may complete the daily rite with water, milk, or buttermilk. In the absence of the five "M" substances, the fifth is prescribed; O Goddess, in the absence of the fifth, one should resort to the fifth mentally.
Now follows the censure of practicing the five principles without the traditional oral instructions and so forth.
In the second chapter of the fifth section of the *Kulārṇava*: "Some here, devoid of the guru’s instruction, cause delusion; others, themselves previously deluded, delude people.
Some, devoted to wicked conduct, being base men, recite [the texts]; many [are] Kaulikas..."

Those who mock the Dharma with false knowledge, devoid of the traditional lineage, attempt to strengthen the Lord through their own intellects. If a man could indeed attain perfection through the drinking of liquor,
then let all base people who delight in drinking liquor attain perfection!

If a meritorious state were attained merely by eating meat, then all meat-eaters in this world would become partakers of merit. O Goddess of the Gods! If indeed one attains liberation through sexual union with women, then all living beings in the world would be liberated simply by indulging in women.

O Goddess! The great Kula path has never been censured by me at any time. Those who are devoid of proper conduct (*ācāra*) in this world are always condemned. Otherwise, I have described the conduct within the Kaulika dharma.
O Goddess! Fools who consider themselves wise act otherwise; [it is as difficult as walking] upon the edge of a sword.

O Mistress of the Gods! That which is called drinking liquor (*surāpāna*)—which is known in the Vedas and other scriptures as a great sin (*mahāpātaka*)—is said to be the useless spilling [of the substance], not the drinking [itself]. It is less grave than going [to the forest], hanging from the neck of a tiger, or carrying a serpent; it is not to be feared for the sake of preserving one's lineage and caste.

It has been described [as follows]: liquor, meat, and the flesh of animals—which are not to be smelled, not to be consumed, not to be touched, and not to be drunk—constitute a great fruit for the Kaulikas. As for that which is said: "There are eleven kinds of liquor that are impure for the twice-born, and the twelfth is the spirituous liquor known as *surā*."

"It is remembered as the lowest of all; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*. This statement prohibiting the drinking [of *surā*] by the twice-born (*dvijāti*) is also, by virtue of being syntactically connected with the preceding statement, intended either for animals or for those who have not been consecrated.
The practice of the *cakra* is as maintained in the *Śyāmārahasya*:
having sat upon separate seats either in a circular (*cakrākāra*) or a linear (*paṅktikāra*) arrangement, accompanied by one's own *śakti*,
in pairs according to the sequence of couples, seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), [one applies] sandalwood paste to the foreheads of the initiates (*sāmayika*).

Having offered [the previous items], one should offer a flower with the thought that it is Śiva-śakti. Then, if the Guru is present there, one should first worship him with perfume and other offerings, place a flower in his vessel, offer it to him along with the purification, and prostrate. In the absence of the Guru, [one should cast] that vessel into water.

p. 1051) one should cast [it]. Then, having given the vessel of Śakti, together with the purification, to Śakti, one should also give the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*), together with the purification, from the *vīrapātra* to the members of the community (*sāmayika*) in order of seniority. Then, the member of the community also, with devotion, with both hands...
Having gathered [the materials] and recited the root mantra eight times over them,

one should satisfy Ānandabhairava and Bhairavī as before, and then satisfy the gurus and the deities. One should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the procedure prescribed in the respective ritual manual (kalpa).
Then the leader of the circle (cakranāyaka) should perform the salutation of the vessel (pātravandana) together with them as follows:

"It is drenched by the nectar of the moon shining from the crest of the glorious Bhairava; it is worshipped by the lords of the fields (kṣetrādhīśvara), the yoginīs, the hosts of gods, and the siddhas."
I bow to this great-souled ocean of bliss, the manifest nectar of the three sections,
the primordial Lord Śrī residing in the lotus of the hand, who bestows purity.

Having thus consecrated [the vessel] and lifted the bowl with the left hand, and having performed a mutual salutation, one should receive the command of the Guru, Śakti, and the Sādhakeśvaras by saying, "I take [it].
They should say, "Enjoy [it]. Then, from the Mūlādhāra, [one should raise] Kuṇḍalinī...

Having visualized the Guru’s sandals (gurupādukā) as having the very form of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) extending to the tip of the tongue, and having reflected "I am Śiva," one should hold the vessel with both hands and,
while reciting the root mantra, offer libations to the Goddess at the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī.

This has been stated in the *Udayākara-paddhati*: "Having fashioned the body of the mantra, one should meditate upon the station of the Guru; thereafter, the Goddess, the digit consisting of pure consciousness, or else the triad [of the Guru, the Goddess, and the Mantra] surrounded by the seat of the heart, joined with lamps and collyrium. And [one should offer] flowers and other items consecrated with mantras."
Those who, having reflected upon it as the dense destroyer of my delusion, drink [it], indeed attain both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.

And in another tantra: "Having applied a vermilion tilaka on the forehead and wine-liquor on the hand, one should drink while meditating upon the Guru and likewise the Goddess who consists of consciousness (*cinmayī*). Then, having placed the vessel upon the support (*ādhāra*), one should again [partake] of the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) in that same sequence."

Having taken [the vessel], one should perform the salutation of the bowl (*pātravandana*). For example: "If wine, which brings the essence of fish, is to be given by her—and if she, whose eyes are like trembling red lotuses, has offered some drink and so forth—then [one should place] the lotus of one's own self-purification in her left hand."

"I now pay homage to the second vessel, which consists of the ritual procedure (vidhā) and whose sole purpose is to increase bliss. Then, having accepted the vessel as before, one should perform another salutation to the vessel (*pātravandana*), as follows:
I ever salute that which is endowed with the entire collection of the arts of all traditions, which illuminates curiosity,
which is served by Candra, Upendra, Mahendra, Śambhu, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and others,
and which is constantly meditated upon by hosts of gods and groups of sages seeking liberation.
Now I am a fit vessel for the third [initiation], capable of realizing the Self.
Having performed the salutation to the third bowl, one should perform another salutation to a bowl, as follows:

May that which brings forth the essence of fish from gold, served by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others; devoted to the practices of ritual gestures (*mudrā*) and sexual union (*maithuna*); the locus of salt, sour, and bitter flavors;
and purified by the flesh of the eight perfected masters (*ācāryāṣṭaka*), Siddhibhairava, and Kālī—protect you.
"Homage to the fourth vessel, accompanied by the fivefold reality.
Having thus performed the salutation to the fourth vessel, one should perform another salutation to the vessels as follows:
"In the support [the skull], upon the strength of the king of serpents, is the vessel, the mandala of the earth, and the wine."

"Contemplating the waters of the seven oceans as my food, as well as the eight elephants of the quarters, and myself likewise— though protected daily by the hosts of stars and by the multitudes of gods and asuras led by the Sun, all acting as my servants"— with these words, one should accept the fifth vessel. Then...

As long as one's vision and other faculties do not waver, one should perform the drinking and other [ritual] acts. Now, its measure is as follows: in the *Rudrajāmala*: "O Goddess, one should give the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) and sandalwood paste to the practitioners (*sādhakas*) and the Śaktis; one should perform [the rite] together with those who observe the covenant (*sāmayikas*)."

The consumption of drinks and so forth. Also elsewhere: "One should enter in the form of a *cakra* (wheel) or in the shape of a row; one may also dwell joined with a *śakti* according to the rule of pairs and pairs.
With the realization that everything is Śiva and Śakti, one should offer it all into the center of the *cakra*. And in another tantra: "Then..."

Having taken a flower, one should offer it into the vessel of the Guru; then, having offered it to the Guru and given some to Śakti, one should take it for oneself. And in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "If the Guru is not personally present, then one should cast [the flower] into water."
Now, the measure of the drinking vessel is as follows, according to the *Kulasāra*:

"O Supreme Goddess! It is stated in the Kula-sādhana that the vessel for the *hetu* (cause/initiation) should be made with a weight of five *karṣas*. Practitioners (*sādhakas*) must not make a vessel of greater weight than this.
One *karṣa* means one *laukika-tola*. Thus it has been said.
p. 1053) In the *Kulottama*: "Twelve *guñjās* shall constitute one *māṣa*, and eight of those are said to be one *karṣa*.
Now, in the *Uttaratantra*: "Having first obtained permission, one should say oneself, 'I shall take [it]';
then, being authorized by the Guru or by those of noble family with the words 'Be pleased,' one should take it oneself."
The wise one is perfected, seated in the bound lotus posture.

In the *Kulārṇava*: "Those who sit upon a single seat, eat from the same vessel, and drink from a single cup—such people go to the lowest hell. Regarding the phrase "a single cup," this means that one should not drink from a single vessel while gathered with all others; it does not mean that one should not drink from the same vessel at every instance of consuming a substance.
A separate vessel must be used for each [participant], because it would result in the fault of performing the rite in a fragmented manner,

because it contradicts established tradition, and because other scriptural statements are observed. Having caused one's own consort, a hero’s consort, an initiated woman, or a preeminent guru to drink first, one should then drink the substance oneself.

This is the definitive conclusion of the scripture: one should eat the remains (ucchiṣṭa) from those endowed with the power of the Guru, as well as from the elder and younger Gurus. One may eat the remains of women, but one should not offer the remains to them.
This must be done regularly within the circle (cakramadhya); otherwise, a downfall will occur for the juniors.

One should indeed give one's own leftovers to one's own disciples; he who out of affection gives them to others becomes a vessel for calamities. Also elsewhere: "One should drink the substance that is the Śakti’s leftover, and chew that which is the Vīra’s leftover. By the grace of the Śakti and the Vīra, what is there that cannot be attained?"
It is accomplished upon the earth.
The Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara) should drink even the remnants of his own power; the measure for that is as follows.

"If the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara) should drink the remains of the *śakti* without deliberation, he will suffer in hell for the duration of a kalpa and be born as a worm in excrement. Regarding the phrase "without deliberation," the author of the *Kaulāvalī* states that it means "without making the investigation of whether this [woman] has been consecrated (*abhiṣiktā*) or not. Having drunk again and again...

Having drunk again, one falls once more to the ground; rising and drinking again, there is no further rebirth. And this statement refers to the occasion of meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth, but not to contact with worldly beings (*paśu*). For it is heard [in scripture] that "if [the practice] is made manifest, there will be a loss of accomplishment," and so on.

"Until the gaze does not waver and until the mind does not waver, one should perform the drinking; beyond this is the drinking of the *paśu*. Because of this statement, and because [the practice] requires meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth.
Then one should recite the Śāntistotra. As it is stated in the Ḍāmara: "Having drunk [the wine] together with one's own people, one should then recite the Śāntistotra:
'May the *preta*s and *kuṣmāṇḍa*s perish; may the malevolent men perish; may there be auspiciousness for the practitioners.'"

May there be victory for those who preserve the sacred tradition! Victorious are all the Mothers; victorious are the hosts of Yoginīs! Victorious are the Siddhi-Ḍākinīs; victorious are the lineages of Gurus! Victorious are the Siddhi-Ḍākinīs; victorious are the Gurus forever! Victorious are all the Sādhakas!
Victorious are those pure Kaulikas, the worshippers endowed with the conduct of the *samaya*.
May those who have attained the power of *aṇimā* rejoice; may the protectors of the *kula* rejoice. May the deities beginning with Indra be present;
may the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*) be satisfied. [May] the moon, the sun, and the others [be satisfied].

May the gods be satisfied through my devotion. May the constellations, the planets, the yogas, the karaṇas, and those who are the lords of the zodiac signs—all of them—attain happiness. May the serpents and other birds, the animals and horses, the mountains, the ravines, and the caves, as well as the sages and the brahmins, likewise find joy.

May they all always grant me peace. Being praised by me, may they be known and remain as perfected ones for my worshippers. As for those who are evil-minded, delighting in great malice, revilers of me, whose hearts are ruined by the destruction of Vedic conduct during worship, and those who have fallen away—may they [be pacified].
Those practitioners who, having seen this unprecedented wheel, have their hearts faint with fear— those Kaulikas who are detractors—
may they meet their destruction here at this moment by the command of the illustrious Bhairava.

May those who hate practitioners, and those who are always defilers of the sacred tradition, go into the mouths of the *ḍākinīs* and be satiated by their flesh. Or, may those who are devoted to Śakti,
those who are devoted to Śiva, and those virtuous Vaiṣṇavas— [all] serve the unborn Lord of all gods, who is to be served by everyone.

May those of pure intellect who constantly worship Śakti with the thought that she is Viṣṇu, and Śiva with the thought that he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa— those whose minds perceive no difference between the two— attain the state beyond the three cities (Tripura) and reach liberation. May my enemies and those who revile me meet their destruction.
May those who hate the practitioners perish by the command of Śiva! Then,

having performed the union of Śiva and Śakti according to the ritual procedure to the best of one's ability, and having offered one's own self at the feet of the Goddess, one should lift the *śrīpātra* vessel, whirl it three times above the Goddess, and then—
Having stabilized [the deity] with the *saṃhāramudrā* and drawn her into one's own heart, one should dismiss her with the words: "O Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā! Forgive me. Oṃ, obeisance to Kālikā.

Now, the *Ānanda-stotra*: I remember with joy the goddess Ānandamayī, the illustrious Sundarī, who wears a digit of the moon as her crest-jewel; she is the seal that is the root of auspiciousness for the mind-born god [Kāma], and she surpasses even the Goddess of Beauty (Lakṣmī) in her loveliness. (1)

May the days pass for us devotees of Maheśvara— those intent on the worship of Śrīsundarī, whose eyes are reddened by the delight of wine, and whose minds are filled with bliss. Having poured a stream of wine into our mouths and having worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa...
Through the lineage tradition, the wise, relishing the flesh and embracing the deer-eyed woman, attain liberation. Day by day may the jar of accomplishment be full;
day by day may there be libation for the Goddess; day by day may the second [consort] be united. Day by day...

May there be union with the practitioner! || 4 || Tasting morsels of flesh and drinking wine until our throats are full, we enjoy the company of beautiful-eyed women, attaining both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.

Let us go! (5) I consider that very day to be a dark and ill-fated day in which there is no gain of sweet meat, where there is no full delight in the five-syllabled mantra, and where there is no union with the deer-eyed woman. (6) Then, the fortune of those who promote [worldly affairs] suddenly departs.
By the mere movement of his feet, the vile life-breaths of those who revile the practitioner of Śrīsundarī go to their destruction here; leprosy and other ailments afflict their limbs,
misfortune their homes, muteness their mouths, and their dwellings become like cremation grounds.
The lifespan of those who revile the practitioners of Śrīsundarī perishes at that very moment.
To whatever extent a person spreads censure against the preeminent practitioners of Śrīsundarī,
together with his sons, wife, and friends, he swiftly meets his destruction.
Drinking liquor in the temples of the initiated, sleeping at night in the houses of courtesans, and eating his meals in house after house, the sovereign of practitioners wanders about. (10)
Thereafter, by the power of time, I shall become whoever I am; I have no dispute about this.

Since I, as Bhairava, remember you, Śrīsundarī, as my mother in birth after birth, those bound souls who move along the banks of the garden of conceptual constructs— (Note: The final fragment "vikalpavāṭītaṭasanniviṣṭe pravartamānāḥ paśavo" appears to be the beginning of a subsequent verse.)

...the wretched ones! Having entered the fathomless ocean of delusion, they wander about, having failed to attain the path of the Kula. I shall not look upon another, nor shall I desire another; remembering none other, I shall never take refuge in anyone else. At no time shall I—
I forget Śrīsundarī, whose form is that of the Supreme Self, within my mind. || 13 ||
Having fashioned the king of Śrīcakras out of vermilion with white powders at night,
and contemplating Śrīsundarī within their hearts, they subjugate people with their playful glances.
We practice the drinking of *aireya*— the uprooting of the trees of sin, the intoxication of the curiosities of the mind,
and the attraction of those with lotus-eyes.

15 || Vārāṇasī, the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā), Prayāga, and Kedāra—all these sacred fords have been visited by him alone who has the contemplation of Śrīsundarī; I consider that by him the entire world has been encompassed. 16 || On his left is the moon-faced woman, in his mouth is sweet nectar, in his lotus-hand is a vessel, and upon his head—

Meditation on the Śrī Guru is the locus for the contemplation of the Goddess within the mind; on the tongue is the practice of recitation (japa); and the transformation [of experience] is the contemplation of the Kaula woman. He who drinks this nectar from the vessel with constancy attains devotion that bestows liberation. (17) On the left...
Skilled in the dalliance with women, a drinking vessel is placed before him along with hot pork seasoned with black pepper; upon his shoulder rests a lute, charming and beautiful—
the profound Kaula doctrine of the true gurus.
It is inaccessible even to yogins. (18) Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation;

where there is liberation, there is no worldly enjoyment. But for those intent on the worship of Śrī Sundarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of their hand. (19) With a single parched grain, I drink a jar [of nectar].
I shall suddenly drink from a jar with salted radish;
I shall taste a piece of roasted fish head; I shall drink from the Ganges and the Yamuna along with the ocean.

20 || The vessel in the hand, the hymn in the mouth, bliss in the lotus of the heart—what is greater than this: the remembrance of the feet of the venerable Lord upon the head? 21 || Having drunk the wine, the practitioner Kulabhairava, devoted to union with a Kula woman, should recite the hymn.
One should perform the duties of the *kula*. "I am devoted to the sacrifice and worship of liquor, meat, and women; I am sustained by the undertaking of the various paths of the *kula*;
I am devoted to the feet of the Guru; I have taken refuge in Bhairavī. (p. 1057)
"I am detached from the ways of common folk; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva. Thus ends the Ānanda-stotra in the Kulārṇava.
Now, the Joy of Bliss (Ānandollāsa), from the seventh chapter of the fifth section of the Kulārṇava.

The beginning, the youthful, the adolescent, and the mature; at the end of that is the "unminded" (unmanā), and beyond that is the "efflorescence of reality" (tattvollāsa). This is to be known as samādhi;
the efflorescence of reality is the seventh. Thus, the beginning is said to consist of three principles (tattvas).
O Kulānāyikā! O Ambikā! The youthful exuberance (*taruṇollāsa*) has indeed been described as the dawn-red face;

O Dear One! youthfulness is said to be the perfect exuberance of the mind. The faltering of sight, mind, and speech is designated as maturity (*prauḍha*). [This occurs] when the wheel is intent upon total exuberance.

One may desire the merging of vessels (*pātramelana*). However, at the outset, one should never perform the intense manifestation of the mature state (*prauḍhasamullāsa*). Likewise, concerning that intense manifestation of the mature state: "When heroes have ascended to that [state], there is no distinction between what should and should not be done; the mere will [of the teacher] is the perfection of the scriptures—this is the Command."

O Supreme Goddess! Whatever action is performed there, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all of that becomes for the pleasure of the Deity, O beautiful one among the gods! Chatter is said to be the fruit of recitation; lethargy is called meditative absorption (samādhi); physical transformation is worship, O Goddess; and vomiting is the offering (bali) to Bhairava.
Liberation occurs through union with Śakti; the hymn is speech at that time;

the ritual placement (nyāsa) is the touching of the limbs; scratching is the act of offering oblations (havana); O Īśānī! gazing is meditation, and lying down becomes prostration. Various [practices] are performed during the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa).
Whatever movement there is, that is its activity. He who deliberates upon what should and should not be done is a sinner.

Those heroes who have entered this wheel are to be known as supreme yogins, by whom men are immersed directly into the nature of Bhairava. [This is] the satiation with supreme bliss through the *sammodaka*.

The turning of knowledge; the playing of flutes, lutes, and other instruments; the composition of poetry and the like; weeping, the flow of speech, rising up, yawning, walking, and transformation—O Goddess!
this is designated as Yoga. In this wheel, the heroines and yoginīs are slow with intoxication.

O Queen of the Gods! They act according to their inner inclination with great joy. Remaining by the side, they inquire slowly, never forgetting their own vision. Placing the vessel upon their mouths, they dwell in a state of liberation (nirvāṇa), intoxicated, perceiving their own Self as the Supreme Person.

She embraces another beloved. In the very same way, a mature man, filled with internal exaltation, might out of delusion embrace one man and then a woman; the innocent woman asks her own husband, "Who are you?"
"Who are you that have come here? What is our business? For what purpose have we arrived and why do we stand here? Is this a garden, alas! Or has it become a house?
Thus women, having filled their mouths with wine, make men drink from their own mouths, using their lips as a vessel for the side-dish.

Having cast [the food], they place it into the mouths of their beloveds; O Śāmbhavī! they take up the vessels and side-dishes belonging to another. Holding wine-jars upon their heads, the yogins dance.
Out of ignorance, they clap their hands and sing songs with indistinct syllables.

The family powers (kula-śaktis) take delight in the faltering placement of steps; intoxicated by passion, the yogins fall upon the breast of the woman in her state of exhilaration. And the yoginīs, agitated by passion, fall upon the man;
they fulfill the complete bliss of their mutual desires.

O Mistress of the Kula! They perform various such actions as these; for when the outpouring [of consciousness] proceeds, having abandoned the agitation of the mind, the foremost of yogis attain the state of the deity through intoxication. As for the fool who reviles the Kaulikas who are possessed by Bhairava—

The Yoginīs, who are the leaders of the *kula*, may have doubts regarding the underlying reality (*tattva*). One should neither criticize nor laugh at those who are intoxicated with passion within the circle (*cakra*). One must never disclose to outsiders the news concerning this circle. One should provide them with food and should not act in a way that is harmful to them.

One should protect these with devotion and guard them with great effort. Seeing those who are intoxicated in the *cakra*, one should regard them with the thought that they are deities. He who rejoices in and worships with devotion shall go to the station of the Yoginīs. O Dear One, the Kaulika who beholds such a *cakra* with devotion [attains the same].

One obtains the fruit of ten million vows, sacred fords, austerities, gifts, and sacrifices. Through intoxication, falling and rising, and repeated fainting, those two who are known as the supreme imperishable syllables remain present for a long time in the sixth *ullāsa*, the field of the madman, which is endowed with heroes. Supreme...

O Mistress of the Lineage! For one who desires to abide in the Self that is Brahman, the state of equilibrium (*samavasthā*) is proclaimed because of the non-abiding of the body, the senses, and the mind. O Beloved! When there is the blossoming of reality (*tattvollāsa*), that supreme resonance (*mūrcchanā*) arises as the very nature of the Supreme Mantra.
Even the proximity of the *mūrcchanās* (melodic scales), they know, is inferior to liberation (*mukti*).

With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from the opening and closing of the eyes—this is the *śāmbhavī-mudrā*, hidden in all the *tantras*. And this is the *khecarī-mudrā* of Śiva.

Flowing together, eternally transcending all, the destroyer, resembling the ocean, the heroic one shining with this [power], is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. Those who are solely intent on meditation upon the Self do not know anything at all; therefore, it is impossible to say that "this is my supreme bliss."
It can be experienced by oneself alone, like drinking sugar-water;

it cannot be described as "such-and-such" happiness. This supreme meditation on Brahman is seen even in the case of a *kulaka* (a low-caste person) and others; whatever bliss exists in that meditation [is the goal].
The Supreme, which transcends body, place, and action, I am truly unable to describe, for I am awakened and composed. Men of merit who are devoted to the nectar-bliss of meditating upon Brahman—
when that [worldly state] has vanished even for a moment— they liberate themselves, though their worldly luster has been destroyed.

For those devotees of that [deity] who possess the sevenfold ecstasy (ullāsa), there is a great fruit. O Mistress of the Kula! Eight signs of realization arising from the knowledge of the three times, as well as the eight states beginning with trembling, arise; of this there is no doubt. What is the use of saying more in this regard?

The eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, having attained the status of female door-keepers, long serve the state of the Sage. Those auspicious qualities of the Supreme Lord, whose body consists of the five elements—O Knower of the Kula-principle! those very qualities are gathered together in those who know the Truth. This is the commencement of the joyful outburst of praise.

"Youth and maturity as well—those who rejoice through yoga are said to be 'unminded' (unmanā), which is called the dream state. Non-abiding is the deep sleep state; from the conjunction of these three states, he who knows the sevenfold manifestation is indeed liberated and is a Kaulika. When the wheel of Bhairavī is set in motion, all castes [are equal]."

The twice-born: when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes are distinct from one another; whether woman, man, eunuch, or even a Cāṇḍāla, they are all twice-born. Within the Cakra there is no distinction; O Dear One, all are equal to the gods. [Just as] the water of city-tanks, mountain streams, and so forth [merges into] the Gaṅgā...
Just as [water] attains oneness [when mixed], so too do human beings attain oneness within the centers of the Śrīcakra. Just as water combined with milk becomes nothing but milk,
so too within the Śrīcakra no distinction of caste exists.

Just as there is no one other than a god among the gods in the meritorious worlds such as heaven, so too within the center of the *cakra*, all deities and all human beings exist. There is no distinction of caste in this *cakra*; all are remembered as equal to Śiva.
Indeed, the Veda has declared that everything established therein is Brahman. What more need be said here?

What need is there for further speech, O Kuleśvarī! Within the circle, all men are my own form and all women are your own form, O beloved! But the foolish soul who creates distinctions of caste within the circle—O Kulnāyikā, the Yoginīs devour him and curse him.

One should seat one woman in a particular place and one man in another separately; or else, having formed a pair, one should seat them in sequence. O Dear One, with the consciousness that they are Śiva and Śakti, all [the deities] should be properly seated in the center of the circle (cakra), either in the form of a male or in the form of a wheel.
One should worship them. O Dear One! Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are inseparable according to tradition;
likewise, Vīra is with Śakti. O Lady of beautiful hips! I am not satisfied by thousands of jars of wine nor even by hundreds of loads of meat, but only by the nectar of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*.
This world is neither marked by the wheel, nor marked by the lotus, nor marked by the thunderbolt; rather, it is marked by the *liṅga* and the *bhaga*. Therefore, it consists of Śakti and Śiva.
At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti arises, that—

For those who abide in the multitude of twilight states (*sandhyā*), that very *samādhi* is prescribed. A lustful man should not approach a woman who is unwilling or uninitiated; he should approach that woman who has been ordained [for union] and is purified by the immediate consecration (*sadyaḥ-saṃskāra*). Thus it is impelled by the various distinctions of drinking from the effulgence of the three principles (*tattva-traya-ullāsa*).
In brief, O Mistress of the Family! What more do you wish to hear? Thus ends the *Ānandollāsa*.
Now follows the practice of the five wheels (*pañcacakra*), as it is taught in the tenth chapter of the *Niruttara-tantra*.
The illustrious Śiva said:

The power arising from every birth is always worshipped by yogis; whichever [power] the lord of yogis beholds, that very one he should worship. Listen specifically, O lady of excellent complexion, regarding the heroic power (vīra-śakti): when the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) has been performed, the heroine (vīrā) is highly praised in the practice of the hero (vīrasādhana).

O Goddess! If they are devoid of the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*), they should not be employed in the Kula practice; if they are so employed, there will be a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and one shall go to the Raurava hell. O Goddess! One should not perform the Kula practice without a Vīra-Śakti; in her absence, a woman of low birth is recommended.
In the *vīrasādhana*, O fair-faced one, listen to those [wheels] which are praised as the five wheels (*pañcacakra*).
